Chapter 1

Rocket Nozzles: Machines that Turn Heat and Pressure into Thrust

The nozzle of a rocket takes the pressure generated by fuel combustion and turns it into thrust for propulsion.

We use rockets to travel to space (Figure 1.1, p. 3) and to launch missles and fireworks. Chemical rockets have a combustion chamber in which fuel is combined with oxidizer (or in which monopropellants decompose) to generate heat and pressure. This hot, high-pressure gas is then sent through the nozzle. The nozzle of a rocket is a machine that converts heat and pressure to speed, so that the gas can be ejected out the back of the rocket to generate thrust.

Rocket nozzles convert pressure and temperature to thrust

The source of thrust in a rocket nozzle comes from ejection of high-momentum gas out the nozzle (Figure 1.2, p. 3). The combustion chamber combines fuel and oxidizer to generate high-pressure, high-temperature gas. This high-\(p\), high-\(T\) gas then travels through a converging-diverging nozzle. This nozzle accelerates the gas and increases its speed \(U\), while reducing its pressure \(p\), its temperature \(T\), and its density \(\rho\). Ejecting this fast fluid at a mass flow rate of \(\dot{m}\), pressure of \(p_e\), and speed of \(U_e\), out of the exhaust of the nozzle with exhaust area \(A_e\), into a domain with ambient pressure \(p_\infty\) causes a thrust force \(F_T\) on the rocket:

F_T = \dot{m}U_e + (p_e - p_\infty)A_e (1.1)

rocket: a propulsion engine that carries its own propellant. Cf. air-breathing engine, which intakes air to serve as oxidizer.

nozzle: a duct with varying cross-section which is designed to control the velocity and its distribution in an exhaust.

machine: as defined in this text, a device that changes direction or magnitude of forces, causes motion or acceleration, or transfers energy to perform a useful action.

thrust: a motive force pointing in the direction of a vehicle or object's desired motion.

thrust: a motive force pointing in the direction of a vehicle or object's desired motion.

converging-diverging nozzle: a nozzle in which the cross-section converges to a throat then diverges from the throat to the exhaust. Synonymous with de Laval nozzle or convergent-divergent nozzle.

speed of sound: the speed with which infinitesimal (isentropic) disturbances propagate in a fluid. Denoted \(a\) by those studying compressible flow, and usually by \(c\) by those studying acoustics. We will use \(a\). Given by \(a^2 = (\partial p/\partial \rho)_s\), or, for ideal gases, as \(a^2 = \gamma RT\).

rocket thrust equation


PDF page 14 — verified

Figure 1.1: Left: a Falcon rocket at an early stage of a launch. Right: Falcon rocket at high altitude.

Rocket analysis highlights the importance of the speed of sound \(a\) of a gas, and the Mach number \(M = U/a\) of any point in a flow. Fluid behaviors at \(M < 1\) (subsonic flow) and at \(M > 1\) (supersonic flow) are different, and these differences are central to nozzle design. Shock waves are a lossy process found in supersonic flows, and avoiding them is central to nozzle design.

Figure 1.2 schematic labels: Fuel; Oxidizer; Combustion chamber; Combustion; high T, high p, M < 1; throat; nozzle; expansion; convert T, p into fluid kinetic energy, M > 1.

F_T = \dot{m}U_{\mathrm{exhaust}} + \Delta p A_{\mathrm{exhaust}}

Thrust primarily generated by maximizing mass flow and exhaust speed.

Figure 1.2: Thrust equation and diagram of a rocket engine.

Although a rocket can derive some thrust from the pressure of the exhausted gas \((p_e - p_\infty)A_e\), the thrust generated by a well-designed rocket nozzle comes from ejection of high-momentum gas out the nozzle \(\dot{m}U_e\). The thrust is optimized when the exhaust flow is supersonic and the exhaust pressure is close to the ambient pressure—in this condition, the nozzle has converted the high-pressure combustion products into fast-moving gas whose ejected

thrust: a motive force pointing in the direction of a vehicle or object's desired motion.

supersonic: having a speed higher than the speed of sound c, a Mach number greater than one.


PDF page 15 — verified

Momentum creates a lot of thrust:

• If the exhaust flow is subsonic, the combustor isn’t running correctly and not generating enough pressure. Alternately, all fluid acceleration that the nozzle created was subsequently lost in a normal shock wave inside the nozzle. We would have been better off with a shorter nozzle that didn’t expand the cross-sectional area so much.

• If the exhaust is supersonic but the exhaust pressure is lower than ambient, the exhaust is still too wide—the nozzle tried to expand the gas too much, and the thrust is nonideal both because the increased speed is offset by the imbalanced pressure force, and because in practice oblique shocks typically are generated inside the nozzle. We are not getting all the thrust we could have generated. This is common at takeoff conditions (Figure 1.1, p. 3, left).

• If the exhaust is supersonic but the exhaust pressure is higher than ambient, the nozzle exhaust isn’t big enough—we should have had more thrust if the nozzle had been longer so that the cross-section could be expanded more. This is common at high-altitude conditions (Figure 1.1, p. 3, right).

The thrust is also optimized by minimizing any process that adds entropy and converts energy unnecessarily to heat. Any shock waves in a nozzle convert mechanical energy to heat, which cannot be used for thrust. Also, the gas very close to the solid surface of the nozzle, in what is called the boundary layer, is slowed and heated by the viscous interaction between the fast-moving gas and the motionless nozzle wall. The kinetic energy lost and converted to heat in the boundary layer also cannot be used for thrust.

The geometry of a rocket nozzle controls both the mass flow rate through the nozzle and the conversion of heat and pressure to speed. The shape of a nozzle can be designed if the pressure generated by the combustor is known, as well as the range of ambient pressures the rocket will operate in. Any rocket that changes elevation must account for the fact that the exhaust pressure changes with elevation, because the density of our atmosphere goes down as we move up in the atmosphere. The size of a nozzle is dictated by the thrust required, and therefore the mass flow rate used in the combustion. For a specific nozzle geometry, the thrust is proportional to the cross-sectional area of the nozzle throat, and the size of the nozzle can be scaled to accommodate whatever thrust is needed.

Rocket nozzles must be converging-diverging nozzles because this geometry is the only way to efficiently extract all of the energy from a high-pressure gas

Rocket nozzles are always converging-diverging nozzles, i.e., de Laval nozzles. By this, we mean that the cross-section of the nozzle converges as the fluid leaves the combustion chamber, leading to a throat, after which the nozzle diverges, leading to the exhaust. During standard operation, the fluid in the combustor and converging section is subsonic, and subsonic fluid moves faster and faster as the cross-section is reduced. In this situation, the fluid is sonic at the throat. Downstream of the throat, the fluid

is supersonic, and supersonic fluid moves faster and faster as the cross section is increased. A rocket nozzle that is poorly designed or being used in conditions that differ from those assumed for the design may not have the subsonic, sonic, and supersonic domains delineated above.

In practice, the combustor of a rocket nozzle always generates gas that has a high enough p and T such that the best way to extract that energy to generate thrust always involves accelerating the fluid to supersonic speeds, and because the converging-diverging geometry is the only way to do this, rocket nozzles always have a converging-diverging geometry.

We can design the combustion chamber conditions, nozzle throat area, and nozzle exhaust area

In introductory fluids, we can develop several key tools that prescribe thrust: (a) the relation between combustor pressure and temperature, throat area, and mass flow rate; and (b) the relation between throat area, mass flow rate, ambient pressure, and thrust. Putting these together, we can show how increasing the combustor pressure, increasing the throat area, and increasing the exhaust area all increase the thrust, but in very different ways with different design tradeoffs.

We will also develop many tools that describe well designed and poorly designed nozzles, and nozzles operating near or far from their design condition, and all of the fluid-mechanical things that happen in many different situations. For a rocket, the most obvious things we observe are what the exhaust looks like—for example whether it has shock waves and/or expansion fans, and whether it is narrow or broad.

Given what we will cover, we will not develop the tools that prescribe what the shape of the rocket has to be to minimize losses. We know that it needs to be converging then diverging, but our analysis does not prescribe the shape of the convergence nor the shape of the divergence. That is the topic of an advanced compressible flow class. Or a Google search for “method of characteristics de Laval nozzle”.

The mass flow, thrust, and exhaust structure generated by a rocket nozzle are prescribed by the pressure ratio between combustor and exhaust and the temperature in the combustor

The mass flow through a rocket is relatively simple, because in all normal rocket operations, the mass flow is choked and independent of ambient conditions. The mass flow for a choked nozzle is

\dot{m} \simeq 1.7 A^* \frac{p_0}{\sqrt{RT_0}} (1.2)

combustor: an area in which fuel is burned, typically to generate pressure and temperature that can be used to do work. Synonymous with combustion chamber.

throat: the narrowest section of a tube or nozzle.

shock wave: a discontinuous transition in which a supersonic flow slows down, with an attendant increase in pressure and density.

expansion fan: also known as a Prandtl–Meyer expansion fan. An infinite set of Mach waves that isentropically turn and accelerate a supersonic flow around a convex corner. Cf. oblique shock.

compressible flow: implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to change significantly in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Cf. incompressible flow.

Editorial source note: Eq. (1.2) is retained as printed with coefficient 1.7. For a calorically perfect ideal gas with a sonic throat and stagnation conditions p₀,T₀, combining continuity with the isentropic relations gives \(\dot m=A^*p_0\sqrt{\gamma}(2/(\gamma+1))^{(\gamma+1)/(2(\gamma-1))}/\sqrt{RT_0}\). The coefficient is about 0.685 for γ=1.4; the printed 1.7 does not follow that model.


PDF page 17 — verified

where A* is the area of the nozzle throat, p₀ and T₀ are stagnation pressure and stagnation temperature in the combustor, and R is the effective gas constant for the gas mixture. This shows that we get maximum thrust at the highest possible stagnation pressure, and (from the dependence of R on molecular weight) from the gases with the highest molecular weight. Those parameters go into combustor design. The nozzle design then controls mass flow simply through the throat area—the mass flow is proportional to the throat area.

Because the thrust of a well designed rocket comes almost entirely from the momentum of the ejected gas (and not the pressure force at the exhaust), what is left to maximize thrust is simply to maximize the exhausted velocity. The speed of the velocity at exhaust is a function of the pressure ratio between the combustor and the ambient fluid.

If there are no shock waves in a nozzle and the pressure at the exhaust matches the environment, the thrust is approximated by a simple relation:

F_T \simeq A^*p_0\,2\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{p_\infty}{p_0}\right)^{0.2}} (1.3)

which tells us that the thrust generated by a nozzle is proportional to the throat area and the stagnation pressure in the combustion chamber. In fact, the factor \(2\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{p_\infty}{p_0}\right)^{0.2}}\) doesn’t get much higher than 1.7 or so, so the product of the stagnation pressure and the throat area is a very reasonable approximation of the thrust that can be generated by a rocket nozzle.

The thrust equation above is for an ideally expanded nozzle which isentropically expands the pressure to an exhaust pressure that is the same as the ambient. Any real nozzle achieves this only for one ambient condition. For ambient conditions different from that one, a variety of interesting phenomena can occur. In the following paragraphs, we describe how the flow changes in a nozzle as the pressure ratio is increased, showing how a nozzle performs both on- and off-design. This particular nozzle is a de Laval nozzle with a 9.4 cm exhaust and a 2.5 cm throat, driven by a combustor generating 1.2 bar gas at 2000 K.

The purpose of a rocket nozzle is to convert pressure (stored ability to do work) and heat (thermal or sensible energy) to speed (kinetic energy) and therefore thrust. Thus when the exhaust pressure is low, the nozzle has converted a large amount of energy and we expect high thrust. When the exhaust pressure is the same as the combustor pressure, the nozzle has extracted no energy and generated no thrust. This dependence is shown in Figure 1.3, p. 7. We describe the performance of the combustor in terms of the stagnation pressure p₀ and stagnation temperature T₀ it generates; because the speed of the fluid in the combustor is low, stagnation pressure is not too different from the static pressure generated in the combustor. We write the pressure of the fluid the rocket is moving through as pₑ. p₀/pₑ = 1 corresponds to no expansion and no thrust. Large p₀/pₑ corresponds to lots of expansion and lots of thrust.

The mass-flow-rate curve (Figure 1.4, p. 7) is strikingly different from the thrust curve. Whereas most of the action in the thrust curve happens at high p₀/pₑ, most of the action in the mass flow rate curve happens at low p₀/pₑ. From this we can infer that when we first increase p₀/pₑ (for this specific nozzle, from 1 to 1.02), it gets the fluid moving and generates some thrust. As we increase p₀/pₑ beyond that, though, the mass flow does not change; what changes is the degree to which the fluid is accelerated. In the context of a nozzle being used for propulsion, the pressure ratio is always high enough that it is in the choked flow regime, and although the mass flow rate is a function of the combustor performance (through p₀), it

stagnation pressure: the pressure \(p_0\) a fluid would have if isentropically slowed to stagnation along a streamline. For a calorically perfect gas, \(p_0 = p\left(1 + \frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}\). For an incompressible fluid, \(p_0 = p + \frac{1}{2}\rho U^2\).

thrust: a motive force pointing in the direction of a vehicle or object’s desired motion.

choked flow: a flow regime in which the mass flow rate and flow properties upstream of the nozzle throat are unaffected by the ambient pressure and exhaust conditions.

Figure 1.5: The structure of shock waves and expansion fans in a de Laval nozzle as a function of pressure ratio p₀/pₑ. At very low pressure ratios, flow is subsonic (a). As the pressure ratio increases, a normal shock forms downstream of the throat (b) and moves toward the exhaust (c, d, e). As pressure ratio continues to increase, the flow becomes overexpanded, meaning that it is isentropic throughout the nozzle, and what was formerly a normal shock inside the nozzle becomes a set of oblique shocks and expansion fans in the nozzle exhaust (f, g). At the nozzle’s design condition, it is ideally expanded, and there are no shock waves; instead, in practice one sees only weak Mach waves in the exhaust from the shear layer between the exhaust and the ambient gas (h). If the pressure ratio is increased even more, the nozzle is underexpanded, and the exhaust has expansion fans first followed by (in some cases) oblique shocks (i). A rocket being used to launch from sea level to outer space typically starts out overexpanded, then as it rises in the atmosphere becomes ideally expanded then underexpanded. Consistent with this, the exhaust is narrow at launch then becomes quite broad in the upper atmosphere.

The flow inside the nozzle is complicated, and changes in the pressure ratio lead to complicated changes in the pressure distribution

Although we typically do not see the flow inside the nozzle directly, its nature is rather complicated and changes in the pressure ratio lead to complicated changes in the pressure distribution.

For small pressure ratios, the flow is purely subsonic (Figure 1.6, p. 9, left). As the flow moves through the converging section of the nozzle, the speed and Mach number increase, and the pressure, density, and temperature decrease. These changes reverse in the diverging section of the nozzle, and the flow properties are not much different at the exit as they are in the combustion chamber. Little energy has been converted from pressure to kinetic energy, and thus there is little thrust.



Figure 1.6: Left: purely subsonic flow at small pressure ratios. Flow properties as a function of distance along the nozzle for p₀/pₑ = 1.013. Right: choked but purely subsonic flow. Flow properties as a function of distance along the nozzle for p₀/pₑ = 1.017. These both correspond to Figure 1.5a, p. 8.

The purely subsonic flow continues until the choked flow regime (Figure 1.6, p. 9, right). Choking is the point at which the Mach number becomes 1 at the throat. As before, the changes in the converging section are largely canceled in the diverging section, and there is still little thrust.

If we keep increasing the pressure ratio, one specific location in the nozzle will exhibit a discontinuity in all flow properties (Figure 1.7, p. 10, left). This discontinuity is a shock wave, specifically a normal shock, i.e., a region in which the fluid suddenly slows down, while increasing density, pressure, temperature, and entropy. Here, the converging section speeds up the flow, and at first the diverging section continues to speed up the flow, but this acceleration is suddenly canceled by the normal shock. The thrust is a little bit higher than the purely subsonic flow, but it is hardly worth it—the thrust is still only about 10% as high as optimum.

As we keep increasing the pressure ratio, we see the normal shock move downstream (Figure 1.7, p. 10, right). As the pressure ratio is increasing, we are getting more and more acceleration in the diverging section, and al-

shock wave: a discontinuous transition in which a supersonic flow slows down, with an attendant increase in pressure and density.

normal shock: short for normal shock wave. A shock wave that is aligned normal to the flow.

These oblique shocks collide with each other and generate expansion fans, and this creates a series of repeating diamond shapes that are sometimes visible as shock diamonds or Mach diamonds (Figure 1.9, p. 11) in the nozzle exhaust. At a pressure ratio of about 30 (for this geometry), the nozzle is ideally expanded, and the pressure at the nozzle exhaust matches that of the environment. At a pressure ratio above that for ideally expanded flow, the nozzle is underexpanded (Figure 1.5i, p. 8), and the pressure at the nozzle exhaust is still above that of the environment. Here the exhaust expands out into a wide pattern. The thrust is high; if the nozzle had been made longer with a larger exit area, even more thrust could have been extracted.

The key design inputs to a rocket nozzle are mass flow and stagnation pressure available; the design parameters are shape, throat area, and exhaust area, and the key output is thrust

Quasi-1D compressible flow combines thermodynamics with mass and momentum conservation to predict performance of systems like rocket nozzles

The engineering system that motivates this chapter is a rocket nozzle. The physics of this chapter is quasi-1D compressible flow, which is the first step of combining mass and momentum conservation with thermodynamics.

Thermodynamics as taught in ENGRD2210 focuses on equations of state (for example the ideal gas law, or the steam tables) and basic conservation principles (mostly mass and energy) with a primarily steady-state, primarily scalar approach.

In MAE3230, we will expand this in multiple ways, by adding a focus on the momentum equation, by considering dynamic and unsteady systems, and by considering vector and dyadic tensor descriptions that manage forces, torques, motion, rotations, deformations, and stresses in one or more directions.

In this chapter, we start by considering fluid moving in one direction only, and because of this geometric simplicity, we can do a strictly scalar analysis with not much need for calculus. We will find that this analysis explains the speed of sound, and how a rocket nozzle works.

We will start by glossing over many of the derivations to get to the results, and simply use the results to understand how sound works and how rocket nozzles work. We will return to the derivations in more detail later in the text.

Sound waves and compressible flows are central to numerous important technologies especially the thrust of a rocket

Understanding how sound waves move and how fluid acts when it is compressible (i.e., moving at a speed comparable to the speed of sound) helps us understand how sound propagates, how sonar works, how musical instruments work, and how rocket nozzles work. Sound is of course central to our human experience; just check Apple’s market evaluation. Sound wave speed and propagation is central to human technology like sonar, is critical to our use of sound to locate items in our surroundings, and is used for

sound wave: an isentropic expansion or compression wave. Equivalent to a Mach wave. Usually used to refer to these waves in the context of acoustics rather than compressible flow.

speed of sound: the speed with which infinitesimal (isentropic) disturbances propagate in a fluid. Denoted \(a\) by those studying compressible flow, and usually by \(c\) by those studying acoustics. We will use \(a\). Given by \(a^2 = (\partial p/\partial \rho)_s\), or, for ideal gases, as \(a^2 = \gamma RT\).

sonar: Sound Navigation And Ranging. A technique for identifying objects using time-of-flight acoustic signals.

Supersonic flows are present in rocket nozzles, which is well known, but also explains the hiss of a shop air nozzle and the pop of a balloon. The speed of sound is 340 m/s in atmospheric air; and this frames the speed of the phenomena we will discuss.

More than anything, this chapter will explain how a rocket nozzle works, specifically by showing the thrust equation, using that to explain why a nozzle exists, and then showing the equations that help us design a nozzle properly. We won’t learn enough to design the shape of the nozzle, but we will learn how big it should be, and why its performance changes as the environment of the rocket changes.

The 1-D conservation equations are needed to figure out the speed of sound and the effects of a shock wave

Consider steady flow in one direction, say left to right, denoted in Figure 1.10, p. 13. We consider a control volume and fluid moving into and out of the control volume. The area A of the entrance and exit control surfaces are the same. The state entering the control volume we denote as state 1, and the state exiting the control volume we denote as state 2. Although we allow the state to change between the entrance and the exit, we assume that state 1 is uniform across the entrance control surface, and we assume that state 2 is uniform across the exit control surface.



Figure 1.10: control volume for 1D flow.

Conservation of mass, momentum, and energy give us three relations that link state 1 and state 2 to each other. We have made many simplifying assumptions (in particular, steady flow, flow only in one direction and uniform conditions in the other direction), and with these simplifying assumptions these relations are all algebraic.

The 1D inviscid compressible conservation equations are algebraic, and derived by considering the fluxes of mass, momentum, and energy into and out of a control volume, combined with the force and work done by pressure on the control surface (see Sidebar 1.1, p. 14).

The results of this analysis include conservation of mass:

control volume: a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.


PDF page 25 — source_issue

SIDEBAR 1.1: FUNDAMENTALS

1D inviscid compressible flow conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy

Conservation of mass is a balance of mass flux into and out of a control volume. Mass is neither created nor destroyed, so the rate of mass flow into the control volume must be equal to the rate of mass flow out of the control volume:

\rho_1 U_1 A = \rho_2 U_2 A (1.4)

The underbrace on the left is labeled “mass flow rate into CV”; the underbrace on the right is labeled “mass flow rate out of CV.”

\rho_1 U_1 = \rho_2 U_2 (1.5)

Conservation of momentum is a balance of momentum flux into and out of a control volume as well as the net force from pressure on the control surface. The net momentum gain of the fluid must be given by the net force on the fluid. The force on the left side from the pressure is \(p_1 A\), and opposing that on the right side is \(p_2 A\). Thus the net force is \((p_1-p_2)A\). The momentum per unit volume is \(\rho U\). The flowrate of momentum out of the right side is \(U_2 A(\rho_2 U_2)\), and the flowrate of momentum into the left side is \(U_1 A(\rho_1 U_1)\), so the net momentum gain of the fluid is \((\rho_2 U_2^2-\rho_1 U_1^2)A\). Thus

(p_1-p_2)A = (\rho_2 U_2^2-\rho_1 U_1^2)A (1.6)

if we consider the pressure force only, no body forces like gravity or electrostatics, and we do not consider fluid viscosity either. Rearranging,

p_1 + \rho_1 U_1^2 = p_2 + \rho_2 U_2^2 (1.7)

Conservation of energy is a balance of energy flux into and out of a control volume combined with the work done by fluid motion across the control surface. Energy is neither created nor destroyed, so the net energy gain of the fluid must be given by the work done on the fluid. The work done on the fluid on the left side is \(p_1 U_1 A\), and the work done by the fluid on the right side is \(p_2 U_2 A\). Thus the net work done on the fluid is \((p_1 U_1-p_2 U_2)A\). The internal energy per unit volume is \(\rho e\), and the kinetic energy per unit volume is \(\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2\), so the total rate of energy entering at left is \(\rho_1(e_1+\frac{1}{2}U_1^2)A\) and leaving at right is \(\rho_2(e_2+\frac{1}{2}U_2^2)A\), so

(p_1U_1-p_2U_2)A = \rho_2U_2(e_2+\frac{1}{2}U_2^2)A - \rho_1U_1(e_1+\frac{1}{2}U_1^2)A (1.8)

as long as we assume that no energy is added to the system through heat conduction. From conservation of mass, \(\rho_1 U_1 A = \rho_2 U_2 A\), so we divide each term by \(\rho_1 U_1 A\) or \(\rho_2 U_2 A\):

\frac{p_1}{\rho_1} - \frac{p_2}{\rho_2} = e_2 + \frac{1}{2}U_2^2 - e_1 + \frac{1}{2}U_1^2 (1.9)

and, defining the specific enthalpy \(h=e+\frac{p}{\rho}\), we rearrange to give

h_1 + \frac{1}{2}U_1^2 = h_2 + \frac{1}{2}U_2^2 (1.10)

Editorial note: equation (1.9) in the source prints a plus before its final kinetic-energy term. Dividing equation (1.8) by the common mass flow rate gives a minus there. The consistent rearrangement is shown below; it agrees with equation (1.10).

\frac{p_1}{\rho_1}-\frac{p_2}{\rho_2}=e_2+\frac{1}{2}U_2^2-e_1-\frac{1}{2}U_1^2 (1.9, corrected)


PDF page 26 — verified

\rho_1 U_1 = \rho_2 U_2 (1.11)

conservation of mass equation, strictly 1D flow

which shows that density and velocity change in opposite directions; conservation of momentum:

p_1 + \rho_1 U_1^2 = p_2 + \rho_2 U_2^2 (1.12)

conservation of momentum equation, strictly 1D flow, no viscosity

which shows that pressure changes generate a force that accelerates or decelerates the fluid; and conservation of energy

h_1 + \frac{1}{2}U_1^2 = h_2 + \frac{1}{2}U_2^2 (1.13)

conservation of energy equation, strictly 1D flow, no heat conduction

which shows that, on a per-mass basis, the sum of internal energy and stored work of compression (i.e., enthalpy) trades off with kinetic energy \(\frac{1}{2}U^2\). Taken together, these relations help us derive the speed of sound.

Acoustics describes sound waves and their fluid-mechanical effects

Sound waves are small disturbances in density and pressure. They propagate with the speed of sound \(a\), which technically is the speed of an isentropic plane wave disturbance:

a = \sqrt{\left.\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right|_s} (1.14)

speed of sound

Equation (1.14) is derived on p. 21 and the subscript s denotes that the derivative is at constant entropy. For an ideal gas, the speed of sound is given by

a = \sqrt{\gamma RT} (1.15)

speed of sound for an ideal gas

where \(\gamma\) is the specific-heat ratio \(\gamma = c_p/c_v\) of the gas (\(\gamma = 7/5\) for air), \(R\) is the gas constant, and \(T\) is the absolute temperature. This speed is a measure of the equation of state of the fluid, specifically how compressible the fluid is. Water is harder to compress than air, and its speed of sound is about 1500 m/s. Air is easier to compress than water, and its speed of sound is about 340 m/s. The relation between the compressibility of the fluid (i.e., \(\partial p/\partial \rho\)) and the speed of sound is microscopically related to the way a fluid responds to a small change in density. If a small change in density leads to a large pressure change, that pressure change will create a large force on the nearby fluid, quickly accelerating it. If a small change in density leads to a small pressure change, that change will generate only small forces which will accelerate the nearby fluid only slowly.

Incompressible flow describes the study of fluid in which pressure changes are unrelated to density changes. This is consistent with fluid motion relative to boundaries at speeds well below the speed of sound. Incompressible flow either assumes that density is fixed (as we have done in this

class), or that density might change but in a way that is unrelated to pressure. The buoyancy force that hot air feels, causing it to rise, is an example of a flow where there are density changes but that is still properly described as an incompressible flow.

Acoustics describes the study of small pressure and density disturbances in a fluid, which propagate through a fluid with the speed of sound, and explain how we hear sound and how microphones and other sensors detect sound.

The incompressible approximation cannot describe acoustics, and incompressible analysis treats disturbances as if they propagate infinitely fast in fluid

A mathematically incompressible fluid (such a thing doesn’t exist, but is a mathematical idealization) has an infinitely fast speed of sound, because it takes infinitely high pressure to affect a density change in a mathematically incompressible fluid. Thus an analysis that assumes \(\rho\) uniform cannot describe acoustics.

After we do rockets and stuff, our analysis for the rest of the term will be incompressible analysis, for which changes in the boundary conditions of a fluid flow instantly change the entire flowfield. However, our compressible analysis in this chapter will show that changes in boundary conditions propagate through a flowfield with a finite speed denoted the speed of sound. This is not particularly important when objects move through air at speeds well below the speed of sound; however, when objects move with speeds near or above the speed of sound, there are significant consequences.

The pressure and density disturbances we hear and detect with microphones are tiny

The approximate human limit of detection of acoustic pressure (i.e., the smallest sound we can hear) is 20 μPa or 2×10⁻¹⁰ atm. Sound pressure level SPL is a measure of the strength of sound waves and is given by

\mathrm{SPL}[\mathrm{dB}] = 20\log_{10}\left(\frac{p_a}{20\,\mu\mathrm{Pa}}\right) (1.16)

definition of sound pressure level

where SPL[dB] denotes “sound pressure level in units of decibels” and \(p_a\) denotes the acoustic pressure, i.e., the magnitude of the sinusoidally varying pressure associated with the sound. A decibel is a unitless “unit” defined in terms of a ratio of an acoustic pressure to this reference pressure. 0 dB corresponds to a sound amplitude just at the human limit of detection. We can invert Equation (1.16) to get

p_a = (20\,\mu\mathrm{Pa})10^{\mathrm{SPL}[\mathrm{dB}]/20} (1.17)

incompressible flow: implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Incompressible flow implies that the motion of the fluid does not cause density to change, in comparison to compressible flow in which fluid moves so quickly and the pressure changes so much that the density is perturbed enough to affect convective fluxes. Incompressible flows may still have nonuniform density, for example if the fluid’s temperature varies; this can affect the conservation of momentum equations. An incompressible flow does not imply that the fluid is mathematically incompressible, only that pressure-induced compression can be ignored. Cf. compressible flow.

acoustics: the study of sound, i.e., small pressure and density disturbances in a fluid.

incompressible: with respect to a flow, implies physically that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations, and is not perturbed by the fluid’s acceleration and deceleration. With respect to a fluid, denotes that the density of the fluid is a mathematical constant.

So 100 dB, which is the sound of a jackhammer to the person using it, and the limit at which workers are required to wear protective earplugs, corresponds to an acoustic pressure of 2 Pa, i.e., 1×10⁵ more than the hearing threshold. This fluctuation is still five orders of magnitude smaller than atmospheric pressure.

Compressible flow is flow in which the fluid is moving fast enough that its motion causes significant changes in the fluid density

Acoustics refers to the limit in which pressure and density change only a very small amount. In this limit, perturbations are isentropic, move with the speed of sound, and remain small. In this limit, we can detect the presence of acoustic disturbances with our ears and with microphones, but the forces acoustic waves generate are small, and the propagation of acoustic waves is largely independent from any other fluid mechanical phenomena.

Consider a whiffle ball thrown at 15 m/s. The whiffle ball causes a disturbance in the velocity and the pressure. We treat flow around the whiffle ball as incompressible, and assume that the density does not change markedly. An incompressible analysis would correctly describe the forces around this ball. The ball makes a sound, though; you can hear a whiffle ball flying through the air; it is about 10 dB. That sound is explained by small perturbations in pressure and density; by the time they get to our ears these perturbations are about 60 μPa pressure variation or about 7×10⁻¹⁰ kg/m³ variation in density. Those perturbations are not enough to invalidate the use of incompressible flow to predict the forces on the ball.

In contrast, consider a bullet shot from a gun moving at about 750 m/s in air (Figure 1.11, p. 19). The speed of sound of air at STP is near 350 m/s, so there is no way for the bullet to make a small perturbation in the density; the bullet is moving faster than an isentropic wave would travel, and it makes a large change in the density. It is like a car moving at 60 mph slamming into a line of cars waiting at a stop light. It makes a big change. As the bullet slams into air molecules, the air is increased to a higher pressure (by about a factor of 5), higher density (by about a factor of 3), and higher temperature (by about a factor of 2).

Compressible flow describes the study of large pressure and density disturbances in a fluid, which result from the superposition of an infinite number of acoustic waves when the speed of the object is not well below the speed of sound. Shock waves are the most interesting part of these flows—they are an inevitable flow phenomenon any time an object moves faster than the speed of sound, in which the pressure, velocity, temperature, and density all change discontinuously.

As soon as we start considering shock waves, we need to bring back thermodynamics of ideal gases from ENGRD2210 (Sidebar 1.2; p. 18).

ideal gas: a gas with negligible intermolecular interaction. Also called perfect gas or dilute gas. Describes the gas’s equation of state p = ρRT. Not equivalent to ideal fluid, which, in contrast, describes a constitutive relation.

SIDEBAR 1.2: FUNDAMENTALS

Let’s review ideal gas thermodynamics!!

The ideal gas law specifies the equation of state for an ideal gas

The ideal gas law specifies that

p = \rho RT (1.18)

where p is pressure, ρ is density, R is the gas constant for the specific gas in question (R for air is R = 287 J/kg K), and T is absolute temperature.

Specific heats, specific heat ratio, and enthalpy are critical fluid parameters that come into play as soon as temperature can change in a fluid flow

Materials have specific heats at fixed volume (\(c_v\)) and pressure (\(c_p\)), which describe partial derivatives of specific internal energy e and specific enthalpy h = e + p/ρ, respectively, with respect to temperature:

c_v = \left.\frac{\partial e}{\partial T}\right|_v,\qquad c_p = \left.\frac{\partial h}{\partial T}\right|_p (1.19)

If we ignore chemical reactions and assume that specific heats are independent of temperature, we can simply define \(e=c_vT\) and \(h=c_pT\). A gas with specific heats that are independent of temperature is called a calorically perfect gas. We will always model gases as calorically perfect, because it makes the math easier. In practice it is often used; however, when using it one should always be aware of its limitations—the exhaust gases of rockets are often not in thermodynamic equilibrium. The specific heat ratio γ is defined as \(\gamma=c_p/c_v\). For diatomic gases at the temperatures we consider, γ = 7/5. Thus γ = 1.4 is typically used for air. As diatomic gases heat up, both their \(c_p\) and \(c_v\) increase, and γ gets smaller. The Argon in air has γ = 5/3, but it is present at low enough concentration that it doesn’t significantly affect air’s behavior. Because \(c_p-c_v=R\), we can rewrite the ideal gas law in terms of specific enthalpy and the specific heat ratio:

p = \frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}\rho h (1.20)

This can be useful when manipulating conservation equations, which are written in terms of p, ρ, and h. The energy carried by a fluid per unit volume is called the stagnation enthalpy \(H_0\), and is given by the sum of the internal energy, work stored in pressure, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy:

H_0 = \rho e + p + \frac{1}{2}\rho U^2 + \rho g (1.21)

Editorial note: the scan clearly prints \(\rho g\) as the last term of (1.21). That term has units of force per volume, unlike the other energy-per-volume terms. If \(z\) is elevation above the reference level, the gravitational term is \(\rho gz\); the dimensionally consistent expression is \(H_0=\rho e+p+\tfrac12\rho U^2+\rho gz\). Equation (1.22) explicitly neglects gravity and is unaffected.

The enthalpy, like the Bernoulli constant (or, equivalently, the total pressure), is a measure of all of the relevant energy the fluid is carrying. Whereas the Bernoulli equation retained the gravity term but neglected internal energy, the enthalpy (which we use for compressible flow analysis) retains internal energy but usually drops gravitational potential energy. Gravitational potential energy is always negligible in compressible flows we consider (which are usually gas flows with low density), but temperature does change and we must keep track of internal energy. Ignoring gravity, and dividing by density to get the energy per unit mass, leads to what we call the specific stagnation enthalpy \(h_0\):

h_0 = e + \frac{p}{\rho} + \frac{1}{2}U^2 = h + \frac{1}{2}U^2 (1.22)

The specific stagnation enthalpy is the specific enthalpy the fluid would have if it were isentropically slowed to zero speed, or, equivalently, the total energy stored in the fluid (per unit mass) from internal energy, stored compression work, and kinetic energy.

Isentropic processes have a specific pressure-density relation

Isentropic processes in calorically perfect ideal gases satisfy

p = C\rho^\gamma (1.23)

where C is a constant.

Sound waves are isentropic disturbances in density and pressure that propagate with a speed dictated by the equation of state of the fluid

Sound waves are small perturbations, and are the easiest to analyze because we can determine their speed with only two equations.

The speed of sound is the speed of an infinitesimally small perturbation of pressure and density

We can combine conservation of mass and conservation of momentum to show that if a fluid transitions from state 1 to state 2 across an infinitesimally strong plane wave, that that wave must be moving at a speed \(U=\sqrt{\left.\frac{\partial p}{\partial\rho}\right|_s}\) (Sidebar 1.3, p. 21). This speed is called the speed of sound and is denoted by a.

We normally discuss acoustic waves as sinusoidally oscillating perturbations that have frequency and wavelength

Pressure and density disturbances can take any form, but the math is simplest for sinusoidally varying perturbations (and any other function can be written in terms of the sinusoidally varying perturbations anyway), so we consider sinusoidally varying perturbations. Acoustic variations have a frequency and wavelength that satisfies

a = f\lambda (1.34)

relation between frequency, wavelength, and wavespeed for a sinusoidal wave

where a is the speed of sound, f is the frequency of the oscillation, and λ is the wavelength of the oscillation. Young humans can hear roughly from \(f=10\text{--}20{,}000\,\mathrm{Hz}\).

The microscopic picture of how an acoustic wave travels is shown in Figure 1.12, p. 22, in which the locations of fluid particles are shown at several points of time for a 1-D column of fluid connected to a vibrating speaker.

Musical notes have well specified frequencies, for example the A₄ note on a piano is tuned to 440 Hz, and each half tone difference on a keyboard (i.e., the difference from one key on a piano keyboard to the next) is different by a frequency ratio of \(2^{1/12}\). This is an example of a well-tempered or equally tempered instrument. Some musical intervals that sound nice include

acoustic: in general, related to sound. When used to modify a field property, e.g., “acoustic pressure,” means the magnitude of the specific small oscillatory variation around the mean value.

SIDEBAR 1.3: FUNDAMENTALS

The speed of sound \(a=\sqrt{\partial p/\partial\rho}=\sqrt{\gamma RT}\) is derived using conservation of mass and momentum for a plane wave

If we allow density to change, we can show that a plane wave of a small perturbation of pressure and density must move at a specific speed dictated by the equation of state of the fluid; this speed is the speed of sound. Assume fluid in one state has an infinitesimally weak transition through a discontinuity into a second state; call these states 1 and 2. Assume also that states 1 and 2 are different but only infinitesimally so. Assume that the disturbance is planar, i.e., the flow varies in only one dimension and it has no dependence tangent to the disturbance. The integral conservation of mass equation says

\rho_1 U_1 = \rho_2 U_2 (1.24)

and the integral conservation of momentum equation says

\rho_1 U_1^2 + p_1 = \rho_2 U_2^2 + p_2 (1.25)

Now assume that the perturbation is infinitesimal, and write \(\rho_2=\rho_1+d\rho\), \(U_2=U_1+dU\), \(p_2=p_1+dp\):

\rho_1 U_1 = (\rho_1+d\rho)(U_1+dU) (1.26)

Keeping only terms that are first order in differentials, this leads for conservation of mass to

0 = U_1d\rho + \rho_1dU (1.27)

or equivalently

\frac{d\rho}{\rho_1} = -\frac{dU}{U_1} (1.28)

which tells us that for conservation of mass, the relative changes in density and speed must be opposite and equal. For substitution later, we could equivalently write

\frac{d\rho}{dU} = -\frac{\rho_1}{U_1} (1.29)

For conservation of momentum, we write

p_1 + \rho_1U_1^2 = (p_1+dp) + (\rho_1+d\rho)(U_1+dU)^2 (1.30)

Keeping only terms that are first-order in differentials, this leads to

0 = dp + U_1^2d\rho + 2\rho_1U_1dU (1.31)

\frac{dp}{d\rho} = -U_1^2 - 2\rho_1U_1\frac{dU}{d\rho} = -U_1^2 + 2U_1^2 = U_1^2 (1.32)

So, this analysis tells us that a plane wave inducing an infinitesimal density perturbation must be moving at speed \(U=\sqrt{dp/d\rho}\). This speed is the speed of sound and is typically denoted by a. This analysis is not valid for a finite discontinuity, i.e., a shock wave. If the fluid is an ideal gas (\(p=\rho RT\)) and the wave is isentropic (\(p=C\rho^\gamma\)), then \(C=RT\rho^{1-\gamma}\) and \(\partial p/\partial\rho=\gamma RT\). Thus for an ideal gas

a = \sqrt{\gamma RT} (1.33)

1.7. Properties of Sound Waves



Figure 1.12: A microscopic picture of a traveling acoustic wave. A 1-D column of fluid is actuated by a speaker at left which is vibrating at cyclic frequency \(f\). The locations of fluid “particles” are shown for several different times from bottom to top. Examining an individual particle’s location with time (i.e., from bottom to top on the diagram) shows that it moves sinusoidally. Examining regions of high or low density show that they propagate from left to right with the speed of sound \(a\). Here the dots denoting “fluid particles” are schematic—really, the system is a continuum. What is propagating is regions of low and high density, and the speed is closely related to how much pressure (i.e., force) is generated when there is a local density gradient. The distance between regions of high (or low) density is referred to as the wavelength \(\lambda\); and these parameters satisfy \(a=f\lambda\).

1.7. Properties of Sound Waves

an “octave” (i.e., 12 half-tones i.e., a frequency ratio of 2), a “major fifth” (i.e., 7 half-tones i.e., a frequency ratio of \(2^{7/12} \simeq 1.498 \simeq 3/2\)), and a “major fourth” (i.e., 5 half-tones i.e., a frequency ratio of \(2^{5/12} \simeq 1.335 \simeq 4/3\)). Each of these frequency ratios (and therefore these combinations of tones) sounds good to our ear because many or all of the harmonics are resonant; these frequency ratios form the physical underpinning of classical music theory and the notion of a chord or a musical key.

Because highlighting a tone is important for music, and because we gain benefit from amplification of acoustic signals, resonance is important in acoustics. Acoustic waves reflect off of solid surfaces and other changes in geometry (for example the open end of a tube), and where the reflected wave interferes constructively with the incoming wave, a standing wave is generated. This standing wave can be much higher amplitude than the original traveling wave. Musical instruments, for example, are designed to create resonances at specific frequencies and have these resonances controllable in various ways (striking a key on a piano, opening and closing keys on woodwind instruments, opening and closing valves on brass instruments, pinning the end of a string with your finger on a violin or against a fret on a guitar). These resonances occur when an acoustic wave is reflected after a distance that corresponds to an integral number of half-wavelengths, because in that case the wave interferes constructively.

This is shown in Figure 1.13, p. 24, in which the oscillations in speed and pressure of fluid in a standing wave inside a tube with two open ends (this is basically what a concert flute is). At nodes, fluid parameters are not changing. At antinodes, fluid parameters change the maximum amount. In a standing acoustic wave, the locations where pressure oscillates the most (i.e., pressure antinodes) correspond to where the fluid is motionless (i.e., velocity nodes), whereas the locations where the fluid sloshes back and forth (i.e., velocity antinodes) correspond to where the pressure does not change (i.e., pressure nodes). Locations of fluid particles are shown at several points of time for a 1-D column of fluid connected to a vibrating speaker.

Introductory mechanical engineering fluid mechanics does not focus too much on acoustics, but we should be aware of the notion that acoustic waves of a specific wavelength can be amplified by a resonant chamber. For example a tube will resonate sound at certain frequencies, depending on whether the tube is open or closed at each end. This is how pipe organs and brass instruments work. Strings vibrate at a frequency dictated by their length, and the properties and tension of the string, so piano wires and guitar strings are tightened until they vibrate at the desired frequency, then both vibrations are amplified and changed by the soundboard.

A string or pipe resonates when its length corresponds to an integral number of half-wavelengths of the acoustic wave. Example Problem 1.1 (p. 25) shows an example calculation of the length of a resonant chamber and its relation to resonant frequencies.

harmonic: in the context of frequencies, a harmonic is a frequency which is an integral multiple of a fundamental frequency. Cf. overtone.

resonance: when an actuation has the same frequency as a system’s natural frequency, leading to an output that is much higher in magnitude than would be expected from the original actuation.

acoustic: in general, related to sound. When used to modify a field property e.g., “acoustic pressure”, means the magnitude of the specific small oscillatory variation around the mean value.

standing wave: a wave (sound wave or shock wave) that is not moving, usually because of the superposition of waves moving in two directions. Cf. traveling wave.

node: the location in space where an oscillation has no amplitude.

antinode: the location in space where an oscillation has maximum amplitude. Cf. node.

An infinite number of standing waves are possible inside this tube; in any real fluid (which has some viscous effects), the strongest resonances will be in the lower-order resonances. This standing wave corresponds to a frequency three times the fundamental i.e., the second overtone; I show an overtone because it is easier to see the patterns of nodes and antinodes if there are several to look at instead of just one. Arrows denote how the fluid sloshes back and forth at the velocity antinodes (which are also pressure nodes). At bottom, graphs show the magnitude of the pressure and velocity oscillations as a function of distance along the tube. The distance between nodes or the distance between antinodes is referred to as the wavelength \(\lambda\); and these parameters satisfy \(a=f\lambda\). The keys on a flute open and close holes along the length of a tube like this, so as to change the effective length of the tube resonator or to preferentially enhance or remove resonances.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 1.1

What is the shortest closed tube that will resonate a \(C_4\) note i.e., a 262-Hz acoustic signal? A C-floor concert flute’s (Figure 1.14, p. 25) lowest note is a \(C_4\) (“middle C”) and the standard length of a concert flute is 66 cm. Does this match your calculation?

Figure 1.14: A C-floor concert flute.

Photograph omitted.

Solution: the shortest tube corresponds to a half-wavelength. At 440 Hz, the wavelength can be calculated from

\lambda = \frac{a}{f} = \frac{340\ \text{m/s}}{262\ \text{Hz}} = 1.3\ \text{m}, (1.35)

and thus the shortest length \(l\) is given by

l = \frac{\lambda}{2} = \frac{1.3\ \text{m}}{2} = 0.65\ \text{m}. (1.36)

This is consistent with the calculation. We did cheat a bit, though. There are a couple sources of small errors, including that flutes operate on air blown from a mouth, which is warmer and has water vapor, which changes the speed of sound. Also there are small “edge effects” that slightly change the resonances of open tubes. Also the embouchure (i.e., mouthpiece) on a flute is near the end but not at the end of the tube. These errors all cancel out almost perfectly, almost as if Theobald Böhm, the designer of the modern flute, wanted to make it work out nicely for an example problem in fluids class.

Editorial note: “At 440 Hz” conflicts with the printed substitution and question. Using their \(f=262\,\mathrm{Hz}\) gives \(\lambda=340/262\approx1.30\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(l=\lambda/2\approx0.65\,\mathrm{m}\), as shown. The tube end conditions matter: equal end types (both open or both closed) give a half-wave fundamental; one open and one closed gives a quarter-wave fundamental, \(l=\lambda/4\approx0.324\,\mathrm{m}\). The word “closed” alone is ambiguous here.

1.8 Isentropic compressible flow through tubes of varying cross sections e.g., nozzles has simple relations relating the Mach number to all other parameters

For a plane wave, there are only two things that can happen to a fluid; it can remain the same, or it can be changed through a wave. An infinitesimal wave (sound wave) causes an infinitesimal perturbation, whereas a shock wave causes a finite change, and causes the fluid to discontinuously change from supersonic to subsonic.

If we assume that fluid is all moving in one direction, but we allow the cross-sectional area of the tube that contains it to change (for example in a nozzle e.g., Figure 1.15, p. 27), then the fluid can change its properties continuously. This analysis is called quasi-1D analysis and is commonly used for nozzles. Nozzles are used to convert pressure and temperature into kinetic energy.

The conservation relations for quasi-1D inviscid compressible flow are, for conservation of mass:

\rho_1 U_1 A_1 = \rho_2 U_2 A_2,\qquad \frac{d}{ds}(\rho U A)=0, (1.37)

for conservation of momentum:

p_1 A_1 + \rho_1 U_1^2 A_1 + \int_{s_1}^{s_2} \frac{pA}{s}\,ds = p_2 A_2 + \rho_2 U_2^2 A_2,\qquad \frac{dp}{ds}+\rho U\frac{dU}{ds}=0, (1.38)

and for conservation of energy:

h_1+\frac{1}{2}U_1^2=h_2+\frac{1}{2}U_2^2,\qquad \frac{dh}{ds}+U\frac{dU}{ds}=0, (1.39)

Quasi-1D isentropic flow relations are important to us because they will explain the physical principles that undermine the design of a rocket nozzle:

• If you want to make a rocket, the fluid should shoot out the back really fast if you want maximum propulsion.
• To shoot fluid out the back really fast, it should be supersonic.
• Subsonic flows get faster when you make the cross-sectional area of a tube smaller, so if you start with slow or quiescent fluid (say the product of combustion in the engine), you can speed it up by making the tube smaller in cross-sectional area.

plane wave: a wave whose wavefront is planar, i.e., a one-dimensional wave.

shock wave: a discontinuous transition in which a supersonic flow slows down, with an attendant increase in pressure and density.

supersonic: having a speed higher than the speed of sound i.e., a Mach number greater than one.

subsonic: having a speed lower than the speed of sound i.e., a Mach number less than one.

nozzle: a duct with varying cross-section which is designed to control the velocity and its distribution in an exhaust.

quasi-1D: a pictorial representation of a (usually 2D) vector field that indicates the vector magnitude and direction through uniformly spaced vector arrows.

isentropic: without increase in entropy. In a fluid system, this means no conduction of heat, no viscous transfer of momentum, and no shock waves.

quiescent: motionless; \(\vec{u}=0\).

quasi-1D inviscid compressible conservation of mass, in integral and differential forms.

quasi-1D inviscid compressible conservation of momentum, in integral and differential forms.

quasi-1D inviscid compressible conservation of energy, in integral and differential forms.

Editorial note: The printed integrand \(pA/s\) has the right units, but the differential momentum equation and constant mass flow instead imply \(d(pA+\dot mU)/ds=p\,dA/ds\). Thus the wall-pressure term in the integral relation should be \(\int_{s_1}^{s_2}p\,(dA/ds)\,ds\). For a constant-area tube this term is zero; the printed \(pA/s\) would generally not be zero. The source expression is retained above.

1.8. Isentropic Nozzle Relations

Figure 1.15: An example of a nozzle which allows isentropic flow exhausting at supersonic speeds. This is the nozzle on the F-1 engines that powered the Saturn V rocket, which we used to go to the Moon.

Photograph omitted.

But... that only works until the fluid is moving at \(M=1\). Supersonic flows get faster when the cross-sectional area gets bigger. So, you need the nozzle to converge (to get the fluid up to \(M=1\)) then you need the nozzle to diverge (to keep accelerating it). Hence rocket nozzles are converging–diverging nozzles.

The quasi-1D isentropic relations and the notations associated with them are also motivated by these observations:

• If the fluid is sonic, it must be at the throat (the narrowest region) of the nozzle.

• Fluid relations in a nozzle are most easily reported by comparing properties everywhere to the properties at the throat or at stagnation.

throat: the narrowest section of a tube or nozzle.

Quasi-1D isentropic relations are a statement of conservation of energy, combined with the ideal gas law and the calorically perfect assumption

The quasi-1D isentropic flow relations are shown below, both in general and for \(\gamma=7/5\).

Isentropic relations link fluid properties as the Mach number changes. Linking values to the stagnation value (\(M=0\), denoted by subscript 0) or that at the throat (\(M=1\), denoted with an asterisk), is often useful in a

solving problems, because we often have information in the high-pressure reservoir (usually a combustion chamber) or at the throat.

\frac{p}{p_0}=\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{-\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}},\qquad \frac{p}{p_0}=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}M^2\right)^{-\frac{7}{2}}, (1.40)

\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}=\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{\gamma-1}},\qquad \frac{\rho}{\rho_0}=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}M^2\right)^{-\frac{5}{2}}, (1.41)

\frac{T}{T_0}=\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{-1},\qquad \frac{T}{T_0}=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}M^2\right)^{-1}. (1.42)

Stagnation-normalized pressure for isentropic quasi-1D flow through a nozzle.

Stagnation-normalized density for isentropic quasi-1D flow through a nozzle.

Stagnation-normalized temperature for isentropic quasi-1D flow through a nozzle.

These equations are derived by starting with conservation of energy (i.e., that \(h+\frac{1}{2}U^2\) is uniform), deriving the temperature relation, then using that to generate the pressure and density relations from the ideal gas law (\(p/\rho=RT\)) and the polytropic relation for an isentropic process (\(p=C\rho^\gamma\)).

The area-velocity relation shows how the shape of a nozzle accelerates or decelerates a fluid

The area-velocity relation links area changes to speed changes:

\frac{1}{A}\frac{dA}{ds}=(M^2-1)\frac{1}{U}\frac{dU}{ds}. (1.43)

area-velocity relation: the relation \(\frac{1}{A}\frac{dA}{ds}=(M^2-1)\frac{1}{U}\frac{dU}{ds}\), which shows how the shape of a nozzle accelerates or decelerates a fluid.

Area-velocity relation for isentropic quasi-1D flow through a nozzle.

This relation comes from a combination of the speed of sound with both conservation of mass and conservation of momentum for quasi-1-D flow (see Sidebar 1.4, p. 29).

This equation is very powerful and central to nozzle design. It shows that the relative changes in cross-sectional area as we move downstream (\(\frac{1}{A}\frac{dA}{ds}\)) are related to the relative changes in speed (\(\frac{1}{U}\frac{dU}{ds}\)) by the multiplicative factor \((M^2-1)\):

• As \(M\to 0\), the multiplicative factor \(M^2-1\) approaches -1, so \(\frac{1}{A}\frac{dA}{ds}=-\frac{1}{U}\frac{dU}{ds}\). This means that if the nozzle is diverging, the fluid is slowing down by the same relative amount, and if the nozzle is converging, the fluid is speeding up by the same relative amount. This expression looks just like quasi-1-D conservation of mass if \(\rho\) is assumed uniform. \(M=0\) is the incompressible limit, in which flow is moving slowly enough that the density of the fluid is not perturbed. Most of the work we will do this term will be in this incompressible limit. Precisely, for a flow to be well approximated as incompressible, \(M^2\) must be much smaller than 1.

• For \(M<1\), the multiplicative factor \(M^2-1\) is negative but smaller in magnitude than -1. This means that if the nozzle is diverging, the fluid is decelerating and the density is dropping, and if the nozzle is converging, the fluid is accelerating and the density is increasing.

• For \(M=1\), the multiplicative factor \(M^2-1\) is zero. This means that the nozzle can neither be converging or diverging. This means that \(M=1\) only at the throat of a nozzle.

incompressible: with respect to a flow, implies physically that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations, and is not perturbed by the fluid’s acceleration and deceleration. With respect to a fluid, denotes that the density of the fluid is a mathematical constant.

throat: the narrowest section of a tube or nozzle.

SIDEBAR 1.4: FUNDAMENTALS

The area-velocity relation is derived by combining conservation of mass, conservation of momentum, and the speed of sound

Quasi-1-D conservation of mass, quasi-1-D conservation of momentum, and the speed of sound can be combined to generate the area-velocity relation, which is the equation that most clearly tells us how a nozzle needs to be designed to accelerate flow to generate propulsion. The differential relation for conservation of mass along a streamline:

\frac{d}{ds}(\rho U A)=0, (1.44)

can be expanded using the chain rule twice and simplifying:

\rho U\frac{dA}{ds}+\rho A\frac{dU}{ds}+UA\frac{d\rho}{ds}=0, (1.45)

then dividing through by \(\rho U A\):

\frac{1}{A}\frac{dA}{ds}+\frac{1}{U}\frac{dU}{ds}+\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{d\rho}{ds}=0. (1.46)

the differential relation for conservation of momentum along a streamline:

\frac{dp}{ds}+\rho U\frac{dU}{ds}=0 (1.47)

can be linked to this by writing \(\frac{dp}{ds}\) in terms of \(\rho\) and recalling that \(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\) is the squared speed of sound:

\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\frac{d\rho}{ds}+\rho U\frac{dU}{ds}=0 (1.48)

a^2\frac{d\rho}{ds}+\rho U\frac{dU}{ds}=0 (1.49)

and dividing through by \(\rho a^2\):

\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{d\rho}{ds}+M^2\frac{1}{U}\frac{dU}{ds}=0 (1.50)

Equation (1.50) can be inserted into Equation (1.46) to obtain

\frac{1}{A}\frac{dA}{ds}=(M^2-1)\frac{1}{U}\frac{dU}{ds}. (1.51)

• For \(M>1\), the multiplicative factor \(M^2-1\) is positive. This means that if the nozzle is diverging, the fluid is accelerating and the density is dropping, and if the nozzle is converging, the fluid is decelerating and the density is increasing.

The area-Mach-number relation shows how the Mach number at any point in a nozzle can be determined by comparing that location’s cross-sectional area to the sonic area

The area-Mach-number relation links area to Mach number. This relation comes from a combination of conservation of mass with sonic and stagnation relations (see Sidebar 1.5, p. 31):

\frac{A}{A^*}=\frac{1}{M}\left[\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)\right]^{\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}},\qquad \frac{A}{A^*}=\frac{1}{M}\left(\frac{M^2+5}{6}\right)^3. (1.59)

Area-Mach-number relation for isentropic quasi-1D flow through a nozzle.

The area-Mach-number relation basically says that for isentropic flow, if the flow is choked through the throat, the area at a location in the nozzle prescribes the Mach number at that location. Because flow through a nozzle is always choked when it is being used for propulsion, this means that (remarkably) the conditions of isentropic flow inside a nozzle can be calculated algebraically as long as we know \(p_0\) and \(T_0\) in the reservoir and \(A/A^*\) throughout.

Example Problem 1.2 (p. 32) shows an example of how the quasi-1D equations can be used to describe flow through nozzles.

A shock wave is a finite discontinuity through which a fluid moving at a speed larger than the speed of sound is suddenly and discontinuously slowed down, heated up, and compressed to higher density and pressure

As we discussed earlier in the chapter, if an object moves through a fluid at a speed faster than the speed of sound, it must create a finite disturbance called a shock wave. We can get away with studying ideal gases because moving faster than the speed of sound is of engineering relevance only in ideal gases. We consider only calorically perfect gases to make the math easier, and we discuss only normal shocks, which are the most straightfor-

shock wave: a discontinuous transition in which a supersonic flow slows down, with an attendant increase in pressure and density.

1.9. Shock Waves

SIDEBAR 1.5: FUNDAMENTALS

The Area-Mach-number relation is derived by combining conservation of mass with sonic and stagnation relations

Quasi-1-D conservation of mass and sonic and stagnation relations can be combined to generate the Area-Mach-number relation, which shows that the cross-sectional area of a section of a nozzle prescribes what Mach number the flow is at. From conservation of mass:

\rho^* U^* A^*=\rho U A, (1.52)

Mass flow at an arbitrary location: \(\rho U A\).

Mass flow at the throat: \(\rho^* U^* A^*\).

we can rearrange to write the area relative to the area at the throat:

\frac{A}{A^*}=\frac{\rho^* U^*}{\rho U} (1.53)

The fluid speed is equal to the speed of sound at the throat, so \(U^*=a^*\). Also, because we have established stagnation and sonic relations, we can rewrite \(\rho^*/\rho\) in terms of the sonic density:

\frac{A}{A^*}=\frac{\rho^*}{\rho_0}\frac{\rho_0}{\rho}\frac{a^*}{U} (1.54)

The stagnation relation for density is

\frac{\rho_0}{\rho}=\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma-1}},\qquad \frac{\rho_0}{\rho}=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}M^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}, (1.55)

which, applied at \(M=1\) for the sonic condition, is

\frac{\rho_0}{\rho^*}=\left(\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma-1}},\qquad \frac{\rho_0}{\rho^*}=\left(\frac{6}{5}\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}=1.58. (1.56)

Finally, the characteristic Mach number \(M^*=U/a^*\) is given by

\frac{U}{a^*}\equiv M^*=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{\gamma+1}{2}M^2}{1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2}},\qquad M^*=\sqrt{\frac{6M^2}{M^2+5}}. (1.57)

Multiplying the appropriate ratios together we get

\frac{A}{A^*}=\frac{1}{M}\left[\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)\right]^{\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}},\qquad \frac{A}{A^*}=\frac{1}{M}\left(\frac{M^2+5}{6}\right)^3. (1.58)

1.9. Shock Waves

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 1.2

A high-pressure chamber has essentially stationary air at 4000 K and 15 atm. It exhausts through an isentropic nozzle and exits out the end at \(1.2\times10^{-2}\) atm. Calculate the Mach number at the exit. Also, calculate the mass flow rate of the gas through the rocket if the area of the exit is \(0.5\ \text{m}^2\). Assume the air is chemically inert and calorically perfect with \(\gamma=1.4\) (this is not really true for 4000 K air).

Solution: We assume isentropic flow throughout. Because the flow is isentropic, the pressure ratio is given by

\frac{p_0}{p_e}=\left[1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right]^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}. (1.60)

For \(p_0=15\) atm, \(p_e=1.2\times10^{-2}\) atm, and \(\gamma=1.4\), this leads to

M=5.78. (1.61)

at the exit,

\dot{m}=\rho A u. (1.62)

at exit,

\frac{T}{T_0}=\left(\frac{p}{p_0}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}}=0.13. (1.63)

Thus \(T=522\) K at the exit and the speed of sound is \(a=458\ \text{m/s}\), making the velocity at the exit \(u=2.64\ \text{km/s}\). The density at the exit is given by

\rho=\frac{p}{RT}=8.12\times10^{-3}\ \text{kg/m}^3. (1.64)

The mass flow rate is thus

\dot{m}=8.12\times10^{-3}\times2.64\times10^3\times0.5\simeq10.7\ \text{kg/s}. (1.65)

1.9. Shock Waves

ward. For more info on shock waves and compressible flow, take MAE4230!

The speed of sound involved only infinitesimal changes to density and pressure, which did not lead to a temperature change or any need to consider energy for the fluid. However, if we consider finite disturbances i.e., shock waves, we must add temperature (and therefore energy), and that requires that we know something about the equation of state of the fluid. The normal shock relations are derived by combining conservation of mass, conservation of momentum and conservation of energy for a plane wave with the equation of state of the fluid—these are four equations, which in turn lead to solution for the four unknowns \(U\), \(p\), \(\rho\), and \(T\). Sidebar 1.6 (p. 34) shows the equations used to derive normal shock relations.

normal shock: short for normal shock wave. A shock wave that is aligned normal to the flow.

The normal shock relations are algebraic relations that describe the ratios of fluid properties before and after a shock wave in terms of the upstream Mach number

The normal shock relations are simple in that they are algebraic relations derived through manipulation of algebraic equations. They can be written in a format such that the properties downstream of the normal shock can be quickly calculated given the properties upstream of the normal shock. They are written in terms of the fluid specific heat ratio \(\gamma\) and the upstream Mach number \(M_1\). The Mach number is the speed normalized by the speed of sound:

M\equiv\frac{U}{a};\qquad M_1=\frac{U_1}{a_1};\qquad M_2=\frac{U_2}{a_2}. (1.71)

Definition of Mach number.

Fluid going through a shock wave heats up and slows down, so the speed of sound downstream of the shock wave is higher than that upstream of the shock wave, and the Mach number after a normal shock is always below one.

The normal shock relations are listed below, both in general and for \(\gamma=7/5\), which is the value for air at standard temperature. The normal shock relations are algebraic; however, unlike equations like the Bernoulli equation or the Navier–Stokes equations, these equations are harder to break apart term by term to isolate the contributions of each part.

\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}=\frac{(\gamma+1)M_1^2}{2+(\gamma-1)M_1^2},\qquad \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}=\frac{6M_1^2}{M_1^2+5}, (1.72)

Density jump across a normal shock wave.

\frac{U_2}{U_1}=\frac{2+(\gamma-1)M_1^2}{(\gamma+1)M_1^2},\qquad \frac{U_2}{U_1}=\frac{M_1^2+5}{6M_1^2}, (1.73)

Speed drop across a normal shock wave.

\frac{p_2}{p_1}=1+\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma+1}(M_1^2-1),\qquad \frac{p_2}{p_1}=\frac{7M_1^2-1}{6}, (1.74)

Pressure jump across a normal shock wave.

\frac{h_2}{h_1}=\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\left[1+\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma+1}(M_1^2-1)\right]\frac{2+(\gamma-1)M_1^2}{(\gamma+1)M_1^2},\qquad \frac{h_2}{h_1}=\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{7M_1^4+34M_1^2-5}{36M_1^2}, (1.75)

Enthalpy/temperature jump across a normal shock wave.

We can also determine that

M_2=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_1^2+1}{\gamma M_1^2-\frac{\gamma-1}{2}}},\qquad M_2=\sqrt{\frac{M_1^2+5}{7M_1^2-1}}. (1.76)

Mach number downstream of a normal shock wave.

speed of sound: the speed with which infinitesimal (isentropic) disturbances propagate in a fluid. Denoted \(a\) by those studying compressible flow, and usually by \(c\) by those studying acoustics. We will use \(a\). Given by \(a^2=\left.\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right|_s\), or, for ideal gases, as \(a^2=\gamma RT\).

1.9. Shock Waves

SIDEBAR 1.6: FUNDAMENTALS

The equations used to derive normal shock relations

Normal shock relations are derived using conservation of mass, momentum, and energy, combined with an equation of state for the fluid. Recall that conservation of mass says mass flux into and out of a control volume must be equal:

\rho_1 U_1=\rho_2 U_2, (1.66)

and conservation of momentum says the difference in momentum flux into and out of a control volume must be explained by the net force caused by pressure variation:

p_1+\rho_1 U_1^2=p_2+\rho_2 U_2^2. (1.67)

Those two equations were enough to derive the speed of sound for an infinitesimal disturbance. However, if state 1 and state 2 are different by a finite amount, i.e., in a normal shock, there are an infinite number of solutions to this system (there are three variables and only two constraints). To specify which solution(s) are possible, we need more constraints. We add conservation of energy, which requires that we add the temperature or enthalpy (so now four variables and three constraints). And then we define an equation of state for the fluid, which leads to the fourth constraint. Then the system is solvable. Conservation of energy is similar to conservation of mass, in that energy flux into and out of the control volume must be equal:

\rho_1U_1h_{01}=\rho_2U_2h_{02}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h_{01}=h_{02}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h_1+\frac{1}{2}U_1^2=h_2+\frac{1}{2}U_2^2, (1.68)

where \(h_0\) is the energy per unit mass of the fluid, referred to as the specific stagnation enthalpy. The equation of state is the ideal gas law, rearranged from its more familiar \(p=\rho RT\) into:

p=\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}\rho h. (1.69)

These equations constitute four equations in four unknowns (\(\rho\), \(U\), \(p\), and \(h\)) and, although the algebra is tedious, these can be solved. The most convenient form involves solving for \(\rho_2/\rho_1\), \(p_2/p_1\), \(U_2/U_1\) and \(h_2/h_1=T_2/T_1\) as a function of the Mach number \(M_1\), where the Mach number is defined as the velocity nondimensionalized by the speed of sound:

M_1=\frac{U_1}{a_1}. (1.70)

1.9. Shock Waves

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 1.3

Following an internet search at [illegible] Professor Kirby purchases a t-shirt Gatling gun (Figure 1.16, p. 35). He uses this to shoot a plush Kirby doll (Figure 1.16, p. 35) at a Mach number of 1.2 through the air. What is the pressure downstream of the normal shock directly in front of the plush Kirby?

Figure 1.16: Left: a t-shirt Gatling gun (only $4000!). Right: a plush Kirby doll.

Photographs omitted.

Solution: The pressure after the normal shock wave is

p_2=p_1\frac{p_2}{p_1}=(1\ \text{atm})\frac{7M_1^2-1}{6}=(1\ \text{atm})\frac{7(1.2)^2-1}{6}=1.5(1\ \text{atm})=1.5\ \text{atm}. (1.78)

and

\frac{a_2}{a_1}=\sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}}=\sqrt{\left[1+\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma+1}(M_1^2-1)\right]\frac{2+(\gamma-1)M_1^2}{(\gamma+1)M_1^2}},\qquad \frac{a_2}{a_1}=\sqrt{\frac{7M_1^4+34M_1^2-5}{36M_1^2}}. (1.77)

Sound-speed jump across a normal shock wave.

These equations do not make any intuitive sense to most students upon an initial read. They did not make sense to me when I took Aerospace Engineering 320 at the University of Michigan in 1992 (I got a C+). They come from algebraic manipulation of the three conservation equations combined with the equation of state—a normal shock must conserve mass, momentum, and energy and if the gas is ideal it must obey the ideal-gas law. Conceptually, these equations are simple, but the algebraic form of the equations provides no insight or clarity into the underpinning concepts. At least not to me. But, again, I got a C+ when I took compressible flow in undergrad. Rocked a 17/100 on the final. BOOM.

To understand these expressions, we benefit most from calculating typical values and/or plotting their functional dependence (Figure 1.17, p. 36). They show that, as the upstream Mach number gets bigger, the downstream Mach number gets smaller, asymptoting to \(\sqrt{1/7}\) for air. When the fluid goes through the shock wave, (at least for modest upstream Mach numbers), the pressure goes up the most, then density, and temperature goes up the least. As a specific example, for an upstream Mach number \(M_1=2\), the temperature goes up by a factor of 1.7, the density by 2.7, and the pressure by 4.5. So \(M_1=2\) air at STP would, after a normal shock wave, be 500 K and 4.5 atm with a density of about \(3.2\ \text{kg/m}^3\). Example Problem 1.3 (p. 35) shows another normal shock calculation.

We implemented many models to obtain the results in this chapter

It isn’t any fun to dwell on the minutia of every single approximation before we get to how a rocket nozzle works. However, after we have some results for how a rocket nozzle works, we should take a moment to reflect on the models that were required to make the analysis in this chapter tractable, and what errors are introduced. These modeling approaches are central to how engineers study all subjects—we develop models that are as simple as possible and that explain as much of engineering analysis and design as possible.

model: a (preferably simple) mathematical construct that explains observed phenomena well enough that it is useful for analysis or design.

The easier the analysis, the more we must have used models to get rid of all the hard parts. This chapter generates algebraic (!!!) solutions that are remarkably good at describing how a rocket nozzle works and how we should design it (or at least how we should pick its throat area and exit area). But to get there, we had to use a large number of engineering models, described below and in a number of sidebars. An enormous amount of physics in this chapter is buried in the prepositional phrases “for quasi-1D flow” “for isentropic flow” “for an ideal gas” “for a calorically perfect gas” and the like.

throat: the narrowest section of a tube or nozzle.

We considered flow through a nozzle. This nozzle can be studied while motionless in a laboratory, but in practice we put nozzles on the end of rockets, and rockets are shooting around doing stuff e.g., sending satellites into orbit. Throughout the analysis, we used the object frame of reference, i.e., the frame of reference aligned with the nozzle itself (see Sidebar 1.7,

frame of reference: WHEN IN DOUBT, ASK DMITRY SAVRANSKY.
