1.10. Models

(p. 42). In this frame of reference, the analysis of the nozzle does not depend on how fast the rocket is moving, which is an important simplification, and this choice builds on tools used in MAE2030 for selection of frame of reference.

In ENGRD2210, we treat the fluid as a continuum material with thermodynamic properties e.g., pressure, temperature, density, entropy. For a rocket nozzle, we use the continuum model as well, but the fluid is moving and has a velocity, and the system strictly speaking is not in thermodynamic equilibrium. If we are going to add velocity into a rocket nozzle analysis, we need to agree on how fluid velocity and mass and momentum flux fits into a thermodynamic context. The continuum approach for doing this in a rocket nozzle context is to give a continuum description of the pressure of the fluid and understand how pressure relates to the molecular fluctuations of velocity (see Sidebar 1.8, p. 43).

Although nozzles are 3D objects, flow moves through them mostly along their axes, and not too much error is generated by ignoring the fact that flow that is expanding must have a small radial velocity component, so we use the quasi-1D flow model (see Sidebar 1.9, p. 44) to simplify the analysis.

The real flow in a rocket nozzle varies somewhat along its cross-section. However, we ignore this and treat the flow as if it is effectively averaged along the cross section (see Sidebar 1.10, p. 45). Again, we choose this to simplify the analysis.

We need an equation of state to describe flow through a rocket nozzle, and we’d like to use the simplest one possible if we can get away with it. Fortunately, a rocket nozzle that launches something into orbit only works when the flow through it is supersonic, and that in practice is not achieved in any situation other than with a gas that is well approximated by the ideal-gas law. So, we use the ideal gas model in doing this analysis (see Sidebar 1.11, p. 46).

From the standpoint of thermodynamic losses, there are two types of flow that are relatively easy to analyze in a rocket nozzle: (1) isentropic flow and (2) normal shocks. Fortunately, for a well designed nozzle, the only analyses we need are (1) isentropic flow, which describes how rocket nozzles work when operating at their design condition and (2) normal shock waves, which describe how rocket nozzles work when they are being used at a condition way off design. Because of this, the isentropic flow model is central to nozzle analysis (see Sidebar 1.12, p. 46).

If we assume that the fluid in a rocket nozzle isn’t very far from thermodynamic equilibrium, then flow through a rocket nozzle can be thought of as a thermodynamic process in \(p\)-\(T\) space. In ENGRD2210 we learn many polytropic processes e.g., isothermal isobaric isentropic processes. We typically treat flow through rocket nozzles as isentropic other than normal shocks, and to mathematically treat that thermodynamic process we need to know what the specific-heat ratio \(\gamma\) is. The calorically perfect model treats this specific-heat ratio as a mathematical constant that is a property of the gas. This is a good approximation for unreacting gases below 1000 K and not really a very good approximation for hot reacting gases that are produced in the combustor of a real rocket. But for MAE3230 we need to make the equations manageable so we can develop an intuition for how these flows work, and we can fix the modest errors later with a computer if we really need to make a rocket nozzle, so our starting point is to use the calorically perfect model (see Sidebar 1.13, p. 47).

pressure: usually used to mean static pressure but can be used metaphorically to describe any force per unit area or energy per unit volume.

continuum: a physical domain whose properties are differentiable. Contrast with atomistic.

radial: related to the radius \(r\) i.e., the distance from the origin of the coordinate system.

supersonic: having a speed higher than the speed of sound i.e., a Mach number greater than one.

ideal-gas law: \(p=\rho RT\). An equation of state for ideal gases i.e., perfect gases i.e., dilute gases that have little intermolecular interaction. \(T\) and \(p\) are absolute temperature and pressure.

isentropic: without increase in entropy. In a fluid system, this means no conduction of heat, no viscous transfer of momentum, and no shock waves.

normal shock: short for normal shock wave. A shock wave that is aligned normal to the flow.

polytropic: obeying a power-law relation of the form \(p=C\rho^n\). Examples include isothermal, isobaric, isentropic, incompressible.

specific-heat ratio: denoted \(\gamma\) and defined as \(\gamma\equiv c_p/c_v\). A measure of how energy in the fluid links back to the equation of state.

calorically perfect: having specific heats that are not a function of temperature, i.e., \(e=c_vT\) and \(h=c_pT\).

Problems with Answers

1. (OBJECTIVE: use isentropic flow relations to predict how properties change with Mach number) If air (\(\gamma=1.4\)) at \(p=1\) atm and \(M=5\) is isentropically slowed to \(M=4\), what will its pressure be?

Solution: We can determine the stagnation pressure as follows. Write the isentropic relation for pressure, assuming γ = 7/5:

\frac{p}{p_0}=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}M^2\right)^{-\frac{7}{2}}, (1.89)

rearrange to write p in terms of p0 and vice versa:

p=p_0\left(1+\frac{1}{5}M^2\right)^{-\frac{7}{2}},\qquad p_0=p\left(1+\frac{1}{5}M^2\right)^{\frac{7}{2}}. (1.90)

So the pressure at point 2 — given the pressure at point 1 and the Mach numbers at points 1 and 2 — is

p_2=p_1\left(\frac{1+\frac{1}{5}M_1^2}{1+\frac{1}{5}M_2^2}\right)^{\frac{7}{2}}=(1\ \text{atm})\left(\frac{6}{21/5}\right)^{\frac{7}{2}}=3.48\ \text{atm}. (1.91)

2. (OBJECTIVE: Determine isentropic channel flow changes) Evaluate the following for calorically perfect air, \(\gamma=1.4\). Consider a quasi-1D flow in a channel with inlet \(M=0.2\), \(T=300\) K, and \(p=1\) atm. Assume that the channel geometry is designed such that the fluid is isentropically accelerated to \(M=0.8\) at the exit. (a) What is the sign of \(dA/dx\) for this channel geometry? (b) What are the temperature and speed of the flow at the exit?

Solution: (a) the sign is negative, because M is increasing and the flow is subsonic. (b) for isentropic flow:

\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{2+(\gamma-1)M_1^2}{2+(\gamma-1)M_2^2}=0.894, (1.92)

thus T2 = 268 K. For the speed:

u_2=M_2a_2=0.8\sqrt{1.4\times287\times268}=263\ \text{m/s}. (1.93)

3. (OBJECTIVE: calculate quasi-1D compressible flow and normal shocks) Evaluate the following for calorically perfect air, \(\gamma=1.4\).

(a) Given \(M=2\), evaluate \(p_0/p\).

(b) Consider a normal shock. Given \(M_1^*=1.5\), evaluate \(M_2^*\) and \(M_2\).

(c) Consider isentropic flow through a nozzle with a stagnant reservoir at left and supersonic flow exiting at right. \(p_0\) in the reservoir is 1 atm and \(T_0\) in the reservoir is 300 K. Given that the areas of the entrance, throat, and exit are 1.0, 0.3, and 3 m², respectively, calculate the pressure at the throat.

(d) Consider isentropic flow through a nozzle with a stagnant reservoir at left and \(M=7\) supersonic flow exiting at right. Assume the area of the throat is 1 m². What are the cross-sectional areas of the points where (a) \(M=0.2\) and (b) \(M=5\)?

Solution:

(a)

\frac{p_0}{p}=\left(1+\frac{M^2}{5}\right)^{7/2}=7.82. (1.94)

(b)

M_2^*=.667,\qquad M_2^2=\frac{2}{\frac{\gamma+1}{(M_2^*)^2}-(\gamma-1)}=0.4,\qquad M_2=0.63. (1.95)

(c)

\frac{p_0}{p}=\left(1+\frac{M^2}{5}\right)^{7/2};\quad M=1,\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=(5/6)^{7/2}p_0=.528\ \text{atm}. (1.96)

(d)

\frac{A}{A^*}=\frac{1}{M}\left[\frac{5}{6}\left(1+\frac{M^2}{5}\right)\right]^3. (1.97)

For \(M=0.2\), \(A/A^*=2.96\). For \(M=5\), \(A/A^*=25\).

4. (OBJECTIVE: Evaluating stagnation properties) What is the stagnation pressure for air at \(T=300\) K, \(p=5\) bar and \(M=4.2\)?

Solution:

The temperature is not needed other than that at this temperature, the flow can be assumed calorically perfect.

p_0=p\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}=(5\ \text{bar})\left(1+\frac{1.4-1}{2}(4.2)^2\right)^{\frac{1.4}{1.4-1}}=987.7\ \text{bar}. (1.98)

Editorial note: Table 1.3 is reproduced as printed. For the calorically perfect gas in Problem 5, \(\gamma\) is constant, so its blank answers should be S/S. The printed S/S answers for \(\rho U\) and \(p+\rho u^2\) are incorrect: each should be D/I for deceleration to \(M=0\) and acceleration to \(M=1\), respectively. With fixed stagnation properties, \(\rho U\propto M(1+0.2M^2)^{-3}\) and \(p+\rho U^2=p_0(1+1.4M^2)(1+0.2M^2)^{-7/2}\); both increase with \(M\) on \(0<M<1\). Continuity keeps \(\rho U A\) constant, not \(\rho U\) when area varies.

(b) What is the ratio of the nozzle exit area to the throat area?

Solution:

We know that \(p/p_0\) is 0.1. From

\frac{p}{p_0}=\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{-\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}, (1.99)

we can determine that \(M=2.16\). The area-Mach-number relation gives a relation between area ratio and Mach number:

\frac{A}{A^*}=\frac{1}{M}\left[\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)\right]^{\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}},\qquad \frac{A}{A^*}=\frac{1}{M}\left(\frac{M^2+5}{6}\right)^3, (1.100)

Which gives

\frac{A}{A^*}=1.94. (1.101)

SIDEBAR 1.7: ENGINEERING MODELS

Object frame of reference

Premise: an object is used as the frame of reference when it is moving relative to the lab frame.

When an object is moving and we want to analyze the fluid mechanics associated with it, we find it much easier to choose a reference frame associated with the object.

Mathematical form: the object frame of reference defines the coordinate system relative to the object.

The mathematical form of the definition of an object frame of reference is to align the coordinate frame with the object:

\vec{u}_{\mathrm{object}}=0. (1.79)

Utility: the object frame is what we use for vehicles and projectiles.

When objects are moving in the lab reference frame (a car, a plane, a boat), using that object reference frame for the coordinate system makes things easy — the velocity at wall is homogeneous (i.e., \(\vec{u}=0\)), the boundary condition is steady, the flow can be steady, etc.

Limitations: using a moving object as a frame of reference means the frame of reference might be accelerating, and it makes the velocity boundary condition at infinity nonhomogeneous.

When a vehicle or projectile moves, the object frame of reference is easy to use, because the boundary conditions at the object are steady. But this makes the velocity at infinity nonzero, i.e., nonhomogeneous. Further, when the object accelerates, that means that the frame of reference is accelerating, and an accounting must be made for that. The simplest example of this is an object moving in a circle, which by definition must be experiencing a centripetal force.


PDF page 54 — source_issue

SIDEBAR 1.8: ENGINEERING MODELS

Temporal and Spatial Averaging in the Continuum Model of Fluid Mechanics

Premise: The Continuum Model Replaces The Motion of Individual Molecules with Velocity, Pressure, and Viscosity, and replaces the mass of individual molecules with Density

An atomistic description of a fluid would include a description of the motion of every atom or molecule in the system. The atoms or molecules of a real fluid are changing constantly, and are quite numerous, so an atomistic description of a fluid is, for most mechanical engineering applications, somewhere between \(1\times10^{12}\) and \(1\times10^{30}\) times more complicated than it needs to be.

The continuum model replaces the motion of individual molecules with their spatially averaged quantities; instead of considering an atom, we say instead that we will average over some spatial dimension, say a nanometer or micron, enough so that we can approximate the fluid velocity and mass as continuous field properties. If all the relevant physical phenomena were linear functions of velocity, there would be nothing else to say. But, the energy of a molecule (or the momentum it carries) are quadratic functions of velocity, and the average energy of the molecules is not equal to the energy associated with molecules moving at the average velocity. So if we time-average the behavior of molecules and replace it with \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\), we get extra terms left over. We made things \(1\times10^{12}\) to \(1\times10^{30}\) times simpler by replacing individual molecular motion with \(\vec{u}\), but we need some extra bookkeeping to keep track of the information we lost when we averaged.

The extra bookkeeping takes two forms. Both account for the fact that, even though a fluid might on average be motionless, that motionlessness only describes the average motion, and in fact the individual molecules are bouncing all over the place and clunking into each other. First, independent of any macroscopic fluid motion, there is an isotropic effect of this which leads to a force per unit area applied to any real or imagined surface anywhere in the fluid—this is called pressure. The microscopic fluctuations, which we ignored when defining velocity, have to be accounted for in an averaged sense. By averaging over space and time, we replace the fluctuations of all of the molecules with one field variable \(p(x,y,z,t)\), which describes the net effect—the molecules bouncing around push on any surface with a force per unit area normal to that surface.

Second, if the velocity is nonuniform, we find that molecules bouncing around leads to both an anisotropic transfer of momentum (i.e., force) as well as a conversion of energy in the form of continuum velocity into energy in the form of increased fluctuations (i.e., increased temperature). This is called viscosity. These are summarized in Figure F.1, p. 529.



Figure 1.18: Momentum flux averaging in fluid mechanics. Averaging over the time and distances associated with molecular collisions (i.e., the continuum approximation) transfers from an atomistic description of fluids to a continuum description (which is what most mechanical engineers use), and introduces pressure and viscosity to account for the effects of the fluctuations that are lost in the process.

Mathematical form: The continuum approximation replaces the velocity vectors of all of the individual molecules with \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\), \(p(x,y,z,t)\), and \(\mu(x,y,z,t)\), and the masses of the molecules with \(\rho(x,y,z,t)\)

Our continuum description of the state of a fluid comprises \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\), \(p(x,y,z,t)\), \(\rho(x,y,z,t)\), and \(\mu(x,y,z,t)\). Here, the spatial coordinates \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) as well as the temporal coordinate \(t\) are both meant to be averaged over the spatial dimension and temporal dimension of molecular collisions (roughly 100 nm and 1 ns in air at STP; about 100–1000 times smaller and shorter in water).

Utility: The continuum approximation simplifies our calculations by many orders of magnitude

To describe the atomistic motion of a few nanometers cubed of water for 100 ps of a simple system might cost about $10,000. That isn’t worth the money for most mechanical engineering applications. The continuum approximation makes description of fluid mechanics possible; simplifying things by as much as \(1\times10^{30}\).

Limitations: The continuum approximation requires that we use constitutive relations to describe fluids

The continuum approximation is useful and simple, and it is tough to get it to break down in any system of routine relevance to a mechanical engineer. Because it corrects for a subset of atomistic motion with a thing called pressure, it often requires thermodynamics and an equation of state—this is central for compressible flow. It corrects for a different subset of atomistic motion with a thing called viscosity, and it requires that we define what that viscosity is. The viscosity is a constitutive relation.

In using the continuum model, we have overlapped the language of thermodynamic equilibrium with the language of continuum flow. A moving fluid is not, strictly speaking, in thermodynamic equilibrium. But it is close enough to thermodynamic equilibrium that the result the continuum approximation gives for “pressure” is, for MAE3230 purposes, equivalent with the one that thermodynamics gives for “pressure”.

Editorial redraw note: This shared drawing was cross-checked against all four source copies (PDF pages 54, 80, 91 and 448). Page 91 recovers the velocity overbar, collision scales and turbulent-viscosity closure that are erased in some copies. Tensor arrows are represented by the tensor key below the drawing.

Editorial note: Molecular momentum is linear in velocity; kinetic energy and momentum flux involve quadratic velocity terms. The source prose confuses momentum with momentum flux.

SIDEBAR 1.9: ENGINEERING MODELS

Quasi-1D Compressible Flow

Premise: Quasi-1D compressible flow approximately describes nozzles

The geometry of a nozzle greatly affects its performance; in fact it is quite easy to show that an improperly designed nozzle will have tons of oblique shocks and will generate much less thrust than a properly designed nozzle. However, if a nozzle is designed correctly, its behavior is captured well by assuming that the fluid motion is largely all in one direction, along the nozzle axis. Although we know that there must be a radial component of the flow for any nozzle whose cross-sectional area varies, this effect can be largely ignored when analyzing nozzles.

Mathematical form: Quasi-1D flow pays attention only to x-momentum and treats fluid properties as if they were only a function of x

Using x as the axial direction, quasi-1D flow assumes

\vec{u}=U(x)\hat{x}\qquad p=p(x)\qquad T=T(x)\qquad \rho=\rho(x)\qquad A=A(x) (1.80)

Utility: Quasi-1D is described by algebraic equations and ODEs and does a good job predicting the overall performance of a well-designed nozzle

In a well-designed nozzle the flow is primarily all in one direction, along the axis of symmetry of the nozzle. Nozzles are typically axially symmetric, and although there is a component of flow in the radial direction, this is both small and axially symmetric, so its net momentum is zero. Thus quasi-1D flow analysis does a good job of predicting the performance of well-designed nozzles.

Limitations: Quasi-1D flow fails everywhere if the nozzle is designed poorly and it fails near the nozzle exit no matter what

Nozzle design is an interesting confluence between performance and analytical simplicity. The number one thing that makes a nozzle perform poorly is oblique shocks located inside the nozzle. The number one thing that makes a nozzle hard to analyze is oblique shocks located inside the nozzle. So... if your nozzle is designed well, a simple analysis is a pretty good predictor of performance. If your nozzle is designed poorly or if the upstream stagnation pressure is off design, a simple analysis will not predict performance well.


PDF page 56 — source_issue

SIDEBAR 1.10: ENGINEERING MODELS

Mean Flow

Premise: often, we don’t need details of spatial variation of a flow and instead we only need the spatial average

Mean flow approximations basically just ignore spatial variation of a fluid flow and instead focus on some sort of a spatial average. Two examples are flow in pipes and flow in porous media. When we pump flow through a pipe, we care primarily about the total flowrate and not so much about the details of the velocity distribution. A fluid-mechanics researcher might look in great detail, but for engineering analysis of flow through pipes, we typically just measure the flow rate and how it relates to the pressure drop, because that tells you what you need to know to design a piping system. And when fluid moves through porous media, for example water being wicked into a paper towel, we care more about the motion of the fluid front than we do about the details of how the water moves around and through individual paper fibers.

Mathematical form: mean flow approximations simply use an area-averaged speed \(\bar U\) instead of \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\)

In pipes, we replace the velocity distribution with the cross-sectional-area-averaged value of the downstream component:

\bar{U}=\frac{Q}{A}=\int_A \vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA. (1.81)

although I will always try to write this as \(\bar{U}\), most fluids texts simply write this as \(U\) with the understanding that everyone knows that the value is an area-averaged one.

In porous media, we replace the velocity field \(\vec{u}\) with an area-averaged velocity field \(\bar{\vec{u}}\), which is understood to give a value that is averaged over a volume \(V\) large relative to the pore structure of the material:

\bar{\vec{u}}(x,y,z,t)=\frac{1}{V}\int_V\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\,dV. (1.82)

Utility: mean flows

The mean-flow approximation lets us write relations for pipe flow in a form

\frac{\partial B}{\partial s}=-f_D\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^2, (1.83)

which helps us understand how much pumping power is required to move flow through a piping system. \(\bar{U}\) is easy to measure because it is directly calculable from the flowrate \(Q\) and the pipe dimensions.

The mean-flow approximations let us write relations for porous-media flow in a form

\bar{\vec{u}}=-\frac{k}{\mu}\vec{\nabla}p, (1.84)

which describes porous media flow using only the material permeability k, and which does not require microscopic measurement of fluid flow.

Limitations: Mean flow analysis usually hides its errors into the definition of a material or flow property like \(f_D\) or \(k\)

Although averaging velocities correctly captures values proportional to velocity, such as the total flowrate, averaging velocities cannot correctly capture values proportional to velocity squared, for example the dynamic pressure \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^2\). \(\overline{U^2}\) is not equal to \(\bar{U}^2\). In pipe flow, there is an inherent limitation: \(\bar{U}\) correctly describes the average velocity and (when multiplied by the cross-sectional area) the total flow rate, but \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^2\) isn’t the cross-section-averaged dynamic pressure exactly. This approach works for calculation of the viscous dissipation factor, but it is not because \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^2\) is equal to the mean dynamic pressure, it is because for any specific flow \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^2\) is always proportional to the mean dynamic pressure. So this error gets folded into the viscous dissipation factor \(f_D\).

Similarly, averaging flow through porous media leads to errors that typically get lumped into some material property. The permeability \(k\) of a porous material can be related back to the pore size and structure but only if those details are known exactly. More often, the permeability of a porous material lets us estimate (but not exactly measure) properties like the pore size.

Editorial source note: Eq. (1.81) omits \(1/A\) before the integral: \(\int_A\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA=Q\), so the mean speed is \(\bar U=(1/A)\int_A\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA\). Eq. (1.83) omits the inverse pipe diameter: with dimensionless Darcy friction factor, \(\partial B/\partial s=-(f_D/D)(\rho\bar U^2/2)\). The printed equations are retained; these same omissions are noted for Eqs. (2.14) and (2.16).


PDF page 57 — verified

SIDEBAR 1.11: ENGINEERING MODELS

Ideal gas

Premise: an ideal gas is a gas whose molecules have no attraction for each other

If the molecules of a gas spend most of their time far apart from each other because the gas is at low density, the molecular attractions or repulsions the molecules feel for each other have no effect on the thermodynamic properties of the system, and the equation of state is simple and algebraic.

Mathematical form: an ideal gas obeys the ideal gas law \(p=\rho RT\)

An ideal gas obeys the ideal-gas law:

\frac{p}{\rho}=RT. (1.85)

where \(R\) is specific to a gas \((R=\bar{R}/MW)\).

Utility: the ideal gas law makes compressible flow relations tractable

In fluid mechanics, if we have to keep track of the equation of state of the fluid it’s a pain. We would rather that the equation of state be as simple as possible. The ideal-gas law is nice in that it is simple and algebraic, and we can use it to describe the relations between pressure, density, and temperature when all three change, as is the case for compressible flow. Outside of the ideal-gas law, we need a complicated equation of state, which can be implemented computationally (Wolfram Alpha, for example, has this no problem) but difficult to implement for back-of-the-envelope calculations.

Limitations: The ideal gas law breaks down at high pressure and low temperature

The ideal-gas law is most accurate when gas molecules are far from each other and when the kinetic energy of the gas molecules is large relative to the intermolecular interactions, and thus the breakdowns of the ideal gas law occur when the pressure is high and the temperature is low. Air’s behavior between 250–1000 K is within 10% of the ideal-gas law for all pressures below 200 bar, and room-temperature air is consistent with the ideal-gas law to one part in 1,000. 1-bar air is described by the ideal-gas law within a couple of percent error even down to 85–90 K, which is approaching the 77 K liquefaction point of nitrogen.

SIDEBAR 1.12: ENGINEERING MODELS

Isentropic flow

Premise: Isentropic flow has no viscous losses, no heat conduction, and no shock waves

Isentropic flow is adiabatic and reversible: it has no thermal diffusion, no viscous diffusion, and no shock waves. This is the best-case scenario for flow in a rocket nozzle.

Mathematical form: Isentropic flow obeys the polytropic relation \(p=C\rho^\gamma\)

Assuming that flow is isentropic means that it obeys the polytropic relation

p=C\rho^\gamma. (1.86)

Utility: for isentropic flow, the link between \(p\) and \(\rho\) means that fluid properties are a function of stagnation properties and Mach number only

For isentropic flow, stagnation properties (e.g., \(p_0\), \(\rho_0\), \(T_0\)) are mathematical constants, and the fluid properties \(p\), \(\rho\), and \(T\) can be written as a function of the stagnation properties and \(M\) alone. This makes \(M\) an all-important parameter that describes everything about a fluid’s properties. Given the area-Mach-number relation, that means that the cross-sectional area of a nozzle basically controls all of the properties of a fluid flow. This is a stunning simplification.

Limitations: real nozzles have viscous losses in the boundary layer as well as weak oblique shocks

In practice, the deviations from isentropy in a well-designed nozzle operating at the design condition aren’t bad, and a nozzle designed using the isentropic flow model will be quite well designed. In reality, nozzles have boundary layers in which the fluid is slowed by viscosity and heated by viscous dissipation. In reality, nozzles often have weak oblique shocks throughout, which slow down the fluid and heat it up and limit the momentum that can be ejected out the nozzle exit. Because of this, the isentropic flow model overestimates the thrust that a real nozzle will provide.


PDF page 58 — verified

SIDEBAR 1.13: ENGINEERING MODELS

Calorically perfect gas

Premise: a material that doesn’t react, is in equilibrium, and whose specific heat doesn’t change with temperature is calorically perfect

The specific heat of a material is a measure of how much energy it stores as its temperature is increased. The specific heat changes with temperature if the ways that energy can be stored change with temperature. This can be quantified with statistical thermodynamics, but the short story is that molecules have more and more ways to store energy as temperature increases. Most diatomic gases, for example, store energy in their translational motions at all temperatures above 1 K or so, in rotational motion at all temperatures above 3 K, and in vibrational motion above 3000 K. Thus the specific heat of diatomic gases change a lot in the 1–5 K range and in the 1000–5000 K range, but not so much in between. So air, for example, from 100 K to 1000 K has a specific heat that changes only 15% or so.

Everything gets more and more complicated as the molecules get bigger—there are more and more different ways to store energy, and these ways of storing energy are activated at more and more different temperatures, and for large molecules the specific heat goes up continuously over all temperature ranges. Everything also gets complicated if the gas reacts (for example air starts dissociating in a hot combustor) or if the system is out of equilibrium (a rapidly expanded and cooled gas sometimes can’t equilibrate the energy it stored in vibrations fast enough to stay in equilibrium).

Mathematical form: a calorically perfect gas has state-independent \(c_p\), \(c_v\), and \(\gamma=c_p/c_v\)

A calorically perfect gas has \(c_p\), \(c_v\), and \(\gamma=c_p/c_v\) that are independent of \(T\) and \(p\) and thus can be treated as mathematical constants. This leads to a number of simple algebraic relations relating specific internal energy and specific enthalpy to temperature:

e=c_vT;\qquad h=c_pT;\qquad \Delta e=c_v\Delta T;\qquad \Delta h=c_p\Delta T. (1.87)

and also introduces the specific-heat ratio \(\gamma=c_p/c_v\) to describe the \(p\)–\(\rho\) relation for an isentropic process:

p=C\rho^\gamma. (1.88)

Utility: the calorically perfect model, combined with the ideal gas law, makes isentropic compressible flow relations algebraic

Ideal nozzle analysis is all about assuming that (1) compressible flow is really only possible in dilute gases where the ideal-gas law is a good model, and (2) if the person that designed the nozzle did it right, the flow is largely isentropic. When this is true, \(p\), \(\rho\), and \(T\) are related by the ideal-gas law and by the isentropic process relation \(p=C\rho^\gamma\). After that, just a little bit of conservation of mass is enough to generate the necessary (algebraic) relations. This is a stunning simplification and one that means an MAE3230 student can do a serviceable job of predicting the performance of a real nozzle. Which is cool.

The calorically perfect model is only as accurate as the state-independent \(c_p\), \(c_v\), and \(\gamma\) approximations. In the 100–1000 K range, \(c_p\) and \(c_v\) only change by 15% or so, and a calculation with a calorically perfect model is likely to only be off by 5–10%. Given how simple the isentropic relations are, this is pretty good accuracy and very useful.

Limitations: air and combustion products are not well approximated by a calorically perfect gas in the 1500–3000 K range

If you burn fuel and oxidizer, the temperatures unfortunately get high, the gas is reacting, the specific heats are changing with the reaction, and the specific heats are going up as temperature increases. This will make isentropic processes at high \(T\) look like they occur at \(\gamma\to1\) and processes at low \(T\) look like they occur at a larger gamma (e.g., 1.4 for air).


PDF page 59 — verified

Chapter 2

Turbomachines: Machines that Inject Energy Into (And Extract Energy From) Fluids

2.1

Turbomachines are machines that add energy to or remove energy from fluid by use of a rotating element

If we examine our day-to-day terrestrial lives and ask what are the fluid mechanical devices around us, we would conclude that maybe 70% of the fluid-mechanical devices around us are turbomachines. Every engine or computer has a fan and/or pump that cools it; every refrigerator or air conditioner has a compressor, every vacuum cleaner has a fan, every fish tank has a dynamic pump. We extract enormous energy from wind turbine farms and hydroelectric power plants. Airplanes fly by use of turbofan or turboprop engines.

These turbomachines are broadly classified either (a) as pumps, i.e., machines that add energy to fluid, or (b) as turbines, i.e., machines that remove energy from fluids.

We treat turbomachines only at system level in this chapter, but turbomachines also motivate much of the more detailed material later in the text. Dams (Chapter 3) build up pressure for hydroelectric turbines and motive the hydrostatic equation; the kinetic energy imparted by a pump impeller to a fluid is correlated to pressure by a process described by the Bernoulli equation (Chapter 5), the airfoils that make up the impellers and runners of turbomachinery are their own design problem, etc.

In this chapter, we broadly discuss first the energy stored in fluids, then we discuss several types of turbomachines, i.e., fluid machines that add to or extract energy from fluid through a rotating element. We do this by considering the system-scale energy transfer, i.e., what is the form and efficiency of energy transfer to or from the fluid.

turbomachine: a machine that adds energy to or extracts energy from a fluid by use of a rotary element. Typically implies dynamic machines not positive-displacement machines.

wind turbine: a turbine that extracts energy from naturally occurring gas motion. If the turbine were driven by a collocated combustion chamber, it would instead be a gas turbine. If by vapor, it would be a steam turbine. If driven by liquid it would be a hydrodynamic turbine.


PDF page 60 — source_issue

2.2 Fluids store energy in four forms: pressure, kinetic energy, potential energy, and internal energy

Energy is stored in a fluid in four forms: pressure, kinetic energy, potential energy, and internal energy. Written in terms of energy per unit volume, these four forms are:

1. internal energy \(\rho e\): the kinetic energy of the isotropic random molecular-scale motion; what we normally think of as “heat”. The specific heat \(c_v\) describes how this changes with temperature, and for a calorically perfect gas \(e=c_vT\).

2. pressure \(p\): the stored ability to do mechanical work, per unit volume.

3. kinetic energy: the kinetic energy of a mass is \(\frac12mU^2\), and written per unit volume is \(\frac12\rho U^2\).

4. potential energy: volumetric potential energy can take multiple forms, including gravitational or electrostatic etc. (volumetric gravitational potential energy of a material of density \(\rho\) at altitude \(z\) is \(\rho gz\); volumetric electrostatic potential energy of a material with charge density \(\rho_e\) at a voltage \(V\) is \(\rho_e V\)). We consider only gravitational potential energy in this class.

The total energy of a fluid can be written using the specific total enthalpy \(h_0\):

\rho h_0=\rho e+p+\frac12\rho U^2+\rho gz, (2.1)

specific total enthalpy: sum of internal energy, work of compression, gravitational potential energy, and kinetic energy, reported per unit mass and denoted \(h_0=e+p/\rho+\frac12\rho U^2+gz\).

Editorial note: The sidebar has an extra \(\rho\) in its kinetic-energy term. Dividing equation 2.1 by density gives \(h_0=e+p/\rho+U^2/2+gz\), whose terms all have units of energy per mass. The sidebar formula above is reproduced literally.

and all of the energy of a fluid except the internal energy is often called the total pressure \(p_0\):

p_0=p+\frac12\rho U^2+\rho gz. (2.2)

Turbomachines have rotating elements (alternately called impellers, rotors, runners, wheels, or a variety of other names) consisting of airfoils (alternately called blades, vanes, buckets, cups, or a variety of other names). These airfoils are solid surfaces that move through the fluid, locally changing the fluid’s pressure \(p\) and/or kinetic energy \(\frac12\rho U^2\). The net action of the rotating element (and, if present, the turbomachine housing) depends on the machine. If it is a pump, its goal is to increase the fluid’s total pressure by injecting power \(P\) from an external motor. If it is a turbine, its goal is to extract power \(P\) by reducing the fluid’s total pressure. In the process, some power goes into heating the fluid—this energy is wasted and is an inherent inefficiency of the turbomachine.

impeller: a rotating airfoil used to trasfer energy from a driveshaft to fluid, typically to generate a pressure jump in a confined duct or volute casing. Compare with propeller.

airfoil: a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes. Roughly synonymous with blade, hydrofoil, wing, and vane. Often chosen over the word hydrofoil when the fluid is air. Often chosen over the word vane when mounted on an airplane.

2.3 The centrifugal pump is the most ubiquitous tool for adding energy to a fluid


PDF page 61 — source_issue

Centrifugal pumps are efficient, inexpensive, and ubiquitous tools to pump water and similar liquids

A centrifugal pump (Figure 2.1, p. 50) consists of an impeller spun by a motor. The spinning impeller pulls liquid in through its inlet, called its eye, and spins the fluid azimuthally so that it exits the radius of the impeller with an increased kinetic energy. The impeller is housed within a volute casing, which steers this spinning fluid to the pump exit, decelerating it and increasing its pressure.

impeller: a rotating airfoil used to trasfer energy from a driveshaft to fluid, typically to generate a pressure jump in a confined duct or volute casing. Compare with propeller.

eye: the inlet of a centrifugal pump, located along the axis of rotation of the impeller.

volute: a casing i.e., housing of a centrifugal pump which has a spiral shape resembling a mollusc. Synonymous with scroll.



Figure 2.1: A centrifugal pump. Fluid enters through the eye. The fluid is spun by the impeller, increasing its kinetic energy. Fluid exits the impeller and is steered by the volute toward the output, during which much of the kinetic energy is converted to an increase in pressure.

A centrifugal pump is designed to do work on fluid and increase the fluid’s total energy. In the mean flow approximation, the volumetric energy of a liquid (liquids can often be approximated as having a fixed density) can be written as

e_{\mathrm{total}}=\rho h_0=p+\frac12\rho U^2+\rho gz+\rho e, (2.3)

Printed annotations for equation 2.3

Term | Source label
\(p\) | stored compression work per vol
\(\frac12\rho U^2\) | kinetic energy per vol
\(\rho gz\) | potential energy per vol
\(\rho e\) | potential energy per vol
volumetric energy of a fixed-density fluid

Editorial note: The printed annotation on \(\rho e\) incorrectly repeats “potential energy per vol”. Here \(e\) is specific internal energy, so the correct label is “internal energy per vol”; the formula itself agrees with equation 2.1.

mean flow: averaged, both to eliminate fluctuations and to average across a cross-section.

volumetric: related to volume, or per unit volume.

In a centrifugal pump, the impeller increases the fluid’s volumetric kinetic energy \(\frac12\rho U^2\), and the volute trades that kinetic energy for pressure \(p\). A perfectly efficient centrifugal pump would put all of the work from the motor into \(p\).

In practice, there are losses in the impeller, and some of the work heats up the fluid (\(\rho e\)) instead of accelerating it. There are also losses in the volute, and some of the kinetic energy (\(\frac12\rho U^2\)) is traded for more heat (\(\rho e\)) instead

volute: a casing i.e., housing of a centrifugal pump which has a spiral shape resembling a mollusc. Synonymous with scroll.


PDF page 62 — source_issue

of pressure p. So a real centrifugal pump puts most of its work into an increase in pressure, but some of its work also heats up the fluid. Energy conservation still applies—this energy did not disappear—but, because that energy is not of any use to us, we describe it as a loss.

The power that the motor puts into the pump is referred to as the brake horsepower \(P_{\mathrm{brake}}\), given by the product of the torque \(T\) and the angular rotation rate \(\omega\):

P_{\mathrm{brake}}=\omega T. (2.4)

The useful power that the pump puts into the fluid is sometimes called water horsepower, and is given by the product of the volumetric flow rate \(Q\) and the pressure change \(\Delta p=p_{\mathrm{outlet}}-p_{\mathrm{inlet}}\):

P_{\mathrm{water}}=Q\Delta p. (2.5)

The difference between the inputted brake horsepower and the useful power extracted is the total heat added to the fluid; which for a liquid system is not mechanically useful. The thermodynamic efficiency \(\eta\) of a centrifugal pump is

\eta=\frac{Q\Delta p}{\omega T}. (2.6)

When designing or building a centrifugal pump, the goal is to generate \(\Delta p\) and \(Q\) that are useful for an application, with the highest \(\eta\) possible.

When selecting a centrifugal pump, the goal is to match the optimum performance of the pump to the system it is driving. The efficiency of a centrifugal pump is widely variable based on what system it drives. If the pump is overpowered, it spins the fluid around in the volute way too much — like a blender, and that extra energy just heats up the fluid. If the pump is underpowered, the impeller spins along with the fluid but hardly accelerates it at all.

In practice, centrifugal pumps can be selected from hydraulic coverage charts and pump performance charts once the performance of the pumped system is known

We can immediately show how a practicing engineer selects a centrifugal pump for an application, even without knowing too many details about how pumps work (we will, of course, discuss those details later). This involves knowing the response of the system, i.e., the set of pipes or whatever is being pumped, as well as looking up the options for the pumps. An immediate challenge, as is the case any time we combine engineering practice with a fluid mechanics class, is that we will spend some time translating back and forth between the language of physics (SI units, dimensional homogeneity, consistent and precise language) and the language of fluids engineering and the skilled trades (imperial units, often inconsistent units, dimensional inhomogeneity, jargon and metaphorical language). In this text we use both— anyone who wants to really get anything done has to know both languages and has to be able to go back and forth between them.

In practice, almost all mechanical-engineering systems are high-Reynolds number systems, meaning that they are big enough

loss: in fluid mechanics, a measure of deviation from inviscid or isentropic behavior. Often used to adjust an inviscid or isentropic model to describe real engineering systems.

brake horsepower: equivalent to brake power. Measure of power produced at the shaft of a motor. \(1\ \mathrm{hp}=746\ \mathrm{W}\).

water horsepower: Measure of useful power produced by a pump, or the useful power needed by a pump to drive flow through a given system. \(1\ \mathrm{hp}=746\ \mathrm{W}\).

efficiency: when describing a turbomachine, the useful work generated normalized by the work inputted.

Reynolds number: \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\). The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(Re_x\), \(Re_d\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

and fast enough that the fluid mechanics is dominated by the fluid inertia in most parts of the flow. We will discuss the hows and whys of that later in the text. See, for example, Appendix C. But in practice, as long as a fluid flow through a set of pipes is mostly controlled by the fluid inertia, it’s pressure–flow relation will always be approximately parabolic (Figure 2.2a, p. 52). Meanwhile, the pressure–flow relation of a centrifugal pump typically is monotonic negative (Figure 2.2b, p. 52)—the pump generates maximum pressure at zero flow rate and maximum flowrate at zero pressure.

inertia: the resistance to acceleration exhibited by objects with mass. In a fluid mechanical context, fluid inertia is often invoked to explain why fluid moving in one direction will continue moving in that direction. Often used to explain separation at sharp corners.



Figure 2.2: (a) The pressure required to pump fluid through a set of pipes, switches, valves, etc., is approximately parabolic when Re is high. (b) in practice, a centrifugal pump will generate higher pressure when flowrates are low and lower pressures when flowrates are high (c) a pump connected to a system generates flowrate \(Q\) and pressure difference \(\Delta p\) defined by the intersection of these two curves.

Any centrifugal pump connected to a system will generate a flowrate \(Q\) and pressure difference \(\Delta p\) defined by the intersection of these two curves (Figure 2.2c, p. 52). As an engineer, there are two ways for us to evaluate the results:

• was this the \(Q\) and \(\Delta p_0\) we wanted? Usually, we want and need a specific flowrate \(Q\) through the system. For example, a cooling system might need a specific flowrate so that there is enough cooling to prevent damage. Or, in other cases, we want a specific pressure at some point. For example, municipal water systems are often designed to be at 45 psig or so; this is a pressure people are used to, which makes for a nice shower, a well-behaved faucet, and pipes that don’t burst.

• is the pump operating at a high efficiency? If not, we are wasting power.

So, we can connect any pump we want and some fluid will flow, but if we want the desired flowrate \(Q\) and we want the pump to operate efficiently, we want to pick the correct pump. An underpowered pump will generate too little flow. An overpowered pump will generate too much, and if we close a valve to reduce the flow, we are just wasting energy. We identify the correct pump by reading the pump performance curve for an individual pump, or the hydraulic coverage chart for a family of pumps.

Reading a very complete dynamic pump performance curve (Figure 2.3, p. 54) tells you many things:

• model and rotation rate. Centrifugal pump performance is a function of too many parameters to graph. It is customary to make a performance curve for a specific model and rotation rate (typically listed as rpm i.e., revolutions per minute). The rotation rate corresponds to the

hydraulic coverage chart: a \(\Delta p_0\)–\(Q\) chart showing the high-efficiency regions of a family of dynamic pumps.


PDF page 64 — source_issue

line voltage (3600 RPM for 60 Hz line voltage and 3000 RPM for 50 Hz line voltage), which can also be divided by 2 or 3 if the AC motor is a four- or six-pole motor (in which case you get 1800/1200 Hz or 1500/1000 Hz). Also, the RPM of the shaft of an induction motor is actually slower than the electric field that drives it, so instead of 3600 RPM you might see 3550 RPM or the like. This information usually is in the header of the performance curve.

• flowrate. The x axis lists flowrate. This is often just called flow or capacity or discharge. This is usually gallons per minute. Sometimes a metric scale (L/min) is also provided.

• pressure. What the pump really does is increase the fluid’s energy, which can take the form of increased elevation, increased temperature, increased fluid speed, or increased fluid pressure. The form most engineers find most convenient is to talk about sum of all the useful forms of energy added to the fluid, in units of how high one could pump the fluid with that energy. This quantity is the total head \(H=\frac{p}{\rho g}+\frac{U^2}{2g}+z\), although most pump performance charts plot this on the y axis and just call it “head”. In practice, pumps rarely change the fluid elevation and rarely change the fluid speed much. So in practice the “head” that is plotted on a pump performance chart is really just the pressure jump the pump creates, described using the language of hydraulic engineers, rather than the language of fluid mechanics students.

• impeller diameter. This is often listed as impeller trim. The same pump often can take impellers of several sizes, and each impeller size will correspond to a single curve on the head–flow (i.e., \(H\)–\(Q\)) axes.

• power required. This is typically listed as brake horsepower.

• net positive suction head. This the minimum total head \(H=\frac{p}{\rho g}+\frac{U^2}{2g}\) required at the inlet of the pump to ensure that it does not cavitate. This is shown either as an inset graph or with isocontours.

• efficiency. This is the ratio of the water power (\(P_{\mathrm{water}}=\Delta p\,Q\)) done divided by the brake power \(P_{\mathrm{brake}}=\omega T\) input into the pump. This is typically shown by use of efficiency isocontours on the performance curve.

• minimum flowrate. Often a mark or line is used to show the minimum recommended flowrate. Below this flowrate, there is not enough flowrate to cool the pump and it can overheat.

To select a pump, we identify the system characteristic of the hydraulic network we are pumping, i.e., the \(\Delta p_0\) vs. \(Q\) graph for the network. For fully turbulent flow, this curve will have a parabolic shape. We identify where on that curve we want to operate, which specifies the \(\Delta p_0\) and the \(Q\) at operating conditions. Then we find that point first on a hydraulic coverage chart (e.g., Figure 2.5, p. 55), which specifies the pump, then on the detailed pump performance chart (e.g., Figure 2.7, p. 57), which specifies the impeller trim.

For example, let’s suppose we have a 500′-long, 3″ diameter, smooth pipe and we want to buy a pump to drive 400 gpm through that pipe. We will show later in the text (Chapter 6) how to predict the pressure drop when fluid moves through a pipe. But for the moment let’s take as given the system performance curve shown in Figure 2.4a, p. 54.

From this curve, we can see that this system will have a flowrate of 400 gpm (\(2.5\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}\)) when a pressure head of 48 ft of water

capacity: term used in the fluids engineering and turbomachine literature, synonymous with volumetric flowrate \(Q\).

total head: a property \(H_{\mathrm{total}}=p_{\mathrm{total}}/\rho g\) which describes the equivalent height whose gravitational potential energy per unit volume is equal to the fluid’s total pressure.

brake horsepower: equivalent to brake power. Measure of power produced at the shaft of a motor. \(1\ \mathrm{hp}=746\ \mathrm{W}\).

net positive suction head: the minimum total head required at the inlet of a pump to ensure that it does not cavitate. Important because it tells you where in a hydraulic circuit the pump needs to be—can it pull from above or does it need to push from below.

2.4 Many classes of dynamic turbopumps exist; the proper class can be selected given the pumped fluid, whether an enclosure is possible, and the specific speed needed

The above example described how we would pick a centrifugal pump if we already knew that we wanted a centrifugal pump, specifically if we knew that we wanted a centrifugal pump from the Kirby family of centrifugal pumps. But in general we have many applications in which we need to identify a turbomachine that adds energy to fluid to achieve a task. We may need to push fluid for the purposes of thrust for an airplane—in which case we need a propeller. Or we may need to push fluid to move it around, for ventilation or cooling—in which case we need a fan or blower. Or we may need to push fluid so as to compress it and change its density, for example to power pneumatic tools—in which case we need a compressor. Or maybe we need to move liquid, but we don’t need the large pressure change that a centrifugal pump would generate, maybe we need high flowrates, as we would need for the pump that drives a jetski. In this case we would want an axial-flow pump.

Analytical tools can help us decide what sort of pump will best complete our task. To do this, we find it convenient to rearrange many of the parameters into nondimensional forms.

propeller: a rotating airfoil that transfers energy from a driveshaft to fluid to generate thrust. Compare to impeller.

fan: an enclosed turbomachine that adds energy to a gas, usually air, primarily for the purpose of fluid motion. The term fan is typically used for open systems, whereas the term blower is typically used for enclosed systems. Fans have a high pump specific speed whereas gas compressors have a lower pump specific speed. The equivalent turbomachine driving a liquid would be called a pump.

pneumatic: related to flow of gases through pipes, especially when the gas is used as an actuator. Cf. hydraulic, which has a similar meaning but implies liquids.

axial-flow pump: a dynamic pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it axially with an impeller. These pumps look approximately like fans or propellers located inside a tube. Typically has high specific speed.


PDF page 68 — verified

INTERSECTION OF PUMP PERFORMANCE CURVE WITH SYSTEM RESPONSE CURVE GIVES THE \(\Delta B\) AND \(Q\) FOR THE PUMP DRIVING THAT SYSTEM.



Figure 2.7: The system characteristic or system response curve is the \(\Delta B\) vs. \(Q\) relation for the driven hydraulic system, in this case different lengths of 3" diameter smooth pipe. The pump performance curves for different impellers show, via the intersections of the pump performance curves and the system characteristics, how the pump will drive the system. For example, with an 8" impeller above, about 50’ of head will drive about 400 gpm through a 500’ pipe at about 78% efficiency. For 2000’ of pipe, this pump is undersized—regardless of the impeller, its flow will be low and its thermodynamic efficiency only 60%. For 100’ of pipe, this pump is a bit oversized—one can dial in the flowrate and head with different impeller sizes, but the efficiency only ranges from about 65-72%.


PDF page 69 — source_issue

The nine parameters of a pump and its performance include inputs, outputs, fluid properties, and design specs; we like to rearrange these parameters into a number of nondimensional parameters that give general insight into how pumps work

A pump has two outputs and one input: we input the power \(P\) to run it, and the pump generates a volumetric flowrate \(Q\) and the total pressure difference created by the pump \(\Delta p_0\).

There are two fluid properties involved, the fluid density \(\rho\) and the fluid viscosity \(\mu\).

There are four design parameters: the pump’s size \(D\), the angular frequency \(\omega\) with which it spins, the surface roughness \(\epsilon\) of the surfaces in the pump, and then the design’s geometry—all of the shapes, angles, and length ratios that define the difference between a centrifugal pump and an axial-flow pump.

Nondimensionalizing the fluid properties and surface roughness tells us alot about the nature of the fluid flow, but we don’t really know the fluid physics yet, and it turns out it doesn’t make a ton of difference in terms of how pumps work, so we won’t dwell on these

Two parameters come out that tell us something about the nature of the fluid flow inside the pump, these are the Reynolds number \(\mathrm{Re}=\rho\omega D^2/\mu\) and the normalized surface roughness \(\epsilon/D\). It turns out that although these are very interesting from a physical standpoint, and very important for fluid mechanics in general, most pump performance is not a strong function of these factors and so they are not of much engineering importance for us in this chapter.

Reynolds number: \(\mathrm{Re}=\rho U\ell/\mu\). The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(\mathrm{Re}_x,\mathrm{Re}_d\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

Nondimensionalizing the flowrate, total pressure change, and power show us how these pump characteristics depend on pump size and speed

Our inputs and outputs are readily nondimensionalized to make the capacity coefficient, the head coefficient, and the power coefficient:

C_Q=\frac{Q}{\omega D^3}\qquad Q=C_Q\omega D^3, (2.7)

capacity coefficient

C_H=\frac{\Delta p_0}{\rho\omega^2D^2}\qquad \Delta p_0=C_H\rho\omega^2D^2, (2.8)

head coefficient

C_P=\frac{P}{\rho\omega^3D^5}\qquad P=C_Q\rho\omega^3D^5. (2.9)

power coefficient

Editorial note: The right side of printed equation (2.9) uses \(C_Q\). Rearranging the definition on its left instead gives \(P=C_P\rho\omega^3D^5\); the power coefficient must be \(C_P\). The printed formula is retained above.

These coefficients are often reported in the hydraulic engineering literature. More important than the coefficients in the equations on the left side, though, is the scalings that are implied by the equations on the right side. For a given pump geometry operating close to its maximum efficiency, these coefficients do not change much as the pump size or speed is changed. Thus


PDF page 70 — verified

the relations in the equations on the right show (at least approximately) how flowrate, total pressure change, and power are related to pump speed and size. For example, the flowrate of a pump is proportional to the motor speed and its size to the third power. If we double the motor speed, we will get double the flowrate. If we scale a pump up to be twice as big, we will get 8 times the flowrate. Similarly, the total pressure change across the pump is proportional to the speed squared and to the diameter squared. And the power required to run the pump is proportional to the speed cubed and the diameter to the 5th power.

total pressure: a property \(p_0=p+\frac12\rho u^2+\rho gz\), having units of pressure (or equivalently volumetric energy), which indicates storage of multiple forms of energy, including \(p\,dV\) work of compression (\(p\)), kinetic energy (\(\frac12\rho u^2\)), and gravitational potential energy \(\rho gz\).

Nondimensionalizing the speed, size, and water horsepower of a pump tells us what the pump is good for and whether it is performing well at a specific condition

Whereas the capacity coefficient, head coefficient, and power coefficient showed us how flowrate, pressure, and power scale with speed and size of the pump, there are three parameters that come out that show us how the pump really performs—whether it good at generating a lot of total pressure, or a lot of flowrate, and when it does this, at what thermodynamic efficiency it performs. These three parameters are the thermodynamic efficiency, the specific speed, and the specific diameter. The thermodynamic efficiency is the ratio of the water power generated \(\Delta p_0Q\) divided by the driving brake horsepower:

\eta=\frac{\Delta p_0 Q}{P_{\mathrm{brake}}}. (2.10)

thermodynamic efficiency

The pump specific speed \(\omega_p\) and the pump specific diameter \(D_p\) are normalized versions of the speed and diameter:

\omega_p=\frac{\omega Q^{1/2}\rho^{3/4}}{\Delta p_0^{3/4}}, (2.11)

pump specific speed

D_p=\frac{D\Delta p_0^{1/4}}{\rho^{1/4}Q^{1/2}}. (2.12)

pump specific diameter

If we run a pump and measure its performance at max efficiency, we can calculate the specific speed and specific diameter of the pump at that condition, and that will tell us what sort of pump it is an what that pump is good at. The specific speed of a pump tells us, compared to other pumps, whether it has to run fast or slow to achieve a standard task. The specific diameter of a pump tells us, compared to other pumps, whether it has to be big or small to achieve a standard task.

Importantly, if you plot the specific speeds and specific diameters of many many turbomachines at their maximum efficicency point, they fall along a thin band (Figure 2.8, p. 60), showing that high specific speed correlates with low specific diameter and vice versa. Axial-flow pumps have high specific speed and low specific diameter. For a given pressure and flowrate, they will be small but run at high speed. For a given speed and size, they will generate high flowrate but low pressure. Centrifugal pumps have low specific speed and high specific diameter. For a given pressure and flowrate, they will be large but run at low speed. For a given speed and size, they will generate low flowrate but high pressure.

specific diameter: a normalized diameter indicative of what diameter would be required to pump a standardized \(\Delta p_0\) for a specific \(Q\) (pump specific diameter); or that diameter required to generate a standardized power \(P\) using a standardized \(\Delta p_0\) (turbine specific diameter).

turbomachine: a machine that adds energy to or extracts energy from a fluid by use of a rotary element. Typically implies dynamic machines not positive-displacement machines.

In practice, pumps all run at approximately the same speed, so specific speed and specific diameter dictate which pumps generate more flow and less pressure or more pressure and less flow

In practice, the speed of a pump is largely fixed. Unless the motor is very small, AC motors are cheaper and more reliable than DC motors, so most

pumps run on AC motors. AC motors run on line frequency at 3600 rpm, so pumps run on 3600 rpm or an even divisor (1800 rpm; 1200 rpm). In practice, we dial in the design of a pump by use of its geometry (axial-flow pump vs. centrifugal pump) and its size (bigger for high flowrate, smaller for low flowrate), not its speed.

axial-flow pump: a dynamic pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it axially with an impeller. These pumps look approximately like fans or propellers located inside a tube. Typically has high specific speed.

Axial-flow pumps are best suited for high-flowrate, low-pressure applications

A single-stage axial-flow pump is basically an impeller inside a pipe (Figure 2.9, p. 61).

impeller: a rotating airfoil used to trasfer energy from a driveshaft to fluid, typically to generate a pressure jump in a confined duct or volute casing. Compare with propeller.



Figure 2.9: Axial-flow pumps. Left: schematic. Right: interior view.

Axial-flow pumps have high pump specific speed and low pump specific diameter, meaning that to generate the same \(\Delta p_0\) and \(Q\) of a centrifugal pump, they need to run fast and be small. Or, conversely, an axial-flow pump driven by the same motor and of the same size as a centrifugal pump will generate higher \(Q\) and lower \(\Delta p_0\). In practice, this means we use axial-flow pumps when we need higher flowrate and lower pressure. Axial-flow pumps for liquids are used, for example, for irrigation, in powerplants, and in jetskis.

centrifugal pump: a pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it centrifugally with an impeller, then decelerating it through a volute. Typically has low specific speed.

Propellers and fans are best suited when the turbopump cannot be enclosed

Propellers and fans are simply axial-flow pumps that are not enclosed. Removing the enclosure makes propellers and fans less efficient but cheaper and lighter. Propellers are used to generate thrust for boats and airplanes. Helicopters and quadcopters use vertical-axis propellers, which in this context are called rotors. We use the term fan usually to describe a propeller whose purpose is to circulate air rather than to generate thrust.

propeller: a rotating airfoil that transfers energy from a driveshaft to fluid to generate thrust. Compare to impeller.

fan: an enclosed turbomachine that adds energy to a gas, usually air, primarily for the purpose of fluid motion. The term fan is typically used for open systems. whereas the term blower is typically used for enclosed systems. Fans have a high pump specific speed whereas gas compressors have a lower pump specific speed. The equivalent turbomachine driving a liquid would be called a pump.


PDF page 73 — verified

Multistage compressors are best suited for compressing gases over large density changes

When we need to energize gases by increasing their pressure, the task is different from pressurizing liquids, simply because gases compress and their density and specific volume change significantly during the process. In practice, the most successful design for compressing gases is to use an axial-flow configuration, but to compress the gas in many stages. Thus gas compressors typically use multiple stages of rotors and stators Figure 2.10, p. 62). Compressors have rotating rotors that do work on fluid to increase its azimuthal kinetic energy, followed by stators that convert the azimuthal kinetic energy to pressure. Each combination of rotor followed by stator is called a stage, and compressors position these stages inside a housing. These gas compressors are used to compress gases for pneumatic tools and in gas turbine engines to facilitate combustion. Compressors are commonly used to compress gas to power pneumatic tools. A supercharged engine is one that uses a compressor to compress the air so that more oxidizer fits inside the engine cylinders and thus more fuel can be used, generating more power. A turbocharged engine is one that uses the exhaust to drive a turbine to generate torque that is then used to power a compressor that compresses the incoming air.

compressor: an enclosed turbomachine that adds energy to a gas, usually air, primarily for the purpose of increasing its pressure. gas compressors have a low pump specific speed whereas fans and blowers have higher pump specific speeds. The equivalent turbomachine driving a liquid would be called a pump.

rotor: in general for a motor or turbomachine, the rotating part. Specifically for a quadcopter or helicopter, the rotating lifting surface. Cf. stator.

stator: a stationary airfoil component of a motor or pump. Cf. rotor.

rotor: in general for a motor or turbomachine, the rotating part. Specifically for a quadcopter or helicopter, the rotating lifting surface. Cf. stator.

stator: a stationary airfoil component of a motor or pump. Cf. rotor.

stage: a combination of a rotor and a stator used in a turbomachine to increase pressure without building up swirl.

2.5 Many classes of turbines exist; the proper class can be selected given the pumped fluid, whether an enclosure is possible, and the specific speed needed

To a first approximation, a turbine is just a pump run in reverse. Whereas a pump is a tool that uses a motor (or other external power source) to drive an impeller, transferring power from the motor to the fluid, a turbine is a tool that uses fluid to drive a runner, transferring power from the fluid to a generator (or other external power sink). There are a few small practical differences between the two (it’s a bit harder to get high efficiency in a turbine and it usually involves turning vanes at the inlet), but for the most part they are just the same thing run in two different directions. Because of this, there are strong analogies between pumps and turbines.

Most turbines are reaction turbines. Reaction turbines are fully immersed in the working fluid. At very high specific diameter and low specific speed, impulse turbines are important. Impulse turbines are not fully immersed in the working fluid, and operate on localized impact of a fluid stream on the buckets or paddles of the runner.

runner: the rotating blade element of a reaction turbine. Analogous to the impeller of a pump.

Francis turbines are best suited for high-pressure, low-flowrate applications

A Francis turbine (Figure 2.11, p. 64) is the analog of a centrifugal pump—a turbine in which the fluid has significant radial motion, not just axial motion.

Francis turbine: a reaction turbine with radial or mixed flow and low turbine specific speed, suitable for extracting energy over a high pressure drop. The turbine analog of a centrifugal pump.

Propeller turbines are best suited for high-flowrate, low-pressure applications

Propeller turbines, most famously the Kaplan turbine, are analogs of axial-flow pumps—turbines in which the fluid’s motion is primarily axial. Relative to Francis turbines, propeller turbines work better when the pressure available is lower. A tall dam would use a Francis turbine to generate hydroelectric power, whereas a short dam would use a propeller turbine.

Kaplan turbine: a propeller turbine with mostly or all axial flow and a relatively low specific speed, suitable for extracting energy over a low pressure drop. Kaplan turbines are a specific propeller turbine design with adjustable blades for operation over a wide range of operating conditions.

Editorial note: The Kaplan sidebar prints “relatively low specific speed.” Figure 2.8 places Kaplan turbines at the high-specific-speed end, consistent with their high-flow, low-head operating range. “Relatively high specific speed” is the consistent comparison with Francis turbines. The original wording is retained above.

Wind turbines are unshrouded propeller turbines

Unlike hydroelectric applications, in which water moves through a contained system to drive a turbine, wind energy involves unshrouded turbines. Wind turbines are essentially propellers or fans running in reverse—rather than driving a propeller with a motor to create thrust, a wind turbine extracts energy from the wind, slowing down the wind and driving a generator.

Impulse turbines have rotors that are not immersed in the driving fluid

An impulse turbine is a turbine whose rotors are not immersed completely in the driving fluid. They are often less efficient but often cheaper and simpler to construct. For example, Pelton turbines (Figure 2.12, p. 65) use high-pressure water that impacts a set of buckets on a wheel to transfer energy. Water wheels (Figure 2.13, p. 65) are impulse turbines from antiquity. Ossberger turbines (Figure 2.14, p. 65) are in use in Ithaca’s powerplant at the base of Beebe Dam.

2.6 Turbomachine loss of efficiency comes from three sources

Real turbomachines might have efficiencies on the order of 0.9 at their optimum conditions, but over wide ranges of performance their efficiency can be quite low. There are three broad categories of losses in a turbomachine:

1. The idealized model ignores friction in the shaft, and treats the flow as being uniform and lossless, but fluid cannot move along a wall without being retarded by the wall and experiencing viscous conversion of mechanical energy to thermal energy. These factors are independent of any design parameters, and set an upper limit of a centrifugal pump’s efficiency at something like 80-90%. In practice, 10-20% of your energy is always dissipated as heat, no matter how well you design your pump and how carefully the performance condition is chosen to optimize the efficiency.

2. The idealized model assumes that fluid moves smoothly along the vanes without any recirculation, i.e., that energy is efficiently added to the fluid. This, in practice, is not always achieved for flow through an impeller. If the rotation rate or vane angle or flow rates are not within an optimal range, the motion of the impeller asks the fluid to follow a path it can’t quite follow, and instead the fluid follows a recirculatory path, which is inefficient and ends up converting more mechanical energy to heat. So the work from the motor is transferred to the fluid with varying efficiency.

3. Most turbomachines, in the end, lead to changes in the total pressure, but locally they often change the fluid kinetic energy and then convert that kinetic energy into pressure later. This is particularly true for radial-flow turbomachines e.g., Francis turbines and centrifugal pumps. The idealized model assumes that the kinetic energy imparted into the fluid by the rotor is then converted with perfect efficiency to pressure in the volute of a centrifugal pump or the scroll of a Francis turbine, but in practice this process is lossy. Similarly, but less dramatically, axial-flow pumps and propeller turbines are supposed to increase pressure without imparting angular momentum into the flow. But in practice, they always impart swirl into the flow, which is dissipated later as heat.

Two limits are useful to consider how a turbomachine can run without efficiently adding energy to or removing energy from a fluid:

Limit 1: Consider a pump filled with fluid but whose input and output is blocked. One can spin the impeller, adding kinetic energy, but if the output is blocked there is no place for this fast fluid to go, and it spins around in the casing until its mechanical energy is dissipated as heat. In this case the pump generates no flowrate and therefore no work, and its overall efficiency is zero. Even if the power from the motor were converted to fluid kinetic energy with perfect efficiency, the system does no work with that energy—it converts none of the kinetic energy into pressure, it converts it all into useless heat. In fact this is a real system — this is what a hydraulic bike trainer is, or a water brake engine dynamometer. Each of these devices takes external work and dissipates it completely as heat.

efficiency: when describing a turbomachine, the useful work generated normalized by the work inputted.

recirculation: when a region of fluid is made to flow largely upstream. Typically associated with separation.

Francis turbine: a reaction turbine with radial or mixed flow and low turbine specific speed, suitable for extracting energy over a high pressure drop. The turbine analog of a centrifugal pump.

centrifugal pump: a pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it centrifugally with an impeller, then decelerating it through a volute. Typically has low specific speed.

Editorial note: Item 3 groups turbines with pumps when saying the rotor imparts energy to the fluid and that the machines increase pressure. In turbine operation the overall energy transfer is reversed: the fluid drives the shaft, as described in Section 2.5. The pump wording should not be applied unchanged to turbines.


PDF page 78 — source_issue

Limit 2: Consider a fixed pump whose input and output are completely open. One can spin the impeller, adding kinetic energy, but if the output is completely open to ambient pressure, there is no pressure change in the fluid, and again no work is done. The kinetic energy is dissipated as heat upstream and downstream of the pump. This is a fixed propeller that coincides with motion but does no work.

In practice, the efficiency of a pump is best roughly at its maximum work point i.e. in the middle of its performance range. At low flow rate, the fluid experiences flow separation at the inner edge of the vane, reducing the work-to-KE conversion, and the fluid undergoes recirculation in the casing, reducing the KE-to-pressure conversion. At high flow rate, the fluid experiences flow separation at the outer edge of the vane, reducing the work-to-KE conversion, and the fluid undergoes recirculation in the casing, reducing the KE-to-pressure conversion.

2.7 Our analysis of turbomachines was a mean-flow, continuum analysis in the object frame of reference

Several models were required to make the analysis in this chapter tractable.

We considered flow through turbomachinery. For stationary turbomachinery e.g., a water pump, the object frame of reference and the laboratory frame of reference are the same; but when the turbomachinery is moving e.g., a propeller on an aircraft, our analysis is always in the object frame of reference, i.e., the frame of reference aligned with the object itself (see Sidebar 2.1, p.68). In this frame of reference, the analysis of the turbomachinery does not depend on whether the machine is moving, which is an important simplification, and this choice builds on tools used in MAE2030 for selection of frame of reference.

For turbomachinery, we use the continuum model, and the pressure is the readout of the molecular fluctuations of velocity (see Sidebar 2.2, p.69).

The real flow in any turbomachine varies significantly along relevant cross-sections. However, when we analyze turbomachines, we ignore this and treat the flow as if its properties are effectively averaged along cross sections and/or at inlets and outlets (see Sidebar 2.3, p.70).

model: a (preferably simple) mathematical construct that explains observed phenomena well enough that it is useful for analysis or design.

Editorial note: Several letters in the model definition are washed out here. The definition above is restored using the matching, more legible definition on PDF page 47.

frame of reference: WHEN IN DOUBT, ASK DMITRY SAVRANSKY.

continuum: a physical domain whose properties are differentiable. Contrast with atomistic.
