SIDEBAR 2.1: ENGINEERING MODELS

Object frame of reference

Premise: an object is used as the frame of reference when it is moving relative to the lab frame

When an object is moving and we want to analyze the fluid mechanics associated with it, we find it much easier to choose a reference frame associated with the object.

Mathematical form: the object frame of reference defines the coordinate system relative to the object

The mathematical form of the definition of an object frame of reference is to align the coordinate frame with the object:

\vec u_{\mathrm{object}}=0. (2.13)

Utility: the object frame is what we use for vehicles and projectiles

When objects are moving in the lab reference frame (a car, a plane, a boat), using that object reference frame for the coordinate system makes things easy—the velocity at wall is homogeneous (i.e., \(\vec u=0\)), the boundary condition is steady, the flow can be steady, etc.

Limitations: using a moving object as a frame of reference means the frame of reference might be accelerating, and it makes the velocity boundary condition at infinity nonhomogeneous

When a vehicle or projectile moves, the object frame of reference is easy to use, because the boundary conditions at the object are steady. But this makes the velocity at infinity nonzero i.e., nonhomogeneous. Further, when the object accelerates, that means that the frame of reference is accelerating, and an accounting must be made for that. The simplest example of this is an object moving in a circle, which by definition must be experiencing a centripetal force.


PDF page 80 — source_issue

SIDEBAR 2.2: ENGINEERING MODELS

Temporal and Spatial Averaging in the Continuum Model of Fluid Mechanics

Premise: The Continuum Model Replaces The Motion of Individual Molecules with Velocity, Pressure, and Viscosity, and replaces the mass of individual molecules with Density

An atomistic description of a fluid would include a description of the motion of every atom or molecule in the system. The atoms or molecules of a real fluid are changing constantly, and are quite numerous, so an atomistic description of a fluid is, for most mechanical engineering applications, somewhere between \(1\times10^{12}\) and \(1\times10^{30}\) times more complicated than it needs to be.

The continuum model replaces the motion of individual molecules with their spatially averaged quantities; instead of considering an atom we say instead that we will average over some spatial dimension, say a nanometer or micron, enough so that we can approximate the fluid velocity and mass as continuous field properties. If all the relevant physical phenomena were linear functions of velocity, there would be nothing else to say. But, the energy of a molecule (or the momentum it carries) are quadratic functions of velocity, and the average energy of the molecules is not equal to the energy associated with molecules moving at the average velocity. So if we time-average the behavior of molecules and replace it with \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\), we get extra terms left over. We made things \(1\times10^{12}\) to \(1\times10^{30}\) times simpler by replacing individual molecular motion with \(\vec{u}\), but we need some extra bookkeeping to keep track of the information we lost when we averaged.

The extra bookkeeping takes two forms. Both account for the fact that, even though a fluid might on average be motionless, that motionlessness only describes the average motion, and in fact the individual molecules are bouncing all over the place and clunking into each other. First, independent of any macroscopic fluid motion, there is an isotropic effect of this which leads to a force per unit area applied to any real or imagined surface anywhere in the fluid—this is called pressure. The microscopic fluctuations, which we ignored when defining \(\vec u\), have to be accounted for in an averaged sense. By averaging over space and time, we replace the fluctuations of all of the molecules with one field variable \(p(x,y,z,t)\), which describes the net effect—the molecules bouncing around push on any surface with a force per unit area normal to that surface.

Second, if the velocity \(\vec u\) is nonuniform, we find that molecules bouncing around leads to both an anisotropic transfer of momentum (i.e., force) as well as a conversion of energy in the form of continuum velocity \(\vec u\) into energy in the form of increased fluctuations (i.e., increased temperature). This is called viscosity. These are summarized in Figure F.1, p. 529.



Figure 2.15: Momentum flux averaging in fluid mechanics. Averaging over the time and distances associated with molecular collisions (i.e., the continuum approximation) transfers from an atomistic description of fluids to a continuum description (which is what most mechanical engineers use), and introduces pressure and viscosity to account for the effects of the fluctuations that are lost in the process.

Mathematical form: The continuum approximation replaces the velocity vectors of all of the individual molecules with \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\), \(p(x,y,z,t)\), and \(\mu(x,y,z,t)\), and the masses of the molecules with \(\rho(x,y,z,t)\)

Our continuum description of the state of a fluid comprises \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\), \(p(x,y,z,t)\), \(\rho(x,y,z,t)\), and \(\mu(x,y,z,t)\). Here, the spatial coordinates \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) as well as the temporal coordinate \(t\) are both meant to be averaged over the spatial dimension and temporal dimension of molecular collisions (roughly 100 nm and 1 ns in air at STP; about 100–1000 times smaller and shorter in water).

Utility: The continuum approximation simplifies our calculations by many orders of magnitude

To describe the atomistic motion of a few nanometers cubed of water for 100 ps of a simple system might cost about $10,000. That isn’t worth the money for most mechanical engineering applications. The continuum approximation makes description of fluid mechanics possible; simplifying things by as much as \(1\times10^{30}\).

Limitations: The continuum approximation requires that we use constitutive relations to describe fluids

The continuum approximation is useful and simple, and it is tough to get it to break down in any system of routine relevance to a mechanical engineer. Because it corrects for a subset of atomistic motion with a thing called pressure, it often requires thermodynamics and an equation of state—this is central for compressible flow. It corrects for a different subset of atomistic motion with a thing called viscosity, and it requires that we define what that viscosity is. The viscosity is a constitutive relation.

In using the continuum model, we have overlapped the language of thermodynamic equilibrium with the language of continuum flow. A moving fluid is not, strictly speaking, in thermodynamic equilibrium. But it is close enough to thermodynamic equilibrium that the result the continuum approximation gives for “pressure” is, for MAE3230 purposes, equivalent with the one that thermodynamics gives for “pressure”.

Editorial note: A molecule’s momentum \(m\vec v\) is linear in its velocity. Kinetic energy is quadratic, and momentum flux involves products of velocity components. The source phrase “the momentum it carries” should distinguish momentum from momentum flux.

SIDEBAR 2.3: ENGINEERING MODELS

Mean Flow

Premise: often, we don’t need details of spatial variation of a flow and instead we only need the spatial average

Mean flow approximations basically just ignore spatial variation of a fluid flow and instead focus on some sort of a spatial average. Two examples are flow in pipes and flow in porous media. When we pump flow through a pipe, we care primarily about the total flowrate and not so much about the details of the velocity distribution. A fluid-mechanics researcher might look in great detail, but for engineering analysis of flow through pipes, we typically just measure the flow rate and how it relates to the pressure drop, because that tells you what you need to know to design a piping system. And when fluid moves through porous media, for example water being wicked into a paper towel, we care more about the motion of the fluid front than we do about the details of how the water moves around and through individual paper fibers.

Mathematical form: mean flow approximations simply use an area-averaged speed \(\bar U\) instead of \(\vec u(x,y,z)\)

In pipes, we replace the velocity distribution with the cross-sectional-area-averaged value of the downstream component:

\bar U=\frac{Q}{A}=\int_A\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA. (2.14)

although I will always try to write this as \(\bar U\), most fluids texts simply write this as \(U\) with the understanding that everyone knows that the value is an area-averaged one.

In porous media, we replace the velocity field \(\vec u\) with an area-averaged velocity field \(\bar{\vec u}\), which is understood to give a value that is averaged over a volume \(V\) large relative to the pore structure of the material:

\bar{\vec{u}}(x,y,z,t)=\frac{1}{V}\int_V\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\,dV. (2.15)

Utility: mean flows

The mean-flow approximation lets us write relations for pipe flow in a form

\frac{\partial B}{\partial s}=-f_D\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2, (2.16)

which helps us understand how much pumping power is required to move flow through a piping system. \(\bar U\) is easy to measure because it is directly calculable from the flowrate \(Q\) and the pipe dimensions.

The mean-flow approximations let us write relations for porous-media flow in a form

\bar{\vec{u}}=-\frac{k}{\mu}\nabla p, (2.17)

which describes porous media flow using only the material permeability \(k\), and which does not require microscopic measurement of fluid flow.

Limitations: Mean flow analysis usually hides its errors into the definition of a material or flow property like \(f_D\) or \(k\)

Although averaging velocities correctly captures values proportional to velocity, such as the total flowrate, averaging velocities cannot correctly capture values proportional to velocity squared, for example the dynamic pressure \(\frac{1}{2}\rho U^{2}\). \(\bar{U}^{2}\) is not equal to \(\overline{U^{2}}\). In pipe flow, there is an inherent limitation—\(\bar{U}\) correctly describes the average velocity and (when multiplied by the cross-sectional area) the total flow rate, but \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^{2}\) isn’t the cross-section-averaged dynamic pressure exactly. This approach works for calculation of the viscous dissipation factor, but it is not because \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^{2}\) is equal to the mean dynamic pressure, it is because for any specific flow \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^{2}\) is always proportional to the mean dynamic pressure. So this error gets folded into the viscous dissipation factor \(f_D\).

Similarly, averaging flow through porous media leads to errors that typically get lumped into some material property. The permeability \(k\) of a porous material can be related back to the pore size and structure but only if those details are known exactly. More often, the permeability of a porous material lets us estimate (but not exactly measure) properties like the pore size.

Editorial note: Equation (2.14) omits \(1/A\) before the integral: \(\int_A\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA=Q\), so \(\bar U=(1/A)\int_A\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA\). Equation (2.16) omits the inverse pipe diameter: the pressure gradient is \(\partial B/\partial s=-(f_D/D)(\rho\bar U^2/2)\), which has pressure-per-length units. The printed expressions above are retained literally.

Chapter 3

Dams: Machines That Store Potential Energy In Fluids

A dam concentrates the potential energy associated with a waterway into a localized region of high-pressure fluid that can be used to drive a turbine

A dam is a wall in a waterway that limits water flowing downhill. It is used to retain water upstream of the dam to control floods or provide a local water resource for drinking or irrigation, or to generate hydroelectric power. In the context of hydroelectric power (our focus in this section), a dam is a machine that concentrates the gravitational potential energy of high-elevation water in a localized region, generating high-pressure fluid. This high-pressure fluid can then be used to drive a turbine. If there were no dam, the gravitational potential energy of high-elevation water would be dissipated as heat as the water flowed downhill. Operating one large hydroelectric plant at a dam is much cheaper and more efficient than the alternative without the dam, which would be to try to extract energy from the river by putting many water wheels throughout this path.

dam: a wall that stops or restricts flow of surface water, e.g., rivers.

machine: as defined in this text, a device that changes direction or magnitude of forces, causes motion or acceleration, or transfers energy to perform a useful action.

water wheel: an impulse turbine, technologically important in antiquity, consisting of a wheel with paddles that water flows over.

The Hoover Dam generates the largest reservoir in the US and generates electricity for Arizona, Nevada, and California

The Hoover Dam (Figure 3.1, p. 72) is an approximately 725-ft-tall dam (base elevation 500′; top elevation 1225′) that sits in the path of the Colorado River. Upstream of the Dam is Lake Mead, an up to 120-mile-long reservoir of water that holds up to 3.2×10¹⁰ m³ of water and gravitational potential energy of about 3×10¹⁶ J, about 300 times the energy of the nuclear bomb the US dropped on Hiroshima. At the dam, water at the base of the dam travels through intake towers through four penstocks to the

penstock: a pipe or other intake structure that feeds water into a hydroelectric turbine.

On June 30, 2022, the height difference between Lake Mead and the Hoover Dam turbines was approximately 400 ft, gauge pressure at the turbine was more like 12 bar, and recent power output averages have been approximately 400 MW.

The Hoover Dam and Lake Mead reservoir provide drinking water and electricity to Arizona, Nevada, and California. They also provide drinking water to Mexico and irrigation water to several other western states. These water outflows are routed through a number of pipes connected directly to Lake Mead. A much-discussed topic is the fact that Lake Mead’s level has dropped over the last 20 years, as the water commitments apportioned to a variety of states and municipal entities for drinking and irrigation have exceeded the water input to the Colorado River from snowmelt and rain.

PDF page 85 — verified

A dam’s machine function is to localize the release of water’s gravitational potential energy at a powerplant

A dam is a machine that localizes the release of water’s gravitational potential energy.

Any mass in a gravitational field has a potential energy given by \(E=mgz\), where z and E are both measured relative to some arbitrary reference point. Any mass moving with a z component \(u_z\) is extracting that gravitational potential energy as power at rate \(P=-mgu_z\). If the mass is accelerating in freefall, the potential energy is being converted to kinetic energy. If the mass is moving at steady speed and not accelerating (as water flowing in a river does), the power being extracted from gravitational potential energy must simultaneously be dissipated. In a river, the power extracted is dissipated mostly as heat and erosion of the riverbed.

If we want to generate hydroelectric power from a river at large scale, we cannot do so at a point in the river at which it is shallow and level—the local rate of extraction of gravitational potential energy is low.

Rather than extract energy from a river in a distributed fashion along the river, we build a dam at one point, and build up an impoundment of fluid. As the hydrostatic equation of fluid mechanics will show us, gravitational forces on this built-up water lead to a pressure distribution throughout the water, and the pressure at the bottom of the reservoir becomes large (Figure 3.4, p. 74). To extract energy in concentrated fashion, we place one or more turbines. What type of turbine works best depends on the scale of the operation and the pressure of the upstream fluid.

machine: as defined in this text, a device that changes direction or magnitude of forces, causes motion or acceleration, or transfers energy to perform a useful action.

Figure 3.4: How a dam facilitates hydroelectric power generation. By holding water at the dam, the height of the water impoundment builds. The hydrostatic distribution of pressure leads to high pressure at the base of the dam, where high-pressure water can be used to drive the turbines.

The hydrostatic equation describes the equilibrium between pressure

and gravity in (effectively) motionless fluid:

\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}=-\rho g,\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p+\rho gz=k,\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p(d)=p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gd (3.1)

where \(d=z_{\mathrm{surface}}-z\) is the (positive) depth underwater. This tells us that a reservoir tall enough to let the intake to the turbine be depth d underwater will lead to an excess pressure of \(\rho gd\) at the turbine. For the Hoover Dam, this is a maximum depth of about 180 m, so the excess pressure at the turbines is

\Delta p=\rho gd=(1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2})(180\ \mathrm{m})=1.76\times10^6\ \mathrm{Pa} (3.2)

meaning that, at maximum reservoir height, the turbines extract the energy of the fluid while reducing its pressure by approximately 1.76×10⁶ Pa.

The Hoover Dam is designed to handle 2000 MW of power through 17 turbines, so 120 MW per turbine. Each turbine is connected to a generator with a 40-pole rotor (Figure 3.5, p. 75), meaning that to generate 60 Hz electricity it needs to spin at 3600 rpm × 2/40 = 180 rpm, so \(\omega=19\ \mathrm{rad/s}\).

Figure 3.5: The 40-pole rotor of a Hoover Dam generator. Almost all pictures of Hoover Dam rotors are of this one, on the sightseeing tour at the Dam. They almost always feature this same yellow forklift.

Dam.

Water that is motionless (or close to motionless) has a well-defined hydrostatic pressure distribution, which stems from momentum equilibrium in the fluid, in which gravity pulls downward while the pressure gradient pushes the fluid upward. For a uniform-density fluid, the pressure increases linearly as we move from the surface (where the pressure is equal to the pressure of the air above it) down below the surface:

p(z)=p(0)-\rho gz (3.4)

The pressure increases approximately 1 bar for every 10 m of depth. When Lake Mead is full, the top of Lake Mead is about 180 m above the intake to the turbines and the pressure drop across the turbines is approximately 18 bar. Total flow capacity through the turbines is about 1700 m³/s. The total work done on the turbines (and thus the maximum energy extractable by perfect turbines at max capacity and max reservoir height) is

W=\Delta p Q=(18\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})(1700\ \mathrm{m^3/s})=3000\ \mathrm{MW} (3.5)

but in practice, peak energy extraction is more like 2000 MW because of imperfect turbine efficiency combined with reservoir heights and flow rates that are not at maximum. And, in practice, typical energy extraction is more like 700 MW. And, the turbines don’t run all the time, so time-averaged energy extraction rates are more like 400 MW. The Hoover Dam is nearly the tallest dam in the US (the Oroville Dam is maybe 30 feet taller) but not close to the most powerful hydroelectric powerplant (the Grand Coulee Dam is rated 3.5 times higher; it is shorter but much wider with higher flowrate).

These calculations illustrate what the purpose is of the dam. The flowrate of a river is specified by the rainfall upstream of it and is largely out of our control. What we can control is the pressure that the water is at when we run it through a turbine. To a first approximation, the pressure drop across the turbine, and therefore the energy generated by every unit volume of fluid that passes through it, is defined by how high of a reservoir of water is maintained upstream of the turbine. A taller dam generates more power, and a waterway with higher flow rate generates more power.

dam: a wall that stops or restricts flow of surface water, e.g., rivers.

Hydrostatics forms our first framework to describe the pressure distribution in fluid systems

The engineering system that motivates this chapter is a dam, which concentrates gravitational potential energy in a location so that it can be used to drive a hydroelectric turbine. The physics of this chapter is hydrostatics, the study of fluids at rest. Fluid at rest is the simplest to study, and is the fluid-mechanical version of MAE2020 (See Sidebar 3.1, p. 78). Although hydrostatics is very limited in its application, it can help us describe the pressure variation in a static fluid, as exemplified by the dependence of air pressure with elevation in the atmosphere, or the depth dependence of water pressure in swimming pools, rivers, and oceans. This explains many of the aspects of hydrological systems like lakes and dams, how altimeters and depth gauges work, how pressure sensors like manometers and barometers work, et cetera. We will build on this in Chapter 4 to show how these

pressure: usually used to mean static pressure but can be used metaphorically to describe any force per unit area or energy per unit volume.

buoyancy: the force opposing gravity felt by an object immersed in a fluid, caused by the nonuniform hydrostatic pressure distribution.

The key equations we develop in this chapter are the differential and integral forms of the hydrostatic equation, which relates the pressure of a fluid to its elevation in a gravitational field.

The premise, mathematical form, utility, and limitations of the hydrostatic model are described in Sidebar 3.2, p. 78.

The hydrostatic equation describes the instantaneous relation between the body forces a system feels and its surrounding pressure distribution

The hydrostatic equation is a critical first component of fluid mechanics because it relates the body forces a system feels to its surrounding pressure distribution. For most systems we analyze in this chapter, the system is motionless in the laboratory reference frame, but is being acted upon by gravitational forces. When we perform hydrostatic analysis, we are analyzing a motionless system; however, it is acted upon by these gravitational forces which try to accelerate the fluid in the system toward the center of the earth. For hydrostatics problems, we typically use Cartesian coordinates (see Sidebar 3.4, p. 79) and align the z axis so that it is pointing upward. Hydrostatic analysis uses pressure and density as key parameters and thus is a manifestation of the continuum model (see Sidebar 3.4, p. 80).

Because we know the system is motionless and not accelerating, we know the gravitational forces must be counteracted by another force. The hydrostatic equation shows that the pressure must vary in the direction of the gravitational acceleration so that imbalances in the pressure surface forces balance out the gravitational body force. We use pressure throughout this course, with many different units; some comments on pressure can be found in Sidebar 3.5, p. 81.

hydrostatic equation: in differential form, \(\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}=-\rho g\). In integral form, \(p+\rho gz=k\).

gravitational acceleration: acceleration due to gravity. Denoted as a vector \(\vec{g}\) or its magnitude \(g\). By our convention, we take g positive pointing downward.

surface force: a force that acts on a control volume through its surface. Examples include viscous stresses and pressure. These forces, at the atomistic level, operate through close interactions when molecules collide with each other. Compare to body force.

body force: a force that acts directly upon all of the mass within a control volume. Examples include gravity and electromagnetic forces. These forces act directly (gravity) or indirectly (electromagnetics) over lengths much longer than molecular diameters. Compare to surface force.

SIDEBAR 3.1: Connections in the MAE curriculum: link to ENGRD2020 Statics

Statics and hydrostatics

Hydrostatics is the fluids version of ENGRD2020. Statics is described in ENGRD2020, and ENGRD2020 in essence is “everything we can calculate for a rigid solid by use of \(\sum \vec{F}=0\) and \(\sum \vec{M}=0\)”. ENGRD2020 doesn’t cover fluid statics because fluid statics requires multivariable differential calculus (MATH 1920), which many sophomores don’t have when taking ENGRD2020. But you should have finished MATH 1920 by now, so we can derive partial differential relations that describe the pressure distribution. This chapter covers hydrostatics, i.e., fluid statics, which basically is the fluid-mechanical version of ENGRD2020. Just as ENGRD2030 is harder than ENGRD2020 for most students, study of moving fluid in later chapters will be more challenging than the study of motionless fluid in this chapter.

SIDEBAR 3.2: ENGINEERING MODELS

Hydrostatic Equation

Premise: The hydrostatic model describes the pressure distribution in quiescent fluid.

The hydrostatic model is a description of fluid that is motionless; it establishes the simplest continuum description of a fluid, incorporating the definition of pressure into an expression of static equilibrium for a fluid.

Mathematical form: Assuming \(\vec{u}=0\) and setting \(\sum \vec{F}=0\) on a control volume leads to the hydrostatic equation.

If we assume fluid is not moving, the only force on the fluid is pressure, and an equilibrium analysis of a differential or finite control volume leads to the hydrostatic equation in differential or integral form, respectively:

\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}=-\rho g;\qquad p+\int_{z_0}^{z}\rho g\,dz=k (3.6)

Utility: The hydrostatic equation describes pressure distributions with altitude and informs calculations of forces on fluid containers.

The hydrostatic equation describes pressure variation with altitude in the atmosphere, and the pressure variation with depth underwater. It describes how pressure varies in pipes in buildings, and why a dam leads to high-pressure water for energy generation.

Limitations: The hydrostatic equation becomes invalid when the dynamic pressure or viscous stresses become significant relative to pressure differences associated with height.

Moving fluid has a dynamic pressure \(\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2\), and fluid that is deforming generates viscous stresses whose components are proportional to components of the velocity gradient, e.g., \(\mu\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\). For quiescent fluid, these terms are identically zero. If fluid is moving a small amount and we still want to use the hydrostatic equation, it is valid only when these terms are still very small relative to \(\rho g\Delta z\) terms and thus can be ignored in terms of their effect on pressure. Or equivalently, the magnitude of these terms tells us the distance \(\Delta z\) over which the hydrostatic equation is relevant. For example, the hydrostatic equation is a poor description of how pressure varies from the bottom to the top of an airplane wing, because \(\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2\) can’t be ignored for flow over an airplane wing (and in fact it is much bigger than \(\rho g\) times the vertical distance between bottom and top of the wing). The hydrostatic equation is a good description of how the pressure at the altitude of the plane differs from the pressure at sea level. There are also other forces that could be applied to fluids (electric fields, magnets, osmotic pressure) that are all ignored here as they are not central to most mechanical engineering fluid mechanical problems.

SIDEBAR 3.4: ENGINEERING MODELS

Temporal and Spatial Averaging in the Continuum Model of Fluid Mechanics

Premise: The Continuum Model Replaces The Motion of Individual Molecules with Velocity, Pressure, and Viscosity, and replaces the mass of individual molecules with Density

An atomistic description of a fluid would include a description of the motion of every atom or molecule in the system. The atoms or molecules of a real fluid are changing constantly, and are quite numerous, so an atomistic description of a fluid is, for most mechanical engineering applications, somewhere between \(1\times10^{12}\) and \(1\times10^{30}\) times more complicated than it needs to be.

The continuum model replaces the motion of individual molecules with their spatially averaged quantities; instead of considering an atom we say instead that we will average over some spatial dimension, say a nanometer or micron, enough so that we can approximate the fluid velocity and mass as continuous field properties. If all the relevant physical phenomena were linear functions of velocity, there would be nothing else to say. But, the energy of a molecule (or the momentum it carries) are quadratic functions of velocity, and the average energy of the molecules is not equal to the energy associated with molecules moving at the average velocity. So if we time-average the behavior of molecules and replace it with \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\), we get extra terms left over. We made things \(1\times10^{12}\) to \(1\times10^{30}\) times simpler by replacing individual molecular motion with \(\vec{u}\), but we need some extra bookkeeping to keep track of the information we lost when we averaged.

The extra bookkeeping takes two forms. Both account for the fact that, even though a fluid might on average be motionless, that motionlessness only describes the average motion, and in fact the individual molecules are bouncing all over the place and clunking into each other. First, independent of any macroscopic fluid motion, there is an isotropic effect of this which leads to a force per unit area applied to any real or imagined surface anywhere in the fluid—this is called pressure. The microscopic fluctuations, which we ignored when defining \(\vec u\), have to be accounted for in an averaged sense. By averaging over space and time, we replace the fluctuations of all of the molecules with one field variable \(p(x,y,z,t)\), which describes the net effect—the molecules bouncing around push on any surface with a force per unit area normal to that surface.

Second, if the velocity \(\vec u\) is nonuniform, we find that molecules bouncing around leads to both an anisotropic transfer of momentum (i.e., force) as well as a conversion of energy in the form of continuum velocity \(\vec u\) into energy in the form of increased fluctuations (i.e., increased temperature). This is called viscosity. These are summarized in Figure F.1, p. 529.



Figure 3.7: Momentum flux averaging in fluid mechanics. Averaging over the time and distances associated with molecular collisions (i.e., the continuum approximation) transfers from an atomistic description of fluids to a continuum description (which is what most mechanical engineers use), and introduces pressure and viscosity to account for the effects of the fluctuations that are lost in the process.

Mathematical form: The continuum approximation replaces the velocity vectors of all of the individual molecules with \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\), \(p(x,y,z,t)\), and \(\mu(x,y,z,t)\), and the masses of the molecules with \(\rho(x,y,z,t)\)

Our continuum description of the state of a fluid comprises \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\), \(p(x,y,z,t)\), \(\rho(x,y,z,t)\), and \(\mu(x,y,z,t)\). Here, the spatial coordinates \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) as well as the temporal coordinate \(t\) are both meant to be averaged over the spatial dimension and temporal dimension of molecular collisions (roughly 100 nm and 1 ns in air at STP; about 100–1000 times smaller and shorter in water).

Utility: The continuum approximation simplifies our calculations by many orders of magnitude

To describe the atomistic motion of a few nanometers cubed of water for 100 ps of a simple system might cost about $10,000. That isn’t worth the money for most mechanical engineering applications. The continuum approximation makes description of fluid mechanics possible; simplifying things by as much as \(1\times10^{30}\).

Limitations: The continuum approximation requires that we use constitutive relations to describe fluids

The continuum approximation is useful and simple, and it is tough to get it to break down in any system of routine relevance to a mechanical engineer. Because it corrects for a subset of atomistic motion with a thing called pressure, it often requires thermodynamics and an equation of state—this is central for compressible flow. It corrects for a different subset of atomistic motion with a thing called viscosity, and it requires that we define what that viscosity is. The viscosity is a constitutive relation.

In using the continuum model, we have overlapped the language of thermodynamic equilibrium with the language of continuum flow. A moving fluid is not, strictly speaking, in thermodynamic equilibrium. But it is close enough to thermodynamic equilibrium that the result the continuum approximation gives for “pressure” is, for MAE3230 purposes, equivalent with the one that thermodynamics gives for “pressure”.

Editorial note: A molecule’s momentum \(m\vec v\) is linear in its velocity. Kinetic energy is quadratic, and momentum flux involves products of velocity components. The source phrase “the momentum it carries” should distinguish momentum from momentum flux.

SIDEBAR 3.5: FUNDAMENTALS

Pressure

Pressure is an isotropic force per unit area felt everywhere in a fluid

Any surface placed anywhere in a fluid will feel an isotropic force per unit area that we refer to as the pressure. The microscopic underpinnings of this force is the kinetic energy of the molecules that make up the fluid bouncing back and forth, and the pressure accounts for our ignoring molecular details when we use a continuum velocity to replace individual molecular velocities.

Many units are used for pressure

The SI unit for pressure is Pa. We also routinely use \(1\ \mathrm{N/m^2}=1\ \mathrm{Pa}\). \(1\ \mathrm{bar}=1\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\), \(1\ \mathrm{atm}=1.013\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\), and \(1\ \mathrm{lb/in^2}=1\ \mathrm{psi}=6.9\ \mathrm{kPa}\). More obscure is \(1\ \mathrm{dyne/cm^2}=0.1\ \mathrm{Pa}\).

Pressure is routinely measured in units of equivalent length or head, because pressure differences are related to lengths by the hydrostatic equation. These lengths are always implicitly understood to be multiplied by the density of the specified fluid plus the acceleration due to gravity \(g=(9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2})\); they imply the height of a static fluid column that would have the specified pressure at its bottom. \(1\ \mathrm{bar}=10200\ \mathrm{mmH_2O}=750\ \mathrm{mmHg}=29.5\ \mathrm{inHg}=402\ \mathrm{inH_2O}\). Absolute pressure is a measure of the isotropic force per unit area. Relative pressure (equivalently gauge pressure) is a measure of a pressure difference compared to some reference pressure, often the local atmospheric pressure. It is common, when quoting gauge pressure in psi, to use the shorthand psig to denote “pounds per square inch greater than the reference pressure” or psia to denote “pounds per square inch absolute”.

We use many metaphors to compare pressure, work, and energy

The units of pressure are equivalent to energy per volume, and the term “pressure” is used metaphorically to refer to many properties that have units of energy per volume and/or which can be converted to pressure. For example, the dynamic pressure, which is a measure of the volumetric kinetic energy of a fluid, is not a description of isotropic force per unit area. However, it has units of energy per volume, which is the same as pressure, and it can be converted to pressure (by stagnating fluid isentropically). So to call the volumetric kinetic energy “dynamic pressure” is a metaphor. Pressure can be thought of as the stored capability to do work that a fluid holds—this is exact for an ideal gas but only approximate for other fluids. So when we discuss the interplay of pressure, velocity, and height in fluid flows (e.g. through the hydrostatic equation and the Bernoulli equation), we find it useful to think of pressure, speed, and height as being measures of stored ability to do work, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy, respectively.

Unlike in introductory thermodynamics, where we treat pressure as a state property, in MAE3230 we treat pressure as a field variable

In introductory thermodynamics, we treat pressure p as a scalar state property, i.e., a property of a system that applies equally to any part of the system. This is likely the analysis used in most of ENGRD2210. In MAE3230, we treat pressure p as a scalar, but we treat it as a field property, i.e., a property that varies in space. For a motionless fluid, pressure is not much more complicated in MAE3230 than it is in the state-property limit: we let it vary in space but that is the only additional complication.

Pressure does not completely describe the state of stress for a moving fluid

Pressure is not sufficient to describe the state of stress in a fluid if the fluid is moving. In fact we need a dyadic tensor with 9 quantities to be able to define the state of stress in a moving fluid. For a moving fluid, we still use pressure to describe the scalar field property that describes the isotropic part of the force per unit area on any surface in the fluid, and then we call everything else a viscous stress.


PDF page 93 — verified

The first form is written to show that we can solve for the pressure gradient if we know the fluid density. The second form (which is equivalent) shows that the net volumetric z force \(f_z\) on the fluid is given by the sum of the net volumetric surface pressure forces \(-\frac{dp}{dz}\) and the volumetric gravitational body force \(-\rho g\). In integral form, the hydrostatic equation is

p+\rho gz=k (3.9)

hydrostatic constant

volumetric work of compression; volumetric gravitational potential energy

where k is the hydrostatic constant. This shows that the pressure of a fluid increases as we decrease z, i.e., move downward in a fluid. The source of this pressure change is the gravitational force acting on the column of fluid.

The hydrostatic equation describes conservation of z momentum in the case in which the fluid velocity \(\vec{u}=0\) and its acceleration is also zero.

To derive the integral hydrostatic equation, we first consider a finite control volume with two surfaces parallel to the xy plane and all other surfaces parallel to the z axis, as shown in Figure 3.9, p. 84 (Sidebar 3.6, p. 83 gives some perspective on how we use control volumes in MAE3230 vs ENGRD2210). Examining z forces, the surfaces parallel to the z axis play no role. There is a z force from gravity given by \(F=-\rho g(z_2-z_1)A\), a z force from the pressure on the bottom surface given by \(F=p_1A\), and a force from the pressure on the top surface given by \(F=-p_2A\). Summing these and setting the result equal to zero at equilibrium, we find

p_1A-p_2A-\rho g(z_2-z_1)A=0 (3.10)

force at bottom; force at top; gravity force

which simplifies to

p_1+\rho gz_1=p_2+\rho gz_2 (3.11)

and because location 1 and location 2 are arbitrary,

p+\rho gz=k (3.12)

hydrostatic constant; volumetric work of compression; volumetric gravitational potential energy

We derive the differential hydrostatic equation by balancing forces on an infinitesimal control volume and using the Taylor-series expansion

volumetric: related to volume, or per unit volume.

integral: as an adjective, relating to the finite difference between two discrete states (e.g., point 1 to point 2) or the integrated effect of something over a finite distance or volume. Compare with differential, meaning related to derivatives.

control volume: a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

Control Volumes and Surfaces

Control volumes and surfaces define a volume and its boundary for the purposes of implementing accounting of quantities and their fluxes into and out of the volume

A control volume \(\mathcal{V}\) is a defined volume in space (Figure 3.8, p. 83). A control surface \(\mathcal{S}\) is the surface that encloses a control volume and is used to define the fluxes of properties into and out of the control volume. The control volume and control surface are a more sophisticated version of a free-body diagram. Whereas a free-body diagram lets us apply discrete forces and moments and evaluate motion of discrete objects, a control volume and its control surface allows application of distributed forces and moments, and consider the effects of field properties such as pressure, velocity, and shear stress. Fluxes across control surfaces are defined using a unit outward normal vector \(\hat{n}\) by convention. You used free-body diagrams in ENGRD2020 and ENGRD2030. In those cases, you rarely or never used distributed loads and you likely never had a flux. You used control volumes and control surfaces in ENGRD2210. However, in ENGRD2210 we always assumed that fluxes were known, so the integration of a distributed flux term was always calculated for you already. In MAE3230, we have to calculate the fluxes using vector analysis.



Figure 3.8: A schematic of a control volume V surrounded by control surface S, with several examples of unit outward normals n-hat.

How much higher than \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) is the pressure at the bottom of a 12-foot-deep swimming pool filled with water?

Solution:

p-p_{\mathrm{atm}}=\rho g\Delta z=(1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2})(12\ \mathrm{ft})\left(\frac{1\ \mathrm{m}}{3.28\ \mathrm{ft}}\right)=35.9\times10^3\ \mathrm{Pa} (3.13)

gradient be for there to be no net force on the control volume. The two forces that apply in this system are the gravitational force on the fluid in the control volume \(F_g=-\rho g\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z\) and the pressure forces (pA) on the six faces of the control surface. We need only consider the z forces, and because four of the faces are parallel to the z axis, we need only consider two of the faces (the top and the bottom). The force caused by the gravitational attraction of the mass of the control volume must be perfectly balanced by the net effect of the pressure if the system is to remain motionless. From the diagram,

0=-\rho g\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z+p_{\mathrm{bottom}}\Delta x\Delta y+(-p_{\mathrm{top}}\Delta x\Delta y) (3.14)

pressure force on bottom face; gravitational force on CV; pressure force on top face

Now we need some way to define \(p_{\mathrm{top}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{bottom}}\). We estimate these values relative to the pressure at the center of the control volume p by using a Taylor-series expansion (see Sidebar 3.7, p. 86):

p_{\mathrm{top}}=p+\frac{1}{2}\Delta z\frac{dp}{dz} (3.20)

pressure at top written as a Taylor-series expansion; distance from center; pressure at center; pressure gradient

and

p_{\mathrm{bottom}}=p+\left(-\frac{1}{2}\Delta z\right)\frac{dp}{dz} (3.21)

pressure at bottom written as a Taylor-series expansion; distance from center; pressure at center; pressure gradient

Putting these into Equation (3.14), we get

0=-\rho g\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z+\left(-\frac{dp}{dz}\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z\right) (3.22)

gravitational force on CV; pressure force on CV; rho and g assumed uniform because fluid element is so small

which leads to

\frac{dp}{dz}=-\rho g (3.23)

downward volumetric pressure force; upward volumetric gravitational force

If \(\rho\) is nonuniform, the differential form can be integrated to show that the integral form of the hydrostatic equation involves an integral of \(\rho\) over the length rather than simply multiplication:

p_2-p_1=-g\int_{z_1}^{z_2}\rho(z)\,dz (3.24)

Nonuniform \(\rho\) is most relevant for (a) the atmosphere (because \(\rho\) is a function of altitude) or (b) stratified fluids (say a layer of oil on top of a layer of water).

SIDEBAR 3.7: FUNDAMENTALS

Taylor-Series Expansions

The Taylor Series prescribes the value of a function (e.g., pressure, density, velocity) everywhere in space if we know all of that function’s derivatives at one point

The Taylor-series expansion for a function \(f(x)\) around a point \(x_0\) is given by

f(x)=f(x_0)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left.\frac{1}{n!}\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial x^n}\right|_x\Delta x^n (3.15)

where \(\Delta x=x-x_0\). The Taylor-series expansion prescribes f at any x if we know f and all of f’s derivatives at \(x_0\). The Taylor series helps us change the mathematical description of a function from one that permeates space (i.e., knowing \(f(x)\) everywhere) to one that involves a ton of information all at one point in space (i.e., all the derivatives of f at one value of \(x=x_0\)). This is helpful because all of our differential equations that describe physical principles (e.g., conservation of momentum) are applied at a specific point in space.

We use the first-order term in the Taylor series to formulate differential equations

In formulating differential relations in physical systems, we use the Taylor-series expansion to relate the properties of f (f is typically the pressure, density, temperature, velocity, or similar fluid property) in different parts of an infinitesimal fluid element. Because the fluid element is vanishingly small, we find that we need not evaluate all the terms of the sum: in fact we need only the first term because all terms beyond the first-order term \((\frac{df}{dx}\Delta x)\) are vanishingly small relative to the first-order term. If we include only the first-order term, the Taylor-series expansion becomes

f(x)\approx f(x_0)+\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{x_0}\Delta x (3.16)

0th-order estimate of f(x); 1st-order (linear) correction for f(x)

and this is the form we use when deriving differential governing equations. One might argue that the first-order term is also vanishingly small relative to the zeroth-order term. The reason why the first-order term must be retained is that, when evaluating the effect of changes in fluid properties when deriving differential forms of the governing equations, we are actually interested in the difference between properties along the surface of a control volume. If we use the Taylor-series expansion to approximate, for example \(f(x_2)-f(x_1)\), we can see why the first-order term is important:

f(x_2)-f(x_1)=\left[f(x_0)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left.\frac{1}{n!}\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}(x_2-x_0)^n\right]-\left[f(x_0)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left.\frac{1}{n!}\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}(x_1-x_0)^n\right] (3.17)

f(x_2)-f(x_1)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left.\frac{1}{n!}\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}\left[(x_2-x_0)^n-(x_1-x_0)^n\right] (3.18)

Here, we see that \(f(x_0)\) cancels. For \(x_2-x_0\) and \(x_1-x_0\) approaching zero, the difference \(f(x_2)-f(x_1)\) can be written as

f(x_2)-f(x_1)\approx\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{x_0}(x_2-x_1) (3.19)

1st-order (linear) approximation

As \(x_2\) and \(x_1\) approach \(x_0\), all terms for n=2 and higher are much smaller than the term for n=1. This is why the n=1 term is necessary but why the n=2 and higher terms are not retained in the sum.

Editorial source note: The evaluation subscript in Eq. (3.15) visibly reads \(x\), whereas a Taylor expansion about \(x_0\) requires evaluation at \(x_0\). The evaluation subscripts in Eqs. (3.18) and (3.19) are damaged in this scan; the displayed \(x_0\) is a reconstruction from the stated expansion point and clearer repeated formulas (5.48)–(5.49), not fully recovered source lettering. The assertion that derivatives at one point prescribe a function elsewhere also requires analyticity and convergence at that point.

The hydrostatic distribution describes pressure differences in columns of liquids

Because columns of liquids can be directly related to pressure differences, columns of liquids have been used as pressure measurement devices. The relation between heights of fluid and pressure is so pervasive that pressure is routinely measured in units of equivalent heights of equivalent fluid, in which case it is typically called head.

head: a quantity (e.g., static head \(H\equiv\frac{p}{\rho g}\) or total head \(H\equiv\frac{p}{\rho g}+\frac{u^2}{2g}+z\)) in units of length that communicates energy per unit volume or, equivalently, pressure of a fluid. It describes the height of a hypothetical fluid that would generate a hydrostatic gauge pressure at its bottom equal to the static pressure or total pressure in the fluid under discussion.

The difference between two pressures can be indicated by the difference in height of two columns of liquid

Consider a U-shaped tube connected at two ends to two regions of air with two different pressures \(p_1\) and \(p_2\), shown in Figure 3.11, p. 87. At equilibrium, the hydrostatic equation must be satisfied in all fluid domains, and the pressure must be continuous at the water–air boundary. At the boundaries, the pressure on either side of the interface must be the same for the interface to be in equilibrium, so

p_1=p_a (3.25)

equilibrium at interface

and

p_2=p_d (3.26)

equilibrium at interface

In the left column, the integral form of the hydrostatic equation tells us

p_b-p_a=\rho gh_1 (3.27)

hydrostatic equation in left column



Figure 3.11: A U-shaped manometer.

equilibrium: a state in which forces are balanced.


PDF page 99 — verified

whereas in the right column, the integral hydrostatic equation tells us

p_c-p_d=\rho gh_2 (3.28)

hydrostatic equation in right column

and at the bottom of the tube

p_b=p_c (3.29)

hydrostatic equation along bottom

Combining these relations, we have

p_1-p_2=\rho g(h_2-h_1) (3.30)

manometer relation

And thus we can see that this configuration means that \(p_1\) is larger than \(p_2\), and we can measure how much larger \(p_1\) is then \(p_2\) as long as we know the difference in height between the two interfaces, the gravitational acceleration, and the fluid density. No information about the tube diameter is involved, and no dimensions of this device in the xy plane affect the result. The only spatial dimension involved is the z dimension.

This U-shaped tube is a manometer, among the simplest devices developed for measuring pressures. It is the simplest system for illustrating the integral hydrostatic equation both mathematically and visually. It was also a staple engineering pressure sensor probably until about 1990, at which point it was systematically replaced with electronic pressure gauges, which started to become inexpensive around that time. That was also about the time I got my driver’s license.

The dependence on fluid density indicates that a manometer is more sensitive (i.e., the level will move more for a given pressure difference) if a fluid of low density is used, and a manometer has larger dynamic range if a fluid of high density is used. Historically, the two most common fluids used in manometers have been mercury (which has a very high density and gives high dynamic range) and gauge oil (which has a density about 80% of water, is usually colored red to make it easy to see, and gives high sensitivity). Water typically isn’t used, because water evaporates.

manometer: a device that measures pressure differences by measuring heights of columns of liquid.

sensitive: producing a large response from a small input.

gauge oil: a (typically red-colored) oil that is chemically inert with low vapor pressure and low density. Used for sensitive manometry.

Multiple-fluid systems can be analyzed by systematically applying the hydrostatic equation in each fluid domain and enforcing pressure continuity at each interface

The analysis of columns of fluid can become more complicated if multiple fluids are involved; however, solution requires only that we systematically apply the hydrostatic equation and pressure continuity at interfaces. continuity: when used to modify a field (e.g., “velocity continuity” or “pressure continuity”), this is a mathematical term that typically means that the field is continuous, and often used to indicate that a field has the same value on both sides of an interface. When used alone, this is a physical term which typically means “conservation of mass”. When used as continuity equation, synonymous with “conservation of mass equation”.

What is the difference in pressure between A and B in Figure 3.12, p. 89? Assume the liquid at A and B is water. Assume the oil has density 827 kg/m³. \(h_1=10\text{ in}, h_2=3\text{ in}, h_3=4\text{ in}, h_4=4\text{ in}, h_5=5\text{ in}, h_6=8\text{ in}\).



Figure 3.12: A manometer with mercury and oil separating two regions of water.

A barometer measures absolute pressure by comparing atmospheric pressure to vacuum, typically with a mercury column

A column can be used to measure absolute pressure by having one of the ports be at vacuum. Because mercury is very heavy and has a very low vapor pressure, this requires only that we fill a tube with mercury, then turn it upside down in a reservoir of mercury, as shown in Figure 3.13, p. 90. The system will equilibrate at a point where the height of the mercury column is given by \(h=p_{\mathrm{atm}}/(\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}}g)\). This is a barometer. When I was a kid, we had a mercury barometer in the living room; when the pressure went down, you expected rain.

absolute pressure: pressure measured relative to vacuum.

barometer: a special case of a manometer. A device that measures ambient pressure by measuring the height of a column of liquid.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 3.3

Pressures are often listed using units of length, for example mmHg: 760 mmHg = 1 atm. Show that the gauge pressure at the bottom of a 760-mm-tall column of mercury, with \(\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}}=13600\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}\), is approximately 1 atm.

Solution: The gauge pressure is equal to the difference between the pressure and the atmospheric pressure, which is equal to the difference between the pressures at the bottom and top of the column. So the gauge pressure is given by

\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}}gh=(13600\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2})(760\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m})\left(\frac{1\ \mathrm{atm}}{1.013\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}}\right)=1\ \mathrm{atm} (3.33)

Because the hydrostatic equation describes pressure differences as proportional to heights of columns of liquids, it is common to describe pressures in terms of lengths

Pressure is routinely described in terms of length, because a height of fluid in a gravitational field generates a hydrostatic pressure difference. The term head is used to describe this length, and it is routine to use units of length (e.g., mm Hg) to describe absolute or relative pressures. For example, all typical weather forecasts in the US describe the pressure in terms of inches of mercury. See for example Figure 3.14, p. 91, in which pressure is reported as 30.01″, implying 30.01 inHg, which in turn really means

(30.01\ \mathrm{in})\left(\frac{0.0254\ \mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{in}}\right)(13600\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2})=0.102\ \mathrm{MPa}

Using in Hg is ubiquitous, but in Hg is a nonstandard unit—a pressure described in terms of head can only be used in a calculation once it is multiplied by the proper \(\rho g\) to get the relevant pressure. Example Problem 3.3 (p. 90) illustrates a calculation of the link between liquid heights and pressure that is focused directly on how length units are used to describe head.

It describes the height of a hypothetical fluid that would generate a hydrostatic gauge pressure at its bottom equal to the static pressure or total pressure in the fluid under discussion.

It describes the height of a hypothetical fluid that would generate a hydrostatic gauge pressure at its bottom equal to the static pressure or total pressure in the fluid under discussion.


PDF page 102 — verified

The hydrostatic equation describes pressure changes in bodies of fluid

From the standpoint of hydrostatics, bodies of fluid, e.g., the atmosphere or the ocean, are equivalent to the columns of fluid described in the previous section. The hydrostatic equation describes how the pressure increases as we go down in z.

hydrostatic equation: in differential form, \(\frac{dp}{dz}=-\rho g\). In integral form, \(p+\rho gz=k\).

The pressure in the Earth’s atmosphere is described by the hydrostatic equation with a height-dependent density

Earth’s atmosphere is a fluid, and it follows the hydrostatic relation

\frac{dp}{dz}=-\rho g (3.34)

as well. However, the density of air is a strong function of pressure and temperature, both of which change as we move from the ground up toward space. The gravitational acceleration changes as well, albeit more subtly. Although we need not treat g as variable between the ground and the altitude, say, of commercial airline flights, we do need to treat g as altitude-dependent in the upper atmosphere. To find the origin of atmospheric pressure at a point, we must integrate the relation for \(\frac{dp}{dz}\) allowing density and gravitational acceleration to be altitude-dependent. Starting from z = ∞, where we know the pressure is zero:

p=\int_{\infty}^{z}\frac{dp}{dz}\,dz (3.35)

substituting \(-\rho g\) in for \(\frac{dp}{dz}\) and reversing the order of integration, we find

p=\int_{z}^{\infty}\rho(z)g(z)\,dz (3.36)

hydrostatic equation, differential form, g positive pointing down.

hydrostatic equation for pressure in the atmosphere.

3.5. HYDROSTATIC EQUATION IN BODIES OF FLUID

Although \(g\) changes by a small enough amount that most calculations don’t bother keeping track, \(\rho\) changes greatly and knowing \(\rho(z)\) is essential to get any atmospheric calculation correct. Equation 3.36 shows that the hydrostatic pressure at any point is basically an integral of the gravitational force per unit area between that point and outer space.

Although we can in principle always calculate \(p\) by use of the integral in Equation (3.36), most engineers use what is called the standard atmosphere, which is a tabulated set of air properties that are agreed upon as being representative of the Earth’s atmosphere. It involves nothing more than the hydrostatic equation, the ideal-gas law, and the experimentally observed mean temperature distribution in the atmosphere. Graphs are shown in Figure 3.15, p. 93 and tabulated values are shown in Table 3.1, p. 92. Wolfram Alpha knows it. The hydrostatic relation thus explains why aerobic activity is more difficult at high elevation (air density is lower so less oxygen) and why our ears pop on airplanes as we descend (airplanes pressurize the cabin roughly to the same pressure that you would find at elevation 6000 ft, then increase upon landing).

Example Problem 3.4 (p.94) calculates how pressure changes in the atmosphere and under water. Example Problem 3.5 (p.95) is a typical homework or exam problem that incorporates the hydrostatic equation in multiple configurations.

Although many hydrostatics problems can be solved with algebra, we should get used to the vector differential operator form of the hydrostatic equation

In this chapter, we have used \(\vec{g}\) as the vector gravitational acceleration and \(g\) its scalar magnitude. In turn, \(\rho\vec{g}\) is the gravitational force per unit volume. In differential form, the hydrostatic form was listed earlier as

\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}=-\rho g, (3.46)

and this differential form can be integrated to lead in general to

p_2-p_1=\int_{z_1}^{z_2}-\rho g\,dz (3.47)

or, for uniform \(\rho\) and \(g\), to

p_2-p_1=-\rho g(z_2-z_1). (3.48)

These relations are one-dimensional, because we consider only the \(z\) direction. But what if we move around in a 3D space and need to formulate how our 3D motion relates to elevation? For example, what if we are hiking through the mountains? We move along the surface of a mountain, but how

hydrostatic equation: in differential form, \(\frac{dp}{dz}=-\rho g\). In integral form, \(p+\rho gz=k\).

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 3.4

A balloon is filled with air to a volume of 1 L by a person standing on the ground at 15 °C and a pressure \(p=(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})\). Assume the tension of the balloon can be neglected and the pressure in the balloon is approximately equal to that of its environment. What is the volume inside the balloon if the balloon is:

1. brought to a depth of 4 ft underwater in a 15° C pool of water?

2. brought to a depth of 20 m underwater in a 15° C pool of water?

3. brought to the top of a building like Upson Hall (60 ft)?

4. brought to the top of Longs Peak in Rocky Mountain National Park (14,300 ft)?

Solution: We know the temperature, pressure, and density of air at its starting state. Because the mass is fixed, we need to know the density change as we increase or decrease elevation, as \(V=m/\rho\) and \(V_2=V_1\rho_1/\rho_2\) if mass is fixed. If we do not know density directly and instead need to determine density through pressure, temperature, and the ideal gas law, then we use

\rho=\frac{p}{RT} (3.37)

and

V_2=V_1\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}=V_1\frac{p_1T_2}{p_2T_1} (3.38)

Underwater, the pressure is specified by the water the balloon is contained in, and the change of pressure of the water is given by the integral hydrostatic equation with uniform density, because the density of water is well approximated as uniform:

p_2=p_1-\rho g\Delta z. (3.39)

So 4 ft underwater, the water is at \(p=(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})-(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(-4\,\mathrm{ft})(1\,\mathrm{m}/3.28\,\mathrm{ft})=1.13\times10^6\,\mathrm{Pa}\), and

V_2=V_1\frac{p_1}{p_2}=1\,\mathrm{L}\times\frac{(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})}{0.113\,\mathrm{MPa}}=0.88\,\mathrm{L}. (3.40)

Editorial note: the source prints 1.13×10⁶ Pa in the preceding 4-ft sentence. Evaluating its displayed expression gives about 0.113 MPa = 1.13×10⁵ Pa; the source’s following Eq. (3.40) also uses 0.113 MPa. The printed exponent is retained above.

At 20 m underwater, the water is at \(p=(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})-(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(-20\,\mathrm{m})=0.297\times10^6\,\mathrm{Pa}\), and

V_2=V_1\frac{p_1}{p_2}=1\,\mathrm{L}\times\frac{(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})}{0.297\,\mathrm{MPa}}=0.34\,\mathrm{L}. (3.41)

In the air, the density cannot be assumed independent of pressure except over tiny ranges of pressure. Over 60 ft, the density of air changes only 0.3%, so we can approximate it as uniform, and the same goes for temperature: \(p=(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})-(1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(60\,\mathrm{ft})(1\,\mathrm{m}/3.28\,\mathrm{ft})=0.1011\,\mathrm{MPa}\), and

V_2=V_1\frac{p_1}{p_2}=1\,\mathrm{L}\times\frac{(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})}{0.1011\,\mathrm{MPa}}=1.002\,\mathrm{L}. (3.42)

But over a distance of 14,300 ft, we can’t assume that density is uniform. Instead the density is changing, as is the temperature and pressure. The integral form of the hydrostatic equation gives

p_2=p_1-\int_{z_1}^{z_2}\rho(z)g(z)\,dz, (3.43)

Where \(\rho(z)\) varies because of both pressure and temperature variation in the atmosphere. The tabulated standard atmosphere gives \(\rho(14{,}300\,\mathrm{ft})=0.79\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), so

V_2=V_1\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}=1\,\mathrm{L}\times\frac{(1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})}{0.79\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}}=1.5\,\mathrm{L}. (3.44)

If we had tried to assume that the sea-level density \(\rho=(1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})\) could be treated as uniform, we would have obtained \(p=(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})-(1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(14300\,\mathrm{ft})(1\,\mathrm{m}/3.28\,\mathrm{ft})=49\times10^3\,\mathrm{Pa}\), and \(V_2=V_1p_1/p_2=2.1\,\mathrm{L}\). Further, if we try to use the sea-level density, our (incorrect) calculation will tell us (incorrectly) that the pressure becomes negative around 28,000 feet.

Editorial source note: Eq. (3.40) also contains a numerical mismatch: \(1\,\mathrm L\times0.1013/0.113\approx0.896\,\mathrm L\), or 0.90 L to two decimal places, rather than the printed 0.88 L. The printed value is retained.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 3.5

Consider the container shown in Figure 3.16, p. 95. Answer the following questions:

1. You fill an empty container to height \(h/2\) with water by pouring water into the top. What happens?

2. Is the result different if, instead of filling from the top, you connected a hose to the bottom, forced water up through the tube in the center until the container was full up to height \(h/2\), then removed the hose?

3. Return to the experiment in which we fill the container from the top. What happens when the container is filled up past height \(h\)?

4. Now reconsider an experiment in which an empty container is filled from the top to height \(h/2\) with mercury. What happens?

5. What if you filled an empty container to height \(h/2\) with mercury, then filled past height \(h\) with water?



Figure 3.16: Top (left) and side (right) view of a container with a siphon in a center column.

Solution:

1. The container fills up to \(h/2\). The rightmost part of the siphon fills to \(h/2\) as well; this has no effect on the gross behavior of the container.

2. Yes, totally different. In this case, the entire central siphon is filled with water, and the hydrostatic equations cannot be solved. The pressure at the bottom of the siphon is \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) if you consider that it is exposed to the atmosphere. The hydrostatic equations say that the fluid would be static only if the pressure at the bottom of the siphon were \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh/2\). Thus the pressure at the outlet is not enough to hold up the water. By definition the water must be flowing out of the cup no matter what height it is filled to. Importantly, all of the water flows out of the cup.

3. In this case, the right part of the central siphon fills with water, and as soon as the height \(h_0\) exceeds \(h\) the hydrostatic equations again cannot be solved. Now the pressure at the top of the siphon is \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) if you consider that it is exposed to the atmosphere, but the hydrostatic equations say that the fluid would be static only if the pressure at the top of the siphon were equal to \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho g(h_0-h)\). Thus the fluid fills the central part of the siphon (making the pressure imbalance even worse) and fluid flows out the siphon. Once the siphon region is full, the water flows out of the cup no matter what height the water level is at in the container, and thus all of the water flows out of the cup.

4. This result is the same as for question 1.

5. There is no siphon effect. Now we have two fluids, and the hydrostatic pressure is the sum of the \(\rho gh\) terms associated with each fluid. Upon filling up to say \(h\) with water, there is a pressure imbalance and the mercury level in the central siphon goes up, but it goes up only a small amount because mercury is 13.6 times as dense than water. So the height difference between the mercury in the siphon and the mercury in the container would be \(h/2/13.6=h/27.2\). Some of this would be from the siphon mercury moving up; some would be from the container mercury going down. So the mercury level in the siphon would go up a distance that is less than \(h/27.2\). This would not be enough to fill the siphon and there would be no siphoning of the fluid out.

For video demonstrations of most of these results, see https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ISfIT3B4v6E.

SIDEBAR 3.8: Connections in the MAE curriculum: link to ENGRD2030 Dynamics

Hydrostatics in a uniformly accelerating fluid

Changing to a uniformly accelerating fluid creates a uniform dynamics problem

Fundamentally, the hydrostatic pressure distribution is a measure of the difference between the rate at which a body of fluid is accelerating and the rate at which it would be accelerating if it moved in response to an external body force. For our typical hydrostatic problem, there is an external body force which would make the fluid accelerate at a rate given by \(-g\hat{z}\), but we consider a fluid that is not accelerating at all, and for this to be true the gravity must be balanced by a pressure distribution such that \(dp/dz=-\rho g\). We chose a coordinate reference frame such that the fluid was not moving, so this was in essence a static problem defined by ENGRD2020: \(\sum\vec{F}=0\). The result is that there is a pressure gradient in the direction of the vector given by the difference between the acceleration the body force would provide \((-g\hat{z})\) and the acceleration of the system \((0)\):

\frac{\partial p}{\partial(-gz)}=\rho,\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\frac{dp}{dz}=-\rho g. (3.45)

We can generalize this relation for any body of fluid that is accelerating uniformly in any direction, at which this becomes a dynamic problem defined by ENGRD2030: \(\sum\vec{F}=m\vec{a}\) (or, actually, \(\sum\vec{f}=\rho\vec{a}\)). To do this, we can rederive the hydrostatic equation, but instead of setting the sum of forces equal to zero, we set the sum of forces equal to the fluid mass times its acceleration. The net effect is that there is a pressure gradient in the direction of the vector given by the difference \(-g\hat{z}-\vec{a}\). This explains why the level of fluid in a container accelerating forward is tilted backward, and why the level of fluid in a container rotating forms a parabola with the fluid higher on the outside and lower on the inside.



Figure 3.17: The direction of the pressure gradient in a hydrostatic system is in the direction of \(\vec{g}-\vec{a}\), where \(\vec{g}\) is the acceleration caused by body forces and \(\vec{a}\) is the uniform acceleration of the fluid system. Back before travel mugs were a thing, you used to have to know how to tilt your coffee mug when you accelerated or braked. In the schematic above, Prof. K is clearly accelerating forward, in which case you have to tilt your coffee mug forward. I used to watch my dad do this in his 1970 Chevy Chevelle.

Editorial notation note: The source expressions are consistent. With the vertical coordinate \(z\) upward and \(g>0\), \(\vec g=-g\hat z\), so \(\vec g-\vec a=-g\hat z-\vec a\). Equation (3.45) differentiates with respect to the scalar \(-gz\), not a vector; by the chain rule, \(\partial p/\partial(-gz)=\rho\) is equivalent to \(dp/dz=-\rho g\).

3.6. VECTOR DIFFERENTIAL OPERATOR FORM

our hiking along a trail affects our elevation, and therefore the pressure, is a function of a 3-dimensional motion in space that isn’t as simple. So we want to formulate the hydrostatic equation in a three-dimensional framework.

To do this, define the gravitational potential energy per unit volume of fluid as

e_{\mathrm{pot}}=\rho gz. (3.49)

This is a measure of how much work is required to elevate that fluid to height \(z\) in the gravitational field. The gravitational potential energy is a scalar field property. We could use this to rewrite the integral hydrostatic equation as:

p+e_{\mathrm{pot}}=k. (3.50)

The opposite of the gradient of any potential energy gives the force, and the gradient of gravitational potential energy per unit volume gives us the gravitational force per unit volume \(f_g\):

\vec{f}_g=-\nabla e_{\mathrm{pot}}=+\frac{\partial(\rho gz)}{\partial x}\,\hat{x}+\frac{\partial(\rho gz)}{\partial y}\,\hat{y}+\frac{\partial(\rho gz)}{\partial z}\,\hat{z}, (3.51)

Editorial note: Eq. (3.51) is transcribed with the positive component signs visible in the source. The next displayed equation gives \(\vec f_g=-\rho g\hat z\); for uniform \(\rho,g\), the z-component of \(-\nabla(\rho gz)\) is negative. The source sign difference is retained rather than silently repaired.

which simplifies to

\vec{f}_g=-\rho g\hat{z}. (3.52)

These results are not really new; we are rewriting the same physical results in different mathematical forms, because these different mathematical forms are useful to us in different contexts.

This analysis is a simple introduction to the gradient operator (see Sidebar 3.9, p. 98). The integral of the gravitational (vector) force along a path gives the (scalar) gravitational potential energy, and the gradient of the (scalar) gravitational potential energy leads to a (vector) gravitational force.

Many more gradients of scalars will be used in later chapters. As one example, for irrotational flow we will later show that the velocity vector can be determined by taking the gradient of a scalar \(\vec{u}=\nabla\phi\). This type of analysis is very powerful and permeates the study of fluid mechanics.

gravitational potential energy: potential energy that fluid has relative to a reference height \(z_0\): \(\int_V\rho g(z-z_0)\,dV\).

gravitational potential energy per unit volume of fluid, \(g\) assumed uniform.

hydrostatic equation, uniform \(\rho\), uniform \(g\), written in terms of gravitational potential energy: \(p+e_{\mathrm{pot}}=k\).

scalar: as a noun, a property with a magnitude only; no direction; as an adjective, having magnitude only but no direction.

gradient: the gradient of a property \(\vec{u}\) is symbolized by \(\nabla\vec{u}\). It denotes the direction(s) in which the property or its components are changing, as well as the magnitude of the spatial derivative in that direction. \(\nabla\vec{u}\) has tensor order one higher than \(\vec{u}\).

vector: a property with magnitude and direction.

SIDEBAR 3.9: FUNDAMENTALS

Gradient

The gradient of a property is a generalized multivariable derivative of that property

The gradient of a scalar is a vector pointing in the direction in which the scalar is changing most rapidly, and has a magnitude equal to how fast the scalar changes in that direction. This is often most easily visualized by thinking of the scalar as an elevation, and thinking of the gradient at any point as pointing directly up the hill in the direction of maximum increase. The gradient of a scalar is a vector pointing in a direction that is normal to an isocontour of that scalar.

The gradient of the pressure of a fluid is a vector denoting the net volumetric force on the fluid stemming from pressure variations

The negative gradient of pressure \(-\nabla p\) denotes the net volumetric pressure force on the fluid.

The gradient of the velocity potential is used to define the velocity for a potential flow

Irrotational flows, i.e., potential flows define the vector velocity by use of a scalar quantity \(\phi\):

\vec{u}=\nabla\phi. (3.53)

One way of thinking about this is that the velocity potential is analogous to elevation, generating mountains and valleys, and the velocity of a fluid always points directly up the mountain.

The gradient takes different forms in different coordinate systems

We can write the gradient both in terms of components and unit vectors, and we can equivalently write it as a matrix representation, which is understood to be shorthand for the components and unit vectors. In Cartesian coordinates, the gradient of a scalar (for example \(\nabla p\)) and its matrix representation (here, \([\nabla p]\)) are

\nabla p=\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\hat{x}+\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}\hat{y}+\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\hat{z},\qquad [\nabla p]=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial p}{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}. (3.54)

In cylindrical coordinates, the gradient of a scalar (for example \(\nabla\phi\)) and its matrix representation (here, \([\nabla\phi]_{r\theta z}\)) are

\nabla\phi=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\hat{r}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\theta}\hat{\theta}+\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}\hat{z},\qquad [\nabla\phi]_{r\theta z}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\\ \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\theta}\\ \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}. (3.55)

We focus on the initial and final states of the water-air interface in the bottle and assume that the fluid has come to rest at both scenarios. In both cases, we must uphold the two pressure boundary conditions defined by the air pressure and the pump. The pressure condition for the lowest point in the cylinder can be obtained using the hydrostatic equation:

p_{\mathrm{air}}+\rho g(0.20\,\mathrm{m}+z)=300000\,\mathrm{Pa}. (3.56)

The pressure condition at the air-water interface can be obtained using Boyle’s Law:

p_{\mathrm{air}}(1.3\,\mathrm{m}-z)=101325\,\mathrm{Pa}(1.3\,\mathrm{m}). (3.57)

Solving one equation and substituting into the other equation gives a quadratic equation with roots \(z\simeq0.85\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(z\simeq30.84\,\mathrm{m}\), the latter of which we can rule out because it corresponds to a nonsensical result (air compressed so much its pressure goes negative and a water column so high its pressure goes negative also). Noting that the water level is already 0.2 m high, we sum these two values to obtain the new height.

The water rises to a height of 1.05 m.

3. (OBJECTIVE: Calculate the horizontal pressure differences (i.e., stack effect associated with temperature variations)) Consider a tall building (400 m) filled with 15°C air, which has a density of 1.225 kg/m³. It is winter, and the 0°C air outside has a density of 1.292 kg/m³. Assume the building is perfectly sealed except that a window on the top floor is open so the pressure inside and outside the building is the same at the top of the building. What is the pressure difference between the inside and outside of the building at the bottom of the building? Solution: Using window and bottom to denote the height of the window and the bottom of the building, and in and out to describe fluid properties inside and outside the building:

p_{\mathrm{out}}+\rho_{\mathrm{out}}gz_{\mathrm{bottom}}=p_{\mathrm{window}}+\rho_{\mathrm{out}}gz_{\mathrm{window}} (3.58)

and

p_{\mathrm{in}}+\rho_{\mathrm{in}}gz_{\mathrm{bottom}}=p_{\mathrm{window}}+\rho_{\mathrm{in}}gz_{\mathrm{window}}. (3.59)

Rearranging,

p_{\mathrm{out}}-p_{\mathrm{in}}=g(z_{\mathrm{window}}-z_{\mathrm{bottom}})(\rho_{\mathrm{out}}-\rho_{\mathrm{in}})=(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(400\,\mathrm{m})(1.292-1.225)\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}=260\,\mathrm{Pa}. (3.60)
