6. (OBJECTIVE: hydrostatics with variable surface pressure boundary condition) A cylindrical tank (Figure 3.27, p. 104) is filled with water by a pump that exhausts at 200 kPa, forcing the pressure at the bottom of the tank to be at 200 kPa. When the water level is as shown in the figure, the air (which is well modeled as an ideal gas) is at 100 kPa and \(H=35\,\mathrm{cm}\). Calculate how high a water level can be generated by the pump. Solution: The water rises to a height \(z\) above the starting point. At that point, denote the pressure above the water as \(p_{\mathrm{air}}\). Then hydrostatic equilibrium implies \(p_{\mathrm{air}}+\rho g(0.35\,\mathrm{m}+z)=2\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\) and Boyle’s Law specifies \(p_{\mathrm{air}}(0.75\,\mathrm{m}-z)=(1\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa})(0.75\,\mathrm{m})\) (because the cross-sectional area is uniform, the volume is always proportional to the height). Solving the first for \(p_{\mathrm{air}}\) and substituting into the second gives a quadratic equation for the solution: \((2\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}-\rho g(0.35\,\mathrm{m}+z))(0.75\,\mathrm{m})=(1\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa})(0.75\,\mathrm{m})\). This has two solutions: \(z=20.44\,\mathrm{m}\) (which would correspond to the water rising past the top of the container, and also the gas being ideal but having negative pressure, so that solution is not realistic) and \(z=0.36\,\mathrm{m}\), corresponding to the water rising 36 cm.

The water rises 36 cm to a height of 71 cm.

Note that the primary pressure change in this problem is the compression of the air. The hydrostatic pressure from the water is minor—in fact, the water is almost identical to a piston compressing the gas. We would not have known this if we had not calculated \(p_{\mathrm{air}}\). The conclusion that the primary pressure change is the air compression might have been different if the starting condition had a lower pressure or the tank were taller.

Calculate and plot the uncertainty of the depth reading as a function of angle from 0° to 270°, which covers up to about 55 m (nitrogen narcosis usually is a factor when diving at or near 30 m, so normal recreational divers rarely go deeper than 30 m).

Figure 3.28: The Oris Aquis depth gauge, shown (left) at depth 0 m and (right) at depth 5 m. [Photographs omitted.]

p=0.1\,\mathrm{MPa}+(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})l, (3.61)

8. (OBJECTIVE: illustrate disconnect between weight and pressure of fluids) A 5-gallon glass carboy has a burst pressure of 4 atm, meaning that it will break if the pressure inside it reaches 4 atm. It is connected by a sealed connection to a 3/4-in-diameter plastic tube. The tube and carboy are filled with water. The end of the plastic tube is lifted up into the air until the carboy breaks. How high does the tube get? Is this different for a 1/4-in tube? Solution: The hydrostatic equation gives

p_2-p_1=\rho g(z_2-z_1). (3.68)

At the top of the tube (call this location 1), the pressure is atmospheric, \(p_1=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\). At the bursting point, \(p_2=4\,\mathrm{atm}\). Rearranging:

z_2-z_1=\frac{p_2-p_1}{\rho g}=\frac{4\,\mathrm{atm}-1\,\mathrm{atm}}{(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})}\times\left(\frac{0.1013\,\mathrm{MPa}}{1\,\mathrm{atm}}\right)=30.6\,\mathrm{m}. (3.69)

The hydrostatic equation does not predict a dependence on the diameter and there is no dependence on the diameter if the tube and carboy are infinitely rigid. This process is unrelated to the weight of the fluid—there is less weight in the tube than there is in the carboy. 9. (OBJECTIVE: Develop intuition for how a siphon will work depending on where the outlet is relative to the reservoir) Figure 3.30, p. 107 shows a container of maple syrup \(\rho=1370\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\) open to the atmosphere that is filled to a height of \(h_1=1\,\mathrm{m}\). You insert one end of a siphon tube filled with maple syrup into the reservoir at a depth \(h_4=0.8\,\mathrm{m}\) below the surface and raise the tube to height \(h_3=1\,\mathrm{m}\). The other end of the tube is placed \(h_2=1.5\,\mathrm{m}\) below the highest point of the tube. Assume that the tube is initially closed at B and the fluid in the siphon is initially at rest.

(a) What are the pressures at points A and B? (b) If the tube is opened to atmospheric pressure at B, will there be flow? Into or out of the tube? (c) To where should the end of the tube at B be moved to make the pressure at point B equal to atmospheric?



Figure 3.30: Siphon placed in maple syrup reservoir.

Solution: Defining \(z=0\) at the top of the reservoir of maple syrup, use the hydrostatic equation to define the pressure at point A:

(0.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})+0=p_A+(1370\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(1\,\mathrm{m})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_A=87900\,\mathrm{Pa}. (3.70)

At point B:

(0.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})+0=p_B+(1370\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(-0.5\,\mathrm{m})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_B=108000\,\mathrm{Pa}. (3.71)

If the tube at point B is opened and exposed to \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}=(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})\), fluid will flow out of the tube. Generally, as long as the other end of the siphon is below the free surface level in the reservoir, syrup will flow out of the reservoir through the tube. In fact, the syrup in the reservoir will continue to flow until either the water level decreases to the same elevation as the other end of the tube or there is no more syrup in the reservoir. Point B could be moved up 0.5 m, at which point \(p_B\) would equal atmospheric.

Chapter 4

Boats: Machines That Turn Nonuniform Pressure into Buoyancy to Transport Freight

A boat is a machine that turns the pressure distribution in a quiescent liquid into a stabilizing force and torque

Boats have existed since antiquity and travel and shipping over water have always been much easier than travel on air or land. For example, I got cargo quotes during summer 2022 to move 1500 tons of spring wheat from Duluth, MN to Toledo, OH. That volume of wheat would go in one barge for $23/ton, in 15 rail cars for $43/ton, and in 75 trucks for $200/ton. Shipping over water is clearly the cheapest. Cargo traveling from China to the US has historically cost about $0.50/kg ($450/ton) by container ship and $7/kg ($6350/ton) by air freight.

A large fraction of North American cities are located where they have easy access to water, for example the Atlantic Ocean (Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Washington, DC, Jacksonville, Miami), the Pacific Ocean (Seattle, Portland, San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego), the Great Lakes (Toronto, Milwaukee, Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland), and the Mississippi River (Minneapolis/St. Paul, St. Louis, Memphis, New Orleans). Similar observations can be made throughout the world. The simple explanation for this is that it is way cheaper and more convenient to build infrastructure at a location that has access to cheap and safe and efficient cargo.

All travel and shipping on boats is based on the very simple idea that there is a buoyancy force that lifts up objects when they are immersed in fluid. Archimedes’ principle states that an object immersed in a fluid in a gravitational field feels an upward buoyancy force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid (Figure 4.1, p. 109). When this buoyancy force balances the gravitational force, the object is in buoyant equilibrium and will neither rise nor descend. This is routinely stable when floating at the interface between a dense fluid (water) and a not-dense fluid (air), because any motion in the \(z\) direction will lead to a stabilizing force that returns the object to the equilibrium height. When the object is in a configuration in which the buoyancy force and the gravitational force combine to make no net torque, it is in rotational equilibrium, and if rotational perturbations create a torque that returns the object to the same configuration, that configuration is referred to as buoyantly stable.

Archimedes’ principle: the principle of buoyancy that an object immersed in fluid feels a buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid.

buoyancy: the force opposing gravity felt by an object immersed in a fluid, caused by the nonuniform hydrostatic pressure distribution.


PDF page 120 — verified

4.1. BOATS

as buoyantly stable.



Figure 4.1: An object immersed in a fluid feels a nonuniform pressure owing to the hydrostatic-equation solution for \(p(z)\). The net effect of this is called the buoyancy of the object. The gravity force is equivalent to a point force downward at the center of gravity, whereas the buoyancy force is equivalent to a point force upward at the center of buoyancy.

Two basic mechanisms can be used to ensure that an object floats on water—one is to construct the vessel out of a material whose density is lower than water, such as plastic foam or wood, and the other is to construct the vessel so that it is hollow. Vessels made from low-density materials are very robust and never sink, but work well only for very small vessels because of material limitations or stability performance. Larger vessels are typically hollow, meaning that they float only because they are filled with so much air. If these vessels take on water, they sink, because the construction materials themselves are denser than water (Figure 4.2, p. 109).



Figure 4.2: Left: foam is less dense than water, and will float regardless of configuration. Center: boats are usually made of metal that is denser than water, but both the hull and the open-air regions inside it displace water, leading to flotation. Right: boats sink when they take on water and the only volume of water displaced by the hull is the hull itself.

For large vessels, designing the boat hull and where cargo is stored is focused on (1) ensuring that the boat floats, i.e., that there is a stable height at which the boat’s buoyancy force balances the weight (called displacement) of the boat and its cargo; and (2) ensuring that the boat is buoyantly stable, meaning that if it rotates to one side it will return to its original position. For a rigid boat hull with fixed cargo, the boat has a well-defined weight and center of gravity. At steady-state, it floats at a height at which the displaced water has a weight equal to the vessel’s weight (Figure 4.3, p. 110). In that configuration, the hull has a center of buoyancy. The weight of the vessel is equivalent to a point force having the weight of the vessel, aligned in the

Hull design for buoyant stability is a central part of naval architecture and marine engineering, involving calculations of the locations of the center of gravity and center of buoyancy for the hull, and how they change when the boat rotates around longitudinal and transverse axes.

The engineering motivations of this chapter are floating vehicles like boats and dirigibles, which are simple and inexpensive tools that make transport of people and cargo easier, safer, and cheaper. The physics of this chapter involves applying the pressure distribution we derived in Chapter 3 and applying that pressure to a control surface to identify the force and torque that the pressure distribution makes on the surface. In making this calculation, we find that the equilibrium described by hydrostatics leads to a mathematical trick (the gradient-field theorem) which in this context is known as Archimedes’ principle:

\vec{F}_{\mathrm{buoyancy}}=\int_S-p\hat{n}\,dA=-\int_V\rho_{\mathrm{SF}}(z)\,\vec{g}\,dV, (4.1)

Total pressure surface force on CV = upward force equal to weight of displaced fluid.

which describes the buoyancy force from the pressure distribution in terms of a spatial integral inside the control volume using the density \(\rho_{\mathrm{SF}}\) of the fluid outside the control volume with the same \(z\).

center of buoyancy: the point around which the net buoyancy force of a body generates no torque.

4.2. HYDROSTATICS. REVISITED

Because we know the equilibrium in a uniform liquid between the force and torque from the hydrostatic pressure distribution (which is determined by an inconvenient vector surface integral) is equal to and opposite from the force and torque from the gravitational force (which is determined by a much-easier scalar volume integral), we find that we can determine the effects of pressure distributions without actually integrating them, and instead finding the gravity forces. This leads to the concept of buoyancy force, buoyancy torque, and the center of buoyancy of an object immersed in a fluid.

The premise, mathematical form, utility, and limitations of the hydrostatic model are described in Sidebar 4.1, p.114.

The key results of hydrostatics are the equilibrium between pressure and gravity, and the pressure distribution that results from that equilibrium

From last chapter, we learned that for static fluid there must be equilibrium \(\sum\vec F=0\):

\int_V\rho\vec{g}\,dV+\int_S-p\hat{n}\,dA=0, (4.3)

total gravitational body force on fluid; total pressure surface force on fluid.

where \(\rho\vec{g}\) is the volumetric gravitational body force applied to the fluid by the gravitational field and \(-p\hat n\) is the areal pressure surface force (or, equivalently, the normal surface stress) applied to the fluid by its surroundings. The gravitational acceleration vector \(\vec{g}=-g\hat z\). \(V\) denotes the control volume whereas \(S\) denotes the control surface.

This led to a general differential expression

\frac{dp}{dz}=-\rho g, (4.4)

and an integral expression that can be used if \(\rho\) is uniform:

p+\rho gz=k. (4.5)

Equation 4.3: integral hydrostatic equilibrium equation for a control volume.

volumetric: related to volume, or per unit volume.

Equation 4.4: differential hydrostatic relation.

Equation 4.5: integral hydrostatic relation, uniform density.

Equation 4.5 can be thought of as a conservation of energy equation that shows: if we move fluid up in a gravitational field (increasing gravitational potential energy) we reduce the pressure (decreasing the stored ability to do mechanical work) commensurately.

body force: a force that acts directly upon all of the mass within a control volume. Examples include gravity and electromagnetic forces. These forces act directly (gravity) or indirectly (electromagnetics) over lengths much longer than molecular diameters. Compare to surface force.

areal: related to area, or per unit area.

normal: orthogonal; perpendicular.


PDF page 123 — verified

4.3. PRESSURE, REVISITED

The definition of pressure is that it describes an isotropic force per unit area that is exerted on any plane in or on the boundary of a fluid

Recall that, if we consider any point \((x,y,z)\) in space in or at the boundary of a fluid, and consider a plane intersecting that point as defined by the outward normal \(\hat n\), the definition of pressure \(p(x,y,z)\) is that \(p\) is a scalar that defines the stress \(p\hat n\) that the “inside” fluid exerts on that plane. By definition, the “outside” fluid exerts an equal and opposite stress i.e., \(-p\hat n\). We have already used this definition in deriving the hydrostatic equation and in the second term of Equation (4.3). This same concept can be applied to determine the total force a fluid exerts on any boundary by integrating \(p\hat n\) along that surface, and we can determine the (equal and opposite) total force the boundary exerts on the fluid by integrating \(-p\hat n\).

The pressure distribution in a fluid can be integrated to determine the force the fluid exerts on a boundary surface

Hydrostatic pressure distributions explain the equilibrium positions of columns of fluid, and the pressure distribution in the atmosphere and underwater. Hydrostatic pressure distributions describe how and where floating objects float. From an engineering standpoint, though, we cannot forget that there is more to it than that. Hydrostatic pressures and forces can be enormous—enough to destroy objects, power powerplants, et cetera. We need to be able to predict the forces that fluids apply to objects immersed in fluids, as well as the forces that fluids apply to the boundaries that contain them. These forces control whether an object will explode when rising in the air, or implode when sinking in water. These forces also form the engineering constraints that define how thick the wall of a water tower or a dam has to be.

In fact, we already calculated the force exerted by pressure on a surface when we considered an infinitesimal control volume to describe the hydrostatic equation; however, we chose a control volume whose geometry was so easy that we essentially avoided using vector calculus. Now we will consider the surface more generally, which will require a vector treatment.

The pressure force a fluid exerts on a surface is in the direction of the unit outward normal of a fluid control surface. Taking \(\hat n\) by convention as the unit outward normal defined for the control surface, the pressure stress the fluid exerts on the surface is given by \(p\hat n\) and the equal and opposite stress applied by the surroundings of the control surface on the fluid is given by \(-p\hat n\). In general, the force a fluid exerts on a surface is given by a vector integral:

\vec{F}=\int_S p(x,y,z)\hat{n}(x,y,z)\,dA, (4.6)

where \(\hat n\) is the unit outward normal defined in the fluid. When \(\hat n\) and \(p\)

stress: in Newtonian fluid mechanics, the word stress is used to denote either (a) a scalar force per unit area on a plane, (b) a vector force per unit area on a plane, and (c) a dyadic tensor that fully describes all forces per unit area that would be applied on any plane. Fluid mechanicians are cavalier about this because so many fluids are effectively incompressible and isotropic. Solid and continuum mechanicians call (a) a stress component, (b) a traction, and (c) the stress tensor. So beware of this in MAE3270 and MAE3280 and MAE4230.

pressure: usually used to mean static pressure but can be used metaphorically to describe any force per unit area or energy per unit volume.

hydrostatic: relating to fluids at rest.

control volume: a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

unit outward normal: a vector of length one that points normal to a control surface, and points outward, away from the control volume.

integral formula for the force on a surface caused by pressure

are uniform (for example a horizontal planar surface), the total force is given simply by the product of the pressure, area, and unit outward normal:

\vec{F}=pA\hat{n}. (4.7)

For a planar surface with nonuniform pressure, \(\hat n\) is still uniform, and the total force is given by a scalar integral of the pressure:

\vec{F}=\left[\int_S p(x,y,z)\,dA\right]\hat{n}. (4.8)

scalar integral of the pressure.

Several example problems are provided to illustrate how the force on an object can be obtained by integrating the pressure force. Example Problem 4.1 (p.114) shows an example of integrating a force on a horizontal planar wall. Example Problem 4.2 (p.115) shows an example of integrating a force on a planar wall not aligned with the coordinate system. Example Problem 4.3 (p.116) shows an example of integrating a force over an entire object.

For a curved surface, \(\hat n\) varies across the surface, and the pressure in general may be nonuniform, and the full vector integration must be performed. Example Problem 4.4 (p.117) shows an example of integrating a force on a curved wall.

The net effect of a hydrostatic pressure distribution is that any object (or, more generally, any control volume) immersed in a fluid feels an upward “buoyancy” force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid

Recall that for a control volume drawn in a body of static fluid there must be equilibrium \((\sum\vec F=0)\):

\int_V\rho\vec{g}\,dV+\int_S-p\hat{n}\,dA=0, (4.21)

total gravitational force on fluid in CV; total pressure surface force on fluid.

As written, Equation 4.21 is meant to describe integrals carried out over the control volume using the properties inside the control volume. Thus here \(\rho\) describes the density inside the control volume. For a single fluid, of course, \(\rho\) inside the control volume and outside the control volume at the same \(z\) are equal, so Equation (4.21) can be written in terms of the density of the surrounding fluid at the same \(z\), which we denote \(\rho_{\mathrm{SF}}(z)\):

\int_V\rho_{\mathrm{SF}}(z)\vec{g}\,dV+\int_S-p\hat{n}\,dA=0, (4.22)

integral hydrostatic equilibrium equation for a control volume.

4.5. ARCHIMEDES’ LAW

SIDEBAR 4.1: ENGINEERING MODELS

Hydrostatic Equation

Premise: The hydrostatic model describes the pressure distribution in quiescent fluid

The hydrostatic model is a description of fluid that is motionless; it establishes the simplest continuum description of a fluid, incorporating the definition of pressure into an expression of static equilibrium for a fluid.

Mathematical form: Assuming \(\vec u=0\) and setting \(\sum\vec F=0\) on a control volume leads to the hydrostatic equation

If we assume fluid is not moving, the only force on the fluid is pressure, and an equilibrium analysis of a differential or finite control volume leads to the hydrostatic equation in differential or integral form, respectively:

\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}=-\rho g;\qquad p+\int_{z_0}^{z}\rho g\,dz=k. (4.2)

Utility: The hydrostatic equation describes pressure distributions with altitude and informs calculations of forces on fluid containers

The hydrostatic equation describes pressure variation with altitude in the atmosphere, and the pressure variation with depth underwater. It describes how pressure varies in pipes in buildings, and why a dam leads to high-pressure water for energy generation.

Limitations: The hydrostatic equation becomes invalid when the dynamic pressure or viscous stresses become significant relative to pressure differences associated with height

Moving fluid has a dynamic pressure \(\frac12\rho U^2\), and fluid that is deforming generates viscous stresses whose components are proportional to components of the velocity gradient e.g., \(\mu\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\). For quiescent fluid, these terms are identically zero. If fluid is moving a small amount and we still want to use the hydrostatic equation, it is valid only when these terms are still very small relative to \(\rho g\Delta z\) terms and thus can be ignored in terms of their effect on pressure. Or equivalently, the magnitude of these terms tell us the distance \(\Delta z\) over which the hydrostatic equation is relevant. For example, the hydrostatic equation is a poor description of how pressure varies from the bottom to the top of an airplane wing, because \(\frac12\rho U^2\) can’t be ignored for flow over an airplane wing (and in fact it is much bigger than \(\rho g\) times the vertical distance between bottom and top of the wing). The hydrostatic equation is a good description of how the pressure at the altitude of the plane differs from the pressure at sea level. There are also other forces that could be applied to fluids (electric fields, magnets, osmotic pressure) that are all ignored here as they are not central to most mechanical engineering fluid mechanical problems.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 4.1

Consider a beaker with radius \(R=4\,\mathrm{cm}\) filled with water to height \(h=20\,\mathrm{cm}\) in surroundings at \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\). What is the pressure force on the bottom surface? Solution: The pressure at the bottom is \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\). Because this pressure is uniform across the surface, and because the surface is a flat surface whose unit outward normal is \(-\hat z\), the integral becomes simple multiplication:

\int_S-p\hat{n}\,dA=pA\hat{n}=\left[(.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})+(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(0.2\,\mathrm{m})\right][\pi(.04\,\mathrm{m})^2](-\hat{z})=-518\,\mathrm{N}\hat{z}. (4.9)

Note this force is more than 100 pounds! Hydrostatic forces tend to be large. We just don’t notice them because these forces are applied on all surfaces so they cancel out in terms of net forces.

Editorial source note: Eq. (4.9) changes sign between \(\int_S-p\hat n\,dA\) and \(pA\hat n\). For uniform pressure and a fixed normal, the integral equals \(-pA\hat n\). The reported downward force is the water’s force on the bottom; using the water volume’s outward bottom normal \(\hat n=-\hat z\), that force is \(pA\hat n\), whereas \(-pA\hat n\) is the opposite force on the water. The source chain is retained literally.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 4.4

Consider a pirate’s treasure chest (Figure 4.6, p. 117) sitting at the bottom of a pool of water such that the base of its lid is d=10 m deep. The main body of the chest measures b=18” deep × c=36” wide × a=12” tall. The lid can be approximated as a half-cylinder with b/2=9” radius and c=36” length. Integrate along the lid surface to quantify the force that the water applies to the top of the lid.



Figure 4.6: Image of a pirate treasure chest.

Solution: Define z=0 at the base of the center of the lid. The semicircle defined by the lid can be written as x=r cos θ and z=r sin θ if we take the center of the lid as x=0. The unit outward normal measured from the fluid points toward the origin: n̂=(−cos θ,−sin θ). The area of a differential surface element is given by rc dθ. The pressure is given by \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}-\rho g(z-d)=p_{\mathrm{atm}}-\rho g(-10+r\sin\theta)\). Separating the x and z components, the integrals become:

F_x=\int_0^\pi p\hat{n}\,dA=[p_{\mathrm{atm}}-\rho g(-d+r\sin\theta)](-\cos\theta)rc\,d\theta=0. (4.17)

because the integrals of cos θ and sin θ cos θ from 0 to π are both zero, and

F_z=\int_0^\pi p\hat{n}\,dA=\int_0^\pi[p_{\mathrm{atm}}-\rho g(-d+r\sin\theta)](-\sin\theta)rc\,d\theta=[rc(-p_{\mathrm{atm}}-d\rho g+r\rho g\sin\theta)\sin\theta]_0^\pi (4.18)

for the z component. The resulting integral gives

F_z=-2p_{\mathrm{atm}}rc-2drc\rho g+\frac{1}{2}\pi r^2c\rho g\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F_z=-bc\left[p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho g\left(d-\frac{\pi}{8}b\right)\right] (4.19)

The lengths in SI are b=18” (0.0254 m/in)=0.46 m, c=36” (0.0254 m/in)=0.91 m. The force evaluates to

F_z=-(0.46\,\mathrm{m})(0.91\,\mathrm{m})\left[(0.1013\,\mathrm{MPa})+(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})\left(10\,\mathrm{m}-\frac{\pi}{8}(0.46\,\mathrm{m})\right)\right] =83\,\mathrm{kN}. (4.20)

This is about 20,000 pounds. This is not necessarily the net force one would have to overcome to open the treasure chest—we calculated the force pushing down on the lid, but we have not calculated the force pushing up on the other side of the lid.

Editorial note: Eq. (4.17) omits the integral sign before its expanded integrand. Eq. (4.18) places the integrand itself inside evaluation brackets rather than an antiderivative; that bracket would give zero at both endpoints. A correct antiderivative is \(rc[(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+d\rho g)\cos\theta+r\rho g(\theta/2-\sin(2\theta)/4)]\). Eq. (4.19) gives the consistent integral result. Eq. Equation (4.22) now relates the total pressure force on the control volume to the gravitational body force of the fluid that would have filled the control volume, whether that fluid is really there or if that space has been replaced by an object. We refer to this hypothetical fluid as the displaced fluid. Rearranging this, we can write an expression for the net force exerted by the pressure distribution in terms of this imagined gravitational body force:

\vec{F}_{\mathrm{buoyancy}}=\int_S-p\hat{n}\,dA=-\int_V\rho_{\mathrm{SF}}(z)\vec{g}\,dV (4.23)

total pressure surface force on CV

upwards force equal to weight of displaced fluid

where \(F_{\mathrm{buoyancy}}\) is the force exerted on the control volume by the pressure distribution in the fluid, commonly referred to as the buoyancy force. Going from Equation (4.21) to Equation (4.23) is mathematically trivial—we just moved a term to the other side. However, these two forms of the equation have very different intended use and the argument that switched from the fluid inside the control volume to the fluid outside the control volume is important. Whereas Equation (4.21) showed how a control volume enclosing fluid has an equilibrium between the pressure force on the fluid and the gravitational force on the same fluid, Equation (4.23) shows that any control volume enclosed by static fluid must have a net pressure force on it that is equal in magnitude to the gravity force that would have been felt by the same fluid if it filled that control volume. In other words, a hot air balloon floating in air feels a buoyancy force equal to a balloon’s volume worth of air, and a dolphin swimming in the ocean feels a buoyancy force equal to a dolphin’s volume worth of seawater. Whatever material fills the control volume will also feel a gravitational force, so the net force on the contents of a control volume are

buoyancy force (points up)

\vec{F}_{\mathrm{total}}=\int_V\rho_{\mathrm{CV}}(z)\vec{g}\,dV-\int_V\rho_{\mathrm{SF}}(z)\vec{g}\,dV=\int_V(\rho_{\mathrm{CV}}(z)-\rho_{\mathrm{SF}}(z))\vec{g}\,dV (4.24)

weight of control volume (points down)

where \(\rho_{\mathrm{CV}}\) is the density of whatever is inside the control volume, and \(\rho_{\mathrm{SF}}(z)\) is the density of the fluid surrounding the control volume, at the same z. Equation (4.24) shows that the net force on the contents of a control volume is given by the downward gravitational force on the control volume contents combined with the net upward force exerted on the control surface by the surrounding fluid. So the net force on the hot air balloon is a downward gravitational force given by the weight of the balloon, and an upward force given by the weight of a balloon’s volume worth of air. The net force on the dolphin is a downward gravitational force given by the weight of the dolphin, and an upward force given by the weight of a dolphin’s worth of seawater. This net force is prescribed by the density difference between the control volume contents and the surrounding fluid. If these densities are equal, the system is in equilibrium and there is no net force—this is the result in a uniform body of liquid. If the control volume contents have a lower density than the surrounding fluid (e.g., a bubble in water), then the buoyancy force pushing up is larger in magnitude than the downward gravity force, and the bubble feels a net upward force. If the control volume contents have a higher density than the surrounding fluid (e.g., a steel ball in water) then the buoyancy force up is smaller in magnitude than the gravity force, and the steel ball feels a net downward force. We know that these objects are not in equilibrium and will be accelerated by this force imbalance, but we don’t know anything more about this system yet because we have no equations yet to manage fluids that are moving (that will come later). Our hydrostatic analysis so far only tells us what happens during that condition in which the fluid and control volume are motionless.

integral hydrostatic equilibrium equation rewritten to show the net pressure force on a control volume, independent of CV contents

Force on a control volume embedded in a fluid, agnostic to contents of CV.

buoyancy: the force opposing gravity felt by an object immersed in a fluid, caused by the nonuniform hydrostatic pressure distribution.

control volume: a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

control surface: the surface that encloses a control volume.

equilibrium: a state in which forces are balanced.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 4.5

The net force is the difference between these two, although the air term hardly matters: \(F_z=(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})\frac43\pi(0.01\,\mathrm{m})^3(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})=0.04\,\mathrm N\).

This analysis can be summarized with the statement that an object immersed in a fluid feels a net upward force from the pressure distribution that is equal to and opposite from the gravity force that would have been felt by the displaced fluid. This is called Archimedes’ principle. Critically, Archimedes’ principle means that, no matter how complicated the control volume geometry and no matter how annoying the vector surface integral of p n̂ would be, we don’t have to perform that vector integral. Instead, we can perform a scalar integral of ρg over the volume, which is almost always easier. Archimedes’ principle: the principle of buoyancy that an object immersed in fluid feels a buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid.

YEET: I do not know what this means, nor whether I am using it correctly, nor do I want to. I am not trying to be cool. I am making fun of you.

This so-called buoyancy force is not a new force; it is simply a way of describing the integrated effect of the pressure distribution that we already calculated; this is shown schematically in Figure 4.8, p. 122. The power of Archimedes’ principle is that it gives us a result for the net effect of the surface pressures without calculating the pressures directly or going through the surface integral required to generate their net effect. In the language of MATH1920, Archimedes’ principle is a specific example of the gradient-field theorem (Sidebar 4.2, p. 120).

Archimedes’ principle dictates how high a hot-air balloon or dirigible/zeppelin/blimp will fly, how deep we dive when scuba diving, and at what height a boat floats on top of water, as a few examples. Example Problem 4.6 (p. 121) shows a buoyancy problem with an added external force.

A body in equilibrium with a multi-fluid system must rest at a position such that the total weight of the fluid(s) displaced is equal to the weight of the object.

A direct consequence of Archimedes’ principle is a description of how objects float at the interface between two fluids, most often the interface between water and air, which is where boats and icebergs and humans float.

Archimedes’ principle: the principle of buoyancy that an object immersed in fluid feels a buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid.

For example, ice has a density approximately 90% that of water, so ice cubes and icebergs float such that about 90% of their volume is below the water surface. A polystyrene pool noodle is about 5% the density of water, so pool noodles float such that about 5% of their volume is below the water surface. Example Problem 4.7 (p. 121) shows a buoyancy problem with multiple fluids.

SIDEBAR 4.2: FUNDAMENTALS

Gradient-Field Theorem

The gradient-field theorem relates the surface integral of a scalar field multiplied by the unit outward normal to a volume integral of the scalar’s gradient field. The gradient of a scalar field results in a vector field; this vector field can be used to evaluate the surface integral of that scalar field multiplied by the unit outward normal. The gradient-field theorem is written in general for a scalar field q as:

\int_V\nabla q\,dV=\int_S q\hat{n}\,dA (4.25)

As is the case for the divergence theorem, the gradient-field theorem is useful for switching back and forth between volume and surface properties. Whereas the divergence theorem is useful when interested in the surface integral of a property that is dotted against the unit outward normal (i.e., orthogonally projected onto the surface), for example a flux across a surface, the gradient-field theorem is useful when interested in the surface integral of a property multiplied by the unit outward normal, for example a surface pressure. For example, the hydrostatic equation prescribes the pressure as a function of space; the gradient-field theorem directly relates the surface integral of the pressure on a surface to the volume integral of ρg, which is the gradient of the pressure. Archimedes’ principle lets one replace the surface integral of p (which can be a pain for complicated surface geometries) with the volume integral of ρg, and because g is uniform, this effectively is the volume integral of a scalar. Written specifically for a hydrostatic case with ∇p=−ρg, the gradient-field theorem helps us identify the force a fluid applies to a control volume:

\vec{F}=\int_S(-p)\hat{n}\,dA=\int_V\nabla(-p)\,dV=\int_V\rho g\hat{z}\,dV (4.26)

and this force is equal in magnitude to (but in the opposite direction of) the gravitational force on the fluid in the control volume. For uniform ρ and g, this gives a total force ρgV ẑ. Thus the pressure force applied to a fluid control volume by the surrounding pressure (\(\int_S p\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA\)) is equal in magnitude to (but of opposite sign to) the gravitational force that would be applied to the enclosed volume if it was filled with the same liquid as its surroundings. This balance is not a new result: we used this balance to derive the differential form of the hydrostatic equation in the first place. But now that we have worked it all out, this example uses a hydrostatics result that we have seen before as an illustrative case of how a scalar and its gradient can be related by surface and volume integrals. Archimedes’ principle is the combination of two analyses: (1) the gradient-field theorem applied to a hydrostatic system combined with (2) the observation that when we consider a motionless object immersed in fluid, the presence of the object does not change the pressure distribution outside it. So the force on an immersed motionless object is identical to the force that would be applied to a control volume filled with the same liquid as its environment.

For those interested in the vector calculus, the gradient-field theorem is really just a special case of the divergence theorem applied to an isotropic dyadic field. If one uses qI as the field in the divergence theorem, a couple of vector identities will get you to Equation (B.111). The force per unit area caused by pressure is an isotropic dyadic and given by −pI, so the version of the divergence theorem that is most immediately useful to evaluate the integrated pressure force on a surface is the gradient-field theorem.

Editorial note: the source phrase “ρg, which is the gradient of the pressure” conflicts with its displayed ∇(−p)=ρg ẑ (equivalently, ∇p=−ρg ẑ). The phrase has been preserved literally above; the consistent statement is that ρg ẑ is the gradient of −p, or the negative gradient of p.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 4.6

Frozen sea water has a density near 925 kg/m³ whereas seawater has a density near 1030 kg/m³. You see a polar bear standing on an ice floe (Figure 4.7, p. 121) that has an area of 100 m² that extends 20 cm above the ocean. What is the mass of the ice floe? If the bear (polar bears weigh about 1000 lbs) jumped off the floe, how much would the floe rise?

Figure 4.7: A polar bear. I mean, that is just... adorable.

Photograph omitted.

Solution: The volume of ice above the water is given by:

V_{\mathrm{ice}}-V_{\mathrm{water}}=(100\,\mathrm{m^2})(0.2\,\mathrm{m})=20\,\mathrm{m^3}. (4.27)

The forces in the z direction sum to zero:

W_{\mathrm{bear}}+\rho_{\mathrm{ice}}gV_{\mathrm{ice}}=\rho_{\mathrm{water}}g(V_{\mathrm{ice}}-20\,\mathrm{m^3}) (4.28)

V_{\mathrm{ice}}=\frac{-W_{\mathrm{bear}}-(20\,\mathrm{m^3})\rho_{\mathrm{water}}g}{g(\rho_{\mathrm{ice}}-\rho_{\mathrm{water}})} (4.29)

m_{\mathrm{ice}}=\rho_{\mathrm{ice}}V_{\mathrm{ice}} (4.30)

The volume of submerged ice that comes out of the water when the bear jumps off is

V=-\frac{W_{\mathrm{bear}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{water}}g} (4.31)

and the distance the floe moves is

\Delta z=\frac{W_{\mathrm{bear}}}{A_{\mathrm{floe}}\rho_{\mathrm{water}}g} (4.32)

V_{\mathrm{ice}}=\frac{-1000\,\mathrm{lb}\left(\frac{\mathrm{N}}{0.22\,\mathrm{lb}}\right)-20\,\mathrm{m^3}(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(1030\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})}{(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(925\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}-1030\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})}=196\,\mathrm{m^3}, (4.33)

m_{\mathrm{ice}}=(925\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(196\,\mathrm{m^3})=1.8\times10^5\,\mathrm{kg}, (4.34)

\Delta z=\frac{1000\,\mathrm{lb}\left(\frac{\mathrm{N}}{0.22\,\mathrm{lb}}\right)}{(100\,\mathrm{m^2})(1030\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})}=4.5\,\mathrm{mm}. (4.35)

Editorial note: evaluating the displayed Eq. (4.33) with the printed inputs gives about 200.5 m³ (using the shown 1000 lb × N/(0.22 lb) conversion), not 196 m³. The printed result is retained above; Eq. (4.34) then uses that printed 196 m³.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 4.7

A layer of mineral oil (ρ=800 kg/m³) rests on top of a layer of perflubron (ρ=1930 kg/m³). A droplet of water is injected into the fluid, at which point buoyancy and gravity cause the droplet to move until it comes to equilibrium. At equilibrium, when the droplet has come to rest, what fraction of the droplet is in the mineral oil and what fraction of the droplet is in the perflubron? Solution: The integral of the density of the material in the control volume must equal the integral of the density of the material outside the control volume at the corresponding z. If we define x as the fraction in mineral oil, then 800x+1930(1−x)=1000, from which we calculate x=0.82. The droplet rests in between the two layers, with 82% of the volume above the interface, in the mineral oil, and 18% below the interface in the perflubron.

The positive magnitude of the volume that emerges when the bear leaves is \(W_{\mathrm{bear}}/(\rho_{\mathrm{water}}g)\), consistent with the positive rise in Eq. (4.32). The present sign is uncertain source transcription, not a verified negative volume.

4.6. HYDRAULIC ACTUATION



Figure 4.8: The pressure distribution on an object is nonuniform, and the net force points upward with magnitude equal to the weight of the displaced liquid. This is called Archimedes’ law.

The hydrostatic equation shows that horizontal fluid connections equate pressures on either end of a fluid (not force)

The hydrostatic equation p+ρgz=k specifies that p is a function of z only and therefore independent of geometric parameters such as the shape of a container or the bore of a cylinder. This is in essence a restatement of Pascal’s law. Example Problem 4.8 (p. 123), for example, illustrates the hydrostatic paradox, which results from this conclusion. This has been termed a paradox because, to some, this is counterintuitive—although the weights of fluids are different, the force on the bottom surface is the same. Forces, of course, always balance at equilibrium, and the reconciliation between the fact that the weights of liquid are different but the forces on the bottom surface are the same comes from the fact that the pressure applies an upward force to side walls of the narrow container and a downward force to the side walls of the wide container.

Returning to the hydrostatic equation, this equation gives a relation for fluid pressure as a function of z and only z. This means that if we change the area over which fluid pressure is applied (for example as in Figure 4.10, p. 124), it is straightforward to change the magnitude of force being applied—this is a simple mechanical advantage device like a pulley or lever. For a pressure that can be approximated with a uniform value p, this gives

p=\frac{F_1}{A_1}=\frac{F_2}{A_2} (4.36)

which means

F_2=F_1\frac{A_2}{A_1} (4.37)

\(\overleftrightarrow{T}=-p\overleftrightarrow{I}\) for quiescent fluid.

\(\vec{\vec{T}}=-p\mathbf{I}\) for quiescent fluid.

force relation for two sides of a hydraulic actuator


PDF page 134 — verified

4.6. HYDRAULIC ACTUATION

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 4.8

The three containers shown in (a)–(c) (Figure 4.9, p. 123) have identical bottom surfaces (and surface areas) but different side geometries as well as different masses and weights of water inside them. Which of these containers has the largest force F on the bottom surface? Or are two of them the same? Or all the same?



Figure 4.9: Three containers with identical bottom geometries and water heights but different side geometries and water weights.

Solution: All the same. Pressure is a function of the height and density as described by the hydrostatic equation. The question doesn’t ask what is the total force caused by all of the fluid (that would be simply equal to the weight of the fluid). The question asks about the fraction of that force that is applied to the bottom surface of the vessel; the differences in weight between (a), (b), and (c) are borne by the sides of the channel. See https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J7ymn6f£2B18 for a fast, silent demonstration. See https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6zeHWVUixXoc#t=3m49s for an equivalent but longer demonstration with narration and more detailed discussion and also giraffes and hydraulic jacks. That demonstration uses a piston to measure the force on the bottom surface alone on a scale.

This is the operational principle behind hydraulic actuators like a hydraulic jack. As long as the solid container is strong enough to hold the pressure of the liquid, one can increase the force arbitrarily. The forces on the two pistons do not match, but the system is in equilibrium (there is a force on the left wall that balances the forces). This system also has matched work input and output because if we displace piston 1 by length d₁, we will displace piston 2 by d₁A₁/A₂, so the work is equal to F₁d₁ on both sides of the system.

A tube with two different bores separated by a solid piston can be used as a pressure amplifier (Figure 4.11, p. 125). Here, force equilibrium requires that

F_2+F_3=F_1\quad\Rightarrow\quad p_2A_2+p_{\mathrm{atm}}(A_1-A_2)=p_1A_1\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{p_2-p_{\mathrm{atm}}}{p_1-p_{\mathrm{atm}}}=\frac{A_1}{A_2}. (4.38)

pressure–area relation for a pressure amplifier

From this, we see that the gauge pressure is amplified by the area ratio of the solid piston.

gauge pressure: pressure difference relative to atmospheric pressure.

3. (OBJECTIVE: Calculate forces from hydrostatics, noting how large forces can be with unremarkable pressures) A Kugel fountain is a prime example of a fluid’s ability to transfer pressure. A granite sphere (ρ=2700 kg/m³) is “levitated” by pressurized water reservoir (Figure 4.20, p. 131). The ball rests in a socket that covers some area of the sphere. If the diameter of the sphere is 2 m, and the socket covers one tenth of the total area of the sphere, what is the water gauge pressure necessary to run the fountain? You will find that (a) hydrostatic variation with height is unimportant in this problem and can be ignored and (b) the bottom of the sphere can be approximated as horizontal to a reasonable approximation, and that prevents us from needing lots of integrals.

Figure 4.20: Kugel fountain!!!

Photograph omitted.

Solution: A uniform pressure applied over the entirety of a solid object always integrates to zero, so the atmospheric pressure can be ignored. The equilibrium comes from a balance between the weight of the sphere and the force caused by the gauge pressure of the water. The weight of the sphere is

F_g=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\rho_{\mathrm{granite}}g (4.53)

The gauge pressure in the reservoir applies a force normal to the surface. It technically is curved, but the areas in this problem were chosen so that it is a fair assumption to just treat the bottom as if it were horizontal. In that case the analysis is scalar:

F_{\mathrm{water}}=\frac{1}{10}4\pi r^2p_{\mathrm{water}} (4.54)

where \(p_{\mathrm{water}}\) is gauge pressure.

\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\rho_{\mathrm{granite}}g=\frac{1}{10}4\pi r^2p_{\mathrm{water}} (4.55)

Solving for \(p_{\mathrm{water}}\) and substituting d=2r,

p_{\mathrm{water}}=\frac{5}{3}d\rho_{\mathrm{granite}}g=\frac{5}{3}(2\,\mathrm{m})(2700\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}) (4.56)

leading finally to

p_{\mathrm{water}}=88.2\,\mathrm{kPa} (4.57)

What might seem remarkable is that this gauge pressure is less than 1 atm, and thus what is required for a Kugel fountain is typically a pump discharging 50–100 gallons per minute at a gauge pressure less than 1 atm; such a pump isn’t remarkable or expensive. What is expensive about a Kugel fountain is a granite ball that is precisely spherical enough to rest and rotate in its socket.

Currently accounting for the curvature would show that actually the pressure needed is about 10% higher than our calculated result, because as we move up the side of the sphere the component of the force pointing up is decreasing.

4. (OBJECTIVE: Link Archimedes’ principle to the operation of the Falkirk Wheel) A caisson holding 500 tons (4.5×10⁶ N) of water when full, has a 10-ton (1×10⁵ N) boat added to it. What volume and weight of water is displaced by the boat? What is the net weight carried by the caisson with the boat? Solution: At equilibrium, the weight of the boat is balanced by the nonuniform pressure distribution in the water: these are at equilibrium when the displaced water weighs 10 tons. That volume of water is

V=\frac{W}{\rho}=\frac{1\times10^5\,\mathrm{N}}{1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}}=100\,\mathrm{m^3}.

The total weight the caisson holds is still 500 tons; now it is 490 tons of water and 10 tons of boat.

5. (OBJECTIVE: use Archimedes’ principle to link weight, volume, and displaced volumes of water in different scenarios) Professor Zehnder sits in a raft floating in a swimming pool. He holds a steel ball in his hands. He throws the steel ball out of the raft and onto the ground that surrounds the swimming pool. Is the height of the water in the swimming pool higher after the ball is thrown, lower after the ball is thrown, or the same before and after? Solution: The height of the water is lower after Zehnder throws the ball. When the ball is added to the raft, the raft sinks down into the water until an additional volume of water is displaced to counteract the weight of the ball, and the water level rises. When the ball is removed, the raft rises and the water level lowers.

6. (OBJECTIVE: Relate hydrostatic forces to other mechanical forces) A tire pressure gauge shown in Figure 4.21, p. 132. One end of the pressure gauge is connected to the tire, and the air pressure from the tire depresses a plunger of area 10 mm² connected to a spring with a spring constant is 200 N/m. If the tire pressure is 3×10⁵ Pa, by what distance is the plunger displaced?



Figure 4.21: Analog “pencil” style tire pressure gauge—schematic.

Solution: The force applied to the plunger from the tire side is F=(3×10⁵ Pa)(10×10⁻⁶ m²)=3 N whereas the force from the atmospheric side is F=(1×10⁵ Pa)(10×10⁻⁶ m²)=1 N. So the net force of 2 N must be balanced by F=kd from the spring. For k=200 N/m, d=1 cm.

Chapter 5

Carburetors and Torque Converters: Machines That Use Accelerating Fluid to Generate Pressure Changes

A carburetor is the standard way to mix fuel and oxidizer in a small engine

Small engines, like the single-cylinder, two-stroke engine in Figure 5.1, p. 136, require that fuel and air be mixed before they are injected into the combustion chamber. A carburetor is a simple and inexpensive way to mix liquid fuel into a stream of air, such that the flowrate of fuel injected into the airstream is proportional to the flowrate of air. Whereas a rocket nozzle is an example of a fluid machine that converts pressure into speed in a compressible flow context, including supersonic flow, for the purpose of thrust, a carburetor is an example of a fluid machine that uses a Venturi to convert pressure into speed in a largely incompressible flow context, using only subsonic flow, for the purpose of mixing two streams of fluids in a controlled manner.

carburetor: a device that mixes fuel and air by passing the air through a Venturi to create a low-pressure region which sucks liquid fuel from a reservoir into the flow. Common in small engines e.g., chainsaws, lawn equipment, motorcycles.

fluid machine: a machine that adds energy to or extracts energy from a fluid.

A carburetor injects fuel into an airstream by connecting the throat of a Venturi to a tank of fuel. The Venturi is a narrowing of a tube—in this case the tube carrying the air intake—that causes the fluid to accelerate and decrease in pressure. You can see it on the side of a lawnmower (Figure 5.2a, p. 136) or find one when taking apart a chainsaw (Figure 5.2b, p. 136). It is directly underneath the air filter on many pre-1980 cars, but not found on current cars, which use fuel injectors. Carburetors work because the decreased pressure of the air in the throat draws fuel into the airstream, and the fuel drawn in is proportional to the airflow.

Venturi: a tube with a constriction whose purpose is to generate a low-pressure region in the throat.

fuel injector: a device that injects fuel directly into a combustion chamber, usually with a spray atomizer.

A Venturi is a tube with a neck region that causes the pressure of the fluid to go down in the neck

If we take a tube and decrease its cross-sectional area in a neck region (A₂<A₁), fluid flowing through the tube will go down in pressure in the neck region. The fluid in the neck moves faster as illustrated by the conservation of mass equation. If we assume that density is approximately uniform:

\rho U_1A_1=\rho U_2A_2\quad\Rightarrow\quad U_2>U_1. (5.1)

conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.


PDF page 147 — verified

5.1. CARBURETORS



Figure 5.1: Exterior view (left) and cutaway view (right) of a single-cylinder two-stroke engine. A mixture of air, gas, and oil must be generated for the engine intake; typically for an engine like this the mixing of gas and oil occurs in the fuel line, and the mixing of fuel/oil and air occurs in the carburetor. Some of these engines use a one-way check valve at the intake port; some simply use the piston to cover the intake port during specific portions of the stroke.

Figure 5.2: Left: (a) a carburetor on a lawnmower. Right: (b) a carburetor from a chainsaw.

Photographs omitted.


PDF page 148 — verified

5.1. CARBURETORS

The Bernoulli equation, which describes the pressure variation in the converging portion of a Venturi at high Reynolds number:

p_1+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_1^2+\rho gz_1=p_2+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_2^2+\rho gz_2, (5.2)

illustrates that the acceleration of the fluid (U₂>U₁; kinetic energy has increased) coincides with a pressure decrease (p₂<p₁; stored ability to do mechanical work has decreased).

A carburetor connects a fuel line to the throat of a Venturi

The simplest carburetor design (which you might find in a cheap lawnmower or chainsaw, as in Figure 5.2, p. 136) consists of a fuel line connected to the throat of a Venturi. In practice, the geometry of these carburetors can be convoluted and compact; to understand the flow more easily we typically envision a simplified geometry as depicted in Figure 5.3, p. 137. Carburetors always have a throttle valve between the Venturi and the intake manifold; this throttle valve controls both the air and fuel flow in proportion. The throttle valve is what is controlled by the accelerator pedal in an old car, the twist throttle on a motorcycle, or the trigger of a chainsaw. Carburetors often also have a choke valve between the Venturi and the inlet air coming from the air filter. The choke valve blocks the airflow into the engine but allows fuel flow—this lets the user inject excess fuel into the engine, which can be necessary when starting a cold engine.

Reynolds number: Re=ρUℓ/μ. The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(\mathrm{Re}_{\ell}\), \(\mathrm{Re}_D\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

throttle: as a verb, means to restrict. As a noun or as an adjective in throttle valve, refers to a valve that restricts airflow (and therefore fuel flow) into an engine. Open or full throttle means maximum airflow rate.

choke: as a verb, means to restrict. In a supersonic nozzle context, choke is used to specifically mean to restrict flow through a sonic throat. As a noun or adjective in choke valve, refers to a valve that restricts intake airflow but allows fuel flow, used to make a very rich intake mixture often needed to start a cold engine.

5.1. CARBURETORS

Carburetors are ingenious because they passively match fuel and air flow rates and keep the chemistry stoichiometric. This works because the air flow rate and the fuel flow rate are both proportional to √Δp, meaning that no matter how slow or fast the air intake, it will generate a pressure difference which then leads to a fuel flow, and (to a first approximation) that fuel flow will always be in the same proportion as the incoming air. If the user opens up the throttle valve (say by pulling the trigger on a chainsaw) and doubles the input air flow, the pressure difference exhibited at the Venturi will quadruple, and the fuel flow will double. Close the throttle valve and halve the input air flow, the pressure difference drops by a factor of four, and the fuel flow is cut in half.

stoichiometric: with respect to a chemical equation, meaning that the reactants are in balance and can react completely to form products.

This chapter uses the Bernoulli equation to show that the change in pressure of the air rushing through the air intake, which is largely inviscid, is proportional to the change in U². Soon, in Chapter 6, we will show that the change in the fuel pressure, as it rushes through the fuel line and experiences viscous losses, is also proportional to the change in U².

In practice, the pressure upstream of the choke valve is approximately \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\), and in the engine manifold during the intake stroke is about \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}/3\). At open throttle, the pressure downstream of the Venturi is about \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}/3\), the air flow rate through the Venturi is high, the pressure at the Venturi is low, pulling a lot of fuel in from the tank, and the engine runs at maximum power. At closed throttle, the pressure throughout the carburetor is approximately \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\), and there is very little airflow. The pressure at the Venturi is approximately \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\), and very little fuel is pulled from the fuel tank, and the engine runs at minimum power. The fuel tank has a float-feed chamber that uses a float valve (Figure 5.4, p. 138) similar to that in a toilet tank. This tank remains at atmospheric pressure.

float valve for industrial storage tank; float valve for carburetor (view from bottom, bowl off); float valve for toilet bowl (cutaway); fill valve; flush handle; toilet bowl; rubber float; overflow; flapper valve; stainless steel float; hinge; plastic float; bowl.



Figure 5.4: Several types of float valves, including the float valve in the float-feed fuel chamber of a lawnmower carburetor.

A carburetor (mostly) fixes the fuel–air ratio in the engine independent of power/throttle (Figure 5.5). Geometric parameters of the Venturi and the fuel line set the fuel–air ratio; these are relatively easy to design to generate a stoichiometric fuel–air ratio over a reasonable fraction of the available throttle

rich: with respect to a combustion reaction, meaning having excess fuel with respect to stoichiometric conditions.

lean: in a combustion reaction, meaning having an excess of oxidizer relative to stoichiometric conditions.

Figure 5.5 plot labels: rich 1.5; stoichiometric 1.0; lean 0.5; x-axis fraction of full throttle (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 100%); max power; compressible flow in throat; Bernoulli prediction; surface tension, raised outlet (fix with idle jet).



Figure 5.5: Fuel–air ratio generated by a carburetor. If the system were described only by the Bernoulli equation in the converging portion of the Venturi, the fuel–air ratio would be the same independent of how open the throttle is. Real carburetors do not quite achieve stoichiometry that is completely independent of throttle. In reality, at closed throttle, surface tension in the fuel stream suppresses the fuel flow and tends to make the mixture lean. At fully open throttle, the Mach number in various parts of the system approaches 0.3 or 0.4, and the air density drops—the velocity–pressure relation in the air changes somewhat, and the effects of varying density lead the mixture to become rich.

In summary, a carburetor takes advantage of the fact that when fluid accelerates along its path in an inviscid flow, the pressure goes down. The carburetor forces the air to accelerate by constricting the airflow and forcing it to accelerate locally, and uses the reduction in pressure to inject fuel into the mixture for combustion. This phenomenon is described by the Bernoulli equation.

Torque converters form the connection between the engine and the transmission of an automatic-transmission car

Bernoulli equation: in differential form 0=d/ds(p+½ρU²+ρgz), in integral form B=p+½ρU²+ρgz, where B is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

torque converter: a turbomachine that transfers torque from an engine to a transmission by exchanging fluid with differing angular momentum back and forth between two sides of the device, one of which is connected to the engine and one to the input shaft of the transmission.

5.2. TORQUE CONVERTERS

the engine to the transmission, amplifying the torque when the vehicle is accelerating. Torque converters use the pressure gradient generated by rotating fluid to throw transmission oil back and forth between the impeller, which is connected to the engine, and the turbine, which is connected to the transmission.

Figure 5.6: Left: an automobile torque converter. Externally, a torque converter looks like a torus (donut) in shape. One side is bolted to the engine flex plate; the other side connects to the input shaft of the transmission. Right: the same torque converter, cut apart to see its components and sitting on a bench in 242 Upson Hall at Cornell. Clockwise from lower left: (1) impeller, welded to half of the outer casing; (2) stator; (3) the other half of the outer casing; (4) turbine.

Photographs omitted.

A standard-transmission automobile connects the engine to the drivetrain through a clutch, which is a frictional contact, combined with a system of gears, and many engineers assume that it is typical for the connection between the engine of an automobile and the drivetrain of the automobile to be a solid–solid connection. In fact, though, most automobiles make this connection using a fluid-mechanical connection.

An automatic transmission, which you find in about 96% of US cars, uses a torque converter. It doesn’t use solid–solid contact or friction, and it doesn’t use solid–liquid contact and viscosity either. It uses the transfer of the angular momentum of transmission oil as that oil moves back and forth in a single casing that holds three turbomachines, in this case called the impeller, the stator, and the turbine (Figure 5.7, p. 141).

Automatic transmissions were developed for several reasons, but one important one is that, relative to standard transmissions, they were easier to use and led to a smoother ride. Rather than a frictional solid–solid connection, which in theory provides infinite torque when the clutch is engaged, a torque converter generates high finite torque when accelerating quickly, but gentler torque when accelerating slowly or when coasting.

A torque converter works by strategically moving oil back and forth between the two sides of the torque converter so as to exchange angular momentum. The impeller is welded to the case, and the impeller and case all spin along with the engine. The impeller’s blades operate as a centrifugal pump, efficiently forcing the fluid to rotate, generating a radial pressure gradient.

centrifugal pump: a pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it centrifugally with an impeller, then decelerating it through a volute. Typically has low specific speed.

Inside a torque converter, the fluid is rotating in a circle, and that must be because of a centripetal force accelerating the fluid toward the center, and that centripetal force is induced by the high pressures on the outside of the torque converter relative to those toward its center. In this case, the fluid also moves in the poloidal direction, spinning from the center of the impeller, to the outside of the impeller, across the midline into the outside of the turbine, in to the center of the turbine, and back to the center of the impeller (Figure 5.9, p. 143). The fluid moving from impeller to turbine has a lot of angular momentum, but the fluid moving back from impeller to turbine doesn’t. So this process effectively sends angular momentum from the impeller to the turbine, and this exchange of angular momentum is the torque that transfers from the engine to the transmission.

poloidal: with reference to a torus (donut) and toroidal–poloidal coordinates, means along the small circle. If a torus is a cylinder bent into a circle, the poloidal direction is the circumferential direction of the original cylinder.

angular momentum: the cross product of radial vector from an axis of rotation with linear momentum in the azimuthal direction.

Figure 5.9 diagram labels: turbine; casing; engine rotation; casing is attached to flex plate and crankshaft and engine; turbine spins freely in casing; transmission input shaft; impeller rotation; outer fluid carries lots of angular momentum from fast element to slow element; inner fluid carries minimal angular momentum from slow element back to fast element; stator affects flow only when impeller speed greatly exceeds that of turbine.



Figure 5.9: A torque converter transfers high-angular-momentum fluid from the fast-spinning element to the slow-spinning element, and transfers low-angular-momentum fluid back. This poloidal motion causes a net transfer of angular momentum from the fast-spinning element to the slow-spinning element. During acceleration (shown in the diagram), the engine and impeller are spinning faster, throwing fluid centrifugally out its exterior and accepting return fluid at the interior. The turbine and transmission input shaft are spinning more slowly, taking fluid in at the exterior and ejecting it back to the impeller towards the interior. When accelerating and the impeller rotation rate is much higher than that of the turbine, the angle through which the fluid has to turn between turbine and impeller is very high, and the stator blades help achieve this. When decelerating or when accelerating gently, this same flow pushes the stator in a different direction, and the stator spins freely and does not affect the flow.

This process would work equally well in both directions, if there were no stator and if the impeller and turbine had symmetric geometries. But, the

5.2. TORQUE CONVERTERS

impeller and turbine have blades aligned at different angles, which are optimized to maximize the angular momentum transfer associated with radial flows during acceleration; these impede angular momentum transfer during deceleration. So, the curvature of the blades make a torque converter asymmetrically effective at transferring angular momentum.

Also, a torque converter has a stator, which is a third rotating element mounted in between the impeller and turbine. The stator is mounted on a one-way clutch. The stator spins freely in the direction of engine rotation but cannot spin against engine rotation, and its blades are set at an angle such that it plays a role only when the impeller is rotating much faster than the turbine. In this condition, the stator combines with the blades of the turbine and impeller to create smooth acceleration of the fluid from the slow angular velocity in the turbine to the high angular velocity in the impeller. The stator itself doesn’t apply a driving torque to the transmission (actually the opposite) but more importantly it leads to a flow that applying a strong retarding torque to the impeller. Whereas the impeller is basically a centrifugal pump, and the turbine is basically a Francis turbine, the stator is basically a one-way propeller turbine whose purpose is to make the impeller perform better when it is rotating much faster than the turbine. The stator makes the torque converter transfer angular momentum better during rapid acceleration. It does not affect how the torque converter transfers angular momentum during rapid deceleration—when a car decelerates rapidly, it is doing so because of the brakes, not the transmission or drivetrain.

A common way of graphing torque converter performance is to graph the torque ratio versus the speed ratio. Rotational power is P=ωT, where P is power, ω is angular velocity, and T is torque. For an engine (and impeller) spinning at angular velocity \(\omega_e\) with torque \(T_e\), and driving the transmission (and turbine) at angular velocity \(\omega_t\) with torque \(T_t\), we can define the speed ratio SR:

\mathrm{SR}=\frac{\omega_t}{\omega_e} (5.5)

and the torque ratio TR:

\mathrm{TR}=\frac{T_t}{T_e} (5.6)

A clutch, as is found in a standard transmission, has SR=1 and TR=1 unless the clutch slips. A gear, as is found in both standard and automatic transmissions has (SR)(TR)=1, assuming no losses. A typical graph of torque converter torque ratio versus speed ratio is shown in Figure 5.10, p. 145. A torque converter has a smoothly varying torque ratio depending on the speed ratio. This leads to a smooth ride for the driver. Its efficiency η=(SR)(TR), however, is significantly less than one, especially at low speed ratios.

Torque converters are purely inertial mechanisms, using the transfer of momentum of the oil to effect a torque. Unlike engine oil, which must have high viscosity to bear heavy loads in the crankshaft, the viscosity of the transmission oil used in torque converters doesn’t matter as much. The transmission oil does lubricate the torque converter parts, but those lubricated surfaces bear less load than in a crankshaft, and transmission oil’s role as a means for transferring angular momentum is not driven by its viscosity.

So, in summary, a torque converter is a strategic combination of a centrifugal pump (called the impeller), a propeller turbine (called the stator) and a Francis turbine (called the turbine) that transfers rotational power back and forth between engine and transmission. Placed together, these three elements ensure that angular momentum is carried from one side to the other depending on which is rotating faster. The torque converter is asymmetric, giving larger torque and faster transfer of power when the impeller is rotating faster than the turbine, and generating smaller torque

blade: a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes. Roughly synonymous with airfoil, hydrofoil, wing, and vane. Often chosen over the word vane when the blade is rotating in a turbomachine.

Francis turbine: a reaction turbine with radial or mixed flow and low turbine specific speed, suitable for extracting energy over a high pressure drop. The turbine analog of a centrifugal pump.

propeller turbine: an axial-flow reaction turbine, typically with relatively high specific speed, suitable for extracting energy over a low pressure drop. The turbine analog of an axial-flow pump.

clutch: a mechanical device that engages and disengages power transmission through a frictional or viscous contact.

inertial: related to the resistance to acceleration exhibited by objects with mass. In a fluid-mechanical context, inertial implies that fluid momentum and fluid pressure are important and viscosity is not.

centrifugal pump: a pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it centrifugally with an impeller, then decelerating it through a volute. Typically has low specific speed.

5.3. INVISCID FLOW ALONG A STREAMLINE

and slower transfer of power when the impeller is rotating more slowly than the turbine. Its behavior is explained by the Euler equation for the pressure distribution normal to a fluid streamline in inviscid flow:

\frac{\partial k}{\partial n}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R} (5.7)

This chapter describes inviscid incompressible flow using a coordinate system aligned to fluid streamlines

This chapter’s engineering motivation includes two fluid machines: a carburetor, which causes a pressure change along the path of airflow when the air is caused to accelerate, and a torque converter, which causes a pressure change normal to the path of oil flow when the oil is caused to rotate as a solid body. These are both fluid machines that are largely explained by the Euler equations, i.e., the equations for inviscid, incompressible fluid flow. The Euler equations are the physics we describe in this chapter.

Whereas hydrostatics prescribes the relation between pressure and gravitational potential energy for fluids at rest, leading to the relation p+ρgz=k, the Euler equations we describe in this chapter describe fluids that are moving and accelerating. In order to describe fluids in motion, we now consider the kinetic energy of fluid in motion and develop a relation between pressure, gravitational potential energy, and kinetic energy. In addition, we consider the acceleration of fluid and develop relations between accelerations, forces, and the gradients of these energies. By inviscid, we mean that the viscous forces in the flow are negligible relative to the momentum of the fluid and the forces caused by pressure gradients. This analysis is much easier if we choose a coordinate system that always aligns our relations relative to streamlines, which describe the instantaneous direction of fluid flow. Also the analysis in this chapter is much easier if we use a Lagrangian reference frame.

The analysis in this chapter is thermodynamically simpler than Chapter 1 but kinematically more complicated. Our description of quasi-1D compressible flow through a rocket nozzle in Chapter 1 considered inviscid flow and allowed the density of the fluid to change. In this chapter, we simplify the analysis by assuming that the density is fixed and the flow is incompressible, so the results of this chapter are relevant only for small Mach numbers. This simplification is quite powerful, though; it simplifies the analysis enough that we can take on the more complicated problem of fluid that changes direction (see Sidebar 5.1, p. 252).

The material in this chapter greatly expands the applicability of our analysis—the Euler equations predict how pressure changes in pipes and ducts whose cross-section changes, as well as the pressure changes on airplanes, automobiles, and projectiles. These pressure changes can be used to create velocity-measurement devices and predict the aerodynamic force on objects, and of course explain the operation of carburetors and torque converters.

The results of this chapter apply only in regions of flow where viscous effects are unimportant because the flow’s momentum overwhelms viscous forces (high-Reynolds number flow) or the structure of the flow eliminates viscous forces (irrotational flow). Generally speaking, the results of this chapter will be quantitatively useful for regions far from walls in flows with

fluid machine: a machine that adds energy to or extracts energy from a fluid.

Euler equations: pronounced OY-ler. The inviscid conservation of momentum equations. Can be written in streamline coordinates (\(dB/ds=0\), \(dk/dn=-\rho U^2/R\), \(dk/d\ell=0\)) or fixed coordinates (\(\rho\,\partial\vec u/\partial t+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\rho\vec g\)).

hydrostatics: the study of fluids at rest.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

Lagrangian: pronounced la-GRAHN-zhee-an. A mode of analysis in which a mass element (i.e., a system) is followed as it moves through a flowfield.

Why is everything named after Euler Haiku: “it’s so confusing / why do we name everything / after just one guy.”

Reynolds number: Re=ρUℓ/μ. The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(\mathrm{Re}_{\ell}\), \(\mathrm{Re}_D\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

irrotational flow: flow in which ω=∇×u=0. The terms irrotational flow (ω=0) and potential flow (u=∇φ) are synonymous—one implies the other.
