5.3. INVISCID FLOW ALONG A STREAMLINE

SIDEBAR 5.1: ENGINEERING MODELS

Incompressible Flow

Premise: At low M, treating ρ as unaffected by pressure or velocity greatly simplifies the math and leads to only very small errors. All of the conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy involve the fluid density, and this density is routinely found inside temporal and spatial derivatives. If we could just assume that ρ were a constant, it would greatly simplify the math. This approximation is surprisingly useful, even for fluids like air, for which the fluid itself is definitely compressible according to the ideal-gas law. We find that, even for a fluid like air which we know can be compressed, the flow of this fluid often does not lead to large density changes, and if we ignore the small density changes, our calculations of the velocity and pressure fields and resulting outputs like forces have only small errors. Importantly, the incompressible flow approximation involves approximating ρ as a constant for the purposes of the conservation equations. It does not involve claims that the fluid cannot be compressed. Just that the amount it is compressed by flow can be ignored without messing up the calculations engineers care about.

Mathematical form: for incompressible flow ρ=constant. Incompressible flow simplifies the conservation equations by taking ρ to be a constant, and is valid when M is small:

\rho=\mathrm{constant}\quad\mathrm{when}\quad M<0.3. (5.8)

Utility: the incompressible flow approximation turns the conservation of mass equation into a kinematic relation and greatly simplifies the conservation of momentum equations

The conservation of mass equation is greatly simplified if we assume that ρ is a constant:

\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\rho\vec{u}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0. (5.9)

In the incompressible flow model, we never actually solve the conservation of mass equation so much as we use what we know about conservation of mass to simplify the conservation of momentum equations. There are many terms in the conservation of momentum equations that are proportional to ∇·u, and these all cancel out. That and taking ρ outside the derivatives greatly simplifies the equations:

\frac{\partial\rho\vec{u}}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\rho\vec{u}\vec{u}=-\nabla p+\nabla\cdot2\mu\mathbf{E}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\rho\frac{\partial\vec{u}}{\partial t}+\rho\vec{u}\cdot\nabla\vec{u}=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec{u}. (5.10)

Limitations: The incompressible flow model fails when M is high

The Mach number M is the governing parameter that tells us how good the incompressible flow approximation is. The errors associated with the incompressible flow approximation end up being roughly proportional to M², and so a rule of thumb is that if M<0.3 then the errors associated with the incompressible flow approximation are below 10% and aren’t that big of a deal. The incompressible flow model is very useful, but requires that M be low. As soon as M gets high, it fails.

Editorial note: Eq. (5.10) is retained literally. If gravitational body force is included, the momentum equation has an additional +ρg⃗ term on the right (or −ρg ẑ in the z-up convention); the source does not state that gravity is being neglected here.

5.4. BERNOULLI EQUATION

large boundaries that have large velocities and low viscosities. Later in the term, we will develop a more formal process for evaluating the validity of the Bernoulli equation.

The Bernoulli equation is also useful when the inviscid approximation isn’t quite correct, because in a number of cases the Bernoulli equation can be modified with a relatively simple correction factor to account for viscous losses. Such approaches are covered in Chapter 6.

The premise, mathematical form, utility, and limitations of the inviscid flow equations are summarized in Sidebar 5.2, p. 149.

Bernoulli’s equation in integral form relates pressure, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy along a streamline

Bernoulli’s equation in integral form states that, along a streamline,

kinetic energy per vol; Bernoulli constant; stored compression work per vol; potential energy per vol

p+\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2+\rho gz=B, (5.14)

steady Bernoulli equation, integral form, flow along a streamline, no viscous effects, uniform density

where B is uniform along the streamline, and is known as the Bernoulli constant. Here p is pressure, ρ is fluid density, U is fluid speed, g is the gravitational acceleration, and z is the coordinate in the direction away from the gravitational center.

Bernoulli’s equation as written in Equation (5.14) is valid for steady incompressible flow along a streamline with no viscous effects. Here, “no viscous effects” means that viscosity does not cause meaningful changes in the velocity, which is a good approximation when the Reynolds number is high and the fluid is far enough away from walls, or when the flow is irrotational. For now, we will consider only those systems for which these approximations are correct. Sidebar 5.3 summarizes key properties of streamlines.

Bernoulli’s equation tells how a fluid element’s pressure, speed, and height in a gravitational field are all related as the fluid flows along a streamline. It can be thought of as a conservation of momentum equation or a conservation of energy equation (when there is no viscosity and no temperature change, one is a multiple of the other). Considering it in terms of energy, each term in Bernoulli’s equation has units of energy per volume, and each term corresponds to a different form of energy:

volumetric stored ability to do work (p). Any fluid could be expanded to p=0, generating a finite amount of work. The pressure is thus a measure of this stored ability to do work, evaluated per unit volume.

volumetric kinetic energy (½ρU²). A mass m moving with a speed U has kinetic energy ½mU², and thus kinetic energy per unit volume is ½ρU².

volumetric gravitational potential energy relative to z=0. The potential energy of a weight mg raised to a height z in a potential field is mgz, and this potential energy per unit volume is given by ρgz.

Bernoulli Haiku: “Newton’s second law / in streamwise coordinates / is super awesome.”

speed: when describing fluid, a scalar description of fluid motion equal to the magnitude of the velocity. When describing a turbomachine, the angular frequency of its rotation.

incompressible flow: implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Incompressible flow implies that the motion of the fluid does not cause density to change, in comparison to compressible flow in which fluid moves so quickly and the pressure changes so much that the density is perturbed enough to affect convective fluxes. Incompressible flows may still have nonuniform density, for example if the fluid’s temperature varies; this can affect the conservation of momentum equations. An incompressible flow does not imply that the fluid is mathematically incompressible, only that pressure-induced compression can be ignored. Cf. compressible flow.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

conservation of momentum: the notion that changes in momentum are brought about by forces as prescribed by Newton’s second law.

volumetric: related to volume, or per unit volume.

5.4. BERNOULLI EQUATION

SIDEBAR 5.2: ENGINEERING MODELS

Steady Euler Equations

Premise: The steady Euler equations describe steady inviscid flow. Inviscid flow is one in which the net viscous forces can be neglected, at least within some important domain. The steady Euler equations describe conservation of mass, i.e., F=ma for steady flow of a fluid with no net viscous force.

Mathematical form: Assuming \(\mu\nabla^2\vec u=0\) and setting \(\sum F=ma\) on a control volume leads to the Euler Equations

If we assume that the net effects of viscous stresses on a control volume can be neglected, then ΣF=ma tells us that any Lagrangian acceleration that happens to fluid moving through a domain in a steady flow is caused by pressure gradients. Or, equivalently, an Eulerian control volume analysis shows that, in steady-state, any net force from pressure gradients is balanced by net momentum outflow. The control volume can be chosen to be differential, and the analysis can be performed with respect to a fixed coordinate system:

\rho\vec{u}\cdot\nabla\vec{u}=-\nabla p, (5.11)

or streamline coordinates:

\frac{\partial B}{\partial s}=0;\quad\frac{\partial k}{\partial n}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R};\quad\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial n}=0. (5.12)

The equation for the streamwise coordinate can be integrated to generate the integral Bernoulli equation:

B=\mathrm{constant};\quad p_1+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_1^2+\rho gz_1=p_2+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_2^2+\rho gz_2. (5.13)

Inviscid flow does not require that there be no viscous stresses; it requires only that the net viscous force on a control volume be zero, i.e., that the divergence of the viscous stresses is zero. The Euler equations describe an inviscid flow assumption for incompressible flow. If a flow is at M>0, a comparable model would be the isentropic flow model.

Utility: The Euler equations describe the idealized exchange of energy between potential energy, kinetic energy, and stored capacity to do work

The Euler equations (specifically the integral form of the Bernoulli equation B=constant on a streamline) describe the idealized exchange of energy between potential energy, kinetic energy, and stored capacity to do work. This is useful because it links directly to engineering applications—we often want to store work, store potential energy, convert these back and forth, and translate that to fluid motion. Although this conversion in the real world cannot be performed with perfect efficiency, and some of the energy is converted to (relatively useless) heat, the Euler equations show what the best possible result could be, and help us understand what the functional forms are and what the material dependences are, especially for fast-moving flows such as those related to cars, planes, boats, and large piping systems.

Utility: The Euler equations relate the spatial orientation of streamlines to pressure, altitude, and the net forces that result from their gradients

The Euler equations (specifically the form written for the normal coordinate n, i.e., ∂k/∂n=−ρU²/R) show that fluid turns in response to gradients of the hydrostatic constant k, i.e., k=p+ρgz, i.e., pressure or potential energy. This helps us know that if we are aware of pressure gradients or potential-energy gradients, we know the fluid will turn in response to it. Or, if we are aware of streamline curvature, we know that it evinces the presence of gradients in p or ρgz. The precise relation of streamline curvature to gradients predicted by the Euler equations is exactly correct only in the complete absence of net viscous forces, so in real flows the Euler equations only approximates this relation. But still, when we look at a flow and see the streamlines turn, we will always find gradients in k, and knowing this is very useful for interpreting fluid flows.

Utility: The Euler equations provide a framework that lets us describe real flows by combining a vector description of inviscid flow with an algebraic loss factor

The Euler equations describe lossless flow, i.e., flow in which energy is never converted to heat; it is always traded back and forth between kinetic energy, potential energy, and stored ability to do work. This is quite good for understanding the functional form of energy exchange, especially as a function of space as described by gradients. This is a vector description. So what happens if we add a little bit of viscous forces? Does everything about the flow change? Are all the conclusions invalid? Well, no. For most mechanical engineering flows, where the Reynolds number is high, the Euler equations describe all the complicated spatial variation of the pressure, speed, and altitude quite well except that the net effect of viscous forces is that the Bernoulli constant gets lower as the fluid moves downstream. So for flow through a pipe, for example, the Euler equations correctly describe how fluid pressure decreases in a constriction where the speed is higher, and the Euler equations correctly describe how fluid pressure increases as fluid moves from high altitude to low. The Euler equations correctly show how, as the fluid zooms around a corner, the pressure must be higher on the outer side of the elbow than on the inner side of the elbow. What the Euler equations do not describe well is how the Bernoulli constant goes down as the fluid moves downstream; however, that in most cases can be described by an algebraic loss factor that describes how the Bernoulli constant drops along that path.

Limitations: The Euler equations become invalid when the Reynolds number is low

The Reynolds number Re=ρUℓ/μ is a measure of the relative importance of viscous forces to the kinetic energy of the fluid. When Re is large, the viscous forces are relatively small in most parts of the fluid. When Re is small, the viscous forces are relatively large in most parts of the fluid. For the Euler equations to be useful, Re must be large.

Limitations: The Euler equations become invalid near a surface

The Euler equations as a model provide useful predictions of fluid phenomena when Re is large and the area of interest is far from walls or some sort of area-averaged quantity. The Euler equations never predict correctly what happens near a surface, because viscous forces always become dominant as the area of interest approaches a wall. Thus we never try to use the Euler equations to describe flow very close to a wall; instead, near the wall, we use the boundary-layer equations, a different engineering model.

Editorial note: the source prints Eq. (5.11) as ρu·∇u=−∇p, omitting the gravitational body-force term. In a z-up coordinate system, the steady Euler equation with gravity is ρ(u·∇)u=−∇p−ρg ẑ; this is consistent with the sidebar’s Bernoulli expression containing ρgz. The printed equation is retained above.

Editorial note: enlarged inspection resolves the printed last relation of Eq. (5.12) as \(\partial\ell/\partial n=0\). This is not the third pressure-potential Euler relation: the Euler sidebar on source page 157 instead prints \(dk/d\ell=0\). The differing source expression is retained literally. The premise also calls \(F=ma\) conservation of mass; it is conservation of momentum.

5.5. STREAMLINE CURVATURE

Bernoulli’s equation linking any two points along a streamline in inviscid flow:

this is uniform along a streamline

p_1+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_1^2+\rho gz_1=p_2+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_2^2+\rho gz_2=B, (5.15)

shows that, as a fluid element moves along a streamline, it trades back and forth among kinetic energy, upward translation in a gravitational field, and stored work of compression.

If we assume that the speed U is zero, Bernoulli’s equation simplifies to become the integral form of the hydrostatic equation, which we have already seen:

p+\rho gz=k. (5.16)

The hydrostatic equation is also an equation that trades forms of energy or work for each other—as we move our observations from the bottom to the top of a quiescent body of fluid, we move from a place where the energy has been stored in compression of the fluid (the bottom) to a place where the energy has been stored in gravitational potential energy (the top).

Although we have cast Bernoulli’s equation as a conservation of energy equation, it is very different from a thermodynamic energy conservation equation we might have used in ENGRD2210. We can guarantee that the Bernoulli constant is uniform only when we move along a streamline in an inviscid flow. It cannot in general be used to compare two points in a fluid flow unless they are on the same streamline.¹

Bernoulli’s equation can also be written in differential form along a streamline:

Bernoulli constant B; streamwise derivative

\frac{d}{ds}\left(p+\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2+\rho gz\right)=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{\partial B}{\partial s}=0. (5.17)

differential form of Bernoulli equation; no viscosity; incompressible; steady. Alternatively, the Euler equation in the streamwise coordinate.

The Bernoulli constant B, which is also called the total pressure p₀ (B≡p₀), is a measure of all of the energy in a fluid other than internal energy. This summed energy does not change along a streamline in inviscid flow.

The curvature of a streamline is related to the normal gradient of the hydrostatic constant

When streamlines curve, the curvature corresponds to a fluid acceleration in the direction of the center of curvature. Denoting the coordinate pointing toward the center of curvature as n, we can show that if the streamline has curvature with a radius of curvature R, then there must be a gradient of the hydrostatic constant given by

¹ Bernoulli’s equation can be used to compare any two points in an irrotational fluid flow, but that’s a special case.

steady Bernoulli equation, integral form, flow along a streamline, no viscous effects, uniform density

hydrostatic equation: in differential form ∂p/∂z=−ρg. In integral form, p+ρgz=k.

hydrostatic equation, k is a constant

quiescent: motionless; u=0.

gravitational potential energy: potential energy that fluid has relative to a reference height z₀.

conservation of energy: the notion that energy is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

hydrostatic constant: the constant k in the hydrostatic equation p+ρgz=k.

5.6. FREE JETS

volumetric centripetal force

\frac{\partial k}{\partial n}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}. (5.18)

normal derivative of the hydrostatic constant

Euler’s equation for the normal coordinate

The hydrostatic constant is a measure of the energy in the form of pressure or gravitational potential energy. This equation tells us that variations of this hydrostatic constant cause forces that cause fluid to change direction, accelerating normal to its current path.

Absent viscous losses, free jets emanating from a static high-pressure source exit their orifice at a speed given by

U=\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}}

The Bernoulli equation, because it governs the conversion between different forms of energy, describes how fluid can be accelerated by a pressure difference or height difference. One classic example of this is a free jet, which is a jet that travels ballistically, usually because it is a water jet moving through air. Free jets occur when a relatively dense, viscous fluid (water is 800 times as dense as air and about 55 times as viscous) moves through a less dense, less viscous medium.

As a first example, we imagine a reservoir of water at a (high) pressure p₁ connected to a low-pressure air environment at p₂ by a lossless valve. If the valve is suddenly opened, how fast does the fluid rush out? We assume that there are no viscous effects, we assume that the fluid rushing out of the reservoir takes the form of a free jet with pressure equal to the environment (p₂). We can show that the fluid issues with speed U=√(2(p₁−p₂)/ρ).

We consider a large reservoir of fluid at pressure p₁ emptying into the atmosphere through a circular orifice of radius r (Figure 5.11, p. 152). Assume r is much smaller than R, the diameter of the reservoir. If we assume that r≪R, then we can assume (because of conservation of mass) that the fluid in the reservoir is moving quite slowly and is well approximated by U₁=0. So at location 1, the fluid velocity is (approximately) zero, and the pressure is p=p₁. Bernoulli’s law along a streamline tells us at what speed the free jet must issue. Along a streamline, B=p+½ρU²+ρgz is uniform. At position 1, B=p₁+ρgz₁. At position 2, B=p₂+½ρU₂²+ρgz₂. Thus

p_1+\rho gz_1=p_2+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_2^2+\rho gz_2\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{1}{2}\rho U_2^2=p_1-p_2. (5.19)

Bernoulli equation: in differential form 0=d/ds(p+½ρu²+ρgz), in integral form B=p+½ρu²+ρgz, where B is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

free jet: a jet emanating from an orifice whose pressure is assumed to be equal to the environment.

Sidebar 5.3: Fundamentals

Streamlines

Streamlines are everywhere tangent to the instantaneous velocity. Streamlines are properties of the instantaneous velocity field, and they serve to illustrate the nature of the flow in several ways. First, because streamlines are everywhere tangent to the instantaneous velocity, one can immediately see the direction of flow. Second, because flow is tangent to the streamline, no mass ever goes through a streamline. Third, for 2D flow, each streamline corresponds to a specific value of the streamfunction, ψ. Fourth, for 2D flow, the difference between the streamfunctions of two streamlines is proportional to the areal flow rate between the streamlines—because of this, we know that where streamlines are close to each other, the fluid speed is high, and where streamlines are far from each other, the fluid speed is low.



Figure 5.11: A free jet issuing from a high-pressure reservoir at p₁ into a low-pressure region at p₂.

Example Problem 5.1

When the button on a drinking fountain is pushed, the water stored in the fountain (in a large reservoir at p = .102 MPa) issues out of its nozzle into the atmosphere at p = .101 MPa. The reservoir and nozzle are at approximately the same height. At what speed U does the water issue from the fountain? Solution: Assuming steady, inviscid, incompressible flow, the fluid issuing from the fountain has a speed given by

U=\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{2(.102\,\mathrm{MPa}-.101\,\mathrm{MPa})}{1\times10^3\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}}}=1.4\,\mathrm{m/s}. (5.20)


PDF page 164 — source_issue

U_2=\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}}, (5.21)

Velocity of a free jet emanating from an orifice from a static reservoir with overpressure Δp; no viscous losses.

where Δp = p₁ − p₂. Equation (5.21) shows that the speed of a free jet driven by a pressure difference Δp exits at a speed proportional to the square root of the pressure difference divided by the density. The size of the orifice and the direction of the jet do not impact the speed, as we have ignored viscous effects. The direction of the jet, of course, determines the path the fluid takes, and the size of the orifice determines the volumetric flow rate. Example Problem 5.1 (p.152) is an example of calculating a fluid velocity from a specified pressure difference.

free jet: a jet emanating from an orifice whose pressure is assumed to be equal to the environment.

Free jets driven by the hydrostatic pressure of a reservoir issue with speed √(2gh)

Consider a liquid reservoir emptying into the atmosphere through a circular orifice of radius r located a distance h below the top of the liquid (Figure 5.12, p.153). Assume r is much smaller than R, the diameter of the reservoir.



Figure 5.12: Left: a free jet emanating from a reservoir. Right: the exchange of volumetric energy among three forms: pressure, volumetric kinetic energy, and volumetric gravitational potential energy.

If we assume that r ≪ R, then we can assume the fluid in the reservoir is moving quite slowly and is well approximated by the hydrostatic equation, as long as it is reasonably far from the orifice. So at location (A), the fluid velocity is (approximately) zero, z ≈ h, and the pressure is \(p_A=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\). Moving from (A) to (B) to (C), the fluid speed is always very low and the kinetic energy is negligible, and gravitational potential energy is being traded for pressure. At location (C), the fluid velocity is (approximately) zero, z ≈ 0, and the pressure has increased to \(p_C=p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\). Moving from (C) to (D), the velocity is still negligible, and p, U, and z are all unchanging. Moving from (D) to (H), the pressure must drop to \(p_H=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) because the fluid issues as a free jet.

hydrostatic equation: in differential form, \(dp/dz=-\rho g\). In integral form, \(p+\rho gz=k\).

gravitational potential energy: potential energy that fluid has relative to a reference height z₀: ∫ᵥ ρg(z−z₀)dV.

Table 5.1: Pressure, speed, and height at various points along a streamline moving from the surface of a reservoir of water out an orifice as a free jet.

Location | Pressure p | Speed U | height relative to orifice z | B = p + ½ρU² + ρgz
A | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) | 0 | h | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\)
B | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\tfrac12\rho gh\) | 0 | h/2 | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\)
C | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\) | 0 | 0 | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\)
D | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\) | 0 | 0 | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\)
H | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) | √(2gh) | 0 | \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\)
Example Problem 5.2

At what speed does water issue from a small orifice located at the bottom of a 1-meter-tall reservoir of water? Solution: per Torricelli’s relation,

U=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(1\,\mathrm{m})}=4.4\,\mathrm{m/s}. (5.24)

The fluid streamlines are horizontal and straight, so they have no curvature, so from Equation (5.73) we know there is no normal gradient of the pressure. As the ambient is at \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\), the free jet must be at \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\).

The Bernoulli equation tells us what velocity the free jet must be at. Along a streamline, B = p + ½ρU² + ρgz is uniform. At position (A), \(B=p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\). At position (C), \(B=p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh\). And at position (H), \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) and z = 0, so \(B=p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\tfrac12\rho U^2\). The speed U observed at (H) must satisfy:

p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh=p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac12\rho U^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac12\rho U^2=\rho gh. (5.22)

Rearranging this to solve for U, we find

U=\sqrt{2gh}. (5.23)

We equivalently could have obtained this result from Equation (5.21) by noting that the pressure difference caused by a height h of fluid is ρgh.

Equation (5.23), which is often called Torricelli’s relation, shows that the speed of a free jet driven by hydrostatic forces exits at a speed proportional to the square root of the height of the fluid column. The size of the orifice and the direction of the jet do not impact the speed, as we have ignored viscous effects. The direction of the jet, of course, determines the path the fluid takes, and the size of the orifice determines the volumetric flow rate. A short example of a free jet calculation is shown in Example Problem 5.2 (p.154), and Sidebar 5.4 (p.157) discusses when it is appropriate to assume that the flow issuing from an orifice is a free jet.

This flow illustrates the Bernoulli equation and the different forms of energy the fluid can hold. At A, the fluid holds gravitational energy. Following a streamline from A to C, the gravitational potential energy is converted to stored work of compression i.e., increased pressure. When the fluid exits the orifice at H, the pressure excess has all been converted to kinetic energy. Table 5.1, p.154 shows all of the intermediate values for the speed and pressure throughout this process.

velocity of a free jet emanating from an orifice a distance h below a surface; no viscous losses.

Torricelli’s relation: the observation that a free jet emanating from an orifice a distance h below the top of a reservoir exits with speed √(2gh).

Absent viscous losses, free jets emanating from a contraction of a high-pressure, finite-diameter source issue at a speed given by \(\frac{A_1}{\sqrt{A_1^2-A_2^2}}\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}}\).

Consider now that r is not so much smaller than R, so the fluid in the reservoir can no longer be assumed quiescent (this can still correspond to Figure 5.11, p.152).

Now, we apply the Bernoulli equation. At position 1, B = p₁ + ½ρU₁² + ρgz. At position 2, B = p₂ + ½ρU₂² + ρgz. If we note that, by mass conservation, ṁ = ρ₁U₁A₁ = ρ₂U₂A₂ and for incompressible flow Q = U₁A₁ = U₂A₂, we can substitute Q/A₁ for U₁ and Q/A₂ for U₂. Rearranging to solve for Q, we find

Q=\frac{A_1A_2}{\sqrt{A_1^2-A_2^2}}\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}}, (5.25)

Or, solving for U₂, we find

U_2=\frac{A_1}{\sqrt{A_1^2-A_2^2}}\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}}. (5.26)

whereas U₁ is given by

U_1=\frac{A_2}{\sqrt{A_1^2-A_2^2}}\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}}. (5.27)

The pressure difference is again defined as Δp = p₁ − p₂. Arithmetic checks will show that as A₂ → 0, these results simplify to that of a fluid emanating from a stagnant chamber. The solution is well-defined as A₂ → A₁, but when A₂ = A₁, both numerator and denominator go to zero and the solution is undefined; the Bernoulli equation cannot describe a pressure difference for inviscid flow through a horizontal pipe with uniform cross-sectional area. There is a real pressure difference in the real flow of a real fluid through a horizontal pipe, but that pressure difference cannot be explained by the Bernoulli equation and we will discuss that later in the text.

Equation (5.26) shows that, if the reservoir is not infinitely large, the fluid inside must have been moving to satisfy conservation of mass, and the extra kinetic energy of the fluid in the reservoir translates to a higher exit speed. Example Problem 5.3 (p.157) shows an example calculation of this kind.

Bernoulli equation: in differential form d/ds(p + ½ρu² + ρgz) = 0, in integral form B = p + ½ρu² + ρgz, where B is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

Conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

Editorial source note: In the limit discussed after Eq. (5.27), the numerator does not go to zero merely because \(A_2\to A_1\). For a fixed nonzero pressure difference, the displayed speeds diverge as \(\sqrt{A_1^2-A_2^2}\to0\). Equal areas in the stated steady, horizontal, inviscid model require zero pressure difference; Bernoulli then does not determine the common speed from the pressure difference alone. The original limiting statement is retained.


PDF page 167 — verified

In practice, free jets emanating from orifices contract and suffer small viscous losses

We are not at this stage in MAE3230 able to perform the analysis to describe in detail why free jets don’t go quite as fast as the Bernoulli equation predicts. However, in practice, the speed of fluid is often about 2% slower than that predicted by the Bernoulli equation, and the velocity coefficient is the term used to describe the ratio of the actual speed to the speed predicted by the Bernoulli equation.

velocity coefficient: ratio of the actual speed of fluid exiting an orifice to that predicted by the Bernoulli equation.

Further, the size of the jet is often not exactly the same as the orifice diameter. If we create the geometry of the orifice carefully, we can make the jet diameter the same as the orifice diameter. However, if we just drill a hole in the side of the container, the jet that comes out contracts in diameter because the fluid can’t make a 90-degree turn at the sharp edges, and, in this initial region while the jet is contracting, the jet is not at \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\). The net area effect of this observation is described by the contraction coefficient, which describes the area ratio of the jet area to the orifice area. For sharp-edged orifices, the contraction coefficient is usually about 0.6, so the flowrate issuing out of a sharp-edged orifice is often significantly smaller than one would predict from the orifice area and Torricelli’s relation alone.

contraction coefficient: the ratio of the area of a free jet issuing from an orifice to the area of the orifice itself.

5.7 A Venturi is a tube with a narrow throat that generates a low-pressure region

In the previous section, we specified the pressure in two places and saw what speed resulted; this describes fluid issuing from a high-pressure reservoir. We can also specify a volumetric flowrate through a tube and ask what the Bernoulli equation predicts when its cross-sectional area changes.

Consider air flowing through a horizontal tube whose diameter decreases then increases (Figure 5.13, p.157). Neglecting gravitational potential energy because the flow is horizontal (and air’s density is low anyway), we have

p+\frac12\rho U^2=B. (5.30)

Bernoulli equation along a horizontal path.

gravitational potential energy: potential energy that fluid has relative to a reference height z₀: ∫ᵥ ρg(z−z₀)dV.

Conservation of mass prescribes that the velocity in the throat must be higher than that in the wider regions of the tube. For mass to be conserved, the mass flow rate through the wide regions of the tube (ρU₁A₁) must be equal to the mass flow rate through the throat (ρU₂A₂):

\rho U_1A_1=\rho U_2A_2, (5.31)

which means

U_2=U_1\frac{A_1}{A_2}. (5.32)

So the velocity in the throat has increased by the ratio of areas. This is why the water comes out faster when you put your thumb on the end of a garden hose (Figure 5.14, p.158).

throat: the narrowest section of a tube or nozzle.

Sidebar 5.4: Fundamentals

When we can approximate a jet as a free jet?

Free jets are inviscid jets in isobaric conditions

• There are no viscous effects. Fluid A issuing into fluid B where \(p_A\gg p_B\) and \(\mu_A\gg\mu_B\) will be largely unaffected by viscous effects. So water issuing into air is well approximated as a free jet. Air issuing into air can be modeled as a free jet but only for a distance approximately equal to the orifice diameter.

• When there are no pressure gradients. Free jets move ballistically because of gravity, but absent gravity their streamlines are straight.

We can assume a jet is a free jet when:

Example Problem 5.3

The impeller of a jetski creates a flow at p₁ = 0.391 MPa in a duct of circular cross-section with diameter 144 mm. This flow is exhausted to atmospheric pressure out a nozzle in the rear of the jetski which is also of circular cross-section but diameter 82 mm. Solution: If we assume steady, inviscid, incompressible flow, the Bernoulli equation applies and Eq. (5.26) is the result:

U_2=\frac{A_1}{\sqrt{A_1^2-A_2^2}}\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}}=\frac{d_1^2}{\sqrt{d_1^4-d_2^4}}\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho}}, (5.28)

so

Because the flow in the throat is faster, the pressure must have gone down, per the Bernoulli equation:

p_1+\frac12\rho U_1^2=p_2+\frac12\rho U_2^2, (5.33)

which, rearranged to show the pressure change, gives

p_1-p_2=\frac12\rho(U_2^2-U_1^2) (5.34)

pressure drop in a Venturi.

The pressure drop in the throat has immediate engineering use—any time we want to mix two fluids, one straightforward way to do this is to take one of the fluids, send it through a tube with a throat, and connect the throat to a reservoir of the second fluid. The pressure drop caused by the fluid acceleration will draw the second fluid into the tube. This approach underpins fuel–air mixing in carburetors, aspiration in water aspirators, and paint–propellant mixing in spray paint guns. We use the term Venturi to describe a tube whose cross-sectional area is reduced with the purpose of reducing the pressure. Example Problem 5.4 (p.159) shows example calculations of a Venturi used to mix liquid and gas.

Venturi: a tube with a constriction whose purpose is to generate a low-pressure region in the throat.

Solution: We need to find the pressure drop from \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) to p₂ for the 10 cm of water.

Using the Bernoulli equation and ignoring the gravity term because the flow is horizontal, we have

Applying continuity i.e., conservation of mass:

5.8 The form of the Bernoulli equation naturally encourages us to define a number of equivalent “pressures” corresponding to different forms of energy of a fluid

Although the pressure p is the only true pressure in the Bernoulli equation, the other terms have units of pressure, and physically can be converted to pressure, so other terms are often given names that include the word “pressure”.

The ½ρU² term describes the volumetric kinetic energy of the fluid. This has units of [Pa] and is referred to as the dynamic pressure. This term is a metaphor—½ρU² is not pressure, but ½ρU² has units of pressure, could be compared to pressure, and can be converted to pressure by deceleration along a streamline as prescribed by the Bernoulli equation.

p + ½ρU² is called the stagnation pressure, because the Bernoulli equation shows that if a fluid were decelerated isentropically to U = 0 along a horizontal streamline, the static pressure would increase to p + ½ρU².

p + ½ρU² + ρgz is the Bernoulli constant and is also called the total pressure. The Bernoulli equation shows that if a fluid were isentropically decelerated to U = 0 along a streamline that terminated at z = 0, the static pressure would become p + ½ρU² + ρgz.

In summary, pressure is a real pressure, dynamic pressure is a metaphor for pressure, and stagnation pressure and total pressure are hypothetical pressures we could achieve by decelerating a fluid to U = 0 along a judiciously chosen streamline.

dynamic pressure: Given by \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\tfrac12\rho U^2\). Denotes the added pressure a fluid would have if it were slowed isentropically to motionlessness. Equivalently, describes the volumetric kinetic energy of a fluid in terms of an equivalent pressure.

stagnation pressure: the pressure p₀ a fluid would have if isentropically slowed to stagnation along a streamline. For a calorically perfect gas, \(p_0=p\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}\). For an incompressible fluid, p₀ = p + ½ρU².

static pressure: equivalent to the thermodynamic definition of pressure. A parameter that describes the force per unit area that the fluid imparts on a control surface in the flow. If positive, describes compressive forces. If negative, describes tensile force.

total pressure: a property p₀ = p + ½ρU² + ρgz, having units of pressure (or equivalently volumetric energy), which indicates storage of multiple forms of energy, including p dV work of compression (p), kinetic energy (½ρU²), and gravitational potential energy ρgz.

5.9 The steady Bernoulli Equation is derived by applying a differential form of Newton’s second law to a fluid element to evaluate acceleration along a streamline

The steady Bernoulli equation makes enough sense as a conservation of energy equation that some may feel no need to see a derivation—it might seem that one is hardly needed. However, examining the derivation brings forward subtleties of the roles of energy and momentum and highlights when and where the Bernoulli equation is valid versus when not. It also sets the stage for later derivations by introducing notation and terminology.

The steady Bernoulli equation can be derived in both differential and integral form by evaluating F = ma for a fluid element along a streamline. This is a conservation of momentum analysis. Relative to derivations we will do later in the term, this one is quite straightforward. Three factors make this relatively easy:

conservation of energy: the notion that energy is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

Top Gun (1984) Haiku with portrait: “worst movie ever / and horrible dialogue / but cool airplane scenes”.


PDF page 172 — verified

1. We choose to do the derivation in streamline coordinates. Streamline coordinates make the math simpler because they automatically align all the coordinates in a way that simplifies and categorizes the forces and accelerations. Sidebar 5.6 (p.181) describes streamline coordinates in detail.

2. We choose to do the derivation in a Lagrangian coordinate frame, which makes F = ma easy to analyze but means that our conclusions describe what happens to fluid as it moves along in a flow and do not immediately link results to a stationary Eulerian reference frame. Sidebar 5.7 (p.182) describes Eulerian and Lagrangian reference frames.

3. We do the analysis for steady, incompressible, and inviscid flow, which makes many derivatives drop out of the analysis. In particular, we omit all analysis of viscous forces associated with any spatial gradients of the fluid velocity u⃗.

Although we most often use the term acceleration to describe a change in velocity with time, the steady Bernoulli equation is designed to give us information about how pressures and speeds of a specified mass of fluid change in space in a steady flow. We derive the Bernoulli equation along a streamline because the streamline is a path that lets us transform time to space easily.

Our derivation, in the end, generates Equation (5.14). En route to Equation (5.14), though, we learn additional things. The differential form of Bernoulli’s equation shows us that

• the fluid acceleration dU/dt is caused by imbalance between the pressure gradient along a streamline and the gradient in ρgz along the streamline. In this sense, the hydrostatic equation told us that for quiescent fluid, there must be no net volumetric force on a fluid, which means that the net force caused by the pressure gradient and the gravitational force must cancel. Now, we see that when the pressure gradient and the gravitational force don’t cancel, the fluid is accelerated. This is analogous to the difference between ENGRD2020 (ΣF⃗ = 0) and ENGRD2030 (a⃗ = ΣF⃗/m).

• along a streamline (but only along a streamline), dU/dt (the acceleration of the fluid) can easily be transformed into a spatial derivative—specifically, the spatial derivative of the dynamic pressure i.e., the volumetric kinetic energy. We then write a differential equation that says that p + ½ρU² + ρgz does not change along a streamline, and it is equal to a constant that we denote as B.

This derivation of the Bernoulli equation is a conservation of momentum formulation in which the net force is translated into a time rate of change of momentum.

Differential analysis of the momentum along a streamline leads to the Bernoulli equation

Our approach to analyzing momentum along a streamline will proceed as follows:

streamline coordinates: the coordinates s, n, and ℓ, indicating streamwise, normal, and binormal directions. These directions refer respectively to s: the direction in which the fluid is moving; n: the direction in which the fluid is turning; ℓ: the direction ŝ × n̂ indicating the axis around which the fluid path turns.

Lagrangian: pronounced la-GRANZH-ee-an. A mode of analysis in which a mass element (i.e., a system) is followed as it moves through a flowfield.

inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don’t significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid has μ = 0; in practice there is no such thing.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

quiescent: motionless; u⃗ = 0.

dynamic pressure: Given by \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\tfrac12\rho U^2\). Denotes the added pressure a fluid would have if it were slowed isentropically to motionlessness. Equivalently, describes the volumetric kinetic energy of a fluid in terms of an equivalent pressure.

conservation of momentum: the notion that changes in momentum are brought about by forces as prescribed by Newton’s second law.


PDF page 173 — verified

1. create a differential control volume with one axis in the direction of fluid flow and two others perpendicular to the fluid flow.

2. write expressions for the pressure on upstream and downstream faces by use of a Taylor-series expansion around the control volume center.

3. sum the surface forces (from the pressure) with the body force (from gravity) to determine the net force in the direction of flow.

4. equate the net force with the product of fluid mass and acceleration.

5. rewrite the fluid acceleration as a spatial derivative of dynamic pressure.

6. show that p + ½ρU² + ρgz does not change along a streamline.

7. conclude that p + ½ρU² + ρgz is uniform along a streamline.

We will do this derivation twice. First, we will do this for flow in the x direction, which is simple because the axes are convenient and gravity can be neglected. Then, we will repeat this for flow in any direction.

We consider steady, inviscid, incompressible flow along a streamline pointing in the x direction, and consider a differential fluid element (Figure 5.18, p.184) aligned along the streamline with sides of differential length Δx, Δy, and Δz, and we consider the x momentum in a Lagrangian frame. Because the streamline is pointing in the x direction, there is no gravitational component along the streamline. In this case, the only forces applied to the fluid element are the surface forces due to pressure. The only forces with a component in the streamwise direction are the pressure forces on the upstream and downstream faces, which have magnitude F = pΔyΔz, evaluated at each face. If we allow the pressure to change along the streamline, then we must write an expression for the pressures on each face. To do this, we write a Taylor-series expansion (See Sidebar 5.8, p.183) for the pressure around the center of the fluid element. Keeping only the first term of this Taylor-series expansion, the pressure at the right face is p + ½(dp/dx)Δx and at the left face is p − ½(dp/dx)Δx. Thus the net streamwise force on the fluid element is

F_x=\left(p-\frac12\frac{dp}{dx}\Delta x\right)\Delta y\Delta z-\left(p+\frac12\frac{dp}{dx}\Delta x\right)\Delta y\Delta z=-\frac{dp}{dx}\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z. (5.50)

In the streamwise direction, we can then set the product of the mass times the Lagrangian acceleration of the fluid element equal to this force:

ma_s=F_s, (5.51)

\rho\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z\frac{dU}{dt}=-\frac{dp}{dx}\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z, (5.52)

Taylor-series expansion: an infinite series that describes the value of a function f near a point x⃗ in terms of the derivatives of f at x⃗.

control volume: a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

differential: relating to how properties are changing locally as expressed by derivatives. Compare with integral, meaning related to finite differences evaluated over finite distances.

fluid element: we use the term fluid element to mean a specified mass of fluid i.e., a system. A fluid element can be finite or infinitesimal.

Lagrangian: pronounced la-GRANZH-ee-an. A mode of analysis in which a mass element (i.e., a system) is followed as it moves through a flowfield.


PDF page 174 — verified

\rho\frac{dU}{dt}=-\frac{dp}{dx}, (5.53)

which tells us that, for a horizontal streamline, the presence of a ∂p/∂x derivative causes a net volumetric force on the fluid (the pressure gradient is not balanced by any gravity force), and therefore an acceleration.

If we can rearrange Equation (5.53) so that the derivatives on both sides are with respect to the same coordinate, we can integrate the differential relation to generate an integral relation. This is possible along a streamline in steady flow because the acceleration can be transformed to a spatial derivative along the streamline. The total derivative can be written in terms of partials:

\frac{dU}{dt}=\frac{\partial U}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}, (5.54)

and because U = ∂x/∂t,

\frac{dU}{dt}=U\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}. (5.55)

Using the inverse chain rule,

\frac{dU}{dt}=U\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac12U^2\right). (5.56)

Multiplying both sides by ρ, we find the relation

\rho\frac{dU}{dt}=\frac{d(\rho U)}{dt}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac12\rho U^2\right)=\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac12\rho U^2\right). (5.57)

Equation (5.57) tells us that, along a streamline, the time rate of change of volumetric fluid momentum (ρU) can equivalently be written as the streamwise derivative of the volumetric kinetic energy. We have thus transformed a temporal derivative into a spatial derivative.

Substituting this back into Eq. (5.53), we get

\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac12\rho U^2\right)=-\frac{dp}{dx}, (5.58)

and therefore

\frac{d}{dx}\left(p+\frac12\rho U^2\right)=0. (5.59)

Integrating, we find

p_{\mathrm{stag}}=p+\frac12\rho U^2. (5.60)

This is called the Bernoulli equation and this version is valid for a horizontal streamline. The pressure p is (for clarity) referred to as the static pressure, ½ρU² is referred to as the dynamic pressure, and their sum, \(p_{\mathrm{stag}}\), is referred to as the stagnation pressure. Because we derived this for a horizontal streamline, there is no gravity term.

differential: relating to how properties are changing locally as expressed by derivatives. Compare with integral, meaning related to finite differences evaluated over finite distances.

integral: as an adjective, relating to the finite difference between two discrete states (e.g. point 1 to point 2) or the integrated effect of something over a finite distance or volume. Compare with differential, meaning related to derivatives.

chain rule: if F(x)=f[g(x)], F′(x)=g′(x)f′[g(x)].

streamwise: in the direction of the flow i.e., along the streamlines.

Bernoulli equation: in differential form d/ds(p + ½ρu² + ρgz)=0, in integral form B=p+½ρu²+ρgz, where B is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.


PDF page 175 — source_issue

So, for steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a horizontal streamline, the sum of p and ½ρU² does not change for a Lagrangian fluid element. This expression shows that, as a fluid speeds up, it exchanges static pressure for kinetic energy, whereas as a fluid slows down, it exchanges kinetic energy for static pressure.

Along a general streamline, the total pressure is uniform

We can extend this analysis for fluid in a gravitational field (Figure 5.19, p.184) and we can consider pressure gradients both parallel to and normal to the streamline.

We start by considering again flow along a streamline, but we allow this streamline to be oriented arbitrarily relative to the gravitational vector. Now we write the equations in terms of the streamwise coordinate s and the normal and binormal coordinates n and ℓ. We define θ as the angle between the x axis and the streamwise coordinate s in the xz plane. Thus dz/ds = sin θ. The component of the gravitational force in the s direction is −ρgΔsΔnΔℓ sin θ. The net force in the s direction from the pressure gradient is −(dp/ds)ΔsΔnΔℓ. Summing these forces, we find that the total streamwise force on the fluid element \(F_s\) is

F_s=\left(-\rho g\sin\theta-\frac{dp}{ds}\right)\Delta s\Delta n\Delta\ell, (5.61)

and the volumetric streamwise force on the fluid element \(f_s\) is

f_s=-\rho g\sin\theta-\frac{dp}{ds}. (5.62)

Setting the streamwise force \(F_s\) equal to mass times streamwise acceleration of the fluid element, we obtain

-\rho g\Delta s\Delta n\Delta\ell\sin\theta-\frac{dp}{ds}\Delta s\Delta n\Delta\ell=\rho\Delta s\Delta n\Delta\ell\frac{dU}{dt}. (5.63)

We can divide out the element volume ΔsΔnΔℓ, and, because dU/dt = (∂U/∂s)(∂s/∂t) = U∂U/∂s = U dU/ds, we obtain

\rho g\sin\theta-\frac{dp}{ds}=\rho U\frac{dU}{ds}. (5.64)

As before, the inverse chain rule can be used to set ρU dU/ds = d/ds(½ρU²). From earlier, sin θ = dz/ds. Thus

-\rho g\frac{dz}{ds}-\frac{dp}{ds}=\frac{d}{ds}\left(\frac12\rho U^2\right), (5.65)

and, gathering terms:

\frac{d}{ds}\left(p+\frac12\rho U^2+\rho gz\right)=0, (5.66)

inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don’t significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid that has μ=0; in practice there is no such thing.

streamwise: in the direction of the flow i.e., along the streamlines.

chain rule: if F(x)=f[g(x)], F′(x)=g′(x)f′[g(x)].

Editorial note: Eq. (5.64) is retained exactly as printed. The leading gravity term is positive in the source, although Eqs. (5.63) and (5.65) require a minus sign. The consistent expression is \(-\rho g\sin\theta-\frac{dp}{ds}=\rho U\frac{dU}{ds}\).


PDF page 176 — source_issue

and we can integrate this with respect to s to obtain

p+\frac12\rho U^2+\rho gz=B. (5.67)

For a general streamline, we see that inviscid flow allows conversion back and forth between p, ½ρU², and ρgz. The sum of these is the total pressure and, equivalently, the Bernoulli constant.

At any point on a streamline, the local streamline curvature is related to the normal pressure gradient

In the previous section, we showed that along a streamline, the momentum equation (i.e., Newton’s second law) could be rearranged to show that total pressure is unchanging; net force from pressure gradients and gravity either accelerate or decelerate the flow, causing an increase or decrease in the volumetric kinetic energy. That led to Equation (5.67).

Normal to a streamline, the momentum equation (i.e., Newton’s second law) tells us how much the streamline is curving. We use the same streamwise coordinates but now we assume that the streamline is curved, and we take the n direction to point toward the center of curvature. We define α as the angle between the x axis and the normal coordinate n in the xz plane. Thus dz/dn = sin α. The component of the gravitational force in the n direction is −ρgΔsΔnΔℓ sin α. The net force in the n direction from the pressure gradient is −(dp/dn)ΔsΔnΔℓ. Summing these forces, we find that the total normal force on the fluid element \(F_n\) is

F_n=\left(-\rho g\sin\alpha-\frac{dp}{dn}\right)\Delta s\Delta n\Delta\ell, (5.68)

and the volumetric normal force on the fluid element \(f_n\) is

f_n=-\rho g\sin\alpha-\frac{dp}{dn}. (5.69)

Streamline coordinates are cylindrical coordinates, which means that the coordinates themselves are a function of time, which means that velocities and accelerations are trickier to evaluate—they require application of the chain rule. Doing that chain-rule analysis, though, generates the centripetal acceleration relation for flow along curved paths; that analysis and its final result are both described from a vector calculus standpoint on p.453. For steady flow, most of the terms in Equation (B.62) drop out, and the centripetal acceleration relation becomes a = U²/R. Setting the normal force \(F_n\) equal to \(F_n=ma_n=mU^2/R\) from the relation for centripetal force for an object moving in a circular orbit:

-\rho g\Delta s\Delta n\Delta\ell\sin\alpha-\frac{dp}{dn}\Delta s\Delta n\Delta\ell=\rho\Delta s\Delta n\Delta\ell\frac{U^2}{R}. (5.70)

We can divide out the element volume, leading to

-\rho g\sin\alpha-\frac{dp}{dn}=\frac{\rho U^2}{R}. (5.71)

From earlier, sin α = dz/dn. Thus

\rho g\frac{dz}{dn}-\frac{dp}{dn}=\frac{\rho U^2}{R}, (5.72)

volumetric: related to volume, or per unit volume.

streamwise: in the direction of the flow i.e., along the streamlines.

centripetal: pointing toward the center of a circular arc.

Vector Calculus isn’t Spooky Haiku with portrait: “vector calculus / shouldn’t be really spooky / it helps for fluids”.

PDF page 177 — source_issue

and, gathering terms:

\frac{d}{dn}(p+\rho gz)=\frac{dk}{dn}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}. (5.73)

Unlike for our relation along a streamline, which was homogeneous and easy to integrate, it is not particularly easy to integrate this relation. Rather, we focus on this differential result. It tells us that the net force normal to the streamline, which comes from a normal variation in the hydrostatic constant k = p + ρgz, is coexistence with streamline curvature away from the region where k is larger, toward the region where k is smaller.

5.10 The different relations we have discussed are all Euler Equations in Streamline Coordinates

In this chapter, we have described the Bernoulli equation, for example the differential form for changes in the Bernoulli constant B = p + ½ρU² + ρgz along a streamline:

\frac{dB}{ds}=\frac{d}{ds}\left(p+\frac12\rho U^2+\rho gz\right)=0. (5.74)

We have also described the changes in the hydrostatic constant k = p + ρgz normal to a streamline, and how that relates to the local streamline curvature:

\frac{dk}{dn}=\frac{d}{dn}(p-\rho gz)=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}. (5.75)

We can write one more relation, for the binormal direction ℓ. By definition, the streamline has no curvature in the binormal direction (R = ∞), so the same arguments that we used for the gradients normal to the streamline give

\frac{dk}{d\ell}=\frac{d}{d\ell}(p+\rho gz)=0. (5.76)

Equations (5.74)–(5.76) constitute the inviscid equations of motion (i.e., the Euler equations) in streamline coordinates. These three relations, in turn, tell us that, at any point in a fluid:

• The Bernoulli constant (i.e., the total pressure) is not changing in the direction of flow; energy is just being traded among stored work, kinetic energy, and potential energy.

• The hydrostatic constant decreases in the direction of the local curvature of the streamline; a gradient in hydrostatic constant means a net force causes the flow to turn.

• The hydrostatic constant is not changing in the binormal direction; the binormal direction in a moving fluid is the one direction where k acts as if the fluid were not moving at all.

homogeneous: with reference to an equation, means there is no constant term. With reference to a fluid property, means uniform.

differential: relating to how properties are changing locally as expressed by derivatives. Compare with integral, meaning related to finite differences evaluated over finite distances.

hydrostatic constant: the constant k in the hydrostatic equation p + ρgz = k.

binormal: the binormal direction is the direction normal to both the tangent and normal to a curve, given by the cross product of the tangent to the normal.

inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don’t significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid that has μ=0; in practice there is no such thing.

Bernoulli constant: the constant B in the Bernoulli equation B = p + ½ρu² + ρgz. A measure of the energy per unit volume of the fluid. Synonymous with total pressure.

hydrostatic constant: the constant k in the hydrostatic equation p + ρgz = k.

Editorial note: Eq. (5.75) is retained exactly as printed. The source prints p−ρgz, conflicting with k=p+ρgz and Eq. (5.73) on the same page. The consistent expression is \(\frac{dk}{dn}=\frac{d}{dn}(p+\rho gz)=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}\).


PDF page 178 — verified

The choice of streamline coordinates leads to very simple equations of motion. Example Problem 5.8 (p.185) characterizes different paths in a system that has well-defined and uniform streamwise, normal, and binormal coordinates. Streamline coordinates, though, can be difficult in that they only let us interpret what is going on in a fluid flow once we know in what direction the flow is moving. For simple systems and geometries, the Euler equations in streamline coordinates generate useful analysis, because sometimes we know the whole velocity field (say, for fluid rotating in a beaker) and sometimes we know just enough to do an analysis (say, for flow issuing from a reservoir, in which case we know almost nothing except that the streamlines at some point need to pass through the orifice). For more complicated systems (in later chapters), we will need to formulate the equations of motion in a fixed Cartesian or cylindrical coordinate system first to determine the velocity field; only after we have determined the velocity field will the equations of motion in streamline coordinates become useful to us.

5.11 The Bernoulli equation fails when viscous effects are present or when moving along a path that is not a streamline

The Bernoulli equation is simple and effective for helping us perform a number of calculations; further, it in many cases helps us to develop an intuition for how fluids behave. It is the most important equation of this chapter. However, the assumptions associated with its implementation are severe, and the Bernoulli equation gives nonsensical answers if it is used incorrectly. Many flows cannot be described by the Bernoulli equation. Because this is a class and we are taking on problems in a prescribed order, we are talking for the moment about flows in which the Bernoulli equation is useful. However, as the term goes on, we will talk about more complicated situations, and whether the Bernoulli equation is applicable will have to be determined by an analysis of the relative importance or unimportance of viscous effects in the flow.

Sometimes, the Bernoulli equation can be adjusted to account for viscous effects; for example the conversion of kinetic energy to pressure in a centrifugal pump is mostly described by the Bernoulli equation except for inefficiencies and viscous losses that make the final pressure not as high as would be expected from an inviscid analysis, while also leading to an increase in the temperature of the pumped fluid. Also, flow through a long straight tube is mostly described by the Bernoulli equation except for viscous losses, which cause the pressure to decrease as fluid moves downstream as the kinetic energy is dissipated as heat. The viscous losses in the pipe are the reason why you always need a pump to move fluid through it; the Bernoulli equation would predict that no pump is needed to move fluid through a horizontal pipe. But a Bernoulli equation with an extra loss term often describes the behavior of these systems quite well.

equations of motion: in fluid mechanics, the (usually dynamic) equations that govern motion of a fluid element.

Euler equations: pronounced OY-ler. The inviscid conservation of momentum equations. Can be written in streamline coordinates (dB/ds=0, dk/dn=−ρU²/R, dk/dℓ=0) or fixed coordinates (ρ(∂u⃗/∂t+u⃗·∇u⃗)=−∇p+ρg⃗).

Bernoulli equation: in differential form 0=d/ds(p+½ρu²+ρgz), in integral form B=p+½ρu²+ρgz, where B is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

PDF page 179 — verified

Don’t try to use ∂B/∂s = 0 along a path that is not a streamline

The most common error students make is to apply the Bernoulli equation along a path that is not a streamline. Unfortunately, this is an easy mistake to make for multiple reasons.

First, we use the Bernoulli equation so much that sometimes it is easy to just panic and use the Bernoulli equation no matter what.

Second, 99% of all YouTube videos ever made that use the word “Bernoulli” also say “fast-moving fluid has low pressure”, which encourages one to think the Bernoulli equation works on any path, if you watch too many YouTube videos.

Third, there are many flows where the fast regions have lower pressure than the slower regions, which makes it seem like maybe the Bernoulli equation applies along any path, but just because a flow has a fast region with low pressure doesn’t mean the Bernoulli equation had much of anything to do with it. Often, these effects are attributed to the Bernoulli equation; it makes it seem like the Bernoulli equation explains everything.

Fourth, just to make things a pain, sometimes the Bernoulli equation does apply along any path. That is not generally true but it is true in special cases. It is true if the flow is irrotational, and it is true if the Bernoulli constant is uniform at infinity, for example for a uniform flow over an object if gravity can be ignored. The Bernoulli equation applies along any path in most inviscid aerodynamic analysis with a uniform freestream, for example (see a large fraction of MAE3050). However, if you are using the Bernoulli equation along a path that is not a streamline, you had better know that the flow is irrotational or the Bernoulli constant is uniform at infinity.

Fifth, sometimes the streamlines in a flow are not obvious, especially when we are assuming that a flow is almost quiescent in a domain—if we are approximating the fluid as quiescent, how can we define a streamline? Here, experienced fluid mechanicians (who teach classes and write fluid textbooks) feel comfortable drawing streamlines as part of a limiting process in which the velocity approaches zero closely enough that ½ρU² goes to zero but is still enough to define a streamline. Fluid mechanics students usually find this not so obvious.

The Reynolds number describes whether viscous effects are important and therefore whether the Bernoulli equation can be used

Our analysis that leads to the Euler equations in streamline coordinates is an inviscid analysis—we ignore viscosity. This is often a completely sound approach, because the engineering outcomes we are trying to calculate (average velocity out an orifice, force on an object) are often well approximated by an inviscid analysis.

Bernoulli equation: in differential form 0=d/ds(p+½ρu²+ρgz), in integral form B=p+½ρu²+ρgz, where B is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

YouTube Haiku with portrait: “YouTubers are nice / but seem to know so little / fluid mechanics”.

irrotational: not rotating, i.e., ω⃗=∇×u⃗=0.

Bernoulli constant: the constant B in the Bernoulli equation B=p+½ρu²+ρgz. A measure of the energy per unit volume of the fluid. Synonymous with total pressure.

quiescent: motionless; u⃗=0.

inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don’t significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid that has μ=0; in practice there is no such thing.


PDF page 180 — verified

flow that is unaffected by viscosity. We can always find a place in the flow where viscosity matters. The question really becomes: even though viscosity matters somewhere, does it matter enough that it affects the calculations we care about. The Reynolds number Re = ρUℓ/μ is the parameter that tells us the answer.

The Reynolds number tells us whether viscous effects can be neglected in many ways. Two key ways to think about it are as follows:

• Far from walls, the Reynolds number tells us the ratio of volumetric fluid kinetic energy (which is proportional to ρU²) to the viscous force per unit area the fluid feels (which we will later show is proportional to μU/ℓ). Fluids that are fast, dense, and moving in and around large objects have a lot of kinetic energy and a lot of inertia, and viscous forces are not enough to affect them much. So fast-moving water in a large river is well described by an inviscid analysis. Slow-moving honey in a microchannel is very poorly described by inviscid flow equations.

• Near walls, the same Reynolds number can be thought of as a ratio of times—the viscous effects of a wall diffuse a length ℓ in a time ρℓ²/μ, whereas fluid moves a distance ℓ in a time ℓ/U. The ratio of these two (which is again equal to the Reynolds number) tells us whether fluid zooms through a tube or over an airfoil in a time so short that viscous effects cannot diffuse very far from the surface. In this sense, the same two examples above can be thought of in terms of how far effects diffuse from a surface. In a large river with fast-moving water, there are viscous effects, they are just restricted to a region very close to the river bed, and in the end the net effect of this tiny region is small. In contrast, the viscous effects of the microchannel wall diffuse throughout the flowfield for the slow-moving honey, and there is no region in the honey flow that remains unaffected by viscosity.

So, when we use the Bernoulli equation for flow through a pipe or flow over an airfoil, we are using an inviscid analysis, and the reason this leads to a good approximation of the correct answer is because, when the Reynolds number is high, most of the fluid flow is dominated by fluid inertia or kinetic energy. There are small domains where viscosity matters, especially very close to any surfaces, but if these domains are very thin, they often do not affect our calculations.

Reynolds number: Re=ρUℓ/μ. The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(\mathrm{Re}_L\), \(\mathrm{Re}_d\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

Reynolds number Haiku 5 with portrait: “dynamic pressure / Newtonian viscous stress / it’s the ratio”.

Reynolds number Haiku 2 with portrait: “inertial/viscous / the Reynolds number tells us / which one dominates”.


PDF page 181 — verified

5.12 Even when we do not know the velocity field, we can often determine enough about streamlines to help us perform a Bernoulli equation analysis

We start by providing a number of definitions and observations relevant to streamlines:

• Streamlines are everywhere tangent to the instantaneous velocity vector u⃗.

• If the flow is steady, a streamline is equivalent to a pathline, meaning that the streamline shows the path that a fluid element would take through the domain.

• If fluid flows from point A to point B in a steady flow, there must be a streamline connecting point A to point B.

• If fluid flows around an embedded solid object, a streamline must terminate on the surface of that object in a stagnation point somewhere on the upstream side of the object.

• If fluid flows around a region of stagnant fluid, a streamline must terminate at the edge of the stagnant fluid in a stagnation point somewhere on the upstream side of the object.

• If a streamline terminates at an impermeable wall or a region of stagnant fluid, the velocity must approach zero along that streamline—it must be a stagnation point.

• If there is a stagnation point i.e., a point where u⃗ = 0 somewhere in the flow, a streamline can be drawn through that point only as part of a limiting process, so saying that a streamline “terminates at a stagnation point” actually requires a bit of attention to the math.

• Streamlines are routinely drawn through stagnation points or to follow the contour of an impermeable wall. These streamlines are understood to be the product of this limiting process, i.e., we take the limit of the streamline contour as we approach the wall, or we take the limit of the streamline contour as we approach the streamline that goes through the stagnation point, or we take the limit as fluid approaches the stagnation point along the streamline.

• A streamline can only have a sharp corner if (a) the sharp corner is at a location where u⃗ = 0 or (b) the fluid is going through an oblique shock wave.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

pathline: a line that traces the Lagrangian motion of a fluid element as it moves in time. Can be imagined as the line that would be traced out if a small particle were placed into a fluid flow.

stagnation point: a point in a flow where the velocity is zero.

shock wave: a discontinuous transition in which a supersonic flow slows down, with an attendant increase in pressure and density.


PDF page 182 — source_issue

When walls and stagnation points seem to create contradictions, the resolution always involves taking a limit as we approach the wall or stagnation point in some way

If you are comfortable with the fact that streamlines are routinely drawn terminating at stagnation points, and drawn at the surfaces of walls, you do not need to read this section.

Contradictions seem to arise when we carefully consider stagnation points and walls in the context of streamlines, especially because fluid mechanicians tend to be cavalier in discussing streamlines in this context.

When u⃗ = 0, the definition of a streamline (tangent to velocity vector) no longer works. How do we define the streamline in this case?

There are two ways we can resolve this problem. The first is that, for incompressible flow, density is fixed and uniform, and thus conservation of mass places kinematic restraints on the fluid flow. In this case, we can use a different definition of the streamline, i.e., as an isocontour of a scalar called a streamfunction; that definition doesn’t have any problem with stagnation points or walls. We need one streamfunction for 2D flow and three streamfunctions for 3D flow.

The second resolution is that, even though it is not possible to define a streamline at a point where u⃗ = 0, we can always take a limit as we approach that point. For example, at a wall, using the “tangent to the velocity vector” definition we technically can’t draw a streamline at an impermeable wall. But we can draw a streamline a tiny distance from a wall, and we can take the limit as that tiny distance becomes as small as we need it to be. So... although there is a mathematical difficulty at the wall, in practice our engineering interpretation of along what path the fluid flows is not affected by this.

Similarly, a streamline that terminates at a wall always approaches u⃗ = 0 at the wall; in fact if we calculate how long it takes the fluid on that streamline to reach the wall, that time is infinite. But, that doesn’t prevent our drawing the contour all the way to the wall.

As an example, consider the velocity field u⃗ = x x̂ − y ŷ, which approximates the 2D flow of fluid impinging from top and bottom. This velocity field has streamlines that are all rectangular hyperbola, and are all defined by y = A/x where each unique value of the constant A defines a streamline. Anywhere in this flow, we can calculate the velocity vector and find that it is tangent to one of those rectangular hyperbola. Along any of those rectangular hyperbola, we can integrate along the curve and follow the path of the particle.

There are streamlines along the y axis and along the x axis; these are most easily obtained by taking the limit as A approaches zero from the positive and negative directions. At the origin, u⃗ = 0, the velocity vector is the zero vector, and the tangent is not defined. However, all of these values are defined everywhere except that point singularity.

conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

streamfunction: [units/short text unreadable]. Scalar function defined for 2D flows equivalently as (a) \(\psi(A)=\int_O^A u\,dy-v\,dx\), or (b) \(u=\partial\psi/\partial y\) and \(v=-\partial\psi/\partial x\), or (c) [displayed vector expression unreadable]. Incompressible 2D flow can be defined [text unreadable] because the existence of [text unreadable] is mathematically equivalent to satisfying conservation of mass.

Editorial note: enlarged inspection recovered the integral and component-derivative streamfunction formulas. The third vector formula and several adjacent words remain erased; they are explicitly marked instead of reconstructed.


PDF page 183 — verified

A short set of guidelines informs most decisions about where streamlines can be drawn to facilitate analysis using the Bernoulli equation

The elegance of the integral form of the Bernoulli equation is that it can be applied at any point along any streamline; often all that is required is to identify whether fluid flows from one point to another and where streamlines stagnate.

If we knew the distribution of u⃗ in space, identifying the streamlines would be trivial—we would simply trace out contours that are tangent to the (known) velocity vectors. But if we knew the distribution of u⃗ in space, we would also know the distribution of p in space, and we wouldn’t need the Bernoulli equation. So, gaining benefit from the Bernoulli equation requires that we figure out enough about where the streamlines go so that we can do an analysis, but that we figure all of this out when we do not know the velocity vectors already.

5.13 The Bernoulli equation in practice is always applied to a Reynolds-averaged flow

The Bernoulli equation in practice is always applied to a Reynolds-averaged flow (see Sidebar 5.9, p.186).

5.14 The steady Bernoulli equation can in practice still be used even with unsteady boundary conditions

We might ask: need the steady Bernoulli equation be thrown away if there is anything unsteady about a flow. For example, if a reservoir is emptying, and the height of the reservoir is changing, does that invalidate the Bernoulli equation? Or can we still use it? The model that governs this question is the quasi-steady flow model (see Sidebar 5.10, p.187).

Bernoulli equation: in differential form 0=d/ds(p+½ρu²+ρgz), in integral form B=p+½ρu²+ρgz, where B is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

7. (OBJECTIVE: Motivate why indicated airspeed is used. Understand practical effects of standard atmosphere in aviation) The Bernoulli equation can be used to understand how speed, pressure, and density change along a streamline. Airplane airspeed indicators calculate IAS from the Pitot–static tube as follows:

\mathrm{IAS}=\sqrt{\frac{2(p_{\mathrm{stag}}-p_{\mathrm{static}})}{\rho_{z=0}}}, (5.81)

where \(\rho_{z=0}\) is the standard density at sea level, not the density of the air around the plane. Because the real ρ is not used in this calculation, IAS is really a measure of the local dynamic pressure expressed in velocity units; it is not a measurement of the airplane’s speed. Because air density doesn’t change too much, though, IAS is still of same order as the airplane’s speed.

2. (OBJECTIVE: Torricelli relation problem but with knowns and unknowns reversed) A water jet in a fountain shoots 4 ft high and travels 6 ft. At what gauge pressure is the reservoir of water? Solution: The z velocity is \(w=w_0-gt\), time at peak is \(t=w_0/g\), z at peak is \(z=w_0^2/(2g)\). Time at return to ground is \(t=2w_0/g\), x position at return to ground is \(x=2u_0w_0/g\). So

4=\frac{w_0^2}{2g},\qquad6=\frac{2u_0w_0}{g}. (5.82)

From this, the speed at exhaust is 6.2 m/s.

\Delta p=\frac12\rho U^2=19\,\mathrm{kPa}=6.4\,\mathrm{ft\ H_2O}. (5.83)

Editorial note: the printed 6.2 m/s and 19 kPa do not follow from a 4 ft peak height and 6 ft range. With \(H=1.2192\,\mathrm m\), \(L=1.8288\,\mathrm m\), \(w_0^2=2gH\), \(u_0=L g/(2w_0)\), and \(U^2=u_0^2+w_0^2\), the speed is about 5.22 m/s and the water gauge pressure is 13.6 kPa (4.56 ft of water). Source values are retained above.
