3. (OBJECTIVE: show ballistic trajectory of fluid jets; relate to mass conservation) If you watch a jet falling out of a faucet (Figure 5.29, p.191), you will find that the radius of the jet decreases as it falls away from the faucet. Define z = 0 as the z-location of the orifice of the faucet with positive z pointing upward, and let a be the diameter of that orifice. Let g be the acceleration due to gravity. Define U₀ as the speed of the fluid issuing from the orifice. Ignore viscosity and surface tension and assume that the speed of the fluid is a function of z but uniform horizontally. Determine the fluid speed U(z) and the jet diameter a(z). Solution: Use Bernoulli because all points in flow can be traced back via a streamline to the orifice exit. Per Bernoulli,

p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac12\rho U^2+\rho gz=p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac12\rho U_0^2. (5.84)

Here we use \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) for the pressures because the liquid is exposed to atmosphere. z = 0 at the orifice so the ρgz term is zero on the RHS. Rearranging,

U(z)=\sqrt{U_0^2-2gz}. (5.85)

The mass flow must be uniform, so at all points UA is the same. From this,

U_0\pi a^2/4=U(z)\pi r(z)^2, (5.86)

which simplifies to

r(z)=\frac{a/2}{\sqrt[4]{1-\frac{2gz}{U_0^2}}}. (5.87)

4. (OBJECTIVE: use ballistic analysis to study free jets; understand engineering utility of free jets) A firefighter stands 15 feet away from a burning house and needs to get a jet of water into an upstairs bedroom that is 13 ft off the ground. How much pressure must be in the water line if this is to be possible? What is the best angle α relative to horizontal for the firefighter to launch the jet at? Solution: An inviscid analysis provides the most optimistic estimate of the water speed and will provide the lowest minimum pressure estimate. Launching a free jet at angle α, the x velocity is U cos α and the z velocity is U sin α − gt. Taking the jet nozzle as the origin, x(t) = Ut cos α and z(t) = Ut sin α − ½gt².

The lowest pressure to get the jet to the window is when the jet’s peak is right at the window (i.e., w = 0). From that t = U sin α/g, which gives x = 15 = U² sin α cos α/g and z = 13 = ½U² sin²α/g. The ratio of these gives 13/15 = ½ tan α which gives α = 60°. Substituting into the x or z expression gives U = 18.4 m/s. From Bernoulli, that speed requires an (overpressure in the hose line of ½ρU² = 1.7 bar. So the water line must be pressured to at least 2.7 bar.

5. (OBJECTIVE: show inviscid draining of a reservoir) A cylindrical reservoir (Figure 5.30, p.191) with cross-section A₁ is filled with water at height z = h₀ at time t = 0. The top is open and exposed to the atmosphere. A water-filled pipe of cross-section [source unreadable; related to A₂] is inserted into the reservoir to siphon it, where the outer pipe terminates at z = 0 and the inner pipe terminates at a small [source unreadable], just enough so that the fluid can enter the pipe unimpeded. Model the flow as steady flow but with a slowly changing reservoir height, and assume that there are no viscous effects. How long does it take for the reservoir to empty? And what is h(t)? Solution: This question can be solved with quasi-steady analysis, i.e., a steady governing equation but time-dependent boundary conditions. This is valid because, although the boundary conditions are changing, they are changing slowly enough that the steady governing equation is still valid, i.e., the Eulerian fluid acceleration is small.

The Bernoulli equation specifies that the Bernoulli constant is uniform along a streamline. Drawing a streamline from top of the reservoir to the exit of the siphon gives \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh=p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\tfrac12\rho U^2\), leading to the Torricelli relation U = √(2gh). The volumetric flow rate out of the siphon is thus A₂√(2gh). This causes the height of the reservoir to drop over time, at a rate A₁ dh/dt = −A₂√(2gh). So we have an ODE for h(t):

A_1\frac{dh}{dt}=-A_2\sqrt{2gh}. (5.88)

This ODE is separable, so put all the h stuff on the left:

h^{-1/2}\frac{dh}{dt}=-\frac{A_2}{A_1}\sqrt{2g}. (5.89)

Editorial note: Problem 4’s claim that minimum pressure occurs when the trajectory peak is at the window is incorrect. For target displacement \((x,z)\), minimizing \(U^2=gx^2(1+\tan^2\alpha)/[2(x\tan\alpha-z)]\) gives \(U_{\min}^2=g(z+\sqrt{x^2+z^2})\) and \(\tan\alpha=(z+\sqrt{x^2+z^2})/x\). With 15 ft horizontal and 13 ft vertical displacement, converted to meters, this gives about 9.90 m/s at 65.46°, and water gauge pressure 49.0 kPa (0.49 bar), or about 1.50 bar absolute at standard atmospheric pressure. The printed 18.4 m/s, 1.7 bar gauge and 2.7 bar absolute also use an inconsistent length conversion. These are idealized source-problem calculations; all printed results remain above.


PDF page 188 — source_issue

Integrate both from start to finish. Call \(t_{\mathrm{empty}}\) the time to empty the reservoir:

\int_{t=0}^{t=t_{\mathrm{empty}}}h^{-1/2}\frac{dh}{dt}\,dt=\int_{t=0}^{t=t_{\mathrm{empty}}}-\frac{A_2}{A_1}\sqrt{2g}\,dt. (5.90)

Do a parameter transform on left from t to h. Change integral bounds to the h bounds, and replace (dh/dt)dt with dh:

\int_{h=h_0}^{h=0}h^{-1/2}\,dh=\int_{t=0}^{t=t_{\mathrm{empty}}}-\frac{A_2}{A_1}\sqrt{2g}\,dt, (5.91)

\left[2h^{1/2}\right]_{h_0}^{0}=\left[-\frac{A_2}{A_1}\sqrt{2g}\,t\right]_0^{t_{\mathrm{empty}}}. (5.92)

0-2h_0^{1/2}=-\frac{A_2}{A_1}\sqrt{2g}\,t_{\mathrm{empty}}, (5.93)

t_{\mathrm{empty}}=\frac{A_1}{A_2}\sqrt{\frac{2h_0}{g}}. (5.94)

We can do this more generally for the time required for the height h₀ to drop to a lower height h, in which case we get

t(h)=\frac{A_1}{A_2}\sqrt{\frac2g}(\sqrt{h_0}-\sqrt h). (5.95)

This can be rearranged algebraically to find

h=h_0+\frac{A_2^2}{A_1^2}\frac{g}{2}t^2-\frac{2A_2}{A_1}\sqrt{h_0}\,t\sqrt{\frac g2}. (5.96)

Here, solutions are only meaningful for positive h. This is a parabolic distribution. At \(t>t_{\mathrm{empty}}\) the solution has no meaning; this analysis loses meaning if h goes negative or if t goes positive because of all the principal square roots and the squaring we did.

6. (OBJECTIVE: Understanding the characteristics of rotating bodies of fluid) A zenith telescope can be made using a rotating mercury tank as the main reflective lens—this can make sense as it is extremely difficult and expensive to make a solid lens of that size without any blemishes. When the system rotates at an angular velocity ω and reaches equilibrium, the mercury inside also rotates with an angular velocity ω. Use the normal Euler equation normal to streamlines to calculate the pressure variation along the radius r (r and n point oppositely, so ∂p/∂r = −∂p/∂n) and use that to predict the height of the mercury. How, if at all, would the height be different if the fluid were water or gallium? How, if at all, would the pressure distribution be different if the fluid were water or gallium (ρ = 5910 kg/m³)? Solution: With angular velocity ω, the speed of the field is U = ωr. Normal to a streamline, we can write

\frac{\partial p}{\partial n}=-\frac{\partial p}{\partial r}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}, (5.97)

where R is the radius of curvature. Given that U = ωr and r = R,

\frac{\partial p}{\partial r}=\frac{\rho U^2}{R}=\frac{\rho\omega^2r^2}{r}=\rho\omega^2r. (5.98)

Integrating,

p-p(r=0)=\frac12\rho\omega^2r^2. (5.99)

In the vertical (binormal) direction, the hydrostatic relation is satisfied, and the height of the water is the height required for the pressure to decrease to \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\):

h-h(r=0)=\frac{\Delta p}{\rho g}=\frac{\omega^2r^2}{2g}. (5.100)

This shows that the shape is independent of ρ and therefore the same for water, mercury, or gallium. The pressure differences are proportional to the density, though, so the pressure changes would be bigger for mercury than gallium and bigger for gallium than with water. The fluid is rearranged by the flow but of course the total amount of fluid is unchanged, so if the radius of the tank were specified, we could calculate the absolute height change, not just the relative height change, by integrating Δh·2πr dr from center to edge and setting the total equal to zero.

Editorial source note: The statement after (5.96) that the analysis loses meaning “if t goes positive” is incorrect as written: the draining solution applies for \(0\le t\le t_{\mathrm{empty}}\). The squared expression must not be continued beyond emptying, where it would predict a rising height.


PDF page 189 — source_issue

7. (OBJECTIVE: Motivate why indicated airspeed is used. Understand practical effects of standard atmosphere in aviation) The Bernoulli equation can be used to understand how speed, pressure, and density change along a streamline. In aviation, the correct density to use is known only approximately and in many cases it is more important for a pilot to know the aerodynamic effects of the plane’s speed more than the speed itself. Because of this, aviation guidelines, flight planning, and critical speeds for takeoff and climb all are expressed in terms of the indicated airspeed IAS rather than true airspeed. Airplane airspeed indicators calculate IAS from the Pitot–static tube as follows:

\mathrm{IAS}=\sqrt{\frac{2(p_{\mathrm{stag}}-p_{\mathrm{static}})}{\rho_{z=0}}}, (5.101)

where \(\rho_{z=0}\) is the standard density at sea level, not the density of the air around the plane. Because the real ρ is not used in this calculation, IAS is really a measure of the local dynamic pressure expressed in velocity units; it is not a measurement of the airplane’s speed. Because air density doesn’t change too much, though, IAS is still of same order as the airplane’s speed.

Because planes typically fly at altitude, and ρ is lower at altitude than at sea level, the indicated airspeed IAS typically underestimates the true airspeed TAS (which we in fluids class would just call the speed U). (a) Derive an expression for the ratio IAS/U. (b) Calculate IAS/U for a plane flying at 10,000 ft, using the standard atmosphere.

Solution: Bernoulli tells us that the speed of air moving past a Pitot–static tube is

U=\sqrt{\frac{2p_{\mathrm{stag}}-p_{\mathrm{static}}}{\rho}}. (5.102)

If \(\mathrm{IAS}=\sqrt{2(p_{\mathrm{stag}}-p_{\mathrm{static}})/\rho_{z=0}}\), then we can substitute and solve, finding

\frac{\mathrm{IAS}}{U}=\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\rho_{z=0}}}. (5.103)

Per the standard atmosphere, ρ(10,000 ft)=0.9046 kg/m³ and ρ(0 ft)=1.225 kg/m³. So

\frac{\mathrm{IAS}}U=\sqrt{\frac{0.9046\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}}{1.225\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}}}=0.86. (5.104)

An aviation rule of thumb (very approximate) is that true airspeed exceeds indicated airspeed by about 2% per 1000 ft. True airspeed is 16% higher at 10,000 ft, 37% higher at 20,000 ft, and 63% higher at 30,000 ft.

8. (OBJECTIVE: intuition for geometry of streamlines, relation to Bernoulli, role of stagnation pressure) Figure 5.31, p.192 shows a Pitot–static tube that is used to measure the velocity of a flow of air using a mercury manometer. What is its velocity in the channel along the streamline that terminates at the inlet to the tube? Solution: Rearranging the Bernoulli equation (p + ½ρU² = B, where B is a constant) we get

U=\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p}{\rho_{\mathrm{air}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}}g\Delta h}{\rho_{\mathrm{air}}}}, (5.105)

U=\sqrt{\frac{2\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}}g\Delta h}{\rho_{\mathrm{air}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(13600\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(0.03\,\mathrm{m})}{1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}}}=81.6\,\mathrm{m^3}. (5.106)

9. (OBJECTIVE: list purpose here) In 1888, Karl Benz patented a thing called a carburetor (Figure 5.32, p.192), which was used to mix air and fuel in an engine (You may have heard of the Mercedes-Benz brand of automobile). It was replaced in automobile engines in the 1980’s by fuel injectors, but is still used in many other engines. A carburetor comprises (a) a float-feed chamber for fuel that works a bit like your toilet tank, (b) a venturi, i.e., a channel with a narrow region in the center, and (c) usually two valves—a butterfly throttle valve that controls the airflow through the system, and a choke valve.

(a) Consider the carburetor with both valves open (open-choke, full throttle) with ρ₁ = 1.2 kg/m³, p₁ = 1×10⁵ Pa. Let the cross-sectional area of the intake A₁ be 10 cm² and the area of the throat A₂ be 3 cm². The piston in the cylinder head (below region 6; not shown) moves down, lowering the pressure in the cylinder (p₆) to 5×10⁴ Pa and drawing in 500 cm³ of air in 15 ms. If you approximate the flow from 1 to 3 as inviscid and approximately steady during this process, what is the pressure p₂?

(b) The reduced pressure at p₂ ensures that fuel (from the reservoir, also at 1×10⁵ Pa) is always drawn into the venturi and mixed with air. If the throttle valve is closed enough to reduce (by a factor of 2) the rate at which air is sucked into the cylinder head, by what factor will the pressure difference drawing in fuel be reduced?

Solution

a) To find p₂, we can first find the velocities at 1 and 2 and then use the Bernoulli equation for horizontal flow to find the pressure at 2. First, the velocity at 2 can be found as

U_2=\frac{500\,\mathrm{cm^3}}{(3\,\mathrm{cm^2})(15\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s})}=11.1\times10^3\,\mathrm{cm/s}=111\,\mathrm{m/s}. (5.107)

Then, by conservation of volume (conservation of mass assuming uniform density), we can find U₁:

U_1=U_2\frac{A_2}{A_1}=(111\,\mathrm{m/s})\frac{3\,\mathrm{cm^2}}{10\,\mathrm{cm^2}}=33.3\,\mathrm{m/s}. (5.108)

Using Bernoulli’s equation for horizontal flow (neglect hydrostatic term) between points 1 and 3:

p_1+\frac12\rho U_1^2=p_2+\frac12\rho U_2^2. (5.109)

p_2=p_1+\frac12\rho(U_2^2-U_1^2). (5.110)

p_2=(1\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa})+\frac12(1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})[(33.3\,\mathrm{m/s})^2-(111\,\mathrm{m/s})^2]. (5.111)

p_2=93\,\mathrm{kPa}. (5.112)

b) The pressure difference is proportional to ½ρU², Δp is 1/4 as large.

Editorial note: Eq. (5.110) prints p₂=p₁+½ρ(U₂²−U₁²), with the velocity-square order reversed. Rearranging Eq. (5.109) gives p₂=p₁+½ρ(U₁²−U₂²), matching the following numerical substitution in Eq. (5.111) and the stated 93 kPa result.

Editorial source note: The sentence introducing (5.109) says “between points 1 and 3,” but the equation and this calculation compare points 1 and 2.

Sidebar 5.5: Common Source of Confusion

Static, Dynamic, Stagnation, and Total Pressure: are they all pressures?

Students often misunderstand which of the numerous “pressures” are actually pressure

Most MAE3230 students have an intuitive sense of what “pressure” is; this intuition, which comes from ENGRD2210, is that pressure is a thermodynamic property that describes the force per unit area on the surface of an enclosure. This thermodynamic pressure is what we call pressure in fluid mechanics. In fluid mechanics, things are more complicated than equilibrium thermodynamics because p is a field property not a state property. For clarity, we also call the thermodynamic pressure the static pressure. The dynamic pressure is not pressure, in the sense that it is not a thermodynamic property that describes force per unit area. It has units that are the same as pressure, but it is not a pressure. Fluid mechanicians find it useful to use the term dynamic pressure because dynamic pressure describes a form of energy that could be converted to pressure. The Bernoulli equation describes how forms of energy that are not pressure could be converted to pressure. The stagnation pressure does not describe the pressure of fluid, it describes a hypothetical pressure the fluid would have if we slowed it down to quiescence isentropically.

If you are wondering whether you understand this, ask yourself whether you can explain everything in Fig. 5.12

…because if you can, you probably understand it.

Sidebar 5.6: Fundamentals

Streamline Coordinates

Streamline coordinates are coordinates everywhere aligned to local streamlines rather than the laboratory frame

Streamline coordinates (Figure B.8, p.455) are coordinates aligned to local streamlines rather than the laboratory frame. We label these coordinates s, n, and ℓ, where ŝ points in the direction of fluid flow (i.e., tangent to the streamline), n̂ points toward the center of curvature of the streamline, and ℓ̂ points in the direction of ŝ × n̂.



Figure 5.16: A schematic of a streamline coordinate system. ŝ points in the streamwise direction of fluid flow. n̂ points in the normal direction i.e., toward the center of the local curvature. ℓ̂ points in the binormal direction i.e., in the direction ŝ × n̂.

Streamline-oriented coordinate systems relate forces to (a) acceleration along the streamline and (b) curvature of the streamline itself

We often use Cartesian coordinate systems aligned to the lab frame, for example x, y, and z. With such a coordinate system the forces and accelerations relate straightforwardly:

F_x=ma_x,\quad F_y=ma_y,\quad F_z=ma_z, (5.43)

where F denotes a force and a denotes acceleration. In Cartesian coordinates, from each force we directly determine an acceleration.

Streamline coordinates are defined by taking the coordinate s in the direction of flow and n and ℓ orthogonal to the flow. At any single point, the path of the streamline can be considered to be a circular path around an origin a distance R away in the n̂ direction; this R is the radius of curvature of the streamline.

From the standpoint of keeping track of where we are and where the origin is, streamline coordinates are profoundly miserable and useless. However, streamline coordinates are very convenient in that they ensure that the flow locally is always in the s direction, and any curvature in the streamline is locally equivalent to an object moving in a circular trajectory prescribed by a centripetal force.

In streamline coordinates, the coordinates play two different roles (and have different units) and unsurprisingly the relations between force and acceleration are different in the radial (normal) and azimuthal (streamwise) directions, as well as the binormal (ℓ) direction:

F_n=-m\frac{U^2}{R},\quad F_s=ma_s,\quad F_\ell=0. (5.44)

Forces and accelerations along a streamline direction are related by an F = ma relation similar to that for Cartesian coordinates; however, in the radial direction we no longer have a relation describing forces and accelerations in the radial direction (we by definition have no motion in the radial direction, because we defined the coordinate system so that the velocity points in the azimuthal direction). Instead, the relation is akin to the centripetal force relation for an object moving in the circle—the radial force dictates how fast the flow is turning, measured through the radius of curvature R.

The figure includes handwritten labels identifying circles denoting local streamline curvature and coordinates s (streamwise), n (normal), ℓ (binormal).

Editorial redraw note: The local geometry is shown in a planar projection. The circled dot denotes the binormal pointing out of the page, consistent with the stated cross product.

Editorial source note: The source defines \(\hat n\) toward the center of curvature but prints \(F_n=-mU^2/R\) in (5.44). With that inward normal, centripetal acceleration and the net normal force are positive: \(F_n=mU^2/R\). The negative sign would instead apply to an outward radial component.

Sidebar 5.7: Fundamentals

Eulerian and Lagrangian depiction of fluid flow

Fluid flows are described alternately with Eulerian (space-referenced) or Lagrangian (fluid-element-referenced)

Two different classes of frames of references are commonly used to describe fluid flow (Figure 5.17, p.182). One, Lagrangian frames of reference, are frames of reference that follow a fluid element as it moves through a flow. They allow analysis of a system, i.e., a mass element. The advantage of a Lagrangian frame of reference is that, because it follows an element of fluid, we can simply apply F⃗ = m a⃗ to that fluid element and we need do no further bookkeeping. The disadvantage of a Lagrangian frame of reference is that it is both difficult to measure experimentally and it can be difficult to visualize—because the frame of reference is zipping along with the fluid, it can be more difficult to keep track of it.



Figure 5.17: Lagrangian analysis moves with the flow; Eulerian analysis watches it go by.

The second class of frames of references are Eulerian frames of reference. Eulerian frames of reference are not fixed to fluid elements: instead they are fixed to a specific time or path in space. They allow analysis of a control volume, i.e., a volume element. Most often, the Eulerian frame of reference we use is one that is motionless relative to the laboratory or to an object (e.g., a vehicle) moving in a fluid. The advantage of an Eulerian frame of reference is that it is easy to measure experimentally and easy to visualize. The disadvantage of an Eulerian frame of reference is that we cannot simply apply F⃗ = ma⃗ to a fixed control volume; in addition to accounting for the forces applied to the mass in the control volume, we must use the Reynolds transport theorem to account for the fluxes of momentum that enter and exit the control volume.


PDF page 194 — source_issue

Sidebar 5.8: Fundamentals

Taylor-Series Expansions

The Taylor Series prescribes the value of a function (e.g., pressure, density, velocity) everywhere in space if we know all of that function’s derivatives at one point

The Taylor-series expansion for a function f(x) around a point x₀ is given by

f(x)=f(x_0)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left.\frac1{n!}\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial x^n}\right|_x\Delta x^n, (5.45)

where Δx = x − x₀. The Taylor-series expansion prescribes f at any x if we know f and all of f’s derivatives at x₀. The Taylor series helps us change the mathematical description of a function from one that permeates space (i.e., knowing f(x) everywhere) to one that involves a ton of information all at one point in space (i.e., all the derivatives of f at one value of x = x₀). This is helpful because all of our differential equations that describe physical principles (e.g., conservation of momentum) are applied at a specific point in space.

We use the first-order term in the Taylor series to formulate differential equations

In formulating differential relations in physical systems, we use the Taylor-series expansion to relate the properties of f (f is typically the pressure, density, temperature, velocity, or similar fluid property) in different parts of an infinitesimal fluid element. Because the fluid element is vanishingly small, we find that we need not evaluate all the terms of the sum; in fact we need only the first term because all terms beyond the first-order term (df/dx Δx) are vanishingly small relative to the first-order term. If we include only the first-order term, the Taylor-series expansion becomes

f(x)\simeq\underbrace{f(x_0)}_{\text{0th-order estimate of }f(x)}+\underbrace{\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{x_0}\Delta x}_{\text{1st-order (linear) correction for }f(x)}, (5.46)

and this is the form we use when deriving differential governing equations. One might argue that the first-order term is also vanishingly small relative to the zeroth-order term. The reason why the first-order term must be retained is that, when evaluating the effect of changes in fluid properties when deriving differential forms of the governing equations, we are actually interested in the difference between properties along the surface of a control volume. If we use the Taylor-series expansion to approximate, for example f(x₂) − f(x₁), we can see why the first-order term is important:

f(x_2)-f(x_1)=\left[f(x_0)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left.\frac1{n!}\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}(x_2-x_0)^n\right]-\left[f(x_0)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left.\frac1{n!}\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}(x_1-x_0)^n\right], (5.47)

f(x_2)-f(x_1)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left.\frac1{n!}\frac{\partial^n f}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}\left[(x_2-x_0)^n-(x_1-x_0)^n\right]. (5.48)

Here, we see that f(x₀) cancels. For x₂ − x₀ and x₁ − x₀ approaching zero, the difference f(x₂) − f(x₁) can be written as

f(x_2)-f(x_1)\simeq\underbrace{\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{x_0}(x_2-x_1)}_{\text{1st-order (linear) approximation}}. (5.49)

As x₂ and x₁ approach x₀, all terms for n = 2 and higher are much smaller than the term for n = 1. This is why the n = 1 term is necessary but why the n = 2 and higher terms are not retained in the sum.

Editorial source note: The evaluation subscript in (5.45) visibly reads \(x\); expansion about \(x_0\) requires derivatives evaluated at \(x_0\). The evaluation subscript in (5.46) and the second bracket of (5.47) are washed out; their displayed \(x_0\) is an explicitly labeled reconstruction from the stated expansion point and the clearer (5.48)–(5.49).

Editorial source note: The claim that all derivatives at one point prescribe the function everywhere requires analyticity and convergence of the Taylor series at the requested point. Smoothness alone does not establish that claim.

Sidebar 5.9: Engineering Models

Reynolds-Averaged Flow

Premise: Although turbulent flow is unsteady, we often need to know only the time-averaged results

In reality, all high-Re flows are turbulent and unsteady. Many flows, however, have fluctuations but still nonetheless have a time-invariant portion, and often that time-invariant portion is of engineering importance. In these cases, we reframe the equations so that we are actually talking about the time-invariant portion. We do not need to know the microsecond-scale or millisecond-scale fluctuations in the instantaneous lift force on a plane—the question is just what is the time-averaged portion and is that enough so that the plane doesn’t crash.

Mathematical form: time-averaging a turbulent flow leads to equations that look just like the Navier–Stokes equations but with an extra term known as the turbulent viscosity

If we have a flow that is stationary but unsteady, we rewrite the equations by decomposing the velocity u⃗ into its time-averaged component ū⃗, and its fluctuation components u⃗′. This changes the Navier–Stokes equations:

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u+\rho\vec g. (5.77)

into the Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations:

\rho\bar{\vec u}\cdot\nabla\bar{\vec u}=-\nabla\bar p+\mu\nabla^2\bar{\vec u}+\rho\vec g+f_t. (5.78)

Here, \(f_t\) is a single term that gathers together all of the effects of the fluctuations. This is shown in Figure A.2, p.437.



Figure 5.22: Averaging over time in turbulent flows transfers from an instantaneous description of a turbulent flow to a Reynolds-averaged description, and introduces a turbulent viscosity to account for the effects of the fluctuations that are lost in the process.

…which is nice and simple except… we don’t know what \(f_t\) is. Turbulence modeling involves trying to develop some sort of prediction for what \(f_t\) is based on other properties of the flow. When using a software package to simulate fluid flow, these turbulence models are often selected from a menu in the program, for example k–ε or k–ω or SST or RDT etc. Each of these models takes properties of the flowfield and predicts what \(f_t\) is, and how accurate that prediction is varies widely depending on what sort of turbulent flow is being modeled. Reynolds-averaging the Navier–Stokes equations is the sort of topic that is often discussed in MAE4230.

At the MAE3230 level, we don’t deal with the fluctuations or turbulence models either. It is just understood that when we are talking about a turbulent flow in MAE3230, we are always talking about ū⃗ not u⃗.

Utility: Reynolds averaging is what makes all of MAE3230 possible

We actually couldn’t analyze anything in MAE3230 if we didn’t have a way to ignore the hard part we can’t analyze well. Reynolds averaging is a formal way to ignore all the fluctuations we don’t know how to handle.

Limitations: Reynolds averaging works only for stationary flow

Reynolds averaging presupposes that there is a time-invariant flow to decompose from fluctuations, and thus Reynolds averaging is possible only if a flow is stationary.

Sidebar 5.10: Engineering Models

Quasi-steady flow

Premise: quasi-steady flow is flow for which the governing conservation equations are well approximated by steady equations, but the boundary conditions are time-dependent

Quasi-steady flow analysis is appropriate when the governing equations can ignore acceleration terms and all time-changing aspects of the flow can be accounted for with changing boundary conditions.

Mathematical form: quasi-steady flow is modeled by setting all time derivatives in the governing equations to zero

Quasi-steady flow implies that time derivatives of velocity can be neglected in the governing equations. This does not mean that the velocity does not change; instead, it means that although the velocity is changing, ρ∂u⃗/∂t is small relative to the other terms in the equation and can be neglected.

For the integral form of the Bernoulli equation,

B_1+\int_{s_1}^{s_2}\rho\frac{\partial U}{\partial t}\,ds=B_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad B_1=B_2. (5.79)

where s is the distance along a streamline, 1 and 2 denote two points along this streamline, and B = p + ½ρU² + ρgz. This is a huge simplification, because in most flows the ∫(ρ ∂U/∂t)ds integral is difficult to integrate. The unsteady Bernoulli equation is useful for confined flows with very well-defined streamlines, for example startup or slowdown of flow in a tube, but not very useful otherwise. The steady Bernoulli equation, on the other hand, is used all the time.

For the Navier–Stokes equations,

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u. (5.80)

This simplification is not as dramatic, as the steady Navier–Stokes equations still have significant complexity to them. But still you’d rather not have to deal with that unsteady term.

Importantly, although these governing equations no longer have a time derivative term, the velocity itself is a function of time (u⃗ = u⃗(x,y,z,t)) and the boundary conditions i.e., pressure or velocity at the boundary can be a function of time.

Utility: Quasi-steady flow can be used when the boundary conditions of a time-varying system vary slowly relative to the time with which the fluid system reaches steady state

We find that fluid flow is immensely simplified when it can be approximated as steady. This is the primary reason why so many fluid-mechanical analyses are performed in the frame of reference that moves along with a moving object. However, if we force everything to be absolutely steady, then nothing can change, and a strictly steady model cannot be applied to describe an airplane that accelerates or a reservoir that empties. Quasi-steady flow helps.

Limitations: the quasi-steady approximation breaks down whenever the acceleration terms are significant contributors to the force balance

Flow over an airfoil on a plane is well described by quasi-steady analysis. Flow over a flapping bird wing is not (the lift on a moving wing is not equal to the lift on a stationary wing in the same position). Steady-state operation of the water pipes in your house are well described by quasi-steady analysis. Water hammer in your pipes is not (it involves wave propagation through the pipes). Quasi-steady analysis describes water entering and exiting a water tower but does not describe the slosh of fuel in a liquid-fueled rocket (cf. Falcon 1 oxygen tank, for example).

Editorial source note: The unsteady Bernoulli integral in (5.79) has the wrong sign. With \(s\) increasing from 1 to 2, \(\partial B/\partial s=-\rho\,\partial U/\partial t\), hence \(B_2=B_1-\int_{s_1}^{s_2}\rho(\partial U/\partial t)\,ds\). The steady limit is still \(B_1=B_2\).

Editorial source note: Equation (5.80) omits gravity on both sides of the displayed implication. It is a version of Navier–Stokes with gravity neglected (or with its conservative contribution absorbed into a modified pressure), whereas (5.77) writes gravity explicitly. Dropping the time derivative does not itself remove the body force.

Chapter 6

Pumps: Machines that Push Fluid Through Pipes

The Bernoulli equation can be modified to describe cross-sectionally averaged flow through pipes

The Bernoulli equation, as derived in the previous chapter, consisted of a steady equation for inviscid flow along a streamline. These three properties led to enormous simplification. The molecular-level fluctuations of fluid molecules, which we call viscosity (see Sidebar 6.1, p. 195), were ignored. Macroscopic fluctuations of fluid parcels, which we call turbulence, were ignored. And we aligned the coordinate system with the flow to make the math easier, without regard for whether the resulting coordinate system was conveniently placed relative to any physical objects (say a wall or container).

Revisiting what we did in the previous chapter, we will find that we skimmed over a number of mathematical and physical details and a couple of key engineering ones as well. In looking at this system more closely, we find that for real engineering systems, the Bernoulli equation is really just a starting point. Whereas the Bernoulli equation describes how stored work (pressure), kinetic energy (speed), and gravitational potential energy (altitude) trade back and forth when fluid flow is lossless, our real observations of fluid flows show us that as fluid moves about and as energy is traded back and forth among \(p\), \(U\), and \(z\), there is also a fluid-mechanical loss as some of this energy is dissipated as heat.

Although there are many situations in which a lossless approximation is appropriate, losses are central to discussion of any system in which pumps push fluid through pipes. The Bernoulli equation predicts (incorrectly) that fluid can be moved through an infinitely long horizontal pipe without using a pump of any kind—clearly, neglecting losses in this context leads to an absurd, incorrect result. However, a modified version of the Bernoulli equation will describe flow through pipes quite well. In fact we will visit and revisit the Bernoulli equation over and over again all term, and each time we revisit it we hopefully will get a more nuanced understanding of what it can and cannot tell us, and develop more ways to apply it or adjust it to help us solve engineering problems. In this chapter, we learn that if we modify the Bernoulli equation with a loss term, we can use it to design pumping systems through pipes.

The inviscid approximation that we used to derive the Bernoulli equa-

Viscosity: if denoted \(\mu\), the dynamic viscosity. A measure of fluid resistance to being deformed. For Newtonian fluids, proportional to the ratio of the fluid stress to fluid strain rate. If denoted \(\nu\), the kinematic viscosity \(\nu=\mu/\rho\). A measure of fluid’s ability to diffuse momentum.

Turbulence: the local instability and chaos of a fluid flow, leading to unsteadiness and fluctuations even if the flow is stationary.

Bernoulli equation: in differential form \(0=\frac{d}{ds}(p+\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2+\rho gz)\), in integral form \(B=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2+\rho gz\), where \(B\) is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

Inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don't significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid that has \(\mu=0\); in practice there is no such thing.


PDF page 205 — verified

6.1. Modified Bernoulli Equation

The inviscid approximation that we used to derive the Bernoulli equation is never exactly correct. In fact, the structure of the mathematics and physics that govern fluid flow means we can essentially never find an approximation that correctly describes all aspects of a mechanical engineering fluid mechanical system (mathematically, we would call such a delightful approximation a regular approximation). The approximation will always be totally wrong somewhere in the fluid flow (and because it always breaks down somewhere, it is mathematically a singular approximation). For example, the Bernoulli equation is always totally wrong right next to a solid surface, for example right next to the wall of a pipe. However, from an engineering standpoint, that detail often doesn't matter—the Bernoulli equation often gives us an accurate description of the overall performance of an engineering system. The Bernoulli equation does correctly describe how a carburetor works and how fast water shoots out of a reservoir of water as a free jet. So the Bernoulli equation is useful for engineers that want real answers and want to build real things, even if it isn't physically perfect.

The Bernoulli equation is also useful because in a number of cases its form can be adjusted to correctly account for the effects of viscosity. In many systems, the Bernoulli equation is close enough to being correct that a proper analysis of a fluid mechanical system consists of the Bernoulli equation with a well-defined loss term. This approach (i.e., Bernoulli equation plus losses) works for well-defined, enclosed flows, for example flow through pipes. Flows through pipes are well suited for Bernoulli-with-some-losses-added analysis for several reasons:

1. We typically do not care about the spatial distribution of speed in such a system; we care only about the volumetric flow rate. I care about how much water comes out of the shower head when I take a shower, but I do not care about the distribution of \(\vec{u}\) in the 90° elbow in the pipe behind the drywall.

2. We typically do not care about detailed temporal fluctuations of fluid flow; we care only about the time-averaged performance. If we studied the instantaneous velocity of fluid moving through the pipes to my shower, we would find that the velocity is always fluctuating. However, that fluctuation isn't perceptible, so as engineers in many contexts we don't care.

3. Pipes are long and have a well-defined direction, and the mean fluid flow inside is approximately unidirectional, so we don't really need a vector description of the fluid flow. The flow is moving from inlet to outlet, and we don't need to describe the direction of the flow in any more detail than that. So the analysis is a scalar analysis and we don't need multivariable calculus.

This approach constitutes a mean-flow approximation (see Sidebar 6.2, p. 195).

These observations make our analysis simpler. (1) means we can describe flow in terms of volumetric flow rate \(Q\) in a pipe or mean speed \(\bar{U}\) at a specific location in a pipe. We do not need \(\vec{u}(x,y,z,t)\). (2) means we really are talking about time averages; we don't need \(Q(t)\) or \(\bar{U}(t)\) either. We can use \(Q\) or \(\bar{U}\) to describe a spatially and temporally averaged flow. (3) means we can have many pipes, pointing in many directions, or pipes that twist and turn, and we can still use scalar variables \(Q\) or \(\bar{U}\) to describe the flow. Taken together, these observations encourage us to define a Bernoulli constant using these spatially and temporally averaged properties:

\bar{B} \equiv p + \frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^{2} + \rho g\bar{z}, (6.5)

where \(\bar{U}\) and \(\bar{z}\) are the cross-sectional averages of speed and altitude. \(\bar{B}\) is

Regular approximation: in a fluid-mechanical context, an approximation that applies to the entire fluid domain.

Singular approximation: in a fluid-mechanical context, an approximation that applies to only part of the fluid domain and fails in the other part.

Loss: in fluid mechanics, a measure of deviation from inviscid or isentropic behavior. Often used to adjust an inviscid or isentropic model to describe real engineering systems.

Speed: when describing fluid, a scalar description of fluid motion equal to the magnitude of the velocity. When describing a turbomachine, the angular frequency of its rotation.

Scalar: as a noun: a property with a magnitude only; no direction; as an adjective: having magnitude only but no direction.

6.1. Modified Bernoulli Equation

Sidebar 6.1: Fundamentals

Viscosity

Viscosity dissipates fluid mechanical energy into heat when a fluid is deformed. Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to deformation. It is the net effect of microscopic variations in molecular motion. Any time a fluid is deformed in any way (stretched, squeezed, sheared), the molecular interactions of fluid molecules lead to a net transfer of momentum from one part of a fluid to another, and lead to dissipation of mechanical energy into heat. Fluid that is all moving uniformly with the same velocity is not deforming, nor is fluid that is all rotating uniformly; but any other flow has fluid deformation. Therefore all flows (other than uniformly translating or rotating fluid) have both (a) viscous transfer of momentum from one place to another and (b) viscous dissipation of fluid mechanical energy into heat.

Fluids deform the most near walls and in regions of recirculation

One obvious source of fluid deformation is the presence of a solid wall. Fluid molecules adhere to surfaces, and the velocity of a fluid element in contact with a wall is zero (this is called the no-slip condition). Fluid rushing past the wall is deformed—it is motionless when it is at the wall but moving when it is near the wall. The viscous outcomes of this deformation are (a) the wall is pulled forward (b) the fluid is pulled backward (c) the fluid heats up. From the standpoint of energy dissipation, mechanical energy is dissipated into heat fastest when the fluid viscosity is high, and fastest when the fluid is deforming rapidly. The regions of highest deformation in fluid systems are (a) the region adjacent to walls and (b) regions of recirculation, where fluid moving in one direction is recirculated upstream.

Sidebar 6.2: Engineering Models

Mean Flow

Premise: often, we don't need details of spatial variation of a flow and instead we only need the spatial average. Mean flow approximations basically just ignore spatial variation of a fluid flow and instead focus on some sort of a spatial average. Two examples are flow in pipes and flow in porous media. When we pump flow through a pipe, we care primarily about the total flowrate and not so much about the details of the velocity distribution. A fluid-mechanics researcher might look in great detail, but for engineering analysis of flow through pipes, we typically just measure the flow rate and how it relates to the pressure drop, because that tells you what you need to know to design a piping system. And when fluid moves through porous media, for example water being wicked into a paper towel, we care more about the motion of the fluid front than we do about the details of how the water moves around and through individual paper fibers.

Mathematical form: mean flow approximations simply use an area-averaged speed \(\bar U\) instead of \(\vec u\). In pipes, we replace the velocity distribution with the cross-sectional-area-averaged value of the downstream component:

\bar U = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{1}{A}\int_A \vec u\cdot\vec n\,dA. (6.1)

Although I will always try to write this as \(\bar U\), most fluids texts simply write this as \(U\) with the understanding that everyone knows that the value is an area-averaged one. In porous media, we replace the velocity field \(\vec u\) with an area-averaged velocity field \(\bar{\vec u}\), which is understood to give a value that is averaged over a volume \(V\) large relative to the pore structure of the material:

\bar{\vec u}(x,y,z,t)=\frac{1}{V}\int_V\vec u(x,y,z,t)\,dV. (6.2)

Utility: mean flows. The mean-flow approximation lets us write relations for pipe flow in a form

\frac{\partial B}{\partial s}=-f_D\frac{1}{D}\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2, (6.3)

which helps us understand how much pumping power is required to move flow through a piping system. \(\bar U\) is easy to measure because it is directly calculable from the flowrate \(Q\) and the pipe dimensions. The mean-flow approximations let us write relations for porous-media flow in a form

\bar{\vec u}=-\frac{k}{\mu}\nabla p, (6.4)

which describes porous media flow using only the material permeability \(k\), and which does not require microscopic measurement of fluid flow.

Limitations: Mean flow analysis usually hides its errors in the definition of a material or flow property like \(f_D\) or \(k\). Although averaging velocities correctly captures values proportional to velocity, such as the total flowrate, averaging velocities cannot correctly capture values proportional to velocity squared, for example the dynamic pressure \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\). \(\bar U^2\) is not equal to \(\overline{U^2}\). In pipe flow, there is an inherent limitation—\(\bar U\) correctly describes the average velocity and (when multiplied by the cross-sectional area) the total flow rate, but \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\) isn't the cross-section-averaged dynamic pressure exactly. This approach works for calculation of the viscous dissipation factor, but it is not because \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\) is equal to the mean dynamic pressure; it is because for any specific flow \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\) is always proportional to the mean dynamic pressure. So this error gets folded into the viscous dissipation factor \(f_D\). Similarly, averaging flow through porous media leads to errors that typically get lumped into some material property. The permeability \(k\) of a porous material can be related back to the pore size and structure but only if those details are known exactly. More often, the permeability of a porous material lets us estimate (but not exactly measure) properties like the pore size.


PDF page 207 — source_issue

6.1. Modified Bernoulli Equation

Calculated from \(\bar U\) and \(\bar z\). \(\bar B\) is close to, but not exactly equal to, the cross-sectional average of \(B\), because the kinetic energy is a nonlinear function of the speed (see Sidebar 6.3, p. 197). All properties in Equation (6.5) are assumed to be time-averaged values. Because streamlines must connect the inlet of a pipe to its outlet, the Bernoulli equation would tell us that \(\bar B\) is the same at the inlet of a pipe and at the outlet if there were no viscous effects whatsoever and if the speed were uniform across every cross section.

However, in real flows through real pipes, there are viscous effects—there is a force per unit area between the fluid and the wall of the pipe, and the pipe is pushed forward while the fluid is pulled backward. A force must be applied to a pipe to hold it in place while fluid moves through it. Also, the kinetic energy in the fluid is dissipated by this interaction with the wall, and work must be done on the fluid to keep it moving at the same speed, so the pressure of the system drops (Figure 6.1, p. 197). The energy loss (in the form of pressure drop) coincides with the fluid heating up, but because it is usually not our goal to heat the fluid, we think of the conversion of pressure to heat as a loss. For now, we will describe these effects in terms of viscous losses, which will take the form of reductions in the Bernoulli constant as fluid moves from upstream to downstream in a pipe. The fact that there are viscous losses when fluid moves through a pipe is the reason why we need pumps to move fluids around.

Whereas the steady differential Bernoulli equation at a point in space for inviscid flow along a streamline is given by

\frac{\partial B}{\partial s}=0, (6.6)

for the cross-section of a pipe, if we incorporate viscous losses, the differential relation becomes

\frac{\partial \bar B}{\partial s}=-f_D\frac{1}{d}\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2. (6.7)

Editorial note: the equality/sign area of (6.7) is damaged in the scan. The displayed negative sign is reconstructed from the readable loss relation (6.9): for a positive downstream coordinate, \(\partial\bar B/\partial s=(\bar B_{\mathrm{outlet}}-\bar B_{\mathrm{inlet}})/L=-f_D\rho\bar U^2/(2d)\). It is not a visually recovered glyph.

Equation (6.7) constitutes the definition of \(f_D\), the viscous dissipation factor of the fluid flow, which is a function of the Reynolds number \(Re_d=\rho\bar U d/\mu\) as well as how smooth or rough the pipe surface is. Written in this form, we see that, for a system with viscous effects, the Bernoulli constant goes down as we move downstream along a streamline, because energy is being dissipated as heat. For most mechanical-engineering flows, this energy dissipation occurs at a rate proportional to the fluid's kinetic energy \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\). The viscous dissipation is larger when the diameter \(d\) is small—it is harder to push fluid through a small-diameter pipe than it is to push fluid through a large-diameter pipe.

Whereas the fact that \(\partial\bar B/\partial s\) is proportional to \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\) and inversely proportional to \(d\) are true for all high-\(Re\) pipe flows, the value of the viscous dissipation factor \(f_D\) is different for pipes of different shapes, cross sections, and surface roughnesses, and the viscous dissipation factor also varies as the interplay between fluid momentum and fluid viscosity changes. Large viscous dissipation factors \(f_D\) are associated with rough walls, cross sections with eccentricity or sharp corners, and viscosity-dominated flows. Small viscous dissipation factors are associated with smooth walls, circular cross sections, and momentum-dominated flows.

For fully developed flow (see Sidebar 6.4, p. 216) through a pipe of uniform cross-sectional geometry, the differential equation Equation (6.7) can be integrated to result in

\frac{\bar B_{\mathrm{inlet}}-\bar B_{\mathrm{outlet}}}{L}=\frac{\Delta\bar B_{\mathrm{loss}}}{L}=f_D\frac{\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2}{d}. (6.9)

The drop in \(\bar B\) must be counteracted by expending gravitational potential energy

Loss: in fluid mechanics, a measure of deviation from inviscid or isentropic behavior. Often used to adjust an inviscid or isentropic model to describe real engineering systems.

Streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

Viscous dissipation factor: a nondimensional coefficient used to characterize drop of the Bernoulli constant (and thus typically pressure) in a pipe. This is typically called the “friction” factor by other texts, but the word “friction” is physically incorrect and misleading so I don't use that term. In this class we use the Darcy factor \(f_D=\frac{\Delta B}{\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2}\frac{d}{L}\), but there are others, e.g., Fanning factor with similar but slightly different definitions.

Differential steady Bernoulli equation for inviscid flow along a streamline.

Modified Bernoulli equation to incorporate viscous losses in a pipe.

Reynolds number: \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\). The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(Re_d\), \(Re_L\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

Mechanical-engineering flow: there is no formal definition of this term. I use this term colloquially to mean high-Reynolds number flows of Newtonian fluids like air and water. In particular, this distinguishes from biological- and chemical-engineering flows, which more often have non-Newtonian flows at low Reynolds number.

Dissipation: in fluid mechanics, an irreversible process in which entropy is increased, and energy is converted from one form to another form that can do less mechanical work.

Integral relation for drop in Bernoulli constant along a pipe.

6.1. Modified Bernoulli Equation

Sidebar 6.3: Fundamentals

Area-averaged speed

Using \(\bar U\) in pipes makes for considerable simplification and doesn't generate much in the way of errors. We use \(\bar U\) to describe the mean velocity in a pipe and we largely pretend that the velocity is uniform across the pipe, even though we know that that cannot really be the case.

You can't use \(\bar U\) without violating conservation of mass or violating conservation of momentum. It's OK though. Mass flow is proportional to the integral of \(U\), and momentum flow is proportional to the integral of \(U^2\). If you replace the distribution of \(U\) with its average, you will get one of those integrals wrong. Because we use the average of \(U\), this treatment gets the transport of momentum wrong. However, the good news is that this doesn't matter too much from an engineering standpoint, for a couple of reasons:

For most mechanical-engineering flows, \(U\) is roughly uniform for most of the domain inside the pipe. Thus for most of the cross section of the pipe, \(U\) is close to \(\bar U\). \(U\) is dissimilar from \(\bar U\) in the region very close to the wall, but this contributes only a small amount to the total mass or momentum flux.

In a pipe of uniform cross section, \(\bar U\) isn't changing as you move downstream, which means there is no net convective influx or outflux of mass or momentum, so it doesn't matter whether you get that integral right or not; no matter what you do, it will sum to zero.

The parts of a pipe for which \(\bar U\) is changing (e.g., contractions, expansions, valves, orifices) are accounted for by experimentally determined loss coefficients anyway.

\(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\) isn't the kinetic energy per unit volume of the fluid, but that's OK too. Whereas \(\bar U\) is the cross-sectionally averaged speed in the pipe, \(\bar p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}\) is not the cross-sectional average of \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}\), because the square of the average \(U\) is not equal to the average of \(U^2\). \(\bar p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}\) is the volumetric kinetic energy associated with the average speed in the pipe. Similar statements hold true for \(\bar B\), \(\bar p_{\mathrm{stagnation}}\), and \(\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}\).

\(\bar B\) is not the cross-sectional average of \(B\), because \(\bar U^2\) isn't the same as \(\overline{U^2}\). We define \(\bar B\) as the Bernoulli constant you would get if you used \(\bar U\) and \(\bar z\) instead of \(U\) and \(z\). Because the cross-sectional average of the kinetic energy isn't exactly the same as \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\), \(\bar B\) isn't exactly the same as \(\overline{U^2}\). In practice, this detail doesn't matter very much.

Editorial note: the last comparison in this paragraph is printed as \(\bar B\) versus \(\overline{U^2}\), which have different dimensions. The preceding definition instead implies that \(\bar B\) generally differs from the cross-sectional average of \(B\): with uniform \(p\) and \(\rho\), the difference is \(\frac12\rho(\overline{U^2}-\bar U^2)\). The two different placements of the overbar on the squared speed are intentional.

6.2. Bernoulli Constant Drop in Pipes

The drop in \(\bar B\) must be counteracted by expending gravitational potential energy (as occurs in an aqueduct that brings water from a high-altitude source to a low-altitude reservoir) or by running a pump that injects some work per unit volume into the fluid to counteract the losses.

Calculation of the drop in Bernoulli constant in pipes is often iterative

In practice, the hydraulic engineering design of pumping and piping systems involves picking the proper pump, pipes, and piping components. The previous section described how the Bernoulli constant decreases as we move downstream in a pipe. Now, we need to quantify how fast that happens (by describing a relation for \(f_D\)), and develop algorithms for solving a variety of pipe flow problems. We start by discussing \(f_D\)'s dependence and using that to frame the approaches we need to use to predict flow through pipes and design the parameters of these systems.

Design changes we might make in a real system are easiest to understand when described using dimensional units

The amount that the Bernoulli constant drops along a pipe is a function of its diameter \(d\), length \(L\), and surface roughness \(\epsilon\), as well as the fluid's density \(\rho\) and viscosity \(\mu\), and the mean velocity \(\bar U\) of the flow. We could, in principle, change one or more of these parameters and hold other parameters fixed, and observe how the drop in the Bernoulli constant changes. As one example, consider flow driven by a positive-displacement pump at fixed flowrate \(Q\) and ask: how does the drop in the Bernoulli constant of a fluid moving through a pipe at flowrate \(Q\) change if we, for example, double the pipe length \(L\), the surface roughness \(\epsilon\), the viscosity \(\mu\), the density \(\rho\), or the pipe diameter \(d\)? Results are summarized in Table 6.1, p. 198. Doubling

Table 6.1: How much \(\bar U\), the Reynolds number, \(\epsilon/d\), and \(\Delta\bar B\) change if that parameter is doubled at fixed \(Q\) for fully developed turbulent flow in a pipe. This replicates how the drop in Bernoulli constant would change if we change the pipe or the fluid for a flow driven by a positive-displacement pump at a fixed flowrate \(Q\).

Parameter doubled | \(\bar U\) | \(Re_d\) | \(\epsilon/d\) | \(\frac{L}{d}\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\) | \(\Delta\bar B\) | Comments
Pipe length \(L\) | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | Simplest case
Pipe surface roughness \(\epsilon\) | 1 | 1 | 2 | 1 | 1–1.5 | \(f_D\) increases as \(\epsilon/d\) increases
Viscosity \(\mu\) | 1 | 1/2 | 1 | 1 | 1.0–1.26 | Reynolds number effect only
Density \(\rho\) | 1 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 1.62–2.0 | \(f_D\) slightly lower when Reynolds number is larger, but dynamic pressure is twice as high
Pipe diameter \(d\) | 1/4 | 1/2 | 1/2 | 1/32 | 0.02–0.05 | Dynamic-pressure change from \(\bar U\) is the largest effect; lower \(\epsilon/d\) also makes \(f_D\) lower
Viscous dissipation: in fluid mechanics, the irreversible process by which fluid kinetic energy is converted to heat by the action of viscosity.

Fully developed: far enough from an inlet or exit such that the flow mimics that of an infinitely long channel.

6.2. Bernoulli Constant Drop in Pipes

Higher \(f_D\). Doubling viscosity increases \(f_D\) and the volumetric work required by up to about 26%. Doubling the density doubles \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}\) of the flow, but reduces \(f_D\) by up to about 19%, so the net \(\bar B\) drop goes up between 62–100%. Finally, doubling the pipe diameter reduces the \(\bar B\) drop by 95–98%, mostly because double the diameter means four times the cross-sectional area, which means one fourth the \(\bar U\), which means 1/16 times as much \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}\). A larger-diameter pipe made of the same material looks relatively smoother, and that lowers \(\Delta\bar B\) even more. Finally, the flow is a bit more viscous-dominated and that leads to a small increase in \(f_D\) which is drowned out by the other effects.

So, if you want to move fluid through a pipe but exert minimum work, the number one design criterion is: use large-diameter pipe. Less important but still useful: make the interior smooth and minimize the length of the pipe. And finally, fluid properties aren't too important, except that the viscosity of fluids varies by a lot—for example, honey's viscosity is 10,000 times that of water, so even if the volumetric work required to pump fluid isn't supersensitive to viscosity, you will find that honey is much harder to move around than water. If the only issue were minimizing work, then piping design would be pretty easy, except large-diameter piping costs a lot and weighs a lot, and the pipes that are cheap and light and have smooth interiors (e.g., PVC pipe) can't hold much pressure. So a large part of design of piping systems is figuring out how to pick pipe that can handle the relevant pressures without exploding, minimizes viscous losses during pumping, and costs and weighs the least.

Formally, the dependence of the drop in Bernoulli constant can be written in terms of its parameters as

\Delta\bar B=f(d,L,\epsilon,\rho,\mu,\bar U), (6.10)

If we continue with this approach, we find that (a) the equations are an enormous pain to write and (b) the resulting functional dependences are an enormous pain to plot. Six dependent parameters makes this system very unwieldy. So an analysis with dimensional parameters helps us quickly get a “feel” for which parameters make the most difference for a specific question (for example, as we did in Table 6.1, p. 198), but writing the equations and dependences formally, or graphing the results to understand these dependences, are both tedious. We address this by using nondimensional parameters—doing so reduces the number of parameters in the system, making the equations and graphs simpler, but means that the parameters we evaluate and plot must be retranslated back to dimensional form before they can be interpreted as part of a physical system.

Evaluating with dimensional parameters is less clearly connected to the engineering of a physical system, but is much easier to plot and generalize

Rather than writing \(\bar B\) in terms of the six parameters \(d\), \(L\), \(\rho\), \(\mu\), \(\epsilon\), and \(\bar U\), we find that the physics of this process is captured by writing the viscous dissipation factor \(f_D\) in terms of the Reynolds number \(Re\) and the nondimensional parameters

Viscous dissipation factor: a nondimensional coefficient used to characterize drop of the Bernoulli constant (and thus typically pressure) in a pipe. This is typically called the “friction” factor by other texts, but the word “friction” is physically incorrect and misleading so I don't use that term. In this class we use the Darcy factor \(f_D=\frac{\Delta B}{\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2}\frac{d}{L}\), but there are others, e.g., Fanning factor with similar but slightly different definitions.

6.2. Bernoulli Constant Drop in Pipes

Nondimensionalized surface roughness \(\epsilon/d\):

f_D=f(Re,\epsilon/d), (6.11)

We defined \(f_D\) as

\frac{d\bar B}{ds}=-\frac{f_D}{d}\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2, (6.15)

and so \(f_D\) is a proportionality factor that (in addition to the dynamic pressure \(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\)) tells us how quickly mechanical energy is being dissipated as heat as we move downstream along a pipe. Equation (6.11) tells us that this proportionality factor is a function of how much the flow is dominated by the fluid's momentum and how much the flow is dominated by the fluid's viscosity. This is described by the Reynolds number \(Re\) (see Sidebar 6.5, p. 217), which is the ratio of the fluid's kinetic energy to the viscous forces that dissipate that kinetic energy:

Re=\frac{\rho\bar U d}{\mu}, (6.16)

The viscous dissipation factor \(f_D\) is also a function of \(\epsilon/d\), which basically indicates how rough the surface is. Rougher surfaces increase viscous dissipation by bringing fast fluid in proximity to slow fluid and increasing local viscous stresses.

The pressure drop in a pipe can be predicted given the Reynolds number and the surface roughness

The pressure drop in a pipe can be predicted given the Reynolds number and the surface roughness. Dimensional analysis does not tell us how the pressure drop varies in a pipe, but it does tell us that the properly nondimensionalized pressure drop is a function of the Reynolds number and the relative roughness \(\epsilon/d\) alone. If we need to predict the pressure drop in a pipe, we typically read the number off a graph (called a Moody diagram) or use an approximate equation. The most famous equation is the Colebrook–White equation (not shown here), but I prefer to use the Haaland equation:

f_D=\left\{-1.8\log_{10}\left[\left(\frac{\epsilon}{3.7d}\right)^{1.11}+\frac{6.9}{Re}\right]\right\}^{-2}, (6.17)

The Haaland equation is an entirely empirical formula that is used to approximate experimental data. Because the relation between flowrate and pressure drop is nonlinear for turbulent flow, and because the most convenient way to summarize and graph the data involves nondimensionalization on both axes, the process of figuring out turbulent flow in a pipe can be iterative. The algorithm for this process is shown in Figure 6.3, p. 219.

6.2. Bernoulli Constant Drop in Pipes

A number of factors, only a small fraction of which are fluid dynamic, drive pipe selection

The fluid-mechanical equations help us calculate what happens given a size of pipe, tube, or hose. There are no hard-and-fast rules for piping system design, but one rule of thumb, especially in water piping systems, is that most piping systems are designed for \(U=1\text{–}3\,\mathrm{m/s}\). If the fluid speed is slower, it is easier for solids to accumulate, and you probably paid too much for a pipe that is unnecessarily big and unnecessarily heavy. If the fluid speed is faster, then the system is less thermodynamically efficient because you are squeezing fluid through a pipe whose diameter is too small. Example Problem 6.1 (p. 220) gives an example linking the surface roughness to the viscous dissipation factor to relate volume flowrate to pressure drop using the Moody chart.

You have to be multilingual if you want to discuss flow through pipes with the rest of the world

Fluid mechanics and hydraulics engineering are two quite different fields. Fluid mechanics is the broad analysis of fluid flow in all forms. MAE3230 is designed to prepare you for many applications of fluid mechanics, ranging from theoretical to applied. Hydraulics engineering is a very applied branch of fluid mechanics that is focused strictly on how to put together hydraulic fluid components like pumps and pipes to control flow in engineered systems, and, in a civil engineering context, how to manage water resources like reservoirs, water towers, and dams.

The language spoken by a theoretical fluid mechanician is very different from the language spoken by a hydraulics engineer. A student of MAE3230 must speak both languages fluently. This section is important, despite having no new physics. This section has new language to describe the same physics we have already discussed. But this language is critical to be able to read any US pump performance chart or US pipe sizing chart or use any US pipe system design software.

The state of fluid in a hydraulic system can be written in terms of Bernoulli constants, pressures, or heads

A fluid flow in a hydraulic system (which, at any point along the pipe's axis, has a density \(\rho\), an averaged velocity \(\bar U\), and a pressure \(p\)) can be described

Pipe: a hollow structure designed to convey a fluid. Usually rigid. Designated by nominal diameter and schedule, which describe approximate inner diameter and material thickness. Usually fitted by threads. Cf. tube, hose.

Tube: a hollow structure. Typically a tube is structural, not fluid-carrying, but the word tubing is sometimes used to describe copper and PVC pipe and hose. Usually rigid when discussed structurally, usually flexible when used to mean hose. Designated by nominal diameter and schedule, which describe approximate inner diameter and material thickness. Cf. pipe, hose.

Hose: a type of pipe that is usually flexible, designated by inside diameter, and normally fitted by stretching it over a rigid surface, e.g., a hose barb. Cf. tube, pipe.

6.2. Bernoulli Constant Drop in Pipes

By a long list of parameters. Because a hydraulic approach to flow through a pipe is by definition a spatially and temporally averaged one, these properties are not meant to describe exactly what is going on at any point in the cross section, but instead are meant to be some measure of cross-sectionally averaged properties.

If you prefer, as I do, to think of the state of the fluid in terms of the Bernoulli equation, the state of the fluid can be described by use of the Bernoulli constant: \(\bar B=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2+\rho g\bar z\). Or, if you prefer to think in terms of pressures, as most aerodynamicists do, you can use:

The static pressure \(p\).

The dynamic pressure \(\bar p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\).

The stagnation pressure \(\bar p_{\mathrm{stagnation}}=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\), or

The total pressure \(\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2+\rho g\bar z\).

Note that \(\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}\) and \(\bar B\) are two names for the same property. As is the case with \(\bar B\), the symbols \(\bar p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}\), \(\bar p_{\mathrm{stagnation}}\), and \(\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}\) refer to values calculated from \(\bar U\) and \(\bar z\); they are similar to but not exactly equal to the cross-sectionally averaged values of \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{stagnation}}\), and \(p_{\mathrm{total}}\). We don't have to put a bar over \(p\) because the static pressure does not vary across the cross section of a pipe in the fully developed region. Although we are careful here to place a bar over properties to be clear that they represent properties of the cross section of the pipe, be aware that most authors and references do not bother to do this, so most references will simply use \(p_0\) or \(B\), and in the context of flow through pipes, it is understood that the symbol implies a cross-sectionally averaged value.

If you prefer, as most hydraulic engineers do, to think in terms of heights of fluid, we can divide all of the pressures by \(\rho g\) to come up with an equivalent height \(H\) whose gravitational potential energy \(\rho gH\) is equivalent to that pressure. In hydraulic engineering, this height is referred to as head, for example:

The static head \(H=p/(\rho g)\).

The velocity head or dynamic head \(\bar H_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\bar U^2/(2g)\).

The stagnation head \(\bar H_{\mathrm{stagnation}}=p/(\rho g)+\bar U^2/(2g)\), or

The total head \(\bar H_{\mathrm{total}}=p/(\rho g)+\bar U^2/(2g)+\bar z\).

Editorial note: each word “or” above connects to the next bullet; it does not introduce another formula on the same line. Parts of the stagnation-head notation are washed out. The displayed relation follows by dividing the readable stagnation pressure by \(\rho g\), giving units of length.

Velocity head should look like a rearrangement of the Torricelli relation \(U=\sqrt{2gh}\). The Torricelli relation describes how gravitational potential energy (altitude) can be converted to kinetic energy, and the velocity head \(\bar H_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\bar U^2/(2g)\) describes the gravitational potential energy (altitude) one can extract from kinetic energy.

“Head” is really a hydraulic engineering term, and hydraulic engineers on average use more colloquial language than fluid mechanicians. So hydraulic engineers often just use the word “head” and one has to figure out from context whether they mean static head, velocity/dynamic head, stagnation head, total head, or total dynamic head. Whereas I use specific symbols for each expression, the symbols \(H\) and \(H_0\) are routinely used broadly to mean all of these properties in the hydraulic engineering literature, which rarely uses precise language and assumes the reader understands the meaning from context.

Dynamic pressure: given by \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2\). Denotes the added pressure a fluid would have if it were slowed isentropically to motionlessness. Equivalently, describes the volumetric kinetic energy of a fluid in terms of an equivalent pressure.

Total pressure: a property \(p_0=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2+\rho gz\), having units of pressure (or equivalently volumetric energy), which indicates storage of multiple forms of energy, including \(p\,dV\) work of compression (\(p\)), kinetic energy (\(\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2\)), and gravitational potential energy \(\rho gz\).

I Add Lots of Stars and Primes and Subscripts and Bars to My Symbols Haiku: “I try to be clear / by using lots of symbols / does it help at all?”

Head: a quantity (e.g., static head \(H=p/(\rho g)\) or total head \(H=p/(\rho g)+U^2/(2g)+z\)) in units of length that communicates energy per unit volume or, equivalently, pressure of a fluid. It describes the height of a hypothetical fluid that would generate a hydrostatic gauge pressure at its bottom equal to the static pressure or total pressure in the fluid under discussion.

Velocity head: given by \(H=U^2/2g\). The height a fluid could be pumped to if the kinetic energy of its mean velocity were converted to gravitational potential energy. Synonymous with dynamic head.

6.2. Bernoulli Constant Drop in Pipes

The differences in the states of fluid at two points in a hydraulic system can be written in terms of Bernoulli constants, pressures, or heads

The differences between the states of fluid at two points in a hydraulic system can also be written in terms of Bernoulli constants, pressures, or heads. Changes in the state of the fluid can be described by use of the Bernoulli constant:

\Delta\bar B=\left(p_1+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_1^2+\rho g\bar z_1\right)-\left(p_2+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_2^2+\rho g\bar z_2\right), (6.22)

Or pressures:

\Delta p=p_1-p_2, (6.23)

\Delta\bar p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_1^2\right)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_2^2\right), (6.24)

\Delta\bar p_{\mathrm{stagnation}}=\left(p_1+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_1^2\right)-\left(p_2+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_2^2\right), (6.25)

\Delta\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}=\left(p_1+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_1^2+\rho g\bar z_1\right)-\left(p_2+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_2^2+\rho g\bar z_2\right), (6.26)

Hydraulic engineers often describe the effect of a length of pipe or an elbow, orifice, or valve in terms of its pressure drop \(\Delta\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}\), where \(\Delta\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}\) is usually by convention positive and equal to \(\bar p_{\mathrm{total,upstream}}-\bar p_{\mathrm{total,downstream}}\). In a hydraulics context, the term “pressure drop” always refers to \(\Delta\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}\), but for horizontal pipes of uniform cross section, \(\Delta p=\Delta\bar p_{\mathrm{stagnation}}=\Delta\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}=\Delta\bar B\). I have never heard a hydraulic engineer refer to a drop in the Bernoulli constant.

The drop in Bernoulli constant or total pressure can be written in terms of head, in which case they are referred to as the head loss:

\Delta\bar H_{\mathrm{total}}=\left(\frac{p_1}{\rho g}+\frac{\bar U_1^2}{2g}+\bar z_1\right)-\left(\frac{p_2}{\rho g}+\frac{\bar U_2^2}{2g}+\bar z_2\right), (6.27)

As was the case with pressure drop, head loss is by convention positive and given by taking the upstream-minus-downstream difference in flow properties. It doesn't make any sense to refer to a change in static, dynamic, or stagnation head as a “loss”—head loss always refers to reduction in total head.

The total dynamic head, abbreviated TDH, is the total head loss in a system, or equivalently the work per unit volume of fluid that the pump must generate. The TDH terminology is common, especially in hydraulics reference charts, but confusing because its usage is not consistent with the terms “total head” or “dynamic head” used to describe the state of a fluid.

Change in Bernoulli constant.

Change in static pressure.

Change in dynamic pressure.

Change in stagnation pressure.

Pressure drop: the reduction of the (typically total) pressure of fluid associated with viscous dissipation of mechanical energy to heat: \(\Delta\bar p_{\mathrm{total}}=\Delta p+\frac{1}{2}\rho\Delta(\bar U^2)+\rho g\Delta\bar z\).

Head loss: the dissipation of mechanical energy to work, written in terms of height change of a fluid that would lead to an equivalent loss of gravitational potential energy per unit volume: \(\Delta\bar H=\frac{\Delta\bar p}{\rho g}+\frac{1}{2g}\Delta(\bar U^2)+\Delta\bar z\).

Total dynamic head: denoted TDH. The work per unit fluid volume \((\Delta p_p)\) that a pump adds to its working fluid, described using the equivalent height \((\mathrm{TDH}=\Delta p_p/(\rho g))\). Equal to the difference in total head between inlet and outlet of the pump. Not equal to total head nor dynamic head, which are both properties of fluids at a location rather than a differential property describing the difference in fluid properties across a pump.

What I call flowrate, hydraulic engineers call capacity or discharge

I typically describe the volumetric flowrate \(Q\). This is routinely called the capacity or discharge of a pump or hydraulic system. The mass flow rate \(\dot m=\rho Q\) is typically not discussed in a hydraulic engineering context.

There is no such thing as friction in a fluid, but you need to know what a “friction factor” is

In this class we define \(f_D\):

f_D=\frac{d\,\Delta\bar B_{\mathrm{loss}}}{\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2 L}, (6.28)

and call it the viscous dissipation factor. It is routinely called the friction factor or Darcy factor by others. I don't call it a friction factor, because there is no such thing as friction in a fluid, and the use of the term “friction” creates an incorrect intuition about what viscosity is. But most references call \(f_D\) a “friction factor”, so take note.

The Darcy factor is exactly four times the Fanning viscous dissipation factor \(f_F\), which is another common factor used in these calculations:

f_D=4f_F. (6.29)

Pipe designers often describe fluid components by use of coefficients that are less general descriptions of fluid flow but are more specific to component sizing and design

It is common in piping systems design to define a resistance coefficient or loss coefficient of a pipe or other element (e.g., flange, elbow, valve, orifice). This resistance coefficient is in general given by

K=\frac{\Delta\bar B}{\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2}, (6.30)

For a length of pipe, the resistance coefficient can be determined from the viscous dissipation factor:
