K=\frac{\Delta\bar B}{\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2}=f_D\frac{L}{d}, (6.31)

and is useful for describing the pressure drop in an element as a function of the dynamic pressure of the fluid:

\Delta\bar B=\frac{1}{2}K\rho\bar U^2, (6.32)

or, similarly, the head loss:

\Delta\bar H_{\mathrm{total}}=K\frac{\bar U^2}{2g}. (6.33)

It is also common to define a flow coefficient, which is like a resistance coefficient raised to the \(-\frac{1}{2}\) power and expressed using nonstandard units. Whereas the resistance coefficient is dimensionless and measures how well a system element resists flow, flow coefficients are typically written in the US using nonstandard English units and used to describe how well a system element allows flow. The flow coefficient is often in the US written as

C_v=Q\sqrt{\frac{SG}{\Delta\bar B}}, (6.34)

where \(SG=\rho_{\mathrm{fluid}}/\rho_{\mathrm{water}}\). Its SI units would be \(\mathrm{m}^{7/2}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1/2}\), but it is typically written as \(\mathrm{gpm}/\sqrt{\mathrm{psi}}\). A hydraulics engineer elsewhere in the world would use a metric version of this, typically called a flow factor, often written as

K_v=Q\sqrt{\frac{SG}{\Delta\bar B}}, (6.35)

Again this in SI units would be \(\mathrm{m}^{7/2}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1/2}\), but it is typically written as \(\mathrm{m^3/hr}/\sqrt{\mathrm{bar}}\). \(C\) is for constant (in English) and \(K\) is for Konstante (in German).

Flow coefficient: in hydraulics, a measure of the flow rate normalized by the square root of the pressure drop: \(C_v=Q\sqrt{SG/\Delta B}\). Typically reported in \(\mathrm{gpm}/\sqrt{\mathrm{psi}}\).

Pressure drops and head losses are sometimes described in terms of equivalent pipe lengths

To determine the pump specifications required to push fluid through a piping system, one needs to sum up the losses from all of the hydraulic components at the specified flow rate. This can be done by summing up pressure drops or head losses. It is also often done by converting to equivalent lengths. Whereas head is the height that leads to a gravitational potential energy per unit volume that is equal to a pressure, an equivalent length is the length of pipe that, at a specific flow condition, leads to a specified pressure drop. Each of these approaches is correct; the question is which approach makes analysis easier. Equivalent lengths are particularly useful when the system is dominated by losses in elements such as pipes, orifices, elbows, valves, and constrictions, because all of these elements produce losses that are similarly dependent on flow rate. Rearranging the definitions of resistance coefficient for a hydraulic element and viscous dissipation factor for a length of straight tube, we find

\frac{L_{\mathrm{eq}}}{d}=\frac{K}{f_D}, (6.36)

6.3. Losses in Pipes

Which shows that a hydraulic element with resistance coefficient \(K\) is equivalent to a length \(L\) of pipe of diameter \(d\) and viscous dissipation factor \(f_D\). This approach is most useful for a standard pipe material and working range of flows, and is most often used by one designing a piping system with a standardized set of elements.

Engineering analysis of pipe networks uses empirical factors to account for losses in valves, elbows, et cetera

The most thermodynamically efficient way to transmit fluid a distance through a tube with given cross-sectional area is to push it through a straight tube of circular cross section, and the process is more efficient as the cross-sectional area is increased. A straight tube is maximally efficient because the only viscous losses are associated with the fact that the fluid moves downstream while the pipe stays motionless. The circular cross section is maximally efficient because the perimeter-to-area ratio is minimized.

Any deviation from that configuration will generate additional viscous losses or, equivalently, will require a stronger pump doing more work for the same volumetric flow rate. A noncircular cross section just increases the perimeter of the pipe, and viscous losses are roughly proportional to the perimeter. Bends, expansions, and contractions in a pipe just serve as additional opportunities for flow patterns to develop that dissipate more energy but don't move any more fluid downstream.

Straight pipes convey fluid most efficiently, and any engineer knows this, but in practice, real hydraulic systems need contractions and expansions, valves, and bends and elbows. In mechanical-engineering flows, these elements cause flow separation, recirculation, and additional viscous losses. Separation refers to when the flow cannot follow the contour of the wall, and instead a streamline extends away from the wall. Separation leads to regions of recirculation, in which fluid is stirred about. Figure 6.4, p. 220 shows where separation occurs for some example geometries. In all of these cases, there is a region of fluid in which the fluid is being stirred (leading to viscous dissipation) but is not moving downstream. These regions do not accomplish any net fluid transport downstream, instead providing only increased volume in which viscous dissipation occurs. Thus this flow phenomenon leads to additional losses, as shown in Figures 6.5 and 6.6. Equivalent lengths of valves (even open valves) vary widely, at times as low as \(L/d=3\) and as high as \(L/d=1000\).

Example Problem 6.2 (p. 222) illustrates a simple calculation incorporating both pressure drop through pipes as well as through other lossy elements.

Recirculation: when a region of fluid is made to flow largely upstream. Typically associated with separation.

Viscous stress: in general, the force per unit area that a fluid applies at a point that is not explained by the thermodynamic pressure. For Newtonian incompressible fluids, this is synonymous with shear stress and is given by the viscosity multiplied by the strain rate.

6.4. Pumps

Fluid piping systems need to get the pressure from somewhere to drive fluid through the system. The simplest is for this to come from height and gravitational potential energy, and this is how gravity-fed aqueducts, like ancient Roman aqueducts, work (Example Problem 6.2). In practice, most engineering systems require a mechanical device (i.e., a pump) to generate flow and pressure. In this section, we discuss various types of pumps. There is some redundancy with the treatment of turbomachines in Chapter 2, but here we include also positive-displacement pumps.

The two major classes of pumps are positive-displacement pumps and dynamic pumps

Pumps come in countless forms; we will discuss only a few of them here. You probably researched and fabricated one of these in MAE2250 (hint: given the manufacturing tools you have, you have to go reciprocating piston pump. Reciprocating piston pump will always win. You HAVE to ask your Uncle Brian about these things). Pumps can roughly be classified as positive-displacement pumps or dynamic pumps. Positive-displacement pumps work by displacing fluid in a controlled way by moving the boundaries of a fluid container. Positive-displacement pumps are flowrate sources; their flowrate output is directly related to the movement of its mechanism, independent of the upstream or downstream load. Fluid properties and load will affect how much power is required to drive the pump, but the relation between pump motion and fluid motion is fixed. Some examples of positive-displacement pump types include reciprocating pumps, rotary vane pumps, gear pumps, and peristaltic pumps. Dynamic pumps work by adding kinetic energy to fluid, then trading that kinetic energy for pressure via deceleration of the flow (i.e., roughly as described by the Bernoulli equation, but with some losses). Two major classes of dynamic pumps are axial-flow pumps and centrifugal pumps. Dynamic pumps are almost always turbomachines.

Positive-displacement pumps, regardless of their configuration, tend to be good in low-flowrate applications, either because the fluid simply need not be moved much, or because the fluid has high viscosity. Positive-displacement pumps do not cause much local variation in fluid speed nor local variation in fluid pressure, so they are relatively robust, and they usually do not need priming. Many positive-displacement pumps produce unsteady output, which is sometimes undesirable, and they do not perform as well as dynamic pumps in high-flowrate applications. Positive-displacement pumps are flowrate sources; a positive-displacement pump run at a specific frequency or rotation rate will generate the same flowrate regardless of its environment; environmental factors (in particular, the fluid viscosity and upstream and downstream pressures) affect only the power required to actuate the pump.

The different configurations of positive-displacement pumps do not involve much fluid physics, but having a working knowledge of these configurations is useful to facilitate understanding of engineering fluid systems. Reciprocating pumps use a central domain whose volume can be changed (typically by motion of a piston, a plunger, or a diaphragm). By alternately filling and emptying this domain, fluid is moved about. If we add two check valves, one on each side of the central domain, we can transduce the periodic filling and emptying of this domain into directional flow. This is the fluid-

Positive-displacement pump: a pump that moves fluid by displacing the boundaries containing the fluid. Generated flowrate is a fixed function of RPM.

Dynamic pump: a pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it with an impeller, then decelerating it to increase pressure.

Reciprocating pump: equivalently, reciprocal pump. A positive-displacement pump that combines oscillation of the volume of a central domain with two check valves to induce flow.

Rotary vane pump: a positive-displacement pump that pushes fluid along an eccentric channel using vanes that press up against the outer housing via centrifugal force.

Gear pump: a positive-displacement pump that moves fluids through interlocking gears.

Bernoulli equation: in differential form \(0=\frac{d}{ds}(p+\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2+\rho gz)\), in integral form \(B=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2+\rho gz\), where \(B\) is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

Priming: the process of filling a pump with fluid as required to enable its operation.

Check valve: a valve that allows flow in one direction but not the other.

6.4. Pumps

Mechanical analog of an AC electrical power supply rectified through two diodes. A number of reciprocating pumps are shown in Figures 6.7–6.8. Reciprocating pumps are some of the simplest and cheapest pumps that can be manufactured—these pumps are integral parts of (for example) a spray bottle or a water pistol.

Rotary vane pumps use a rotor rotating inside a cavity with multiple vanes that extend to the edge of the cavity by centrifugal force. Rotary vane pumps are shown in Figure 6.9, p. 223. Gear pumps use one or more gears rotating inside a cavity to displace fluid. Schematics and images of gear pumps are shown in Figure 6.10, p. 223. Rotary vane pumps and gear pumps are common choices for oil pumps in automotive engines. Peristaltic pumps displace fluid by squeezing a flexible hose in a wavelike pattern from upstream to downstream, normally by encasing a semicircle of the hose inside a housing and rotating rollers over the hose. They are common choices for pumping corrosive or dangerous fluids. A peristaltic pump is shown in Figure 6.11, p. 223.

Dynamic pumps increase pressure by first (1) increasing the kinetic energy of the fluid, then immediately (2) trading kinetic energy (fluid speed) for stored work of compression (pressure). The Bernoulli equation qualitatively explains this tradeoff, although this process does have losses, and some of the energy imparted into the fluid is dissipated as heat. The pressure generated is thus less than would be predicted by the Bernoulli equation. Dynamic pumps are more well suited for large-flowrate applications, work well for low-viscosity fluids like air and water and poorly for high-viscosity fluids (don't use them in your corn-syrup-processing facility). Dynamic pumps lead to large local changes in fluid speed and pressure, and can induce cavitation if they are run improperly. Dynamic pumps often need priming, i.e., they only run properly if they are filled with the working fluid before they are turned on. Dynamic pumps are neither ideal pressure sources nor ideal flowrate sources; a dynamic pump run at a specific frequency or rotation rate will generate different pressures and flowrates depending on its environment. Environmental factors and working fluid affect not only the power required to actuate a dynamic pump, but also its pressure and flowrate outputs.

There are two primary classes of dynamic pumps—axial-flow pumps and centrifugal pumps. A single-stage axial-flow pump is basically an impeller inside a pipe (Figure 6.12, p. 224). An impeller inside a pipe works mostly like a propeller in open fluid, but it is significantly more efficient. Multi-stage axial-flow pumps consist of multiple rotors and stators, where the rotors are essentially moving airfoils, and the stators are motionless airfoils that increase efficiency by preventing the fluid from rotating and instead driving it forward. Centrifugal pumps (Figure 6.13, p. 224) bring fluid in near the axis of a rotating impeller (this section of the pump is called the eye) and throw the fluid out centrifugally into the volute casing. The volute casing is named after a spiral shape; it takes the fluid that is ejected out centrifugally from the impeller and moves it through a channel of expanding area to decelerate it and increase its pressure. Importantly, both axial-flow pumps and centrifugal pumps decrease the pressure of the fluid locally even if they eventually increase it.

Picking a positive-displacement pump is pretty simple

Positive-displacement pumps are pretty simple to select for several reasons. Their performance doesn't vary much with fluid viscosity; the power

6.4. Pumps

Required to drive them is just proportional to the viscosity; regardless of what fluid you want to drive, if you have a strong enough motor and the right gear ratio you are set. If the system can tolerate fluctuations, reciprocating pumps are acceptable whereas if fluctuations are not acceptable, a rotary pump, e.g., a gear pump or a rotary vane pump, is required. If the fluid being pumped is incompatible with the pump materials, a diaphragm reciprocating pump or a peristaltic pump will keep the pumped fluid separate from the workings of the pump.

Positive-displacement pumps are not ideal for high-flowrate applications. A key failure mode for a positive-displacement pump is bursting—the pump itself can typically generate higher pressure than it or the connecting pipes can mechanically withstand, and the local pressures required to squeeze the fluid through the pump are typically larger than the pressures needed elsewhere in the system. Because of this, positive-displacement pumps typically need a safety valve that releases fluid before the pump bursts, and if you try to run them at high flowrate, you just end up shooting fluid out the safety valve.

Dynamic pumps are sensitive to environment and best results require a pump matched well for its intended use

In contrast to positive-displacement pumps, dynamic pumps must be chosen properly if they are to work well, and their performance is a strong function of the upstream and downstream pressures. If the upstream pressure is too low, they cavitate. If the downstream pressure is too high, they generate very little flow and their efficiency goes to zero. If the downstream pressure is too low, they generate very little pressure increase and their efficiency goes to zero. So a properly sized and designed dynamic pump operates in the middle of its performance range, generating roughly 50–75% of its maximum pressure change and roughly 50–75% of its maximum flowrate. These maximum pressure changes and flowrates are a function primarily of the impeller size and rotation rate. Dynamic pumps work poorly in very low flowrate applications and for high-viscosity fluids, but very well for water and air in high-flowrate applications.

One can analyze dynamic pumps with MAE3230-level fluid mechanical analysis and be within 20–30% of the right answer, but we won't do it, and in practice pumps are selected from performance charts. Some examples of these charts are shown in Figures 6.15–6.16.

Reading a very complete dynamic pump performance curve tells you many things:

Model and rotation rate. Dynamic pump performance is a function of too many parameters to graph. It is customary to make a performance curve for a specific model and rotation rate (typically listed as rpm, i.e., revolutions per minute). The rotation rate corresponds to the line voltage (3600 RPM for 60 Hz line voltage and 3000 RPM for 50 Hz line voltage), which can also be divided by 2 or 3 if the AC motor is a four- or six-pole motor (in which case you get 1800/1200 Hz or 1500/1000 Hz). Also, the RPM of the shaft of an induction motor is actually slower than the electric field that drives it, so instead of 3600 RPM you might see 3550 RPM or the like. This information usually is in the header of the performance curve.

Reciprocating pump: equivalently, reciprocal pump. A positive-displacement pump that combines oscillation of the volume of a central domain with two check valves to induce flow.

Peristaltic pump: a positive-displacement pump that moves fluid along by wavelike compression of the tube that holds the fluid.

Positive-displacement pump: a pump that moves fluid by displacing the boundaries containing the fluid. Generated flowrate is a fixed function of RPM.

Dynamic pump: a pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it with an impeller, then decelerating it to increase pressure.

Cavitate: to transition in phase from liquid to gas. Physically identical to boil, but we use boil when the cause is increased temperature and cavitate when the cause is decreased pressure.

Impeller: a rotating airfoil used to transfer energy from a driveshaft to fluid, typically to generate a pressure jump in a confined duct or volute casing. Compare with propeller.

6.5. Averaging

Flowrate. The \(x\) axis lists flowrate. This is often just called flow or capacity or discharge. This is usually gallons per minute. Sometimes a metric scale is also provided.

Pressure. The pressure the pump generates is shown on the \(y\) axis. This is usually reported as total head, i.e., \(H=\frac{p}{\rho g}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{U^2}{g}+z\).

Impeller diameter. This is often listed as impeller trim. The same pump often can take impellers of several sizes, and each impeller size will correspond to a single curve on the head–flow (i.e., \(H\)–\(Q\)) axes.

Power required. This is typically listed as brake horsepower.

Net positive suction head. This is the minimum total head \(H=\frac{p}{\rho g}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{U^2}{g}\) required at the inlet of the pump to ensure that it does not cavitate. This is shown either as an inset graph or with isocontours.

Efficiency. This is the ratio of the work \((\Delta p\,Q)\) done divided by the brake power input into the pump. This is typically shown by use of efficiency isocontours on the performance curve.

Minimum flowrate. Often a mark or line is used to show the minimum recommended flowrate. Below this flowrate, there is not enough flowrate to cool the pump and it can overheat.

To select a pump, we identify the system characteristic of the hydraulic network we are pumping, i.e., the \(\Delta p\) vs. \(Q\) graph for the network. For fully turbulent flow, this curve will have a parabolic shape. We identify where on that curve we want to operate, which specifies the \(\Delta p\) and the \(Q\) at operating conditions. Then we find that point first on a hydraulic coverage chart (e.g., Figure 6.15, p. 226), which specifies the pump, then on the detailed pump performance chart (e.g., Figure 6.17, p. 228), which specifies the impeller trim.

Example Problem 6.3 (p. 228) contains a simple pump design question (i.e., impeller diameter selection) that can be directly read off of a pump performance chart.

6.5. Flow through most industrial and commercial pipes is typically analyzed using the Reynolds-averaged flow

Flow through most industrial and commercial pipes is typically analyzed using Reynolds-averaged flow (see Sidebar 6.6, p. 229).

Head: a quantity (e.g., static head \(H=p/(\rho g)\) or total head \(H=p/(\rho g)+U^2/(2g)+z\)) in units of length that communicates energy per unit volume or, equivalently, pressure of a fluid. It describes the height of a hypothetical fluid that would generate a hydrostatic gauge pressure at its bottom equal to the static pressure or total pressure in the fluid under discussion.

Brake horsepower: equivalent to brake power. Measure of power produced at the shaft of a motor. \(1\,\mathrm{hp}=746\,\mathrm{W}\).

Net positive suction head: the minimum total head required at the inlet of a pump to ensure that it does not cavitate. Important because it tells you where in a hydraulic circuit the pump needs to be—can it pull from above or does it need to push from below.

(a) The volumetric flow rate if the flow is assumed to be inviscid.

(b) The pressure distribution as a function of distance along the siphon tube (call 0 cm the tube inlet, 30 cm the top of the reservoir, and 60 cm the point at which the water issues from the tube). 3. (OBJECTIVE: Use the viscous dissipation factor in a simple problem related to case studies) The Aqueduct-de-Nîmes carried water from the springs at Fontaine-d’Eure to Nîmes. The height difference from start to finish was 12 m. The aqueduct was 50 km long. It delivered 40,000 m³ of water per day. Although the aqueduct is partially covered and partially uncovered, and is of variable cross section, and isn't always circular in cross section, for simplicity we will approximate the aqueduct as having a uniform closed circular cross section. This aqueduct was made about two thousand years ago; it was roughly made, and its viscous dissipation factor was pretty high, estimated at about \(f_D=0.0155\). Estimate the diameter the duct must have had, and estimate how many days it took water to get from Fontaine-d’Eure to Nîmes.

Problems with Answers

1. (OBJECTIVE: highlight how important large diameter is in maximizing flow in engineering piping systems) A horizontal 50'-long garden hose connects high-pressure water from the municipal water system at 3 bar gauge pressure to an atmospheric-pressure outlet to water a garden. Calculate the flow rate of water if the hose is 3/4” diameter versus 1/2” diameter. Garden hose interiors are smooth.

Solution: The hose length is \(L=50\,\mathrm{ft}\left(\frac{1\,\mathrm{m}}{3.28\,\mathrm{ft}}\right)=15.2\,\mathrm{m}\). The pressure difference between inlet and outlet is \(0.3\times10^6\,\mathrm{Pa}\). The diameters under consideration are \(d=0.019\,\mathrm{m}\) or \(d=0.013\,\mathrm{m}\). Estimate \(\bar U\) by guessing \(f_D=0.03\) (you can guess anything; I always guess .03):

\bar U=\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta p d}{\rho}\frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{f_D}}=\sqrt{\frac{2(\text{0.3e-6}\,\mathrm{Pa})(0.019\,\mathrm{m})}{(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(15.2\,\mathrm{m})(0.03)}}=5\,\mathrm{m/s}, (6.41)

For 1/2” hose we instead get \(\bar U=1.1\,\mathrm{m/s}\). With these \(\bar U\) values we can calculate the Reynolds number. For 3/4” pipe

Re=\frac{(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(5\,\mathrm{m/s})(0.019\,\mathrm{m})}{1\,\mathrm{mPa\,s}}=9.5\times10^4. (6.42)

For 1/2” pipe we get \(Re=5.4\times10^4\). From the Moody chart \(Re=9.5\times10^4\) predicts \(f_D=0.018\), whereas \(Re=5.4\times10^4\) predicts \(f_D=0.0205\). Refining our estimate using these values, we get \(\bar U=6.5\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and \(\bar U=5.3\,\mathrm{m/s}\). That leads to \(Re=1.2\times10^5\) for 3/4” and \(Re=6.9\times10^4\) for 1/2”. Both of those lead to updated \(f_D\) values that aren't much different, so we take these as close enough. The flow rate is thus given by

Q=\bar U A=(6.5\,\mathrm{m/s})\frac{\pi(0.019\,\mathrm{m})^2}{4}=1.8\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3/s}=1.8\,\mathrm{L/s}, (6.43)

and for 1/2” we get \(Q=0.7\,\mathrm{L/s}\). So the 3/4” hose leads to 2.5 times as much water flow, mostly from 2.2 times the area and then another 10% or so from a reduced viscous dissipation factor because the Reynolds number is higher for the larger-diameter hose.

Anyone doing many turbulent pipe calculations would use a computer function or program to iteratively solve until the correct \(f_D\) is obtained. However, one guess followed by one update is typically sufficient to get \(f_D\) accurate enough that the primary source of error in your calculation is no longer the solution for \(f_D\) but rather the roughness of the pipe or some other geometric uncertainty. For a garden hose, which is pretty flexible, the primary uncertainty is kinks in the hose.

2. (OBJECTIVE: place viscous losses in the context of siphon flow) A siphon made of 1/2” diameter smooth-surface tubing and length 60 cm is connected to a \(h_0=30\)-cm-tall reservoir with large cross section that holds water that is \(h=20\,\mathrm{cm}\) deep (Figure 6.21, p. 232). The tubing extends from a tiny bit above the bottom of the reservoir, to the top of the reservoir, over the edge of the reservoir, and then straight down the outside. The siphon issues at an elevation that matches the bottom of the reservoir of water. Calculate the following:

(a) The volumetric flow rate if the flow is assumed to be inviscid. (b) The pressure distribution as a function of distance along the siphon tube (call 0 cm the tube inlet, 30 cm the top of the reservoir, and 60 cm the point at which the water issues from the tube). You may, for the purposes of this calculation, assume the flow is fully developed throughout. In practice this will lead to a small error when calculating the pressure distribution in the first section of the tubing.

Editorial source clarification: (6.41) prints \(\text{0.3e-6}\,\mathrm{Pa}\), inconsistent with the stated 3 bar pressure difference and the reported speed. The intended pressure is \(0.3\times10^6\,\mathrm{Pa}\). The following 1/2-inch-hose speed has a damaged leading digit and is transcribed as \(1.1\,\mathrm{m/s}\); substituting its stated diameter into (6.41) with the intended pressure gives about \(4.1\,\mathrm{m/s}\), consistent with the following \(Re=5.4\times10^4\). The derived value is an editorial calculation, not a certified reading of that damaged digit.


PDF page 224 — source_issue

6.6. Practice Problems

(c) The volumetric flow rate if the viscous losses in the tubing are accounted for. (d) The pressure distribution if the viscous losses in the tubing are accounted for. Comment on how accurate the Bernoulli equation is for a system like this, and whether the Bernoulli equation underestimates or overestimates (a) the flow rate, (b) the pressure at the exit of the siphon, (c) the pressure at the inlet of the siphon.

Solution: (a) If inviscid, the speed is given by the Torricelli relation:

\bar U=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(0.2\,\mathrm{m})}=2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}. (6.44)

The area is

A=\pi\frac{(0.013\,\mathrm{m})^2}{4}=1.3\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}, (6.45)

so the flowrate is

Q=\bar U A=(2.0\,\mathrm{m/s})(1.3\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2})=2.6\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3/s}=0.26\,\mathrm{L/s}. (6.46)

(b) The pressure difference associated with 20 cm is 0.02 bar. Figure 6.22, p. 233 shows the pressure variation for both this case and the case with viscous effects.

(c) If viscous effects are to be accounted for, we note that in a pipe \(\bar B_{\mathrm{inlet}}-\bar B_{\mathrm{outlet}}=f_D\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U^2\frac{L}{d}\), so, denoting condition 1 at the top of the reservoir and condition 2 at the outlet of the siphon and condition 3 in the siphon, we can write

p_1+\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_1^2+\rho gz_1-p_2-\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_2^2+\rho gz_2=f_D\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_3^2\frac{L}{d}, (6.47)

The tube is of uniform cross section so \(\bar U_3=\bar U_2\). Pressure at the reservoir top and siphon outlet are the same, so those pressures cancel. The fluid is motionless at condition 1, so \(\bar U_1=0\). Call the height difference \(h=z_1-z_2\). That leads to

\rho gh-\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_2^2=f_D\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_2^2\frac{L}{d}. (6.48)

We can rearrange to find

\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar U_2^2=\frac{\rho gh}{1+f_D\frac{L}{d}}, (6.49)

which shows that the dynamic pressure is equal to the volumetric gravitational potential energy from the surface, divided by a factor that gets bigger as the pipe's aspect ratio gets longer. The term \(f_D L/d\) dominates when \(L/d\gg1/f_D\). The term \(f_D L/d\) is negligible when \(L/d\ll1/f_D\). And that term is 1, meaning half of the gravitational potential energy is dissipated, when \(L/d=1/f_D\). For most conditions \(f_D\) ranges between 0.01–0.1. So when \(L/d\) is small relative to 10 or 100, the viscous effects are small and the Bernoulli equation might be an OK approximation. When \(L/d\) is big relative to 10 or 100, viscous effects are large and only a small fraction of the gravitational potential energy of the fluid at the surface remains in the form of kinetic energy at the outlet; most of it is dissipated as heat. The formula for the mean fluid speed is

\bar U_2=\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+f_D\frac{L}{d}}}, (6.50)

which should look like the Torricelli relation with a viscous correction term in the denominator. If the pipe is extremely short, i.e., \(L/d\to0\), we recover the Torricelli relation. As the pipe gets long, i.e., \(L/d\to\infty\), then \(\bar U_2\to0\). For this tube \(L/d=0.6/0.013=46\). I first guess \(f_D=0.022\) because I am nerdy and 0.22 is approximately 1/46. This leads to \(\bar U_2=\sqrt{gh}=1.4\,\mathrm{m/s}\), which implies \(Re\) [partially unreadable substitution] \(=1.8\times10^4\).

Editorial note: Equation (6.47) prints \(+\rho gz_2\). Since the left side is inlet energy minus outlet energy, this term should be \(-\rho gz_2\), consistent with \(h=z_1-z_2\) and (6.48). The prose also prints “0.22 is approximately 1/46”; \(1/46\approx0.0217\), consistent with the stated guess \(f_D=0.022\).

Editorial note: The faint bottom substitution is recoverable mathematically as \(Re=\rho\bar U_2d/\mu\approx(1000)(1.4)(0.013)/(0.001)=1.82\times10^4\). This reconstruction agrees with the legible printed result; it is not a literal recovery of every washed-out symbol.

which per Moody diagram gives \(f_D = 0.027\), which leads to a recalculated \(U = \sqrt{2gh/2.21} = 1.3\,\text{m/s}\). Recalculating \(Re\) again wouldn’t lead to much of a change. So the flowrate is

The Bernoulli equation overpredicts the speed and flowrate by a factor \(\sqrt{1+f_D L/d}\), which in this case is \(\sqrt{2.24}\) or about a factor of 1.5. The pressure at the exit of the siphon is the atmospheric pressure and is unaffected by whether there are viscous losses. The pressure at the inlet of the siphon is atmospheric in the inviscid case, but is higher than atmospheric in the viscous case, consistent with the notion that there are losses in the Bernoulli constant when viscous effects are present, and there is no way to end up at 1 bar with viscous losses unless the fluid enters the tubing at a pressure higher than atmospheric. The flow rate in a real system matches the flow rate in the inviscid approximation only when \(L/d\) is small. Any pipe with a long aspect ratio always has viscous losses.

3. (OBJECTIVE: Use the viscous dissipation factor in a simple problem related to case studies) The Aqueduct-de-Nîmes carried water from the springs at Fontaine-d’Eure to Nîmes. The height difference from start to finish was 12 m. The aqueduct was 50 km long. It delivered 40,000 m³ of water per day.

Although the aqueduct is partially covered and partially uncovered, and is of variable cross-section, and isn’t always circular in cross-section, for simplicity we will approximate the aqueduct as having a uniform closed circular cross-section.

This aqueduct was made about two thousand years ago; it was roughly made, and its viscous dissipation factor was pretty high, estimated at about \(f_D = 0.0135\). Estimate the diameter the duct must have had, and estimate how many days it took water to get from Fontaine-d’Eure to Nîmes. Solution: The volumetric flowrate \(Q\) can be related to the speed \(U\) by

U = \frac{Q}{\pi d^2/4};\qquad U^2 = \frac{16Q^2}{\pi^2d^4}. (6.53)

From the definition of the viscous dissipation factor \(\Delta p = \frac{1}{2}\rho U^2 f_D L/d\) and the hydrostatic pressure difference \(\Delta p = \rho gh\), we can relate the diameter to the velocity with

d=U^2 2gh f_D L. (6.54)

Substituting and solving for \(d\), we find

d = \sqrt[5]{\frac{16Q^2 f_D L}{2\pi^2gh}}. (6.55)

For the given parameters:

d = \sqrt[5]{\frac{16(4\times10^4\,\mathrm{m^3/day})^2(1\,\mathrm{day}/24\,\mathrm{hr})^2(1\,\mathrm{hr}/60\,\mathrm{min})^2(1\,\mathrm{min}/60\,\mathrm{s})^2(0.0135)(50\times10^3\,\mathrm{m})}{2\pi^2(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})\,\mathrm{m/s^2}(12\,\mathrm{m})}} = 1\,\mathrm{m}. (6.56)

From the diameter, we can calculate the speed

U = \frac{4Q}{\pi d^2} = \frac{4(4\times10^4\,\mathrm{m^3/day})(1\,\mathrm{day}/24\,\mathrm{hr})(1\,\mathrm{hr}/60\,\mathrm{min})(1\,\mathrm{min}/60\,\mathrm{s})}{\pi(1\,\mathrm{m})^2} = 0.59\,\mathrm{m/s}, (6.57)

Editorial note: Equation (6.54) prints the product \(U^2 2gh f_D L\). Rearranging the preceding pressure balance instead gives \(d=U^2 f_D L/(2gh)\), which agrees with the fifth-root expression in (6.55). Equation (6.56) prints a second \(\mathrm{m/s^2}\) after the already dimensioned acceleration; this duplicate unit should be omitted. Its faint root index is shown as 5 following (6.55).

Editorial note: For the siphon, \(f_D L/d=0.027\cdot46=1.242\). The fraction of the reservoir head dissipated is \(1.242/(1+1.242)\approx0.554\); \(1/2.24\approx0.446\) is the fraction retained as outlet kinetic energy. The printed pressure loss of about 0.01 bar is consistent to its stated precision.

(OBJECTIVE: how to read Moody chart to solve flow problems in pipes with viscous loss) Fluid moves through a smooth pipe (surface roughness \(\epsilon = 0\)) with a circular cross section, length \(L = 1\,\mathrm{m}\), and diameter \(d = 20\,\mathrm{mm}\). The flow is driven by a pump generating a gauge pressure 1 atm higher than ambient (equivalently, this could be a column of fluid of height \(h = \text{[formula illegible]}\)). What is the volumetric flow rate \(Q\) if the fluid is:

(a) water (\(\rho = 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(\mu = 1\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}\))? (b) air (\(\rho = 1.2\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(\mu = 1.8\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}\))? (c) maple syrup (\(\rho = 1370\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(\mu = 1\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}\))? (d) mercury (\(\rho = 13500\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(\mu = 1.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}\))?

The Moody diagram will be useful; see Figure 6.23, p. 234. The value of the viscous dissipation factor is specified by the blue line; the black curved line is a reference line that denotes different domains of flow that have been described by fluid mechanicians over the years. Solution: For this problem, we need to find the average velocity for all of the flows with the provided condition. This is done by taking an iterative approach. The non-dimensional viscous dissipation factor is [parenthetical definition illegible in scan] and the Reynolds number using the diameter of the pipe as the characteristic length is [parenthetical definition illegible in scan]. (Note: this is the Darcy viscous dissipation factor where the pressure drop of a pipe with diameter \(D\) over a characteristic length is normalized by the dynamic pressure. This is not the same as the Fanning viscous dissipation factor; however, they are closely related—the Darcy viscous dissipation factor is exactly four times larger than the viscous dissipation factor in a circular pipe.)

(a) One recommended algorithm is to guess \(f_D\) and see if there is a contradiction, and adjust as needed. (b) Next we need to see whether our calculated \(f_D\) matches our guessed \(f_D\). (c) Repeat this step until the Reynolds number converges, which will provide you the average velocity. Alternatively, you can use the Haaland or Colebrook equation and use MATLAB’s fzero or fsolve command to solve for the viscous dissipation factor for the Reynolds number you have calculated. Note that these equations typically have only a specific \(Re\) range in which they are valid.

Now that the average velocity is found, it is relatively simple to find the volumetric flow rate as

Q = UA. (6.59)

So for our fluids: (a) Water: (turbulent) \(U = 17\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(Q = 0.0053\,\mathrm{m^3/s}\), \(f_D = 1.3\times10^{-2}\). (b) Air: (turbulent) \(U = 520\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(Q = 0.163\,\mathrm{m^3/s}\), \(f_D = 1.22\times10^{-2}\). (c) Maple syrup: (laminar) \(U = 1.25\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(Q = 3.93\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3/s}\), \(f_D = 1.87\). (d) mercury: (turbulent) \(U = 5\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(Q = 0.0016\,\mathrm{m^3/s}\), \(f_D = 1.2\times10^{-2}\).

SIDEBAR 6.4: ENGINEERING MODELS

Fully Developed Flow

Premise: it is easier to describe flow in pipes in regions that are far away from the entrance. The velocity distribution in a pipe changes as the fluid moves through the pipe (analogous comments can be made for flow between two plates). The changes are seen at the entrance and at any location that deviates from a straight line and uniform cross-section. Regions of flow that we refer to as fully developed are far from entrances or exits, far from turns, and far from locations at which the cross-section changes. Because of this, the fully developed region of a flow has no downstream gradients of velocity.

Mathematical form: for fully developed flow, the streamwise derivative of velocity is zero

For fully developed flow:

\frac{\partial \bar{u}}{\partial s} = 0. (6.8)

The fully developed flow model can be applied to both laminar and turbulent flow; for turbulent flow a Reynolds average must be used.

Utility: fully developed flow is universal and easy to measure experimentally

Whereas flow at entrances and exits and through turns is complicated and hard to replicate, the fully developed region of the flow through a pipe is universal and easy to replicate. Also, for many engineering systems, the primary behavior of the system is explained by the fully developed region. For example, the pressure drop through a long pipe is dominated by the pressure drop in the fully developed region. Although the details at the entrance and exit might be harder to predict, they are not the dominant source of pressure drop, and therefore have little engineering impact. Because the fully developed region of flow through a pipe is universal and useful, we have many tools to analyze this aspect of flows. The Moody chart or the Haaland equation or the Colebrook–White equation, for example, describes head losses for fully developed flow.

Limitations: the domain downstream of an entrance, turn, or change in cross-section has a finite entrance length or development length associated with it

The domain downstream of an entrance, turn, or change in cross-section has a finite entrance length or development length associated with it. The length of this domain is approximately 10 diameters long, although the precise length varies with Reynolds number and pipe cross-section. In this region, the velocity distribution changes, and the pressure drop associated with viscous losses is different (typically higher) than that of the fully developed region.


PDF page 228 — source_issue

SIDEBAR 6.5: FUNDAMENTALS

Reynolds Number

The Reynolds Number describes whether the behavior of a fluid is dominated by its momentum or by the viscous stresses it feels; it is the most ubiquitous nondimensional parameter in fluid mechanics.

Without attempting to write any equations, we can think of the Reynolds number as a measure of whether fluid behavior is dominated by the fact that the fluid has momentum or dominated by the fact that the fluid exhibits viscosity. Fluid has mass that is proportional to its density \(\rho\) and proportional to its volume (say \(\ell^3\) for a cube with sides of length \(\ell\); \(\pi\ell^3/6\) for a sphere of diameter \(\ell\)). Fluid has momentum that is proportional to its speed \(U\) and kinetic energy that is proportional to its speed squared \((U^2)\). So, fluid has more momentum and is harder to accelerate or change directions if it is dense, if it is moving quickly, and if it is large in scope. On the other hand, fluid feels viscous stresses in response to fluid deformation, which is proportional to velocity gradients. These stresses are proportional to the viscosity \(\mu\) and are surface forces that are proportional to the area enclosing a fluid system. Fluid feels viscous effects more strongly when the viscosity is high. The definition of the Reynolds number:

Re = \frac{\rho U\ell}{\mu}, (6.12)

is consistent with these observations. Dense, fast, big flows will have a large numerator and the Reynolds number will be high. These flows are momentum-dominated. Flows with high viscosity or that are slow or small will have a large denominator and small numerator and the Reynolds number will be low. These flows are viscous-dominated.

The Reynolds Number is proportional to the ratio of a fluid’s kinetic energy to the viscous stresses that would dissipate that energy

One way of quantitatively evaluating the heuristic above is to think about fluid kinetic energy and its dissipation by viscosity. The kinetic energy per unit volume in a fluid is given by \(\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2\). The viscous stresses in fluid are proportional to viscosity times strain rate which is a measure of local velocity gradients. Local velocity gradients are proportional to velocity differences divided by the length over which the velocity changes. A parcel of fluid moving at speed \(U\) that is a distance \(\ell\) from a wall might experience a viscous stress proportional to \(\mu U/\ell\). The ratio of these two parameters is:

Re = \frac{\text{twice the volumetric kinetic energy}}{\text{an approximation of local viscous stresses}} = \frac{2(\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2)}{\mu U/\ell} = \frac{\rho U\ell}{\mu}. (6.13)

The Reynolds number is thus a measure of how much kinetic energy is in a fluid proportional to the viscous process that would dissipate that energy. When Reynolds number is high, the fluid has a lot of kinetic energy and viscosity has a tough time changing the fluid’s direction or speed very much. When Reynolds number is low, the fluid has very little kinetic energy and viscosity has no problem changing the fluid’s direction or speed.

The Reynolds Number is often described as the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces

[Partially unreadable sentence beginning] at top is to consider the forces a fluid element feels when it is moving along a curved path. Most texts say that the Reynolds number is “the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces” but “inertial force” is actually a hard concept and most students don’t know what “inertial force” means in this context. Inertial forces, i.e., fictitious forces, describe the apparent force on an object if it is viewed in an accelerating reference frame. A classic example is the centrifugal force—if we define an accelerating coordinate frame associated with a mass moving with radius of curvature \(R\), in that frame the mass appears to feel an outward centrifugal force given by \(mU^2/R\). Imagine a fluid moving at speed \(U\) along the centerline of a pipe of diameter \(\ell\) with an elbow that has a radius of curvature \(\ell\) equal to the diameter. The centrifugal force on the fluid per unit volume would be given by \(\rho U^2/\ell\), and integrating this over a distance \(\ell\) would give a centrifugal force per unit area \(\rho U^2\). The viscous stress, i.e., viscous force per unit area, might again be proportional to \(\mu U/\ell\). Taking the ratio of the two:

Re = \frac{\text{inertial force associated with steering a cube of fluid with speed }U\text{ and side length }\ell\text{ along a curved path with radius }\ell}{\text{viscous force on a side of that cube if the local strain rate is approximated as }U/\ell} = \frac{(\rho U^2/\ell)\ell^3}{(\mu U/\ell)\ell^2} = \frac{\rho U\ell}{\mu}. (6.14)

The Reynolds number is thus a measure of what force is bigger: the force required to turn fluid moving at \(U\) along a circular path with radius \(\ell\), or the viscous force generated when fluid moving at speed \(U\) a distance \(\ell\) from a wall. When the Reynolds number is high, the centrifugal force the fluid feels if you try to steer it along that curved path is very high and the local viscous forces are not enough to control the flow. When the Reynolds number is low, the centrifugal force the fluid feels if you try to steer it along that curved path is low, and the local viscous forces are enough to control the flow.

The Reynolds number has only one length scale; it communicates size but cannot communicate shape

The Reynolds num[partially unreadable] has one length scale in it, which is chosen differently depending on what flow we are trying to characterize—for example the diameter of a pipe, the distance between two surfaces, the chord length of an airfoil, the downstream distance along a boundary layer. The Reynolds number alone is not sufficient to describe any system with two length scales, e.g., the length and thickness of an airfoil, and is of course not sufficient to describe the difference between differently shaped pipes or airfoils or jets or pickup trucks. The examples above are contorted to try to describe the physical systems explained by the Reynolds number alone; the contortions all come from using the same length scale \(\ell\) to try to describe everything. Real systems have Reynolds numbers but also need a description of the system geometry before we can solve anything.

The Reynolds number dictates transition from laminar to turbulent flow

Viscosity is linear and viscosity takes a mathematical form that smoothes out any fluctuations in velocity. Viscosity describes the diffusion of momentum. Viscosity, i.e., the diffusion of momentum, is thus a stabilizing phenomenon. The fluid kinetic energy is nonlinear in the velocity, and convection of momentum takes a mathematical form that allows variations in velocity to grow. Convection is thus a destabilizing phenomenon. Laminar flow results when the stabilizing effects of viscosity outweigh the destabilizing effects of momentum convection, and turbulent flow (i.e., disorderly, chaotic flow that is observed in most mechanical engineering flows) results when the destabilizing effects of momentum convection outweigh the stabilizing effects of momentum diffusion. Thus \(Re\) is the defining parameter that prescribes transition from laminar to turbulent flow.

Editorial note: Some printed symbols in the denominator of (6.14) are washed out. The displayed denominator \((\mu U/\ell)\ell^2\) is reconstructed from the preceding explanation of viscous stress and cube-face area; it gives the legible final \(\rho U\ell/\mu\). Partial sentence beginnings are marked rather than supplied as certain source text.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 6.1

Back when Roman aqueducts were the height of technology, the Aqueduct-de-Nîmes transported 40,000 m³ of water daily through a 50-km-long pipe, driven by a height difference of 12 m. If we assume that the aqueduct can be approximated as a pipe with diameter of 1.3 m, what is the approximate surface roughness of the aqueduct? Solution: A flowrate of 40,000 m³ of water daily corresponds to a mean speed \(U\) given by

U = Q/A = \frac{40{,}000\,\mathrm{m^3/day}}{\pi(0.65\,\mathrm{m})^2}\left(\frac{1\,\mathrm{day}}{24\,\mathrm{hr}}\right)\left(\frac{1\,\mathrm{hr}}{60\,\mathrm{min}}\right)\left(\frac{1\,\mathrm{min}}{60\,\mathrm{s}}\right) = 0.35\,\mathrm{m/s}. (6.18)

The Reynolds number is

Re = \rho Ud/\mu = \frac{(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(0.35\,\mathrm{m/s})(1.3\,\mathrm{m})}{(1\,\mathrm{mPa\,s})} = 4\times10^5. (6.19)

The viscous dissipation factor is given by

f_D = \frac{\Delta p}{\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2}\frac{d}{L} = \frac{(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(12\,\mathrm{m})}{\frac{1}{2}(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(0.35\,\mathrm{m/s})^2}\frac{1.5\,\mathrm{m}}{50000\,\mathrm{m}} = 0.05. (6.20)

For \(Re = 4\times10^5\) and \(f_D = 0.05\), the Moody chart indicates that the relative roughness \(\epsilon/d = 0.02\). Hence the surface roughness

\epsilon = 0.02(1.3\,\mathrm{m}) = 2.6\,\mathrm{cm}. (6.21)

So the surfaces of the aqueduct had average roughness of about 1 in. This result is very approximate; the Aqueduct-de-Nîmes had varying cross-sections and hydraulic diameters; the circular approximation we used was for expediency.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 6.2

Consider flow of \(7.5\times10^5\,\mathrm{m^3}\) of water through a smooth pipe of diameter 10 cm and length 3.8 m, which has a globe valve with effective length \(l_v = 50d\) upstream of the pipe. A 45° flanged turn is placed midway along the pipe. What is the pressure difference between inlet and outlet?

Solution: Per the figure, a 45° flange has an equivalent length of \(12d\). Adding a globe valve with equivalent length of \(50d\) to the pipe and a pipe with length equal to \(38d\) gives a total length of \(100d\). The average speed of the flow is

U = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{7.5\times10^5\,\mathrm{m^3}}{\pi(5\,\mathrm{cm})^2} = 1\,\mathrm{m/s}. (6.37)

The Reynolds number is \(Re = \rho Ud/\mu = (1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(1\,\mathrm{m/s})(0.1\,\mathrm{m})/(1\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}) = 1\times10^5\). The viscous dissipation factor from the Moody chart is \(f_D = 0.018\). The pressure drop is given by

\Delta p = \frac{1}{2}\rho U^2 f_D\frac{L}{d} = \frac{1}{2}(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(1\,\mathrm{m/s})(0.018)(100) = 900\,\mathrm{Pa}. (6.38)

Figure 6.14: The full performance curve of a dynamic pump, like the one above, is illustrative of the relevant physics. Efficiency is maximum in the middle of the performance curve because work output is the product of head and flowrate. The peak of the efficiency curve is sometimes labeled BEP—best efficiency point. However, a curve like this is not actually used for design, because the efficiency is so poor at low head and low flowrate that under those conditions you should really be using a different pump. The shaded regions correspond to the recommended operation range for pumps, incorporating all of the possible impeller diameters, and allow selection of the appropriate pump as long as the location in \(\Delta B-Q\) space is known.

SIDEBAR 6.6: ENGINEERING MODELS

Reynolds-Averaged Flow

Premise: Although turbulent flow is unsteady, we often need to know only the time-averaged results

In intro fluids, we are almost always pretending that flow is steady. In reality, all high-\(Re\) flows are turbulent and unsteady. Many flows, however, have fluctuations but still nonetheless have a time-invariant portion, and often that time-invariant portion is of engineering importance. In these cases, we reframe the equations so that we are actually talking about the time-invariant portion. We do not need to know the microsecond-scale or millisecond-scale fluctuations in the instantaneous lift force on a plane—the question is just what is the time-averaged portion and is that enough so that the plane doesn’t crash.

Mathematical form: time-averaging a turbulent flow leads to equations that look just like the Navier–Stokes equations but with an extra term known as the turbulent viscosity

If we have a flow that is stationary but unsteady, we rewrite the equations by decomposing the velocity \(\vec{u}\) into its time-averaged component \(\bar{\vec{u}}\), and its fluctuation components \(\vec{u}^{\prime}\). This changes the Navier–Stokes equations:

\rho\frac{\partial \vec{u}}{\partial t} + \rho\vec{u}\cdot\nabla\vec{u} = -\nabla p + \mu\nabla^2\vec{u} + \rho\vec{g}. (6.39)

into the Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations:

\rho\bar{\vec{u}}\cdot\nabla\bar{\vec{u}} = -\nabla\bar{p} + \mu\nabla^2\bar{\vec{u}} + \rho\vec{g} + f_t. (6.40)

Here, \(f_t\) is a single term that gathers together all of the effects of the fluctuations. This is shown in Figure A.2, p. 437.



Figure 6.18: Averaging over time in turbulent flows transfers from an instantaneous description of a turbulent flow to a Reynolds-averaged description, and introduces a turbulent viscosity to account for the effects of the fluctuations that are lost in the process.

Which is nice and simple except... we don’t know what \(f_t\) is. Turbulence modeling involves trying to develop some sort of prediction for what \(f_t\) is based on other properties of the flow. When using a software package to simulate fluid flow, these turbulence models are often selected from a menu in the program, for example \(k\text{-}\epsilon\) or \(k\text{-}\omega\) or SST or RDT etc. Each of these models takes properties of the flowfield and predicts what \(f_t\) is, and how accurate that prediction is varies widely depending on what sort of turbulent flow is being modeled. Reynolds-averaging the Navier–Stokes equations is the sort of topic that is often discussed in MAE4230. At the MAE3230 level, we don’t ever deal with the fluctuations or turbulence models either. It is just understood that when we are talking about a turbulent flow in MAE3230, we are always talking about \(\bar{\vec{u}}\), not \(\vec{u}\).

Utility: Reynolds averaging is what makes all of MAE3230 possible

We actually couldn’t analyze anything in MAE3230 if we didn’t have a way to ignore the hard part we can’t analyze well. Reynolds averaging is a formal way to ignore all the fluctuations we don’t know how to handle.

Limitations: Reynolds averaging works only for stationary flow

Reynolds averaging presupposes that there is a time-invariant flow to decompose from fluctuations, and thus Reynolds averaging is possible only if a flow is stationary.

Equation (6.39) annotations: \(-\nabla p\), “net volumetric pressure force”; \(\mu\nabla^2\vec u\), “net volumetric viscous force”; \(\rho\vec g\), “net volumetric gravity force”.

Equation (6.40) annotations: \(-\nabla\bar p\), “net volumetric pressure force”; \(\mu\nabla^2\bar{\vec u}\), “net volumetric viscous force”; \(\rho\vec g\), “net volumetric gravity force”; \(f_t\), “time-avgd mom outflow from corr. vel flucts”.

Chapter 7

Helicopter/Quadcopter Rotors: Turbomachines That Lift Vehicles Into the Air

The rotor of a quadcopter or helicopter is a turbomachine that lifts the vehicle into the air

Helicopters and quadcopters all fly by use of rotors, spinning sets of blades that push air down so as to generate a net reactive force up (Figure 7.1, p. 235).



Figure 7.1: Helicopters and quadcopters use rotors to push air down (downwash), thereby generating lift.

A quadcopter rotor has fixed geometry, and controlling its thrust is simply a matter of changing the power applied to the shaft. In this sense, a quadcopter rotor is essentially the same as a desk fan, but with a different purpose. A desk fan is designed to move air, and incidentally generates a force. A quadcopter rotor is designed to generate a force, and incidentally causes a downwash of fluid. Quadcopter rotors have fixed geometry relative to the vehicle, and vehicle control is effected only by varying the motor power (and therefore rotor spin rate) of at least four rotors in different combinations.

rotor: in general for a motor or turbomachine, the rotating part. Specifically for a quadcopter or helicopter, the rotating lifting surface. Cf. stator.

downwash: the downward motion of air consistent with a lift-generating aerodynamic object, e.g., a wing or rotor.


PDF page 247 — verified

7.1. ROTORS

A quadcopter is controlled by controlling the rotation rate of (at least) four independent fixed-geometry rotors

Quadcopters are the simplest and most common drone modality. They are easy for users to fly, and the software involved in their stabilization and control is relatively straightforward. They typically use fixed-pitch blades—this configuration works fine for small vehicles but is very ineffective for large vehicles—and quadcopters are an appropriate design only for small vehicles. Quadcopters are less thermodynamically efficient than helicopters and much less thermodynamically efficient than airplanes.

A handheld controller is all that is needed to control a quadcopter (Figure 7.2, p. 236). Two thumb-actuated joysticks control throttle, yaw, pitch, and roll through independent control of the power supplied to each rotor. Combinations of these can achieve climb, descent, steering (yaw rotation), pitching for forward or backward flight, and rolling for sideways flight (Figure 7.3, p. 237).



Figure 7.2: A quadcopter controller. Left: example image. Right: schematic representation. Two joysticks each have four-direction actuation; the eight different inputs each refer to a different combination of increased and decreased power to the four rotors.

[The controller photograph at left in Figure 7.2 is omitted.]

Forward and backward on the left joystick is the throttle—it controls the sum of the powers to the four rotors. Left and right on the left joystick is the yaw control—it controls balance between power to clockwise-spinning (front left, rear right) and counterclockwise-spinning (front right, rear left) rotors. Forward and backward on the right joystick is the pitch control—it controls balance between front two and back two rotors. Left and right on the right joystick is the roll control—it controls balance between left two and right two rotors.

A helicopter has a main rotor that provides the primary forces, and a tail rotor that stabilizes the helicopter in yaw

A helicopter uses a main rotor, which spins counterclockwise when viewed from above, to provide its primary forces, and a tail rotor to counteract the

pitch: for an aircraft, pitch implies nose-up and nose-down rotation of an aircraft, i.e., rotation around the wing–wing axis. For a propeller or rotor, pitch implies the angle of attack of the propeller blades.

torque caused by the main motor. The main and tail rotor spin rates are each approximately steady in normal operation. The main rotor generates thrust by pushing fluid downward and generating upward lift; the fluid mechanical analysis behind that is a prime motivator for integral control volume analysis.

The main rotor is on a gimbaled mount that can be tilted relative to the helicopter fuselage. As indicated previously, the main rotor primarily provides lift, but it also provides thrust in whatever direction the rotor is tilted towards. The blades of the main rotor experience drag as they rotate and the motor must apply a counterclockwise torque to keep the rotor in motion; there is an equal and opposite clockwise torque induced on the helicopter. If this were the only rotor, this clockwise torque on the fuselage would make the fuselage spin out of control. The tail rotor balances this torque by pushing air left, leading to a thrust vector to the right, and thus applying counterclockwise torque.



Figure 7.4: Schematic of yaw equilibrium, i.e., longitudinal trim. The main rotor spins counterclockwise (viewed from above). The motor is applying a counterclockwise torque to the rotor and the rotor applies a clockwise torque to the motor and fuselage. To stabilize this, the tail rotor pushes fluid to the left, creating thrust to the right, and therefore a counterclockwise torque on the fuselage that cancels the main rotor torque.

A helicopter is controlled by controlling the blade pitch angle and thus the tilt and lift of the main rotor plane

A helicopter rotor is much more sophisticated than a propeller, fan, or quadcopter rotor. Other than yaw control, which is handled by the tail rotor, all of the control of a helicopter is caused by a single rotor whose spin rate is largely fixed. This is possible because a helicopter rotor’s blades can change their pitch angle, which is the angle the blades make relative to horizontal.

lift: the component of a force a fluid exerts on an immersed object that is normal to the flow.

integral: as an adjective, relating to the finite difference between two discrete states (e.g., point 1 to point 2) or the integrated effect of something over a finite distance or volume. Compare with differential, meaning related to derivatives.

control volume: a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

gimbal: a pivoted support that permits rotation of an object about an axis.

fuselage: the main body of an aircraft.

yaw: left–right rotation of an aircraft, i.e., rotation around the vertical axis.

pitch: for an aircraft, pitch implies nose-up and nose-down rotation of an aircraft, i.e., rotation around the wing–wing axis. For a propeller or rotor, pitch implies the angle of attack of the propeller blades.


PDF page 250 — verified

7.1. ROTORS

The average pitch angle can be increased and decreased, which is generally called collective control (Figure 7.5, p. 239), and the pitch angle can be made to vary sinusoidally as the rotor spins, which is generally called cyclic control (Figure 7.6, p. 240). Collective control increases and decreases the force that the rotor generates, causing climb or descent. Cyclic control causes the rotor to tilt relative to the helicopter fuselage, causing the thrust vector from the rotor to tilt relative to the helicopter and lead to flight in an arbitrary direction.

collective control: control of a helicopter’s lift magnitude, coming from control of all of the rotor blade rotation-independent angle of attacks.

cyclic control: control of a helicopter’s lift angle, resulting from tilting of the rotor plane coming from sinusoidal variation of the rotor blade angle of attacks during blade rotation.

fuselage: the main body of an aircraft.



Figure 7.5: Collective control changes rotor blade pitch angle throughout the rotor path, causing uniform change in the blade lift. A: The pilot’s collective lever is pulled up to make the helicopter climb. B: Pushing the collective lever up actuates the swash plate and makes the blade pitch angle increase throughout the rotor path. The rotor has high pitch angle throughout. C: The increased lift causes the helicopter to climb.

The lift on a rotor blade is linearly related to the pitch angle of the blades

As described previously, the rotor of a helicopter spins at a mostly constant speed. The local forces generated by the rotor are controlled primarily of the blade pitch angle. An important observation from thin-blade aerodynamics is that, within the normal operating range of a rotor blade or an airplane wing (say −5° to 12°), the lift generated by a blade moving through air varies approximately linearly with the blade pitch angle. Because the rotor blade pitch angle can be actuated very quickly, even for a large rotor, controlling lift through blade pitch angle is a fast, effective, and agile strategy for actuating a helicopter. Trying to control a helicopter by increasing power to the motor would be very slow and ineffective. In comparison, a quadcopter can spin up the rotor speed quickly because quadcopters are small and spinning up a small rotor is feasible. Also, quadcopters tend to be much cheaper and less sophisticated than helicopters, and use four or more rotors instead of the mechanical complexity of a swash plate.

blade: a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes. Roughly synonymous with airfoil, hydrofoil, wing, and vane. Often chosen over the word vane when the blade is rotating in a turbomachine.

pitch: for an aircraft, pitch implies nose-up and nose-down rotation of an aircraft, i.e., rotation around the wing–wing axis. For a propeller or rotor, pitch implies the angle of attack of the propeller blades.

swash plate: an angled disk attached to a shaft, which transduces rotating motion into oscillatory motion. In a helicopter, causes rotor blade pitch angle to vary sinusoidally with rotor rotation.

B: Pushing the cyclic forward actuates the swash plate and makes the blade pitch angle vary sinusoidally. The rotor, which spins counterclockwise when viewed from above, has low pitch angle when advancing through 0° but high pitch angle when receding through 180°, generating low lift when advancing and high lift when receding. C: The \(\theta\)-dependent lift tilts the rotor plane so that its rotation axis points forward, and its lift vector points forward.

Figure 7.7: Graph of the lift coefficient \(C_L = \frac{F_L}{\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2 A}\) as a function of pitch angle, i.e., angle of attack, for a Hughes Helicopter HH-02 airfoil. Within a finite range, the lift coefficient (and therefore lift) varies linearly with pitch angle. At the limits, the airfoil stalls, meaning that it loses lift owing to separation on the low-pressure surface.

Antitorque pedals controlled by the feet control the pitch of the tail rotor blades, changing tail rotor thrust and torque and causing the helicopter to yaw

The side thrust of the tail rotor is controlled by the pitch angle of the tail rotor blades. The pitch is always varied uniformly throughout the tail rotor’s path. The pilot changes the tail rotor pitch through foot pedals (i.e., anti-torque pedals) which connect to the tail rotor blades through the tail gearbox (Figure 7.8, p. 242). Depressing the right pedal forward reduces the tail rotor pitch, and the tail rotor thrust undercompensates for the torque caused by the main rotor, so the fuselage rotates clockwise and the helicopter turns right. Depressing the left pedal forward increases the tail rotor pitch, and the tail rotor thrust overcompensates for the torque causes by the main rotor, so the fuselage rotates counterclockwise and the helicopter turns left.

To describe the basic aspects of quadcopter and helicopter control, we use a model of a rotor that describes the thrust vector it generates and how it induces fluid flow, and then use that thrust to describe basic vehicle control. The simplest model of a rotor is an actuator disk, a fluid machine that translates power to thrust by use of the actuated fluid.

antitorque pedals: pedals that control the pitch angle of the tail rotor of a helicopter, controlling by how much the main rotor torque is counteracted by the tail rotor.

fuselage: the main body of an aircraft.

actuator disk: a simplified model of a turbomachine, e.g., a propeller, as an infinitely thin disk that creates a pressure discontinuity.

fluid machine: a machine that adds energy to or extracts energy from a fluid.

Propellers, rotors, and fans can all be modeled as actuator disks whose force is determined from a control-volume analysis of entering and exiting flow

The actuator disk model of a rotor treats the rotor as if it were an infinitely thin disk that uniformly increases the pressure of the air that passes through it (Figure 7.9, p. 243). With this approximation, experimental observations and control volume analysis of the fluid that passes through the rotor immediately leads to several key conclusions:



Figure 7.9: A drawing of the rotor of a helicopter as an actuator disk, including control surfaces that are used to analyze this system. Key observations from an inviscid control volume analysis include: (a) the velocity increases from approximately zero in the far upstream region to a speed \(U_{\mathrm{rotor}}\) at the rotor, and continues increasing until it is twice that speed in the wake downstream of the rotor; (b) fluid upstream of the rotor comes from all directions but flows as a column of fluid downstream of the rotor, with a cross-sectional area that reduces by a factor of 2 downstream of the rotor; (c) the lift force generated is \(F = 2\dot{m}U_{\mathrm{rotor}} = 2\rho U_{\mathrm{rotor}}^2 A_{\mathrm{rotor}}\); (d) the pressure drop upstream of the rotor is 1/3 of the pressure rise downstream of the rotor.

If we assume that the rotor generates a mass flow \(\dot{m} = \rho U_{\mathrm{rotor}} A_{\mathrm{rotor}}\), then:

Conservation of mass between surfaces \(S_2\) and \(S_3\) implies \(\rho A_2 U_2 =\)

Conservation of mass between surfaces \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), plus the assumption that \(A_1 \to \infty\), implies \(\rho A_1 U_1 = \rho A_2 U_2\) and

Conservation of momentum between surfaces \(S_2\) and \(S_3\), given a downward force \(F\) applied by the rotor to the air, implies \(p_2 A_2 + \rho U_2^2 = p_3 A_3 + \rho U_3^2 + F\), so

which means the lift force caused by the air on the rotor is \(L = A_{\mathrm{rotor}}(p_3 - p_2)\).

Conservation of momentum between surfaces \(S_1\) and \(S_4\), given that the integrated effect of the pressure along this contour is zero, implies \(\rho U_1^2 = \rho U_4^2 + F\), so the lift force can also be written as

L = \dot{m}U_4 = \rho A_4 U_4^2 (7.5)

Setting the two expressions for \(L\) equal to each other leads to

U_4 = 2U_3 = 2U_2 (7.6)

Applying the Bernoulli equation between \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) and between \(S_3\) and \(S_4\) leads to

p_2 = p_{\mathrm{atm}} - \frac{1}{2}\rho U_2^2 (7.7)

p_3 = p_{\mathrm{atm}} + \frac{3}{2}\rho U_2^2 (7.8)

Editorial source correction: Both inline momentum balances above omit the areas multiplying the momentum-flux terms. Their dimensionally consistent forms are \(p_2A_2+\rho U_2^2A_2=p_3A_3+\rho U_3^2A_3+F\) and \(\rho U_1^2A_1=\rho U_4^2A_4+F\), using the source’s force sign convention. The printed balances are retained; \(\rho U^2\) has pressure units whereas each complete force term has units of newtons.


PDF page 256 — verified

We have skipped ahead and shown the results, without showing any of the detailed analysis. The actuator disk adds negative \(z\) momentum to the fluid, and net negative momentum of the fluid leaves the control volume at \(S_4\). The lift force can be calculated by tracking this negative momentum using a large control volume that encapsulates the entire flow. The lift force can equivalently be calculated by examining the pressure drop using an infinitesimally thin control volume that encapsulates only the actuator disk. These lift forces are by definition identical. Although the rotor increases the speed of the air, the air does not have a velocity discontinuity at the rotor. The velocity varies continuously through the flow. The rotor does have the effect of accelerating the fluid, but it does so gradually, starting far upstream of the rotor and ending far downstream of the rotor. The speed of the air at the rotor \(U_{\mathrm{rotor}}\) is one-half as fast as the speed the fluid eventually obtains.

We found it useful to approximate the flow generated by the actuator disk is inviscid, and the Bernoulli equation is a good approximation for the transfer of energy within the fluid. This leads to a prediction of pressure and velocity distributions generated by the rotor (Figure 7.10, p. 246). The Bernoulli equation applies before and after the rotor, but it does not apply at the actuator disk, because the actuator disk does work on the fluid. Thus the integral form of the Bernoulli equation is correct only if states 1 and 2 of that equation are on the same side of the actuator disk. Upstream of the actuator disk, the flow accelerates, streamlines converge, and the pressure drops below atmospheric. At the actuator disk, the work done by the actuator disk increases the fluid pressure above atmospheric. Downstream of the actuator disk, the flow continues to accelerate, the streamlines continue to converge, and the pressure returns to atmospheric. The fluid speed at the propeller is half of the maximum speed downstream of the propeller.

These results motivate a detailed discussion of control volume analysis for at least three reasons: first, this control volume was carefully drawn to make the math easy, and we need to learn how to do that. Second, even if we make the math easy, we need to get the accounting right, especially the signs of all the terms, and we need to practice that. Third, any slight deviation from flow moving uniformly normal to a surface will make the math much more complicated, and we have to in general know how to handle that aspect of the dyadic/vector calculus.

We performed this analysis using inviscid analysis, but real flows are viscous, and we should immediately wonder—is this inviscid analysis any good? Figure 7.11, p. 247 compares the inviscid solution (which we just wrote out) with the viscous solution (which is reproduced from a full simulation). We can see from this comparison that, for an actuator disk, the inviscid solution does a good job of predicting the lift force and the velocity and pressure variation from upstream to the actuator disk and a bit past it. Then where the inviscid solution completely fails is predicting what happens in the wake. The real fluid slows down, dissipates its kinetic energy as heat, and the effect of the actuator disk propagates only a finite distance downstream. The inviscid solution cannot properly describe this, and predicts that the fluid just zooms along forever.

This chapter focuses attention on integral conservation equations

The key engineering motivation of this chapter is quadcopters and helicopters, two vehicles which use a rotor to generate lift. The same principles

actuator disk: a simplified model of a turbomachine, e.g., a propeller, as an infinitely thin disk that creates a pressure discontinuity.

Bernoulli equation: in differential form \(0 = \frac{d}{ds}(p + \frac{1}{2}\rho u^2 + \rho gz)\), in integral form: \(B = p + \frac{1}{2}\rho u^2 + \rho gz\), where \(B\) is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

rotor: in general for a motor or turbomachine, the rotating part. Specifically for a quadcopter or helicopter, the rotating lifting surface. Cf. stator.

The stagnation pressure is uniform along streamlines upstream and downstream of the rotor, but changes discontinuously at the rotor. The static pressure drops everywhere in the flowfield as the fluid moves and accelerates, but also has a discontinuous increase at the rotor. The velocity increases continuously throughout. The Bernoulli equation describes the fluid properties in the fluid domain, but does not describe what happens at the rotor, because the rotor adds energy to the fluid, and the Bernoulli equation does not account for this.

PDF page 259 — verified

apply to a propeller, which an airplane might use to generate thrust, a fan, which we use to circulate air and cool equipment, and a wind turbine, which is basically just a propeller with negative input power because it is connected to a generator instead of a motor.

In all of these cases, a rotor leads to a net increase in fluid momentum in one direction, and a thrust in the opposite direction. This flow is best quantified with an integral control volume analysis, which we formalize in this chapter. The physics of this chapter includes the concepts of conservation of mass and conservation of momentum. The key mathematics of this chapter is the Reynolds transport theorem, a tool for converting back and forth between Lagrangian and Eulerian frames of reference, a fluid-mechanics-specific version of the chain rule from calculus.

Whereas previous chapters used control volumes ad hoc, using the level of expertise we developed in ENGRD2210, the complex spatial variation of real fluid mechanical systems requires us to formulate more complicated equations, and these formulations invariably involve more formal control volume analysis. So we pursue this control volume analysis in two steps. In this chapter, we present integral analysis of control volumes. By integral, we mean that the control volume will be finite in size, and the properties of fluids entering and leaving will typically be known. In the following chapter, we will move to differential analysis of control volumes, which will imply that the control volumes will be infinitesimally small and the properties of fluids entering and leaving will be related by Taylor-series expansions. We take these two topics in this order because integral control volumes help us develop intuition for the needed accounting processes without too much differential calculus. In the next chapter, we overlay differential calculus onto what is (hopefully) a well-understood control volume accounting framework.

This chapter is not focused primarily on predicting the velocity field in a fluid; rather, it provides a bridge between the fluid flow itself and the other components of a fluid system—it helps us understand how quickly a reservoir fills if we know the flow rates at its inlet and exit, or what the force is on a wall if we hit it with a jet of fluid, or how the thickness of a constriction in a pipe changes the velocity of the fluid in the pipe.

The key mathematical results of this chapter are the integral forms of the governing equations for conservation of mass and conservation of momentum. These will not only allow the analysis in this chapter, but these integral conservation laws will form the basis for the equivalent differential conservation laws to follow in the next chapter.

The integral conservation of mass equation we use for a control volume comes from combining the Reynolds transport theorem with the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed

The fundamental statement of conservation of mass is that the mass of a system is neither created nor destroyed. Stated in terms of a total derivative, this means

integral: as an adjective, relating to the finite difference between two discrete states (e.g., point 1 to point 2) or the integrated effect of something over a finite distance or volume. Compare with differential, meaning related to derivatives.

conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

conservation of momentum: the notion that changes in momentum are brought about by forces as prescribed by Newton’s second law.

Taylor-series expansion: an infinite series that describes the value of a function \(f\) near a point \(\vec{x}\) in terms of the derivatives of \(f\) at \(\vec{x}\).
