SIDEBAR 7.1: FUNDAMENTALS

The key derivatives we use are partial, total, and material derivatives

Partial derivatives and total derivatives are mathematical concepts. A function of several variables \(f(x,y,z,t)\) has partial derivatives with respect to each variable. The partial derivative with respect to a variable measures how much function \(f\) changes if that single variable is changed while all other variables are held constant:

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,y,z,t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{f(x,y,z,t+\frac{1}{2}\Delta t)-f(x,y,z,t-\frac{1}{2}\Delta t)}{\Delta t} (7.9)

The function also has total derivatives with respect to each variable. The total derivative of the function with respect to a variable measures how much the function \(f\) changes as a function of a single variable if it is assumed that all other variables are themselves functions of the first variable:

\frac{df}{dt}(x,y,z,t)=\lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{f\left[x(t+\frac{1}{2}\Delta t),y(t+\frac{1}{2}\Delta t),z(t+\frac{1}{2}\Delta t),t+\frac{1}{2}\Delta t\right]-f\left[x(t-\frac{1}{2}\Delta t),y(t-\frac{1}{2}\Delta t),z(t-\frac{1}{2}\Delta t),t-\frac{1}{2}\Delta t\right]}{\Delta t} (7.10)

This can equivalently be written as:

\frac{df}{dt}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial t} (7.11)

Equation 7.11 annotations: “partial deriv of f”; “total deriv of f”; “how f changes because of x-motion”; “how f changes because of y-motion”; “how f changes because of z-motion.”

In fluid mechanics, we define a material derivative (or some authors use the term substantial derivative), which is a physical, kinematic concept. The material derivative, denoted \(D/Dt\), reports the rate at which a property in which a moving control mass changes as a function of time, written not in terms of properties of the moving control mass, but instead in terms of an Eulerian control volume. Mathematically, it is a special case of a total time derivative taken on a fluid element, where \(\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}=u\), \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}=v\), and \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial t}=w\):

\frac{Df}{Dt}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+u\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial f}{\partial z} (7.12)

Equation 7.12 annotations: “partial deriv of f”; “material deriv of f”; “convective deriv of f in x dir”; “convective deriv of f in y dir”; “convective deriv of f in z dir.”

Because \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) form the basis for a spatial vector, it is convenient to notate this definition using Gibbs notation (i.e., vector notation), in which the material derivative is

\frac{Df}{Dt}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\vec{u}\cdot\nabla f (7.13)

Equation 7.13 annotations: “material deriv of f”; “partial deriv of f”; “velocity”; “f gradient”; “rate of change of f from outward flux of f.”

“Material derivative of a fluid property” is no different from “total derivative of a fluid property with respect to time”. Material derivative, however, is the term typically used in fluid mechanics. The material derivative communicates a kinematic concept. If we simply rearrange Equation (7.13):

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\frac{Df}{Dt}-\vec{u}\cdot\nabla f (7.14)

Equation 7.14 annotations: “Eulerian derivative”; “Lagrangian derivative”; “net convective outflux.”

We see that this relation prescribes how a change of fluid property in an Eulerian reference frame is given by the Lagrangian derivative minus a correction factor that corrects for the flux of that property that leaves or enters the Eulerian control volume. It prescribes how we move back and forth between asking “how does a fluid element’s property \(f\) change with time as it moves through a flowfield?” (Answer: \(Df/Dt\)) and “how the the property \(f\) of a fluid at a specific point in space change as time elapses?” (Answer: \(\partial f/\partial t\)). The material derivative is essentially a frame-of-reference transform between a Lagrangian frame of reference (a specific mass element, moving with the flow) and an Eulerian frame of reference (a specific control volume, whose shape and location and velocity are not tied to any mass element). The material derivative is the differential equivalent of the Reynolds transport theorem.


PDF page 261 — verified

\frac{dm}{dt}=0 (7.15)

Equation 7.15 label: “total derivative of mass with respect to time”; conservation of mass for a system.

Here we use the total derivative. Central to this chapter is the difference between total and partial derivatives, which is also discussed in Sidebar 7.1, p. 249. We can restate the mass of a system contained within a control volume \(\mathcal{V}\) as the integral of its density:

\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathcal{V}}\rho\,dV=0 (7.16)

Equation 7.16 label: “integrated mass in control volume”; conservation of mass for a system in terms of density.

For a system, as the fluid moves about, the volume \(\mathcal{V}\) that encapsulates the fluid changes with time.

The total derivative is the time derivative of a system, and is sufficient if we are following a defined chunk of fluid as it moves about. However, as engineers, we are much more likely to monitor a specific volume in space, i.e., a control volume. This control volume may be fixed at a specific location, or moving on an arbitrary path that is not identical to the motion of the fluid. Because of this, we need a way to recast conservation of mass in terms of the control volume. To do this, we use the Reynolds transport theorem (see Sidebar 7.3, p. 251), which relates the total derivative of the system to the partial derivative of the control volume:

\frac{Dm}{Dt}=\frac{dm}{dt}=\frac{\partial m}{\partial t}+\int_S\rho\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA (7.22)

Equation 7.22 annotations: “partial deriv of mass”; “total deriv of mass”; “net outflux of mass.” Caption: Reynolds transport theorem for transport of mass.

Substituting, this leads to

\frac{\partial m}{\partial t}+\int_S\rho\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA=0 (7.23)

Equation 7.23 annotations: “partial deriv of mass”; “net outflux of mass.” Caption: integral conservation of mass equation.

which is the integral control volume form of conservation of mass. The density \(\rho\) is often assumed uniform and constant for flows of single fluids as long as the pressure variations are not large enough to compress the fluid, i.e., for incompressible flow (see Sidebar 7.3, p. 252). If \(\rho\) is fixed, and the control volume is fixed, \(\frac{\partial m}{\partial t}=0\). The conservation of mass relation for fixed \(\rho\) and a fixed control volume thus simplifies to

\int_S\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA=0 (7.24)

Equation 7.24 annotation: “net outflux of mass.” Caption: integral conservation of mass equation, fixed density, fixed control volume.

For fixed density and a fixed control volume, conservation of mass is satisfied if the net volume outflow of fluid over the surface of the control volume is zero.

system: an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass. Compare to control volume, which is a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass.

SIDEBAR 7.2: FUNDAMENTALS

Reynolds Transport Theorem

The Reynolds Transport Theorem is an integral relation that relates the total derivative of an extensive property of a control volume to its partial derivative

The Reynolds transport theorem is the integral analog of the material derivative. It relates the total and partial derivatives of an extensive property of a control volume by accounting for transport of the property across the control surface. It is a vector accounting concept; essentially it says that, in a finite control volume, the total derivative of a quantity is given by the sum of its partial derivative plus the net outward flux of the quantity through the control surface. The total derivative tells us how the affected mass would experience changes in property \(Q\) if we followed it around; the partial derivative tells us how the fixed control volume experiences changes in extensive property \(Q\) if we remain fixed on the control volume, and the flux through the control surface is the difference between these two. The Reynolds transport theorem expressed for an extensive property \(Q\) (and intensive, i.e., per-unit-volume property \(q\)) in a control volume denoted by \(\mathcal{V}\) and bounded by a control surface \(S\) is

\frac{dQ}{dt}\equiv\frac{DQ}{Dt}=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{\mathcal{V}}q\,dV+\int_S q\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA (7.17)

Equation 7.17 annotations: “material deriv of Q”; “total deriv of Q”; “summed temporal changes in q happening inside the CV”; “summed rate at which q is leaving the CV.”

or, because \(Q=\int_{\mathcal{V}}q\,dV\),

\frac{dQ}{dt}\equiv\frac{DQ}{Dt}=\frac{\partial Q}{\partial t}+\int_S q\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA (7.18)

Equation 7.18 annotations: “material deriv of Q”; “Lagrangian deriv of Q”; “Eulerian deriv of Q”; “summed rate at which q is leaving the CV.”

This relation says that the total derivative of an extensive property \(Q\) can be found by evaluating the partial derivative of \(Q\) and adding the net outward flux of \(q\) through the control surface. \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\) is the component of the fluid velocity moving outward through the control surface, \(q\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\) is the flux of \(q\) moving outward through the control surface, and \(\int_S q\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA\) is the total of this flux integrated over the control surface \(S\).

We can obtain the material derivative from the Reynolds transport theorem by shrinking the control volume to be infinitesimally small. This process is most convenient if the infinitesimally small control volume is aligned with a coordinate system, e.g., a Cartesian coordinate system, making the \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\) terms easy to determine. This illustrates that the vector operator \(\vec{u}\cdot\nabla\) operating on an intensive quantity \(q\) gives \(\vec{u}\cdot\nabla q\), the net outward flux of \(q\).

We need the Reynolds transport theorem because the basic principles of conservation of mass and conservation of momentum are stated in a Lagrangian reference frame—the Lagrangian form is the one that most closely relates to relations from ENGRD2020 and ENGRD2030. For example, in ENGRD2030 we might say that

[First example formula is unreadable in the source] or [second example formula is unreadable in the source].

However, we usually study fluid mechanics in an Eulerian reference frame, and the Reynolds transport theorem helps us make the transition.

SIDEBAR 7.3: ENGINEERING MODELS

Incompressible Flow

Premise: At low \(M\), treating \(\rho\) as unaffected by pressure or velocity greatly simplifies the math and leads to only very small errors

All of the conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy involve the fluid density, and this density is routinely found inside temporal and spatial derivatives. If we could just assume that \(\rho\) were a constant, it would greatly simplify the math. This approximation is surprisingly useful, even for fluids like air, for which the fluid itself is definitely compressible according to the ideal-gas law. We find that, even for a fluid like air which we know can be compressed, the flow of this fluid often does not lead to large density changes, and if we ignore the small density changes, our calculations of the velocity and pressure fields and resulting outputs like forces have only small errors. Importantly, the incompressible flow approximation involves approximating \(\rho\) as a constant for the purposes of the conservation equations. It does not involve claims that the fluid cannot be compressed. Just that the amount it is compressed by flow can be ignored without messing up the calculations engineers care about.

Mathematical form: for incompressible flow \(\rho\) = a constant

Incompressible flow simplifies the conservation equations by taking \(\rho\) to be a constant, and is valid when \(M\) is small:

\rho=\text{a constant}\qquad\text{when }M<0.3 (7.19)

Utility: the incompressible flow approximation turns the conservation of mass equation into a kinematic relation and greatly simplifies the conservation of momentum equations

The conservation of mass equation is greatly simplified if we assume that \(\rho\) is a constant:

\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\rho\vec{u}=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0 (7.20)

In the incompressible flow model, we never actually solve the conservation of mass equation so much as we use what we know about conservation of mass to simplify the conservation of momentum equations. There are many terms in the conservation of momentum equations that are proportional to \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}\), and these all cancel out. That and taking \(\rho\) outside the derivatives greatly simplifies the equations:

\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\rho\vec{u})+\nabla\cdot(\rho\vec{u}\vec{u})=-\nabla p+\nabla\cdot 2\mu\dot{\epsilon}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\rho\frac{\partial\vec{u}}{\partial t}+\rho\vec{u}\cdot\nabla\vec{u}=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec{u} (7.21)

Limitations: The incompressible flow model fails when \(M\) is high

The Mach number \(M=U/a\) is the governing parameter that tells us how good the incompressible flow approximation is. The errors associated with the incompressible flow approximation end up being roughly proportional to \(M^2\), and so a rule of thumb is that if \(M<0.3\) then the errors associated with the incompressible flow approximation are below 10% and aren’t that big of a deal. The incompressible flow model is very useful, but requires that \(M\) be low. As soon as \(M\) gets high, it fails.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 7.1

Consider a control volume defined by the contents of a water glass. Water flows in a stream from a faucet; when the water crosses the boundary at the top of the glass, its velocity is uniformly \(-15\hat{z}\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and the cross-sectional area of the stream is \(1\,\mathrm{cm}^2\). What is \(\frac{\partial m}{\partial t}\) for the control volume? Now imagine a fluid element in the water stream. What is \(\frac{dm}{dt}\) for the fluid element? Solution: conservation of mass says that \(\frac{dm}{dt}\) for any mass is zero, so \(\frac{dm}{dt}=0\) for the fluid element. The control volume formulation of conservation of mass is

\frac{\partial m}{\partial t}=-\int_S\rho\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA (7.25)

At the top of the glass, \(\hat{n}=\hat{z}\). Within the stream, \(\vec{u}=-15\hat{z}\,\mathrm{m/s}\). The integral becomes

\frac{\partial m}{\partial t}=\rho U A=(1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3})(15\,\mathrm{m/s})(1\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2})=1.5\,\mathrm{kg/s} (7.26)

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 7.2

The pipe network shown in Figure 7.12, p. 253 has several known volumetric flow rates of a fixed-density fluid. If \(Q_1=3\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3/s}\) and \(Q_2=1\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3/s}\), what are the rest of the flow rates?



Figure 7.12: A simple pipe network.

Solution: If density is fixed, conservation of mass is equivalent to conservation of volume. Drawing a control volume around the node at left gives \(Q_1=Q_2+Q_5\). For the node at right \(Q_4+Q_7=Q_8\). Along the top branch \(Q_2=Q_3=Q_4\). Along the bottom branch \(Q_5=Q_6=Q_7\). From these relations,

Q_1=Q_8=3\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3/s} (7.27)

Q_5=Q_6=Q_7=2\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3/s} (7.28)

Q_2=Q_3=Q_4=1\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3/s} (7.29)

Example Problem 7.1 (p. 252) draws a contrast between conservation of mass for a moving fluid element vs conservation of mass for a control volume, and shows a straightforward mass flux calculation. Example Problem 7.2 (p. 253) highlights how conservation of mass plays out in terms of discrete flow elements, e.g., pipe networks.

Revisiting the Venturi, we see that we used conservation of mass to determine that fluid accelerates in the throat

In describing a Venturi in Section 5.7, we said: For mass to be conserved, the mass flow rate through the wide regions of the tube (\(\rho U_1 A_1\)) must be equal to the mass flow rate through the throat (\(\rho U_2 A_2\)):

\rho U_1 A_1=\rho U_2 A_2 (7.30)

which means

U_2=U_1\frac{A_1}{A_2} (7.31)

So the velocity in the throat has increased (relative to the wider section) by the ratio of areas. This is why the water comes out faster when you put your thumb on the end of a garden hose.

Although we didn’t say so at the time, this was an integral conservation of mass analysis. It was straightforward because we implicitly drew a control volume with edges normal to the flow, so for flow out of the control volume \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}=U\) and for flow into the control volume \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}=-U\). The velocity was assumed uniform at the inlet and uniform at the outlet, so the integral of \(U\) over each surface was simply \(UA\). This analysis was easy because we chose the control volume judiciously and the flow and geometry are simple.

If the control volume moves and/or deforms, we must be careful to evaluate surface fluxes and volume integrals correctly

The terms for flux across a surface (e.g., \(\rho\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\)) require that the velocity \(\vec{u}\) be evaluated relative to the control surface. If the control surface is not moving, \(\vec{u}\) can simply be measured with respect to a motionless laboratory frame of reference. But if the control surface is moving, \(\vec{u}\) must be measured relative to the control surface.

Similarly, the volume integral of a property is often more complicated to evaluate when the control volume changes with time. Something like mass, which is unchanging for a flow of uniform density in a fixed, unchanging control volume, will of course change if the control volume expands and contracts.

The integral conservation of momentum equation comes from the Reynolds transport theorem combined with Newton’s second law

The fundamental statement of conservation of momentum is that the time rate of change of momentum in a system is specified by the external forces applied to it. This is Newton’s second law, often written for discrete objects as \(F=ma\) or \(\vec{F}=m\vec{a}\) or \(\vec{F}=\frac{d(m\vec{u})}{dt}\). The form that relates best to fluid mechanics is

\vec{F}=\frac{d}{dt}(m\vec{u}) (7.32)

Equation 7.32 annotation: “fluid momentum.” Caption: Newton’s second law written as a time derivative of momentum.

which just says that force equals the time derivative of momentum. Although physics classes use the symbol \(p\) for momentum, in fluid mechanics we use \(p\) for pressure. In fact, in fluid mechanics we talk about momentum all the time but never use a symbol for it. We write the total momentum of a system as \(\int_{\mathcal{V}}\rho\vec{u}\,dV\) and the momentum per unit volume at any point is \(\rho\vec{u}\). Writing the conservation of momentum equation in terms of a total derivative of momentum, we get:

control surface: the surface that encloses a control volume.

control volume: a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

system: an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass. Compare to control volume, which is a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass.

total derivative: a derivative that indicates how a function changes as an argument changes, including indirect contributions from changes in other arguments.

¹ Momentum is easy to define in any coordinate frame of reference that is not accelerating, which is how we will implement it. If the frame of reference is accelerating, then we either need to adjust Newton’s second law, or we have to redefine what we mean by momentum.


PDF page 266 — verified

\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathcal{V}}\rho\vec{u}\,dV=\sum\vec{F} (7.33)

Equation 7.33 annotations: “derivative of total system momentum”; “total forces applied to system.” Newton’s 2nd law written as conservation of momentum for a system.

This is a vector equation, and is equivalent to three separate scalar equations for three components of the momentum. The three most common forces applied to a fluid element are gravity, pressure, and viscosity. Gravity applies a downward force to a fluid system, pressure pushes on any surface we define in any fluid, and, when parts of a fluid deform, there is usually a viscous stress transmitted between the components of the fluid.

For a system, the volume \(\mathcal{V}\) that encapsulates the fluid changes with time as the fluid moves about. We usually find it easier to focus on a static control volume. To recast conservation of momentum in terms of a control volume of our choosing, we again use the Reynolds transport theorem (see Sidebar 7.3), which for momentum is:

\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathcal{V}}\rho\vec{u}\,dV=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{\mathcal{V}}\rho\vec{u}\,dV+\int_S(\rho\vec{u})(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA (7.34)

Equation 7.34 annotations: “partial deriv of momentum”; “total deriv of momentum”; “net outflux of momentum.” Caption: Reynolds transport theorem for momentum.

which tells us that the time rate of change of momentum of a system is equal to the time rate of change of momentum of the control volume plus the net flow rate of momentum out of the control volume through the control surface. Using Equation (7.34), we can write Newton’s second law for a control volume as

\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{\mathcal{V}}\rho\vec{u}\,dV+\int_S(\rho\vec{u})(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA=\sum\vec{F} (7.35)

Equation 7.35 annotations: “partial deriv of momentum in CV”; “net flux of momentum out of CV”; “summed force applied to CV.” Caption: Newton’s 2nd law written as conservation of momentum for a control volume.

This tells us that the force applied to a control volume either leads to a temporal change in the momentum inside the control volume, or a net outflow of momentum. Or, equivalently, we could state the the momentum inside the control volume changes based on the difference of momentum added by forcing and momentum lost by convective flux.

viscous stress: in general, the force per unit area that a fluid applies at a point that is not explained by the thermodynamic pressure. For Newtonian incompressible fluids, this is synonymous with shear stress and is given by the viscosity multiplied by the strain rate...

The three most common forces applied to a fluid control volume are pressure, gravity, and viscosity

Three forces are ubiquitous in fluid flows: pressure, gravity, and viscosity. As a rough first estimate, pressure is always important in fluid flows. Gravity is important except when the fluid has very low density (air) or the system is very small. Viscosity is important except when the fluid’s speed is high and the system is very big. We will prescribe (later in the term) rigorous mathematical definitions of when different forces must be included and when they can be ignored.

The force that pressure applies to a control volume is given by the surface integral of \(-p\) times the unit outward normal:

\vec{F}_p=\int_S -p\hat{n}\,dA (7.36)

Equation 7.36 annotation: “vector pressure force per unit area exerted on CV.” Caption: net pressure force on a control volume.

The force that gravity applies to a control volume is given by the volume integral of \(\rho\) times \(-g\hat{z}\):

\vec{F}_g=\int_{\mathcal{V}}-\rho g\hat{z}\,dV (7.37)

Equation 7.37 annotation: “volumetric gravitational body force exerted on CV.” Caption: net gravity force on a control volume.

Viscous forces we will leave until later because (a) they require a bunch of multivariable calculus we have to discuss over some time and (b) many mechanical engineering flows can be described without it, so we have plenty to do in the meantime.

Combining these forces with Equation (7.35) indicates that, for inviscid flows, conservation of momentum can be written for a control volume as:

\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{\mathcal{V}}\rho\vec{u}\,dV+\int_S(\rho\vec{u})(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA=\int_S-p\hat{n}\,dA+\int_{\mathcal{V}}-\rho g\hat{z}\,dV (7.42)

Equation 7.42 annotations: “time deriv of momentum”; “convective outflux of momentum”; “net pressure surface force”; “net gravitational body force.” Caption: conservation of momentum for a control volume, inviscid.

As we have already mentioned, we can add viscous forces to the right-hand side of this equation as well, and we will do this in Appendix F.

Successful implementation of control volume analysis is strongly dependent on judicious choice of control volume

unit outward normal: a vector of length one that points normal to a control surface, and points outward, away from the control volume.

inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don’t significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid that has \(\mu=0\); in practice there is no such thing.


PDF page 268 — verified

how the control volume is chosen. Picking the control volume strategically can make impossible analysis possible, and difficult analysis simple. Poor control volume choices can make analysis difficult or impossible. Some rules of thumb follow which can guide you in choosing control surfaces for your control volume. None of these can be used in all cases, and often one can follow some of but not all of these guidelines. However, using these rules of thumb will often make your control volume analysis easier.

Choose control surfaces at locations at which you know or can parameterize velocity information

The integral conservation equations relate values at the control surface. Because of this, your control surface must be drawn in a location where either you know the key parameters, or you are solving for the key parameter. Otherwise, the control surface is useless and poorly chosen. Note in Example Problem 7.3, p. 268 how we used control surfaces at left and right where the speed was known.

Choose control surfaces normal to or parallel to streamlines

Control surfaces drawn along streamlines simplify mass flux calculations because there is no mass flux across a streamline. Control surfaces drawn along a streamline simplify momentum flux calculations because there is no convective flux of momentum across a streamline (although there can be viscous flux and pressure forces). Control surfaces drawn normal to streamlines simplify flux calculations because the velocity vector is normal to the surface, making the dot product simple, and \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\) is either \(U\) or \(-U\). Note in Example Problem 7.3 how the use of the streamlines at top and bottom to bound the control volume made analysis of top and bottom simple, and surfaces normal to streamlines at left and right made analysis of left and right straightforward.

Choose control surfaces aligned with coordinate systems

If one must integrate surface fluxes, choosing control surfaces aligned with coordinate systems makes the math easier. Recall when we derived the hydrostatic equation, in Figure 3.9, p. 84 we drew a control volume with two surfaces normal to \(\hat{z}\) (which we used to isolate the pressure forces in the \(z\) direction) and one surface tangent to \(\hat{z}\) (so that we could ignore it for the purposes of \(z\) equilibrium).

control volume: a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

control surface: the surface that encloses a control volume.

What is a TikTok Haiku: I just don’t get it / just how is it different / from making a vine.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

flux: in fluid mechanics, flux is defined as rate of flow of a property per unit area across a surface. Flux is defined differently in other physical fields and in mathematics.

convective: in fluid mechanics, relating to transport caused by bulk fluid motion. In heat and mass transfer, relating to total transport in the presence of fluid motion, i.e., both convection and diffusion.

What I Just Said Haiku: for surface fluxes / align surface with axes / makes math easier.


PDF page 269 — verified

Choose control surfaces along which field variables are uniform

If one must integrate surface fluxes, choosing control surfaces along which a variable is uniform makes the math easier as well. Note how Example Problem 7.3 was made quite simple by the fact that the velocities were uniform at inlet and outlet.

Try to replace vector surface integrals with simple algebraic relations

When flows and geometries are simple, we often can write algebraic relations for mass and volume flux and we needn’t perform vector surface integrals. For uniform flow across a surface aligned normal to the flow, we routinely describe a volume flow rate \(Q\) by

Q=UA (7.45)

Equation 7.45 caption: volume flow rate, uniform flow at velocity U moving normally to surface of area A.

and, if density is uniform, we can similarly define a mass flow rate \(\dot{m}\) by

\dot{m}=\rho U A (7.46)

Equation 7.46 caption: volume flow rate, uniform density, uniform flow at velocity U moving normally to surface of area A.

If we study a problem in which fluid moves into and out of the control volume only through discrete surfaces for which \(\dot{m}=\rho U A\) is correct, then we can treat conservation of mass for the system by saying that the total mass flowing into the control volume must equal the total mass flowing out:

\sum_{\mathrm{inlet}}\dot{m}=\sum_{\mathrm{outlet}}\dot{m} (7.47)

Equation 7.47 annotation: “the conservation of mass relation.” This relation is essentially identical to Kirchhoff’s first law for current at a node of an electrical circuit: \(\sum_{\mathrm{in}} I=\sum_{\mathrm{out}} I\), which you study in MAE3780.

Equation (7.47) is useful for systems with discrete flows, for example networks of jets or pipes.

When flows and geometries are simple, we often can write algebraic relations for momentum flux and pressure force as well. For uniform pressure, the force on a surface of area \(A\) has magnitude \(pA\) and the force points into the control volume. For flow normal to a control surface, the magnitude of momentum flux is given by \(\rho U^2 A\). Relative to conservation of mass, conservation of momentum leads to more bookkeeping challenges because it is a vector equation, so (a) it has multiple coordinate components and (b) we must keep track of the signs of the components correctly.

uniform: unchanging in space. Compare to the adjective constant, which means unchanging with time.

We use integral conservation equations when we know (or can parameterize) fluid information at the boundaries

The concepts behind integral conservation equations are not particularly complicated—just that if we want to keep track of how a control volume is changing, we must keep track not only of changes to systems (e.g., applied forces) but also the net flux into and out of the control volume. So integral control volume analysis problems in essence require us to set up the accounting to keep track of inflows and outflows at boundaries. Integral control volume analysis is powerful when we want to relate holistic effects (e.g., the force on a body caused by fluid flow) to surface fluxes (e.g., inflows and outflows). Integral control volume analysis is completely powerless when we need to determine details about what is going on inside the control volume (e.g., the shear stress at the centerline of a pipe).

The challenge of integral conservation comes from two aspects of the analysis. First, the vector calculus behind net outflux (although technically covered in MATH 1920/2930) benefits from practice, and most MAE3230 students need more practice at this. Second, the process of setting up the control volume analysis to get the answers you need has its own rules of thumb (see previous section); students benefit from practice in this regard as well.

When we know fluid flow into and out of a control volume, we can determine the force the fluid made on its boundaries

We often use integral conservation of momentum when we know the fluid’s properties as it is flowing into and out of a control volume. This is simplest when the control volume is used to surround flow moving through pipes or other geometries where inflows and outflows are well defined. This is also straightforward when we are studying isolated jets, for example jets of water moving in air. When information at the boundary is known, determining the force that the fluid applies to the boundary is simply a matter of integrating the surface fluxes. An example of this would be using conservation of momentum to calculate the force on a bend in a pipe. We use integral conservation of momentum to show that if pressure is uniform, the net force from the pressure on an enclosed volume of any shape is zero (see Sidebar 7.4, p. 267).

Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

system: an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass. Compare to control volume, which is a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass.

flux: in fluid mechanics, flux is defined as rate of flow of a property per unit area across a surface. Flux is defined differently in other physical fields and in mathematics.


PDF page 271 — verified

Because mass is conserved, we can often determine velocity–area relations straightforwardly

As long as we are considering incompressible flow of single-fluid systems (just air, or just water, but not combinations of the two), then a control volume’s mass will not change with time. This prescribes that the net mass flux out of a control volume is always zero, and that the volumetric flux out of the control volume is also zero. This gives us straightforward relations, e.g., that the volumetric flow rate \(Q\) is uniform along a pipe. Even for compressible flow, if the flow is steady, we can derive relatively simple relations for conservation of mass for flow in a nozzle.

Conservation of mass and momentum can tell us which state transitions are possible

Often, fluid flows transition between states (flow speeds up, turns a corner, transitions to turbulent flow, etc.). Although the physics of how these transitions is often beyond the analytical techniques in an introductory fluid mechanics class, conservation of mass and momentum in a control volume often can tell us which inlet/outlet states are possible. Integral conservation analysis tells us, for example, what the relations can be between velocities before and after a shock wave, or before and after an ocean wave crashes on a beach.

incompressible flow: implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Incompressible flow implies that the motion of the fluid does not cause density to change, in comparison to compressible flow in which fluid moves so quickly and the pressure changes so much that the density is perturbed enough to affect convective fluxes. Incompressible flows may still have nonuniform density, for example if the fluid’s temperature varies; this can affect the conservation of momentum equations. An incompressible flow does not imply that the fluid is mathematically incompressible, only that pressure-induced compression can be ignored. Cf. compressible flow.

compressible flow: implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to change significantly in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Cf. incompressible flow.

turbulent flow: a fluid flow characterized by local instability and chaos, which exhibits unsteadiness even if the flow is stationary.

shock wave: a discontinuous transition in which a supersonic flow slows down, with an attendant increase in pressure and density.

Practice Problems

Problems

1. (OBJECTIVE: integral conservation analysis with mass and momentum) Consider a rectangular channel of width \(w\) in the \(y\) direction, which contains a flow of fluid with depth \(h_1\) in the \(z\) direction (gravity points in the downward \(z\) direction); this fluid is moving in the \(x\) direction with a uniform speed \(U_1\). Ignore viscous and surface tension effects. At a downstream point, consider the possibility that the fluid might have a different depth \(h_2\). Use conservation of mass and momentum on a judiciously selected control volume to establish whether this is possible. Solve for \(h_2\) and \(U_2\) as a function of \(h_1\) and \(U_1\). Identify all possible solutions—according to this analysis, can \(h_2\) be the same as \(h_1\)? Larger than \(h_1\)? Smaller than \(h_1\)? How do these solutions depend on the upstream Froude number \(Fr = \frac{U_1}{\sqrt{g h_1}}\)?

2. (OBJECTIVE: Apply conservation of momentum and mass to a hydraulic jump system where only heights are known) If you knew a riverbreak well, a single photo of the break would tell you both the height difference \(h_2-h_1\) (from the height of the waves) and the height \(h_1\) (from where the water intersected the bank). A 1-s-long video would tell you how fast the upstream water was moving. Assume you know both \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) and find an expression for the Froude Number in terms of the ratio \(h_2/h_1\) alone. How deep is the upstream water if \(h_2/h_1=6\) and the water is moving at \(10\,\mathrm{m/s}\)? Would you feel safe surfing on the wave in these conditions?

3. (OBJECTIVE: Calculating fluid velocity through pipes) Professor Kirby is what the internet calls a “slow shaver”, taking pretty much forever to complete the task. While he does so, water flows into the sink with the drain plugged as shown in Fig. 7.14 below. The water flows into the sink at a constant rate of \(Q=2\) gallon/min. Fortunately, after the sink fills up, the system doesn’t overflow into the bathroom; instead it comes to steady state because the sink has \(n=3\), \(d=0.4\)-in.-diameter overflow holes. Determine the area-averaged velocity of the fluid passing through the overflow holes when the system is at steady state.

4. (OBJECTIVE: Evaluate reaction forces associated with fluid momentum steering through control volumes) Professor Bouklas likes to build small objects that vibrate when air passes across them (e.g., reed instruments like saxophones) as well as air-driven vehicles (e.g., the four in Figure 7.15, p. 269). Each starts from rest, has frictionless wheels, and moves along only the \(x\) axis. Model flow through each device as incompressible and inviscid, and model inlets and outlets as having pressure \(p=0\). Will any of these vehicles move? If so, in what direction?

5. (OBJECTIVE: control volume analysis of momentum conservation) Professor Kirby just purchased a super soaker for a MAE 3230 demonstration in which he knocks over stuff. He practices by shooting the super soaker normal to a fixed metal plate, creating a jet with uniform speed \(U=8\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and diameter \(d=10\,\mathrm{cm}\) as shown in Figure 7.16. If we neglect gravity and friction, what is the force \(F\) felt by the plate when the super soaker is shooting? By the way, the super soaker in this problem is bigger and more powerful than a toy super soaker.

Problems with Answers


PDF page 273 — source_issue

1. (OBJECTIVE: integral conservation analysis with mass and momentum) Consider a rectangular channel of width \(w\) in the \(y\) direction, which contains a flow of fluid with depth \(h_1\) in the \(z\) direction (gravity points in the downward \(z\) direction); this fluid is moving in the \(x\) direction with a uniform speed \(U_1\). Ignore viscous and surface tension effects. At a downstream point, consider the possibility that the fluid might have a different depth \(h_2\). Use conservation of mass and momentum on a judiciously selected control volume to establish whether this is possible. Solve for \(h_2\) and \(U_2\) as a function of \(h_1\) and \(U_1\). Identify all possible solutions—according to this analysis, can \(h_2\) be the same as \(h_1\)? Larger than \(h_1\)? Smaller than \(h_1\)? How do these solutions depend on the upstream Froude number \(Fr=\frac{U_1}{\sqrt{g h_1}}\)? Solution: We know that the fluid is entering the rectangular channel with uniform speed \(U_1\) and we ignore viscous effects. We also assume that the fluid exits with a uniform speed. Using the following control volume we can use conservation of mass to solve for \(h_2\) and \(U_2\) as a function of \(h_1\) and \(U_1\). Note that \(h_2\) is not necessarily greater than \(h_1\). From conservation of mass, we arrive at the following

\rho U_1 h_1 w = \rho U_2 h_2 w (7.48)

There is no mass transfer from top and bottom, because mass does not cross streamlines. Simplifying, we arrive at the following relationship

U_1 h_1 = U_2 h_2 (7.49)

From conservation of momentum in the \(x\)-direction, we end up with the following with the left hand side containing the momentum terms and the right hand side containing the force from the pressures

\rho U_1^2 h_1 w - \rho U_2^2 h_2 w = \left(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac{1}{2}g h_2\right)w h_2 - \left(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac{1}{2}g h_1\right)w h_1 - p_{\mathrm{atm}}w(h_2-h_1) (7.50)

Note that the RHS needs the third term as top of our control volume still experiences a pressure force in the \(x\)-direction. As a result, \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\) drops out from our momentum balance. Dividing the equation through by density, width \(w\), and gravitational acceleration we arrive with the following

\frac{U_1^2 h_1}{g} - \frac{U_2^2 h_2}{g} = \frac{1}{2}h_2^2 - \frac{1}{2}h_1^2 (7.51)

Applying the conservation of mass and a lot of algebra we can simplify the relationship using \(Fr=\frac{U_1}{\sqrt{g h_1}}\) as shown

\frac{U_1^2 h_1}{g} - \frac{U_2^2 h_2}{g} = \frac{1}{2}h_2^2 - \frac{1}{2}h_1^2 (7.52)

\frac{2U_1^2}{g h_1} - \frac{2U_2^2 h_2}{g h_1^2} = \frac{h_2^2}{h_1^2} - 1 (7.53)

2Fr^2 - \frac{2(U_2 h_2)^2}{g h_1^2 h_2} = \frac{h_2^2}{h_1^2} - 1 (7.54)

Here we use conservation of mass to eliminate \(U_2\):

2Fr^2 - \frac{2(U_1 h_1)^2}{g h_1^2 h_2} = \frac{h_2^2}{h_1^2} - 1 (7.55)

\left(2Fr^2 - \frac{2U_1^2 h_1}{g h_1 h_2} = \frac{h_2^2}{h_1^2} - 1\right)\frac{h_2}{h_1} (7.56)

Editorial note: Equation (7.50) prints \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac12gh_i\) in each pressure term. These sums are dimensionally inconsistent; hydrostatic pressure requires \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac12\rho gh_i\). With that correction, division by \(\rho wg\) produces (7.51). Equations (7.51) and (7.52) are identical in the source. In (7.56), the denominator really is \(gh_1h_2\), and the outside \(h_2/h_1\) means to multiply both sides by that ratio. This yields \(2Fr^2(h_2/h_1)-2Fr^2=(h_2/h_1)^3-h_2/h_1\). No control-volume drawing is present on this source page despite the wording “the following control volume.”


PDF page 274 — verified

2Fr^2\left(\frac{h_2}{h_1}-1\right)=\frac{h_2}{h_1}\left(\frac{h_2}{h_1}+1\right)\left(\frac{h_2}{h_1}-1\right) (7.57)

We can divide out \(h_2/h_1-1\), noting that one possible solution is \(h_2=h_1\), in which case there is no jump and the fluid just flows from inlet to outlet with no change.

2Fr^2=\frac{h_2^2}{h_1^2}+\frac{h_2}{h_1} (7.58)

Using the quadratic equation with respect to \(h_2/h_1\) we arrive at the following by rejecting the negative answer (we can’t have a negative ratio of heights)

\frac{h_2}{h_1}=\frac{-1+\sqrt{1+8Fr^2}}{2} (7.59)

If the Froude number is greater than one, a hydraulic jump with \(h_2/h_1>1\) is possible. It is never guaranteed, because \(h_2=h_1\) is always possible (remember that we divided out \(h_2/h_1-1\)).

If the Froude number is equal to one, all solutions point to \(h_1=h_2\).

If the Froude number is below one, the math says that \(h_1>h_2\) is possible, a “hydraulic jump” in which the fluid speeds up and the height goes down. The analysis we just did does not tell us there is anything wrong with this solution. A separate analysis, though, would show that this solution violates the 2nd law of thermo. You can have a hydraulic jump in which fluid slows and height increases. You cannot have one in which fluid accelerates and height decreases. Again, mass and momentum alone do not tell us this, only an entropy analysis would (i.e., there wasn’t a way for you to know this given the analysis the problem asked you to perform). When the Froude number is below 1, we actually find that \(h_2=h_1\) from the term we divided out.

As you can see, by calculating the Froude number, we are able to determine whether a hydraulic jump is possible or not (possible only if Froude>1). The Froude number is just one of many nondimensional-terms-named-after-some-person-you-don’t-know that we will be using in this class to describe flows.

2. (OBJECTIVE: Apply conservation of momentum and mass to a hydraulic jump system where only heights are known) If you knew a riverbreak well, a single photo of the break would tell you both the height difference \(h_2-h_1\) (from the height of the waves) and the height \(h_1\) (from where the water intersected the bank). A 1-s-long video would tell you how fast the upstream water was moving. Assume you know both \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) and find an expression for the Froude Number in terms of the ratio \(h_2/h_1\) alone. How deep is the upstream water if \(h_2/h_1=6\) and the water is moving at \(10\,\mathrm{m/s}\)? Would you feel safe surfing on the wave in these conditions? Solution: In a hydraulic jump, mass is conserved, so we can write:

Q_1=Q_2 (7.60)

U_1h_1w=U_2h_2w (7.61)

Because the width is assumed to be uniform, this expression becomes:

U_1h_1=U_2h_2 (7.62)

Apply the conservation of momentum equation on a control volume between the inlet and exit:

\rho U_1^2h_1+\frac{1}{2}\rho g h_1^2=\rho U_2^2h_2+\frac{1}{2}\rho g h_2^2 (7.63)

Cancelling and rearranging terms leads to:

U_1^2h_1+\frac{1}{2}g h_1^2=U_2^2h_2+\frac{1}{2}g h_2^2 (7.64)


PDF page 275 — verified

U_1^2h_1-U_2^2h_2=\frac{1}{2}g\left(h_2^2-h_1^2\right) (7.65)

Conservation of mass gave \(U_1h_1=U_2h_2\) so \(U_2^2=U_1^2\frac{h_1^2}{h_2^2}\). Plugging this in leads to:

U_1^2h_1-U_1^2\frac{h_1^2}{h_2^2}h_2=\frac{1}{2}g\left(h_2^2-h_1^2\right) (7.66)

U_1^2\left(h_1-\frac{h_1^2}{h_2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}g\left(h_2^2-h_1^2\right) (7.67)

The Froude number can be defined as \(Fr=\frac{U_1}{\sqrt{g h_1}}\). Plugging this in results in:

\frac{1}{2}\frac{h_2}{h_1}\left(\frac{h_2}{h_1}+1\right)-Fr^2=0 (7.68)

Rearranging gives the solution to the problem:

Fr=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{h_2^2}{h_1^2}+\frac{h_2}{h_1}\right)} (7.69)

3. (OBJECTIVE: Calculating fluid velocity through pipes) Professor Kirby is what the internet calls a “slow shaver”, taking pretty much forever to complete the task. While he does so, water flows into the sink with the drain plugged as shown in Fig. 7.18 below. The water flows into the sink at a constant rate of \(Q=2\) gallon/min. Fortunately, after the sink fills up, the system doesn’t overflow into the bathroom; instead it comes to steady state because the sink has \(n=3\), \(d=0.4\) in diameter overflow holes. Determine the area-averaged velocity of the fluid passing through the overflow holes when the system is at steady state. Solution: Since the sink level remains constant, that means that the flow rate of the water flowing into the sink is equal to the flow rate of water flowing through the overflow holes. This leads to the equation \(Q_1=Q_2\) where \(Q_1=2\) gal/min. Converting from gal/min to ft³/s yields a flow rate of \(Q_1=0.00446\) ft³/s. Now, it is possible to solve for the velocity of the water

Q_2=A_2U=\frac{3}{4}\pi d^2U (7.70)

Solving the expression for \(U\) gives

U=\frac{Q_2}{\frac{3}{4}\pi d^2} (7.71)

Plugging in values and solving gives the answer for the velocity:

U_2=1.70\;\mathrm{ft/s} (7.72)

4. (OBJECTIVE: Evaluate reaction forces associated with fluid momentum steering through control volumes) Professor Bouklas likes to build small objects that vibrate when air passes across them (e.g., reed instruments like saxophones) as well as air-driven vehicles (e.g., the four in Figure 7.19, p. 271). Each starts from rest, has frictionless wheels, and moves along only the \(x\) axis. Model flow through each device as incompressible and inviscid, and model inlets and outlets as having pressure \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\). Will any of these vehicles move? If so, in what direction? Solution: For each case, we can draw a control volume around the device and define an applied force \(F_A\) in the \(x\) direction analyze the momentum balance along the \(x\) axis. (a) The \(x\) momentum balance for this device is:

\rho U_1^2A_1+\rho U_2^2A_2+F_A=0 (7.73)

Thus, \(F_A<0\) meaning that it is acting towards the left. If we then remove \(F_A\) the device will move to the right.






PDF page 276 — source_issue

(b) The \(x\) momentum balance for this device is:

\rho U_1^2A_1-\rho U_2^2A_2+F_A=0 (7.74)

Then, from conservation of mass we find:

\rho U_1A_1=\rho U_2A_2 (7.75)

Plugging (7.75) into (7.74) we find:

\rho U_2^2\frac{A_2^2}{A_1}-\rho U_2^2A_2+F_A=0 (7.76)

\rho U_2^2A_2\left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}-1\right)+F_A=0 (7.77)

Because \(A_2>A_1\), \(\frac{A_2}{A_1}-1>0\) meaning that \(F_A<0\). Because \(F_A\) is acting towards the left, if we remove \(F_A\) the device will move to the right.

(c) The \(x\) momentum balance for this device is:

\rho U_1^2A_1+F_A=0 (7.78)

because \(A_2\) is not normal to the \(x\) axis. Thus, \(F_A<0\) meaning that it is acting towards the left. If we then remove \(F_A\) the device will move to the right.

(d) This case is very similar to 4b. Using \(x\) momentum balance and conservation of momentum we obtain:

\rho U_2^2A_2\left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}-1\right)+F_A=0 (7.79)

However, in this case \(A_2<A_1\), so \(\frac{A_2}{A_1}-1<0\) meaning that \(F_A>0\). Because \(F_A\) is acting towards the right, if we remove \(F_A\) the device will move to the left.

5. (OBJECTIVE: control volume analysis of momentum conservation) Professor Kirby just purchased a super soaker for a MAE 3230 demonstration in which he knocks over stuff. He practices by shooting the super soaker normal to a fixed metal plate, creating a jet with uniform speed \(U=8\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and diameter \(d=10\,\mathrm{cm}\) as shown in Figure 7.20. If we neglect gravity and friction, what is the force \(F\) felt by the plate when the super soaker is shooting? By the way, the super soaker in this problem is bigger and more powerful than a toy super soaker. Solution: Conservation of momentum is Newton’s second law, written for a system enclosed in volume \(V\) as

\vec{F}=\frac{d}{dt}\int_V \rho\vec{u}\,dV (7.80)

If we choose to focus on a fixed control volume rather than a fixed mass, we use the Reynolds transport theorem:

\vec{F}=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V \rho\vec{u}\,dV+\int_S(\rho\vec{u})(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA (7.81)

Here \(\rho\vec{u}\) is the momentum per unit volume and \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\) is the component of velocity in the direction of the outward normal. If we consider only the \(x\) momentum, this becomes

\vec{F}=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V \rho u\,dV+\int_S(\rho u)(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA (7.82)

Note that we are considering \(x\) momentum which is given by \(\rho u\). The \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\) term describes the volume flux across the control surface; this does not change from \(\vec{u}\) to \(u\); \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\) is a scalar whereas \(u\cdot\hat{n}\) is nonsensical. The flow is steady so the partial derivative term is zero:

F_x=\int_S(\rho u)(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA (7.83)



Editorial source correction: (7.82) projects momentum onto the x direction, so its left side should be the scalar \(F_x\), as in (7.83). The printed vector \(\vec F\) is retained above. The right side correctly uses scalar x momentum \(\rho u\) and vector normal velocity \(\vec u\cdot\hat n\).


PDF page 277 — source_issue

Drawing a control volume enclosing the plate and the jet (Figure 7.21, p. 272, we find that the water shooting out at top and at bottom has no \(x\) component, so those terms are zero. The term that is nonzero is the jet entering at right:

F_x=\int_S(\rho u)(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA=(\rho u)(-u)A (7.84)

So the force applied to the control volume by the plate \(F_x\) is \(\rho u^2A\). The force applied to the plate by the control volume is \(-F_x\) or \(\rho u^2A=(1000)(8)^2\pi(0.05)^2=500\,\mathrm{N}\). That is a PRETTY SWEET SUPER SOAKER. That’s over 100 lbs of force.



Editorial note: Figure 7.21 shows the jet entering from the left and travelling right, so “entering at right” is a source wording error. The sign before the prose force expression is washed out in the scan and cannot be read reliably. Equation (7.84) and the handwritten analysis in Figure 7.21 give \(F_x=-\rho u^2A\) for the force on the fluid; the reaction on the plate is \(-F_x=+\rho u^2A\), approximately 500 N. The prose expression above retains the legible part rather than silently supplying a sign.

SIDEBAR 7.4: FUNDAMENTALS

The force caused by the integral of a uniform pressure around a closed surface is zero

The force caused by the integral of a uniform pressure around a closed surface is zero. Because of this, when analyzing control volumes, we often ignore a reference pressure (e.g., \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\)), and only bother integrating deviations from this reference pressure. Many find it intuitively obvious that the integral of a uniform pressure on a control surface is zero. If you would benefit from a derivation, the divergence theorem from MATH1920 is helpful (yay MATH1920!!!). We start with the surface integral of the force:

\vec{F}=\int_S p\hat{n}\,dA (7.38)

Here we benefit from reversing a simplification we normally use. The isotropic time-averaged effect of molecular fluctuations is called pressure \(p\). It is really an isotropic tensor \(p\vec{I}\), but instead of keeping track of \(p\vec{I}\) all the time and evaluating its effect on a plane by taking its dot product with the unit vector \((p\vec{I}\cdot\hat{n})\), we note that \(p\vec{I}\cdot\hat{n}=p\hat{n}\) and we use that expression instead, because it is simpler and many students haven’t yet learned what a dyadic tensor is. But here let’s rewrite the surface integral in terms of the dyadic tensor:

\vec{F}=\int_S p\vec{I}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA (7.39)

In this form, we can immediately use the divergence theorem to show that this integral is zero. Applying the divergence theorem:

\vec{F}=\int_S p\vec{I}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA=\int_V \nabla\cdot p\vec{I}\,dV (7.40)

Because \(\vec{I}\) is a constant and \(p\) was defined as a uniform pressure, the divergence of \(p\vec{I}\) is zero, so the integral of the effect of a uniform pressure around a closed contour is zero:

\vec{F}=\int_S p\hat{n}\,dA=\int_V 0\,dV=0 (7.41)

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 7.3

Consider a control volume (Figure 7.13, p. 268) drawn around the flow generated by a propeller that applies a force \(F\) to the fluid. Assume that the net force caused by pressure around the control volume is negligible. Assume also that the flow entering and exiting the control volume is uniform and only in the \(x\) direction. Ignore viscous effects, and use integral conservation of mass and conservation of momentum to calculate by how much the fluid accelerates, given \(U_1\), \(U_2\), \(A_1\), and \(A_2\).



Figure 7.13: A control volume used to analyze a propeller.

Solution: There is no mass flow through streamlines, nor convective momentum flux. Absent viscosity, there is no momentum transfer across streamlines. The outflow of mass at left is \(-\rho U_1A_1\) and at right is \(\dot{m}=\rho U_2A_2\); these sum to zero. Momentum exits at left at a rate \(-\rho U_1^2A_1\) and at right at a rate \(\rho U_2^2A_2\); these summed must equal \(F\). So

U_1A_1=U_2A_2,\qquad \rho U_2^2A_2-\rho U_1^2A_1=\rho U_1A_1(U_2-U_1)=F (7.43)

U_2-U_1=\frac{F}{\rho U_1A_1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Delta U=\frac{F}{\dot{m}} (7.44)

The velocity change is given by the applied force normalized by the mass flow rate.

Chapter 8

Flow Visualization: Looking at How Fluid Machines Work

Visualizing fluid flow is an immensely powerful way to understand fluid machines

Among the most important tools we use to understand and measure fluid machines and the fluid mechanics associated with them is flow visualization. Visualizing flow is often the fastest way to experimentally observe key flowfield features that affect how a fluid machine (or any other fluid mechanical phenomenon) works. Techniques such as particle-image velocimetry, schlieren imaging, planar laser-induced fluorescence, streakline imaging, and pathline imaging are all critical ways we learn about the fluid flows around us.

An instantaneous image of smoke or dye released from a point visualizes a streakline of a flow

A streakline is the instantaneous location of all of the fluid elements that went through a specific point at any time. This is visualized experimentally by continuously releasing smoke or dye or some other visual element from a point in the flow, then visualizing it with a short-exposure image. Figure 8.1, p. 274 is a very famous visualization of a von Kármán vortex street seen behind a circular cylinder. In this case, dye is released from the surface of the cylinder, and the pattern that the dye forms tells us enormous information about the flow. In this case, the dye rolls up into alternating swirls—these are associated with alternating vortex shedding from this cylinder, as the fluid that passes near the surface is forced to rotate by the viscous forces at the surface. This alternating vortex shedding explains why cables vibrate in the wind, and why Aeolian harps make sounds. Figure 8.2, p. 274 shows flow over an airfoil at a positive angle of attack. In this case, the flow is water and dye is released from several points upstream of the airfoil. On the rear of the top surface, we can see that the flow has separated—rather than the flow following the top surface, the flow at the separation point turns away from the surface, coincident with recirculating flow. This separation is associated with stall and a loss of lift on an airfoil surface. In both of these cases, watching where all of the fluid elements that went through a specific point tells us critical aspects of the flow. In the first case, it highlighted that the fluid passing by the shoulders of the cylinder was made to rotate, and in the second case, it highlighted that the inclined airfoil was likely losing lift.

von Kármán vortex street: the alternating pattern of vortexes seen in the wake of bluff bodies in certain Reynolds number ranges.

vortex shedding: the process by which the vorticity created in a boundary layer of an object leaves the surface, creating a region of rotating fluid in the wake of the object.

angle of attack: the angle that the chord line of an airfoil makes with the oncoming fluid flow.

separate: the process by which a streamline emanates normal to a surface. Most often, separation is used only to describe streamlines resulting from flow that moves upstream.

stall: the aerodynamic phenomenon in which the lifting surfaces (e.g., wings) exceed a critical angle of attack and the lift is drastically reduced. Stall is defined as high angle of attack, but is associated with low aircraft speed because aircraft often use high angle of attack when at low speed.

shoulder: on an object immersed in a fluid flow, the surfaces at the widest point measured normal to the prevailing fluid velocity.


PDF page 285 — verified

Figure 8.1: Flow from left to right over a circular cylinder, \(Re=140\). The resulting von Kármán vortex street highlights the alternating vortex shedding caused by the viscous effects in the boundary layer at the surface. Photo by Sadatoshi Taneda.

Figure 8.2: Laminar flow from left to right over an NACA64A015 airfoil at angle of attack \(\alpha=5^\circ\). Separation is apparent on the rear of the top surface. Photograph by Henri Werlé. Colored dye in water.


PDF page 286 — verified

An long-exposure image of particles visualizes pathlines of a flow

A pathline is the path through time of a specific fluid element that went through a specific point at a specific time. This is visualized by taking a long-exposure image of a visual element in a flow. Figure 8.3, p. 275 is a long-exposure image of small particles in the flow over a circular cylinder. Whereas a short exposure would show a uniform distribution of tiny bright dots, the long exposure turns these dots into curves that show the direction of flow. Here, the flow has a clearly defined, symmetric recirculation region in the wake of the cylinder, in which the fluid spins in a circle.

Figure 8.3: Flow from left to right over a circular cylinder, \(Re=26\). Photo by Sadatoshi Taneda.

Fluid mechanicians often discuss three different lines that can be defined for a fluid flow: streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines. A streamline is a contour that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneously fluid velocity. A pathline is the path through time of a specific fluid element that went through a specific point at a specific time. And a streakline is the instantaneous location of all of the fluid elements that went through a specific point at any time. These three things can be different from each other if the velocity field varies with time. Fortunately for us in MAE3230, we consider almost exclusively steady flows, for which all three of these ideas are the same thing. In a steady flow, we can release dye from a point and see where the dye goes. Or we can take a long-exposure image of some particles that move through that point. Or we can evaluate the trajectory of the vector field. In a steady flow, all of these techniques will produce the same lines.

One thing we can conclude from this is that streamlines are relatively easy to measure, especially in steady flows, and streamlines give quite a bit of information about how a fluid-mechanical system is operating. This chapter thus builds an engineering motivation to calculate, predict, and measure streamlines. The physics that underpins this chapter is conservation of mass. The mathematics of this chapter has two parts: first, we use the divergence theorem to convert the integral conservation of mass equations into the differential conservation of mass equations. Second, that equation ends up being simple enough that it leads immediately to the streamfunction, a way to simplify our analysis of velocity fields that works because any velocity field

pathline: a line that traces the Lagrangian motion of a fluid element as it moves in time. Can be imagined as the line that would be traced out if a small particle were placed into a fluid flow.

Streamline Haiku: “take the streamfunction / then plot its isocontours / what a nice picture”

trajectory: for a vector field, a trajectory is a contour that is everywhere tangent to the vector field.

streamfunction: denoted \(\psi\). Scalar function defined for 2D flows equivalently as (a) \(\psi(A)=\int_{O}^{A}u\,dy-v\,dx\) or (b) \(u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\) and \(v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\), or (c) \(\vec{u}=\nabla\times\psi\hat{z}\). Incompressible 2D flows can be defined by \(\psi(x,y)\) because the existence of \(\psi(x,y)\) is mathematically equivalent to satisfying conservation of mass.


PDF page 287 — verified

That satisfies differential conservation of mass can be represented most easily with this streamfunction.

The differential conservation of mass equation is weird because we don’t solve it—instead, we use it to make solving other equations easier

In previous chapters, we have implemented a dynamic analysis, both for static fluid (\(\sum F=0\); Chapter 3) and for moving fluid (\(\sum F=ma\); Chapter 5). We also used integral analysis of control volumes and control surfaces to evaluate the forces on containers and immersed objects, for static fluids (Chapter 4), and in general, to link the inputs and outputs of a control volume to its temporal derivatives in general (Chapter 7).

In this chapter, we focus on conservation of mass and extend the analysis from integral analysis of a finite control volume to differential analysis of an infinitesimal fluid element. By moving to a differential analysis, we develop a differential equation that can be applied anywhere in the flow field—this differential equation generates a kinematic constraint on the velocity field.

Whereas integral conservation of mass can be used to solve fluids problems directly (e.g., a tube narrows to one-half the cross-sectional area, what happens to the fluid speed? Ans: it doubles), differential conservation of mass rarely gives us an equation we can just solve. Compare to other analysis you are used to:

• MAE2020: solving \(\sum F=0\) to find the force on a hinge

• MAE2030: solving \(\sum F=ma\) to find the acceleration of an object

• ENGRD2210: solving \(PV=RT\) to find the new pressure after a piston compresses an ideal gas

• MAE3230 Chapter 7: solving \(\int_S \vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA=0\) to find the new fluid speed after the cross-sectional area of a tube is decreased.

In each of those cases, we had a key equation, we solved the equation, and got the answer. That is not the way that differential conservation of mass helps us. Instead, differential conservation of mass changes and simplifies the way we prescribe velocity fields and conservation of momentum equations, but we do not obtain \(\vec{u}\) or \(p\) fields directly by solving the conservation of mass equations directly.¹ There are only certain types of velocity fields that satisfy conservation of mass, and we only need to consider those velocity fields when trying to analyze a fluid flow problem. In fact, conservation of mass simplifies things so much that, for 2D flows, we can describe an entire vector velocity field with a single scalar quantity. And for all flows, there are a bunch of terms in the conservation of momentum equations that we can just cross out because the conservation of mass equation tells us that they must sum to zero.

So conservation of mass is largely a tool that makes conservation of momentum analysis easier. In this chapter, we list out the differential conservation

dynamic: involving forces and accelerations.

conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

differential: relating to how properties are changing locally as expressed by derivatives. Compare with integral, meaning related to finite differences evaluated over finite distances.

kinematic: related to the motion of objects without consideration of forces.

Flash Mob Haiku: “I want a fluids flash mob / feels sort of two-thousand nine / but lets bring it back”

conservation of momentum: the notion that changes in momentum are brought about by forces as prescribed by Newton’s second law.

vector: a property with magnitude and direction.

scalar: as a noun: a property with a magnitude only; no direction; as an adjective: having magnitude only but no direction.

conservation of momentum: the notion that changes in momentum are brought about by forces as prescribed by Newton’s second law.

¹There is one key exception. When flow is irrotational, we actually can solve for the velocity field by use of the conservation of mass equation. That is super-awesome but a special case; it is described later in Chapter 9.


PDF page 288 — verified

of mass equation and show how it makes it easier to prescribe velocity fields and visualize fluid streamlines by use of the streamfunction, then we go back and show the derivation that underpins the differential conservation of mass equation.

For an incompressible flow, conservation of mass requires that there is no net outflow from a control volume

The integral conservation of mass relation for a control volume \(\mathcal{V}\) bounded by a control surface \(S\) in an incompressible flow is given by

\int_S \underbrace{\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}}_{\text{rate at which volume is crossing }S}\,dA=0 (8.1)

The differential conservation of mass relation at any point in an incompressible flow is given by

\underbrace{\nabla\cdot\vec{u}}_{\text{net outflow of volume from an infinitesimally small fluid element}}=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=0 (8.2)

Both of these relations indicate that there can be no net volumetric outflow: in Equation (8.1) there must be no net volumetric outflow through a control surface of a finite control volume, so our expression is an integral expression relating volume flux across the control surface, and in Equation (8.2) we take the limit of the control volume as it becomes infinitely small, leading to a relation involving the divergence of the velocity. Section 8.5, later, shows the derivation of Equation (8.2) from Equation (8.1). Sidebar 8.1, p. 278 reviews the divergence operator, because it is so central to this chapter.

For incompressible flows, conservation of mass creates a kinematic constraint, meaning that it places a constraint on the types of velocity fields that are possible (see Example Problem 8.1, p. 279, for an example of how conservation of mass can be used to evaluate whether a velocity field is possible in an incompressible flow). It is not a dynamic condition; it does not have anything to do with \(F=ma\).

Because conservation of mass is much simpler than conservation of momentum, we consider conservation of mass first (in this chapter) and consider conservation of momentum later. Remarkably, in this chapter we will show that because we know that conservation of mass must be satisfied, we can define velocity fields using only a single scalar parameter. In Chapter 9, we will show that in some cases we can solve a differential equation for the velocity field with that one scalar parameter, and we won’t even need conservation of momentum at all. So we can get surprisingly far with just conservation of mass.

streamfunction: denoted \(\psi\). Scalar function defined for 2D flows equivalently as (a) \(\psi(A)=\int_{O}^{A}u\,dy-v\,dx\) or (b) \(u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\) and \(v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\), or (c) \(\vec{u}=\nabla\times\psi\hat{z}\). Incompressible 2D flows can be defined by \(\psi(x,y)\) because the existence of \(\psi(x,y)\) is mathematically equivalent to satisfying conservation of mass.

integral conservation of mass, incompressible flow

differential conservation of mass, incompressible flow

divergence: the divergence of \(\vec{u}\) is denoted \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}\). The divergence of \(\vec{u}\) describes the normalized expansion rate of the fluid.

kinematic: related to the motion of objects without consideration of forces.

dynamic: involving forces and accelerations.

SIDEBAR 8.1: FUNDAMENTALS

Divergence

The divergence of the velocity field is the net volumetric expansion of the fluid at any point

The mathematical definition of divergence of a vector (or higher-order tensor) is

\nabla\cdot\vec{u}\equiv\lim_{\mathcal{V}\to0}\left(\frac{\int_S\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA}{V}\right) (8.3)

where \(\mathcal{V}\) denotes a control volume with control surface \(S\) and volume \(V\), and \(\hat{n}\) is the unit outward normal along the surface. The limit makes the control volume infinitesimal, making the divergence a differential vector operation. Here \(\vec{u}\) is used as an example, but one can take a divergence of any field variable that has tensor rank of 1 or higher. The verbal definition of the divergence is tricky—the definition mathematicians use is succinct but uses the word “flux” in a way that contradicts how fluid mechanicians use the word “flux”. Rather than attempt a general definition, Table 8.1, p. 278 and 8.2 list some examples. Engineers define flux to mean the rate of flow of a property per unit area across a control surface (in 3D) or the rate of flow of a property per unit length across a surface (in 2D). Consider a property \(P\) and consider a vector field property \(\vec{q}\) such that \(\vec{q}\cdot\hat{n}\) describes the flux of \(P\) across the surface. For example, in 3D, volume flux is described by \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\) and momentum flux is described by \(\rho\vec{u}\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\). With these definitions, \(\nabla\cdot\vec{q}\) describes the net outflow of \(P\) per unit volume (3D) or the net outflow of \(P\) per unit area (2D). The divergence has units equal to the units of \(P\) times \([1/L]\). The divergence of \(\vec{q}\) has a tensor rank one lower than that of \(\vec{q}\); the divergence of a vector is a scalar, and the divergence of a dyadic tensor is a vector.

Table 8.1: Examples of properties, the vectors that transport them across control surfaces, and the resulting divergences for 3D control volumes.

CV dimension | property \(P\) | property \(\vec{q}\) such that \(\vec{q}\cdot\hat{n}\) gives flux of \(P\) through control surface | \(\nabla\cdot\vec{q}\)
3 | volume | \(\vec{u}\) | net volume outflow rate per volume
3 | mass | \(\rho\vec{u}\) | net mass outflow rate per volume
3 | momentum | \(\rho\vec{u}\vec{u}\) | net momentum outflow rate per volume
Table 8.2: Examples of properties, the vectors that transport them across control surfaces, and the resulting divergences for 2D control volumes.

CV dimension | property \(P\) | property \(\vec{q}\) such that \(\vec{q}\cdot\hat{n}\) gives flux of \(P\) through control surface | \(\nabla\cdot\vec{q}\)
2 | area | \(\vec{u}\) | net area outflow rate per area
2 | mass per unit length | \(\rho\vec{u}\) | net mass outflow rate per volume
2 | momentum per unit length | \(\rho\vec{u}\vec{u}\) | net momentum outflow rate per volume
The divergence of the fluid velocity is a measure of how much the fluid is expanding or contracting

If \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}>0\), the fluid is expanding (and density is going down). If \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}<0\), the fluid is contracting (and density is going up). If density is fixed (because the flow is incompressible), then \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0\).

The divergence of the shear stresses is a measure of the net viscous force on a fluid element

The shear stresses on a fluid element are given by a dyadic \(\vec{\tau}_{\mathrm{visc}}\), and the divergence \(\nabla\cdot\vec{\tau}_{\mathrm{visc}}\) of this tensor is a vector that describes the net volumetric force on the fluid from viscous effects. In fluid mechanics, we care about stresses themselves only at walls and interfaces. In the body of a fluid, we care only about the divergences of the stresses. Contrast with solid mechanics, where we care primarily about stresses themselves, because stresses relate to yield and fracture.

The divergence takes different forms in different coordinate systems

In Cartesian coordinates and cylindrical coordinates,

\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=\underbrace{\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}}_{\text{net expansion in }x}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}}_{\text{net expansion in }y}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}}_{\text{net expansion in }z},\qquad \nabla\cdot\vec{u}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(ru_r)}{\partial r}}_{\text{net expansion in }r}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial\theta}}_{\text{net expansion in }\theta}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z}}_{\text{net expansion in }z} (8.4)
