Example Problem 8.1

Indicate whether these are possible incompressible flows from the standpoint of conservation of mass:

1. \(\vec{u}=(x,0,0)\)

2. \(\vec{u}=(x,-y,0)\)

3. \(\vec{u}=(x,y,-2z)\)

Solution:

1. no, \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=1\). This flow is expanding everywhere, which violates conservation of mass if the density is uniform and constant, so this velocity field is not possible in an incompressible flow. This velocity field is what you would find if you had a piston-cylinder system filled with gas and aligned horizontally, and you pulled the piston to the right—the density would have to decrease.

2. yes, \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=1-1+0=0\). This flow is expanding in the \(x\) direction but contracting in the \(y\) direction; these two effects balance. This velocity field is what you find when two plane-symmetric jets aligned in the \(\pm y\) directions impinge on each other.

3. yes, \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=1+1-2=0\). This flow is expanding isotropically in the \(xy\) plane but contracting in the \(z\) direction; again these balance. This velocity field is what you find when two axially symmetric jets aligned in the \(\pm z\) directions impinge on each other.

I don’t expect you to yet be able to look at these velocity fields and tell what flow they correspond to: that is discussed in Appendix E. I describe what these velocity fields correspond to so that you know that these are all real flows; they are not arbitrary mathematical trivia.

For 2D flow, the stream function is a scalar function that simplifies analysis because it simultaneously defines the velocity field and guarantees conservation of mass

Now that we know that \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0\) for incompressible flow, we immediately look to develop tools to take advantage of this. Incompressible flow makes our lives much easier, because it places a strict kinematic constraint on what velocity fields are possible. The restriction that the velocity field must be divergence-free provides us with tools that simplify fluid mechanical analysis. The first example of this is the streamfunction, which greatly simplifies analysis of plane-symmetric 2-D flows by prescribing a 2D velocity field through use of a single scalar variable.

Plane-symmetric flows are often used to describe systems that are very long in one direction or whose properties change very little in one direction. For example, fluid flowing over most of the wing of an airplane can be approximated as plane-symmetric—the shape of the wing changes only slowly along its length, and the flow is well approximated by assuming that there are no velocity components along the wing axis, and no gradient along the wing axis.

Suppose that, rather than trying to define the velocity vector \(\vec{u}\) by defining \(u\), \(v\), and \(w\) as a function of \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\), we instead defined a scalar field variable \(\psi(x,y)\), which we will call the streamfunction, defined \(\vec{u}\) with

u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y},\qquad v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x},\qquad w=0 (8.5)

and used \(\psi\) to describe a plane-symmetric flow in the \(xy\) plane. This is arguably

incompressible flow: implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Incompressible flow implies that the motion of the fluid does not cause density to change, in comparison to compressible flow in which fluid moves so quickly and the pressure changes so much that the density is perturbed enough to affect convective fluxes. Incompressible flows may still have nonuniform density, for example if the fluid’s temperature varies; this can affect the conservation of momentum equations. An incompressible flow does not imply that the fluid is mathematically incompressible, only that pressure-induced compression can be ignored. Cf. compressible flow.

plane-symmetric: independent of a Cartesian coordinate.

2-D flow: A flow that is independent of one of the coordinates, for example a function of \(x\) and \(y\) but not \(z\) (plane-symmetric), or a function of \(r\) and \(\theta\) but not \(z\) (plane-symmetric), or a function of \(r\) and \(z\) but not \(\theta\) (axially symmetric).

streamfunction: denoted \(\psi\). Scalar function defined for 2D flows equivalently as (a) \(\psi(A)=\int_O^A u\,dy-v\,dx\), or (b) \(u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\) and \(v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\), or (c) \(\vec{u}=\nabla\times\psi\hat{z}\). Incompressible 2D flows can be defined by \(\psi(x,y)\) because the existence of \(\psi(x,y)\) is mathematically equivalent to satisfying conservation of mass.

easier than defining \(\vec{u}\), because \(\psi\) is a scalar. Example Problem 8.2 (p. 280) shows how we can prescribe the velocity vector by use of \(\psi\).

If we prescribe \(\vec{u}\) by use of \(\psi\), we immediately find multiple convenient results:

• If the flow is incompressible, conservation of mass will always be satisfied. \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\) is always zero by definition.

• If we plot an isocontour of \(\psi\), that isocontour will be a streamline of the velocity field prescribed by \(\psi\). Equivalently, \(\psi\) never changes in the direction of flow. \(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial s}\) is always zero.

• The areal flow rate between a streamline \(A\) and a streamline \(B\) is given by \(\psi_A-\psi_B\).

• If we plot these isocontours of \(\psi\) at uniform spacing of \(\psi\), we will see that the flow is fast where the streamline density is high, and the flow is slow where the streamline density is low.

Velocity, mass flow, and streamlines can be defined in terms of derivatives of the streamfunction because the streamfunction is actually a measure of areal flow rate

incompressible: with respect to a flow, implies physically that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations, and is not perturbed by the fluid’s acceleration and deceleration. With respect to a fluid, denotes that the density of the fluid is a mathematical constant.

isocontour: a curve along which a property is uniform.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

areal: related to area, or per unit area.

Sidebar 8.2: Fundamentals

Streamfunction

The streamfunction is defined as a measure of the areal flowrate through a contour between points

For any point \(A\) in a flow, consider a path between an arbitrary origin point (which we call \(O\)) and \(A\). Then, presuming we know \(\vec{u}\), let’s figure out the clockwise areal flowrate that crosses that path if the path were a control surface. It turns out that that relation is simple! Call that integral \(\psi\): (see Figure B.9, p. 468):

\psi(A)=\int_O^A \vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,ds=\int_O^A u\,dy+\int_O^A -v\,dx (8.6)

Handwritten Figure 8.5 annotations: ‘part of areal flux explained by x velocity component’; ‘areal flux’; ‘part of areal flux explained by y velocity component’. The left sketch labels the path from O to point A, the increments dx and dy, and the differential flux contributions u dy and (−v) dx; the combined element is marked u dy−v dx.

Handwritten labels in the right sketch: ‘STREAMLINES FOR FLOW OVER BACKWARD-FACING STEP’, ‘INLET FLOW’, and ‘OUTLET’. The recirculation region is labeled ψ=−6, ψ=−5, and ψ=−4. The downstream streamline labels, confirmed in the enlarged source, are ψ=2,1,0,−1,−2,−3. A lower note reads ‘streamlines far apart / U small’.

Additional handwritten derivation: ‘DEFN OF ψ ⇒ \(\psi(A)=\int_O^A(\text{areal flux})\,ds\)’; ‘C.O. MASS ON OAB C.V. ⇒ \(\psi(A)=\int_O^B(\text{areal flux})\,ds\)’; ‘CONCLUDE ψ CONST ON AB ⇒ ψ(A)=ψ(B)’.



Figure 8.5: Left: a differential section of the path from an arbitrary origin to a point \(A\), showing how the volume flux across the element \(ds\) is given by \(u\,dy-v\,dx\). Right: some observations of the streamfunction in a flow. The net flow into the surface \(OAB\) must be zero, consistent with \(\psi(A)=\psi(B)\) along the streamline \(AB\). Streamlines are close to each other at left, consistent with high speed; streamlines are farther away at right, consistent with low speed.

This is because for a differential distance along the path \(ds\) with components \(dx\) and \(dy\), \(\hat{n}\,ds\) (which is normal to the path) has x component \(dy\) and y component \(-dx\) (i.e., \(\hat{n}\,ds=dy\,\hat{x}-dx\,\hat{y}\)). The integrand \(u\,dy-v\,dx\) is just the dot product of \(\vec{u}\) with \(\hat{n}\,ds\).

We haven’t specified the path from \(O\) to \(A\). But, at fixed density, conservation of mass says that the areal flowrate through all of these paths has to be the same, so this integral should not be a function of the path. This is the key thing. For 2D plane-symmetric incompressible flows, \(\psi\) is well defined and single-valued. If \(\psi\) is well defined and single-valued, it describes a velocity field that satisfies conservation of mass.

With this definition, derivatives of \(\psi\) are straightforward, as \(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}=-v\) and \(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}=u\). So

u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y};\qquad v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x};\qquad \vec{u}=\nabla\times\psi\hat{z} (8.7)

If we solve incompressible flow problems in terms of \(\psi\), we never have to solve the conservation of mass equation.

Editorial redraw note: Enlarged source labels resolve the outlet levels as ψ=2,1,0,−1,−2,−3. Contour shapes are schematic.


PDF page 293 — verified

For plane-symmetric flow in the \(xy\) plane, we define the two components of the velocity in terms of the streamfunction \(\psi\). This satisfies continuity and provides a convenient delineation of streamlines and areal flow rate. The reason this works is because the fundamental definition of \(\psi\) is the measure of areal flowrate relative to an arbitrary origin. Sidebar 8.2, p. 281 describes the streamfunction and several facets of its interpretation.

Isocontours of the streamfunction are streamlines

We can prove that the velocity is tangent to the isocontour of the streamfunction, i.e., that a streamline is an isocontour of the streamfunction. If the derivative of \(\psi\) along a streamline is by definition zero, then this confirms that the streamline is an isocontour of \(\psi\). The streamwise derivative of the streamfunction can be written as:

\frac{d\psi}{ds}=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s} (8.8)

Substituting the definition of \(u\) and \(v\) from above, we find

\frac{d\psi}{ds}=-v\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}+u\frac{\partial y}{\partial s} (8.9)

Because \(\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}=\frac{u}{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}\) and \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}=\frac{v}{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}\), we find

\frac{d\psi}{ds}=\frac{-vu}{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}+\frac{uv}{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}=0 (8.10)

This confirms that, by definition, \(\psi\) does not change along a streamline. Thus if a path is everywhere tangent to the fluid flow (i.e., if it is a streamline), then moving along the path does not change \(\psi\) (i.e., the streamline is an isocontour) and vice versa. Thus streamlines are isocontours of the streamfunction. This makes it very easy to plot the streamlines of a flow defined by \(\psi\)—we just calculate \(\psi\) and plot isocontours, for example in MATLAB using \(`contour(psi)`\). Example Problem 8.3 (p. 283) shows how we can plot isocontours of \(\psi\) to denote streamlines of a flow.

Example Problem 8.4 (p. 284) shows how the location of streamlines and our understanding of the streamfunction can be used to infer fluid velocity from streamline patterns.

2D velocity fields can be prescribed completely by specifying \(\psi(x,y)\)

The net result of the above analysis is that \(\psi\) is enough to completely specify the 2D velocity field \(\vec{u}(x,y)\). It is a scalar field that has all the information of the 2D vector field. We can specify the vector flowfield (which has two components) by use of only a scalar field (which has only one), because there is a kinematic constraint (\(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0\)) that gives us additional information.

For 3D flows, things are not so simple, and we need two scalar streamfunctions to prescribe the velocity field, and finding two scalar fields ends up being difficult. Because of this, streamfunctions are not commonly used in 3D flow analysis.

streamfunction: denoted \(\psi\). Scalar function defined for 2D flows equivalently as (a) \(\psi(A)=\int_O^A u\,dy-v\,dx\), or (b) \(u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\) and \(v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\), or (c) \(\vec{u}=\nabla\times\psi\hat{z}\). Incompressible 2D flows can be defined by \(\psi(x,y)\) because the existence of \(\psi(x,y)\) is mathematically equivalent to satisfying conservation of mass.

continuity: when used to modify a field (e.g., ‘velocity continuity’ or ‘pressure continuity’), this is a mathematical term that typically means that the field is continuous, and often used to indicate that a field has the same value on both sides of an interface. When used alone, this is a physical term which typically means ‘conservation of mass’. When used as continuity equation, synonymous with ‘conservation of mass equation’.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

isocontour: a curve along which a property is uniform.

We can derive the differential conservation of mass equation by use of the divergence theorem or a judiciously chosen control volume aligned with a specific coordinate system

The derivation of \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0\) is important because it is the simplest example in which we derive a differential conservation equation by use of the divergence theorem.

This is the point where you realize that that super-boring section in MATH1920 where they made you learn the divergence theorem is actually super-useful, almost magical.

The differential forms of the conservation equations come directly from their integral forms. Two different but equivalent approaches for deriving differential conservation equations are (1) to use the divergence theorem to convert integral relations to differential relations and (2) to analyze a control volume aligned with a specific coordinate system, combined with liberal use of Taylor-series expansions. In either case, we conclude that conservation of mass for an incompressible flow is satisfied if

\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0 (8.11)

The divergence theorem turns the integral conservation of mass equation into a general differential conservation of mass equation

For those who like things abstract and mathematical, the divergence theorem quickly converts the integral forms of the equations to differential form. Those not familiar with vector theorems might find this approach less intuitive, and might want to read the next section first.

Rewriting Equation (7.23) strictly in terms of density, the integral conservation of mass equation is

\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V \rho\,dV+\int_S \rho\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA=0 (8.13)

Equation 8.13 labels: ‘change of mass of CV’ under the first term and ‘net outflux of mass’ above the surface-flux term. The equation is identified as the integral conservation of mass equation.

We cannot simplify this further because we have one volume integral and one surface integral. However, we can make the two integrals of this equation both become volume integrals over the same volume. Writing the divergence theorem for \(\rho\vec{u}\):

\int_V \nabla\cdot(\rho\vec{u})\,dV=\int_S (\rho\vec{u})\cdot\hat{n}\,dA (8.14)

Equation 8.14 is labeled ‘divergence theorem for ρu’.

we can turn the surface integral of the flux term into a volume integral:

\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V \rho\,dV+\int_V \nabla\cdot(\rho\vec{u})\,dV=0 (8.15)

Then, because the derivative and integral commute:

\int_V \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}\,dV+\int_V \nabla\cdot(\rho\vec{u})\,dV=0 (8.16)

which means

\int_V\left[\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot(\rho\vec{u})\right]dV=0 (8.17)

Equation (8.17) must be true for any control volume, and for that to be true, the integrand must be zero:

\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot(\rho\vec{u})=0 (8.18)

Equation 8.18 labels: ‘local volumetric outflux of mass’ above the divergence term and ‘local increase in density’ below the time-derivative term. It is labeled ‘conservation of mass, differential form’.

incompressible flow: implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Incompressible flow implies that the motion of the fluid does not cause density to change, in comparison to compressible flow in which fluid moves so quickly and the pressure changes so much that the density is perturbed enough to affect convective fluxes. Incompressible flows may still have nonuniform density, for example if the fluid’s temperature varies; this can affect the conservation of momentum equations. An incompressible flow does not imply that the fluid is mathematically incompressible, only that pressure-induced compression can be ignored. Cf. compressible flow.

This differential form of the equation now applies everywhere in the fluid. If we were to integrate this equation over a control volume, we would recover the integral form of this conservation equation.

For fixed density, Equation (8.18) simplifies to

\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0 (8.19)

Equation 8.19 is labeled ‘net expansion of fluid’ and ‘conservation of mass, differential form, fixed density’.

From this, we can see that fluids at fixed density move with a divergence-free velocity field—everywhere in the fluid, the net expansion or contraction of the fluid is zero. In Cartesian coordinates, Equation (8.19) is

\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=0 (8.20)

The terms in Eq. 8.20 are labeled ‘expansion in x dir.’, ‘expansion in y dir.’, and ‘expansion in z dir.’ Equation 8.20 is labeled ‘conservation of mass, differential form, fixed density, Cartesian coords’.

whereas in cylindrical coordinates, Equation (8.19) is

\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(ru_r)}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial\theta}+\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z}=0 (8.21)

The terms in Eq. 8.21 are labeled ‘expansion in r-dir.’, ‘expansion in θ-dir.’, and ‘expansion in z-dir.’ Equation 8.21 is labeled ‘conservation of mass, differential form, fixed density, cylindrical coords’.

The flux of mass through each face is relatively easy to write because only one component of the velocity vector is normal to each surface:

Sidebar 8.3: Fundamentals

Divergence Theorem

The divergence theorem transforms integral relations to differential relations by changing the surface integral of surface fluxes to a volume integral of flux divergences

Given an infinitesimal control surface \(S\) with an outward unit normal \(\hat{n}\), a property \(P\), and a vector field \(\vec{q}\) such that \(\vec{q}\cdot\hat{n}\) is the flux of \(P\) outward across \(S\), \(\nabla\cdot\vec{q}\) gives the volumetric outflow of \(P\). The divergence theorem is basically what happens when you integrate this definition over a finite control volume:

\int_V \nabla\cdot\vec{q}\,dV=\int_S \vec{q}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA (8.12)

If the divergence of a vector is its local net outflow, then we should be able to add up all of those net outflows to get the total net outflow. Similarly, we can evaluate the total net outflow by adding up the fluxes at the surface (that is what we did in the previous chapter). The divergence theorem is a statement that these two ways of adding up the net outflow are equivalent. We use this to transfer back and forth between whichever integral is easier. The volume integral is usually mathematically easier, so we often do that. Sometimes, though, we only have information about the boundaries, so then we need to use the surface integral. The divergence theorem lets us pick and choose. The divergence theorem is powerful in that it converts the surface integrals in the integral conservation equations into volume integrals, making all of the terms in those equations volume integrals over the same volume. Because those conservation equations must apply over any volume, that means the integrand itself must satisfy an equality.



Figure 8.9: A differential Cartesian control element and fluxes for conservation of mass with fixed density.

+x face outward mass flux:

\rho\left(u+\frac{\Delta x}{2}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)\Delta y\Delta z

-x face outward mass flux:

-\rho\left(u-\frac{\Delta x}{2}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)\Delta y\Delta z

+y face outward mass flux:

\rho\left(v+\frac{\Delta y}{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)\Delta x\Delta z

-y face outward mass flux:

-\rho\left(v-\frac{\Delta y}{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)\Delta x\Delta z

+z face outward mass flux:

\rho\left(w+\frac{\Delta z}{2}\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\Delta x\Delta y

-z face outward mass flux:

-\rho\left(w-\frac{\Delta z}{2}\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\Delta x\Delta y

• left face: \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}=-u\).

• top face: \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}=v\).

• bottom face: \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}=-v\).

• front face: \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}=w\).

• back face: \(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}=-w\).

We evaluate the magnitudes of the velocity components by use of Taylor-series expansions around the center of the cuboid (see Sidebar 8.3, p. 183 describes the streamfunction and several facets of its interpretation.). Assuming that density is fixed, analyzing this control volume leads to the conclusion that the net mass flux out of the control volume is \(\rho\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\) (see Sidebar 8.4, p. 289), and thus conservation of mass is satisfied if

\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=0 (8.24)

Equation 8.24 is labeled ‘conservation of mass, differential form, fixed density, Cartesian coords’.

which is identical to Equation (8.20). By inference, we could generalize the result by noting that \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\) can be written generally as \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}\), which would lead to the general vector equation

\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0 (8.25)

Deriving the differential form through a specific control volume is less general than using the divergence theorem, but it is more concrete in terms of directly writing and integrating fluxes. The two approaches are completely equivalent.

Several flow visualization techniques don’t measure streamlines but are really useful anyway

This chapter used flow visualization and the experimental determination of streamlines to motivate differential conservation of mass, and the definition of the streamfunction. But there are multiple other ways to visualize fluid flow that are worth mentioning as well. We add these here at the end of the chapter.

Particle-image velocimetry measures a velocity field by cross-correlating images of particles taken immediately after each other

There is a very easy way to estimate the velocity of something, which is to take a picture of it at one time, then take another picture of it a little bit later, and then say that its velocity must be approximated by the distance between its locations in the two pictures divided by the elapsed time. This is a first-order Taylor-series expansion approximation of the velocity, and if the elapsed time is small, this measurement technique can very precisely measure the speed of a particle. Particle-image velocimetry (commonly called

Sidebar 8.4: Fundamentals

How we got that the flux of mass is \(\rho\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\)

We sum the net outflows and set them equal to the change of mass of the control volume

Conservation of mass says \(\frac{dm}{dt}=0\), which, following the Reynolds transport theorem, means that \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V \rho\,dV+\int_S \rho\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n}=0\). This control volume has 6 discrete faces, so we can write the surface integral as a sum over the 6 faces:

\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V \rho\,dV+\sum_{\text{6 faces}}\dot{m}=0 (8.22)

where \(\dot{m}\) is measured positive outward. The outward fluxes for the six faces (assuming \(\rho\) is uniform) are:

• right: \(\rho\left(u+\frac{1}{2}\Delta x\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)\Delta y\Delta z\).

• left: \(\rho\left[-\left(u-\frac{1}{2}\Delta x\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)\right]\Delta y\Delta z\).

• top: \(\rho\left(v+\frac{1}{2}\Delta y\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)\Delta x\Delta z\).

• bottom: \(\rho\left[-\left(v-\frac{1}{2}\Delta y\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)\right]\Delta x\Delta z\).

• front: \(\rho\left(w+\frac{1}{2}\Delta y\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\Delta x\Delta y\).

• back: \(\rho\left[-\left(w-\frac{1}{2}\Delta y\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\right]\Delta x\Delta y\).

Summing these six fluxes, we get \(\rho\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\). If we assume that \(\rho\) is not changing, then this flux must sum to zero, which means

\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=0 (8.23)

Editorial note: the introductory surface integral omits \(dA\) in print. In the front/back face Taylor terms, the printed \(\Delta y\) must be \(\Delta z\), since the derivative is with respect to \(z\). With that correction their sum is \(\rho\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z\,\partial w/\partial z\), consistent with the final divergence formula. The source expressions above are retained literally.

PIV) is essentially a very fancy version of this idea. A fluid flow is filled with particles which serve as Lagrangian flow tracers. Then, two images are taken of the same field of view, separated by a duration of tens of microseconds (Figure 8.10, p. 290). Then, these two images are split into domains and each domain is cross-correlated with the same domain in the paired image. The cross-correlation \(\Phi(\Delta x,\Delta y)\) of two fields of view \(f(x,y)\) and \(g(x,y)\) is given by

\Phi(\Delta x,\Delta y)=\iint f(x,y)g(x+\Delta x,y+\Delta y)\,dx\,dy (8.26)

The cross-correlation is a mathematical way of taking one image \((f)\) on a piece of paper, and a second image \((g)\) on a transparency sheet, and offsetting the transparency sheet by \((\Delta x,\Delta y)\), and seeing how well the two images overlap. At the offset \((\Delta x,\Delta y)\) that makes \(g\) look the most like \(f\), \(\Phi\) is maximized. This function tells us what is the average velocity of the particles in that domain of an image (Figure 8.11, p. 291). In practice, particle-image velocimetry often just takes one image and autocorrelates the image with itself to get the same information; the cross-correlations are handled mathematically with 2D Fourier transforms.

cross-correlation: given two fields, the cross-correlation measures how well the two fields are aligned with each other as a function of displacement.

Figure 8.10: Schematic of PIV setup. Two laser pulses are expanded and focused into sheets, and illuminate a plane in the flow. Two images are taken and cross-correlated, or one image is taken and autocorrelated. Either way, the result is a velocity field.

Planar laser-induced fluorescence (usually) records the concentration of a fluorescent species

The same laser sheet that can be used to reflect off of particles to generate particle-image velocimetry can also be used to excite fluorescent species—for example water can be seeded with a fluorescent dye such as fluorescein, which fluoresces yellow when hit with green light, or air can be seeded with acetone, which fluoresces blue when hit with ultraviolet light. This can be used to generate streaklines or otherwise image the structure of a flow. If you want to make things hard on yourself, you can take pictures of things that are really hard to make fluoresce, like say carbon monoxide. That’s what I did for my Ph.D. dissertation (Figure 8.12, p. 292).

Hydrogen-bubble and laser tagging visualize material lines in a flow

A material line is the location of a curve drawn in a flow after a specified time has elapsed. Whereas a streamline is an instantaneous measure of the velocity field, a streakline gives a time history of all the fluid that passed through a specific point, and a pathline gives the time history of a specific chunk of fluid, a material line is halfway between a pathline and a streakline—it tells us where a finite chunk of fluid is at one specific point in the future. A material line can be visualized by tagging fluid in some way. This is easiest to do in liquid phase—two common examples are (a) generating hydrogen bubbles in water by electrolysis on a wire (Figure 8.13, p. 292) or using a laser to create a local chemical reaction to change a chemical from nonfluorescent to fluorescent (Figure 8.14, p. 293). In each of these figures, a laminar Poiseuille flow is used, which has a well-known parabolic speed distribution. Now that I think about this, I laser-tagged air flow in hard disk drives using acetone-sensitized biacetyl phosphorescence back in 1996 when I worked for Hewlett-Packard. That was cool. But I recorded it on a VCR and I no longer have the tape…

streakline: a line that traces the Eulerian time history of the velocity of a location in a fluid flow as time elapses. Can be imagined as the line that would be traced out if a small trace of dye were released slowly into a fluid flow.

laminar: occurring in orderly sheets or lamina.

Poiseuille flow: pronounced PWAH-zyoil. Laminar, pressure-driven flow through a duct or pipe.

Schlieren imaging transduces refraction associated with nonuniform density into increased or decreased image brightness

Most people are familiar with the optical effect when looking in the distance through air that is next to a hot object. The image shimmers; a phenomenon called heat distortion.

The reason for this shimmering is that light’s speed is different through air that has different temperature, so local variations in temperature act as a weak lens, bending the light toward the colder air. The hot air convecting off the top of a gas grill, or the exhaust from a jet engine bends the light in random directions.

When we are looking at a fluid-mechanical system, this bending of light can be used to measure density fluctuations in the system, which can be useful when two different colorless gases are mixing, or when there are slight temperature fluctuations in the system, or when there are acoustic or shock waves in the system. In these cases, schlieren imaging can be used to see things (slight temperature variations, or shock waves) that we couldn’t see otherwise (Figure 8.15, p. 294).

The optical setup used to generate such an image can be seen in Figure 8.16, p. 295. Light from a point source is collimated, and collimated light passes through the flow to be visualized. When that light is focused, any light that passed through a density gradient has been deflected a bit, and its location at the focus will be shifted. A razor blade inserted partially into the focus transduces density gradients to light intensity in the image. Bright spots in a schlieren image correspond to the light being bent away from the razor blade. Dark spots correspond to the light being bent toward the razor blade.

schlieren: an imaging mode in which density gradients correspond to either bright or dark regions of the image.

shock wave: a discontinuous transition in which a supersonic flow slows down, with an attendant increase in pressure and density.

The central model of this chapter is the incompressible flow approximation

This chapter mostly uses flow visualization to motivate differential conservation of mass and the streamfunction. In addition to a number of models that have become routine (e.g., the continuum approximation), this chapter leans heavily on the incompressible flow model (see Sidebar 8.5, p. 297). By assuming that the Mach number is low and the pressures of the flow don’t change the density much, we can treat \(\rho\) as uniform without introducing problematic errors, and this empowers us to use the streamfunction to formulate 2D incompressible flow problems.


PDF page 308 — verified

Sidebar 8.5: Engineering Models

Incompressible Flow

Premise: At low \(M\), treating \(\rho\) as unaffected by pressure or velocity greatly simplifies the math and leads to only very small errors

All of the conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy involve the fluid density, and this density is routinely found inside temporal and spatial derivatives. If we could just assume that \(\rho\) were a constant, it would greatly simplify the math. This approximation is surprisingly useful, even for fluids like air, for which the fluid itself is definitely compressible according to the ideal-gas law. We find that, even for a fluid like air which we know can be compressed, the flow of this fluid often does not lead to large density changes, and if we ignore the small density changes, our calculations of the velocity and pressure fields and resulting outputs like forces have only small errors. Importantly, the incompressible flow approximation involves approximating \(\rho\) as a constant for the purposes of the conservation equations. It does not involve claims that the fluid cannot be compressed. Just that the amount it is compressed by flow can be ignored without messing up the calculations engineers care about.

Mathematical form: for incompressible flow \(\rho=\text{a constant}\). Incompressible flow simplifies the conservation equations by taking \(\rho\) to be a constant, and is valid when \(M\) is small:

\rho=\text{a constant}\qquad\text{when}\qquad M<0.3 (8.27)

Eq. 8.27 is labeled ‘Incompressible flow simplifies the conservation equations by taking ρ to be a constant, and is valid when M is small’.

Utility: the incompressible flow approximation turns the conservation of mass equation into a kinematic relation and greatly simplifies the conservation of momentum equations

The conservation of mass equation is greatly simplified if we assume that \(\rho\) is a constant:

\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\rho\vec{u}=0;\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0 (8.28)

In the incompressible flow model, we never actually solve the conservation of mass equation so much as we use what we know about conservation of mass to simplify the conservation of momentum equations. There are many terms in the conservation of momentum equations that are proportional to \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}\), and these all cancel out. That and taking \(\rho\) outside the derivatives greatly simplifies the equations:

\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho\vec{u}+\nabla\cdot\rho\vec{u}\vec{u}=-\nabla p+\nabla\cdot 2\mu\vec{\vec{\varepsilon}}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\rho\frac{\partial\vec{u}}{\partial t}+\rho\vec{u}\cdot\nabla\vec{u}=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec{u} (8.29)

Limitations: The incompressible flow model fails when \(M\) is high

The Mach number \(M\) is the governing parameter that tells us how good the incompressible flow approximation is. The errors associated with the incompressible flow approximation end up being roughly proportional to \(M^2\), and so a rule of thumb is that if \(M<0.3\) then the errors associated with the incompressible flow approximation are below 10% and aren’t that big of a deal. The incompressible flow model is very useful, but requires that \(M\) be low. As soon as \(M\) gets high, it fails.

Practice Problems

Problems

1. (OBJECTIVE: role of expansion/contraction in flow; relation between stream function and conservation of mass) Evaluate \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}\) for each of these flows and determine whether they satisfy conservation of mass:

(a) Stagnation flow: If you take two 2D jets and shoot them into each other, at the centerline where the two jets meet, the flow is well approximated by a streamfunction \(\psi=Axy\).

(b) Stagnation flow rotated 45 degrees: \(\psi=\frac{1}{2}A(y^2-x^2)\). This describes the collision between two 2D jets aligned along the line \(y=-x\).

(c) Solid-body rotation: If you look from above at the flow in a beaker of water rotating, the flow is described by the streamfunction \(\psi=\frac{1}{2}A(x^2+y^2)\).

(d) Irrotational vortex: If you look from above at water rotating around a drain, or the flow in a tornado or hurricane, the flow is described by the streamfunction \(\psi=-\frac{1}{2}A\ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\).

2. (OBJECTIVE: Identify mathematical framework of properties of the streamfunction) Show that the streamfunction does not change in the streamwise direction.

3. (OBJECTIVE: list purpose here) Show that a velocity field \(\vec{u}\) of an incompressible fluid in the \(xy\) plane defined by the streamfunction \(\psi\) satisfies conservation of mass.

Problems with Answers

1. (OBJECTIVE: role of expansion/contraction in flow; relation between stream function and conservation of mass) Evaluate \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}\) for each of these flows and determine whether they satisfy conservation of mass:

(a) Stagnation flow: If you take two 2D jets and shoot them into each other, at the centerline where the two jets meet, the flow is well approximated by a streamfunction \(\psi=Axy\).

(b) Stagnation flow rotated 45 degrees: \(\psi=\frac{1}{2}A(y^2-x^2)\). This describes the collision between two 2D jets aligned along the line \(y=-x\).

(c) Solid-body rotation: If you look from above at the flow in a beaker of water rotating, the flow is described by the streamfunction \(\psi=\frac{1}{2}A(x^2+y^2)\).

(d) Irrotational vortex: If you look from above at water rotating around a drain, or the flow in a tornado or hurricane, the flow is described by the streamfunction \(\psi=-\frac{1}{2}A\ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\).

Solution:

These flows are solutions written in terms of the streamfunction \(\psi\), which by definition conserves mass. It would be sufficient to say that all flows by definition have \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0\). In general the definition of \(\psi\) is

u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y},\qquad v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x} (8.30)

thus \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\) always is zero by definition. This is true for each individual flow as well and we evaluate these specifically below. In each case, \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=0\); this can be seen from the fact that the upper left


PDF page 310 — verified

term is always opposite of the lower right term, when the matrix representation of the velocity gradient is written below in the form

[\nabla\vec{u}]=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{bmatrix} (8.31)

(a) \(\nabla\vec{u}=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\0&-A\end{bmatrix}\) — satisfies conservation of mass.

(b) \(\nabla\vec{u}=\begin{bmatrix}0&A\\ A&0\end{bmatrix}\) — satisfies conservation of mass.

(c) \(\nabla\vec{u}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-A\\ A&0\end{bmatrix}\) — satisfies conservation of mass.

(d) \(\nabla\vec{u}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{Axy}{(x^2+y^2)^2}&\frac{A}{2}\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}\\ \frac{A}{2}\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}&-\frac{Axy}{(x^2+y^2)^2}\end{bmatrix}\) conservation of mass.

2. (OBJECTIVE: Identify mathematical framework of properties of the streamfunction) Show that the streamfunction does not change in the streamwise direction. Solution: The derivative of streamfunction in the streamwise direction is \(\frac{d\psi}{ds}\). Thus

\frac{d\psi}{ds}=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}=-v\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}+u\frac{\partial y}{\partial s} (8.32)

\(\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}=\frac{u}{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}\) and \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}=\frac{v}{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}\), so

\frac{d\psi}{ds}=\frac{-vu}{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}+\frac{uv}{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}=0 (8.33)

3. (OBJECTIVE: list purpose here) Show that a velocity field \(\vec{u}\) of an incompressible fluid in the \(xy\) plane defined by the streamfunction \(\psi\) satisfies conservation of mass. Solution: This can be shown by substitution, starting with the definition of velocities in terms of streamfunction:

u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y},\qquad v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x},\qquad w=0 (8.34)

Taking the divergence, we find

\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y\,\partial x}-\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x\,\partial y}+0=0 (8.35)

Chapter 9

Wings, Blades, and Airfoils: The Machines Inside the Turbomachines

The most fundamental fluid machine is an airfoil, which turns fluid and generates a force

In Chapter 2 we discussed turbomachines, for example, propellers, impellers, rotors, fans, blowers, turbines, and compressors. These turbomachines comprise a large fraction of all fluid machines. The fundamental component inside each of these turbomachines is a set of airfoils, alternatively called blades, vanes, rotors, stators, or hydrofoils. Each of these airfoils is itself one of the simplest fluid machines possible—a surface that locally turns the fluid and creates a pressure difference between its two sides, creating a net force in which the fluid applies a force to the airfoil, and an equal and opposite force is applied by the airfoil to the fluid.

Beyond turbomachines, airfoils also serve as the fundamental lifting and control surface on airplanes and hydrofoils serve as fundamental lifting and control surfaces on submarines.

Airfoils are streamlined

Airfoils come in many shapes (Figure 9.1, p. 301), but they share several features. First, they are streamlined, and are usually designed to turn fluid without separation. Second, they are relatively thin, and their thickness is usually set by the minimum thickness for mechanical integrity. Third, their trailing edge typically comes to a sharp point. Fourth, their leading edge (except in the cheapest, least-efficient systems like cheap desk fans) is typically rounded and has no sharp point.

In describing airfoils as streamlined, we imply that their shape is similar to a path a fluid could naturally take with only subtle accelerations, and the surface does not accelerate the fluid very sharply in any direction as the fluid follows the surface of the airfoil (Figure 9.2, p. 301). A bluff body, in contrast, has a shape dissimilar to the paths a fluid normally would take. In particular, the trailing edge of a bluff body requires that the fluid turn sharply at the trailing edge to follow the surface, and the fluid often cannot do this. Instead of following the surface, the fluid separates, and the separation is evidenced by a streamline that departs the surface perpendicular to the surface, combined with a recirculation zone, i.e., a region downstream of the separation point in which fluid is actually moving upstream.

turbomachine: a machine that adds energy to or extracts energy from a fluid by use of a rotary element. Typically implies dynamic machines, not positive-displacement machines.

streamlined: in describing the shape of an object, implies that the shape of the object is roughly similar to the shape of naturally occurring streamlines—smooth, with gentle curvature.

separation: when a streamline emanates normal to a surface. Most often, separation is used only to describe streamlines resulting from flow that moves upstream.

trailing edge: the rearward-most part of an object in a fluid flow.

recirculation: when a region of fluid is made to flow largely upstream. Typically associated with separation.

Airfoil performance depends on chord, camber, thickness, and angle of attack

Airfoil geometries are defined by their chords, camber, and thicknesses (Figure 9.3, p. 302), and their performance is a strong function of their angle of attack \(\alpha\), defined as the angle the chord line makes with the incident flow. Airfoils typically perform well only in a limited range of angle of attack, usually 15–−20° or so from minimum to maximum. Once the airfoil is at a very large angle of attack, it is effectively a bluff body because its geometry no longer echoes the path the fluid would take if experiencing subtle accelerations.



Figure 9.3: An airfoil, its chord, camber, thickness, and angle of attack. NACA airfoils, named after the National Advisory Council on Aeronautics (the precursor to NASA) define airfoil geometry using a four-digit code that describes the airfoil’s camber and thickness. Angle of attack is a property of how the airfoil is aligned relative to the oncoming freestream velocity.

There are several measures of what an airfoil is designed to do to an oncoming flow (Figure 9.4, p. 303):

An airfoil accelerates the fluid, both in front of and behind the airfoil. Here acceleration can mean increasing the speed, but in general means a vector acceleration leading to a change of speed or a change in direction. For example, the wing of an airplane makes the air upstream of the wing move upward, then turns that fluid so that it is moving downward once it is downstream of the wing. The impeller blades on a centrifugal pump cause the fluid moving through the impeller to gain azimuthal speed. The cups on a Pelton turbine are often designed to make jets of fluid reverse direction.

An airfoil causes a pressure difference between the two sides of the airfoil. The wing of an airplane causes the pressure at the top of the airfoil to be low and the pressure at the bottom of the airfoil to be high. The blades of a propeller cause the pressure on the upstream face to be lower than the freestream whereas they make the pressure on the downstream face higher than the freestream.

When used as part of a turbomachine, the local action of the airfoil (accelerating

Handwritten labels in Figure 9.3: FREESTREAM (three arrows); AIRFOIL; ANGLE OF ATTACK α; MAXIMUM THICKNESS POINT; MAXIMUM CAMBER; CAMBER LINE; CHORD LINE; CHORD LENGTH. Handwritten NACA note: “NACA 4-DIGIT AIRFOIL CODE: E.G. NACA 2418. 2: MAX CAMBER IS 2% OF CHORD LENGTH. 4: MAX CAMBER IS 4/10 ALONG CHORD. 18: MAX THICKNESS IS 18% OF CHORD.”

chord: a straight line connecting the leading and trailing edges of an airfoil.

camber: the curvature of the chord line of an airfoil.

angle of attack: the angle that the chord line of an airfoil makes with the oncoming fluid flow.

azimuthal: related to the angle \(\theta\) (cylindrical coordinates) or \(\phi\) (spherical coordinates); in both cases, the angle away from the \(x\) axis in the \(xy\) plane toward the \(y\) axis.

freestream: used in two ways to describe flows around objects, i.e., external flows. In specifying a problem, the freestream value of a quantity (usually \(\bar{u}\) or \(p\)) is the quantity infinitely far away from the object. In discussing the boundary layer adjacent to the object, freestream means the value just outside the boundary layer, which is often not equal to the value infinitely far from the object.

Editorial redraw note: NACA 2418 geometry reconstructed from the stated code. The printed angle range “15–−20°” remains unchanged because its endpoint/dash notation is ambiguous.


PDF page 314 — source_issue



Figure 9.4: Effects airfoils have on incident flow. (a): wing. (b): centrifugal pump. (c): Pelton turbine. (d): propeller.

Handwritten labels in Figure 9.4: panel (a), LOW PRESSURE and HIGH PRESSURE; panel (b), LOW PRESSURE, HIGH PRESSURE, IMPELLER, AIRFOIL, EYE, FLUID, ROTATION, and FLUID SPIRALS OUT; panel (c), LOW PRESSURE and HIGH PRESSURE are legible near the jet/turbine; panel (d) shows a propeller and streamlines.

When used as part of a turbomachine, the local action of the airfoil (accelerating fluid and changing local pressures) then leads to a device-level outcome, such as the pressure increase associated with a pump or propeller, or the pressure decrease associated with a turbine. The device-level outcomes we discussed in Chapter 2 are not exactly the same as the local changes of the airfoil, because the housing that contains the turbomachine also plays a role. Also, the airfoil locally causes some accelerations and pressure components that are undesirable or inefficient, and these result in undesired flow patterns (e.g., swirl after a propeller or wind turbine) or energy dissipated as heat. When used as part of a vehicle, the desired accelerations and pressures caused by the flow generate vehicle propulsion and control (e.g., the lift on an airplane wing), and the undesired accelerations and pressure generate losses that must be overcome by the engines (e.g., the drag on an airplane wing).

Airfoils, in summary, are carefully designed flat surfaces that turn fluid and generate force

So, an airfoil is a thin, streamlined object with a rounded leading edge and a sharp trailing edge, whose camber and angle of attack lead to the acceleration of oncoming fluid and attendant changes in pressure, each of which explain the forces the airfoil generates, which can be used for vehicle control, doing work on a fluid, or extracting energy from a fluid.

pump: usually an enclosed fluid machine that adds energy to a liquid, generating flow and pressure rise. The equivalent turbomachine driving a gas would normally be called a fan, blower, or compressor. However, the term pump is sometimes used as a completely general term for any turbomachine that adds energy to a fluid. Cf. turbine, which removes energy from a fluid.

turbine: a general term for any turbomachine that extracts energy from a fluid.

swirl: the azimuthal motion added to a fluid moving through a turbomachine by the rotary element.

camber: the curvature of the chord line of an airfoil.

Airfoil performance is often predicted well by irrotational flow theory

The engineering motivation of this chapter is airfoils and, more generally, the forces moving fluid makes on objects. The physics includes irrotational flow theory and a descriptive treatment of separation, downstream of which irrotational flow predictions are incorrect and unusable. The mathematics of this chapter first focuses on the vector calculus associated with incompressible irrotational flow, then uses separation of variables to find fundamental solutions to the 2D Laplace equation in terms of cylindrical harmonics.

Airfoils at high Reynolds numbers don’t make much of the fluid rotate

An airfoil operating correctly causes fluid to accelerate, but in the airfoil frame of reference, the airfoil for the most part does not cause the fluid to rotate, and the small regions of the flow in which the fluid rotates don’t make much difference in the airfoil’s desired outcome. To predict an airfoil’s performance, for example the lift on an airplane wing, we often use the equations of irrotational flow, which assume that fluid is not rotating at any point, i.e., \(\nabla\times\vec{u}=\vec{\omega}=0\). And we quantify the effect of the airfoil by quantifying the circulation caused by the airfoil, i.e., the degree to which the fluid is induced to move in a circle around the airfoil. This chapter provides the mathematical framework and solutions for irrotational flow.

An example of the solution of the irrotational flow equations around an airfoil is shown in Figure 9.5, p. 305, which shows 2D irrotational flow over a NACA4412 airfoil at an angle of attack of 10 degrees. There are a number of features of this flow that are typical for flow around an airfoil:

A streamline emanates from the sharp trailing edge, and the direction of the flow at the trailing edge is approximately in the direction of the chord at the trailing edge. This is commonly referred to as the Kutta condition. Accelerating around a sharp convex corner requires enormously high accelerations, which would require enormously high pressure gradients, and you can’t have an enormously high pressure gradient in a subsonic flow. So fluid always separates at a sharp convex corner.

The rounded leading edge has a stagnation point at which a streamline terminates at the wall. Whereas the downstream separation point is always at the sharp edge and not a function of the angle of attack, the location of this stagnation point is a function of the angle of attack.

Fluid is turned in a direction—in this case from ascending to descending—and there are pressure gradients consistent with the Euler equations. Where the fluid is turning, there is a pressure gradient pointing away from the center of curvature of the streamlines \(\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial n}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}\right)\). And, because the Bernoulli constant \(B=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2+\rho gz\) is uniform in the farfield and uniform everywhere in the flow, fluid moving fast with closely packed streamlines has a low pressure, and fluid moving slowly with wide-apart streamlines has a high pressure.

The engineering strategy behind an airfoil, then, is actually pretty simple. An airfoil is designed to turn fluid by making the flow separate at precisely one location—the sharp trailing edge. By turning the chord line of the airfoil

separation: when a streamline emanates normal to a surface. Most often, separation is used only to describe streamlines resulting from flow that moves upstream.

circulation: a measure of the total flow rotation in a closed region. Given by the line integral around a closed clockwise contour \(C\) of the velocity field: \(\Gamma=\oint_C\vec{u}\cdot d\vec{s}\). If the region is filled with fluid, circulation is related by Stokes’ theorem to the area integral of the vorticity in the enclosed area.

angle of attack: the angle that the chord line of an airfoil makes with the oncoming fluid flow.

Kutta condition: the experimental observation that a stagnation streamline will always emanate from a sharp trailing edge. The physical underpinnings of this are viscous, but this is used most to specify the circulation for an irrotational flow analysis of a lifting object.

convex: for a wall bounding a fluid, having a center of curvature inside the boundary.

chord: a straight line connecting the leading and trailing edges of an airfoil.

From the streamlines and velocity vectors, it is clear that the airfoil forces the flow to rise upstream of the airfoil, be turned by the airfoil, and descend downstream of the airfoil. A surface integral performed a distance away from the airfoil (for example, where the velocity vector arrows are) would primarily show positive fluid \(y\) momentum entering and negative fluid \(y\) momentum leaving, indicating that the fluid \(y\) momentum is decreased; the fluid is thrown downward and by Newton’s third law the airfoil feels an upward force. From the pressure isocontours, the pressure on the top of the airfoil is below \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\), whereas the pressure on the bottom of the airfoil is above \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\). relative to the oncoming flow, the airfoil attempts to turn the fluid by that angle. That leads to a force. A sharp corner at the trailing edge makes the flow separate at that point because the accelerations required to turn the corner are too large for the flow to remain attached. The rest of the airfoil is designed to have smooth, rounded surfaces and require only subtle accelerations from the fluid, so that the flow remains attached everywhere other than at the trailing edge. Any geometry that requires too much acceleration from the fluid because its radius of curvature is too small will lead to separation.

We use irrotational flow to estimate the lift on airfoils because it works and it is easy

Irrotational incompressible flow generates an enormous simplification because it lets us turn the equations of fluid mechanics into the Laplace equation, as long as we are willing to solve this equation for a carefully chosen scalar rather than for the vector velocity \(\vec{u}\). For incompressible, irrotational flow, the Laplace equation is satisfied by the streamfunction \(\psi\):

\nabla^2\psi=0, (9.1)

as well as by the velocity potential \(\phi\):

\nabla^2\phi=0, (9.2)

where the velocity \(\vec{u}\) can be calculated directly by taking the gradient of this velocity potential \(\vec{u}=\nabla\phi\) or the curl of a vector streamfunction \(\vec{u}=\nabla\times\psi\hat{z}\). If we want to determine the flow around an airfoil, we can solve the relatively easy equation \(\nabla^2\psi=0\) or \(\nabla^2\phi=0\). We can then calculate \(\vec{u}\) from \(\psi\) or \(\phi\). Figure 9.5, p. 305 is an example of a numerical solution of the Laplace equation for \(\phi\), which then can be used to calculate \(\vec{u}\), which can then be used to calculate \(p\) from the Bernoulli equation.

Irrotational flow also simplifies the calculation of the total force on an airfoil through the Kutta–Zhukovsky theorem, which relates the lift per unit depth on an airfoil to the fluid density, freestream fluid speed, and the circulation induced by the airfoil:

L'=-\rho U\Gamma. (9.3)

generates an enormous simplification because it lets us turn the equations of fluid mechanics into the Laplace equation, which is the same equation as from electricity and magnetism. This equation is easier to solve analytically and easier to solve computationally than other fluids equations. Analytically, we can create flowfields out of combinations of sources/sinks, vortexes, and doublets, which are similar to point charges and magnets. A source is a point singularity in which the flow expands, a vortex is a point singularity that causes the flow to move along a circular path (but not to rotate), and a doublet is like a tiny point propeller that sucks fluid in from one direction and shoots in out the other.

Viewed through this lens, an airfoil is defined fluid-mechanically by the space it takes up (which is defined by its doublet or its distribution of doublets) and the degree by which it makes fluid move along a circular path (which is defined by the vortex or distribution of vortexes buried inside the airfoil).

separate: the process by which a streamline emanates normal to a surface. Most often, separation is used only to describe streamlines resulting from flow that moves upstream.

attached: describing a flow locally, means having a velocity on the surface that runs parallel to the surface and has no stagnation point. Describing a flow globally, means the flow has no separation point associated with flow moving upstream.

Laplace equation: in general, \(\nabla^2\phi=0\). Satisfied by the streamfunction and velocity potential in irrotational flows. A linear, elliptic partial differential equation which is the easiest of all fluid-mechanical equations to solve.

Laplace equation for velocity potential for incompressible irrotational flow.

circulation: a measure of the total flow rotation in a closed region. Given by the line integral around a closed clockwise contour \(C\) of the velocity field: \(\Gamma=\int_C\vec{u}\,ds\). If the region is filled with fluid, circulation is related by Stokes’ theorem to the area integral of the vorticity in the enclosed area.

Kutta–Zhukovsky theorem for irrotational flow.

vortex: in irrotational flow: an idealized point or line doublet of vorticity. From the \(\lambda=0\) separation-of-variables solution of the Laplace equation. More generally: a region of vorticity.

Velocity fields are sometimes irrotational, and it is (comparatively) very easy to analyze fluid flows when this is the case

We find that in a number of special cases, fluid moves in an irrotational manner, meaning that no part of the fluid is rotating. Rotating has a precise mathematical definition which we will describe below.

For the most part, we find that if fluid is made to rotate, that rotation usually comes from interaction between the fluid and a solid wall. We can ensure that a domain of fluid doesn’t rotate if we stay upstream of walls or if the domain we care about is far enough from walls that the effect of the walls can be ignored. For example, considering the flow generated by a helicopter main rotor, although the flow below the main rotor is downstream of the rotor and is not remotely irrotational, the fluid above the rotor is upstream of the rotor and well approximated as irrotational. Also, flow over an airplane (except for the region proximal to the wall, say within 10 cm) is largely unaffected by the wall because the viscous effects at the wall diffuse into the flowfield slowly relative to the speed of the fast air rushing by, and the gross properties of the structure of the flow can be described by use of irrotational flow analysis. Because a significant fraction of mechanical engineering flows satisfy this condition, at least in some part of the domain, it is of engineering importance to consider flows that are not rotating. It is also convenient, because it turns out that analysis of flow that is not rotating is much easier than most other fluid mechanical analysis.

Irrotational flow is particularly useful for aerodynamic analysis of objects and vehicles, and we often use object frames of reference (see Sidebar 9.1, p. 308) when performing irrotational flow analysis.

Irrotational flow underpins all aerodynamic analysis and is the central tool that has been used to design every airplane in use today.

The premise, mathematical form, utility, and limitations of the irrotational flow model are summarized in Sidebar 9.2, p. 308.

Irrotational flow is defined mathematically by the equation

\nabla\times\vec{u}=\vec{\omega}=0, (9.11)

i.e., irrotational flow has no vorticity. Curl is reviewed and vorticity is defined in Sidebar 9.3 (p. 309), and an example vorticity calculation is shown in Example Problem 9.1 (p. 309).

Irrotational flows offer a number of compelling simplifications relative to flows with vorticity. In particular, we can solve for the velocity field \(\vec{u}\) of an irrotational flow without ever using conservation of momentum, i.e., without ever using Newton’s second law, i.e., without using dynamics of any kind. We can use entirely kinematic arguments to get the velocity field, and we need conservation of momentum only if we want to find the pressure field. The ability of conservation of mass and its kinematic result to define the velocity field of an irrotational flow is very important, because conservation of mass is much simpler than conservation of momentum, and we want to get as far with just conservation of mass as possible. The equations that govern irrotational flow are much easier than those for flow with vorticity.

This is worth repeating. For fixed-density irrotational flow, we can describe all of the velocities of a fluid flow without using any dynamical equations.

irrotational: not rotating, i.e., \(\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{u}=0\).

Sidebar 9.1: Engineering Models — Object frame of reference

Premise: an object is used as the frame of reference when it is moving relative to the lab frame

When an object is moving and we want to analyze the fluid mechanics associated with it, we find it much easier to choose a reference frame associated with the object.

Mathematical form: the object frame of reference defines the coordinate system relative to the object

The mathematical form of the definition of an object frame of reference is to align the coordinate frame with the object:

\vec{u}_{\mathrm{object}}=0. (9.4)

Utility: the object frame is what we use for vehicles and projectiles

When objects are moving in the lab reference frame (a car, a plane, a boat), using that object reference frame for the coordinate system makes things easy—the velocity at the wall is homogeneous (i.e., \(\vec{u}=0\)), the boundary condition is steady, the flow can be steady, etc.

Limitations: using a moving object as a frame of reference means the frame of reference might be accelerating, and it makes the velocity boundary condition at infinity nonhomogeneous

When a vehicle or projectile moves, the object frame of reference is easy to use, because the boundary conditions at the object are steady. But this makes the velocity at infinity nonzero, i.e., nonhomogeneous. Further, when the object accelerates, that means that the frame of reference is accelerating, and an accounting must be made for that. The simplest example of this is an object moving in a circle, which by definition must be experiencing a centripetal force.

Sidebar 9.2: Engineering Models — Irrotational Flow

Premise: At high Re, flow around an object has very little vorticity outside the boundary layer and wake

A number of situations involving high-Reynolds number flow over surfaces or flow far from surfaces result in flow with no rotational component in some domain of the flow, and these flow domains are relatively easy to analyze mathematically. Flow far from a surface is often irrotational: for example, for flow over a moving object, the farfield flow is uniform. A rotational component (vorticity) is introduced into a flow by fluid motion tangent to a surface combined with the no-slip condition, but the diffusion of this vorticity competes with the convection of the flow downstream. Some domains of the flow never see an appreciable effect of this vorticity.

Mathematical form: for irrotational flow \(\vec{\omega}=0\)

Irrotational flow assumes that there is no vorticity, i.e., \(\vec{\omega}=0\), or equivalently that the velocity can be represented in terms of a velocity potential:

\vec{\omega}=0;\qquad \vec{u}=\nabla\phi. (9.5)

Utility: the velocity field for incompressible irrotational flow can be solved by use of the Laplace Equation, which is relatively easy to solve analytically and computationally

Combining the potential form of \(\vec{u}\) with the conservation of mass relation (or definition of streamfunction with irrotationality) leads to the Laplace equation for streamfunction or velocity potential:

\nabla^2\phi=0;\qquad \nabla^2\psi=0. (9.6)

The Laplace equation is linear and elliptic and very easy to solve. Analytical Green’s function solutions in the form of Legendre polynomials exist, and numerical solutions of linear elliptic equations are easy and fast. A Laplace equation solution for fluid flow might take 5 orders of magnitude less time to simulate than a Navier–Stokes equations solution for turbulent flow.

Limitations: Irrotational flow doesn’t predict boundary layers, viscous drag, the Kutta condition, or separation

No nonzero fluid flow with any surface present is ever truly irrotational. However, many flows have a domain that is so close to irrotational that the approximations associated with irrotational flow are excellent. Unlike many other models (say the incompressible flow model), which can be regular approximations which are valid everywhere in a flow, the irrotational flow approximation is always singular, meaning it might be appropriate in part of the flow domain but it will never be appropriate everywhere in a flow. The irrotational flow approximation is never designed to properly describe all aspects of a flow. It is always meant to describe only part of a flowfield.

Because of this, an irrotational flow model is always just a partial description of a flowfield and irrotational flow analysis is stitched together with other models (often boundary-layer analysis) to get a full picture.

Irrotational flow can only be valid if the location in the flow is far enough from a wall that the vorticity generated at the wall is carried downstream before it can diffuse to that location. At high \(Re\), the fluid moves fast and diffuses slowly, and the vorticity diffuses only a very small distance from the wall before it is carried downstream. This thin layer is a boundary layer, and the irrotational flow approximation ignores the boundary layer entirely. There is a velocity gradient component normal to a surface which generates a tangential viscous stress at a surface; irrotational flow ignores this. Experimentally, we observe that flow over bluff bodies separates; irrotational flow ignores this. And experimentally, we observe that flow over an aerodynamic body has a streamline emanating from a sharp trailing edge (the Kutta condition); irrotational flow doesn’t specify where the separation streamline on an aerodynamic body is.

These limitations are serious, but they don’t make the irrotational flow model useless; they just place a spatial limit on its application in the flow field (far from the wall: away from boundary layers and wakes) and make the irrotational flow model good for part of an analysis (force on an aerodynamic object with attached flow caused by the pressure gradient) and bad for other things (viscous drag force; form drag in the presence of separation).
