Sidebar 9.3: Fundamentals — Curl and Vorticity

The curl of the velocity field describes the magnitude and direction of fluid rotation

\(\nabla\times\vec{u}\) is a pseudovector that points in the direction of the axis of rotation of a fluid:

\nabla\times\vec{u}=\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\right)\hat{x}+\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}-\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right)\hat{y}+\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\hat{z}, (9.7)

We use the term vorticity to describe this rotation—the vorticity \(\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{u}\). Vorticity is double the angular rotation rate of the fluid. The fluid rotates around this axis as prescribed by the right-hand rule. The curl of \(\vec{u}\) is a pseudovector, meaning that its sign is defined by the handedness of the coordinate system. This makes it almost as cool as a vector, but not quite as cool as a vector. The rotation-rate tensor \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) is an antisymmetric dyadic tensor that describes fluid rotation; its components are proportional to the components of the vorticity.

Whether a fluid is rotating and whether a fluid is moving in a circular orbit are completely unrelated

Vorticity (and, equivalently, the curl of \(\vec{u}\)) describe whether fluid is rotating. Rotation is different than motion in a circular orbit. Objects and fluids can rotate, or move in a circular orbit, or both, or neither. The center of a wheel on a car, for example, rotates while it moves in a straight line. The cabins on a Ferris wheel, for example, move in circular orbits but do not rotate.

The curl of the vector streamfunction can be used to define the velocity for a divergence-free flow

Incompressible flows, i.e., divergence-free flows, can define a 2-D vector velocity by use of a vector streamfunction:

\vec{u}=\nabla\times\psi\hat{z}=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\hat{x}-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\hat{y}. (9.8)

In fact, a 3D vector velocity can be defined in terms of cross products of two streamfunctions, but this ends up not being particularly useful.

Example Problem 9.1

Low-Reynolds number flow between two infinite plates, one motionless at \(y=0\) and one moving in the \(x\) direction at speed \(U\) at \(y=h\), is given by \(u=U\frac{y}{h}\). Does this flow have vorticity? If so, what is the vorticity and the angular rotation rate? Solution:

\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{u}=\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\right)\hat{x}+\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}-\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right)\hat{y}+\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\hat{z}, (9.9)

which simplifies to

\vec{\omega}=-\frac{U}{h}\hat{z}. (9.10)

Yes, there is vorticity. The fluid everywhere is rotating at an angular velocity of \(-\frac{U}{2h}\) rad/s around the \(z\) axis.


PDF page 321 — verified

Another result that is remarkable to me: the Bernoulli equation applies along any path in an irrotational flow, not just along a streamline. We show this result at the end of the chapter.

If a velocity field of an incompressible flow is irrotational, its velocity can be found by solving the Laplace Equation

When a velocity field of an incompressible flow is irrotational, we can determine the velocity field by solving only the Laplace equation. This is good news, because the Laplace equation is easier to solve than any other partial differential equation used in fluid mechanics.

The streamfunction satisfies the Laplace Equation for 2D irrotational flow

Consider the streamfunction \(\psi(x,y)\). Defining \(\vec{u}\) through the streamfunction guarantees that we satisfy continuity. What must be true about \(\psi\) to guarantee that a flow is irrotational? Recalling that \(u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\) and \(v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\), we calculate the curl of \(\vec{u}\):

\nabla\times\vec{u}=\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\hat{z}=-\left(\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y^2}\right)\hat{z}, (9.12)

and for a flow to be irrotational, the curl must be zero:

\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y^2}=0, (9.13)

or, equivalently,

\nabla^2\psi=0. (9.14)

For a 2D uniform-density flow to conserve mass, it must be definable by a streamfunction, and for that flow to be irrotational, the streamfunction must satisfy the Laplace equation.

Thus any \(\vec{u}\) defined by \(\psi\) where \(\nabla^2\psi=0\) conserves mass and has no rotation; a solution of \(\nabla^2\psi=0\) describes an incompressible, irrotational flow. As you know from MATH2930, a solution must satisfy both the governing equation and boundary conditions. So the boundary conditions will specify which of the infinite possibilities of solutions to the Laplace equation is appropriate in each specific case. To find an irrotational flow specified by boundary conditions, we must solve \(\nabla^2\psi=0\) as well as those boundary conditions. Once we know \(\psi\), we can directly calculate \(\vec{u}\), and because the Bernoulli equation applies everywhere in the flowfield, it is straightforward to use \(\vec{u}\) to calculate \(p\).

Boundary conditions for the streamfunction involve its derivatives along walls and at infinity

Irrotational flow can satisfy a number of boundary conditions:

Bernoulli equation: in differential form \(0=\frac{d}{ds}\left(p+\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2+\rho gz\right)\), in integral form: \(B=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2+\rho gz\), where \(B\) is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

irrotational: not rotating, i.e., \(\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{u}=0\).

Laplace equation: in general, \(\nabla^2\phi=0\). Satisfied by the streamfunction and velocity potential in irrotational flows. A linear, elliptic partial differential equation which is the easiest of all fluid-mechanical equations to solve.

continuity: when used to modify a field (e.g., “velocity continuity” or “pressure continuity”), this is a mathematical term that typically means that the field is continuous, and often used to indicate that a field has the same value on both sides of an interface. When used alone, this is a physical term which typically means “conservation of mass”. When used as continuity equation, synonymous with “conservation of mass equation”.

vorticity for 2D flow written in terms of the streamfunction.

zero curl condition expressed using streamfunction.

Laplace equation for streamfunction for 2D incompressible irrotational flow.

governing equation: a catchall for any equation that describes a physical process. In mechanical engineering, this often means conservation equations such as those for mass, momentum, and energy. These can be solved when coupled with boundary conditions.

boundary condition: a mathematical prescription of the conditions on flow parameters (e.g., \(\vec{u}\) or \(p\)) at the boundary of a fluid.

normal: orthogonal; perpendicular.


PDF page 322 — verified

In an irrotational flow, impermeable walls are streamlines; the fluid moves along the wall but not normal to the wall. Thus, at a wall, \(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial s}=0\), where \(s\) is the coordinate tangent to the wall. In other words, \(\psi\) is uniform along a surface.

In unbounded flows, we often have a velocity specified at infinity, which specifies the derivatives of \(\psi\) at infinity.

The velocity potential also satisfies the Laplace Equation for incompressible flow

It is a vector identity that the curl of the gradient of a scalar is zero (this comes from equality of mixed partials). Because of this, if we define the velocity field as the gradient of a scalar (we will call this scalar the velocity potential), we guarantee that the resulting velocity field must be curl-free (the gradient is reviewed in Sidebar 9.4, p. 312). As was the case with the definition of the streamfunction, the definition of the velocity potential describes the vector velocity field in terms of a single scalar, while simultaneously guaranteeing a vector property of the velocity field.

We define the scalar velocity potential \(\phi\) and relate it to the velocity by the relation:

\vec{u}=\nabla\phi;\qquad u=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x},\quad v=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y},\quad w=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}. (9.20)

Or, in cylindrical coordinates,

\vec{u}=\nabla\phi;\qquad u_r=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r},\quad u_\theta=\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\theta},\quad u_z=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}. (9.21)

This velocity potential is directly analogous to the electrical potential, i.e., the voltage, and the velocity is directly analogous to the electric field \(\vec{E}=-\nabla\phi\). See Sidebar 9.5 (p. 313).

The existence of a velocity potential guarantees irrotationality; to guarantee that a fluid is not expanding and therefore conserves mass at fixed density, the velocity potential must satisfy Laplace’s equation. The roles of streamfunction and velocity potential in generating the Laplace equation are summarized in Figure 9.6, p. 313. The velocity potential must satisfy the Laplace equation if an irrotational, incompressible flow is to satisfy conservation of mass. We can show this by setting the divergence of the velocity equal to zero:

\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0, (9.24)

and substituting in \(\vec{u}=\nabla\phi\):

\nabla\cdot\nabla\phi=0, (9.25)

leading to

\nabla^2\phi=0. (9.26)

Thus an irrotational flow that satisfies conservation of mass has a velocity potential that satisfies the Laplace equation.

Boundary conditions for the velocity potential involve its derivatives normal to walls and at infinity

Irrotational flow can satisfy a number of boundary conditions:

In an irrotational flow, impermeable walls are streamlines; the fluid cannot be moving normal to the wall. Thus, at a wall, \(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial n}=0\), where \(n\) is the coordinate normal to the wall.

equality of mixed partials: the notion that taking partial derivatives of a function with respect to one coordinate then a second coordinate is equivalent to taking the partial derivatives in the opposite order, e.g., \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y}=\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\partial x}\).

velocity potential: denoted \(\phi\). Scalar function that specifies the velocity through \(\vec{u}=\nabla\phi\). Irrotational flows can be defined by \(\phi(\vec{r})\) because the existence of \(\phi(\vec{r})\) is mathematically equivalent to specifying \(\nabla\times\vec{u}=0\).

Getting Lost in the Math Haiku: “my head hurts so much / when Kirby goes blah blah blah / about all the math.”

incompressible flow: implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Incompressible flow implies that the motion of the fluid does not cause density to change, in comparison to compressible flow in which fluid moves so quickly and the pressure changes so much that the density is perturbed enough to affect convective fluxes. Incompressible flows may still have nonuniform density, for example if the fluid’s temperature varies; this can affect the conservation of momentum equations. An incompressible flow does not imply that the fluid is mathematically incompressible, only that pressure-induced compression can be ignored. Cf. compressible flow.

Laplace equation for velocity potential for incompressible irrotational flow.

Laplace equation: in general, \(\nabla^2\phi=0\). Satisfied by the streamfunction and velocity potential in irrotational flows. A linear, elliptic partial differential equation which is the easiest of all fluid-mechanical equations to solve.

normal: orthogonal; perpendicular.

Sidebar 9.4: Fundamentals — Gradient

The gradient of a property is a generalized multivariable derivative of that property

The gradient of a scalar is a vector pointing in the direction in which the scalar is changing most rapidly, and has a magnitude equal to how fast the scalar changes in that direction. This is often most easily visualized by thinking of the scalar as an elevation, and thinking of the gradient at any point as pointing directly up the hill in the direction of maximum increase. The gradient of a scalar is a vector pointing in a direction that is normal to an isocontour of that scalar. The gradient of a vector is a dyadic that captures both the directionality of the original vector and the directionality of each component’s gradient.

The gradient of the pressure of a fluid is a vector denoting the net volumetric force on the fluid stemming from pressure variations

The negative gradient of pressure \( -\nabla p\) denotes the net volumetric pressure force on the fluid.

The gradient of the velocity potential is used to define the velocity for a potential flow

Irrotational flows, i.e., potential flows, define the vector velocity by use of a scalar quantity \(\phi\):

\vec{u}=\nabla\phi. (9.15)

One way of thinking about this is that the velocity potential is analogous to elevation, generating mountains and valleys, and the velocity of a fluid always points directly up the mountain.

The gradient takes different forms in different coordinate systems

We can write the gradient both in terms of components and unit vectors, and we can equivalently write it as a matrix representation, which is understood to be shorthand for the components and unit vectors. In Cartesian coordinates, the gradient of a scalar (for example \(\nabla p\)) and its matrix representation (here, \([\nabla p]\)) are:

\nabla p=\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\hat{x}+\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}\hat{y}+\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\hat{z},\qquad [\nabla p]=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial p}{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}. (9.16)

In cylindrical coordinates, the gradient of a scalar (for example \(\nabla\phi\)) and its matrix representation (here, \([\nabla\phi]_{r\theta z}\)) are:

\nabla\phi=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\hat{r}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\theta}\hat{\theta}+\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}\hat{z},\qquad [\nabla\phi]_{r\theta z}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\\ \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\theta}\\ \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}. (9.17)

The gradient of the velocity vector is a dyadic tensor called the velocity-gradient tensor

The velocity-gradient tensor \(\nabla\vec{u}\) is a dyadic tensor. The symmetric part of this tensor tells us how the fluid is being stretched and squeezed, and the antisymmetric part of this tensor tells us how the fluid is being rotated. The viscous stresses in a Newtonian fluid are proportional to the symmetric part of this tensor. The gradient of a vector (for example \(\nabla\vec{u}\)) can be written in terms of unit dyads. The gradient and its matrix representation are, in Cartesian coordinates:

\begin{aligned}\nabla\vec{u}={}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\hat{x}\hat{x}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\hat{y}\hat{x}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\hat{z}\hat{x}\\ \ &+\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\hat{x}\hat{y}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\hat{y}\hat{y}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\hat{z}\hat{y}\\ \ &+\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\hat{x}\hat{z}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\hat{y}\hat{z}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\hat{z}\hat{z},\qquad [\nabla\vec{u}]=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} (9.18)

The gradient of a vector (for example \(\nabla\vec{u}\)) and its matrix representation are, in cylindrical coordinates:

\begin{aligned}\nabla\vec{u}={}&\frac{\partial u_r}{\partial r}\hat{r}\hat{r}+\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial r}\hat{r}\hat{\theta}+\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial r}\hat{r}\hat{z}\\ \ &+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial u_r}{\partial\theta}\hat{\theta}\hat{r}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial\theta}\hat{\theta}\hat{\theta}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial\theta}\hat{\theta}\hat{z}\\ \ &+\frac{\partial u_r}{\partial z}\hat{z}\hat{r}+\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial z}\hat{z}\hat{\theta}+\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z}\hat{z}\hat{z},\qquad [\nabla\vec{u}]_{r\theta z}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial u_r}{\partial r}&\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial r}&\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial r}\\ \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial u_r}{\partial\theta}&\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial\theta}&\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial\theta}\\ \frac{\partial u_r}{\partial z}&\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial z}&\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} (9.19)

Editorial source note: Equation (9.19), retained literally above, omits derivatives of the cylindrical basis vectors. In the source’s row-as-derivative convention, the corrected cylindrical gradient matrix is shown below. The pressure force per unit volume is −∇p, as the following prose states; the sidebar heading’s description of ∇p as the force lacks that minus sign.

[\nabla\vec u]_{r\theta z}=\begin{bmatrix}\partial u_r/\partial r&\partial u_\theta/\partial r&\partial u_z/\partial r\\(\partial u_r/\partial\theta-u_\theta)/r&(\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta+u_r)/r&(\partial u_z/\partial\theta)/r\\ \partial u_r/\partial z&\partial u_\theta/\partial z&\partial u_z/\partial z\end{bmatrix}\quad\text{(editorial correction)}

Sidebar 9.5: Fundamentals — Analogy between potential flow and electrostatics

Potential flow for irrotational flowfields is analogous to electrostatics

In MAE3230, we define the velocity potential as:

\vec{u}=\nabla\phi, (9.22)

where \(\phi\) is the velocity potential and \(\vec{u}\) is the velocity. This solution is valid for irrotational flow because by definition \(\nabla\times\vec{u}=\nabla\times\nabla\phi=0\). It is consistent with a flow with no vorticity. In PHYS2213, you probably defined the electrical potential as

\vec{E}=-\nabla\phi, (9.23)

where \(\vec{E}\) is the electric field and \(\phi\) is the electrical potential, i.e., voltage. This definition is analogous to that of the velocity potential but has a different sign. Current flows from high voltage to low; but the fluid velocity vector points from low potential to high (in all honesty, fluid mechanicians basically got the sign wrong, and we are stuck with it). The electric field has no curl, which is why it is conveniently expressed in terms of an electrical potential. This is true for all electrostatic fields, but only some fluid flows. In your physics class, they may not have spent much time on the details of the electric field being curl-free. In fluids, we have to make this distinction clear, because many flows have vorticity and the notion of a velocity potential is incorrect if vorticity exists in a fluid.

There are analogies between divergence of the electric field in electrostatics and the velocity field in potential flow. If density is fixed, there is no net expansion in a fluid, which means \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0\), whereas if there is no free charge, then Gauss’s law says \(\nabla\cdot\vec{E}=0\). There are also analogies in the boundary conditions for Laplace equation for electrostatics and for potential flow. The potential flow boundary condition at an impermeable wall is \(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial n}=0\), where \(n\) is the coordinate normal to the wall. The electrostatic boundary condition at an insulating wall is \(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial n}=0\).

Electric fields can be used to drive fluid flows. One example of this is electroosmotic flow, which describes the motion of fluid relative to solid surfaces caused by an externally applied electric field and usually driven by surface charge at the wall. In some electroosmotic flows, there is a direct proportionality between the applied electric field and the local velocity, and the local fluid velocity is given by \(\vec{u}=-\frac{\epsilon\zeta}{\mu}\vec{E}\), where \(\epsilon\) is the electrical permittivity of the fluid, \(\zeta\) is the electrical potential at the solid–liquid interface, \(\mu\) is the viscosity of the fluid, and \(\vec{E}\) is the local electric field.

Figure 9.6 concept-map labels: “Define a streamfunction in 2D”; “Require that the flow be irrotational, i.e., curl-free”; “Assume conservation of mass, i.e., divergence-free velocity”; “Streamfunction must satisfy Laplace equation”; “Assume flow is irrotational, i.e., curl-free velocity”; “Require that the flow conserve mass, i.e., be divergence-free”; “Assume flow is irrotational and define a velocity potential”; “Velocity potential must satisfy Laplace equation”; “IRROTATIONAL FLOW”; “DIVERGENCE-FREE FLOW”.



Figure 9.6: Concept map: divergence, curl, and how we show that the velocity potential and streamfunction both satisfy the Laplace equation.

u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y},\quad v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x},\quad \nabla\times\vec u=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \nabla^2\psi=0;\qquad \vec u=\nabla\phi,\quad\nabla\cdot\vec u=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \nabla^2\phi=0.

Example Problem 9.2

Consider a 2D irrotational flow of fluid moving at a uniform velocity \(\vec{u}=U\hat{x}\) over a circular cylinder with radius \(a\) whose center is at the origin of the \(xy\) plane. Prescribe the boundary conditions that the streamfunction must satisfy to solve for the \(\psi\) that defines this velocity field. The same problem can be framed in terms of the velocity potential. Prescribe the boundary conditions that the velocity potential must satisfy to solve for the \(\phi\) that defines this velocity field.

Solution: This problem is most conveniently solved with a combination of Cartesian and cylindrical coordinates. At infinity, \(u=U\) and \(v=0\), so \(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}=U\) and \(-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}=0\). Thus at infinity

\psi(r=\infty)=Uy+C_1. (9.27)

At the surface of the cylinder \((r=a)\), \(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial s}\equiv\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\theta}=0\). So the boundary conditions are

\psi(r=\infty)=Uy+C_1,\qquad \left.\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\theta}\right|_{r=a}=0. (9.28)

In terms of velocity potential, the process is analogous. At infinity, \(u=U\) and \(v=0\), so \(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}=U\) and \(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}=0\). Thus at infinity

\phi(r=\infty)=Ux+C_2. (9.29)

At the surface of the cylinder \((r=a)\), \(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial n}\equiv\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}=0\). So the boundary conditions are

\phi(r=\infty)=Ux+C_2,\qquad \left.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right|_{r=a}=0. (9.30)

In unbounded flows, we often have a velocity specified at infinity, which specifies the derivatives of \(\phi\) at infinity. Example Problem 9.2 (p. 314) gives an example of prescribing boundary conditions in terms of \(\psi\) and \(\phi\).

The streamfunction and velocity potential help to visualize fluid flows

For all 2D flows, the streamfunction helps to visualize flows because isocontours of the streamfunction are streamlines of the flow, i.e., curves everywhere tangent to the local fluid velocity.

For irrotational flows, the velocity potential helps to visualize flows because isocontours of the velocity potential are everywhere normal to the fluid velocity and therefore normal to the streamlines.

See Figure 9.7, p. 316, in which the streamlines and isopotentials are sketched for irrotational flow over a circular cylinder where \(\vec{u}=U_\infty\hat{x}\) and \(p=p_\infty\) far from the cylinder. This flow is a solution of the Laplace equation given boundary conditions \(u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}=U_\infty\) at \(r\to\infty\) and \(u_r=\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\theta}=0\) at \(r=a\). The solution is

\phi(r,\theta)=U_\infty r\left(1+\frac{a^2}{r^2}\right)\cos\theta, (9.31)

Annotations to equation 9.31: “change due to cylinder” points to the \(a^2/r^2\) term; “uniform-flow part” points to the \(1\) term.

isocontour: a curve along which a property is uniform.

velocity potential: denoted \(\phi\). Scalar function that specifies the velocity through \(\vec{u}=\nabla\phi\). Irrotational flows can be defined by \(\phi(\vec{r})\) because the existence of \(\phi(\vec{r})\) is mathematically equivalent to specifying \(\nabla\times\vec{u}=0\).

Editorial source clarification: The inline polar-coordinate relations omit a scale factor. In general, \(u_r=\partial\phi/\partial r=(1/r)\partial\psi/\partial\theta\), and along the cylinder wall \(\partial\psi/\partial s=(1/a)\partial\psi/\partial\theta\). The printed equalities without these factors remain above. Because both derivatives are set to zero at the impermeable wall, the zero-velocity boundary conditions (9.28) and (9.30) are unchanged.

\psi(r,\theta)=U_\infty r\left(1-\frac{a^2}{r^2}\right)\sin\theta, (9.32)

u_r=U_\infty\left(1-\frac{a^2}{r^2}\right)\cos\theta, (9.33)

u_\theta=-U_\infty\left(1+\frac{a^2}{r^2}\right)\sin\theta. (9.34)

In each of the solutions above, the first term corresponds to the uniform flow defined by the boundary conditions at infinity, whereas the second term describes the disturbance in the flow caused by the cylinder. For the pressure:

p=p_\infty+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_\infty^2\left(2\frac{a^2}{r^2}\cos 2\theta-\frac{a^4}{r^4}\right). (9.35)

Annotations to equation 9.35: “ambient pressure” points to \(p_\infty\); “change caused by cylinder” points to the pressure correction term.

There are many immediate physical interpretations we can make for any flowfield visualized in this way.

The fluid velocity is everywhere tangent to streamlines, i.e., \(\psi\) isocontours.

The fluid velocity is everywhere normal to isopotentials, i.e., \(\phi\) isocontours.

If streamlines are plotted at equal spacings in \(\psi\), the areal flowrate in between any two streamlines is the same everywhere in the flowfield.

Streamlines and isopotentials intersect at right angles.

The flowfield in Figure 9.7, p. 316 affords the opportunity to make a number of specific physical interpretations as well:

Assuming that gravity is not a factor, the pressure in the front and back of the cylinder must be higher than \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\), as streamlines curve away from those locations (recall Euler’s equation for the normal coordinate: \(\frac{\partial p}{\partial n}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}\), where \(R\) is the radius of curvature and \(\hat{n}\) points toward the center of curvature).

The pressure at the shoulders of the cylinder (i.e., top and bottom in this figure) must be lower than \(p_{\mathrm{atm}}\), as streamlines curve toward the cylinder shoulders.

Per the Bernoulli equation, the low-pressure region at the shoulders must have the highest fluid speed of any region of this flow, because the Bernoulli constant is uniform everywhere in this flow.

The region at the shoulders must coincide with a high fluid speed, because the areal flowrate between streamlines is the same everywhere, and the streamlines near the shoulders are close to each other.

Per the Bernoulli equation, the high-pressure region at the front and back of the cylinder must coincide with the lowest fluid speed of any region in this flow, because the Bernoulli constant is uniform everywhere in this flow. The speed goes to zero (and pressure to its maximum) at the stagnation point.

streamfunction for irrotational flow at speed \(U_\infty\) around a circular cylinder of radius \(a\).

radial velocity for irrotational flow at speed \(U_\infty\) around a circular cylinder of radius \(a\).

azimuthal velocity for irrotational flow at speed \(U_\infty\) around a circular cylinder of radius \(a\).

pressure for irrotational flow at speed \(U_\infty\) around a circular cylinder of radius \(a\).

isocontour: a curve along which a property is uniform.

isopotential: a curve along which the velocity potential is uniform.

areal: related to area, or per unit area.

shoulder: on an object immersed in a fluid flow, the surfaces at the widest point measured normal to the prevailing fluid velocity.

Bernoulli constant: the constant \(B\) in the Bernoulli equation \(B=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2+\rho gz\). A measure of the energy per unit volume of the fluid. Synonymous with total pressure.

stagnation point: a point in a flow where the velocity is zero.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.


PDF page 327 — verified

The region at the front and back of the cylinder must coincide with a low fluid speed, because the areal flowrate between streamlines is the same everywhere, and the streamlines near the front and back are far from each other.

The streamlines in front of the cylinder are diverging as we move downstream, which means the fluid is expanding in the \(y\) direction and contracting in the \(x\) direction. The expansion rate in \(y\) is exactly counterbalanced by the contraction in \(x\) (this is what \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=0\) means).

The streamlines in back of the cylinder are converging as we move downstream, which means the fluid is contracting in the \(y\) direction and expanding in the \(x\) direction. The contraction rate in \(y\) is exactly counterbalanced by the expansion in \(x\) (this is, again, what \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=0\) means).

All of these conclusions can be quantitatively confirmed by plugging flowfield locations into the formulas for \(\psi\), \(\phi\), \(\vec{u}\), and \(p\) above. For example, at the surface of the cylinder \((r=a)\), the velocity component normal to the surface is zero \((u_r=0)\), and the velocity component tangent to the surface is \(-2U_\infty\sin\theta\). The surface-tangent velocity component at the stagnation points \((\theta=0,\pi)\) is zero. At the shoulders \((\theta=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2})\), the surface-tangent velocity component has magnitude \(2U_\infty\). The maximum pressure is found at \((r=a,\theta=0,\pi)\) and is \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac{1}{2}\rho U_\infty^2\). The minimum pressure is found at \((r=a,\theta=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2})\) and is \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}-\frac{3}{2}\rho U_\infty^2\).

The claim that the solution above satisfies the Laplace equation can be confirmed by plugging the solutions for \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) into the 2D cylindrical Laplace equation, e.g.:

\nabla^2\phi=\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right)+\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial\theta^2}=0. (9.36)

Analytical and numerical solutions to the Laplace Equation are relatively easy to find

The Laplace equation is a linear elliptic equation; because it is linear, it affords superposition of solutions (remember MATH2930, separation of variables, superposing homogeneous solutions to differential equations...). Because it is elliptic, it is very stable when solved numerically. It is also amenable to very fast numerical solution techniques. Overall, the Laplace equation is essentially the best possible differential equation to have to solve. Solutions of the Laplace equation for aeronautical design were common even in the 1960s, one or two decades before people had computers in their homes and only a decade and a half after ENIAC.

A program like XFOIL can predict the lift coefficient on an airfoil in less than 10 seconds because it uses the solutions we derive in the next few pages

XFOIL uses the solutions we derive in the next few pages to predict the lift and drag on an airfoil. Although there is more to it than we describe here, most of the analysis comprises a vortex-panel analysis of the airfoil. A vortex-panel analysis breaks the airfoil surface into chunks called panels, and replaces the wall with a vortex as described by Equation (9.53) (Figure 9.8, p. 318). A vortex-panel analysis then calculates how strong each vortex needs to be to reproduce the flow around the airfoil. Because this process only involves adding together known solutions, it is computationally very efficient.

Although we will detail some general analytical solutions below, we don’t want to get too bogged down in the general analytical solutions. Some key takeaways are:

The solution for uniform flow is easy to determine.

Separation of variables in Cartesian coordinates is mathematically straightforward but not very useful, because we don’t build rectangular airplanes or have many irrotational flows in rectangular ducts.

Separation of variables in cylindrical coordinates leads to a big long equation, but we only have to look at a couple of the terms to get useful solutions.

The cylindrical solutions help us figure out flow over circular cylinders, rotating flow in tornadoes and hurricanes and toilets, and the flow inside a reservoir that leads to exit through an orifice.

Numerical solutions to the Laplace Equation are straightforward to code in MATLAB, C, or even Excel, and commercial solvers easily solve the Laplace Equation

Commercial packages like COMSOL (and a million others) can solve the Laplace equation quite easily. This class does not detail numerical methods,

Footnote 1: Technically it isn’t exactly a point vortex, it is a distributed line of vorticity, but we needn’t get every detail correct.

elliptic: for a 2D PDE of form \(A\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+B\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x\partial y}+C\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}+D\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+E\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+Fu+G\), one where \(B^2-4AC<0\). Corresponds to physical phenomena (e.g., diffusion) in which information propagates infinitely fast and a change in the system in one place affects all other places simultaneously.

lift: the component of a force a fluid exerts on an immersed object that is normal to the flow.

drag: the component of a force a fluid exerts on an immersed object that is tangent to the flow.

irrotational flow: flow in which \(\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{u}=0\). The terms irrotational flow (\(\vec{\omega}=0\)) and potential flow (\(\vec{u}=\nabla\phi\)) are synonymous—one implies the other.

But more information on numerical solutions for fluid mechanics is given in MAE4230. For airfoils, XFOIL is a long-standing shareware package that solves the Laplace Equation by use of vortex-panel techniques.

The Laplace Equation can be solved by separation of variables, and several of the simplest analytical solutions immediately give solutions to real flows and object geometries

One solution is simple: the Laplace equation is a homogeneous 2nd-order equation with only second-order derivatives, and any linear function is a solution (e.g., \(\phi=x\) or \(\psi=y\)). Any \(\phi\), for example, varying linearly in a direction corresponds to a uniform flow in that direction, and that flow satisfies the Laplace equation. Any \(\psi\) that varies linearly in a direction corresponds to a uniform flow at right angles to that direction.

The harder solutions are the nonlinear solutions.

When the geometry has Cartesian symmetry, we can solve the Laplace equation by separating variables in x and y

Separation of variables in \(x\) and \(y\) makes sense if the geometry has Cartesian symmetry, for example if there is a rectangular object. That actually is not that common, so this section is here not because we use Cartesian separation of variables much, but because seeing the Cartesian form sometimes helps students get their head around the cylindrical form, which can be harder to manipulate. We use the solutions in the next section way more often than those in this section.

If we consider the Laplace equation in 2D:

\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial y^2}=0, (9.37)

and try a solution of form \(\phi(x,y)=X(x)Y(y)\), we find that

\frac{d^2X}{dx^2}=\lambda^2X (9.38)

and

\frac{d^2Y}{dy^2}=-\lambda^2Y, (9.39)

which gives a general solution

X=D\cosh\lambda x+E\sinh\lambda x (9.40)

and

Y=F\cos\lambda y+G\sin\lambda y. (9.41)

The general solutions with \(\lambda\ne0\) are useful for irrotational flows in finite domains, especially rectangular domains. For \(\lambda=0\), there also is the solution that any linear function of \(x\) and/or \(y\) satisfies the equation—these solutions are useful for irrotational flows in infinite domains. Thus a general solution is:

\phi(x,y)=A+Bx+Cy+Dxy+\sum_{\lambda\ne0}(E\cosh\lambda x+F\sinh\lambda x)(G\cos\lambda y+H\sin\lambda y). (9.42)

The domain itself will specify what \(\lambda\)’s are possible. The terms in this equation correspond to solutions as follows:

Annotations to equation 9.42: “doesn’t matter” under \(A\); “uniform flows” under the linear \(Bx+Cy\) terms; “stagnation flow” under \(Dxy\); “solutions for rectangular domains” over the summation terms.

separation of variables: a method of solving a partial differential equation in which a function of multiple variables is assumed to be the product of multiple single-variable functions, so that functional dependences of variables can be separated on different sides of equations.

A doesn’t matter because only derivatives of \(\phi\) make any difference.

The \(B\) and \(C\) terms correspond to linear solutions; they describe uniform flow. For example, \(\phi = Bx\) corresponds to a uniform flow with speed \(B\) in the \(x\) direction.

The \(D\) term corresponds to a stagnation flow in which flow approaches the origin from the upper left and lower right and exits at upper right and lower left. This flow, for example, is plotted in Figure 8.6, p. 283.

The \(E\), \(F\), \(G\), and \(H\) terms we will not use in this class. They are rarely used for potential flow.

When the geometry has cylindrical symmetry, we can solve the Laplace equation by separating variables in \(r\) and \(\theta\)

Separation of variables in \(r\) and \(\theta\) makes sense if the geometry has cylindrical symmetry, for example if there is a circular object or a point singularity. If we consider the Laplace equation in cylindrical 2D coordinates:

\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right)+\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial\theta^2}=0, (9.43)

and try a solution of form \(\phi(r,\theta)=R(r)\Theta(\theta)\), we find that

r\frac{d}{dr}\left(r\frac{dR}{dr}\right)=\lambda^2R (9.44)

and

\frac{d^2\Theta}{d\theta^2}=-\lambda^2\Theta (9.45)

must both be satisfied. The \(\Theta(\theta)\) equation leads to sine and cosine solutions, and the \(R(r)\) equation leads to polynomial solutions with both positive and negative exponents. Also, for \(\lambda=0\), the \(R(r)\) equation leads to a natural logarithm solution with a constant and the \(\Theta(\theta)\) equation allows for a linear solution with a constant. Adding all of these solutions up, the general solution is:

\phi(r,\theta)=A+B\ln r+C\theta+\sum_{\lambda=1}\left[(E_\lambda r^\lambda+F_\lambda r^{-\lambda})(G_\lambda\cos\lambda\theta+H_\lambda\sin\lambda\theta)\right], (9.46)

Annotations to equation 9.46: “\(\lambda=0\); R eqn” under \(B\ln r\); “\(\lambda=0\) eqn” above \(C\theta\); “R solutions” under the radial terms; “\(\Theta\) solutions” over the angular terms.

where the \(\lambda\)’s are positive integers. One of these constants is also redundant (we only really need three of the set of \(E\), \(F\), \(G\), and \(H\)). Although we write a solution above for \(\phi\), one could equivalently write the same general form for \(\psi\)—it satisfies the same equation as \(\phi\), but of course \(\psi\) has different boundary conditions.

Unlike the Cartesian solutions, which weren’t immediately useful to us, this general solution immediately solves fluid mechanics problems:

The \(A\) term doesn’t matter because only derivatives of \(\phi\) make any difference.

The \(B\) term describes irrotational flow exiting a point source of mass or entering a point sink of mass. If reporting the solution in terms of \(\phi\), setting \(B=\frac{\Lambda}{2\pi}\) corresponds to a point sink absorbing an areal flowrate of \(\Lambda\). It approximates, for example, the flow inside a reservoir as it approaches an orifice issuing a free jet, or the flow you generate outside your mouth if you purse your lips and suck air in, or the flow above a quadcopter propeller if you view the propeller from far away.

The \(C\) term describes an “irrotational vortex”, which is what you get if you insert a cylinder with infinitesimal radius in the flow and rotate it infinitely fast. If reporting the solution in terms of \(\phi\), setting \(C=-\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\) corresponds to a point irrotational vortex generating a clockwise circulation with magnitude \(\Gamma\). This describes the circular orbits observed in tornadoes and hurricanes and toilets.

There is a \(D\theta\ln r\) term in theory, but it doesn’t matter because it describes velocities that are multiply valued and nonphysical (velocities have to be the same for \(\theta=0\) as they are for \(\theta=2\pi\), for example, which this term doesn’t satisfy). I didn’t write this term above because I couldn’t fit it on the line.

The \(F_1\) and \(G_1\) terms multiplied together describe a point doublet aligned along the \(x\) axis. This describes the way potential flow is affected by the presence of a circular physical obstacle. For the \(\phi\) solution, setting \(F_1G_1=\frac{\kappa}{2\pi}\) generates a doublet of strength \(\kappa\), and if there is a uniform flow at speed \(U\), a doublet of strength \(\kappa=2\pi Ua^2\) will help describe flow around a circular cylinder of radius \(a\). Flow around circular cylinders are important because we build many circular-cylinder-shaped things and we need to know the aerodynamic forces on them.

We won’t discuss anything else.

Sinks and sources can describe flow entering or exiting from small orifices

Sinks are excellent approximations of flow entering a small orifice, because the flow entering an orifice tends to be irrotational. Sources are usually poor approximations of flow exiting a small orifice, because flow exiting an orifice tends to have vorticity. The terms source and sink have essentially the same mathematical form; we use source to denote \(\Lambda>0\) and sink to denote \(\Lambda<0\).

As described above, one solution of the 2D Laplace equation is a point source or sink, described by the \(B=\frac{\Lambda}{2\pi}\) solution for the velocity potential or the \(C=\frac{\Lambda}{2\pi}\) solution for the streamfunction:

\phi=\frac{\Lambda}{2\pi}\ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\frac{\Lambda}{2\pi}\ln r, (9.47)

and

Vortex: in irrotational flow: an idealized point or line doublet of vorticity. From the \(\lambda=0\) separation-of-variables solution of the Laplace equation. More generally: a region of vorticity.

Circulation: a measure of the total flow rotation in a closed region. Given by the line integral around a closed clockwise contour \(C\) of the velocity field: \(\Gamma=\int_C\vec{u}\,ds.\) If the region is filled with fluid, circulation is related by Stokes’ theorem to the area integral of the vorticity in the enclosed area.

Doublet: an idealized point (in 2D) or line (in 3D) source of flow polarity. From the \(\lambda=1\) separation-of-variables solution of the Laplace equation.

Source: an idealized point or line source of volumetric flow. From the \(\lambda=0\) separation-of-variables solution of the Laplace equation.

Irrotational vortexes can describe flow in tornadoes and toilet bowls

Even though tornadoes and toilet bowls involve flows with circular orbits, the flow inside them is mostly or entirely irrotational. Because of this, irrotational vortexes approximate these flows well.

As described above, one solution of the Laplace equation is a point vortex, described by the \(C=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\) solution for the velocity potential or the \(B=-\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\) solution for the streamfunction.

\phi=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\theta, (9.53)

where atan2 denotes the four-quadrant inverse tangent, which is similar to \(\arctan(y/x)\) but defined from 0 to \(2\pi\). In terms of streamfunction,

\psi=-\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=-\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\ln r. (9.54)

The velocities are

u=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, (9.55)

v=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}, (9.56)

u_r=0, (9.57)

Irrotational: not rotating, i.e., \(\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{u}=0\).

Circulation

Circulation describes to what extent fluid has net clockwise or counterclockwise motion along a closed contour. The definition of the circulation \(\Gamma\) is

\Gamma=\oint_C\vec{u}\cdot d\vec{s}, (9.59)

Equation 9.59 annotations: “counterclockwise integral around closed contour” over the integral; “circulation” under \(\Gamma\); “component of fluid velocity moving along contour” under \(\vec{u}\cdot d\vec{s}\).

where \(C\) is a closed counterclockwise contour around a control volume and \(d\vec{s}\) is a differential vector length along the contour \(C\). This is a right-handed definition: if the thumb of one’s right hand points in the direction of the normal to the plane in which this integral is being performed, the fingers point in the counterclockwise direction. For the \(xy\) plane, the normal to the plane is the positive \(z\) direction and the counterclockwise direction is the positive \(\theta\) azimuthal direction. Circulation is a holistic measure of how much the fluid is moving in a counterclockwise direction along that path. It does not directly measure whether the fluid is locally rotating as it moves around the contour, but it does measure whether the fluid has net counterclockwise motion around a loop. Circulation has units of \(\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}\); equivalently velocity \(\times\) length; equivalently vorticity \(\times\) area.

For any domain entirely filled with fluid, Stokes’ theorem relates the circulation to the area integral of the vorticity

Recall the divergence theorem, which related the volume integral of the local fluid expansion \((\nabla\cdot\vec{u})\) to the net outflow at the control surface. Stokes’ theorem has function similar to the divergence theorem, in that it relates the integrated vorticity to the net circulation at the control surface. Stokes’ theorem is

\int_A(\nabla\times\vec{u})\cdot\hat{n}\,dA=\int_C\vec{u}\cdot\hat{s}\,ds, (9.60)

Equation 9.60 annotations: “vorticity” over the area-integral integrand; “integral over area inside contour” under the left integral; “circulation” under the contour integral.

where \(A\) is a 2D control volume and \(dA\) is a differential area. The unit normal vector \(\hat{n}\) defines the counterclockwise direction of the contour integral. Just as the divergence theorem related local fluid expansion to the net outflow, Stokes’ theorem relates local fluid rotation inside the control volume to the net counterclockwise motion at the control surface.

Fluid rotation and fluid circulation are different concepts, but they are related by Stokes’ equation

Circulation is a measure of whether fluid is moving in a net clockwise direction along a path. It does not imply anything about whether the fluid at the control surface is rotating. Vorticity is a local measure of whether fluid is locally rotating. For a domain filled with fluid, Stokes’ theorem relates these two—it says that, even though the extent to which a fluid moves counterclockwise around a path doesn’t tell you whether fluid at the control surface is rotating, it does tell you what the sum of all the vorticity is within the control volume.

The link (Stokes’ equation) between circulation and vorticity is broken by the presence of a solid object inside a control volume

Stokes’ theorem only applies if the domain is continuously filled with fluid. As soon as there is a solid object inside the fluid, there is no theorem that specifies the relation between the fluid vorticity and the circulation around a control volume. Because of this, an entirely irrotational flow can still have circulation around a contour, as long as there is an object inside the contour. This is consistent with the notion that an object (e.g., an airfoil) can make fluid have circulation, even in irrotational flow. No irrotational flow analysis alone can predict what circulation will be observed around an object; the circulation is always a consequence of viscous effects near the surface.

The lift on an object in an irrotational flow is given by the Kutta–Zhukovsky theorem

Kutta–Zhukovsky theorem: it isn’t really hard, but to derive it teaches intro applied math more than it teaches intro fluid mechanics. The Kutta–Zhukovsky theorem relates, in an irrotational flow, the circulation around an object to the lift force it feels:

Handwritten annotation beside the Kutta–Zhukovsky heading: “We will not derive the”.

L'=-\rho U_\infty\Gamma, (9.61)

where \(U_\infty\) is the fluid speed (assumed positive in \(x\) direction), \(\Gamma\) is the circulation (positive counterclockwise), and \(L'\) is the magnitude of the lift force (positive in \(y\) direction) per unit depth normal to the flow. It could be written more generally as

\vec{F}'=\rho\vec{\Gamma}\times\vec{u}. (9.62)

where \(\vec{\Gamma}\) points in the direction of the net circulation. The Kutta–Zhukovsky theorem can be used to evaluate the force on an object through a velocity integral around a contour. It correctly gives the lift force per unit depth as long as there are no viscous effects at the contour or anywhere outside the contour. In real flows with viscous effects, fluid flow is never irrotational everywhere; however, the domain in which viscous effects is important is very thin at high Reynolds numbers for streamlined objects. In cases with highly localized vorticity, the Kutta–Zhukovsky theorem can still be used by considering a contour that is close to the surface of the object but just far enough away from the surface to avoid all of the viscous effects.

Editorial source clarification: In (9.60), the faded operator in the source’s expanded vorticity expression is restored as \(\nabla\times\vec u\). Equation (9.62) prints \(\rho\vec\Gamma\times\vec u\), but this reverses the force sign relative to (9.61) with the stated right-handed, counterclockwise-positive circulation: for \(\vec\Gamma=\Gamma\hat z\) and \(\vec u=U_\infty\hat x\), it gives positive y force. The consistent vector force on the body is \(\vec F^{\prime}=\rho\vec u_\infty\times\vec\Gamma\). The printed formula is retained. Stokes’ theorem can still be applied to a fluid region with an internal hole when its inner boundary circulation is included; it does not simply cease to apply in multiply connected fluid domains.

The basic idea of irrotational flow is that

Irrotational flow happens sometimes, especially if there are large parts of our flow unaffected by the presence of walls.

Assuming \(\nabla\times\vec{u}=\vec{\omega}=0\) greatly restricts the possible \(\vec{u}\) solutions, and makes the governing equation a Laplace equation for a scalar, which is relatively easy to solve.

We can determine \(\vec{u}\) in these cases without using \(F=ma\), only solving the Laplace equation.

The Laplace equation is pretty easy to solve using MATH2930 techniques, and several simple analytical solutions immediately help us understand some important fluid flows. Solutions we want to find take seconds.

We need to use \(F=ma\) (in the form of the Bernoulli equation) only if we want to also determine the pressure, and even if we need this, the two equations (conservation of mass and conservation of momentum) are decoupled—we can solve one, then solve the other. Nothing later will be this easy.

Irrotational flow gives one description of the pressure distribution, but we need to understand other dominant features that control pressure forces on objects moving through fluid

The irrotational flow equations give us a first technique for describing forces on objects moving through fluid. Irrotational flow leads to analytical solutions for some geometries, and efficient computational approaches for the rest. With irrotational flow equations, we can calculate an estimated pressure field and predict the force on an object that comes from the pressure distribution (\(\vec{F}_p\)), by taking the surface of the object as the control surface \(S\) and integrating the pressure:

\vec{F}_p=-\int_S p\hat{n}\,dA, (9.71)

Equation 9.71 annotations: “net force from the pressure distribution” over \(\vec{F}_p\); “net pressure surface stress integrated over control surface” under the integral.

However, there are two important limitations. First, the force from the pressure is not the only force; there are viscous stresses at the surface which also generate forces on the object. For the moment, we will ignore viscous stresses and discuss them instead in Chapter 10. Second, the irrotational flow model breaks down everywhere the fluid is caused to rotate. Streamlined bodies often experience this breakdown only in a very thin boundary layer, and when that is the case, irrotational flow analysis gives a

Irrotational flow: flow in which \(\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{u}=0\). The terms irrotational flow \(\vec{\omega}=0\) and potential flow \(\vec{u}=\nabla\phi\) are synonymous—one implies the other.

Laplace equation: in general, \(\nabla^2\phi=0\). Satisfied by the streamfunction and velocity potential in irrotational flows. A linear, elliptic partial differential equation which is the easiest of all fluid-mechanical equations to solve.

Bernoulli equation: in differential form \(0=\nabla\left(p+\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2+\rho gz\right)\), in integral form: \(B=p+\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2+\rho gz\), where \(B\) is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

Girl Explaining Meme Haiku: “this meme is so old / from 11 years ago / why did it come back.”

Viscous stress: in general, the force per unit area that a fluid applies at a point that is not explained by the thermodynamic pressure. For Newtonian incompressible fluids, this is synonymous with shear stress and is given by the viscosity multiplied by the strain rate.

Example Problem 9.3

Consider two cylindrical reservoirs of radius \(R\) filled with water at rest to a height \(h\). We make this water rotate in two different ways:

1. We rotate the first cylindrical reservoir around its axis of symmetry at an angular frequency \(\omega\) and allow the system to come to a steady state in which all of the fluid is rotating with angular frequency \(\omega\).

2. Along the axis of symmetry of the second reservoir, we insert a cylinder of radius \(r_0\) spinning at an angular frequency \(\omega=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r_0^2}\). In the fluid (i.e., for all \(r>r_0\)), this cylinder generates a flow in the \(xy\) plane that is predicted by an irrotational vortex of strength \(\Gamma\).

What is the equation for the height of the fluid \(h(r)\) in each reservoir? The first simulates mercury zenith telescopes; the second simulates the flow in a bathtub drain or a toilet or a kiddie vortex generator toy, e.g., https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0LfZFGcGc_I, or Figure 9.15, p. 328.

Figure 9.15: The shape of water issuing through a drain in the presence of circulation.

Figure 9.15 is a photograph; photograph omitted in the reader.

Solution: The water inside a steadily rotating beaker of water rotates with the beaker in solid-body rotation. All streamlines are circles centered at \(r=0\). The speed of any point in the fluid is \(\omega r\). The \(r\) direction is normal to the streamlines, pointing away from the center of curvature, so everywhere \(\hat{r}=-\hat{n}\). The Euler equation normal to a streamline is

\frac{\partial}{\partial n}(p+\rho gz)=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\partial p}{\partial n}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\partial p}{\partial r}=\frac{\rho U^2}{r}, (9.63)

The streamlines are circles centered on \(r=0\), so \(R=r\). \(U=\omega r\), so

\frac{\partial p}{\partial r}=\frac{\rho(\omega r)^2}{r}=\rho\omega^2r;\qquad p=p_1+\frac{\rho\omega^2}{2}r^2. (9.64)

Per the hydrostatic equation, the height is given by the height of fluid at which \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\). Using \(h_1\) to specify the height at the center:

h_{\mathrm{solid\ body}}=h_1+\frac{\omega^2}{2g}r^2;\qquad h_1=h-\frac{\omega^2R^2}{4g};\qquad h_{\mathrm{solid\ body}}=h+\frac{\omega^2}{2g}\left(r^2-\frac{1}{2}R^2\right), (9.65)

as long as \(\frac{\omega^2R^2}{4g}\) is not bigger than \(h\), in which case we can still solve the problem but the integrals become more inconvenient because our equation predicts a negative \(h\) and we have to account for the possibility that the height of fluid in the center goes to zero but doesn’t go negative.

The water inside a beaker, a cylinder of radius \(r_0\) spinning at an angular frequency \(\omega=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r_0^2}\), is predicted by a vortex of strength \(\Gamma\). All streamlines are circles centered at \(r=0\). The speed of any point in the fluid is \(\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\). The \(r\) direction is normal to the streamlines, pointing away from the center of curvature, so everywhere \(\hat{r}=-\hat{n}\). The Euler equation normal to a streamline is

\frac{\partial}{\partial n}(p+\rho gz)=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\partial p}{\partial n}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\partial p}{\partial r}=\frac{\rho U^2}{r}, (9.66)

The streamlines are circles centered on \(r=0\), so \(R=r\). \(U=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\), so

\frac{\partial p}{\partial r}=\frac{\rho\Gamma^2}{4\pi^2r^3};\qquad p=C_1-\frac{\rho\Gamma^2}{8\pi^2r^2}. (9.67)

We could have done this another, equivalent way. This flow is irrotational, so the Bernoulli equation applies (use \(z=0\)):

p+\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2=B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p+\frac{1}{2}\rho\left(\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\right)^2=B, (9.68)

which leads to the same result and shows that \(C_1\) is the Bernoulli constant at \(z=0\). Per the hydrostatic equation, the height is given by the height of fluid at which \(p=p_{\mathrm{atm}}\).

h_{\mathrm{vortex}}=C_2-\frac{\Gamma^2}{8\pi^2gr^2}, (9.69)

Integrating this height and setting the value equal to the original volume of liquid \((\pi R^2h)\) gives

C_2=h+\frac{\Gamma^2}{4\pi^2gR^2}\ln\frac{R}{r_0};\qquad h_{\mathrm{vortex}}=h+\frac{\Gamma^2}{4\pi^2g}\left(\frac{1}{R^2}\ln\frac{R}{r_0}-\frac{1}{2r^2}\right), (9.70)

as long as \(\Gamma\) is not bigger than \(\sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2gh}{\frac{1}{2r_0^2}-\frac{1}{R^2}\ln\frac{R}{r_0}}}\), in which case it gets tricky because the problem is ill-posed—the center cylinder is rotating too fast for the velocity to be as specified and for the fluid to touch the inner cylinder.

Also, this solution assumes that \(R\gg r_0\) because we are ignoring that the fluid doesn’t move at the surface of the cylinder, when in fact the vortex solution predicts that it moves with speed \(\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi R}\). So this is a good approximation only if \(R\) is big and \(\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi R}\) is close to zero.

Editorial source note: The final paragraph’s \(\Gamma/(2\pi R)\) concerns the stationary outer reservoir wall at radius R. It is consistent with the discussion of a large reservoir: the rotating inner cylinder at r₀ already matches the specified vortex speed. Equation (9.70) uses the stated small-core approximation R≫r₀.


PDF page 340 — verified

good prediction for \(\vec{F}_p\). But bluff bodies and streamlined bodies at high angles of attack lead to large regions of rotating fluid, and we cannot ignore the attendant breakdown in the irrotational flow model.

We now need to complement irrotational flow modeling with an understanding of separation. Separation describes the phenomenon in which fluid near the surface of an object moves upstream and a streamline emanates normal to the surface. In contrast to attached flow, in which fluid follows along the surface of the object, flow with separation happens when the pressure distribution at the surface cannot generate the accelerations required for the fluid to follow along the wall (Figure 9.16, p. 329). Instead of following the wall, the fluid follows a path with gentler acceleration—it separates from the wall and the fluid behind the separation point has to recirculate. This recirculation zone is filled with rotating fluid and typically dissipates energy into heat. The irrotational flow model is of no use there, and the process dissipates energy that could have otherwise generated a useful force.

Separation: when a streamline emanates normal to a surface. Most often, separation is used only to describe streamlines resulting from flow that moves upstream.

Recirculate: flow upstream. Typically associated with separation.

Figure 9.16 handwritten labels: attached flow over a circular cylinder, Re = 1; separated flow over a circular cylinder, Re = 26; the fluid follows the wall in the attached case; separation points and downstream recirculation in the separated case; “fluid here is moving upstream”; the pressure gradients were not enough to turn the flow around the back side of the cylinder.



Figure 9.16: Attached flow (left) follows the object surface. When flow separates, there is a point on the surface at which the fluid does not follow the surface because the acceleration required to do so is not provided by the local pressure gradients. Instead, the flow separates from the surface and the fluid downstream of the separation point recirculates.

The aerodynamic forces on an object are strongly dependent on whether and where separation occurs. Separation is why airplane wings stall, meaning that their lift stops increasing as we increase angle of attack. Separation is why parachutes work—they are designed to guarantee separation at the parachute edge. Separation is why golf balls with dimples fly longer than smooth golf balls. Separation is why a curveball curves. To predict where separation occurs, we have to study the boundary layer around a surface, which is a thin region in which the viscosity plays an important role. But we haven’t described what viscosity even is yet, and we won’t discuss the boundary layer until the next chapter. So we are talking about fluid physics that we are unprepared to mathematically describe.

We start here with a very descriptive treatment of separation. We will

describe observed fluid mechanical phenomena related to flow over objects, and we will describe how flow features change the pressure distribution, and from that we will describe both aerodynamic lift (e.g., the lift that keeps a plane flying) and form drag, the component of drag on an aerodynamic object that comes from the pressure distribution and not directly from viscosity. For now, we will not derive the governing equations or prove why all of these effects happen. Once we have a handle on what happens, we can then in later chapters start to talk about why.

We will primarily focus on two geometries: airfoils and circular cylinders. Airfoils, as we have discussed, are used in wings, turbines, pumps, fans, wind turbines, and propellers, and are very effective at turning fluid speed into force and vice versa. Circular cylinders are not necessarily great aerodynamic tools, but they are ubiquitous (flow over a cable, flow past a lightpost), can be efficiently actuated (flow over a Flettner rotor), have been studied experimentally to great extent, have simple analytical solutions for irrotational flow, and capture most of the physics of flow around spheres (sports balls, droplets, cannonballs); they are easier to study and have 2D results that are easier to plot. Although there are countless other objects that move through fluids, these are good models to start with. We study these flows in the frame of reference of the object (see Sidebar 9.1, p. 333, for the rationale), with the goal of calculating or predicting the aerodynamic force of fluids on objects.

We have three basic approaches to manage flow over objects

We will typically not find aerodynamic forces on objects by solving the continuity equation and Navier–Stokes equations, simply because the Navier–Stokes equations are too difficult to solve analytically. Instead, we will strategically identify three ways to simplify the system under study, and combine experimental observations with simplified analysis of parts of the problem we have judiciously selected for tractability:

We will look to identify parts of the flow without vorticity, or aspects of the flow that are well approximated by the irrotational flow equations. In these cases, we can solve \(\nabla^2\phi=0\) or \(\nabla^2\psi=0\). This, for example, is often suitable for calculating the lift on an aerodynamic object (but not the drag).

We will look to identify parts of the flow that are nearly unidirectional because the flow is moving parallel to a nearly flat surface. In this case, we can assume that the magnitude of the velocity parallel to the surface (typically denoted as \(u\)) is much larger than the velocity normal to the surface (typically denoted as \(v\)), and velocity derivatives normal to the surface (i.e., with respect to \(y\)) are much larger than velocity derivatives parallel to the surface (i.e., with respect to \(x\)). These approximations allow the Navier–Stokes equations to be replaced with the much simpler boundary-layer equations, which we can solve analytically in a way that helps calculate the drag on an aerodynamic object (but not the lift). We will do this in the next chapter.

We will use dimensional analysis to reduce the number of parameters in our system such that we can correlate experimental data.

We will also make observations of a number of general aspects of flows around objects, which help us to interpret experimental data. In particular, in Chapter-

Lift: the component of a force a fluid exerts on an immersed object that is normal to the flow.

Airfoil: a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes. Roughly synonymous with blade, hydrofoil, wing, and vane. Often chosen over the word hydrofoil when the fluid is air. Often chosen over the word vane when mounted on an airplane.

Irrotational flow: flow in which \(\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{u}=0\). The terms irrotational flow \(\vec{\omega}=0\) and potential flow \(\vec{u}=\nabla\phi\) are synonymous—one implies the other.

Continuity equation: synonymous with “conservation of mass equation”.

The force on an object is calculated by integrating the surface stress along the surface of the object

The aerodynamic force on a body is a surface force that can be calculated by integrating the surface stresses on the body over its surface:

\vec{F}=\int_S\vec{\vec{\tau}}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA, (9.72)

Equation 9.72 note: “how surface stresses can be integrated to generate the force on a body.”

where \(\vec{\vec{\tau}}\) is the stress tensor, which, when dotted with \(\hat{n}\), describes the magnitude and direction of the force per unit area applied to any plane, and \(\hat{n}\) is the unit outward normal for control surface \(S\) that defines the body. For reviews of vector and dyadic tensor calculus, see Appendix B.

In the absence of viscosity, \(\vec{\vec{\tau}}=-p\vec{\vec{I}}\), and the only stress in the fluid is the isotropic effect of pressure. As described in Appendices E–F, if we include viscosity, we find \(\vec{\vec{\tau}}=-p\vec{\vec{I}}+2\mu\vec{\vec{E}}\), where \(\vec{\vec{E}}\) is the strain-rate tensor, and the fluid also has stresses associated with its resistance to deformation.

The surface stresses on a body can be resolved into two components: one normal to the surface and one tangent to the surface. For a Newtonian fluid, the normal stress at any plane in a fluid is given by

\vec{\tau}_n=\left(-p+2\mu\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial n}\right)\hat{n}, (9.73)

Equation 9.73 annotations: “pressure” under \(-p\); “normal viscous stress” under \(2\mu\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial n}\).

where \(u_n\) is the velocity component normal to the wall. At an impermeable wall, though, \(u_n=0\) and \(\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial n}=0\), so the surface normal stress is simply −1 times the pressure multiplied by the unit outward normal:

\vec{\tau}_n=-p\hat{n}, (9.74)

where \(\hat{n}\) is the unit outward normal. Basically this means that even though there are viscous stresses in a flow with viscosity, they do not play a role in the normal stress at a motionless impermeable wall. The integrated effect of the normal stresses is called the pressure force; it is independent of viscosity.

For a Newtonian fluid, the tangential stress at the surface is caused by the viscosity of the fluid and comes from the fluid’s resistance to the deformation associated with flow near a wall. The tangential stress is given by

\vec{\tau}_t=\mu\left(\frac{\partial u_t}{\partial n}+\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial t}\right)\hat{t}, (9.75)

where \(t\) is the coordinate tangent to the surface and \(n\) is the coordinate normal to the surface. For a motionless wall, \(u_n=0\), and the magnitude of the tangential stress becomes

\tau_t=\mu\frac{\partial u_t}{\partial n}, (9.76)

So the tangential stress is given by the viscosity times the partial derivative of the tangential velocity in the direction of the outward-facing normal to the

Surface force: a force that acts on a control volume through its surface. Examples include viscous stresses and pressure. These forces, at the atomistic level, operate through close interactions when molecules collide with each other. Compare to body force.

Stress tensor: denoted \(\vec{\vec{\tau}}\). A dyadic tensor that describes the magnitude and direction of the force per unit area that a fluid would put on any surface at that point. \(\vec{\vec{\tau}}\cdot\hat{n}\) is a vector that describes the magnitude and direction of the force per unit area that the fluid would put on a surface drawn normal to the unit outward normal vector \(\hat{n}\).

surface. As an example, flow along a surface aligned with the \(x\) axis facing in the positive \(y\) direction would lead to a viscous stress whose magnitude is given by

\tau_{yx}=\mu\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}, (9.77)

The net effect of the normal stresses is called the form drag, whereas the net effect of the tangential stresses is called the viscous drag or skin-friction drag. The form drag describes how the pressure distribution controls the aerodynamic forces, and to some extent can be predicted by irrotational flow analysis. The viscous drag describes how the velocity distribution at the surface controls the aerodynamic forces, and is predicted by boundary layer analysis.

The gross aerodynamic properties of an object in a fluid flow are strongly affected by attachment and separation

At relatively high Reynolds numbers, the gross features of flow over an object depend on the object geometry and the Reynolds number. On the upstream part of the object, the flow is for the most part irrotational, and irrotational flow analysis does a good job of predicting the pressure along this part of the object. There is a very thin layer near the surface whose velocity is affected by viscosity, and where the no-slip condition at the wall reduces the fluid speed significantly. However, this layer is so thin it is hard to see, and it has little effect on the pressure distribution. There is a viscous drag associated with this boundary layer, but we will not calculate it in this chapter. The fluid stagnates at a point on the upstream portion of the object, and the pressure there is high per the Bernoulli equation. The fluid that moves past the shoulders of the object has a high speed, and the pressure at the shoulders is low per the Bernoulli equation.

On the downstream part of the object, the behavior of the flow depends greatly on the Reynolds number and the geometry and alignment of the object. Of particular importance is where flow is attached or separated. For streamlined objects, the streamlines of the flow follow the surface, the flow remains irrotational everywhere except in the boundary layer, and irrotational flow analysis does a good job of predicting the pressure distribution on the surface of the object. We describe flow in which the streamlines of the flow follow the surface, as attached (Figure 9.17, p. 333, left). There is always a thin boundary layer, for example seen in the thin dark band at left in Figure 9.18, p. 334 of slower-moving fluid. Similarly, the flat plate at left in Figure 9.18, p. 334, when it is rotated on the right side of the figure, causes flow separation.

Attached flow is the result of a geometry that does not require that the fluid accelerate sideways very quickly—a streamlined surface that is aligned with the flow lets the fluid experience only gentle side acceleration, and the forces acting on the fluid are enough to keep it attached to the wall. However, if we increase the demands for acceleration of the fluid, by making the fluid move faster, or making the fluid denser (so it has more inertia), or by changing the geometry or alignment of the object, sometimes attached flow is no longer possible. In Figure 9.17, p. 333, the right image shows the same airfoil as in the image at left, but with the airfoil rotated to an angle of attack. The fluid streamlines follow the surface geometry about halfway along the top

Form drag: the component of fluid force on an object that (a) is in the direction of flow and (b) is explained by only the pressure distribution on the surface of the object. Synonymous with pressure drag.

Skin-friction drag: the component of fluid force on an object that (a) is in the direction of flow and (b) is explained by only the viscous stress on the surface of the object. Friction here is a metaphor; the viscous stress is in some ways analogous to friction, but it is not friction.

Irrotational: not rotating, i.e., \(\vec{\omega}=\nabla\times\vec{u}=0\).

No-slip condition: a dynamic condition specifying that the component of velocity tangent to a solid surface is zero. Equivalent to saying that fluid, at molecular level, sticks to the surface.

Boundary layer: a thin layer of fluid near a boundary in which the conservation of momentum equation is simplified because of the nearly unidirectional flow parallel to the surface.

Shoulder: on an object immersed in a fluid flow, the surfaces at the widest point measured normal to the prevailing fluid velocity.

Attached: describing a flow locally, means having a velocity on the surface that runs parallel to the surface and has no stagnation point. Describing a flow globally, means the flow has no separation point associated with flow moving upstream.

Angle of attack: the angle that the chord line of an airfoil makes with the oncoming fluid flow.

Sidebar 9.1: Fundamentals

Why we study fluid flow over objects in the object reference frame

In fluid mechanics, we usually use the object reference frame when studying moving objects

If I throw a ball at 10 m/s through air, is it better to assume the air is stagnant and the ball is moving through it, or should I assume the ball is stationary and the air moves with respect to the ball? The laws of physics can be cast in either form. We almost always use a frame of reference in which the object is stationary and fluid moves past it.

We pick the object reference frame because it makes the boundary conditions steady and often makes the flow steady

If we make the object stationary, the boundary conditions are steady, and there is a chance that the flow will be steady. This is much easier to analyze. If we have the object move, then the boundary conditions will always be unsteady, the flow will always be unsteady, and the problem will always be much more difficult.

We go back and forth with language but our analysis is always the same

We often will vary our language between reference frames—we might say we are studying an airplane flying at 175 m/s, or we might say we are studying fluid flow over an airplane at 175 m/s. In either case, the physics is the same. In either case, the way we will study it is to assume the airplane is motionless in the airplane reference frame, and study what happens to fluid moving past the airplane.

Objects that are not streamlined are called bluff bodies; there is no way to align a bluff body in a flow such that the fluid has an easy path that requires no sharp turns. Anything with a sharp corner or edge (other than its trailing edge) is called a bluff body; spheres and cylinders are bluff bodies. This graph is typical for bluff bodies, and this drag (called form drag or pressure drag) is the drag that is eliminated when we design an object to be streamlined.

These distributions exhibit fore-aft symmetry.

Separation: when a streamline emanates normal to a surface. Most often, separation is used only to describe streamlines resulting from flow that moves upstream.

Dynamic pressure: given by \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\frac{1}{2}\rho U^2\). Denotes the added pressure a fluid would have if it were slowed isentropically to motionlessness. Equivalently, describes the volumetric kinetic energy of a fluid in terms of an equivalent pressure.

Fore-aft symmetry: having fluid properties (velocity, pressure) that are the same on the upstream side of the object as they are on the downstream side. Possible only in irrotational flow or Stokes flow.
