Problems with Answers

1. (OBJECTIVE: simplification of NS eqns., steady and isobaric approximations, conservation of mass) Solve for flow between two plates, with one moving relative to the other, as follows: (a) Write out the Navier–Stokes equation (conservation of momentum equation) for \(x\)-momentum. (b) Consider unidirectional, isobaric, steady flow of fluid between two infinite flat plates, one located at \(y=0\) that is motionless and one at \(y=h\) moving with \(x\) velocity \(U\). Use the \(x\)-momentum equation to solve for the velocity distribution. (c) We did not directly use conservation of mass in solving for the velocity field. Is conservation of mass satisfied?

Solution: The Navier–Stokes equations are:

\rho\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}+\rho\left(u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)=-\frac{dp}{dx}+\mu\left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}+\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial z^2}\right) (11.56)

Isobaric and steady means

\rho\left(u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)=\mu\left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}+\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial z^2}\right) (11.57)

If the plates are infinite, it is reasonable to take as an ansatz that \(\partial/\partial x\) and \(\partial/\partial z\) of any velocity component is likely zero:

\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=0,\qquad\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}=0 (11.58)

and that the only nonzero component of velocity is \(u\):

0=\mu\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2} (11.59)

so we look for solutions to this equation. If we find a solution to this equation, this, combined with \(\partial u/\partial x=0,\ \partial u/\partial z=0\), is a solution to the Navier–Stokes equations, and we confirm that our ansatz is of some value. We provide no evidence that this solution is unique. We integrate twice:

0=\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2} (11.60)

C_1=\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} (11.61)

C_1y+C_2=u (11.62)


PDF page 416 — source_issue

u=U\frac{y}{h} (11.63)

woohoo! Yes, this flow conserves mass. \(\nabla\cdot\vec{u}=0\). Conservation of mass was implicitly solved when we assumed that the flow was unidirectional (\(v\) and \(w\) are zero so all derivatives of them are zero) and that \(u\) did not vary with \(x\) (so \(\partial u/\partial x\) is also zero). Really, we used conservation of mass as part of our ansatz. This is a common use of conservation of mass—we use it to frame the possible answers, rather than starting from the complete range of possible answers and then explicitly solving the conservation of mass equation.

2. (OBJECTIVE: Use solution of the Couette flow equations to illustrate how uniformity of shear stress translates to nonuniform velocity when viscosity is nonuniform) Figure 11.14, p. 418 shows what happens when your lubricating oil phase-separates into two components in your bearing. Two fluids flow between two infinite horizontal parallel plates. Both fluids are immiscible, incompressible, and viscous with different viscosities. For the purposes of this problem, assume the fluid configuration is stable (although configurations like this are unstable, they can exist long enough for the solution you will calculate to be relevant). The bottom plate (\(y=0\)) is fixed and the upper plate (\(y=2h\)) moves along the \(x\) axis with a constant velocity \(U\) as depicted. Find the steady-state velocity at the interface of the two fluids in terms of \(U,\rho_1,\rho_2,\mu_1,\) and \(\mu_2\) if there is no pressure gradient in the \(x\) direction and flow is laminar.

Solution: Steady, unidirectional, laminar, isobaric flow leads to the governing equation

\mu\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}=0 (11.64)

which leads to a general solution

u=C_1y+C_2 (11.65)

This solution can be specified through the boundary conditions. At solid surfaces, the no-penetration condition and no-slip condition set the velocity of the fluid equal to the velocity of the wall. At liquid–liquid interfaces, the no-penetration condition and no-slip condition set the velocity of each fluid equal to that of the other fluid. Conservation of momentum at the interface also requires that the state of stress be the same at the interface regardless of the direction from which we take the limit. In other words, the stress on the fluid 1 side has to be equal to the stress on the fluid 2 side, otherwise the interface will feel a net force and (because the interface is infinitely thin and has no mass) an infinite acceleration. The shear stress \(\tau_{xy}=\tau_{yx}=\mu\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\right)=\mu C_1\) in each interface, so the \(\tau_{xy}\) evaluated on either side of the interface must be equal. Denoting the speed of the interface as \(U_I\), we have

\mu_1\left(\frac{U-U_I}{h}\right)=\mu_2\left(\frac{U_I}{h}\right) (11.66)

Implicitly when we say \(U_I\) is the “speed at the interface” we mean that \(U_I\) is the speed at the interface when the limit is taken from both above and below the interface. The speed at the interface is thus

U_I=U\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_1+\mu_2} (11.67)

Some limits are illustrative: if the two viscosities are equal, then \(U_I=\frac{1}{2}U\). If \(\mu_1\gg\mu_2\), then \(U_I\approx U\). If \(\mu_1\ll\mu_2\), then \(U_I\approx0\). This highlights that the velocity is continuous in a subsonic fluid, and the stress is continuous in a subsonic fluid, but the velocity gradient can be discontinuous if the viscosity is continuous, for example at a liquid–liquid interface.

Editorial note: the last sentence prints “if the viscosity is continuous,” but the stated two-fluid problem has different viscosities. From stress continuity, \(\mu_1(du/dy)_1=\mu_2(du/dy)_2\). Thus a nonzero common shear stress permits different velocity gradients when viscosity is discontinuous; equal viscosities require equal gradients in this example. The printed wording is retained above.

3. (OBJECTIVE: Translate Couette flow solutions to tribological applications) A journal bearing of diameter 6 cm rotates at 200 RPM in a motionless 4-cm-long housing, with a gap of \(10\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) in between the bearing and the housing. Lubricating oil (\(\rho=800\ \mathrm{kg/m^3};\ \mu=0.1\ \mathrm{Pa\,s}\)) fills the gap. The velocity distribution is well approximated by assuming that the surfaces are flat and planar but moving with a speed


PDF page 417 — source_issue

prescribed by the rotation speed of the bearing surface. What is the torque required to keep this system rotating at a constant rate? Solution: The surface moves at a velocity given by \(2\pi r f=2\pi(0.03)(200/60)=0.63\ \mathrm{m/s}\). The Reynolds number is \(\mathrm{Re}=\rho U h/\mu=0.05\). Thus a laminar Couette flow solution is stable and would be observed in practice. For a narrow gap very small relative to a large radius, this can be approximated with minimal error as the Couette flow between two flat plates. In this case, the shear stress everywhere is \(\mu\Delta U/h\), where \(h=10\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) is the gap width. The total force being applied at the surface is this stress multiplied by the area: \(2\pi r\mu\Delta U\ell/h\), where \(r=3\ \mathrm{cm},\ \ell=4\ \mathrm{cm}\). The torque is multiplied by the radius \(r\): \(T=2\pi r^2\mu\Delta U\ell/h=1.4\ \mathrm{N\,m}\).

4. (OBJECTIVE: Evaluate pipe flow to determine laminar vs. turbulent flow) For oil (\(\mathrm{SG}=\rho/\rho_{\mathrm{water}}=0.86,\ \mu=0.025\ \mathrm{N\,s/m^2}\)) flowing at \(0.3\ \mathrm{m^3/s}\) through a pipe of circular cross-section with diameter of 500 mm, determine the Reynolds number. Is the flow laminar or turbulent? Solution: The definition of specific gravity is:

\mathrm{SG}=\rho/\rho_{\mathrm{water}}=0.86 (11.68)

So the density of the oil is

\rho_{\mathrm{oil}}=0.86(\rho_{\mathrm{water}})=0.86(999\ \mathrm{kg/m^3})=859\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} (11.69)

The average speed is

\bar{U}=Q/A=\frac{0.3}{\frac{\pi}{4}(0.5)^2}=1.53\ \mathrm{m/s} (11.70)

Thus the Reynolds number is

\mathrm{Re}=\frac{\rho U D}{\mu}=\frac{(859)(1.53)(0.5)}{0.025}=2.63\mathrm{e}4 (11.71)

Based on the criterion that Re < 4000 unambiguously represents laminar flow, this flow is clearly turbulent.

5. (OBJECTIVE: Use laminar–turbulent threshold to determine operating range of a viscometer) A viscometer can be made from a long tube with a very small diameter. The viscometer works by measuring the flow rate of fluid as a function of pressure drop in the tube. We can define a calibration constant, \(k=Q/\Delta p\), but this constant is informative only if the flow of the fluid in the tube is laminar. Given diameters of 0.5 mm, 1 mm, and 2 mm, determine the maximum flow rate that can be used for an effective measurement if the fluid is (a) water and (b) air at STP. Solution: We take that the maximum Reynolds number for laminar flow is \(\mathrm{Re}\approx2100\). This is somewhat arbitrary—any threshold between 1000 and 4000 is reasonable, and the volumetric thresholds vary linearly with what threshold we pick. 2100, 2300, and 4000 are the most common numbers used. We calculate the Reynolds number with

\mathrm{Re}=\frac{\rho U d}{\mu} (11.72)

We can also write the flow rate through the pipe as:

Q=\frac{\pi}{4}d^2\bar{U} (11.73)

Combining these two equations we get:

\mathrm{Re}=\frac{4\rho Qd}{\pi d^2\mu}=\frac{4\rho Q}{\pi d\mu} (11.74)

Solving for Q gives us:

Q=\frac{\pi d\mu\mathrm{Re}}{4\rho} (11.75)

Using the expression for flow rate, we have for air:

Q_{0.5\,\mathrm{mm}}=0.83\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} (11.76)

Editorial note: The threshold sentence is reproduced as printed. Its conclusion at \(Re=2.63\times10^4\) is not inconsistent with its inequality, but the sentence does not justify treating every \(Re<4000\) as unambiguously laminar: the next problem explicitly discusses a range of thresholds and chooses 2100.

Editorial note: The “air” and “water” labels for (11.76)–(11.81) appear reversed. With the water properties printed on source page 222, (11.75) gives \(Q=\pi(0.0005)(0.001)(2100)/(4\cdot1000)=0.825\,\mathrm{cm^3/s}\), matching the printed 0.83. The air properties there give \(12.37\,\mathrm{cm^3/s}\), close to the 12.04 grouped under “water” on the next page. Exact values depend on the chosen fluid properties.

Q_{1\,\mathrm{mm}}=1.66\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} (11.77)

Q_{2\,\mathrm{mm}}=3.32\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} (11.78)

For water, we have:

Q_{0.5\,\mathrm{mm}}=12.04\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} (11.79)

6. (OBJECTIVE: return from nondimensional relationships to dimensional results: generation of intuition between \(Q\)–\(\Delta p\) relationship) If a volumetric flowrate \(Q\) through a pipe of known and fixed cross-section is specified, what is the power-law dependence of pressure drop through a tube of circular cross-section depend on \(R\) if (a) flow is laminar? (You can describe the exponent exactly.) (b) flow is turbulent? (You can describe the exponent only approximately, but please specify a range.)

Solution: If the flow is laminar, the area-averaged speed is linearly proportional to the gradient of the hydrostatic constant (if the pipe is horizontal, this is the gradient of the pressure):

\bar{U}=\left(-\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\right)\frac{R^2}{8\mu} (11.82)

so \(\Delta p\propto Q\). If the flow is turbulent, the losses are proportional to both the viscous dissipation factor \(f_D\) and the dynamic pressure:

\frac{\partial B}{\partial s}=f_D\frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{U}^2\frac{1}{d} (11.83)

so if \(f_D\) doesn’t change, \(\Delta p\propto Q^2\). \(f_D\) isn’t a function of \(\mathrm{Re}\) when \(\mathrm{Re}\) is very large. However, \(f_D\) does change in the \(10^3<\mathrm{Re}<10^7\) range. \(f_D\) goes down a bit as \(\mathrm{Re}\) increases, which means it goes down a bit as \(Q\) increases for fixed cross-sectional area. So if we write \(\Delta p\propto Q^n\), \(n\) is close to 2 but a little bit smaller than 2. \(n\) approaches 2 as the Reynolds number approaches2.

and rearrange to get

SIDEBAR 11.1: ENGINEERING MODELS

No-Slip Condition

Premise: the molecules in fluids and solids interact with each other enough that we do not see velocity discontinuities at interfaces

Velocity is generally continuous in fluids—discontinuities are not possible because the molecules interact with each other and exchange momentum and a discontinuity is only possible if there is no momentum exchange between molecules. The premise of the no-slip condition is that this is true at interfaces as well as within a fluid domain.

Mathematical form: the no-slip condition says that the tangent velocity component of a fluid at a solid wall is zero

The no-slip condition says that at an interface between two materials, numbered 1 and 2:

u_{t,1}=u_{t,2} (11.4)

This is equivalent to saying that the velocity is continuous, i.e., that there is no discontinuity of velocity at an interface. We use this most often in the frame of reference of a motionless solid wall, where this is equivalently

u_t=0\quad\text{at a solid wall} (11.5)

At a fluid–fluid interface, we might not immediately know the fluid velocities, but we know that they are the same on either side of the interface:

u_{t,1}=u_{t,2}\quad\text{at a fluid interface} (11.6)

In the context of a fluid–fluid interface, this is often termed continuity rather than the no-slip condition, but the two terms are equivalent.

Utility: the no-slip condition is an excellent model and provides a simple mathematical boundary condition

The no-slip condition is mathematically simple and matches experimental data.

Limitations: the no-slip condition isn’t quite right when there is no molecular interaction between the fluid and the solid

The no-slip condition basically says the fluid “sticks” to the wall. This is correct as long as there is even the tiniest bit of interaction between the two materials. However, there are some cases for which the no-slip condition breaks down. If the fluid is a rarefied gas, in particular if the mean free path of the gas is large relative to the size of the flow domain, then the no-slip condition breaks down. Or, alternately, at the interface between, say, Teflon and water, then the no-slip condition breaks down. But both of these breakdowns are minor and hard to achieve anyway, and the bottom line is that the no-slip condition is great.

Consider a hockey puck 25.4 mm thick and 38.1 mm in radius that is sliding along a sheet of freshly Zamboni-ed ice at 25 m/s. Assume that the puck floats on a 10 \(\mu\)m-thick layer of water between the ice and the puck. Model the flow of water between the puck and the ice as a Couette flow. Assume that the viscosity of water in the thin film is 1 mPa s and the density is 1000 kg/m³.

1. What is Re for this flow?

2. What is the total drag force on the puck?

we have used the half-height (5 μm) as the characteristic height:

SIDEBAR 11.2: FUNDAMENTALS

Laminar and Turbulent Flow

Fluid flow can roughly be classified into two classes: laminar and turbulent. We classify fluid into two modes, each describing dominant physics and the analytical tools that are appropriate for its analysis.

Laminar flow describes flow that proceeds in orderly sheets or lamina. Laminar flow is stable, and a small perturbation to a laminar flow will fade away over time as the system reverts to its former state. Laminar flow is steady if the boundary conditions are steady. Laminar flow can be analytically tractable if the boundary conditions are conveniently aligned with a coordinate axis or some other convenient shape. This means that we can sometimes find solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations for laminar flow. Momentum transfer in laminar flow is primarily through viscous diffusion of momentum.

Turbulent flow describes flow that is inherently disorganized and unstable. Turbulent flow is unstable, and a small perturbation to a turbulent flow will change the long-term details of the flow. Turbulent flow is never steady. If the boundary conditions are steady, though, turbulent flow can be stationary, meaning that although the details of the flow fluctuate with time, the flow’s long-time-frame average properties are steady. Turbulent flow can never be solved, meaning that we can never analytically solve the Navier–Stokes equations. We make no attempt at MAE3230 level to resolve the fluctuations of a turbulent flow; we only concern ourselves with the stationary solution. We can measure turbulent flows experimentally, we can analyze the results, we can interpret the results in terms of physical and mathematical analysis of the system, we can just never analytically calculate it from scratch. Momentum transfer in turbulent flow is primarily through convective mixing of fast- and slow-moving fluid, which in regions far from walls might be more than three orders of magnitude more efficient than viscous diffusion of momentum.

The distinction between laminar and turbulent flow is often clear, but it is also possible to have a middle ground, typically termed transitional flow. Transitional flow is used to describe a flow that doesn’t quite fit into the two other categories—it fluctuates unlike laminar flow but isn’t quite as unstable or chaotic as turbulent flow. Transitional flow is very interesting from a physical standpoint but doesn’t affect too much engineering analysis—flows mechanical engineers care about rarely or never are in the transitional regime. It is much more common for flows we care about to be fully turbulent, and clearly so. My research involves flows that are fully laminar, and clearly so.

Because the transition from laminar to turbulent flow can have a not-very-well-defined domain, our descriptions of when a flow will be laminar or when a flow will be turbulent are typically approximate. We might say a flow becomes turbulent at a Reynolds number of “about Re = xxx”. This is not sloppiness; this is acknowledgement that the physics is a bit complicated, and knowing the exact transition actually isn’t necessary for most engineering analysis.

Couette flow between two plates transitions at about \(Re_h = 1000\)

Couette flow is the flow between two infinite parallel flat plates. The laminar solution is that the fluid velocity varies linearly from the velocity of one plate to the velocity of the other plate. This laminar solution is observed at \(Re_h \ll 1000\). For \(Re_h \gg 1000\), Couette flow goes turbulent, and the time-averaged velocity profile is different. It has a large domain in the center of the flow that has a much smaller velocity gradient, and most of the velocity changes happen near the wall.

Poiseuille flow in a tube of circular cross-section transitions at about \(Re_d = 1000\text{–}4000\)

Poiseuille flow is the steady laminar flow through a pipe. The laminar solution is that the fluid velocity varies parabolically from zero at the wall to a maximum at the center of the pipe. This laminar solution is observed at \(Re_d \ll 1000\). For \(Re_d \gg 4000\), Poiseuille flow goes turbulent, and the time-averaged velocity profile is different. It has a large domain in the center of the flow that has a much smaller velocity gradient, and most of the velocity changes happen near the wall.

A flat-plate boundary layer transitions at about \(Re_x = 5\times10^5\text{–}5\times10^6\), or, equivalently, \(Re_\theta = 700\text{–}2000\)

A boundary layer formed on a surface is laminar upstream, and eventually becomes turbulent downstream. As was the case for Couette and Poiseuille flow, transition to turbulence makes momentum transport more efficient, so turbulent boundary layers grow faster and concentrate more of their velocity changes near the wall.



Figure 11.7: Laminar vs. turbulent flows. Left: steady laminar and time-averaged stationary turbulent Couette flows with the same velocity boundary condition. Right: steady laminar and time-averaged stationary turbulent Poiseuille flow with the same flowrate. In both cases, the center of the turbulent flow has large turbulent fluctuations, leading to extensive momentum transfer, making the stationary velocity vary rapidly near the wall but only slowly in the center of the flow.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM 11.2

The governing equation for unsteady flow between two infinite parallel plates is \(\rho\,\partial u/\partial t=\mu\,\partial^2u/\partial y^2\). Solve this equation for two plates, one at \(y=0\) and one at \(y=2h\). Use as an initial condition the steady-state solution corresponding to the top plate moving at \(U=1\) and the bottom plate motionless, which is: \(u(t=0)=1-y/(2h)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(2/(n\pi))\sin(n\pi y/(2h))\), and boundary condition \(u(y=0)=u(y=2h)=0\). This describes what happens when the bottom plate, which is sliding relative to the top plate, stops doing so.

Solution: This is a separation of variables problem you already solved in MATH2930; probably you had a metal bar connected to ice water at one end and boiling water at the other end, then you dunk the hot end in ice water. We separate variables and assume multiple possible modes, and plug back into the governing equation:

u_n(y,t)=Y_n(y)T_n(t),\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_n\frac{dT_n}{dt}=\frac{\mu}{\rho}T_n\frac{d^2Y_n}{dy^2},\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{1}{T_n}\frac{dT_n}{dt}=\frac{\mu}{\rho Y_n}\frac{d^2Y_n}{dy^2}=-k_n (11.24)

The LHS is a function of \(t\) only, and the RHS is a function of \(y\) only. There is no way for either side to be a function of \(t\) or \(y\) and still be equal to the other side. Thus each side must be equal to a constant (which we write as \(-k_n\)). The \(Y\) equation gives

\frac{\mu}{\rho Y_n}\frac{d^2Y_n}{dy^2}=-k_n,\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{d^2Y_n}{dy^2}=-k_nY_n\frac{\mu}{\rho},\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_n=A_n\cos\left(\sqrt{k_n\frac{\rho}{\mu}}y\right)+B_n\sin\left(\sqrt{k_n\frac{\rho}{\mu}}y\right) (11.25)

where \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) are constants. All \(A_n=0\) because the cosine function does not satisfy the no-slip condition at \(y=0\). The sine function satisfies the no-slip condition at \(y=0\) for all \(k_n\). The sine function satisfies the no-slip condition at \(y=2h\) only when

\sqrt{k_n\frac{\mu}{\rho}}\,2h=n\pi,\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_n=B_n\sin\frac{n\pi y}{2h},\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k_n=\left(\frac{n\pi}{2h}\right)^2\frac{\mu}{\rho} (11.26)

where \(n\) is an integer. The \(T_n\) equation is given by

\frac{1}{T_n}\frac{dT_n}{dt}=-k_n,\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{dT_n}{dt}=-k_nT_n,\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_n=C_n\exp(-k_nt) (11.27)

Writing the product of \(Y_n\) and \(T_n\) and summing over modes, we have

u=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}B_n\sin\frac{n\pi y}{2h}C_n\exp(-k_nt)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}D_n\sin\frac{n\pi y}{2h}\exp\left[-\left(\frac{n\pi}{2h}\right)^2\frac{\mu}{\rho}t\right] (11.28)

where \(D_n=B_nC_n\). At \(t=0\), we have

u(t=0)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}D_n\sin\frac{n\pi y}{2h}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2}{n\pi}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{2h}\exp\left[-\left(\frac{n\pi}{2h}\right)^2\frac{\mu}{\rho}t\right] (11.29)

Figure 11.9, p. 414 shows the solution as a function of time.



Figure 11.9: Decay of a Couette flow after the bottom plate is stopped.

Editorial note: The initial condition has \(u(0,0)=1\) and \(u(2h,0)=0\); the boundary at \(y=0\) is therefore the initially moving boundary. Both boundaries become stationary afterward. The source alternates between calling the moving/stopped plate “top” and “bottom”; the coordinates and initial condition identify the mathematical problem unambiguously.

Editorial note: Two printed ratios are inverted. From the first equality of (11.25), \(Y_n^{\prime\prime}=-k_n(\rho/\mu)Y_n\); its middle equality prints \(\mu/\rho\). The first expression of (11.26) should correspondingly be \(\sqrt{k_n\rho/\mu}\,2h=n\pi\). The printed final decay rate \(k_n=(n\pi/(2h))^2\mu/\rho\) and the final modal solution use the consistent ratios. The source takes \(U=1\), so its modal coefficient is \(2/(n\pi)\).

Editorial redraw note: The curves are regenerated from (11.29) at representative dimensionless times 0.003, 0.012, 0.035, 0.07, 0.14 and 0.24. The stopped wall is drawn at the bottom, as in the source figure and caption; see the existing note about inconsistent prose.

SIDEBAR 11.1: ENGINEERING MODELS

No-Slip Condition

Premise: the molecules in fluids and solids interact with each other enough that we do not see velocity discontinuities at interfaces.

Velocity is generally continuous in fluids—discontinuities are not possible because the molecules interact with each other and exchange momentum and a discontinuity is only possible if there is no momentum exchange between molecules. The premise of the no-slip condition is that this is true at interfaces as well as within a fluid domain.

Mathematical form: the no-slip condition says that the tangent velocity component of a fluid at a solid wall is zero.

The no-slip condition says that at an interface between two materials, numbered 1 and 2:

u_{t,1}=u_{t,2} (11.30)

This is equivalent to saying that the velocity is continuous, i.e., that there is no discontinuity of velocity at an interface. We use this most often in the frame of reference of a motionless solid wall, where this is equivalently

u_t=0\quad\text{at a solid wall} (11.31)

At a fluid–fluid interface, we might not immediately know the fluid velocities, but we know that they are the same on either side of the interface:

u_{t,1}=u_{t,2}\quad\text{at a fluid interface} (11.32)

In the context of a fluid–fluid interface, this is often termed continuity rather than the no-slip condition, but the two terms are equivalent.

Utility: the no-slip condition is an excellent model and provides a simple mathematical boundary condition.

The no-slip condition is mathematically simple and matches experimental data.

Limitations: the no-slip condition isn’t quite right when there is no molecular interaction between the fluid and the solid.

The no-slip condition basically says the fluid “sticks” to the wall. This is correct as long as there is even the tiniest bit of interaction between the two materials. However, there are some cases for which the no-slip condition breaks down. If the fluid is a rarefied gas, in particular if the mean free path of the gas is large relative to the size of the flow domain, then the no-slip condition breaks down. Or, alternately, at the interface between say Teflon and water, then the no-slip condition breaks down. But both of these breakdowns are minor and hard to achieve anyway and the bottom line is that the no-slip condition is great.

SIDEBAR 11.2: ENGINEERING MODELS

Fully Developed Flow

Premise: it is easier to describe flow in pipes in regions that are far away from the entrance.

The velocity distribution in a pipe changes as the fluid moves through the pipe (analogous comments can be made for flow between two plates). The changes are seen at the entrance and at any location that deviates from a straight line and uniform cross-section. Regions of flow that we refer to as fully developed are far from entrances or exits, far from turns, and far from locations at which the cross-section changes. Because of this, the fully developed region of a flow has no downstream gradients of velocity.

Mathematical form: for fully developed flow, the streamwise derivative of velocity is zero.

For fully developed flow:

\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=0 (11.33)

The fully developed flow model can be applied to both laminar and turbulent flow; for turbulent flow a Reynolds average must be used.

Utility: fully developed flow is universal and easy to measure experimentally.

Whereas flow at entrances and exits and through turns is complicated and hard to replicate, the fully developed region of the flow through a pipe is universal and easy to replicate. Also, for many engineering systems, the primary behavior of the system is explained by the fully developed region. For example, the pressure drop through a long pipe is dominated by the pressure drop in the fully developed region. Although the details at the entrance and exit might be harder to predict, they are not the dominant source of pressure drop, and therefore have little engineering impact. Because the fully developed region of flow through a pipe is universal and useful, we have many tools to analyze this aspect of flows. The Moody chart or the Haaland equation or the Colebrook–White equation, for example, describes head losses for fully developed flow.

Limitations: the domain downstream of an entrance, turn, or change in cross-section has a finite entrance length or development length associated with it.

The domain downstream of an entrance, turn, or change in cross-section has a finite entrance length or development length associated with it. The length of this domain is approximately 10 diameters long, although the precise length varies with Reynolds number and pipe cross-section. In this region, the velocity distribution changes, and the pressure drop associated with viscous losses is different (typically higher) than that of the fully developed region.
