This balance is not a new result: we used this balance to derive the differential form of the hydrostatic equation \(\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}=-\rho g\) in the first place. But now that we have worked it all out, this example uses a hydrostatics result that we have seen before as an illustrative case of how a scalar and its gradient can be related by surface and volume integrals.

Archimedes’ principle is the combination of two analyses: (1) the gradient-field theorem applied to a hydrostatic system combined with (2) the observation that when we consider a motionless object immersed in fluid, the presence of the object does not change the pressure distribution outside it. So the force on an immersed motionless object is identical to the force that would be applied to a control volume filled with the same liquid as its environment.

For those interested in the vector calculus, the gradient-field theorem is really just a special case of the divergence theorem applied to an isotropic dyadic field. If one uses \(q\vec{I}\) as the field in the divergence theorem, a couple of vector identities will get you to Equation (B.111). The force per unit area caused by pressure is an isotropic dyadic and given by \(p\vec{I}\), so the version of the divergence theorem that is most immediately useful to evaluate the integrated pressure force on a surface is the gradient-field theorem.

Two vector identities are useful to remember to be able to quickly understand many fluid mechanical techniques and approaches

The divergence of the curl of any vector or dyadic is zero:

\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\vec{u})=\frac{\partial^2w}{\partial y\partial x}-\frac{\partial^2v}{\partial z\partial x}+\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial z\partial y}-\frac{\partial^2w}{\partial x\partial y}+\frac{\partial^2v}{\partial x\partial z}-\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y\partial z}=0 (B.113)

The curl of the gradient of any scalar, vector, or dyadic is zero:

\nabla\times(\nabla\phi)=\left(\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial z\partial y}-\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial y\partial z}\right)\hat{x}+\left(\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial x\partial z}-\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial z\partial x}\right)\hat{y}+\left(\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial y\partial x}-\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial x\partial y}\right)\hat{z}=0 (B.114)

Both of these identities are readouts of equality of mixed partials.

Streamfunction

The streamfunction is defined as a measure of the areal flowrate through a contour between points

For any point A in a flow, consider a path between an arbitrary origin point (which we call O) and A. Then, presuming we know \(\vec{u}\), let’s figure out the clockwise areal flowrate that crosses that path if the path were a control surface. It turns out that that relation is simple! Call that integral \(\psi\): (see

areal: related to area, or per unit area.


PDF page 479 — source_issue

Figure B.9, p. 468:

\psi(A)=\int_O^A\underbrace{\vec u\cdot\hat n}_{\text{areal flux}}\,ds=\overbrace{\int_O^A u\,dy}^{\text{part of areal flux explained by x velocity component}}+\underbrace{\int_O^A-v\,dx}_{\text{part of areal flux explained by y velocity component}} (B.115)

This is because for a differential distance along the path \(ds\) with components \(dx\) and \(dy\), \(\hat{n}ds\) (which is normal to the path) has x component \(dy\) and y component \(-dx\) (i.e., \(\hat{n}ds=dy\hat{x}-dx\hat{y}\)). The integrand \(u\,dy-v\,dx\) is just the dot product of \(\vec{u}\) with \(\hat{n}ds\).



Figure B.9: Left: a differential section of the path from an arbitrary origin to a point O, showing how the volume flux across the element ds is given by u dy − v dx. Right: some observations of the streamfunction in a flow. The net flow into the surface OAB must be zero, consistent with ψ(A) = ψ(B) along the streamline AB. Streamlines are close to each other at left, consistent with high speed; streamlines are farther away at right, consistent with low speed.

We haven’t specified the path from O to A. But, at fixed density, conservation of mass says that the areal flowrate through all of these paths has to be the same, so this integral should not be a function of the path. This is the key thing. For 2D plane-symmetric incompressible flows, \(\psi\) is well defined and single-valued. If \(\psi\) is well defined and single-valued, it describes a velocity field that satisfies conservation of mass.

With this definition, derivatives of \(\psi\) are straightforward, as \(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}=-v\) and \(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}=u\). So

u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y},\qquad v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x},\qquad \vec{u}=\nabla\times\psi\hat{z} (B.116)

If we solve incompressible flow problems in terms of \(\psi\), we never have to solve the conservation of mass equation.

conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

If we think about the velocity potential as a scalar field that corresponds to elevation, fluid is always moving up the mountain

We often find it intuitive to think of a scalar field as an elevation, and I often find it intuitive to think of the ways a hiker could hike through mountainous terrain as analogies for how fluids move through a scalar field. In this context, fluids behave in a velocity potential field like a powerful, ambitious hiker that wants to always go straight up the “mountain”. The definition \(\vec{u}=\nabla\phi\) shows that the velocity vector \(\vec{u}\) points in the same direction as the direction of maximum rate of increase of \(\phi\). So regions of high positive \(\phi\) are like “attractors” that fluids move toward, just like an ambitious hiker or climber wants to get to the top of the mountain.

If we think about the streamfunction as a scalar field that corresponds to elevation, fluid moves along flat surfaces with the “mountains” to the left

Continuing the analogies of a scalar field as an elevation and of the ways a hiker could hike through mountainous terrain, we now turn to the streamfunction. The streamfunction and velocity potential are orthogonal functions, and isocontours of these two functions are orthogonal to each other, and the hiking analogy is orthogonal as well. In the context of the scalar streamfunction field, fluids behave in a streamfunction field like a lazy recreational hiker that wants to always move along a flat surface with the mountain to their left and the valleys to their right. We can show that the streamfunction does not change along a streamline, and thus fluids move along streamfunction isocontours. The streamfunction isocontours by definition are orthogonal to the gradients of the streamfunction, which in this analogy point up the “mountain”. Regions of high positive \(\psi\) are like “scenery” that fluids circle around and look at—a recreational hiker wants to walk around the mountain but is too tired to climb up it. This “circling around” behavior is consistent with the observation that, in 2D, the definitions \(u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\) and \(v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\) are equivalent to \(\vec{u}=\nabla\times(\psi\hat{z})\).

B.16 One can define a vector streamfunction that prescribes a divergence-free velocity in 3D, but it isn’t very useful

We use the streamfunction primarily for 2D flows, but a vector streamfunction can be prescribed for 3D flows as well. It is rarely used and not a part of MAE3230. But sometimes students ask about it.

In general, we can define the velocity for a 3D flow in terms of a vector streamfunction \(\vec\psi\):

\vec u=\nabla\times\vec\psi. (B.117)

If we want to define \(\vec\psi\) so that the resulting \(\vec u\) is divergence-free, we can achieve that by defining \(\vec\psi\) in terms of two scalars \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\):

\vec\psi=\psi_1\nabla\psi_2. (B.118)

If we define \(\vec\psi\) this way, we can evaluate \(\vec u\) and show that it must be divergence-free. This uses vector identities that most MAE3230 students don’t have memorized. The velocity \(\vec u\) ends up being the cross product of the gradients of \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\):

\vec u=\nabla\times\vec\psi=\nabla\times(\psi_1\nabla\psi_2)=\nabla\psi_1\times\nabla\psi_2. (B.119)

The divergence of this velocity field is identically zero, because we can show by vector identities that it involves curls of gradients, which are all identically zero:

\nabla\cdot(\nabla\psi_1\times\nabla\psi_2)=(\nabla\times\nabla\psi_1)\cdot\nabla\psi_2-(\nabla\times\nabla\psi_2)\cdot\nabla\psi_1=0. (B.120)

So, by defining \(\vec\psi=\psi_1\nabla\psi_2\), we guarantee that \(\vec u=\nabla\psi_1\times\nabla\psi_2\) is divergence-free.

An incompressible velocity field thus prescribes two scalar fields \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\). An irrotational velocity field prescribes one scalar field \(\phi\). For a 3D incompressible, irrotational flow, there are three scalars: \(\phi\), \(\psi_1\), and \(\psi_2\), whose gradients are everywhere orthogonal to each other:

\vec u=\nabla\psi_1\times\nabla\psi_2=\nabla\phi. (B.121)

The 2D streamfunction that is typically used can be recovered by defining \(\psi_1=\psi(x,y)\) and \(\psi_2=z\), in which case \(\nabla\psi_2=\hat z\) and \(\vec\psi=\psi\hat z\). For a 2D flow, \(\nabla\psi\) can be thought of as a vector which, when crossed with \(\hat z\), yields \(\vec u\). It is straightforward to define boundary conditions for \(\psi\) in two dimensions to satisfy the no-slip and/or no-penetration conditions, and thus the streamfunction is useful for 2D incompressible flows.

The two scalar functions \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\) prescribe that \(\psi_1\) is the clockwise areal flowrate between a point and an arbitrary origin along a surface defined everywhere by a normal given by \(\nabla\psi_2\). In 2D, the surface is the \(xy\) plane, prescribed normal to \(\psi_2=\hat z\). Because the spatial orientation and meaning of \(\psi\) and \(\vec u\) in 2D is relatively easy to visualize and easy to align relative to the geometry of a specified object, the streamfunction in 2D is useful.

In 3D, although the vector streamfunction can in principle always be defined, prescribing \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\) to satisfy the no-slip and no-penetration boundary conditions becomes quite unwieldy, and it is usually easier to use other tools to guarantee conservation of mass. So the vector streamfunction in a 3D fluid-mechanical context is mostly a vector-calculus curiosity.

Yer Gettin’ Pretty Esoteric There Aren’tcha Professor Kirby Haiku: these three scalars are / all you need to define u / \(\phi,\psi_1,\psi_2\)

streamfunction: denoted \(\psi\). Scalar function defined for 2D flows equivalently as (a) \(\psi(A)=\int_O^A u\,dy-v\,dx\) or (b) \(u=\partial\psi/\partial y\) and \(v=-\partial\psi/\partial x\), or (c) \(\vec u=\nabla\times\psi\hat z\). Incompressible 2D flows can be defined by \(\psi(x,y)\) because the existence of \(\psi(x,y)\) is mathematically equivalent to satisfying conservation of mass.

conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

For example, \(\psi_1=x,\psi_2=x+y,\phi=z\) satisfies (B.121), while the first two gradients have dot product 1. B.17 Pressure

Pressure is an isotropic, diagonal dyadic tensor

In general, the force per unit area that a plane or surface feels in a motionless fluid is described by an isotropic second-order tensor i.e., dyadic called the pressure. Because this tensor is isotropic, it can equivalently be described as a simple scalar, and most fluid mechanicians describe pressure as a scalar. The microscopic underpinnings of this force is the kinetic energy of the molecules that make up the fluid bouncing back and forth.

If we want to describe a vector property that a fluid applies to a surface, at minimum this requires a second-order tensor. The dot product of this second order tensor with the unit normal to the surface leads to a vector that relates to that plane. For example, pressure describes a force per unit area that is applied to any surface in a fluid. The pressure can be written as a dyadic \(\vec{\vec p}\):

\begin{aligned}\vec{\vec p}={}&p\widehat{xx}+0\widehat{yx}+0\widehat{zx}\\&+0\widehat{xy}+p\widehat{yy}+0\widehat{zy}\\&+0\widehat{xz}+0\widehat{yz}+p\widehat{zz}=p\widehat{xx}+p\widehat{yy}+p\widehat{zz},\end{aligned} (B.122)

or, in Cartesian coordinates, as its matrix representation \([\vec{\vec p}]\):

[\vec{\vec p}]=\begin{bmatrix}p&0&0\\0&p&0\\0&0&p\end{bmatrix}. (B.123)

matrix representation of the pressure dyadic

The unit dyads describe properties that are related to two directions. In this case, the two directions being related are (a) the orientation of the plane in question (as described by the normal \(\hat n\)) and (b) the orientation of the resulting force per unit area, which is a vector. the force per unit area \(\vec F^{\prime\prime}\) is given by the dot product of the pressure vector and the unit normal:

\vec F^{\prime\prime}=\vec{\vec p}\cdot\hat n=(p\widehat{xx}+p\widehat{yy}+p\widehat{zz})\cdot(n_x\hat x+n_y\hat y+n_z\hat z)=pn_x\hat x+pn_y\hat y+pn_z\hat z. (B.124)

Or, using matrix notation:

[F^{\prime\prime}]=[p]^{\mathsf T}[n]=\begin{bmatrix}p&0&0\\0&p&0\\0&0&p\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}n_x\\ n_y\\ n_z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}pn_x\\ pn_y\\ pn_z\end{bmatrix}. (B.125)

matrix representation of force on a plane

As stated above, the pressure is simple enough that it can be described as a scalar and the force per unit area that pressure applies to a surface can be written as \(p\hat n\). This is because the effects of pressure are isotropic and the pressure dyadic is isotropic.

isotropic: equivalent in all directions.

dyadic: a second-order tensor comprising a set of unit dyads.

dyad: a fundamental element that describes two directions, e.g., [example notation too faded to read].

scalar: as a noun: a property with a magnitude only; no direction; as an adjective: having magnitude only but no direction.

Editorial note: The source’s phrase “pressure vector” refers here to the pressure dyadic \(\vec{\vec p}=p\mathbf I\). The sign of the traction depends on which body and normal direction are chosen: for force on fluid with its outward control-volume normal, pressure traction is \(-p\hat n\); the opposite force on the bounding surface is \(+p\hat n\).

B.18 The velocity gradient dyadic is closely related to the Jacobian of the dynamic function \(\vec u=\partial\vec P/\partial t\)

We use gradients to describe spatial variations of stuff, and we use the Jacobian to describe the dynamic behavior of systems. These are significantly different contexts. However, the spatial variation of fluid velocity and the dynamic behavior of a fluid element are very closely related results—they start from different contexts but converge. We don’t use Jacobians in MAE3230, but some students enjoy seeing the parallels.

A gradient is a generalized directional derivative that describes how a function varies in multiple spatial coordinates. When the function in question is the velocity vector, the velocity gradient is a dyadic which can be represented in terms of unit dyads and associated components:

\begin{aligned}\nabla\vec u={}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\widehat{xx}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\widehat{yx}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\widehat{zx}\\&+\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\widehat{xy}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\widehat{yy}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\widehat{zy}\\&+\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\widehat{xz}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\widehat{yz}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\widehat{zz},\end{aligned} (B.126)

or, for convenience, a matrix representation consisting of a matrix of the components:

[\nabla\vec u]=\begin{bmatrix}\partial u/\partial x&\partial v/\partial x&\partial w/\partial x\\ \partial u/\partial y&\partial v/\partial y&\partial w/\partial y\\ \partial u/\partial z&\partial v/\partial z&\partial w/\partial z\end{bmatrix}. (B.127)

The Jacobian matrix of a vector-valued function is a matrix of the partial derivatives of the components of the function with respect to its dependent variables. It mathematically is much more general; it doesn’t have to have anything to do with space. It doesn’t even have to be dimensionally homogeneous.

A common example of a useful Jacobian matrix that is quite different from a gradient comes from coordinate transformation—the position vector in Cartesian coordinates can be written as a function of the coordinates in cylindrical coordinates:

x=r\cos\theta;\qquad y=r\sin\theta;\qquad z=z. (B.128)

and the Jacobian is defined as

J=\begin{bmatrix}\partial x/\partial r&\partial x/\partial\theta&\partial x/\partial z\\ \partial y/\partial r&\partial y/\partial\theta&\partial y/\partial z\\ \partial z/\partial r&\partial z/\partial\theta&\partial z/\partial z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta&0\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}. (B.129)

Jacobians are most often used for coordinate transforms and analysis of dynamical systems. For coordinate transforms, Jacobians help identify how to properly integrate in a transformed coordinate system (the determinant of the Jacobian matrix helps specify a unit volume element for integration). For dynamical systems, if we define a function \(\vec f(\vec P)=\partial\vec P/\partial t\), the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix of \(\vec f\) describes the stability of steady-state values of \(\vec P\).

Jacobian Haiku: the Jacobian / of u as a function of P / it’s grad u transpose

Editorial note: The leading sign of the third displayed row of (B.126) is degraded. It is shown as a plus here, reconstructed from the definition of \(\nabla\vec u\) and the fully legible matrix (B.127). The source defines the Jacobian using “dependent variables”; its columns differentiate with respect to the input (independent) variables, as (B.129) illustrates.


PDF page 484 — source_issue

There is a special case in which a gradient and a Jacobian appear very similar. For the special case where \(\vec P\) is the position vector in Cartesian coordinates and \(\vec u\) is the velocity vector in Cartesian coordinates, the Jacobian of the velocity vector is the transpose of the matrix representation of the velocity gradient dyadic:

J[\vec u(\vec P)]=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}=[\nabla\vec u^{\mathsf T}]. (B.130)

Fluid mechanicians talk about Jacobians primarily in the context of wave propagation—i.e., acoustics, shock waves, surface waves, or in formulation of numerical solvers, and do not use the term “Jacobian” very often otherwise. Fluid mechanicians describe velocity gradients all the time.

B.19 Dyadics we can describe with lower-order vectors or scalars

Pressure: A property that, when orthogonally projected onto a plane, describes the force per unit area on that plane, is properly described by a dyadic:

\vec{\vec p}=p\vec{\vec I}=p\widehat{xx}+p\widehat{yy}+p\widehat{zz};\qquad[\vec{\vec p}]=\begin{bmatrix}p&0&0\\0&p&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}, (B.131)

Editorial correction: The source prints 0 in the bottom-right entry of (B.131). It must be \(p\) for the isotropic tensor \(p\vec{\vec I}\).

where the force per unit area on a surface is given by \(\vec{\vec p}\cdot\hat n\). However, because \(\vec{\vec p}\) is isotropic, \(\vec{\vec p}\cdot\hat n=p\hat n\), and we find that the scalar \(p\) is sufficient to describe the force per unit area on a plane.

Vorticity: The rate at which fluid rotates is properly described by the rotation-rate dyadic:

\vec{\vec\omega}=\frac12\left(\nabla\vec u+\nabla\vec u^{\mathsf T}\right). (B.132)

Editorial correction: The printed plus sign produces the symmetric strain-rate tensor. The antisymmetric rotation-rate tensor uses \(\tfrac12(\nabla\vec u-(\nabla\vec u)^{\mathsf T})\) in the book’s gradient convention.

However, because an antisymmetric tensor has only three unique components, the rotation of fluid can also be described by the vorticity pseudotensor:

\vec\omega=\nabla\times\vec u. (B.133)

Transcription note: The operators in (B.133) are washed out in the scan. The equals and cross-product signs above are reconstructed from the stated vorticity definition; they cannot be certified visually from this source.

Each component of the vorticity corresponds to (and is twice as big as) one of the components of the rotation-rate tensor.

The rotation-rate dyadic does not require definition of a coordinate system. The vorticity does, and the sign of the vorticity is dependent on the handedness of the coordinate system. We always use right-handed coordinate systems.

9. (OBJECTIVE: become used to dyadic manipulation of the terms in the Navier–Stokes equations)

The Navier–Stokes equations describe incompressible flow of a viscous fluid:

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u. (B.137)

We will manipulate this many times over in the lines below. The idea is that we need to become familiar with this equation if we are to use it successfully going forward. These exercises might be easy, might be hard, might be repetitive, might be challenging and disorienting. I think they are important.

(a) Write \(\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}\) in terms of its scalar components and unit Cartesian vectors, i.e., \(\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}=\text{blah}\,\hat x+\text{dee}\,\hat y+\text{blah}\,\hat z\).

(b) Write \(\rho\vec u\) in terms of its scalar components and unit Cartesian vectors.

(c) Write the matrix representation of \(\rho\vec u\) as a column matrix.

(d) Write the Cartesian representation of \(\nabla\) in terms of partial derivative operators and unit Cartesian vectors.

(e) Write this Cartesian representation of \(\nabla\) as a column matrix.

(f) Evaluate the operator \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\) by dotting term by term and using the dot product results for unit Cartesian vectors (i.e., \(\hat x\cdot\hat y=0\) and \(\hat x\cdot\hat x=1\)). The result is not a value, the result is an operator which can be used to operate on a scalar or vector.

(g) Evaluate the operator \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\) by matrix multiplication of the transpose of the matrix representation of \(\vec u\) (a \(1\times3\) row matrix) with the matrix representation of \(\nabla\) (a \(3\times1\) column matrix).

(h) \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\) is an operator that operates on \(\vec u\) to produce a vector. Write out \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) using unit Cartesian vectors.

(i) Write out \(\nabla p\) in terms of unit vector components.

(j) Evaluate the operator \(\nabla^2\), which is shorthand for \(\nabla\cdot\nabla\), by taking the dot product of \(\nabla\) with itself term by term and using the dot product results for unit Cartesian vectors (i.e., \(\hat x\cdot\hat y=0\) and \(\hat x\cdot\hat x=1\)). The result is not a value, the result is an operator that can be used to operate on a scalar or vector.

(k) Evaluate the operator \(\nabla^2\), which is shorthand for \(\nabla\cdot\nabla\) by matrix multiplication of the transpose of the matrix representation of \(\nabla\) (a \(1\times3\) row matrix) with the matrix representation of \(\nabla\) (a \(3\times1\) column matrix).

(l) Write out \(\mu\nabla^2\vec u\) in terms of unit Cartesian vectors.

(m) Write \(\nabla\vec u\), which is a dyadic (i.e., 2nd-order tensor) by taking the dyadic product of \(\nabla\) and \(\vec u\), and noting that the dyadic product of two unit vectors is a unit dyad (for example \(\hat x\hat z=\widehat{xz}\)).

(n) Write the transpose of the dyadic (i.e., \(\nabla\vec u^{\mathsf T}\)) by switching each of the dyads in \(\nabla\vec u\) (i.e., replacing \(\widehat{xz}\) with \(\widehat{zx}\) and so on).

(o) Evaluate the strain rate dyadic (i.e., strain rate tensor) \(\vec{\vec\varepsilon}\) by finding the average of \(\nabla\vec u\) with its transpose, i.e., \(\vec{\vec\varepsilon}=\frac{\nabla\vec u+\nabla\vec u^{\mathsf T}}2\).

(p) Evaluate the rotation rate dyadic (i.e., rotation rate tensor) \(\vec{\vec\omega}\) by evaluating \(\vec{\vec\omega}=\frac{\nabla\vec u-\nabla\vec u^{\mathsf T}}2\).

Problems with Answers

1. (OBJECTIVE: MATH1910 review; helps us derive differential conservation equations used for fluid mechanics) Write the first two terms of the Taylor-series expansion of \(y=\exp x\) around \(x=1\). Solution: Hint: this is plug and chug from defn of T-S expansion. Answer:

y(x)=y(1)+\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=1}(x-1)+\left.\frac12\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right|_{x=1}(x-1)^2+\cdots (B.138)

The TS expansion has infinite terms but problem only asked for two. Derivative of \(\exp x\) is \(\exp x\), conveniently:

y(x)=e+e(x-1)+\frac12e(x-1)^2+\cdots (B.139)

Keeping just the first two terms,

y(x)=e+e(x-1) (B.140)

y(x)=ex (B.141)

Editorial clarification: In (B.140)–(B.141), \(ex\) denotes the first-order Taylor approximation near \(x=1\), not equality to \(e^x\) for all \(x\).

2. (OBJECTIVE: MATH1920 review for conservation of mass equations) Consider a 3D vector field \(\vec u\) with Cartesian components of the form \([\vec u]^{\mathsf T}=[x,0,0]\). This is a flow that is uniformly expanding in the \(x\) direction, which could be approximated by an explosion in a tube aligned in the \(x\)-direction.

(a) In terms of Cartesian derivatives, write out \(\nabla\cdot\vec u\), and integrate it over a cubic volume \(V\) with side length 1 and its center at the origin.

(b) Using the divergence theorem, rewrite the volume integral \(\int_V\nabla\cdot\vec u\,dV\) above in terms of a surface integral over the faces of the cube \(S\). Integrate and confirm the equivalency of both integrals.

Solution:

(a) The divergence in Cartesian coordinates is the sum of the partial derivatives along every axis:

\nabla\cdot\vec u=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=1. (B.142)

Because the divergence is uniform everywhere, you can either directly integrate or just multiply it by the volume of the cube, which is 1:

\int_V\nabla\cdot\vec u\,dV=\int_{-\frac12}^{\frac12}\int_{-\frac12}^{\frac12}\int_{-\frac12}^{\frac12}1\,dx\,dy\,dz=1. (B.143)

(b) The divergence theorem states:

\int_V\nabla\cdot\vec u\,dV=\int_S\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA, (B.144)

where \(\hat n\) represents a unit vector pointing out of the surface of the cube \(S\). This surface integral technically represents 6 different integrals over each cube face, but \(\vec u\) is perpendicular to the unit normals of four of those cube faces, leaving only 2 integrals.

Because \(\vec u\) is parallel to the \(\hat n\) vectors of the remaining 2 faces, and uniform over them as well, you can either directly integrate and add up each contribution, or just multiply the magnitude of the function at each cube face (located at \(x=\pm\frac12\)) by the face area and add up:

\int_S\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA=\int_{-\frac12}^{\frac12}\int_{-\frac12}^{\frac12}\frac12\,dy\,dz+\int_{-\frac12}^{\frac12}\int_{-\frac12}^{\frac12}\frac12\,dy\,dz=1. (B.145)


PDF page 489 — source_issue

Both integrals give the same result.

The divergence equation tells us that the net outflow from a control volume can be calculated in two equivalent ways: by keeping track of what leaves the control volume through the bounding surface, or by summing up all the little net outflows in every individual element inside the control volume. \(\nabla\cdot\vec u\) is the local net outflow, which when summed over a volume, gives us the total net outflow. We will use this to derive the differential forms of the mass and momentum conservation equations that form the foundation of fluid mechanics.

3. (OBJECTIVE: MATH1920 review; helps understand the lift force that makes a plane fly) Consider a 3D vector velocity field \(\vec u\) with Cartesian components of the form \([\vec u]^{\mathsf T}=[0,x,0]\). This is a simple shear flow in the \(y\)-direction.

(a) Write out \(\nabla\times\vec u\) (\(\nabla\times\vec u\) is the vorticity of a fluid flow). Evaluate the integral of \(\nabla\times\vec u\), i.e., the integral of the vorticity over a 2D square-shaped domain \(S\) on the \(x\)-\(y\) plane with side length 1 and its bottom-left corner on the origin.

(b) Consider a 2D region \(S\). Write the surface integral \(\int_S\nabla\times\vec u\,dA\) in terms of a contour integral around the boundary \(C\) of \(S\). Evaluate and verify both integrals are the same.

Solution:

(a) From the definition of the curl, only one term survives:

\nabla\times\vec u=\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\hat z=1\hat z. (B.146)

The curl is uniform on the domain, so we can either directly integrate, or dot-product the curl with the unit normal vector of the square and multiply by its area:

\int_S(\nabla\times\vec u)\cdot\hat n\,dA=\int_0^1\int_0^1 1\hat z\,dx\,dy=1\hat z. (B.147)

Editorial correction: The left-hand side of (B.147) is a scalar. With \(\hat n=\hat z\), both occurrences of \(1\hat z\) on its right should be the scalar \(1\); the source has retained a vector after the dot product.

(b) This question basically asks you to use Stokes’ theorem. It is stated as:

\int_S(\nabla\times\vec u)\cdot\hat n\,dA=\int_C\vec u\cdot\hat s\,ds, (B.148)

where \(\hat s\) is a unit vector pointing along the boundary such that it forms a counterclockwise path around the square’s edges.

Performing this line integral would normally involve four integrals around each line segment on the edge of the square, but luckily both of the horizontal segments cancel out and the vertical segment at the origin is zero because \(\vec u=\vec0\) there. Thus, we find everything comes from the vertical segment at \(x=1\):

\int_C\vec u\cdot\hat s\,ds=\int_0^1 1\,dy=1. (B.149)

Both integrals match.

The Stokes equation tells us that the net rotation in a control volume can be calculated in two equivalent ways: by keeping track of the net circular motion around its enclosing contour, or by summing up all the little net rotations acting on every individual element in the control volume. \(\nabla\times\vec u\) is the local vorticity i.e., the local fluid rotation, which summed over a volume, gives the total circulation i.e., total rotation. The Kutta–Zhukovsky theorem says that the lift generated by a body e.g., airplane is given by \(\rho\) times the circulation times the freestream velocity, so calculating this rotation-y-ness is central to telling whether the plane flies or not.

Editorial clarification: Stokes’ theorem integrates the normal component of vorticity over a surface, not a volume. In this example each horizontal line integral is individually zero. The Kutta–Zhukovsky relation \(L^{\prime}=\rho U_\infty\Gamma\) gives lift per unit span in the two-dimensional ideal-flow setting.


PDF page 490 — source_issue

4. (OBJECTIVE: Remind students what a gradient is. Introduce students to dyadic tensors. Prepare students to evaluate fluid deformation as a means to predict viscous forces) Write out an expression for \(\nabla\vec u\). Is this a scalar, vector, or dyadic tensor? Evaluate \(\nabla\vec u\) for the following velocity fields.

(a) \(\vec u=x\hat x+y\hat y+z\hat z\)

(b) \(\vec u=y\hat x+x\hat y\)

(c) \(\vec u=x\hat x-y\hat y\)

(d) \(\vec u=y\hat x-x\hat y\)

You can evaluate the gradient of a vector by “multiplying” a “matrix” \(\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}\) with a “matrix” \(\begin{bmatrix}u&v&w\end{bmatrix}\).

This is an OK heuristic for Cartesian vectors/tensors but it isn’t real math. I use it to remember how to find the gradient in Cartesian coordinates. It will fail horribly if you try it in cylindrical or spherical coordinates.

Solution:

In matrix form:

[\nabla\vec u]=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}. (B.150)

Transcription note: Several derivative characters in (B.150) are washed out. The matrix is restored from the identical, legible gradient matrix in (B.127) and its unit-dyad expansion, not independently certified from this faded copy.

The velocity gradient is a dyadic tensor.

For \(\vec u=x\hat x+y\hat y+z\hat z\),

[\nabla\vec u]=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}. (B.151)

For \(\vec u=y\hat x+x\hat y\),

[\nabla\vec u]=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}. (B.152)

For \(\vec u=x\hat x-y\hat y\),

[\nabla\vec u]=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}. (B.153)

For \(\vec u=y\hat x-x\hat y\),

[\nabla\vec u]=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}. (B.154)

Editorial correction: In the gradient convention explicitly shown in (B.150), differentiating \(u=y,\ v=-x\) gives row 1 \([0,-1,0]\) and row 2 \([1,0,0]\). The two off-diagonal signs in the source’s (B.154) are reversed.

5. (OBJECTIVE: Remind students what a curl is and prepare them to use vorticity to evaluate the applicability of irrotational flow) Write out an expression for \(\nabla\times\vec u\). Is this a scalar, vector, or dyadic tensor? Or none of these What does this property describe about a fluid? Give a spatial interpretation, using the following as examples.

(a) \(\vec u=y\hat x+x\hat y\)

(b) \(\vec u=y\hat x-x\hat y\)


PDF page 491 — source_issue

Solution:

The curl of a vector is a pseudovector. A pseudovector is similar to a vector; however, a pseudovector’s signs depend on whether the coordinate system is right-handed or left-handed. Many sources (incorrectly) say that the curl of a vector is a vector: this is a little sloppy but not the end of the world. It is more important that we know that the curl of a vector is not a scalar and is not a dyadic tensor than that we get the vector vs. pseudovector part correct.

\(\nabla\times\vec u\) describes the rotation of the fluid. The three components of \(\nabla\times\vec u\) describe twice the angular rotation rate around the \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) axes, respectively.

\(\nabla\times\vec u\) is given by

\begin{aligned}\nabla\times\vec u={}&\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\right)\hat x\\ &+\left(-\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)\hat y\\ &+\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\hat z,\end{aligned}

Transcription note: The leading minus sign in the expanded y component is washed out; it is restored from the legible matrix form (B.155) immediately below.

or, written in matrix form:

[\nabla\times\vec u]=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\\ -\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\end{bmatrix}. (B.155)

For \(\vec u=y\hat x+x\hat y\), \(\nabla\times\vec u=0\), which means that the fluid is not rotating anywhere. This flow is shearing in the \(xy\) plane, extending along the line \(y=x\) and compressing along the line \(y=-x\).

Transcription note: The beginning of this example is faded; the velocity field is restored from Problem 5(a) on the preceding page, and its zero curl is confirmed by direct differentiation.

For \(\vec u=y\hat x-x\hat y\), \(\nabla\times\vec u=-2\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\). This flow is everywhere rotating clockwise around the \(z\) axis at 1 rad/s.

Editorial correction: The source omits the direction in the last curl. Its vector value is \(-2\hat z\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\).

6. (OBJECTIVE: matrix and unit dyad operations; projection of stress tensor onto a plane) When continua are in a state of stress (this is equally true for solids and fluids) defined by \(\vec{\vec\tau}\), \(\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\hat n\) measures the force per unit area that stress state generates on a plane normal to \(\hat n\). For Hookean solids, the stress is proportional to the strain (and often denoted as \(\vec{\vec\sigma}\)). For Newtonian liquids, \(\vec{\vec\tau}\) is proportional to the strain rate. Anyway, we use \(\vec{\vec\tau}\) to calculate the viscous forces in fluid flow. Show that

\begin{aligned}\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\hat n={}&(\tau_{xx}n_x+\tau_{yx}n_y+\tau_{zx}n_z)\hat x\\ &+(\tau_{xy}n_x+\tau_{yy}n_y+\tau_{zy}n_z)\hat y\\ &+(\tau_{xz}n_x+\tau_{yz}n_y+\tau_{zz}n_z)\hat z;\\ [\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\hat n]={}&\begin{bmatrix}\tau_{xx}n_x+\tau_{yx}n_y+\tau_{zx}n_z\\ \tau_{xy}n_x+\tau_{yy}n_y+\tau_{zy}n_z\\ \tau_{xz}n_x+\tau_{yz}n_y+\tau_{zz}n_z\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} (B.156)

Do this in two separate ways:

(a) First do this by multiplying it out term-by-term (yes there are 27 terms: multiply them all out), using unit dyad–vector dot product relations to eliminate 18 of the terms, and grouping the remaining 9.

(b) Then do this by manipulating the matrix representations using matrix operations as specified above.

Describe what physical quantity each of the following describes, and specify the tensor rank of each.

(a) \(\tau_{xy}\)

(b) \((\tau_{xz}n_x+\tau_{yz}n_y+\tau_{zz}n_z)\hat z\)

(c) \(\vec{\vec\tau}\)

Solution:


PDF page 492 — source_issue

To use unit dyad–vector dot product relations, we take the dot product, noting that the dot product commutes with scalar multiplication and distributes over addition. This means it is somewhat like multiplying a sum of 9 terms times another sum of three terms to get 27 total terms:

\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\hat n=\left(\begin{aligned}&\tau_{xx}\widehat{xx}+\tau_{yx}\widehat{yx}+\tau_{zx}\widehat{zx}\\ &+\tau_{xy}\widehat{xy}+\tau_{yy}\widehat{yy}+\tau_{zy}\widehat{zy}\\ &+\tau_{xz}\widehat{xz}+\tau_{yz}\widehat{yz}+\tau_{zz}\widehat{zz}\end{aligned}\right)\cdot\left(\begin{aligned}&n_x\hat x\\ &+n_y\hat y\\ &+n_z\hat z\end{aligned}\right), (B.157)

but, when we get these 27 terms, each includes a unit dyad dotted with a unit vector, and those dot products all become zero or become unit vectors:

\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\hat n=\begin{aligned}&\tau_{xx}n_x\underbrace{\widehat{xx}\cdot\hat x}_{\hat x}+\tau_{xx}n_y\underbrace{\widehat{xx}\cdot\hat y}_{0}+\tau_{xx}n_z\underbrace{\widehat{xx}\cdot\hat z}_{0}\\ &+\tau_{xy}n_x\underbrace{\widehat{xy}\cdot\hat x}_{\hat y}+\tau_{xy}n_y\underbrace{\widehat{xy}\cdot\hat y}_{0}+\tau_{xy}n_z\underbrace{\widehat{xy}\cdot\hat z}_{0}\\ &+\tau_{xz}n_x\underbrace{\widehat{xz}\cdot\hat x}_{\hat z}+\tau_{xz}n_y\underbrace{\widehat{xz}\cdot\hat y}_{0}+\tau_{xz}n_z\underbrace{\widehat{xz}\cdot\hat z}_{0}\\ &+\tau_{yx}n_x\underbrace{\widehat{yx}\cdot\hat x}_{0}+\tau_{yx}n_y\underbrace{\widehat{yx}\cdot\hat y}_{\hat x}+\tau_{yx}n_z\underbrace{\widehat{yx}\cdot\hat z}_{0}\\ &+\tau_{yy}n_x\underbrace{\widehat{yy}\cdot\hat x}_{0}+\tau_{yy}n_y\underbrace{\widehat{yy}\cdot\hat y}_{\hat y}+\tau_{yy}n_z\underbrace{\widehat{yy}\cdot\hat z}_{0}\\ &+\tau_{yz}n_x\underbrace{\widehat{yz}\cdot\hat x}_{0}+\tau_{yz}n_y\underbrace{\widehat{yz}\cdot\hat y}_{\hat z}+\tau_{yz}n_z\underbrace{\widehat{yz}\cdot\hat z}_{0}\\ &+\tau_{zx}n_x\underbrace{\widehat{zx}\cdot\hat x}_{0}+\tau_{zx}n_y\underbrace{\widehat{zx}\cdot\hat y}_{0}+\tau_{zx}n_z\underbrace{\widehat{zx}\cdot\hat z}_{\hat x}\\ &+\tau_{zy}n_x\underbrace{\widehat{zy}\cdot\hat x}_{0}+\tau_{zy}n_y\underbrace{\widehat{zy}\cdot\hat y}_{0}+\tau_{zy}n_z\underbrace{\widehat{zy}\cdot\hat z}_{\hat y}\\ &+\tau_{zz}n_x\underbrace{\widehat{zz}\cdot\hat x}_{0}+\tau_{zz}n_y\underbrace{\widehat{zz}\cdot\hat y}_{0}+\tau_{zz}n_z\underbrace{\widehat{zz}\cdot\hat z}_{\hat z}\end{aligned} (B.158)

Note in Equation (B.157) we are using parentheses not square brackets—these are groups of terms being added together; these are not matrices. These terms can then be gathered together to get the final answer:

\begin{aligned}\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\hat n={}&(\tau_{xx}n_x+\tau_{yx}n_y+\tau_{zx}n_z)\hat x\\ &+(\tau_{xy}n_x+\tau_{yy}n_y+\tau_{zy}n_z)\hat y\\ &+(\tau_{xz}n_x+\tau_{yz}n_y+\tau_{zz}n_z)\hat z.\end{aligned} (B.159)

Transcription note: The bottom line of (B.159) is largely erased. It is restored from the identical, legible expansion in (B.156) and the surviving terms of (B.158). Annotations in (B.158) are presented below each dot product instead of as diagonal cancellation arrows.

Or, using matrix multiplication, we can use matrix representations, which arrange the scalar components and leave the unit dyads as implied. Then matrix multiplications can mimic the unit dyad and unit vector operations, as long as we use the correct matrix operation:

[\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\hat n]=[\vec{\vec\tau}]^{\mathsf T}[\hat n], (B.160)

which leads directly to

[\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\hat n]=\begin{bmatrix}\tau_{xx}&\tau_{xy}&\tau_{xz}\\ \tau_{yx}&\tau_{yy}&\tau_{yz}\\ \tau_{zx}&\tau_{zy}&\tau_{zz}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}n_x\\ n_y\\ n_{\text{[faded]}}\end{bmatrix}, (B.161)

[\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\hat n]=\begin{bmatrix}\tau_{xx}n_x+\tau_{yx}n_y+\tau_{zx}n_z\\ \tau_{xy}n_x+\tau_{yy}n_y+\tau_{zy}n_z\\ \tau_{xz}n_x+\tau_{yz}n_y+\tau_{zz}n_z\end{bmatrix}. (B.162)

Editorial correction: To produce (B.162), the matrix printed in (B.161) must be transposed, as (B.160) specifies; its first row would then be \([\tau_{xx},\tau_{yx},\tau_{zx}]\). The last component of the normal vector has an erased subscript; the preceding expansions identify it as \(n_z\). The book’s dot-product convention here contracts the first dyad index; read the transpose consistently with that convention.

The matrix multiplication is faster but you only use the matrix operations on Cartesian tensors and you can only use it if you make note of what matrix operations correspond to what tensor operations.

Editorial clarification: Algebraic component matrix operations also apply in any orthonormal basis at a point; derivatives in spatially varying bases require additional care.


PDF page 493 — source_issue

(a) \(\tau_{xy}\) is the magnitude of the \(x\) component of the force per unit area that the state of stress would generate on a plane normal to \(\hat y\). It is a scalar.

(b) \((\tau_{zx}n_x+\tau_{zy}n_y+\tau_{zz}n_z)\hat z\) is the \(z\) component of the vector force per unit area that the state of stress would generate on a plane specified by \(\hat n\). It is a vector.

(c) \(\vec{\vec\tau}\) describes the state of stress in a fluid. It is a dyadic tensor.

Editorial clarification: These two answers switch the off-diagonal stress-index convention used in the question and (B.159)/(B.162). There the \(z\) component uses \(\tau_{xz}n_x+\tau_{yz}n_y+\tau_{zz}n_z\), and \(\tau_{xy}\) contributes a \(y\)-directed force on an \(x\)-normal plane. For a symmetric stress tensor the numerical off-diagonal components coincide, but the notation should remain consistent.

7. (OBJECTIVE: evaluate Eulerian momentum loss by outflow; practice dyadic operations via matrix approaches and unit dyad operations) For incompressible flow, \(\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) is a measure of the net momentum outflow per unit volume at any point in a flowfield. We show that by applying the divergence theorem to the \(\int_S\rho\vec u\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA\) integral form. Unlike the Bernoulli equation, which helped us in a Lagrangian sense understand how a fluid mass element accelerates, this expression helps us understand in an Eulerian sense how an infinitesimal control volume loses momentum by outflow. 8. (OBJECTIVE: Establish a formal vector method for simplifying a vector equation to consider only one component of momentum) Rewrite the vector integral conservation of momentum equation

\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V\rho\vec u\,dV}_{\text{time deriv of momentum}}+\underbrace{\int_S(\rho\vec u)(\vec u\cdot\hat n)\,dA}_{\text{convective outflux of momentum}}=\underbrace{\int_S-p\hat n\,dA}_{\text{net pressure surface force}}+\underbrace{\int_V-\rho g\hat z\,dV}_{\text{net gravitational body force}} (B.170)

as an equation for the \(x\) momentum only. You can do this by inspection if it is obvious to you. If you want to do this formally, take the dot product of \(\hat x\) with this equation term by term. Once you have written this equation, what are each of its four terms? Scalars? Vectors? Dyadic tensors?

Solution:

The momentum equation is a vector equation; if we take a dot product of it with a unit vector we get a


PDF page 495 — verified

scalar equation. Start with the vector equation and take the dot product of it with \(\hat x\):

\hat x\cdot\left[\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V\rho\vec u\,dV}_{\text{time deriv of momentum}}+\underbrace{\int_S(\rho\vec u)(\vec u\cdot\hat n)\,dA}_{\text{convective outflux of momentum}}=\underbrace{\int_S-p\hat n\,dA}_{\text{net pressure surface force}}+\underbrace{\int_V-\rho g\hat z\,dV}_{\text{net gravitational body force}}\right]. (B.171)

Partial differentiation with time, integration in space, and the dot product operation all commute, so we can simply move the dot product inside all of the integrals:

\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V\rho\hat x\cdot\vec u\,dV}_{\text{time deriv of }x\text{ momentum}}+\underbrace{\int_S(\rho\hat x\cdot\vec u)(\vec u\cdot\hat n)\,dA}_{\text{convective outflux of }x\text{ momentum}}=\underbrace{\int_S-p\hat x\cdot\hat n\,dA}_{x\text{ component of net pressure surface force}}+\underbrace{\int_V-\rho g\hat x\cdot\hat z\,dV}_{x\text{ component of net gravitational body force}}, (B.172)

and simplify:

\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_V\rho u\,dV}_{\text{time deriv of }x\text{ momentum}}+\underbrace{\int_S(\rho u)(\vec u\cdot\hat n)\,dA}_{\text{convective outflux of }x\text{ momentum}}=\underbrace{\int_S-pn_x\,dA}_{x\text{ component of net pressure surface force}}. (B.173)

9. (OBJECTIVE: become used to dyadic manipulation of the terms in the Navier–Stokes equations)

The Navier–Stokes equations describe incompressible flow of a viscous fluid:

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u. (B.174)

We will manipulate this many times over in the lines below. The idea is that we need to become familiar with this equation if we are to use it successfully going forward. These exercises might be easy, might be hard, might be repetitive, might be challenging and disorienting. I think they are important.

(a) Write \(\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}\) in terms of its scalar components and unit Cartesian vectors, i.e., \(\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}=\text{blah}\,\hat x+\text{dee}\,\hat y+\text{blah}\,\hat z\).

(b) Write \(\rho\vec u\) in terms of its scalar components and unit Cartesian vectors.

(c) Write the matrix representation of \(\rho\vec u\) as a column matrix.

(d) Write the Cartesian representation of \(\nabla\) in terms of partial derivative operators and unit Cartesian vectors.

(e) Write this Cartesian representation of \(\nabla\) as a column matrix.

(f) Evaluate the operator \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\) by dotting term by term and using the dot product results for unit Cartesian vectors (i.e., \(\hat x\cdot\hat y=0\) and \(\hat x\cdot\hat x=1\)). The result is not a value, the result is an operator which can be used to operate on a scalar or vector.

(g) Evaluate the operator \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\) by matrix multiplication of the transpose of the matrix representation of \(\vec u\) (a \(1\times3\) row matrix) with the matrix representation of \(\nabla\) (a \(3\times1\) column matrix).


PDF page 496 — source_issue

(h) \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\) is an operator that operates on \(\vec u\) to produce a vector. Write out \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) using unit Cartesian vectors.

(i) Write out \(\nabla p\) in terms of unit vector components.

(j) Evaluate the operator \(\nabla^2\), which is shorthand for \(\nabla\cdot\nabla\), by taking the dot product of \(\nabla\) with itself term by term and using the dot product results for unit Cartesian vectors (i.e., \(\hat x\cdot\hat y=0\) and \(\hat x\cdot\hat x=1\)). The result is not a value, the result is an operator that can be used to operate on a scalar or vector.

(k) Evaluate the operator \(\nabla^2\), which is shorthand for \(\nabla\cdot\nabla\) by matrix multiplication of the transpose of the matrix representation of \(\nabla\) (a \(1\times3\) row matrix) with the matrix representation of \(\nabla\) (a \(3\times1\) column matrix).

(l) Write out \(\mu\nabla^2\vec u\) in terms of unit Cartesian vectors.

(m) Write \(\nabla\vec u\), which is a dyadic (i.e., 2nd-order tensor) by taking the dyadic product of \(\nabla\) and \(\vec u\), and noting that the dyadic product of two unit vectors is a unit dyad (for example \(\hat x\hat z=\widehat{xz}\)).

(n) Write the transpose of the dyadic (i.e., \(\nabla\vec u^{\mathsf T}\)) by switching each of the dyads in \(\nabla\vec u\) (i.e., replacing \(\widehat{xz}\) with \(\widehat{zx}\) and so on).

(o) Evaluate the strain rate dyadic (i.e., strain rate tensor) \(\vec{\vec\varepsilon}\) by finding the average of \(\nabla\vec u\) with its transpose, i.e., \(\vec{\vec\varepsilon}=\frac{\nabla\vec u+\nabla\vec u^{\mathsf T}}2\).

(p) Evaluate the rotation rate dyadic (i.e., rotation rate tensor) \(\vec{\vec\omega}\) by evaluating \(\vec{\vec\omega}=\frac{\nabla\vec u-\nabla\vec u^{\mathsf T}}2\).

Solution:

(a) Write \(\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}\) in terms of its scalar components and unit Cartesian vectors, i.e., \(\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}=\text{blah}\,\hat x+\text{dee}\,\hat y+\text{blah}\,\hat z\).

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}=\rho\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\hat x+\rho\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}\hat y+\rho\frac{\partial w}{\partial t}\hat z.

(b) Write \(\rho\vec u\) in terms of its scalar components and unit Cartesian vectors.

\rho\vec u=\rho u\hat x+\rho v\hat y+\rho w\hat z.

(c) Write the matrix representation of \(\rho\vec u\) as a column matrix.

[\rho\vec u]=\begin{bmatrix}\rho u\\ \rho v\\ \rho w\end{bmatrix}

(d) Write the Cartesian representation of \(\nabla\) in terms of partial derivative operators and unit Cartesian vectors.

\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\hat x+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\hat y+\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\hat z.

(e) Write this Cartesian representation of \(\nabla\) as a column matrix.

[\nabla]=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}.

Transcription note: The last velocity component in (b), the last derivative in (d), and parts of the operator column in (e) are washed out. They are restored from the legible component matrix (c) and the explicit Cartesian derivative formulas on the next two pages.

(f) Evaluate the operator \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\) by dotting term by term and using the dot product results for unit Cartesian vectors (i.e., \(\hat x\cdot\hat y=0\) and \(\hat x\cdot\hat x=1\)). The result is not a value, the result is an operator,

which can be used to operate on a scalar or vector.

\vec u\cdot\nabla=\left(\begin{aligned}&u\hat x\\ &+v\hat y\\ &+w\hat z\end{aligned}\right)\cdot\left(\begin{aligned}&\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\hat x\\ &+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\hat y\\ &+\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\hat z\end{aligned}\right), (B.175)

\vec u\cdot\nabla=\begin{aligned}&u\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\hat x\cdot\hat x)+u\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\hat x\cdot\hat y)+u\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(\hat x\cdot\hat z)\\ &+v\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\hat y\cdot\hat x)+v\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\hat y\cdot\hat y)+v\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(\hat y\cdot\hat z)\\ &+w\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\hat z\cdot\hat x)+w\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\hat z\cdot\hat y)+w\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(\hat z\cdot\hat z)\end{aligned}, (B.176)

\vec u\cdot\nabla=u\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial}{\partial z}. (B.177)

(g) Evaluate the operator \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\) by matrix multiplication of the transpose of the matrix representation of \(\vec u\) (a \(1\times3\) row matrix) with the matrix representation of \(\nabla\) (a \(3\times1\) column matrix).

[\vec u\cdot\nabla]=\begin{bmatrix}u&v&w\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}, (B.178)

\vec u\cdot\nabla=u\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial}{\partial z}. (B.179)

(h) \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\) is an operator that operates on \(\vec u\) to produce a vector. Write out \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) using unit Cartesian vectors.

\vec u\cdot\nabla=u\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial}{\partial z}, (B.180)

\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=\left(u\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\right)\left(\begin{aligned}&u\hat x\\ &+v\hat y\\ &+w\hat z\end{aligned}\right), (B.181)

\begin{aligned}\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u={}&\left(u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)\hat x\\ &+\left(u\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\right)\hat y\\ &+\left(u\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\hat z.\end{aligned} (B.182)

(i) Write out \(\nabla p\) in terms of unit vector components.

\nabla p=\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\hat x+\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}\hat y+\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\hat z. (B.183)

(j) Evaluate the operator \(\nabla^2\), which is shorthand for \(\nabla\cdot\nabla\), by taking the dot product of \(\nabla\) with itself term by term and using the dot product results for unit Cartesian vectors (i.e., \(\hat x\cdot\hat y=0\) and \(\hat x\cdot\hat x=1\)). The result is not a value, the result is an operator that can be used to operate on a scalar or vector.

Appendix C

Using Units and Unitless Ratios to Make Fluid Mechanics Easier

C.1 Introduction

Dimensional analysis describes a process by which we gain insight, convenience, or advantage from considering the dimensions of particular aspects of a physical problem. The most common use of dimensional analysis is in defining the nondimensional parameters of the system, which are useful for two key reasons. First, one can describe a physical system with a smaller number of nondimensional parameters than one can with the dimensional parameters. In this sense, nondimensionalizing the system simplifies our analysis. As a specific example, we don’t need to describe flow through a tube as a function of all four relevant parameters (speed, pipe diameter, fluid viscosity, and fluid density), we can describe it as a function of the Reynolds number \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\) alone. Second, because systems can be defined by these nondimensional parameters, they allow us to show that systems with different dimensions (different sizes, different fluid properties, different velocities or pressure gradients) can be shown to be dynamically similar to each other, which means that, although the absolute values of each dimensional parameter are not the same in these problems, the properly nondimensionalized paramaters are the same. For example, we can replicate flow over a big object if we use a small model and simply increase the velocities properly, or we can replicate flow over a microscopic object with a laboratory-scale model if we simply increase the fluid viscosity properly.

dimensional analysis: a mode of analysis centered on using dimensional homogeneity to reduce the parameters needed to analyze a system.

nondimensional parameter: a parameter generated by a process to remove units. Typically denotes the ratio of two or more parameters and therefore their relative importance.

Reynolds number: \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\). The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(Re_x,Re_d\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

dynamically similar: having identical dynamics when properly nondimensionalized.

C.2 Dimensional analysis is used to generalize theoretical and experimental results so a finite number of results can be used to explain an infinite number of physical situations

Dimensional similitude generalizes theoretical or experimental results. Consider the following very simple fluids engineering question: I need to

dimensional similitude: the notion that two physical systems with different parameters can be shown to be similar if the relevant nondimensional parameters are equal.


PDF page 501 — source_issue

pump fluid with density \(\rho\) and viscosity \(\mu\) at a mean speed \(U\) through a smooth tube of diameter \(d\) and length \(L\). What pressure gradient \(\Delta p/L\) and therefore what pressure difference \(\Delta p\) must my pump generate? If the speed is very low, diameter is small, and fluid is very viscous, then this fluid flow is laminar, and it can be solved analytically, and we can determine a general solution. However, if the speed is high, the diameter is large, and the fluid is not very viscous, then this fluid flow is turbulent, and it cannot be solved analytically; we must study it computationally or experimentally. Alas there are many fluids we might want to pump, each of which has its own density and viscosity. Further, there are many many diameters of pipes I might use, and various applications could have any of a variety of needed pipe lengths and mean speeds. If we had to perform an experiment or cluster simulation every time we wanted to predict what pump we needed, then design of these systems would be extraordinarily difficult.

laminar: occuring in orderly sheets or lamina.

turbulent: characterized by local instability and chaos.

Fortunately, we can reduce the parameter space enormously if we reframe the question properly. Instead of trying to determine \(\Delta p/L\) as a function of \(U\), \(d\), \(\rho\), and \(\mu\):

\frac{\Delta p}{L}=\frac{\Delta p}{L}(U,d,\rho,\mu), (C.1)

we endeavor to determine the viscous dissipation factor \(f_D\) as a function of the Reynolds number \(Re\):

f_D=f_D(Re). (C.2)

This change reduces the number of dependent parameters from 4 to 1. The definitions we use to perform this simplification are

Re=\frac{\rho Ud}{\mu} (C.3)

and

f_D=\frac{\Delta p}{\frac12\rho U^2}\frac dL. (C.4)

viscous dissipation factor: a nondimensional coefficient used to characterize drop of the Bernoulli constant (and thus typically pressure) in a pipe. This is typically called the “friction” factor by other texts, but the word “friction” is physically incorrect and misleading so I don’t use that term. In this class we use the Darcy factor \(f_D=\frac{\Delta B}{\frac12\rho U^2}\frac dL\) but there are others e.g., Fanning factor with similar but slightly different definitions.

The Reynolds number \(Re\) is a measure of how much the fluid dynamics are governed by (a) the fluid’s mass and its inertia and therefore its tendency to continue in whatever direction it is going, and (b) the fluid’s viscosity and therefore its tendency to average out the fluid’s velocity over space. \(Re\) is essentially the ratio of multiple phenomena. The viscous dissipation factor is a measure of (a) how much fluid slows down in a pipe relative to its kinetic energy and (b) the aspect ratio of the pipe. As was the case for \(Re\), \(f_D\) is the ratio of these two phenomena. If this parameterization works, the only experiments we need to perform are enough to map out how \(f_D\) varies with \(Re\). Everything else is just normalizing the inputs, plugging it into the \(f_D(Re)\) function, getting \(f_D\), and then un-normalizing \(f_D\) to get the pressure gradient.

Reynolds number: \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\). The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(Re_x,Re_d\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

I have provided no argument for why this will work. If it does, however, it leads to a clear path for how we would solve the posed problem. I go into the lab and measure \(f_D\) for a bunch of pipes and fluids, whatever is needed to get \(f_D\) as a function of \(Re\). Then, when I need to know what pump to buy, I take all of the input parameters, and combine \(\rho\), \(U\), \(d\), and \(\mu\) together to learn what phenomena dominate the dynamics of the flow. That specifies \(f_D\), and I use \(f_D\) to calculate \(\Delta p/L\), and from \(L\), I calculate \(\Delta p\), which tells me what sort of pump I need to buy. This is discussed in detail in Chapter 6.

Reynolds number Haiku 4: Navier and Stokes / I nondimensionalize / get Reynolds number

It turns out this mostly works. However, when we study flow through pipes, we find that the pressure drop, especially at high \(Re\), is also a function of the surface roughness \(\epsilon\), typically normalized as \(\epsilon/d\). In this sense, study of turbulent flow in a pipe indicates the strengths and limitations of dimensional analysis—it is so powerful that, even though pressure drop in a tube is

pipe: a hollow structure designed to convey a fluid. Usually rigid. Designated by nominal diameter and schedule, which describe approximate inner diameter and material thickness. Usually fitted by threads. Cf. tube, hose.

Editorial clarification: The four quantities reduced to one dimensionless input are independent parameters in the functional relation. In a steady incompressible pipe of uniform area, viscous losses reduce pressure/total head; they do not require the mean speed to decrease downstream.


PDF page 502 — source_issue

a function of \(\rho\), \(\mu\), \(L\), \(d\), \(\epsilon\), and \(U\), we can still summarize all results in one figure (see the figure later in this Appendix). However, dimensional analysis is completely dependent on our knowing what the relevant parameters are—if we don’t realize that \(\epsilon\) is an important parameter, dimensional analysis won’t help us.

C.3 Dynamic similitude is used to facilitate cheap or easy experiments that replace difficult, expensive, or impossible experiments

The approach above reduces the experimental parameter space that must be explored, so if we want to know how hot water going through a 1-inch pipe at 10 cm/s, we can figure that out from data on cold water going through a 1/2-inch pipe at 12 cm/s. Dynamic similitude also makes it possible to understand fluid systems that are difficult or impossible to test. For example, one can model a \(1\ \mu\mathrm m\) E. coli bacterium moving in water with a lab-scale model, as long as we move the model slowly and use very viscous fluid.

dynamic similitude: the notion that the dynamics of two physical systems are fundamentally the same if all of its nondimensional parameters are the same, allowing us to study systems through experiments at different (and more convenient) conditions.

Dimensionless groups make analysis easier by reducing the number of parameters we must know and by making our analysis independent of units

The parameters we are used to thinking of (velocities, lengths, viscosities, densities, forces, et cetera) usually have units. These units are important and useful, but because units must be used, our answers are dependent on the unit system (say SI vs English engineering). Units help us check our analysis to ensure that it makes sense, and we have extensive experience describing parameters with units. However, dimensional parameters introduce unnecessary complexity, specifically they create more parameters than we need. We can eliminate many of these parameters through a process that examines just the units of these parameters. We can make dimensionless groups i.e., nondimensional parameters in a way that makes analysis easier, simpler, and more general. This process also reduces the number of parameters. That part helps us. In exchange for this benefit, we sacrifice the ability to use units to check our analysis, and we introduce new parameters. We must develop an intuition for what these new parameters mean, and this intuition comes primarily from experience i.e., homework problems.

nondimensional parameter: a parameter generated by a process to remove units. Typically denotes the ratio of two or more parameters and therefore their relative importance.

Nondimensional Parameter Angst Haiku: [The poem is erased/illegible in the source scan.]

Dimensionless groups, which we call Pi groups, may be formed from any set of parameters by systematically eliminating units

We can show that any list of parameters that govern a fluid-mechanical problem can be nondimensionalized by systematically eliminating units. When we do this, we will shorten the list of parameters each time we eliminate a unit.

Unit elimination is a systematic way to identify nondimensional groups

In unit elimination, we make a table of the parameters in an equation and systematically eliminate units by multiplying or dividing parameters through. As an example, consider the drag force \(F_D\) on a sphere of radius \(l\)

drag: the component of a force a fluid exerts on an immersed object that is tangent to the flow.


PDF page 503 — source_issue

moving at velocity \(U\) in a fluid of density \(\rho\) and viscosity \(\mu\). As stated, there are five parameters in this problem: \(F_D\), \(l\), \(U\), \(\rho\), and \(\mu\). We can put these in a table, below (Table C.1). In each case, we write in brackets the units of each parameter in terms of fundamental units of mass (kg), length (\(L\)), and time (s).¹

Table C.1: Five original parameters with their units.

Step | \(F_D\) | \(l\) | \(U\) | \(\rho\) | \(\mu\)
start | \(F_D\ [\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}]\) | \(l\ [\mathrm m]\) | \(U\ [\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}]\) | \(\rho\ [\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}]\) | \(\mu\ [\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}]\)
We now systematically eliminate units. We can, in principle, do this in many different ways. We start by eliminating units of length. We take one of the parameters (in this case, \(l\)) and multiply or divide each term by \(l\) enough to remove the units of m. The first three terms we divide by \(l\), the density we multiply by \(l^3\), and the viscosity we multiply by \(l\) (Table C.2):

Table C.2: Parameters after units of length are eliminated. Four parameters remain: \(F_D/l\), \(U/l\), \(\rho l^3\), and \(\mu l\).

Step | \(F_D\) | \(l\) | \(U\) | \(\rho\) | \(\mu\)
start | \(F_D\ [\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}]\) | \(l\ [\mathrm m]\) | \(U\ [\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}]\) | \(\rho\ [\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}]\) | \(\mu\ [\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}]\)
eliminate lengths | \(F_D/l\ [\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}]\) |  | \(U/l\ [\mathrm{s^{-1}}]\) | \(\rho l^3\ [\mathrm{kg}]\) | \(\mu l\ [\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}]\)
We next eliminate units of time. We divide each term through by \(U/l\) as needed to eliminate time—in this case we divide the first term by \(U^2/l^2\), and divide the third and fifth by \(U/l\) (Table C.3).

Table C.3: Parameters after units of time are eliminated. Three parameters remain: \(F_Dl/U^2\), \(\rho l^3\), and \(\mu l^2/U\).

Step | \(F_D\) | \(l\) | \(U\) | \(\rho\) | \(\mu\)
start | \(F_D\ [\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}]\) | \(l\ [\mathrm m]\) | \(U\ [\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}]\) | \(\rho\ [\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}]\) | \(\mu\ [\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}]\)
eliminate lengths | \(F_D/l\ [\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}]\) |  | \(U/l\ [\mathrm{s^{-1}}]\) | \(\rho l^3\ [\mathrm{kg}]\) | \(\mu l\ [\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}]\)
eliminate time | \(F_Dl/U^2\ [\mathrm{kg}]\) |  |  | \(\rho l^3\ [\mathrm{kg}]\) | \(\mu l^2/U\ [\mathrm{kg}]\)
We finally eliminate units of mass. We divide each term through by \(\rho l^3\) as needed to eliminate mass—in this case we divide the first, fourth, and fifth terms through by \(\rho l^3\) (Table C.4):

Following this process, two parameters remain: \(\Pi_1=F_D/(\rho U^2l^2)\) and \(\Pi_2=\mu/(\rho Ul)\). These groups form the basis of two parameters we use in many engineering analyses: We call \(F_D/(\frac12\rho U^2A)\) the drag coefficient \(C_D\) and we call \(\rho Ul/\mu\) the Reynolds number \(Re\). The one-half in the drag coefficient is arbitrary and is typically used to evoke the dynamic pressure, and we usually use the cross-sectional area \(A\) which has units of m².

Reynolds number: \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\). The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(Re_x,Re_d\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

The original problem, which could have been prescribed verbally as “the drag force on a sphere moving through a fluid is a function of the fluid’s viscosity and density and the sphere’s velocity and radius” or mathematically as

F_D=f(l,U,\rho,\mu), (C.5)

has now been rearranged. Now the problem would be prescribed verbally as “the drag coefficient of a sphere moving through a fluid is a function of \(Re\)”, or:

C_D=f(Re). (C.6)

dynamic pressure: Given by \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\frac12\rho U^2\). Denotes the added pressure a fluid would have if it were slowed isentropically to motionlessness. Equivalently, describes the volumetric kinetic energy of a fluid in terms of an equivalent pressure.

This problem started with \(n=5\) parameters (one independent, four dependent) written in terms of \(m=3\) dimensions. Each elimination of a dimension

¹ If you prefer, you can avoid a specific system of units and write the symbols \(M\), \(L\), and \(T\) for mass, length, and time.

The length unit in the tables is m; L denotes the length dimension. The dynamic-pressure interpretation as the full stagnation-pressure increase applies to the incompressible limit.

Table C.4: Parameters after units of mass are eliminated. Two parameters remain: \(\Pi_1=F_D/(\rho U^2l^2)\) and \(\Pi_2=\mu/(\rho Ul)\).

Step | \(F_D\) | \(l\) | \(U\) | \(\rho\) | \(\mu\)
start | \(F_D\ [\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}]\) | \(l\ [\mathrm m]\) | \(U\ [\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}]\) | \(\rho\ [\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}]\) | \(\mu\ [\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}]\)
eliminate length | \(F_D/l\ [\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}]\) |  | \(U/l\ [\mathrm{s^{-1}}]\) | \(\rho l^3\ [\mathrm{kg}]\) | \(\mu l\ [\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}]\)
