reduced the total number of parameters. After we did this three times, only \(n-m=5-3=2\) parameters were left, and they both were dimensionless. Importantly, the parameters of the problem cannot influence each other in any other way than the one listed. For example, the drag coefficient is only a function of the viscosity through \(\rho Ul/\mu\). There is no other way to add the viscosity into this problem and keep dimensional homogeneity.

This process took advantage of units only. No physical process was assumed, and no conservation equation was solved. These dimensionless groups are called Pi groups: \(\Pi_1=F_D/(\rho U^2l^2)=C_D\) and \(\Pi_2=\mu/(\rho Ul)=1/Re\). The Buckingham Pi theorem is the theorem that says that the number of parameters may be reduced by the number of units in the system. As engineers, the theorem that tells us that this works is probably less important than knowing a systematic way to make unit elimination work.

Editorial correction: With the preceding definition \(C_D=F_D/(\tfrac12\rho U^2A)\), \(C_D=(2l^2/A)\Pi_1\). Thus \(\Pi_1\) is proportional to \(C_D\), not generally equal; for a sphere of radius \(l\), \(A=\pi l^2\). The number removed by the Pi theorem is the rank of the dimensional-exponent matrix (three here).

Buckingham Pi Theorem Haiku: Pi theorem says / unit elimination / gets rid of m terms

Pi group: one of a set of nondimensional groups used to parameterize a physical problem.

Pi groups can equivalently be found by solving a set of linear algebraic equations

We can perform an analysis identical to unit elimination by solving a set of algebraic equations. In fact, unit elimination is basically Gaussian elimination applied to an underconstrained set of algebraic equations. I hate this way, but many students prefer it.

Dimensional homogeneity requires that each dimension is present in equal amounts in all terms in the equation. This sets a number of linear algebraic constraints on the terms in an equation—one for each unit. Consider for example the drag force \(F_D\) as a function of \(\rho\), \(U\), \(\ell\), and \(\mu\). If we assume that a dimensionless Pi group can be written as the product of these parameters raised to unknown powers:

dimensional homogeneity: the property of an equation such that all terms in the equation have the same units and dimensions.

Pi group: one of a set of nondimensional groups used to parameterize a physical problem.

\Pi=k\rho^aU^b\ell^c\mu^dF_D^e, (C.7)

where \(k\) is an arbitrary dimensionless constant, then ensuring dimensional homogeneity sets algebraic restrictions on the possible values of \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\), and \(e\). This equation has units of mass (kg), length (m), and time (s), and each of these three dimensions must be the same for both sides of the equation. Writing in terms of fundamental units kg, m, and s, we have for mass

dimensional homogeneity: the property of an equation such that all terms in the equation have the same units and dimensions.

0=a+0+0+0+d+e, (C.8)

for length

0=-3a+b+c-d+e, (C.9)

and for time

0=0-b+0-d-2e. (C.10)

This creates three algebraic equations, each of which guarantees homogeneity of a specific unit/dimension.

a+d+e=0, (C.11)

dimensional homogeneity for mass

-3a+b+c-d+e=0, (C.12)

dimensional homogeneity for length

-b-d-2e=0. (C.13)

dimensional homogeneity for time

(C.14) is printed beside an empty equation line in the source.


PDF page 505 — source_issue

We have three equations, so if we rewrite these equations with precisely three variables on the left-hand side:

a=-d-e, (C.15)

-3a+b+c=d-e, (C.16)

-b=d+2e, (C.17)

(C.18) is printed beside an empty equation line in the source.

we can pretend that we know \(d\) and \(e\) and rearrange the system by Gaussian elimination. Here is the matrix equation:

\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\-3&1&1\\0&-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\ b\\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-d-e\\ d-e\\ d+2e\end{bmatrix}, (C.19)

and here it is after Gaussian elimination:

\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\ b\\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-d-e\\-d-2e\\-d-2e\end{bmatrix}. (C.20)

In this form, we can pick any combination of \(d\) and \(e\) we want, and that will define a Pi group. For example if I arbitrarily pick \(d=0\) and \(e=1\), we get \(a=-1,b=-2,c=-2,d=0,e=1\). That defines a Pi group

\Pi_1=k_1\frac{F_D}{\rho U^2\ell^2}, (C.21)

Pi group: one of a set of nondimensional groups used to parameterize a physical problem.

which, if \(k_1=2\), is the drag coefficient. If I arbitrarily pick \(d=-1\) and \(e=0\), we get \(a=1,b=1,c=1,d=-1,e=0\), which defines a Pi group

\Pi_2=k_2\frac{\rho U\ell}{\mu}. (C.22)

Transcription note: Some characters in (C.22) are washed out; the displayed expression is reconstructed directly from the five exponents stated immediately above.

drag coefficient: a measure of the ability of a physical object to generate a force tangent to a flow passing over it. Defined by \(C_D=\frac{F_D}{\frac12\rho U^2A}\).

which, if \(k_2=1\), is the Reynolds number. For this to work, the matrix we make on the left hand side must be diagonalizable, or equivalently, it must have a full complement of eigenvalues and eigenvectors (MATH2940). Restated equivalently in terms of units instead of linear algebra, that means the set of variables we put on the left-hand side has to include all of the relevant units, in this case mass, length, and time. Further, it must not be possible to make a dimensionless group from the parameters on the left-hand side.

Reynolds number: \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\). The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(Re_x,Re_d\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

Editorial corrections: For the stated sphere radius \(\ell\) and projected area \(A=\pi\ell^2\), (C.21) equals the conventional drag coefficient when \(k_1=2/\pi\), not 2. Gaussian elimination to a unique solution requires an invertible, full-rank coefficient matrix; diagonalizability is a different property and is not the requirement here. The repeating variables must have linearly independent dimensional-exponent columns.

Other than the requiement listed in the previous paragraph, we can set up these equations in any way we want—we could have picked other \(d\) and \(e\) values, or we could have moved other variables to the right-hand side; no approach is mathematically superior to the other. I picked the \(d\) and \(e\) values I did to make the Pi groups I found immediately take the form that we use in fluid mechanics, but those choices are mathematically arbitrary.

The method of repeating variables is a specific algorithm for the above process usually used to describe it to students that don’t know linear algebra

If you don’t know linear algebra, the diagonalizability constraint must be explained to you with some sort of algorithm. One popular algorithm is the “method of repeating variables”, in which we

1. Count the number of parameters \(n\).


PDF page 506 — source_issue

2. Count the number of units \(m\).

3. Pick \(m\) parameters to be “repeating variables”. These variables between them must include all of the relevant units, and they must not be rearrangeable into a dimensionless group.

4. Write \(n-m\) dimensional homogeneity equations, one for each of the parameters not used as a repeating variable, to determine how each can be nondimensionalized. Each solution will generate a Pi group.

For example, the above system could be analyzed as follows: we have 5 parameters, and 3 units. We could say that \(\rho\), \(\mu\), and \(\ell\) are our repeating variables, and \(F_D\) and \(U\) the two leftover parameters we want to nondimensionalize.

With this approach, one Pi group is

\Pi_1=F_D\rho^a\mu^b\ell^c, (C.23)

leading to three sets of equations for (in turn) mass, length, and time:

\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\-3&-1&1\\0&-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\ b\\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\-1\\2\end{bmatrix}. (C.24)

The solution to this system is \(a=1,b=-2,c=0\), giving \(\Pi_1=\frac{F_D\rho}{\mu^2}\).

The other Pi group is

\Pi_1=U\rho^a\mu^b\ell^c, (C.25)

leading to three sets of equations for (in turn) mass, length, and time:

\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\-3&-1&1\\0&-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\ b\\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\-1\\1\end{bmatrix}. (C.26)

The solution to this system is \(a=1,b=-1,c=1\), giving \(\Pi_2=\frac{\rho U\ell}{\mu}\). \(\Pi_2\) is the Reynolds number; the \(\Pi_1\) we ended up with is \(\Pi_1=C_DRe^2/2\).

Editorial corrections: The “other” group in (C.25) is \(\Pi_2\), although the source prints \(\Pi_1\). With the book’s conventional projected-area drag coefficient and sphere radius \(\ell\), \(\Pi_1=(\pi/2)C_DRe^2\); the printed relationship omits the area factor. In the general algorithm, \(m\) is the dimensional-matrix rank, and each of the \(n-m\) groups requires a system of dimensional-exponent constraints.

These techniques are really all the same thing

The method of repeating variables is equivalent to the general matrix approach; it picks \(m\) “repeating variables” to go in the left-hand side, and in turn sets the multipliers of the remaining \(n-m\) parameters to all be zero except one which is 1. It is just an algorithm for solving an underconstrained set of linear equations that fluids textbooks have for when the students haven’t taken linear algebra. The method of unit elimination is also equivalent to the general matrix approach, it is basically row reduction via unit row operations.

Salsa Verde Haiku: [The poem is erased/illegible in the source scan.]

For those trying to pick which technique they choose to use, I find that unit elimination always works for me, but the link to linear algebra is weak and indirect. The general matrix approach links to linear algebra more cleanly, we do, though, have to pick parameters to guarantee diagonalizability. The repeating variables technique is my least favorite; it fails if diagonalizability is not achieved, but because its links to linear algebra are weak, when it fails it is harder to see why.

Editorial correction: The required condition is invertibility/full rank of the selected dimensional matrix, not diagonalizability.

Once Pi groups are established, each of them must be a function only of the other Pi groups

Given Pi groups, we can hypothesize that one Pi group can only be a function of other Pi groups:

C_D=f(Re\ \text{only}), (C.27)


PDF page 507 — verified

and that hypothesis will be correct as long as we didn’t miss any relevant parameters when we set up our initial assumed functional form. It is easy to miss nondimensional geometric parameters like length ratios and angles. Less often, we might forget a fundamental physical constant. If we leave a parameter out, we will find the nondimensional parameters we have defined are insufficient. When that happens, it is the fault of our setup, not of the approach of forming Pi groups.

nondimensional parameter: a parameter generated by a process to remove units. Typically denotes the ratio of two or more parameters and therefore their relative importance.

The purpose of all of this was to simplify the functional dependences and reduce the number of parameters

By writing the Pi groups in terms of each other, we end up with a simpler functional dependence with fewer parameters. Rather than writing \(F_D\) as a function of four parameters, we wrote \(C_D\) as a function of one parameter.

Pi groups are not unique; they are the solution of an underconstrained set of equations

Pi groups are the solution of a unit-elimination process that can be performed in multiple different ways, leading to different Pi groups. The examples above use unit elimination or a set of linear algebraic equations or repeating variables, all of which boil down to solution of a set of underconstrained linear algebraic equations. The process has more free parameters than it has constraints. Thus there is never a uniquely “correct” set of Pi groups. There are, many Pi groups that we use by convention or because they have a useful physical interpretation, e.g., the Reynolds number and the drag coefficient in this case, but there is no mathematical reason why those Pi groups have to be used. In the examples above we got different Pi groups after three different approaches; however each of the sets of Pi groups we obtained is equivalent to any other set we could obtain.

Pi group: one of a set of nondimensional groups used to parameterize a physical problem.

Reynolds number: \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\). The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(Re_x,Re_d\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

Any Pi group can be raised to any power and it is still a correct Pi group.

Pi groups are dimensionless; if they are raised to a power, they are still dimensionless. Thus any Pi group raised to a power is still a correct Pi group. It is no more formally correct to say that \(C_D\) is a function of \(Re\) than it is to say it is a function of \(Re^{2.81}\). Each is mathematically correct.

Pi group: one of a set of nondimensional groups used to parameterize a physical problem.

Any Pi group can be multiplied by itself or another Pi group and it is still a correct Pi group.

Pi groups are dimensionless; if one multiplies one Pi group by another the result is still dimensionless. Thus any Pi group can be multiplied by another Pi group and it is still a correct Pi group. It is no more formally correct to say that \(C_D=f(Re)\) than it is to say that \(C_D/Re=f(Re^3)\). Each is mathematically correct.

Many famous nondimensional groups result from nondimensionalization of governing equations

Governing equations can be nondimensionalized by dividing all of their variables by characteristic values. When this is done, we find that certain terms in the equation are multiplied by nondimensional parameters, and the magnitude of these nondimensional parameters tell us which of the terms in the equations are more important. Some examples are in Table C.5, p. 497.

As a specific example, consider the Navier–Stokes equations for uniform-viscosity, Newtonian fluids, neglecting gravity:

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u. (C.28)

Navier–Stokes equations: pronounced NAH-vee-ay STOKES. Usually used to mean the incompressible conservation of momentum equation with the Newtonian model of viscous effects included: \(\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u+\rho\vec g\).

Newtonian: in fluid mechanics, describes a fluid whose shear stress is proportional to its strain rate; \(\vec{\vec\tau}=2\mu\vec{\vec\varepsilon}\).

We can nondimensionalize these equations by considering reference parameters \(\rho\), \(\mu\), \(U\), and \(\ell\). We can define nondimensional variables denoted by


PDF page 508 — source_issue

starred properties:

x^*=\frac x\ell,\qquad y^*=\frac y\ell,\qquad z^*=\frac z\ell,\qquad\nabla^*=\frac\nabla{1/\ell},\qquad\nabla^{*2}=\frac\nabla{1/\ell^2}, (C.29)

\vec u^*=\frac{\vec u}U,\qquad t^*=\frac t{\ell/U},\qquad p^*=\frac p{\rho U^2+\mu U/\ell}. (C.30)

Transcription note: The coordinate definitions and several equals signs in (C.29) are faded, but are recoverable from the visible numerators and common length scale. The last numerator visibly shows \(\nabla\), with no squared exponent. Editorial correction: It must be \(\nabla^2\), so \(\nabla^{*2}=\ell^2\nabla^2\).

Most of these are straightforward, but the pressure is not so simple. The pressure is affected by both the dynamic pressures of the system or the viscous stresses, so we nondimensionalize \(p\) by the sum of \(\frac12\rho U^2\) and \(\mu U/\ell\) to cover both effects.²

dynamic pressure: Given by \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\frac12\rho U^2\). Denotes the added pressure a fluid would have if it were slowed isentropically to motionlessness. Equivalently, describes the volumetric kinetic energy of a fluid in terms of an equivalent pressure.

viscous stress: in general, the force per unit area that a fluid applies at a point that is not explained by the thermodynamic pressure. For Newtonian incompressible fluids, this is synonymous with shear stress and is given by the viscosity multiplied by the strain rate.

If we substitute in these relations, we can rearrange the Navier–Stokes equations to find:

Re\frac{\partial\vec u^*}{\partial t^*}+Re\,\vec u^*\cdot\nabla^*\vec u^*=-(Re+1)\nabla p^*+\nabla^{*2}\vec u^*, (C.31)

where the Reynolds number is defined as \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\).

If we include the gravity term in the Navier–Stokes equations:

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u+\rho\vec g. (C.32)

Then the nondimensionalized equation also includes the Froude number \(Fr=U/\sqrt{g\ell}\):

Re\frac{\partial\vec u^*}{\partial t^*}+Re\,\vec u^*\cdot\nabla^*\vec u^*=-(Re+1)\nabla p^*+\nabla^{*2}\vec u^*+\frac{Re}{Fr^2}\hat z. (C.33)

Editorial corrections: The prose and footnote use \(\tfrac12\rho U^2+\mu U/\ell\), but (C.30) uses \(\rho U^2+\mu U/\ell\). The coefficient \(Re+1\) in (C.31)/(C.33) matches (C.30); the prose’s scale would give \(Re/2+1\). Both pressure-gradient operators must be \(\nabla^*p^*\), with the missing star restored. The gravity term should generally be \((Re/Fr^2)\hat g\), where \(\hat g\) points with gravity; for the book’s usual upward \(z\) axis it is \(-(Re/Fr^2)\hat z\).

Froude number | \(Fr=\frac U{\sqrt{g\ell}}\) | Navier–Stokes with significant effects of gravity
Mach number | \(M=\frac Ua\) | Navier–Stokes with compressibility
The output of an engineering analysis is often nondimensionalized for generality

When we write the parameters of an engineering analysis and use unit conversion to eliminate paramters, we are typically left with some sort of normalized output. These normalized outputs are themselves nondimensional parameters, and they are typically referred to as coefficients, as in Table C.6, p. 498.

I think the sum is by far the most sensible and elegant. I mention the uniqueness to you not to imply that I have done anything interesting, but just so you are unsurprised if you don’t find this expression in other sources.

Engineering result | Nondimensional parameter | definition
pressure drop in a pipe | friction factor | \(f_D=\frac{\Delta p}{\frac12\rho U^2}\frac dL\)

drag force on an object | drag coefficient | \(C_D=\frac{F_D}{\frac12\rho U^2A}\)
local shear stress at a wall | friction coefficient | \(C_f=\frac{\tau_w}{\frac12\rho U^2}=\frac{\tau_{xy}|_{\mathrm{wall}}}{\frac12\rho U^2}\)
The Reynolds Number describes whether the behavior of a fluid is dominated by its momentum or by the viscous stresses it feels; it is the most ubiquitous nondimensional parameter in fluid mechanics

Without attempting to write any equations, we can think of the Reynolds number as a measure of whether fluid behavior is dominated by the fact that the fluid has momentum or dominated by the fact that the fluid exhibits viscosity. Fluid has mass that is proportional to its density \(\rho\) and proportional to its volume (say \(\ell^3\) for a cube with sides of length \(\ell\); \(\frac16\pi\ell^3\) for a sphere of diameter \(\ell\)). Fluid has momentum that is proportional to its speed \(U\) and kinetic energy that is proportional to its speed squared (\(U^2\)). So, fluid has more momentum and is harder to accelerate or change directions if it is dense, if it is moving quickly, and if it is large in scope. On the other hand, fluid feels viscous stresses in response to fluid deformation, which is proportional to velocity gradients. These stresses are proportional to the viscosity \(\mu\) and are surface forces that are proportional to the area enclosing a fluid system. Fluid feels viscous effects more strongly when the viscosity is high. The definition of the Reynolds number:

Re=\frac{\rho U\ell}{\mu}, (C.34)

deformation: for fluid mechanics, we typically mean deformation rate, the rate at which parts of the fluid move relative to each other, exclusive of solid-body rotation or uniform translation.

is consistent with these observations. Dense, fast, big flows will have a large numerator and the Reynolds number will be high. These flows are momentum-dominated. Flows with high viscosity or that are slow or small will have a large denominator and small numerator and the Reynolds number will be low. These flows are viscous-dominated.

The Reynolds Number is proportional to the ratio of a fluid’s kinetic energy to the viscous stresses that would dissipate that energy

One way of quantitatively evaluating the heuristic above is to think about fluid kinetic energy and its dissipation by viscosity. The kinetic energy per unit volume in a fluid is given by \(\frac12\rho U^2\). The viscous stresses in fluid are proportional to viscosity times strain rate which is a measure of local velocity gradients. Local velocity gradients are proportional to velocity differences divided by the length over which the velocity changes. A parcel of fluid moving at speed \(U\) that is a a distance \(\ell\) from a wall might experience a viscous stress

heuristic: as a noun, an approach to problem-solving involving searching for an immediate, approximate, informal, non-rigorous, or trial-and-error solution. As an adjective, having the property of being immediate, approximate, or non-rigorous.


PDF page 510 — source_issue

proportional to \(\mu U/\ell\). The ratio of these two parameters is:

Re=\frac{\text{twice the volumetric kinetic energy}}{\text{an approximation of local viscous stresses}}=\frac{2(\frac12\rho U^2)}{\mu U/\ell}=\frac{\rho U\ell}{\mu}. (C.35)

The Reynolds number is thus a measure of how much kinetic energy is in a fluid proportional to the viscous process that would dissipate that energy. When Reynolds number is high, the fluid has alot of kinetic energy and viscosity has a tough time changing the fluid’s direction or speed very much. When Reynolds number is low, the fluid has very little kinetic energy and viscosity has no problem changing the fluid’s direction or speed.

The Reynolds Number is often described as the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces

Another way of evaluating the heuristic at top is to consider the forces a fluid element feels when it is moving along a curved path. Most texts say that the Reynolds number is “the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces” but “inertial force” is actually a hard concept and most students don’t know what “inertial force” means in this context. Inertial forces i.e., fictitious forces describe the apparent force on an object if it is viewed in an accelerating reference frame. A classic example is the centrifugal force—if we define an accelerating coordinate frame associated with a mass moving with radius of curvature \(R\), in that frame the mass appears to feel an outward centrifugal force given by \(mU^2/R\).

centrifugal: pointing away from the center of a circular arc.

Imagine a fluid moving at speed \(U\) along the centerline of a pipe of diameter \(\ell\) with an elbow that has a radius of curvature \(\ell\) equal to the diameter. The centrifugal force on the fluid per unit volume would be given by \(\rho U^2/\ell\), and integrating this over a distance \(\ell\) would give a centrifugal force per unit area \(\rho U^2\). The viscous stress i.e., viscous force per unit area might again be proportional to \(\mu U/\ell\). Taking the ratio of the two:

Re=\frac{\substack{\text{inertial force associated with steering a cube of fluid with speed }U\\ \text{and side length }\ell\text{ along a curved path with radius }\ell}}{\substack{\text{viscous force on a side of that cube}\\ \text{if the local strain rate is approximated as }U/\ell}}=\frac{(\rho U^2/\ell)\ell^3}{(\mu U/\ell)\ell^2}=\frac{\rho U\ell}{\mu}. (C.36)

Transcription note: The equals signs between the three ratios in (C.36) are washed out. They are reconstructed from the stated ratio and the algebraically identical forms; all surviving factors and powers were inspected.

The Reynolds number is thus a measure of what force is bigger: the force required to turn fluid moving at \(U\) along a circular path with radius \(\ell\), or the viscous force generated when fluid moving at speed \(U\) a distance \(\ell\) from a wall. When the Reynolds number is high, the centrifugal force the fluid feels if you try to steer it along that curved path is very high and the local viscous forces are not enough to control the flow. When the Reynolds number is low, the centrifugal force the fluid feels if you try to steer it along that curved path is low, and the local viscous forces are enough to control the flow.

The Reynolds number has only one length scale; it communicates size but cannot communicate shape

The Reynolds number has one length scale in it, which is chosen differently depending on what flow we are trying to characterize—for example the diameter of a pipe, the distance between two surfaces, the chord length of an airfoil, the downstream distance along a boundary layer. The Reynolds number alone is not sufficient to describe any system with two length scales, e.g., the length and thickness of an airfoil, and is of course not sufficient to describe the difference between differently shaped pipes or airfoils or jets or pickup trucks. The examples above are contorted to try to describe the physical systems explained by the Reynolds number alone; the contortions all come from

chord: a straight line connecting the leading and trailing edges of an airfoil.


PDF page 511 — source_issue

using the same length scale \(\ell\) to try to describe everything. Real systems have Reynolds numbers but are also need a description of the system geometry before we can solve anything.

The Reynolds number naturally appears when we perform unit elimination on the parameters in fluid mechanics problems

Fluids have two properties that affect all fluids problems: \(\rho\) and \(\mu\). All fluids problems have at least two properties of the boundaries, objects, or input conditions: the object at minimum has a characteristic size characterized by the length scale \(\ell\), and the flow at minimum has a velocity field characterized by a representative speed \(U\). Using unit elimination on \(\rho\), \(\mu\), \(\ell\), and \(U\) leads to one parameter: \(Re=\rho U\ell/\mu\).

The Reynolds number naturally appears when the Navier–Stokes equations are nondimensionalized

The Reynolds number \(Re\) naturally appears upon nondimensionalization of the Navier–Stokes equations, as we convert

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u (C.37)

to

Re\frac{\partial\vec u^*}{\partial t^*}+Re\,\vec u^*\cdot\nabla^*\vec u^*=-(Re+1)\nabla p^*+\nabla^{*2}\vec u^*. (C.38)

Editorial correction: As in (C.31), the pressure-gradient operator in (C.38) needs a star: \(\nabla^*p^*\). The coefficient shown uses the pressure scale in (C.30).

We refer to two flows as being dynamically similar if they have the same Reynolds number and if their geometry is similar. The nondimensional solution to the Navier–Stokes equations will be identical for two systems if the geometry and Reynolds number are matched. Thus fluid-mechanical results can be meaningfully compared across many different experimental realizations.

dynamically similar: having identical dynamics when properly nondimensionalized.

The \(Re\to0\) and \(Re\to\infty\) limits lead to the Stokes and Euler Equations, respectively

From the format of Equation (C.38) the Reynolds number can, in certain limits, lead to simplification of the equation. If \(Re\to0\), then the terms on the LHS go away, and we have the Stokes equations:

0=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u, (C.39)

and if \(Re\to\infty\), then the viscous term goes away, and we have the Euler equations:

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p. (C.40)

The pressure term never goes away because of a limiting value of the Reynolds number.

Editorial clarification: Similarity also requires matching the dimensionless boundary/initial conditions and any other relevant parameters. The Stokes limit here uses the chosen convective time scale; rapid unsteadiness may retain a time derivative. The inviscid limit need not apply inside thin boundary layers.

The Reynolds number dictates transition from laminar to turbulent flow

Viscosity is linear, and viscosity takes a mathematical form that smoothes out any fluctuations in velocity. Viscosity describes the diffusion of momentum. Viscosity i.e., the diffusion of momentum is thus a stabilizing phenomenon. The fluid kinetic energy is nonlinear in the velocity, and convection of momentum takes a mathematical form that allows variations in velocity to grow. Convection is thus a destabilizing phenomenon. Laminar flow results when


PDF page 512 — verified

the stabilizing effects of viscosity outweigh the destablizing effects of momentum convection, and turbulent flow (i.e., disorderly, chaotic flow that is observed in most mechanical engineering flows) results when the destabilizing effects of momentum convection outweigh the stabilizing effects of momentum diffusion. Thus \(Re\) is the defining parameter that prescribes transition from laminar to turbulent flow.

laminar: occuring in orderly sheets or lamina.

C.5 The viscous dissipation factor in a pipe is a classical example of nondimensional parameters facilitating engineering analysis

The pressure drop in a pipe can be predicted given the Reynolds number and the surface roughness

The pressure drop in a pipe can be predicted given the Reynolds number and the surface roughness. Dimensional analysis does not tell us how the pressure drop varies in a pipe, but it does tell us that the properly nondimensionalized pressure drop is a function of the Reynolds number and the relative roughness \(\epsilon/d\) alone. If we need to predict the pressure drop in a pipe, we typically read the number off a graph (called a Moody diagram) or use an approximate equation. The most famous equation is the Colebrook–White equation (not shown here), but I prefer to use the Haaland equation:

f_D=\left\{-1.8\log_{10}\left[\left(\frac\epsilon{3.7d}\right)^{1.11}+\frac{6.9}{Re}\right]\right\}^{-2}. (C.41)

Haaland equation for Darcy friction factor for flow through a pipe

The Haaland quation is an entirely empirical formula that is used to approximate experimental data.

This question can be answered with dimensional analysis alone.

2. (OBJECTIVE: show how far dimensional analysis can get you; explain drag coefficient curve limits) Consider motion of a sphere of radius \(r\) moving though a fluid with viscosity \(\mu\) at speed \(U\). Assume this fluid is a magical fluid with zero density. Within a constant, what must the drag force be as a function of \(\mu\), \(U\), and \(r\)? This question can be answered with dimensional analysis alone.

Solution:

If there is no density, then

F=f(\mu,U,r). (C.42)

If we divide out \(r\) to eliminate length:

F/r^2=f(\mu r,U/r,1). (C.43)

Editorial correction: Force has one power of length, so eliminating length requires \(F/r\), not the printed \(F/r^2\). The next line (C.44) uses the result obtained from \(F/r\).

If we divide out by \(U/r\) to eliminate time:

Fr/U^2=f(\mu r^2/U,1,1). (C.44)

Then if we divide out by \(\mu r^2/U\) to eliminate mass:

F/(\mu Ur)=f(1,1,1). (C.45)

\(f(1,1,1)\) can only be a constant. So this means \(F/(\mu Ur)=C\) where \(C\) is a constant. That means

F=C\mu Ur. (C.46)

So, if a fluid has no density , the force must be proportional to \(\mu Ur\).

3. (OBJECTIVE: show how far dimensional analysis can get you; explain drag coefficient curve limits) Consider motion of a sphere of radius \(r\) moving though a fluid with density \(\rho\) at speed \(U\). Assume this fluid is a magical fluid with zero viscosity. Within a constant, what must the drag force be as a function of \(\rho\), \(U\), and \(r\)? This question can be answered with dimensional analysis alone.

Solution:

If there is no viscosity:

F=f(\rho,U,r). (C.47)

If we divide out \(r\) to eliminate length:

F/r^2=f(\rho r^3,U/r,1). (C.48)

Editorial correction: As in (C.43), the force should be divided by \(r\), not \(r^2\), to eliminate its length unit. The following (C.49) is consistent with \(F/r\).

If we divide out by \(U/r\) to eliminate time:

Fr/U^2=f(\rho r^3,1,1). (C.49)


PDF page 517 — source_issue

If we divide out by \(\rho r^3\)to eliminate mass:

F/(\rho U^2r^2)=f(1,1,1). (C.50)

\(f(1,1,1)\) can only be a constant. So this means \(F/(\rho U^2r^2)=C\) where \(C\) is a constant. That means

F=C\rho U^2r^2. (C.51)

So, if a fluid has no viscosity, the force must be proportional to \(\rho U^2r^2\).

4. (OBJECTIVE: Apply dimensional analysis to find system parameters) Wind blowing past a rectangular traffic sign (Figure C.3, p. 506 can cause the sign to oscillate with a frequency \(\omega\). This happens all the time; one example is shown in snapshots it Figure C.3, p. 506. Assume that \(\omega\) is a function of the sign width, \(b\); sign height, \(h\); wind speed, \(U\); air density, \(\rho\); and the torsional rigidity, \(GJ\), for the supporting pole. The torsional rigidity, \(GJ\), has dimensions of [N][m] and describes the torque required to deform the system by a radian. It is a combination of a material property (shear modulus of the material) and a geometric measure (the second moment of area of the sign). Develop a suitable set of nondimensional (i.e., pi) terms for this problem.

STREET SIGN OSCILLATION, CEDAR KEY, FL / HURRICANE ELSA, 6 JULY 2021. Photo angles, left to right: \(\theta=95^\circ\), \(\theta=0^\circ\), \(\theta=-30^\circ\). Schematic labels: DO NOT ENTER; width \(b\); height \(h\); wind speed \(U\); rotation frequency \(\omega\); pole torsional parameter \(GJ\).



Figure C.3: Street sign oscillation in Hurricane Elsa, 6 July 2021, Cedar Key, FL. This street sign oscillated at a cyclic frequency of approximately 1.5 Hz.

The three photographs are omitted; their angle labels are transcribed above.

Solution:

Based on the problem statement, we know that \(\omega=f(b,h,U,\rho,GJ)\), where the units of each variable are: \(\omega=[\mathrm{s^{-1}}],b=[\mathrm m],h=[\mathrm m],U=[\mathrm{m/s}],\rho=[\mathrm{kg/m^3}],GJ=[\mathrm{N\,m}]=[\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}]\).

We have 6 variables and 3 units. From the Buckingham Pi Theorem, there are \(6-3=3\) pi terms required. We will solve using the method of repeating variables. Using \(b\), \(U\), and \(\rho\) as repeating variables, we find:

\Pi_1=\omega b^aU^b\rho^c, (C.52)

[\mathrm{s^{-1}}][\mathrm m]^a([\mathrm{m/s}])^b([\mathrm{kg/m^3}])^c=[\mathrm m]^0[\mathrm{kg}]^0[\mathrm s]^0. (C.53)

Editorial clarification: As in the problem statement, the worked solution treats \(GJ\) as a stiffness with units N·m. The usual product of shear modulus and torsion constant has units N·m². Also, the source uses \(b\) for both the sign width and an unknown exponent; they are distinct roles.


PDF page 518 — source_issue

We can then generate the following system of equations: \(c=0,a+b-3c=0,-1-b=0\). Solving this system of equations we find that \(a=1,b=-1,c=0\), and therefore

\Pi_1=\frac{\omega b}{U}. (C.54)

This is what we normally would call a Strouhal number—it defines a characteristic frequency \(U/b\) and uses that to normalize the oscillation frequency.

For \(\Pi_2\):

\Pi_2=hb^aU^b\rho^c, (C.55)

[\mathrm m][\mathrm m]^a([\mathrm m][\mathrm s]^{-1})^b([\mathrm{kg}][\mathrm m]^{-3})^c=[\mathrm m]^0[\mathrm{kg}]^0[\mathrm s]^0, (C.56)

We can then generate the following system of equations: \(c=0,1+a+b-3c=0,-b=0\). Solving this system of equations we find that \(a=-1,b=0,c=0\), and therefore

\Pi_2=\frac{h}{b}. (C.57)

This is an aspect ratio.

For \(\Pi_3\):

\Pi_3=GJb^aU^b\rho^c, (C.58)

[\mathrm{kg}][\mathrm m]^2[\mathrm s]^{-2}[\mathrm m]^a([\mathrm m][\mathrm s]^{-1})^b([\mathrm{kg}][\mathrm m]^{-3})^c=[\mathrm m]^0[\mathrm{kg}]^0[\mathrm s]^0. (C.59)

We can then generate the following system of equations: \(1+c=0,2+a+b-3c=0,-2-b=0\). Solving this system of equations we find that \(a=-3,b=-2,c=-1\), and therefore

\Pi_3=\frac{GJ}{\rho U^2b^3}. (C.60)

This parameter is a ratio of the mechanical resistance to torsion (\(GJ\), units of torque per radian) compared to a measure of the magnitude of the torque applied by the wind (think dynamic pressure \(\tfrac12\rho U^2\) times a characteristic area \(b^2\) to get a force, times a characteristic moment arm \(b\) to make a torque).

The oscillation of the sign is thus most efficiently reported in the functional form:

\frac{\omega b}{U}=\phi\left(\frac hb,\frac{GJ}{\rho U^2b^3}\right) (C.61)

which shows that the oscillation frequency is a function of the aspect ratio and the nondimensionalized torsional rigidity of the beam.

This set of nondimensional parameters isn’t unique, and probably isn’t ideal. Vorticity sheds off of a bluff body at a frequency defined by the smallest dimension of the cross section; as drawn that’s \(b\), so \(\omega b/U\) is probably the right Strouhal number, better than \(\omega h/U\). We could have ended up with \(\omega h/U\); the nondimensionalization process doesn’t know the difference. [faded ratio] is a sensible parameter, and if the other parameters are defined well, the Strouhal number will not be a strong function of [faded ratio]. \(\Pi_3\), though mathematically correct, is probably not the most physically insightful parameter. The forces are surely proportional to the dynamic pressure, the frontal area of the sign, and the moment arm \(b\). So \(\Pi_3\) would be more physically insightful if it were \(\Pi_3=\) [faded fraction]. Again, the math doesn’t know any better. And, given that \(b/h\) is a nondimensional parameter, any set of Pi groups is enough to describe the system. However, picking what set we actually use requires physical insight in addition to the math.

Transcription note: The erased aspect-ratio expressions cannot be certified visually. The final torque-group fraction is consistent with \(GJ/(\rho U^2b^2h)\), using frontal area \(bh\) and moment arm \(b\), but this is a reconstruction from the surrounding explanation. As on the preceding pages, the source uses \(GJ\) for a torsional stiffness in N·m, rather than the usual rigidity in N·m².

5. (OBJECTIVE: ) A scaled version of a submarine will be tested in a wind tunnel where the size is 1/15 of the actual model, the wind speed is 180 ft/s, and the air is standard sea-level. A different prototype will be tested underwater. Determine the speed of the second prototype to ensure they will have a


PDF page 519 — source_issue

similar Reynolds Number

Solution:

Since we want to match the Reynolds number in the air and water conditions;

Re_w=Re_a\Rightarrow\left(\frac U\nu\right)_w=\left(\frac U\nu\right)_a (C.62)

Editorial correction: The Reynolds numbers require the respective lengths: \((Ul/\nu)_w=(Ul/\nu)_a\). The printed (C.62) omits \(l\); (C.63) correctly includes its effect.

Where:

l_a=\tfrac1{15}l_w

\nu_a=1.57\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{ft^2/s}\qquad\nu_w=1.26\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{ft^2/s}\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}

Editorial correction: The trailing kg/m³ is extraneous; both kinematic viscosities have units ft²/s.

Plugging into the previous equation gives:

U_a=\left(\frac{\nu_a}{\nu_w}\right)\left(\frac{l_w}{l_a}\right)U_w=187U_w (C.63)

So the velocity is \(\frac{180\,\mathrm{ft/s}}{187}=.963\,\mathrm{ft/s}\).

Appendix D

How to Derive the Differential Inviscid Conservation of Momentum Equation

In the first few chapters of the text, we determined relations that describe hydrostatic conditions (Chapters 3–4), relations that describe inviscid flow along a streamline (Chapter 5), and integral techniques for analyzing control volumes (Chapter 7). We converted integral relations for conservation of mass into differential forms (Chapter 8). However, we cannot generate descriptions of complicated flow systems without differential governing equations for fluid flow in fixed coordinates (not just the streamline coordinates we used for the Bernoulli equation). In essence, we need to be able to develop equations that describe the fluid velocities and other properties as field variables—for example the velocity field \(\vec u(x,y,z,t)\) and the pressure field \(p(x,y,z,t)\). Chapters 3–8, though useful, fall short of this. Hydrostatic relations give us \(p\) if \(\vec u=0\), but hydrostatic relations are not applicable if the fluid moves. The Bernoulli equation helps us know how \(u\) and \(p\) change along a streamline but we can only calculate one if we know the other. Integral conservation analysis helps us relate inlet and outlet flows to forces on objects, but gives us no detail about what is happening inside a control volume. And differential conservation of mass is not sufficient to derive a velocity field.

inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don’t significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid that has \(\mu=0\): in practice there is no such thing.

control volume: a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

Analyzing fluid mechanics in terms of field variables empowers us in several ways. First, we generate more detailed information at every point in the fluid. Second, by studying the velocity field, we understand the kinematics of fluid deformation—how the fluid is being squeezed, stretched, and rotated. The kinematics of fluid flow help us choose what sorts of analysis to use—we find, for example, that we can simplify our analysis if we can show that the fluid is not rotating (Chapter 9), and we can show that viscous effects in most fluid systems are caused by a specific type of deformation (Appendix F).

kinematics: the study of the motion of objects without consideration of forces.

For conservation of mass, the equations weren’t that complicated, and the derivation wasn’t much of a distraction when we did it in Chapter 8. Also, the differential form could immediately be put to use to solve irrotational flow (Chapter 9). So that narrative arc seems pretty clear. For conservation of momentum, the equations are more complicated, and we actually can’t use the result right away. So as a student, this analysis can appear tiresome or distracting or tedious. The only homework problems I can assign on this material are of the form of “rederive this or that” or “prove this kinematic detail that Professor Kirby finds interesting but maybe students won’t find it relevant”. Differential conservation of momentum analysis gets useful as soon as we add viscosity, but that requires that we formalize the mathematics of fluid deformation, which is another set of derivations. So deriving the differential form of the conservation of momentum, although important, feels like an appendix. So... welcome to the Appendices.

irrotational flow: flow in which \(\vec\omega=\nabla\times\vec u=0\). The terms irrotational flow (\(\vec\omega=0\)) and potential flow (\(\vec u=\nabla\phi\)) are synonymous—one implies the other.


PDF page 521 — verified

In this appendix, we convert the integral conservation of momentum relations from Chapter 7 to differential relations. The differential governing equations for mass and momentum, combined with boundary conditions, form a well-posed system of partial differential equations, and all that is left is to solve these equations. Unfortunately, solving these equations still poses a significant challenge, and we can solve these analytically only for a small subset of fluid-flow problems.

Importantly, though, the differential conservation of momentum equations are the equations solved by computational fluid dynamics software. So the equations in this appendix (usually with the viscous terms from Appendix F) are the ones software packages solve.

The key mathematical result of this appendix is the differential form of the governing equations for conservation of momentum (the Euler equations) in fixed coordinates. These equations are the fundamental underpinnings of a significant fraction of engineering fluid mechanical analysis.

Euler equations: pronounced OY-ler. The inviscid conservation of momentum equations. Can be written in streamline coordinates (\(dB/ds=0,dk/dn=-\rho U^2/R,dk/d\ell=0\)) or fixed coordinates (\(\rho\partial\vec u/\partial t+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\rho\vec g\)).

D.1 We can derive the differential conservation of momentum equation by use of the divergence theorem or a judiciously chosen control volume aligned with a specific coordinate system

As was the case for conservation of mass, we can derive the differential form of conservation of momentum by using the divergence theorem or a control volume aligned with the coordinate system we want to use.

conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

conservation of momentum: the notion that changes in momentum are brought about by forces as prescribed by Newton’s second law.

The divergence theorem turns the integral vector conservation of momentum equation into a general differential vector conservation of momentum equation

As was the case for conservation of mass, the divergence theorem quickly converts the integral forms of the conservation of momentum equation to differential form.

divergence theorem: the divergence theorem, applied to a fluid velocity field: \(\int_\mathcal V\nabla\cdot\vec u\,dV=\int_\mathcal S\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA\) indicates that the net outflow of fluid across a control surface is equal to the integral of the divergence of velocity over the control volume.

Rewriting Equation (7.35), the integral conservation of momentum equation is

\underbrace{\frac\partial{\partial t}\int_\mathcal V\rho\vec u\,dV}_{\text{change of vector momentum in CV}}+\overbrace{\int_\mathcal S(\rho\vec u)(\vec u\cdot\hat n)\,dA}^{\text{outflux of vector momentum through CS}}=\underbrace{\sum\vec F}_{\text{total force applied to CV}}, (D.1)

Newton’s 2nd law written as conservation of momentum for a control volume

As we did previously for mass, we can turn the surface flux integral into a volume integral by use of the divergence theorem:


PDF page 522 — verified

\frac\partial{\partial t}\int_\mathcal V\rho\vec u\,dV+\int_\mathcal V\nabla\cdot\underbrace{\rho\vec u\vec u}_{\text{this is a dyadic}}\,dV=\sum\vec F. (D.2)

Then, because the derivative and integral commute:

commute: two operators commute if they can be applied in any order and the result is the same.

\int_\mathcal V\frac{\partial(\rho\vec u)}{\partial t}\,dV+\int_\mathcal V\nabla\cdot\rho\vec u\vec u\,dV=\sum\vec F. (D.3)

We can write the force as a volume integral of the volumetric force \(\vec f\):

\int_\mathcal V\frac{\partial(\rho\vec u)}{\partial t}\,dV+\int_\mathcal V\nabla\cdot\rho\vec u\vec u\,dV=\int_\mathcal V\vec f\,dV, (D.4)

which means

\int_\mathcal V\left(\frac{\partial(\rho\vec u)}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\rho\vec u\vec u-\vec f\right)dV=0, (D.5)

Equation (D.5) must be true for any control volume, and for that to be true, the integrand must be zero:

\underbrace{\frac{\partial(\rho\vec u)}{\partial t}}_{\text{rate of change of momentum}}+\overbrace{\nabla\cdot\rho\vec u\vec u}^{\text{net rate of outflow of momentum}}=\underbrace{\vec f}_{\text{volumetric force applied to fluid}}. (D.6)

conservation of momentum, differential form

This differential form of the equation now applies everywhere in the fluid. If we integrated this equation over a control volume, we would recover the integral form of this conservation equation.

For fixed density, Equation (D.6) simplifies to

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=\vec f. (D.7)

conservation of momentum, differential form, fixed density

Ok so you should make note of what just happened. I said “For fixed density, Equation (D.6) simplifies to...” That is the typical way we use conservation of mass. We don’t solve \(\nabla\cdot\vec u=0\) in most cases. Instead, we use \(\nabla\cdot\vec u=0\) to simplify the conservation of momentum equation. That is what led to Equation (D.7). \(\nabla\cdot\rho\vec u\vec u\) is more complicated than \(\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\), but some of the parts of \(\nabla\cdot\rho\vec u\vec u\) become zero if \(\nabla\cdot\vec u=0\), so we can write \(\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) instead. The same is true later, when we add viscosity, as a bunch of terms in the viscous force term also go away if \(\nabla\cdot\vec u=0\).

conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

As we described earlier, \(\vec f\) is the sum of all volumetric forces, most commonly net pressure force, gravity, and net viscous forces. The net volumetric gravitational force is

\vec f_{\mathrm{gravity}}=\rho\vec g, (D.8)

net volumetric gravitational force

where \(\vec g=-g\hat z\).

To get the net volumetric pressure force, we again use the divergence theorem. The pressure force on a control volume is given by \(\int_\mathcal S-p\hat n\,dA\). We can use the identity tensor \(\vec{\vec I}\) to put this in a form where the divergence theorem helps us. First, we rewrite \(-p\hat n\) in terms of a dot product:¹

-p\hat n=-p\left(\vec{\vec I}\cdot\hat n\right). (D.9)

divergence theorem: the divergence theorem, applied to a fluid velocity field: \(\int_\mathcal V\nabla\cdot\vec u\,dV=\int_\mathcal S\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA\) indicates that the net outflow of fluid across a control surface is equal to the integral of the divergence of velocity over the control volume.

¹ Pressure really is an isotropic dyadic tensor and \(-p\vec{\vec I}\cdot\hat n\) is arguably the most proper way to thing of the effect of pressure on a surface. We typically write this force per unit area as \(-p\hat n\) just because it is simpler.


PDF page 523 — source_issue

Now this is in a form such that the divergence theorem helps us. By the divergence theorem, \(\int_\mathcal S-p\vec{\vec I}\cdot\hat n\,dA\) is equivalent to \(\int_\mathcal V\nabla\cdot(-p\vec{\vec I})\,dV\). Then, because \(\nabla\cdot\vec{\vec I}(-p)=-\nabla p\):

\vec f_{\mathrm{pressure}}=-\nabla p. (D.10)

net volumetric gravitational force

Editorial correction: The caption for (D.10) should say “pressure force”; the formula itself is correct.

Putting all terms together, we have (for flow without viscous effects):

\underbrace{\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}}_{\text{rate of change of momentum at a point}}+\overbrace{\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u}^{\text{net outflow of momentum at a point}}=\underbrace{-\nabla p}_{\text{net volumetric pressure force}}+\overbrace{\rho\vec g}^{\text{net volumetric gravity force}}. (D.11)

conservation of momentum, differential form, fixed density, no viscous forces

From this, we see that the time change in momentum of a control volume is affected by (1) net outflow of momentum from the control volume, (2) a net volumetric pressure force, and (3) a net volumetric gravitational body force. In Appendix F we will add a net volumetric viscous force to this equation as well. We relate surface fluxes to volume effects through the divergence theorem; the divergence is reviewed again in Sidebar D.1.

volumetric: related to volume, or per unit volume.

Equation (D.11) is quite compact—it is a vector equation, which is equivalent to a set of three scalar equations (In Cartesian coordinates, for x momentum, y momentum, and z momentum). In Cartesian coordinates, Equation (D.11) can be written out for each component, leading to

\rho\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}+\rho\left(u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)=-\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}, (D.14)

\rho\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}+\rho\left(u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\right)=-\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}, (D.15)

Editorial correction: The first convective term in the printed y-momentum equation (D.15) is \(u\,\partial u/\partial x\); it should be \(u\,\partial v/\partial x\).

\rho\frac{\partial w}{\partial t}+\rho\left(u\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)=-\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}-\rho g. (D.16)

The source prints (D.17) on an empty equation line.

conservation of momentum, differential form, fixed density, no viscous forces, Cartesian coords

Applying the integral vector conservation of momentum equation to a control volume aligned with a coordinate system generates a differential conservation of momentum equation specific to the coordinate system

Although the use of the divergence theorem is quick and general, it doesn’t concretely visualize forces and momentum fluxes. An equivalent approach that is coordinate-specific is to analyze a differential control volume aligned with the coordinate system.

As an example, consider the differential Cartesian control volume in Figure D.1, p. 515. We draw a cuboidic control volume and pick faces that are

divergence theorem: the divergence theorem, applied to a fluid velocity field: \(\int_\mathcal V\nabla\cdot\vec u\,dV=\int_\mathcal S\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA\) indicates that the net outflow of fluid across a control surface is equal to the integral of the divergence of velocity over the control volume.

Cartesian: for a vector or coordinate system: fixed, orthogonal, and right-handed.

cuboid: a three-dimensional object with six rectangular faces, all aligned at right angles.

SIDEBAR D.1: FUNDAMENTALS

Divergence

The divergence of the velocity field is the net volumetric expansion of the fluid at any point

The mathematical definition of divergence of a vector (or higher-order tensor) is

\nabla\cdot\vec u\equiv\lim_{V\to0}\left(\frac{\int_\mathcal S\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA}{V}\right). (D.12)

where \(\mathcal V\) denotes a control volume with control surface \(\mathcal S\) and volume \(V\), and \(\hat n\) is the unit outward normal along the surface. The limit makes the control volume infinitesimal, making the divergence a differential vector operation. Here \(\vec u\) is used as an example, but one can take a divergence of any field variable that has tensor rank of 1 or higher. The verbal definition of the divergence is tricky—the definition mathematicians use is succinct but uses the word “flux” in a way that contradicts how fluid mechanicians use the word “flux”. Rather than attempt a general definition, Table D.1, p. 513 and D.2 list some examples. Engineers define flux to mean the rate of flow of a property per unit area across a control surface (in 3D) or the rate of flow of a property per unit length across a surface (in 2D). Consider a property \(P\) and consider a vector field property \(\vec q\) such that \(\vec q\cdot\hat n\) describes the flux of \(P\) across the surface. For example, in 3D, volume flux is described by \(\vec u\cdot\hat n\) and momentum flux is described by \(\rho\vec u\vec u\cdot\hat n\). With these definitions, \(\nabla\cdot\vec q\) describes the net outflow of \(P\) per unit volume (3D) or the net outflow of \(P\) per unit area (2D). The divergence has units equal to the units of \(P\) times \([1/L]\). The divergence of \(\vec q\) \(\nabla\cdot\vec q\) has a tensor rank one lower than that of \(\vec q\); the divergence of a vector is a scalar, and the divergence of a dyadic tensor is a vector.

Editorial correction: The divergence has units of the flux field \(\vec q\) divided by length, not of the transported total property \(P\) divided by length. Momentum flux is a dyadic field, as the source’s own example shows.



CV dimension | property P | property \(\vec q\) such that \(\vec q\cdot\hat n\) gives flux of P through control surface | \(\nabla\cdot\vec q\)
3 | volume | \(\vec u\) | net volume outflow rate per volume

Editorial clarification: The last two rows use three-dimensional density and describe a two-dimensional section per unit depth. Outflow per unit depth, divided by section area, has the same units as outflow per volume.

The divergence of the fluid velocity is a measure of how much the fluid is expanding or contracting

If \(\nabla\cdot\vec u>0\), the fluid is expanding (and density is going down). If \(\nabla\cdot\vec u<0\), the fluid is contracting (and density is going up). If density is fixed (because the flow is incompressible), then \(\nabla\cdot\vec u=0\).

The divergence of the shear stresses is a measure of the net viscous force on a fluid element

The shear stresses on a fluid element are given by a dyadic \(\vec{\vec\tau}_{\mathrm{visc}}\), and the divergence \(\nabla\cdot\vec{\vec\tau}_{\mathrm{visc}}\) of this tensor is a vector that describes the net volumetric force on the fluid from viscous effects. In fluid mechanics, we care about stresses themselves only at walls and interfaces. In the body of a fluid, we care only about the divergences of the stresses. Contrast with solid mechanics, where we care primarily about stresses themselves, because stresses relate to yield and fracture.

The divergence takes different forms in different coordinate systems

In Cartesian coordinates and cylindrical coordinates,

\nabla\cdot\vec u=\underbrace{\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}}_{\text{net expansion in }x}+\overbrace{\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}}^{\text{net expansion in }y}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}}_{\text{net expansion in }z},\qquad\nabla\cdot\vec u=\underbrace{\frac1r\frac{\partial(ru_r)}{\partial r}}_{\text{net expansion in }r}+\overbrace{\frac1r\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial\theta}}^{\text{net expansion in }\theta}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z}}_{\text{net expansion in }z}. (D.13)

SIDEBAR D.2: FUNDAMENTALS

Taylor-Series Expansions

The Taylor Series prescribes the value of a function (e.g., pressure, density, velocity) everywhere in space if we know all of that function’s derivatives at one point

The Taylor-series expansion for a function \(f(x)\) around a point \(x_0\) is given by

f(x)=f(x_0)+\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n!}\left.\frac{\partial^nf}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}\Delta x^n, (D.18)

where \(\Delta x=x-x_0\). The Taylor-series expansion prescribes \(f\) at any \(x\) if we know \(f\) and all of \(f\)’s derivatives at \(x_0\). The Taylor series helps us change the mathematical description of a function from one that permeates space (i.e., knowing \(f(x)\) everywhere) to one that involves a ton of information all at one point in space (i.e., all the derivatives of \(f\) at one value of \(x=x_0\)). This is helpful because all of our differential equations that describe physical principles (e.g., conservation of momentum) are applied at a specific point in space.

Editorial qualification: An infinite Taylor series equals the function only where the function is analytic and the series converges to it. Knowing all derivatives at one point does not determine an arbitrary smooth function everywhere. The local first-order approximation below needs differentiability, rather than this stronger global claim.

We use the first-order term in the Taylor series to formulate differential equations

In formulating differential relations in physical systems, we use the Taylor-series expansion to relate the properties of \(f\) (\(f\) is typically the pressure, density, temperature, velocity, or similar fluid property) in different parts of an infinitesimal fluid element. Because the fluid element is vanishingly small, we find that we need not evaluate all the terms of the sum: in fact we need only the first term because all terms beyond the first-order term (\(\frac{df}{dx}\Delta x\)) are vanishingly small relative to the first-order term. If we include only the first-order term, the Taylor-series expansion becomes

f(x)\simeq\underbrace{f(x_0)}_{\text{0th-order estimate of }f(x)}+\underbrace{\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{x_0}\Delta x}_{\text{1st-order (linear) correction for }f(x)}, (D.19)

and this is the form we use when deriving differential governing equations.

One might argue that the first-order term is also vanishingly small relative to the zeroth-order term. The reason why the first-order term must be retained is that, when evaluating the effect of changes in fluid properties when deriving differential forms of the governing equations, we are actually interested in the difference between properties along the surface of a control volume. If we use the Taylor-series expansion to approximate, for example \(f(x_2)-f(x_1)\), we can see why the first-order term is important:

\begin{aligned}f(x_2)-f(x_1)&=\left[f(x_0)+\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n!}\left.\frac{\partial^nf}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}(x_2-x_0)^n\right]\\ &\quad-\left[f(x_0)+\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n!}\left.\frac{\partial^nf}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}(x_1-x_0)^n\right],\end{aligned} (D.20)

f(x_2)-f(x_1)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n!}\left.\frac{\partial^nf}{\partial x^n}\right|_{x_0}\left[(x_2-x_0)^n-(x_1-x_0)^n\right]. (D.21)

Here, we see that \(f(x_0)\) cancels. For \(x_2-x_0\) and \(x_1-x_0\) approaching zero, the difference \(f(x_2)-f(x_1)\) can be written as

f(x_2)-f(x_1)\simeq\underbrace{\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{x_0}(x_2-x_1)}_{\text{1st-order (linear) approximation}}. (D.22)

As \(x_2\) and \(x_1\) approach \(x_0\), all terms for \(n=2\) and higher are much smaller than the term for \(n=1\). This is why the \(n=1\) term is necessary but why the \(n=2\) and higher terms are not retained in the sum.

divergence theorem: the divergence theorem, applied to a fluid velocity field: \(\int_\mathcal V\nabla\cdot\vec u\,dV=\int_\mathcal S\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA\) indicates that the net outflow of fluid across a control surface is equal to the integral of the divergence of velocity over the control volume.

The inviscid conservation of momentum equation i.e., the Euler equations can be used to rederive Bernoulli and show that Bernoulli applies everywhere in an irrotational flow

The Bernoulli equation we derived was a steady, inviscid, conservation of momentum equation that came from applying \(F=ma\) to a moving fluid system along a streamline. The Euler equations are a set of inviscid conservation of momentum equations that come from applying \(F=ma\) to a control volume, normally written as one vector equation. As these different equations are simply different forms of the same analysis, we can rederive the steady Bernoulli equation from the steady form of the Euler equations. This is useful, because this derivation will highlight that the Bernoulli equation applies everywhere in an irrotational flow.

steady: unchanging with time. Compare to unsteady, meaning changing with time, and stationary, meaning statistically unchanging in time.

inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don’t significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid that has \(\mu=0\): in practice there is no such thing.

Euler’s equations in Gibbs notation were listed in Equation (D.11) and are repeated here:

\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\rho\vec g. (D.28)

inviscid, fixed-density, conservation of momentum, Gibbs notation

The steady form is:

\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\rho\vec g. (D.29)

inviscid, fixed-density, conservation of momentum, Gibbs notation

Recall that the Bernoulli equation in differential form has a term showing how pressure changes and term showing how gravitational potential energy changes; these terms are still apparent in the Euler equations. What is different is that the Euler equations are written for a control volume and therefore the term that becomes \(\tfrac12\rho U^2\) is now in a form that describes convective flux of momentum.

Bernoulli equation: in differential form \(0=\frac d{ds}(p+\tfrac12\rho u^2+\rho gz)\), in integral form: \(B=p+\tfrac12\rho u^2+\rho gz\), where \(B\) is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

How we got that the flux of x momentum is

The x-, y-, and z-momentum are all determined similarly. Here we evaluate the x-momentum as an example.

We sum the net momentum flowing out of the control volume

This control volume has 6 discrete faces, so we can write the surface integral as a sum over the 6 faces:

\int_\mathcal S\rho\vec u\vec u\cdot\hat n=\sum_{\text{6 faces}}(\text{outward momentum flux}), (D.27)

Editorial correction: The surface integral in (D.27) is missing its area element \(dA\).

The outward momentum fluxes for the six faces (assuming \(\rho\) is uniform) are:

right:

\rho\left(u+\tfrac12\Delta x\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)\left(u+\tfrac12\Delta x\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)\Delta y\Delta z.

left:

\rho\left(u-\tfrac12\Delta x\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)\left[-\left(u-\tfrac12\Delta x\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)\right]\Delta y\Delta z.

top:

\rho\left(u+\tfrac12\Delta y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\left(v+\tfrac12\Delta y\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)\Delta x\Delta z.

bottom:

\rho\left(u-\tfrac12\Delta y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\left[-\left(v-\tfrac12\Delta y\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)\right]\Delta x\Delta z.

front:

\rho\left(u+\tfrac12\Delta z\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)\left(w+\tfrac12\Delta z\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\Delta x\Delta y.

back:

\rho\left(u-\tfrac12\Delta z\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)\left[-\left(w-\tfrac12\Delta z\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right)\right]\Delta x\Delta y.

Multiplying these out and keeping only terms with a single differential element, we have

right:

\rho\Delta y\Delta z\left(uu+\tfrac12\Delta x u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\tfrac12\Delta x u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)

left:

\rho\Delta y\Delta z\left(-uu-\tfrac12\Delta x u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\tfrac12\Delta x u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)

top:

\rho\Delta x\Delta z\left(uv+\tfrac12\Delta y u\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\tfrac12\Delta y v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)

bottom:

\rho\Delta x\Delta z\left(-uv-\tfrac12\Delta y u\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\tfrac12\Delta y v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)

front:

\rho\Delta x\Delta y\left(uw+\tfrac12\Delta z u\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}+\tfrac12\Delta z w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)

back:

\rho\Delta x\Delta y\left(-uw-\tfrac12\Delta z u\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}+\tfrac12\Delta z w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)

Summing these six fluxes, we get \(\rho\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z(u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z})\).

Editorial correction: In the expanded left, bottom and back expressions, the first linear derivative term should have a plus sign. For example, \(-(u-a)(v-b)=-uv+ub+av-ab\). After correcting those signs, the sum is \(\rho\Delta V[(\vec u\cdot\nabla)u+u\nabla\cdot\vec u]\). The stated final result then follows from constant-density continuity, \(\nabla\cdot\vec u=0\). The printed negative signs cancel these continuity terms artificially.

• Turn the Euler equations into a form where there is a gradient of the Bernoulli constant. This is trivial if you already know the vector identity \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=\nabla(\tfrac12U^2)+\vec\omega\times\vec u\), not so trivial if you don’t.

• Show that the gradient of the Bernoulli constant is zero in an irrotational flow no matter what the direction is.

• Show that that the gradient of the Bernoulli constant is zero along a streamline regardless of whether there is vorticity.

Bernoulli constant: the constant \(B\) in the Bernoulli equation \(B=p+\tfrac12\rho u^2+\rho gz\). A measure of the energy per unit volume of the fluid. Synonymous with total pressure.

We first note that \(\vec g=-g\nabla z\); this puts the gravitational potential energy term into gradient form:

\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p-\rho g\nabla z (D.30)

inviscid, fixed-density, conservation of momentum, Gibbs notation

Now we want to convert \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) into a form that has the gradient of something, and wow we’d like it to be \(\nabla(\tfrac12U^2)\) because that is where we know we want to end up. Unfortunately, \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) isn’t quite equal to \(\nabla(\tfrac12U^2)\), but there is a vector identity of use here:

\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=\nabla\left(\frac12U^2\right)+\vec\omega\times\vec u. (D.31)

Euler equations: pronounced OY-ler. The inviscid conservation of momentum equations. Can be written in streamline coordinates (\(dB/ds=0,dk/dn=-\rho U^2/R,dk/d\ell=0\)) or fixed coordinates (\(\rho\partial\vec u/\partial t+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\rho\vec g\)).

See Sidebar D.4 for a description of why this identity is true. Substituting this into the Euler equations, we have

\rho\nabla\left(\frac12U^2\right)+\rho\vec\omega\times\vec u=-\nabla p-\rho g\nabla z. (D.36)

almost there. it will all be over soon

We can rearrange this to show what the gradient of the Bernoulli constant is:

\nabla\left(p+\frac12\rho U^2+\rho gz\right)=\rho\vec u\times\vec\omega. (D.37)

general expression for gradient of Bernoulli constant, inviscid, fixed-density flow

Equation (D.37) is now a result that is reminiscent of the Bernoulli equation but much more general. Two specific results immediately follow from it:

• If the vorticity is everywhere zero, i.e., if the flow is irrotational, then the RHS of this equation is zero, which means the gradient of the Bernoulli constant is everywhere zero, which means that the Bernoulli equation applies along any path in the flow, not just a streamline.

vorticity: A pseudovector denoted by \(\vec\omega\) and defined by \(\vec\omega=\nabla\times\vec u\), whose direction describes the axis around which the fluid is locally rotating and whose magnitude indicates exactly twice the angular rotation rate of the fluid around that axis.

• If the vorticity is nonzero, we can still explain why the Bernoulli equation applies along a streamline. The velocity \(\vec u\) points in the direction of the streamline. The curl of a vector with any other vector is always normal to the original vector. Which means that \(\vec u\times\vec\omega\) is always normal to the streamline. Which means that the gradient of the Bernoulli constant is always normal to the streamline, which means that the Bernoulli constant is not changing along the streamline.

Editorial correction: “The curl of a vector with any other vector” means the cross product of two vectors. Curl is a differential operator on one vector field. The cross-product equations and perpendicularity argument are correct.

streamline: a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

Bernoulli equation: in differential form \(0=\frac d{ds}(p+\tfrac12\rho u^2+\rho gz)\), in integral form: \(B=p+\tfrac12\rho u^2+\rho gz\), where \(B\) is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

So, reexamining the Bernoulli equation through a more general analysis that comes from the Euler equations reaffirms that the Bernoulli equation is correct, and shows furthermore that the Bernoulli equation applies everywhere in an irrotational flow.

SIDEBAR D.4: FUNDAMENTALS

Why \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=\nabla(\tfrac12U^2)+\vec\omega\times\vec u\)

We are looking for gradients of volumetric energy terms, so let’s compare \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) to \(\nabla(\tfrac12U^2)\) and see what is left

The net convective flux of momentum (\(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\)) has the form

\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=\begin{bmatrix}u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\\ u\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\\ u\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix} (D.32)

To derive the Bernoulli equation, we would like this to be the gradient of a volumetric energy term. It would be particularly convenient if \(\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) were equal to the gradient of \(\tfrac12\rho U^2\). The gradient of \(\tfrac12U^2\) (note \(U^2=u^2+v^2+w^2\)), unfortunately, is not equal to \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\):

\nabla\left(\frac12U^2\right)=\begin{bmatrix}u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}+w\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\\ u\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+v\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+w\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\\ u\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}+v\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}+w\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix} (D.33)

The difference between the two, though, has some familiar parts:

\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u-\nabla\left(\frac12U^2\right)=\begin{bmatrix}w\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}-\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right)-v\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\\ u\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)-w\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\right)\\ v\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}-\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\right)-u\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right)\end{bmatrix} (D.34)

Editorial correction: The first parenthesis in the last row of (D.34) has its subtraction reversed. It should be \(v(\partial w/\partial y-\partial v/\partial z)\). The final identity (D.35) is correct. Transcription note: The faded last row of (D.33) and first row of (D.34) are restored from the legible operands and their stated difference; the visibly incorrect last row is preserved.

Equation (D.34) has the components of the velocity vector (\(u,v,\) and \(w\)) and also the components of the vorticity vector \(\vec\omega\), namely \((\partial w/\partial y-\partial v/\partial z)\), \((\partial u/\partial z-\partial w/\partial x)\), and \((\partial v/\partial x-\partial u/\partial y)\). In fact, the result when we subtract \(\nabla(\tfrac12U^2)\) from \(\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u\) is equal to \(\vec\omega\times\vec u\). Because of this, we can write the vector identity

\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=\nabla\left(\frac12U^2\right)+\vec\omega\times\vec u. (D.35)

A graduate student should be able to prove this in like two lines instead of the half a page I write above. Take MAE6010 to acquire these superhuman abilities a.k.a. Einstein notation. My professor colleagues would roll their eyes at how long and drawn out the discussion above is; we have all learned much easier mathematical ways to analyze these expressions.

Appendix E

The velocity gradient dyadic can be split up into parts that help us distinguish between translation, rotation, and shear

The surface of any control volume in a fluid experiences surface stresses that we call viscous stresses. Although we do not talk about viscosity or viscous stresses in this appendix, we set the stage to do so by describing fluid deformation mathematically. This discussion ramps up the partial differential calculus, and folds in dyadic mathematics. In exchange, we get very clean and clear descriptions of how a fluid deforms in a way that translates directly to the forces and accelerations that a fluid experiences.

Viscosity is the relation between a fluid’s strain rate and the attendant viscous stress. Because viscous stress and strain rate are both dyadics, we must incorporate tensor mathematics into the discussion (see Sidebar E.1; p. 522).

Students working with dyadics often use matrices as heuristic devices to remember how to perform tensor operations, but one has to be careful to understand what is really going on when we do this (Sidebar E.2, p. 523).

deformation: for fluid mechanics, we typically mean deformation rate, the rate at which parts of the fluid move relative to each other, exclusive of solid-body rotation or uniform translation.

dyadic: a second-order tensor comprising a set of unit dyads.

E.1 Deformation of a fluid is related to velocity gradients

Fluid deformation is described by partial derivatives of velocity components. Given three velocity components \(u,v,\) and \(w\) and three coordinates \(x,y,\) and \(z\), there are nine different ways we can describe how velocity components are changing in space. These form the nine components of the velocity gradient dyadic \(\nabla\vec u\):

\nabla\vec u=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}&\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{bmatrix}. (E.11)

velocity-gradient tensor

Three of these nine terms can be immediately interpreted:

• \(\partial u/\partial x\) describes expansion in the x direction.

• \(\partial v/\partial y\) describes expansion in the y direction.

• \(\partial w/\partial z\) describes expansion in the z direction.
