“Viscous”, “inviscid”, “ideal”, and “frictionless” are adjectives of varying merit that are best used to describe the dynamics of fluid flows rather than the constitutive properties of a fluid

A fluid is viscous if it has a viscosity. Viscosity is a constitutive property of a fluid. This is in contrast to something that is (for example) elastic, meaning it has an elastic modulus, or something that is viscoelastic, meaning it has both elastic and viscous properties. All fluids (excepting some quantum fluids, which are not central to common mechanical engineering systems) have viscosity, so the term viscous is essentially redundant with fluid. Some use the adjective viscous to imply “high-viscosity”, but this is colloquial and not technical terminology.

A flow is viscous if it has a net volumetric viscous force somewhere in the flow. This is true for all flows that are not irrotational. Sometimes “viscous flow” is sloppily used to imply low-Re flow—one should instead use “low-Re flow”, “creeping flow”, or “Stokes flow”.

An inviscid flow is a mathematical model of a flow that has no net volumetric viscous force anywhere in the flow nor a viscous stress at any wall; such a flow has no viscous effects and does not really exist, but is often a useful model. An inviscid flow can have viscous stresses in the fluid as long as they cancel and generate no net volumetric force. Irrotational flows are inviscid. Some flows with vorticity are inviscid, but there are few. The solid-body rotation flow \(\phi=\Gamma\theta\) is one example. High-\(Re\) flows can have large regions of the flow far from walls that are inviscid. Inviscid flow is an approximation that can be correct far from solid walls; it can never be correct near a solid wall.

There is no such thing as an inviscid fluid (excepting some quantum fluids), I strongly dislike terms such as “inviscid fluid”, “ideal fluid”, and “frictionless fluid”, although they are commonly used. I find these terms misleading.

Editorial corrections: “All flows that are not irrotational” is too broad: rotational linear shear or solid-body rotation can have \(\nabla^2\vec u=0\). The printed \(\phi=\Gamma\theta\) represents an irrotational free vortex (away from the axis), not solid-body rotation; solid-body rotation instead has \(u_\theta=\Omega r\). An inviscid wall approximation can hold in special flows with zero shear; “never” is also too broad.

viscosity: if denoted \(\mu\), the dynamic viscosity. A measure of fluid resistance to being deformed. For Newtonian fluids, proportional to the ratio of the fluid stress to fluid strain rate. If denoted \(\nu\), the kinematic viscosity \(\nu=\mu/\rho\). A measure of fluid’s ability to diffuse momentum.

constitutive: relating two properties of a material. For example viscosity relates stress to strain rate and thermal conductivity relates temperature gradient to heat flux.

viscous: related to the generation of local fluid stresses by local fluid shear strain rate.

irrotational: not rotating, i.e., \(\vec\omega=\nabla\times\vec u=0\).

Stokes flow: flow in which \(Re\to0\). Synonymous with creeping flow.

inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don’t significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid that has \(\mu=0\); in practice there is no such thing.

stress: in Newtonian fluid mechanics, the word stress is used to denote either (a) a scalar force per unit area on a plane, (b) a vector force per unit area on a plane, and (c) a dyadic tensor that fully describes all forces per unit area that would be applied on any plane. Fluid mechanicians are cavalier about this because so many fluids are effectively incompressible and isotropic. Solid and continuum mechanicians call (a) a stress component (b) a traction and (c) the stress tensor. So beware of this in MAE3270 and MAE3280 and MAE4230.

“Compressible” and “incompressible” are adjectives that are best used to describe the kinematics of fluid flows rather than the equations of state of fluids

All fluids are compressible, meaning that their density is a function of pressure. An incompressible fluid is a mathematical concept that is not particularly useful.

A compressible flow is one in which the fluid moves fast enough that its interaction with obstacles creates density changes big enough that \(\rho\) can not be assumed uniform in the conservation of mass equation. An incompressible

compressible: when describing a fluid, means density changes with pressure. All fluids are compressible. When describing a flow, means density changes enough in the flow that density changes must be considered in the conservation of mass equation.

Editorial clarification: Incompressibility means material density is conserved, \(D\rho/Dt=0\), hence \(\nabla\cdot\vec u=0\), and need not mean spatially uniform density. Compressibility effects can also arise from unsteadiness, heating, or pressure changes without an obstacle.


PDF page 554 — source_issue

flow is one in which \(\rho\) can be assumed uniform in the conservation of mass equation with minimal error.

conservation of mass: the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

Many terms are used to describe potential flow, some of which describe kinematics and some of which describe their dynamic consequences

Potential flow is a kinematic descriptor that means \(\vec u=\nabla\phi\). Potential flow is a mathematical description of fluid flow that can be correct far from solid walls and is never correct near solid walls. It is useful because the errors associated with the approximation can often be neglected or managed with a complementary analysis technique like boundary layer analysis. Irrotational flow is a kinematic descriptor that means \(\vec\omega=0\). Those two statements can be shown to be mathematically equivalent (with accommodations for point singularities e.g., an irrotational vortex).

Inviscid flow is a dynamic descriptor which means \(\vec f_{\mathrm{viscous}}=0\). It is nearly synonymous with irrotational flow and potential flow, but rather than describing the kinematics of the velocity field, it describes the dynamics of the viscous forces.

potential flow: flow in which \(\vec u\) can be written as \(\vec u=\nabla\phi\). The terms irrotational flow (\(\vec\omega=0\)) and potential flow (\(\vec u=\nabla\phi\)) are synonymous—one implies the other.

kinematic: related to the motion of objects without consideration of forces.

boundary layer: a thin layer of fluid near a boundary in which the conservation of momentum equation is simplified because of the nearly unidirectional flow parallel to the surface.

irrotational: not rotating, i.e., \(\vec\omega=\nabla\times\vec u=0\).

inviscid flow: A flow in which viscous effects can be neglected. Often means irrotational flow, which means \(\nabla^2\phi=0\) and therefore \(\mu\nabla^2\vec u=0\), so there is no net volumetric viscous force. Often means a high-\(Re\) flow in which the viscous effects are confined to boundary layers that do not significantly affect the flow. Does not mean \(\mu=0\).

Appendix G

Glossary of Terms You Should Know

Fluid mechanics has its own language, just like biology and chemistry and physics and solid mechanics and electronics and every other field. There are many terms that are the same from field to field, but unfortunately some terms (like flux or vector) mean different things in MAE3230 than they do in MATH1920, and others (like convection) mean different things in MAE3230 and MAE3240. Also, many words depend totally on context (a mathematical constant is different from a constant parameter in a fluids problem).

Interestingly, some fields like biology take great pains to encourage study of the language of the field, with the effect that students are given the tools they need to learn the language but students perceive that the class involves “memorization not concepts”. I know this first-hand; the other class I teach (MAE6680) is on cancer biology and clinical practice. Fluid mechanics classes and texts typically do not focus on prescription of language: these fields claim to involve “concepts not memorization” but usually expect that students will absorb this language without any effort or systematic prescription.

My experience is that fluids textbooks are full of words and phrases that are not explained; this is the language that fluids professors speak, but perhaps not the language that fluids students speak at the beginning of the term. I think I help you if I provide these definitions, and I do not think that providing these definitions and expecting you to know them means I am requiring “memorization”. I think I am teaching you the language of fluid mechanics 👣 👣 👣.

I provide this glossary in the hopes that it makes it easier to learn these terms and understand the text. As much as is possible with the finite area on a page, these terms are defined in callouts in the margins.

1. absolute pressure : pressure measured relative to vacuum.

2. acceleration : change of velocity with respect to time. If a partial derivative with respect to time, this is Eulerian acceleration. If a total derivative with respect to time, this is Lagrangian acceleration.

3. acoustic : in general, related to sound. When used to modify a field property e.g., “acoustic pressure”, means the magnitude of the specific small oscillatory variation around the mean value.

4. acoustics : the study of sound i.e., small pressure and density disturbances in a fluid.

5. actuator disk : a simplified model of a turbomachine e.g., a propeller as an infinitely thin disk that creates a pressure discontinuity.

6. advection : the transport of a fluid property induced by fluid motion itself.

7. advective : relating to the transport of a fluid property induced by fluid motion itself.

8. adverse pressure gradient : a pressure gradient in which the pressure increases in the downstream direction. Notable because it can make flow separate.

9. airfoil : a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes. Roughly synonymous with blade, hydrofoil, wing, and vane. Often chosen over the word hydrofoil when the fluid is air. Often chosen over the word vane when mounted on an airplane.

Editorial clarification: The partial time derivative is the local acceleration. The acceleration of a fluid particle expressed in Eulerian variables is the material derivative \(D\vec u/Dt=\partial_t\vec u+(\vec u\cdot\nabla)\vec u\); “Eulerian acceleration” should not imply the convective contribution disappears. The three small footprint ornaments in the introduction are represented by text symbols.


PDF page 556 — source_issue

10. altimeter : a device that measures altitude by measuring pressure and comparing to the standard atmosphere.

11. angle of attack : the angle that the chord line of an airfoil makes with the oncoming fluid flow.

12. angular momentum : the cross product of radial vector from an axis of rotation with linear momentum in the azimuthal direction.

13. anisotropic : having different properties depending on orientation in space.

14. ansatz : an educated guess that is verified later. Typically in fluid mechanics this is a simplifying approximation which is useful if a solution to the equations is possible following that approximation. Sometimes an ansatz facilitates an answer. Other times it leads nowhere and we abandon it. The ansatzes you see in textbooks are the ones that were helpful.

15. anticommutative : for a binary algebraic or calculus operation, having the property that when the order of operands is switched, the result changes sign.

16. anticorrelated : two quantities are anticorrelated when the integral of their product sums to a negative number. If this integral is performed over time, the quantities are temporally anticorrelated. If over space the quantitites are spatially anticorrelated.

17. antinode : the location in space where an oscillation has maximum amplitude. Cf. node.

18. antisymmetric : for a tensor or matrix, retains magnitude but changes sign upon permutation of any two indices. For a dyadic element, means that if the dyad is switched (i.e., \(xy\) for \(yx\)), that the value changes but not magnitude. For a 2D matrix, means changes sign upon flipping over the diagonal.

19. antitorque pedals : pedals that control the pitch angle of the tail rotor of a helicopter, controlling by how much the main rotor torque is counteracted by the tail rotor.

20. antitranspose : for a dyadic tensor or a matrix, means that the index order is switched (i.e., \(yz\) for \(zy\)) and the result is multiplied by —1.

21. Archimedes’ principle : the principle of buoyancy that an object immersed in fluid feels a buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid.

22. area–Mach-number relation: the relation \(\frac A{A^*}=\frac1M\left[\frac2{\gamma+1}\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}2M^2\right)\right]^{\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}}\), which shows how the cross-sectional area of any region of a nozzle divided by the area of the throat prescribes what the local Mach number must be.

23. area–velocity relation: the relation \(\frac1A\frac{dA}{ds}=(M^2-1)\frac1U\frac{dU}{ds}\), which shows how the shape of a nozzle accelerates or decelerates a fluid.

24. areal : related to area, or per unit area.

25. associative : for algebraic or calculus expressions with two or more operations, having the property that the result is the same regardless of which operation is executed first.

26. atomistic : means related to atoms i.e., indivisible objects. Used in fluid mechanics to describe analysis that resolves individual atom or molecule motion and interaction. Compare with continuum.

27. attached : describing a flow locally, means having a velocity on the surface that runs parallel to the surface and has no stagnation point. Describing a flow globally, means the flow has no separation point associated with flow moving upstream.

28. attached flow: locally, means flow that runs parallel to a surface and has no stagnation point. Globally, means flow has no separation point associated with flow moving upstream.

29. axial-flow pump : a dynamic pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it axially with an impeller. These pumps look approximately like fans or propellers located inside a tube. Typically has high specific speed.

Transcription note: The numerator of the exponent in entry 22 is erased. \(\gamma+1\) is an editorial restoration of the isentropic area–Mach relation, not a fully visible glyph. Here \(A^*\) is the critical sonic area; it equals the geometrical throat area when that throat is sonic. A given area ratio can have subsonic and supersonic solutions.

Editorial qualifications: Anticorrelation normally refers to a negative covariance of deviations from their means; an uncentered product integral alone is insufficient. Attached flow can include a stagnation point, and no-slip velocity is zero at a stationary wall; entries 27–28 describe outer-flow behavior too loosely.


PDF page 557 — source_issue

30. axial-flow turbomachine : a turbomachine in which the flow path of the fluid at the point of energy transfer is primarily in the axial direction relative to the rotary element.

31. axially symmetric: independent of \(\theta\).

32. azimuthal: related to the angle \(\theta\) (cylindrical coordinates) or \(\vartheta\) (spherical coordinates); in both cases, the angle away from the \(x\) axis in the \(xy\) plane toward the \(y\) axis.

33. ballistic : moving as a projectile (i.e., like a ball) under the influence of gravity only.

34. bathymeter : a device that senses depth underwater by measuring pressure.

35. bar: a unit of pressure: \(1\ \mathrm{bar}=1\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\).

36. barometer : a special case of a manometer. A device that measures ambient pressure by measuring the height of a column of liquid.

37. beam : for a boat, a measure of the width of the hull at the widest point.

38. Bernoulli constant: the constant \(B\) in the Bernoulli equation \(B=p+\frac12\rho u^2+\rho gz\). A measure of the energy per unit volume of the fluid. Synonymous with total pressure.

39. Bernoulli equation: in differential form \(0=\frac d{d\ell}(p+\frac12\rho u^2+\rho gz)\), in integral form: \(B=p+\frac12\rho u^2+\rho gz\), where \(B\) is the Bernoulli constant. Applies to a path along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and to any path if the flow is irrotational.

40. Bernoulli integral: the integral form of the Bernoulli equation: \(B=p+\frac12\rho u^2+\rho gz\), where \(B\) is a constant for flow along a streamline if viscosity is neglected, and \(B\) is uniform throughout an irrotational flow domain.

41. binormal : the binormal direction is the direction normal to both the tangent and normal to a curve, given by the cross product of the tangent to the normal.

42. blade : a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes. Roughly synonymous with airfoil, hydrofoil, wing, and vane. Often chosen over the word vane when the blade is rotating in a turbomachine.

43. blower : an enclosed turbomachine that adds energy to a gas, usually air, primarily for the purpose of fluid motion. The term blower is typically used for enclosed systems, whereas the term fan is typically used for open systems. Blowers have a high pump specific speed whereas gas compressors have a lower pump specific speed. The equivalent turbomachine driving a liquid would be called a pump.

44. bluff body : an object with a blunt trailing edge whose drag is dominated by pressure drag. Contrast with airfoil or streamlined body.

45. bluff bodies : objects with blunt trailing edges whose drag is dominated by pressure drag. Contrast with airfoil or streamlined body.

46. body force : a force that acts directly upon all of the mass within a control volume. Examples include gravity and electromagnetic forces. These forces act directly (gravity) or indirectly (electromagnetics) over lengths much longer than molecular diameters. Compare to surface force.

47. boundary condition : a mathematical prescription of the conditions on flow parameters (e.g., \(\vec u\) or \(p\)) at the boundary of a fluid.

48. boundary layer : a thin layer of fluid near a boundary in which the conservation of momentum equation is simplified because of the nearly unidirectional flow parallel to the surface.

49. boundary-layer equations : simplified equations for flow near a wall derived by assuming flow is primarily along the wall and velocity gradients are primarily normal to the wall.

50. boundary-layer thickness : the thickness of the thin boundary layer of fluid near a boundary in which the governing equation is simplified because of the nearly unidirectional flow parallel to the surface. Can be defined in multiple ways, but in this class we define the boundary-layer thickness \(\delta\) as the distance from the surface at which the fluid is moving at 99% of the speed of the freestream.

Editorial qualification: These Bernoulli expressions assume steady, constant-density flow and conservative gravity. Stagnation (total) pressure is usually \(p+\frac12\rho U^2\), whereas the Bernoulli constant here also includes gravitational potential per volume \(\rho gz\).


PDF page 558 — source_issue

51. Bourdon tube : a coiled, flattened tube which extends upon pressurization and can be used to generate a mechanical pressure gauge.

52. bow shock : the curved shock seen in front of a bluff body in a supersonic flow..

53. Boyle’s Law: the ideal gas relation \(PV=k\) at constant temperature.

54. brake horsepower : equivalent to brake power. Measure of power produced at the shaft of a motor. 1 hp = 746 W.

55. bucket : a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes, typically in an impulse turbine. Functionally synonymous with airfoil, hydrofoil, wing, and vane, but used when the surface is roughly hemispherical.

56. Buckingham Pi theorem: a theorem stating that an equation written in \(n\) physical variables based on \(r\) fundamental physical dimensions can be rewritten in terms of \(n-r\) dimensionless parameters.

57. bulk modulus: a description of the static compressibility of a fluid in terms of its equation of state. Denoted \(\kappa\) and described by \(\kappa=\rho\,dp/d\rho\).

58. bulk viscosity : a measure of fluid resistance to being expanded and compressed. For Newtonian fluids, proportional to the ratio of the fluid stress to fluid strain rate. Not used in MAE3230.

59. buoyancy : the force opposing gravity felt by an object immersed in a fluid, caused by the nonuniform hydrostatic pressure distribution.

60. calibrated leak : a porous material or capillary tube designed to give a calibrated flow rate that is proportional to the pressure difference across it. Mathematically equivalent to a hydraulic resistance.

61. calorically perfect: having specific heats that are not a function of temperature, i.e., \(e=c_vT\) and \(h=c_pT\).

62. camber : the curvature of the chord line of an airfoil.

63. capacity : term used in the fluids engineering and turbomachine literature, synonymous with volumetric flowrate \(Q\).

64. capacity coefficient: the nondimensional coefficient \(C_Q=Q/(fD^3)\). It nondimensionalizes the flowrate (i.e., capacity) of a turbomachine by a factor proportional to the swept volume of the spinning rotor impeller/runner.

65. carburetor : a device that mixes fuel and air by passing the air through a Venturi to create a low-pressure region which sucks liquid fuel from a reservoir into the flow. Common in small engines e.g., chainsaws, lawn equipment, motorcycles.

66. Cartesian : for a vector or coordinate system: fixed, orthogonal, and right-handed.

67. Cartesian coordinate : a fixed, orthogonal, right-handed coordinate system e.g., \(xyz\).

68. casing : an enclosure. In a fluids context, usually an enclosure that contains the rotary elements of a turbomachine. Synonymous with housing.

69. cavitate: to transition in phase from liquid to gas. Physically identical to boil, but we use boil when the cause is increased temperature and cavitate when the cause is decreased pressure.

70. cavitation: phase transition from liquid to gas. Physically identical to boiling, but we use boiling when the cause is increased temperature and cavitation when the cause is decreased pressure.

71. center of buoyancy: the point around which the net buoyancy force of a body generates no torque.

72. center of gravity : for uniform gravitational fields, typically used to mean center of mass, specifically in context to mean the point around which the gravitational force of a body generates no torque independent of orientation.

73. center of mass : the arithmetic mean position of the mass of a body.

Transcription note: Several mathematical glyphs are erased: the minus in \(n-r\), most of \(e=c_vT\), and the equals and division signs in \(C_Q=Q/(fD^3)\). These are restored from their definitions and corresponding earlier formulas; the source is not fully legible here.

Editorial corrections: Camber is the curvature of the mean camber line; the chord line is straight. The center of mass is the mass-weighted mean position \(\int\vec r\,dm/\int dm\), not an unweighted average of arbitrary spatial sample points. Calorically perfect relations can include reference-energy constants; the displayed forms choose zero reference constants.


PDF page 559 — source_issue

74. centrifugal : pointing away from the center of a circular arc.

75. centrifugal pump: a pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it centrifugally with an impeller, then decelerating it through a volute. Typically has low specific speed.

76. centripetal : pointing toward the center of a circular arc.

77. centroid : the arithmetic mean position of the volume of a body.

78. chain rule: if \(F(x)=f[g(x)]\), \(F'(x)=g'(x)f'[g(x)]\).

79. characteristic area: an area chosen to be representative of a geometry, often as part of nondimensionalization.

80. characteristic length: a length chosen to be representative of a geometry, often as part of nondimensionalization.

81. check valve : a valve that allows flow in one direction but not the other.

82. choke : as a verb, means to restrict. In a supersonic nozzle context, choke is used to specifically mean to restrict flow through a sonic throat. As a noun or adjective in choke valve, refers to a valve that restricts intake airflow but allows fuel flow, used to make a very rich intake mixture often needed to start a cold engine.

83. choked : when describing flow or a nozzle, meaning that the system is in a flow regime in which the mass flow rate and flow properties upstream of the nozzle throat are unaffected by the ambient pressure and exhaust conditions.

84. choked flow : a flow regime in which the mass flow rate and flow properties upstream of the nozzle throat are unaffected by the ambient pressure and exhaust conditions.

85. chord : a straight line connecting the leading and trailing edges of an airfoil.

86. clutch : a mechanical device that engages and disengages power transmission through a frictional or viscous contact.

87. circulation: a measure of the total flow rotation in a closed region. Given by the line integral around a closed clockwise contour \(\mathcal C\) of the velocity field: \(\Gamma=\int_{\mathcal C}\vec u\,ds\). If the region is filled with fluid, circulation is related by Stokes’ theorem to the area integral of the vorticity in the enclosed area.

88. Coandă effect : the tendency of a jet to turn towards a wall parallel to the jet owing to a negative pressure region in the entrainment zone.

89. colatitudinal: related to the angle \(\phi\), i.e., the angle from the \(z\) axis toward the \(xy\) plane. Complementary to latitudinal angle, like latitude in geography, which is the angle from the \(xy\) plane toward the \(z\) axis.

90. collective control : control of a helicopter’s lift magnitude, coming from control of all of the rotor blade rotation-independent angle of attacks .

91. collimated : moving parallel, in a straight line.

92. combustor: an area in which fuel is burned, typically to generate pressure and temperature that can be used to do work. Synonymous with combustion chamber.

93. commutative : for a binary algebraic or calculus operation, having the property that the result is the same regardless of the order of operands.

94. commute : two operators commute if they can be applied in any order and the result is the same.

95. compliance : measure of non-rigidity of a system, mathematically described as a change of system volume upon changing pressure. Zero for systems of rigid containers holding incompressible fluids.

96. compressible : when describing a fluid, means density changes with pressure. All fluids are compressible. When describing a flow, means density changes enough in the flow that density changes must be considered in the conservation of mass equation.

Editorial correction: Scalar circulation requires the tangential projection: \(\Gamma=\oint_{\mathcal C}\vec u\cdot d\vec s=\oint_{\mathcal C}\vec u\cdot\hat t\,ds\). Entry87 prints \(\vec u\,ds\) without that projection. Clockwise orientation is a sign convention; Stokes’ normal must follow the right-hand rule (into the page for a clockwise contour viewed on the page). The partly erased colatitude symbol in entry89 is restored as \(\phi\), the convention used in Appendix B.


PDF page 560 — source_issue

97. compressible flow : implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to change significantly in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Cf. incompressible flow.

98. compressor : an enclosed turbomachine that adds energy to a gas, usually air, primarily for the purpose of increasing its pressure. gas compressors have a low pump specific speed whereas fans and blowers have higher pump specific speeds. The equivalent turbomachine driving a liquid would be called a pump.

99. concavity: second derivative of a property with respect to a coordinate. Different from curvature, which is a function of both first and second derivatives.

100. conservation of energy : the notion that energy is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

101. conservation of mass : the notion that mass is neither created nor destroyed, absent nuclear reactions.

102. conservation of momentum : the notion that changes in momentum are brought about by forces as prescribed by Newton’s second law.

103. constant : used as a noun, means a mathematical constant which is a fixed and defined number, in contrast with a variable. Used as an adjective, means unchanging with time. Compare to the adjective uniform, which means unchanging in space.

104. constitutive : relating two properties of a material. For example viscosity relates stress to strain rate and thermal conductivity relates temperature gradient to heat flux.

105. constitutive relation : a relation between physical quantities that is specific to a material. In fluid mechanics, this is typically the constitutive relation for viscosity.

106. contact angle : the angle, measured through the dense fluid, that an interface makes with a solid surface.

107. continuity : when used to modify a field (e.g., “velocity continuity” or “pressure continuity”), this is a mathematical term that typically means that the field is continuous, and often used to indicate that a field has the same value on both sides of an interface. When used alone, this is a physical term which typically means “conservation of mass”. When used as continuity equation, synonymous with “conservation of mass equation”.

108. continuity equation : synonymous with “conservation of mass equation”.

109. continuum : a physical domain whose properties are differentiable. Contrast with atomistic.

110. continuum hypothesis : the hypothesis that fluids are well approximated as continua even though we know they are composed of atoms/molecules.

111. contraction coefficient : the ratio of the area of a free jet issuing from an orifice to the area of the orifice itself.

112. control mass : a mass element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular volume. Synonymous with system.

113. control surface : the surface that encloses a control volume.

114. control volume : a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass. Compare to system, which is an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass.

115. control-volume : (adjective) related to a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass.

Editorial correction: Energy remains conserved in nuclear reactions when mass-energy is included. The “absent nuclear reactions” qualification in entry100 belongs to a nonrelativistic mass-conservation approximation, not to total energy conservation.


PDF page 561 — source_issue

116. convection : in fluid mechanics, convection is typically synonymous with advection, meaning transport of a property based on bulk fluid motion, distinguished from viscous transport of momentum. In MAE3240, though, convection heat transfer will mean total transport including both fluid motion and conduction. Just keeping you on your toes.

117. convective : in fluid mechanics, relating to transport caused by bulk fluid motion. In heat and mass transfer, relating to total transport in the presence of fluid motion, i.e., both convection and diffusion.

118. convergent-divergent nozzle : a nozzle in which the cross-section converges to a throat then diverges from the throat to the exhaust. Synonymous with converging—diverging nozzle or de Laval nozzle.

119. converging-diverging nozzle : a nozzle in which the cross-section converges to a throat then diverges from the throat to the exhaust. Synonymous with de Laval nozzle or convergent—divergent nozzle.

120. convex : for a wall bounding a fluid, having a center of curvature inside the boundary.

121. correlated : two zero-sum fluctuations are correlated when the integral of their product sums to a positive number. If this integral is performed over time, the quantities are temporally correlated. If over space the quantitites are spatially correlated.

122. Couette flow : pronounced KOO-ett. Flow between two infinite parallel plates.

123. creeping flow: flow in which \(Re\to0\). Synonymous with Stokes flow.

124. cross-correlation : given two fields, the cross-correlation measures how well the two fields are aligned with each other as a function of displacement.

125. cross product : given two vectors, a vector pointing in the direction normal to both of the two vectors and having the magnitude equal to the area of the parallelpiped formed by the two vectors.

126. cuboid : a three-dimensional object with six rectangular faces, all aligned at right angles.

127. cup : a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes, typically in an impulse turbine. Functionally synonymous with airfoil, hydrofoil, wing, and vane, but used when the surface is roughly hemispherical.

128. curl: the curl of \(\vec u\) is denoted \(\nabla\times\vec u\). The curl of \(\vec u\) describes the axis and rate of rotation of the fluid.

129. cyclic control : control of a helicopter’s lift angle, resulting from tilting of the rotor plane coming from sinusoidal variation of the rotor blade angle of attacks during blade rotation.

130. cylindrical: with reference to a coordinate system, refers to the coordinates \(r,\theta,z\).

131. dam : a wall that stops or restricts flow of surface water, e.g., rivers.

132. decay : the process by which a flow changes from steady-state motion to quiescence following the removal of pressure or the ceasing of boundary motion. Cf. startup. Alternatively, can be used to describe how a function decreases with distance from a point, usually a boundary.

133. decibel: a “unit” which describes the magnitude of an acoustic pressure variation (typically denoted sound pressure level SPL) to the reference pressure used as the limit of human hearing. \(\mathrm{SPL[dB]}=20\log_{10}\frac{p_a}{20\ \mu\mathrm{Pa}}\).

134. deformation : for fluid mechanics, we typically mean deformation rate, the rate at which parts of the fluid move relative to each other, exclusive of solid-body rotation or uniform translation.

135. de Laval nozzle : a nozzle in which the cross-section converges to a throat then diverges from the throat to the exhaust. Synonymous with converging–diverging nozzle or convergent—divergent nozzle.

136. density: denoted \(\rho\). Mass per unit volume.

137. depth gauge : device that measures depth underwater, usually by measuring pressure.

Editorial clarifications: Entry125’s “parallelpiped” should be parallelogram; the direction follows the right-hand rule. The local angular velocity equals half the curl, \(\vec\Omega=\tfrac12\nabla\times\vec u\). Couette flow specifically involves shear driven by relative wall motion. Sound pressure level uses RMS acoustic pressure with the standard airborne reference \(20\ \mu\mathrm{Pa}\).


PDF page 562 — source_issue

138. determinant: for a linear mapping defined by an \(n\)-dimensional matrix, the volume of the parallelotope that a cube maps to when transformed by the matrix. If the relevant linear mapping maps the position of elements of a fluid flow from one moment in time to a moment an infinitesimal time later (i.e., \([\vec{\vec I}+\nabla\vec u\,t]\)), the determinant of that linear mapping maps the expansion of the fluid. For small \(t\), this can be manipulated back to the identity that the trace of the velocity gradient tensor describes the rate of expansion of the fluid.

139. development: the process by which the flow in a tube changes from the inlet distribution to the distribution it would have in an infinitely long tube. Compare with startup.

140. development length : the length over which the flow in a tube changes from the inlet distribution to the distribution it would have in an infinitely long tube. .

141. deviatoric : what is left when the isotropic component is removed. An anisotropic tensor is the sum of its isotropic component and its deviatoric component.

142. differential : relating to how properties are changing locally as expressed by derivatives. Compare with integral, meaning related to finite differences evaluated over finite distances.

143. differential equation : an equation relating functions with their derivatives.

144. differential fluid element: A control volume or control mass of infinitesimal size such that properties in the element can be approximated by Taylor-series expansions around a central point.

145. diffusion : net movement of a property from a region of higher value to a region of lower value.

146. dilatation : synonymous with dilation or expansion. “Dilatation” is most often used in fluid mechanics.

147. dimensional analysis : a mode of analysis centered on using dimensional homogeneity to reduce the parameters needed to analyze a system.

148. dimensional homogeneity : the property of an equation such that all terms in the equation have the same units and dimensions.

149. dimensional similitude : the notion that two physical systems with different parameters can be shown to be similar if the relevant nondimensional parameters are equal.

150. directrix: a line used in generation of a curve. For a parabola, the parabola is the locus of points equidistant from the focus and the directrix.

151. discharge : the volume flow rate of a pump.

152. discharge coefficient : a measure of the flowrate observed through an orifice normalized by what would be predicted by the Bernoulli equation with no jet contraction.

153. displacement : in general, a distance. For a boat, the weight of the boat, usually measured by use of displacement volume.

154. displacement volume : the volume of water displaced by the submerged portion of a boat.

155. dissipation : in fluid mechanics, an irreversible process in which entropy is increased, and energy is converted from one form to another form that can do less mechanical work.

156. distributive : an operation that is distributive over another operation can be applied independently to the operands of the second operation. In algebra and calculus, usually the distributive property is used to refer to distribution over addition, meaning that an operation is described as distributive if it can be applied to the different parts of a sum.

157. divergence: the divergence of \(\vec u\) is denoted \(\nabla\cdot\vec u\). The divergence of \(\vec u\) describes the normalized expansion rate of the fluid.

158. divergence theorem: the divergence theorem, applied to a fluid velocity field: \(\int_{\mathcal V}\nabla\cdot\vec u\,dV=\int_{\mathcal S}\vec u\cdot\hat n\,dA\) indicates that the net outflow of fluid across a control surface is equal to the integral of the divergence of velocity over the control volume.

Editorial clarification: The determinant is a signed volume scale factor; its absolute value is the volume obtained from a unit cube. The infinitesimal map gives \(\det(I+t\nabla\vec u)=1+t\nabla\cdot\vec u+O(t^2)\). The equals sign in entry158 is erased and restored from the named divergence theorem.


PDF page 563 — source_issue

159. dot product : given two vectors, a scalar giving the magnitude of one vector multiplied by the orthogonal projection of the second onto the first. Given a dyadic and a vector, a vector resulting from the product of the magnitude of the vector and the orthogonal projection of the dyadic onto the plane defined normal to the vector.

160. doublet: an idealized point (in 2D) or line (in 3D) source of flow polarity. From the \(\lambda=1\) separation-of-variables solution of the Laplace equation.

161. downstream : in the direction of fluid motion.

162. downwash : the downward motion of air consistent with a lift-generating aerodynamic object, e.g., a wing or rotor.

163. draft : for a boat, the distance from the waterline to the bottom of the hull.

164. drag : the component of a force a fluid exerts on an immersed object that is tangent to the flow.

165. drag coefficient: a measure of the ability of a physical object to generate a force tangent to a flow passing over it. Defined by \(C_D=\frac{F_D}{\frac12\rho U^2A}\).

166. drag crisis : a point at which if the Reynolds number of a moving bluff body is increased, the drag decreases dramatically, owing to a transition from laminar to turbulent boundary layer leading to a boundary layer separation point located further downstream.

167. dyad: a fundamental element that describes two directions, e.g., \(\widehat{xz}\).

168. dyadic : a second-order tensor comprising a set of unit dyads.

169. dyadic product : given two vectors, a dyadic that encodes information related to two directions. In fluid mechanics, dyadics usually are flowfield properties that find use when they are orthogonally projected onto a plane (through the dot product with the normal vector) to generate a vector property at that plane, e.g., force or momentum flux.

170. dynamic : involving forces and accelerations.

171. dynamic head: given by \(H_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\bar U^2/(2g)\). The height a fluid could be pumped to if the kinetic energy of its mean speed were converted to gravitational potential energy. Synonymous with velocity head. Largely unrelated to total dynamic head.

172. dynamic pressure: Given by \(p_{\mathrm{dynamic}}=\tfrac12\rho U^2\). Denotes the added pressure a fluid would have if it were slowed isentropically to motionlessness. Equivalently, describes the volumetric kinetic energy of a fluid in terms of an equivalent pressure.

173. dynamic pump: a pump that increases fluid pressure by accelerating it with an impeller, then decelerating it to increase pressure.

174. dynamic range : the range of values over which a sensor or measurement can be applied.

175. dynamic similitude : the notion that the dynamics of two physical systems are fundamentally the same if all of its nondimensional parameters are the same, allowing us to study systems through experiments at different (and more convenient) conditions.

176. dynamic viscosity : a measure of fluid resistance to being deformed. For Newtonian fluids, proportional to the ratio of the fluid stress to fluid strain rate.

177. dynamically similar : having identical dynamics when properly nondimensionalized.

178. efficiency : when describing a turbomachine, the useful work generated normalized by the work inputted.

179. eigenfunction : a function that satisfies a homogeneous differential equation and can thus be summed to satisfy initial and/or boundary conditions.

Transcription note: The equal signs in the dynamic-head and dynamic-pressure definitions are erased. They are restored from the definitions; the mean-speed bar on \(\bar U\) in entry171 is visible.

Editorial qualifications: Dynamic pressure equals the stagnation-pressure increment only under the incompressible approximation; compressible isentropic stagnation pressure has a different relation. An eigenfunction satisfies \(L[f]=\lambda f\) with the relevant boundary conditions; the broader statement in entry179 describes homogeneous linear solution superposition, not a complete eigenfunction definition.


PDF page 564 — source_issue

180. elliptic: for a 2D PDE of form \(A\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+B\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x\partial y}+C\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}+D\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+E\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+Fu+G\), one where \(B^2-4AC<0\). Corresponds to physical phenomena (e.g., diffusion) in which information propagates infinitely fast and a change in the system in one place affects all other places simultaneously.

181. enthalpy: sum of internal energy and work of compression. Per unit mass i.e., specific enthalpy, denoted \(h=e+p/\rho\).

182. entrain : to pull in and carry along in a flow of fluid.

183. entropy : measure of irreversibility of a system. Increased by dissipative processes such as viscosity and shock waves.

184. envelope : with respect to a family of curves, the envelope is a single curve that is tangent to each member of the family.

185. equality of mixed partials: the notion that taking partial derivatives of a function with respect to one coordinate then a second coordinate is equivalent to taking the partial derivatives in the opposite order, e.g.,: \(\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x\partial y}=\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial y\partial x}\).

186. equation of state: an equation that governs the relationship between \(\rho,p,\) and \(T\) for a fluid.

187. equations of motion : in fluid mechanics, the (usually dynamic) equations that govern motion of a fluid element.

188. equilibrium : a state in which forces are balanced.

189. Eulerian : a means of defining a frame of reference based on a control volume.

190. Euler equations: pronounced OY-ler. The inviscid conservation of momentum equations. Can be written in streamline coordinates (\(\frac{dB}{ds}=0,\ \frac{dk}{dn}=-\frac{\rho U^2}{R},\ \frac{dk}{d\ell}=0\)) or fixed coordinates (\(\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\rho\vec g\)).

191. expansion : in a thermodynamic or bubble-blowing context, an increase in volume. In a compressible-flow context, reduction in pressure associated with decreasing density and increasing specific volume. In a nozzle context, reduction in pressure to generate speed and thrust.

192. expansion fan : also known as a Prandtl–Meyer expansion fan. An infinite set of Mach waves that isentropically turn and accelerate a supersonic flow around a convex corner. Cf. oblique shock.

193. extensive : describing properties that depend on the extent of a system, for example mass or energy. Distinguished from intensive, which is independent of extent, for example density or energy per unit volume.

194. external flow : the inlet to a centrifugal pump, aligned along its axis.

195. eye : the inlet of a centrifugal pump, located along the axis of rotation of the impeller.

196. fan : an enclosed turbomachine that adds energy to a gas, usually air, primarily for the purpose of fluid motion. The term fan is typically used for open systems, whereas the term blower is typically used for enclosed systems. Fans have a high pump specific speed whereas gas compressors have a lower pump specific speed. The equivalent turbomachine driving a liquid would be called a pump.

197. favorable pressure gradient : a pressure gradient in which the pressure decreases in the downstream direction. Notable because it helps flow remain attached.

198. field property : a property that varies spatially and is described by a field.

199. float valve : a valve mechanically connected to a float, such that when a reservoir fills and the float is raised, the valve switches. Often used to keep a reservoir filled to a steady height, as in a toilet tank or a carburetor float-feed chamber.

200. flow coefficient: in hydraulics, a measure of the flow rate normalized by the square root of the pressure drop: \(C_v=Q\sqrt{SG/\Delta B}\). Typically reported in \(\mathrm{gpm}/\sqrt{\mathrm{psi}}\).

Editorial corrections: Entry194 accidentally defines a pump’s eye. External flow means flow around a body rather than inside a duct. Entry180’s elliptic classification describes a spatial boundary-value equation; time-dependent diffusion is parabolic, while steady diffusion can be elliptic. Equality of mixed partials requires sufficient regularity (for example continuous second partials). The streamline form in entry190 additionally assumes steady flow, constant density, and the book’s inward-normal convention.


PDF page 565 — source_issue

201. flow factor: in hydraulics, a measure of the flow rate normalized by the square root of the pressure drop: \(K_v=Q\sqrt{SG}\,\Delta B\). Typically reported in \(\mathrm{m^3/hr}/\sqrt{\mathrm{bar}}\).

202. flowrate : the rate at which a property flows across a surface. Equivalently, the integral of the flux of a property over the surface.

203. fluid element: we use the term fluid element to mean a specified mass of fluid i.e., a system. A fluid element can be finite or infinitesimal.

204. fluid machine : a machine that adds energy to or extracts energy from a fluid.

205. flux: in fluid mechanics, flux is defined as rate of flow of a property per unit area across a surface. flux is defined differently in other physical fields and in mathematics.

206. force coefficient: a general coefficient to normalize force, normally \(C_f=F/(\tfrac12\rho U^2A)\).

207. fore-aft symmetry : having fluid properties (velocity, pressure) that are the same on the upstream side of the object as they are on the downstream side. Possible only in irrotational flow or Stokes flow.

208. form drag : the component of fluid force on an object that (a) is in the direction of flow and (b) is explained by only the pressure distribution on the surface of the object. Synonymous with pressure drag.

209. frame of reference : WHEN IN DOUBT, ASK DMITRY SAVRANSKY.

210. Francis turbine : a reaction turbine with radial or mixed flow and low turbine specific speed, suitable for extracting energy over a high pressure drop. The turbine analog of a centrifugal pump.

211. free jet : a jet emanating from an orifice whose pressure is assumed to be equal to the environment.

212. freestream : used in two ways to describe flows around objects i.e., external flows. In specifying a problem, the freestream value of a quantity (usually \(\vec u\) or \(p\)) is the quantity infinitely far away from the object. In discussing the boundary layer adjacent to the object, freestream means the value just outside the boundary layer, which is often not equal to the value infinitely far from the object.

213. friction factor: a nondimensional coefficient used to characterize drop of the Bernoulli constant (and thus typically pressure) in a pipe. Two common “friction” factors are used: the Fanning “friction” factor and the Darcy “friction” factor. In this class we use the Darcy “friction” factor \(f_D=\frac{\Delta B}{\frac12\rho U^2}\frac dL\) and call it the viscous dissipation factor. “Friction” is a misnomer here, or at best a metaphor. There is no such thing as friction in a fluid.

214. Froude number: a nondimensional coefficient used to characterize the relation between flow speed and surface wave speed: \(Fr=U/\sqrt{gh}\).

215. fuel injector : a device that injects fuel directly into a combusion chamber, usually with a spray atomizer.

216. fully developed : far enough from an inlet or exit such that the flow mimics that of an infinitely long channel.

217. fulcrum : the pivot point of a lever.

218. full-slip condition : a dynamic condition specifying that the normal derivative of velocity tangent to a solid surface or interface is zero. Equivalent to saying that fluid, at molecular level, feels no force at the surface/interface and slides by unaffected. This is never really the case, but this is a good approximation for liquids at interfaces with gases, and this is what is mathematically implied by the use of an irrotational flow analysis near a wall.

219. fuselage : the main body of an aircraft.

220. gallon per minute: unit of volumetric flow rate. Nonstandard but ubiquitous in pump sizing so... get used to it. abbreviated gpm. \(1\ \mathrm{gpm}=6.3\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^3/s}\).

221. gas constant: the constant \(R\) in the ideal gas law \(p=\rho RT\). 287 J/kgK for air..

Editorial corrections: Entry201 prints \(Q\sqrt{SG}\,\Delta B\); the flow-factor definition requires \(K_v=Q\sqrt{SG/\Delta B}\), with pressure drop inside the denominator of the square root. Entry220 has the wrong exponent sign: one US gallon per minute is approximately \(6.3\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}\), not \(10^5\).

Editorial qualification: Full slip means zero tangential traction, not zero total surface force. On a flat impermeable boundary this can reduce to a zero normal derivative of tangential velocity; curved surfaces require curvature terms. Pressure can still exert a normal force.


PDF page 566 — source_issue

222. gas turbine : a turbine that extracts energy from a gas with significant attendant density change. Typically, gas turbine implies that a combustion chamber in the same housing is generating the high-energy gas that drives the turbine. If the turbine were driven by vapor it would be a steam turbine. If by naturally occurring gas motion it would be a wind turbine. If driven by liquid it would be a hydrodynamic turbine.

223. gauge oil : a (typically red-colored) oil that is chemically inert with low vapor pressure and low density. Used for sensitive manometry.

224. gauge pressure : pressure difference relative to atmospheric pressure.

225. gear pump: a positive-displacement pump that moves fluids through interlocking gears.

226. gimbal : a pivoted support that permits rotation of an object about an axis.

227. governing equation : a catchall for any equation that describes a physical process. In mechanical engineering, this often means conservation equations such as those for mass, momentum, and energy. These can be solved when coupled with boundary conditions.

228. gradient: the gradient of a property \(\vec u\) is symbolized by \(\nabla\vec u\). It denotes the direction(s) in which the property or its components are changing, as well as the magnitude of the spatial derivative in that direction. \(\nabla\vec u\) has tensor order one higher than \(\vec u\).

229. gradient-field theorem: the gradient field theorem applied to a scalar field [formula largely erased] indicates that the surface integral of a scalar is equal to the volume integral of its gradient.

230. gravitational acceleration: acceleration due to gravity. Denoted as a vector \(\vec g\) or its magnitude \(g\). By our convention, we take \(g\) positive pointing downward.

231. gravitational potential energy: potential energy that fluid has relative to a reference height \(z_0\): \(\int_{\mathcal V}\rho g(z-z_0)\,dV\).

232. grease : usually oil emulsified with a soap or detergent. Grease is often designed to be shear-thinning, i.e., its viscosity drops when it is sheared, so it is solid or highly viscous but when sheared in a bearing it does not generate alot of resistance to rotation.

233. Hagen–Poiseuille law: the relation for laminar flow through a long, straight tube (\(\Delta p=QR_h\)). Analogous to Ohm’s law for current through a resistor.

234. harmonic : in the context of frequencies, a harmonic is a frequency which is an integral multiple of a fundamental frequency. Cf. overtone.

235. head: a quantity (e.g., static head \(H\equiv\frac p{\rho g}\) or total head \(H\equiv\frac p{\rho g}+\frac{U^2}{2g}+z\)) in units of length that communicates energy per unit volume or, equivalently, pressure of a fluid. It describes the height of a hypothetical fluid that would generate a hydrostatic gauge pressure at its bottom equal to the static pressure or total pressure in the fluid under discussion.

236. head coefficient: the coefficient \(C_H=\Delta p/(\rho f^2D^2)\). It normalizes the pressure difference generated by a turbomachine by a factor proportional to the dynamic pressure of fluid moving at the blade tip. Or equivalently, normalizes the head difference generated by a turbomachine by a factor proportional to the dynamic head at the blade tip.

237. head loss: the dissipation of mechanical energy to work, written in terms of height change of a fluid that would lead to an equivalent loss of gravitational potential energy per unit volume: \(\Delta H\equiv\frac{\Delta p}{\rho g}+\frac12\Delta(U^2)+\Delta z)\).

238. heuristic :as a noun, an approach to problem-solving involving searching for an immediate, approximate, informal, non-rigorous, or trial-and-error solution. As an adjective, having the property of being immediate, approximate, or non-rigorous.

239. homogeneous : with reference to an equation, means there is no constant term. With reference to a fluid property, means uniform.

Transcription note: Entry229’s formula is too erased to identify all glyphs. The correct gradient theorem is \(\int_{\mathcal V}\nabla\phi\,dV=\int_{\mathcal S}\phi\hat n\,dA\), which includes the outward normal on the surface. Faded equals/division signs and denominator powers in entries233/236 are restored from the named resistance and head-coefficient definitions.

Editorial correction: Entry237 omits \(1/g\) from the speed-change term and prints an unmatched closing parenthesis. The dimensional head change is \(\Delta H=\Delta p/(\rho g)+\Delta(U^2)/(2g)+\Delta z\), with signs set by the chosen upstream/downstream convention. Dissipation converts mechanical energy to internal energy; it is not useful work output.


PDF page 567 — source_issue

240. hose : a type of pipe that is usually flexible, designated by inside diameter, and normally fitted by a stretching it over a rigid surface e.g., a hose barb. Cf. tube, pipe.

241. housing : an enclosure. In a fluids context, usually an enclosure that contains the rotary elements of a turbomachine. Synonymous with casing.

242. hydraulic : related to flow of fluid through pipes. Often implies liquids, in contrast to pneumatic, which implies gases.

243. hydraulic coverage chart: a \(\Delta p_0\)–\(Q\) chart showing the high-efficiency regions of a family of dynamic pumps.

244. hydraulic jump : a sharp increase in the depth of a fluid observed when the upstream fluid velocity is larger than the shallow-water wavespeed of the downstream fluid. Typically seen in dam spillways and rivers.

245. hydraulic radius : a characteristic length, which is the property of a 2D pipe cross-section and analogous to the radius of a circle, that describes the cross-section’s resistance to laminar pressure-driven flow.

246. hydraulic resistance : a linear hydraulic circuit element that allows a flow rate linearly proportional to the pressure drop across it, or the property itself. In electronics, there is an element called a resistor which has the property of resistance. In fluid mechanics, the element and its property are usually both described with the word resistance.

247. hydrodynamic turbine : a turbine that extracts energy from a fluid (usually a liquid) without significant density change. Cf. gas turbine or steam turbine.

248. hydrofoil : a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes. Roughly synonymous with blade, airfoil, wing, and vane. Often chosen over the word airfoil when the fluid is water. Often chosen over the word vane when mounted on a boat or submarine.

249. hydrostatic constant: the constant \(k\) in the hydrostatic equation \(p+\rho gz=k\).

250. hydrostatic equation: in differential form, \(\partial p/\partial z=-\rho g\). In integral form, \(p+\rho gz=k\).

251. hydrostatic : relating to fluids at rest.

252. hydrostatics : the study of fluids at rest.

253. ideal fluid: A theoretical fluid with zero viscosity; such a fluid does not in practice exist. Not equivalent to the term ideal gas, which, in contrast, is a description of an equation of state.

254. ideal gas: A gas with negligible intermolecular interaction. Also called perfect gas or dilute gas. Describes the gas’s equation of state \(p=\rho RT\). Not equivalent to ideal fluid, which, in contrast, describes a constitutive relation.

255. ideal-gas law: \(p=\rho RT\). An equation of state for ideal gases i.e., perfect gases i.e., dilute gases that have little intermolecular interaction. \(T\) and \(p\) are absolute temperature and pressure.

256. ideally expanded : referring to a nozzle or the jet that comes out of the nozzle: means that the pressure of the exhaust is the same as the ambient, so that there are no oblique shocks or expansion fans.

257. impulse turbine: a turbine in which the driving fluid interacts primarily only with the vanes/blades/etc. Cf. reaction turbine, which is fully immersed in the driving fluid.

258. impeller : a rotating airfoil used to trasfer energy from a driveshaft to fluid, typically to generate a pressure jump in a confined duct or volute casing. Compare with propeller.

259. impeller trim : the outer diameter of an impeller.

260. impoundment: the water held back by a dam. If the water is used for drinking or irrigation, it is ofter referred to as a reservoir. From the standpoint of local geography, it is often, called a lake.

Editorial clarification: The integrated hydrostatic form assumes constant \(\rho\) and \(g\), with \(z\) upward. The hydraulic radius is a geometric scale, not an exact universal predictor of laminar resistance for different cross-sectional shapes. The conventional hydraulic radius is \(A/P_{\mathrm{wetted}}\); earlier book pages use a radius-like \(2A/P\). Faded equals signs in the ideal-gas formulas are restored from their definitions.


PDF page 568 — source_issue

261. incompressible : with respect to a flow, implies physically that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations, and is not perturbed by the fluid’s acceleration and deceleration. With respect to a fluid, denotes that the density of the fluid is a mathematical constant.

262. incompressible flow : implies that the density of the fluid may be assumed to be a constant in the convective terms of the conservation of mass and conservation of momentum equations. Incompressible flow implies that the motion of the fluid does not cause density to change, in comparison to compressible flow in which fluid moves so quickly and the pressure changes so much that the density is perturbed enough to affect convective fluxes. Incompressible flows may still have nonuniform density, for example if the fluid’s temperature varies; this can affect the conservation of momentum equations. An incompressible flow does not imply that the fluid is mathematically incompressible, only that pressure-induced compression can be ignored. Cf. compressible flow.

263. incompressible fluid : an incompressible fluid is a mathematical idealization of a fluid whose density does not vary with pressure.

264. indicated airspeed : the air speed that, if the density were that at sea level, would correspond to the measured dynamic pressure from a Pitot—static tube.

265. inertia : the resistance to acceleration exhibited by objects with mass. In a fluid mechanical context, fluid inertia is often invoked to explain why fluid moving in one direction will continue moving in that direction. Often used to explain separation at sharp corners.

266. inertial : related to the resistance to acceleration exhibited by objects with mass. In a fluid-mechanical context, inertial implies that fluid momentum and fluid pressure are important and viscosity is not.

267. inertial reference frame : non-accelerating reference frame i.e., a frame of reference where a body experiencing no force exhibits no acceleration.

268. integral : as an adjective, relating to the finite difference between two discrete states (e.g. point 1 to point 2) or the integrated effect of something over a finite distance or volume. Compare with differential, meaning related to derivatives.

269. integrand: the expression that is integrated in an integral; in the integral \(\int f(x)\,dx\), the integrand is \(f(x)\).

270. integral governing equation : a governing equation applied to a finite volume or two discrete states (e.g., point 1 to point 2).

271. intensive : describing properties that do not depend on the extent of a system, for example density or energy per unit volume. Distinguished from extensive, which is dependent on extent, for example mass or energy.

272. interior angle: the ordinary angle \(0\le\theta\le\pi\) between two nonzero vectors when arranged tail to tail.

273. internal flow : flow contained inside a finite boundary whose boundary conditions are inlet and outlet conditions combined with specifications at the walls.

274. inviscid: a property of a flow meaning having no net volumetric viscous force, typically because the flow is irrotational or because viscous effects don’t significantly affect the net result of an analysis. Inviscid does not mean a fluid that has \(\mu=0\); in practice there is no such thing.

275. inviscid flow: A flow in which viscous effects can be neglected. Often means irrotational flow, which means \(\nabla^2\phi=0\) and therefore \(\mu\nabla^2\vec u=0\), so there is no net volumetric viscous force. Often means a high-\(Re\) flow in which the viscous effects are confined to boundary layers that do not significantly affect the flow. Does not mean \(\mu=0\).

276. irrotational: not rotating, i.e., \(\vec\omega=\nabla\times\vec u=0\).

277. irrotational flow: flow in which \(\vec\omega=\nabla\times\vec u=0\). The terms irrotational flow (\(\vec\omega=0\)) and potential flow (\(\vec u=\nabla\phi\)) are synonymous—one implies the other.

Transcription note: Entry269’s integral and entry272’s inequality symbols are largely erased. The integral is restored from the stated integrand, and the standard inclusive interior-angle range is an explicit reconstruction; the scan cannot distinguish strict from inclusive signs. Faded curl/equality glyphs in entry277 are restored from the clear identical definition in276.

Editorial qualification: The Laplace-potential conclusion in275 assumes incompressibility. A curl-free field has a potential locally; a globally single-valued potential requires appropriate domain topology.


PDF page 569 — source_issue

278. isentropic : without increase in entropy. In a fluid system, this means no conduction of heat, no viscous transfer of momentum, and no shock waves.

279. isobar : a curve along which pressure is uniform.

280. isobaric : having uniform pressure.

281. isocontour : a curve along which a property is uniform.

282. isopotential : a curve along which the velocity potential is uniform.

283. isotherm : a curve along which temperature is uniform.

284. isothermal : having uniform temperature.

285. isotropic : equivalent in all directions.

286. jet: fluid emanating from an orifice that is coherent and directional and defined primarily by its integrated momentum flux.

287. Kaplan turbine : a propeller turbine with mostly or all axial flow and a relatively low specific speed, suitable for extracting energy over a low pressure drop. Kaplan turbines are a specific propeller turbine design with adjustable blades for operation over a wide range of operating conditions.

288. keel : the bottom-most part of a boat’s hull.

289. kinematic : related to the motion of objects without consideration of forces.

290. kinematics : the study of the motion of objects without consideration of forces.

291. kinematic viscosity: defined as \(\nu=\mu/\rho\). A measure of momentum diffusivity of a fluid.

292. kinetic energy: energy of motion of a mass, i.e., \(\tfrac12mU^2\).

293. Kirchoff’s current law : for a node in an electrical circuit, the current entering a node must be equal to the current leaving a node.

294. Kutta condition : the experimental observation that a stagnation streamline will always emanate from a sharp trailing edge. The physical underpinnings of this are viscous, but this is used most to specify the circulation for an irrotational flow analysis of a lifting object.

295. Kutta–Zhukovsky theorem: an irrotational flow theorem that describes the lift force per unit depth of an object as a function of fluid density, freestream speed, and circulation: \(L^\prime=-\rho U\Gamma\).

296. Lagrangian : pronounced la-GRAHN-zhee-an. A mode of analysis in which a mass element (i.e., a system) is followed as it moves through a flowfield.

297. Laplacian: the Laplacian of a vector \(\vec u\) is \(\nabla^2\vec u\) or \(\nabla\cdot\nabla\vec u\).

298. laminar: occuring in orderly sheets or lamina.

299. laminar flow : flow in which fluid moves in orderly sheets or lamina because viscosity dominates over inertia enough that any small perturbations to the flow quickly disappear.

300. Laplace equation: in general, \(\nabla^2\phi=0\). Satisfied by the streamfunction and velocity potential in irrotational flows. A linear, elliptic partial differential equation which is the easiest of all fluid-mechanical equations to solve.

301. leading edge : the forward-most part of an object in a fluid flow.

302. lean : in a combustion reaction, meaning having an excess of oxidizer relative to stoichiometric conditions.

303. lift : the component of a force a fluid exerts on an immersed object that is normal to the flow.

304. lift coefficient: a measure of the ability of a physical object to generate a force normal to a flow passing over it. Defined by \(C_L=L/(\tfrac12\rho U^2A)\).

Editorial corrections: Kaplan turbines normally have high turbine specific speed; entry287 says low. The sign in \(L^\prime=-\rho U\Gamma\) assumes counterclockwise-positive circulation and upward-positive lift with rightward freestream; this conflicts with the clockwise-positive circulation wording in entry87 unless the lift direction is also changed. Laminar flow need not be inertia-free or stable to every perturbation.

Transcription note: The potential symbol and equals sign in entry300 are partly erased and restored from the named Laplace equation. Harmonic velocity potential additionally assumes incompressibility; harmonic scalar streamfunction here applies to two-dimensional incompressible irrotational flow.


PDF page 570 — source_issue

305. lock : a part of a canal system that facilitates raising and lowering of boats.

306. loss : in fluid mechanics, a measure of deviation from inviscid or isentropic behavior. Often used to adjust an inviscid or isentropic model to describe real engineering systems.

307. loss coefficient: a nondimensional factor relating pressure drop in a pipe to dynamic pressure: \(K=f_DL/d\). Also called resistance coefficient.

308. machine: as defined in this text, a device that changes direction or magnitude of forces, causes motion or acceleration, or transfers energy to perform a useful action.

309. Mach number: speed normalized by the speed of sound: \(M=U/a\).

310. Mach wave : an isentropic expansion or compression wave. Equivalent to a sound wave. Usually used to refer to a feature that is weak enough to be approximated as isentropic but strong enough to be apparent in a schlieren image.

311. manometer : a device that measures pressure differences by measuring heights of columns of liquid.

312. material derivative: a term in fluid mechanics used to represent the total derivative of a quantity \(q(x,y,z)\) with respect to time: \(\frac{dq}{dt}=\frac{\partial q}{\partial t}+\vec u\cdot\nabla q\).

313. material line : the location of a curve drawn in a flow after a specified time has elapsed..

314. matrix : a set of numbers that follows a specific set of interaction rules and is often used in physics to represent tensors.

315. matrix representation : the use of a matrix as shorthand to gather the components of a vector or dyadic into an array. For Cartesian coordinates, matrix multiplication can be used as a heuristic to generate a number of vector operations. The matrix representation of a scalar is equivalent to the scalar itself.

316. mean flow : averaged, both to eliminate fluctuations and to average across a cross-section.

317. mechanical advantage : ratio of force exerted by a machine to the force input into it.

318. mechanical-engineering flow : there is no formal definition of this term. I use this term colloquially to mean high-Reynolds number flows of Newtonian fluids like air and water. In particular, this distinguishes from biological- and chemical-engineering flows, which more often have non-Newtonian flows at low Reynolds number.

319. metacenter : the point through which the lines of action of the buoyancy always point when a buoyant object is rotated away from its equilibrium point.

320. model : a (preferably simple) mathematical construct that explains observed phenomena well enough that it is useful for analysis or design.

321. molecular viscosity : synonymous with dynamic viscosity. Used in turbulence context to distinguish from turbulent viscosity.

322. monotonic : when describing a function, implying that its slope is always positive or always negative.

323. Navier–Stokes equations: pronounced NAH-vee-ay STOKES. Usually used to mean the incompressible conservation of momentum equation with the Newtonian model of viscous effects included: \(\rho\frac{\partial\vec u}{\partial t}+\rho\vec u\cdot\nabla\vec u=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u+\rho\vec g\).

324. Newtonian: in fluid mechanics, describes a fluid whose shear stress is proportional to its strain rate: \(\vec{\vec\tau}=2\mu\vec{\vec\varepsilon}\).

325. net positive suction head : the minimum total head required at the inlet of a pump to ensure that it does not cavitate. Important because it tells you where in a hydraulic circuit the pump needs to be—can it pull from above or does it need to push from below.

326. node : the location in space where an oscillation has no amplitude.

Editorial qualifications: The Navier–Stokes form shown assumes spatially uniform viscosity and incompressibility. The Newtonian formula denotes viscous stress; total stress also contains \(-pI\). Entry325 describes required NPSH, measured as inlet total head above the vapor-pressure head, rather than an arbitrary absolute head. A single fixed metacenter is a small-heel approximation; it can move at finite heel. Monotonic functions may have zero slope as well as one sign of slope.


PDF page 571 — source_issue

327. nondimensional parameter : a parameter generated by a process to remove units. Typically denotes the ratio of two or more parameters and therefore their relative importance.

328. no-penetration condition : a kinematic condition specifying that the component of fluid velocity normal to a solid surface is zero relative to the surface. A restatement of the definition of what a ”solid surface” is.

329. normal : orthogonal; perpendicular.

330. normal shock : short for normal shock wave. A shock wave that is aligned normal to the flow.

331. normal stress : in general, the force per unit area that a fluid applies normal to a specified plane. Specifically, often used to describe the force per unit area that a fluid applies normal to a solid surface. Equal in magnitude to the fluid pressure if the fluid is Newtonian and at a surface.

332. no-slip condition : a dynamic condition specifying that the component of velocity tangent to a solid surface is zero. Equivalent to saying that fluid, at molecular level, sticks to the surface.

333. nozzle: a duct with varying cross-section which is designed to control the velocity and its distribution in an exhaust.

334. oblique shock : short for oblique shock wave. A shock wave that is aligned at an angle that is not normal to the flow.

335. operand : the thing an operator operates upon.

336. operator : a function that takes an operand and generates an output.

337. ordinaryangle: an angle between 0 and \(\pi\).

338. orifice plate : a plate with a hole in it, usually fitted into a tube. Typically used to control mass flow through the system.

339. outward-facing normal : the normal vector used at a control surface, which, by convention, is drawn pointing outward.

340. overexpanded : referring to a nozzle or the jet that comes out of the nozzle: means that the pressure of the exhaust is lower than ambient, leading to oblique shocks. The generated thrust could have been larger if the nozzle had simply been shorter with a smaller exhaust area.

341. overtone : a frequency higher than the fundamental, usually a harmonic.

342. overtopping : when water spills over a dam.

343. parabolic: for a 2D PDE of form \(A\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+B\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x\partial y}+C\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}+D\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+E\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+Fu+G\), one where \(B^2-4AC=0\). Corresponds to physical phenomena (e.g., boundary layers) in which information propagates with a finite rate in at least one dimension, so a change in the system in one place affects some other places only after a finite time.

344. partial derivative : a derivative of a function with respect to a single coordinate.

345. particle-image velocimetry : often abbreviated PIV. A measurement technique that determines the velocity field by taking two images of suspended particles in succession and inferring velocity from displacement and elapsed time.

346. Pascal’s law: the notion that for fluids at rest the force per unit area caused by pressure is isotropic i.e., of same magnitude in all directions and can be denoted by a scalar \(p\). Mathematically, Pascal’s law says \(\vec{\vec\tau}=-p\vec{\vec I}\) for quiescent fluid.

347. pathline : a line that traces the Lagrangian motion of a fluid element as it moves in time. Can be imagined as the line that would be traced out if a small particle were placed into a fluid flow.

348. Pelton turbine : an impulse turbine in which jets of fluid impinge on cups mounted on a rotor.

Editorial qualifications: A Newtonian fluid can have viscous normal stress, so normal stress is not universally just pressure. No slip means zero relative tangential velocity between fluid and wall, including moving walls. Parabolic diffusion equations have instantaneous spatial tails; entry343’s “finite rate” should not be read as finite propagation speed in every spatial direction.


PDF page 572 — source_issue

349. penstock : a pipe or other intake structure that feeds water into a hydroelectric turbine.

350. peristaltic pump : a positive-displacement pump that moves fluid along by wavelike compression of the tube that holds the fluid.

351. permeability : a property of a porous medium that describes its resistance to pressure-driven laminar flow.

352. Pi group : one of a set of nondimensional groups used to parameterize a physical problem.

353. pipe : a hollow structure designed to convey a fluid. Usually rigid. Designated by nominal diameter and schedule, which describe approximate inner diameter and material thickness. Usually fitted by threads. Cf. tube, hose.

354. piston : a disk fitted into a tube that allows motion to change a system volume.

355. pitch : for an aircraft, pitch implies nose-up and nose-down rotation of an aircraft i.e., rotation around the wing—wing axis. For a propeller or rotor, pitch implies the angle of attack of the propeller blades.

356. Pitot tube : a tube with an opening aligned parallel to the local fluid velocity and connected at its closed end to a pressure sensor. The static pressure measured at the sensor is a measure of the total pressure or equivalently the stagnation pressure at the opening.

357. Pitot-static tube : A device for measuring fluid speed consisting of an annular two-tube system with two openings, one aligned tangent to the local fluid velocity and one aligned normal to the local fluid velocity, each opening connected at its closed end to a pressure sensor.
