The static pressure measured at the sensor connected to the normal orifice is a measure of the static pressure at the opening: the static pressure measured at the sensor connected to the tangent orifice is a measure of the total pressure or equivalently the stagnation pressure at the opening.

358. plane-symmetric : independent of a Cartesian coordinate.

359. plane wave : a wave whose wavefront is planar, i.e., a one-dimensional wave.

360. planform : as projected onto the horizontal plane.

361. plenum : a chamber where pressurized fluid is held for distribution.

362. pneumatic : related to flow of gases through pipes, especially when the gas is used as an actuator. Cf. hydraulic, which has a similar meaning but implies liquids.

363. Poiseuille flow : pronounced PWAH-zyoil. Laminar, pressure-driven flow through a duct or pipe.

364. polar coordinate : a 2D coordinate system in which location is specified with one angle (\(\theta\)) and one distance (\(r\)) from the origin.

365. poloidal : with reference to a torus (donut) and toroidal-poloidal coordinates, means along the small circle. If a torus is a cylinder bent into a circle, the poloidal direction is the circumferential direction of the original cylinder.

366. polytonic : when describing a function, implying that its slope varies from positive to negative.

367. polytropic: obeying a power-law relation of the form \(p=C\rho^n\). Examples include isothermal, isobaric, isentropic, incompressible.

368. positive-displacement pump : a pump that moves fluid by displacing the boundaries containing the fluid. Generated flowrate is a fixed function of RPM.

369. potential flow: flow in which \(\vec u\) can be written as \(\vec u=\nabla\phi\). The terms irrotational flow (\(\vec\omega=0\)) and potential flow (\(\vec u=\nabla\phi\)) are synonymous—one implies the other.

370. power coefficient: the coefficient \(C_P=P/(\rho f^3D^5)\). It normalizes the power generated by a turbine by a factor proportional to the volume of hte runner multiplied by the dynamic pressure of fluid moving at the runner tip.

Transcription note: The polytropic equality/exponent, potential-flow equality symbols, and power-coefficient subscript/operators are partly erased. They are restored from their definitions and earlier formulas. The source uses frequency \(f\) here rather than angular speed \(\omega\) used in (2.9); numerical coefficient conventions differ by factors of \(2\pi\).

Editorial qualifications: A pressure times a volume is energy; the power coefficient’s denominator also contains an inverse-time scale, here \(f\). Incompressibility is a limiting case of the polytropic description, not generally a finite exponent relation with varying pressure and fixed density. Rotor pitch is its geometric blade setting; angle of attack also depends on the incoming relative flow direction.


PDF page 573 — source_issue

371. PPPT : the Party-People-Pickup-Truck model: a heuristic model that describes mean velocity as the motion of pickup trucks, and molecular velocity fluctuations as “party people” who jump around in between the pickup trucks. Party People in the House: Say Yeah.

372. pressure : usually used to mean static pressure but can be used metaphorically to describe any force per unit area or energy per unit volume.

373. pressure altitude : the altitude in the US standard atmosphere that corresponds to a static pressure reading.

374. pressure coefficient: a pressure difference (typically caused by the interaction of an object with a fluid flow) normalized by the dynamic pressure of the freestream. Defined by \(C_p=\Delta p/(\tfrac12\rho U^2)\).

375. pressure drag : the component of fluid force on an object that (a) is in the direction of flow and (b) is explained by only the pressure distribution on the surface of the object. Synonymous with form drag.

376. pressure drop: the reduction of the (typically total) pressure of fluid associated with viscous dissipation of mechanical energy to heat: \(\Delta p_{\mathrm{total}}=\Delta p+\tfrac12\rho\Delta(\bar U^2)+\rho g\Delta z\).

377. pressure force: the net force on a body caused by the integrated normal component of the surface stresses.

378. pressure head: synonymous with “head” or “hydrostatic head”. Head \(H\) is given by \(H=\frac{p_1-p_2}{\rho g}\). The pressure difference between two points (usually the inlet 1 and outlet 2 of a tube or tube network) in terms of the height of a column of fluid of density \(\rho\) in a gravitational acceleration field \(g\) that would generate the equivalent pressure at the bottom of the column.

379. priming : the process of filling a pump with fluid as required to enable its operation.

380. propeller : a rotating airfoil that transfers energy from a driveshaft to fluid to generate thrust. Compare to impeller.

381. propeller turbine : an axial-flow reaction turbine, typically with relatively high specific speed, suitable for extracting energy over a low pressure drop. The turbine analog of a axial-flow pump.

382. pseudotensor : a quantity otherwise identical to a tensor, but which changes sign if we switch from a right-handed to a left-handed coordinate system.

383. pseudovector : a quantity otherwise identical to a vector, but which changes sign if we switch from a right-handed to a left-handed coordinate system.

384. pump : usually an enclosed fluid machine that adds energy to a liquid, generating flow and pressure rise. The equivalent turbomachine driving a gas would normally be called a fan, blower, or compressor. However, the term pump is sometimes used as a completely general term for any turbomachine that adds energy to a fluid. Cf. turbine, which removes energy from a fluid.

385. pump specific diameter : often just called specific diameter. A speed-independent measure of whether a pump’s output at max efficiency corresponds more to volumetric flowrate or more to pressure difference. For equivalent performance, a high-specific-diameter pump will be larger and operate at lower speed than a low-specific-diameter pump. Given by \(D_p=\Delta p^{1/4}D/\rho^{1/4}Q^{1/2}\). .

386. pump specific speed: often just called specific speed. A size-independent measure of whether a pump’s output at max efficiency corresponds more to volumetric flowrate or more to pressure difference. For equivalent performance, a high-specific-speed pump will be smaller and operate at higher speed than a low-specific-speed pump. Given by \(\omega_p=\rho^{3/4}Q^{1/2}\omega/\Delta p^{3/4}\). .

387. quiescent: motionless; \(\vec u=0\).

388. quasi-1D : a pictorial representation of a (usually 2D) vector field that indicates the vector magnitude and direction through uniformly spaced vector arrows.

389. quiver plot : a pictorial representation of a (usually 2D) vector field that indicates the vector magnitude and direction through uniformly spaced vector arrows.

Editorial corrections: Entry388 repeats the quiver-plot definition. Quasi-1D means a model treating flow as varying primarily along one coordinate, often with cross-sectional averaging. The conventional specific-diameter grouping is \(D_p=D(\Delta p/\rho)^{1/4}/\sqrt Q\); the inline division in385 is ambiguous without grouping. Entry376 includes gravitational potential and therefore describes a Bernoulli-pressure change. General normal stress can also contain a viscous part, so entry377 is exact for pressure force only when that additional normal contribution is absent or excluded.


PDF page 574 — source_issue

390. radial : related to the radius r i.e., the distance from the origin of the coordinate system.

391. radial-flow turbomachine : a turbomachine in which the flow path of the fluid at the point of energy transfer is primarily in the radial direction relative to the rotary element.

392. radius of curvature : for a point on a curve, the radius of curvature is the radius of the equivalent circle that has the same Gaussian curvature as the curve.

393. reaction turbine : a turbine that is fully immersed in the driving fluid. Cf. impulse turbine, in which the driving fluid interacts primarily only with the vanes/blades/etc.

394. reciprocating pump : equivalently, reciprocal pump. A positive-displacement pump that combines oscillation of the volume of a central domain with two check valves to induce flow.

395. recirculate : flow upstream. Typically associated with separation.

396. recirculation : when a region of fluid is made to flow largely upstream. Typically associated with separation.

397. refraction : bending of light when passing through index-of-refraction gradients (typically density gradients).

398. regular approximation : in a fluid-mechanical context, an approximation that applies to the entire fluid domain.

399. regulator : a device that sets a (lower) output pressure given a variable (higher) input pressure.

400. reservoir : a body of water stored for drinking or irrigation, often impounded by a dam.

401. resistance coefficient: a nondimensional factor relating pressure drop in a pipe to dynamic pressure: \(K=f_DL/d\). Also called loss coefficient.

402. resonance : when an actuation has the same frequency as a system’s natural frequency, leading to an output that is much higher in magnitude than would be expected from the original actuation.

403. Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations : a set of equations that comes from writing the Navier-Stokes equations in terms of time-averaged field variables combined with fluctuations around those means.

404. Reynolds number: \(Re=\rho Ul/\mu\). The primary parameter that dictates the properties of an incompressible fluid flow. A measure of fluid inertia relative to the viscous stresses that accelerate and decelerate it. Indicates which terms in the Navier–Stokes equations are largest. Indicates whether flow is laminar or turbulent. Often written with a subscript (e.g., \(Re_x,Re_d\)) to clarify what length scale is used in the calculation.

405. Reynolds transport theorem : an integral description of a total derivative for a control volume, applied specifically to fluid mechanical systems which allows the governing equations for a system to be written in terms of the governing equations for a control volume. Allows transformation between Eulerian and Lagrangian frames of reference.

406. rich : with respect to a combustion reaction, meaning having excess fuel with respect to stoichiometricconditions.

407. rocket : a propulsion engine that carries its own propellant. Cf. air-breathing engine, which intakes air to serve as oxidizer.

408. roll : tilting rotation of an aircraft i.e., rotation around the nose—tail axis.

409. rotor : in general for a motor or turbomachine, the rotating part. Specifically for a quadcopter or helicopter, the rotating lifting surface. Cf. stator.

410. rotary vane pump: a positive-displacement pump that pushes fluid along an eccentric channel using vanes that press up against the outer housing via centrifugal force.

Editorial correction: Entry392 should say the curve’s curvature, not Gaussian curvature (a surface quantity). The radius of curvature is \(R=1/|\kappa|\). The equality in the partly faded Reynolds-number definition is restored from the definition; transition also depends on geometry and disturbances, not a universal Reynolds-number threshold.


PDF page 575 — source_issue

411. rotation-rate tensor: a dyadic tensor that describes the manner in which a fluid rotates. Given by \(\tfrac12(\nabla\vec u-\nabla\vec u^T)\).

412. runner : the rotating blade element of a reaction turbine. Analogous to the impeller of a pump.

413. scalar: as a noun: a property with a magnitude only; no direction; as an adjective: having magnitude only but no direction.

414. schlieren: an imaging mode in which density gradients correspond to either bright or dark regions of the image.

415. scroll : a casing i.e., housing of a centrifugal pump which has a spiral shape resembling a mollusc. Synonymous with volute.

416. self-similar : having a functional dependence that can be written in terms of a single similarity variable.

417. semi-infinite : having a well-defined finite starting point and extending infinitely in one direction.

418. sensitive : producing a large response from a small input.

419. separate: the process by which a streamline emanates normal to a surface. Most often, separation is used only to describe streamlines resulting from flow that moves upstream.

420. separated flow : locally, flow separates at a stagnation point at a surface, which always has a separation streamline emanating normal to the surface rather than parallel to it. Globally, we describe flow as separated if it has a separation point associated with flow moving upstream. Regionally, in a separated flow the separation region is the region in which the flow moves upstream at the wall.

421. separation : when a streamline emanates normal to a surface. Most often, separation is used only to describe streamlines resulting from flow that moves upstream.

422. separation of variables : a method of solving a partial differential equation in which a function of multiple variables is assumed to be the product of multiple single-variable functions, so that functional dependences of variables can be separated on different sides of equations.

423. shaft : in a turbomachine, the mechanical element that forms the axis of rotation. It receives from, or transmits work to, the exterior of the turbomachine.

424. shear : relative to a solid surface, means a force parallel to that surface. In general, refers to deformation in which the fluid is flattened in one direction while being elongated in a perpendicular direction. For incompressible fluids, shear strain rate is usually used specific to off-diagonal components of the strain rate tensor, because the on-diagonal strain rates must sum to zero (\(\nabla\cdot\vec u=0\)) and thus the on-diagonal strain rates can be ignored when calculating viscous forces.

425. shear stress : in general, the force per unit area that a fluid applies tangent to a specified plane. Specifically, often used to describe the force per unit area that a fluid applies tangent to a solid surface. For Newtonian fluids at motionless surfaces, given by the viscosity multiplied by the partial derivative of the tangential velocity in the direction of the outward normal to the surface. Synonymous with tangential stress.

426. shear-thickening : having an effective viscosity (stress-strain rate relation) that increases as the magnitude of shear strain rate increases.

427. shear-thinning : having an effective viscosity (stress— strain rate relation) that decreases as the magnitude of strain rate increases.

428. shop air : a supply of high-pressure (usually about 70 psi) air normally provided in most laboratories and shops from a standard compressor. Used to drive pneumatic tools and blowers.

429. shock wave : a discontinuous transition in which a supersonic flow slows down, with an attendant increase in pressure and density.

Editorial corrections: In entry411 the transpose means \((\nabla\vec u)^T\), the transpose of the full velocity-gradient tensor. Incompressibility makes its trace zero; it does not make individual diagonal strain rates or their viscous contributions vanish, contrary to entry424. Separation streamlines need not leave a wall at exactly90°, and a stationary no-slip wall itself has zero velocity; reverse flow occurs near it.


PDF page 576 — source_issue

430. shoulder : on an object immersed in a fluid flow, the surfaces at the widest point measured normal to the prevailing fluid velocity.

431. singular approximation : in a fluid-mechanical context, an approximation that applies to only part of the fluid domain and fails in the other part.

432. sink: an idealized point or line sink of volumetric flow. From the \(\lambda=0\) separation-of-variables solution of the Laplace equation.

433. skin-friction drag: the component of fluid force on an object that (a) is in the direction of flow and (b) is explained by only the viscous stress on the surface of the object. Friction here is a metaphor, the viscous stress is in some ways analogous to friction, but it is not friction.

434. sonar : SOund Navigation And Ranging. A technique for identifying objects using time-of-flight acoustic signals.

435. sonic: having a speed equal to the speed of sound, or corresponding to a location where the fluid has a speed of sound equal to the speed of sound.

436. sound wave: an isentropic expansion or compression wave. Equivalent to a Mach wave. Usually used to refer to these waves in the context of acoustics rather than compressible flow.

437. source: an idealized point or line source of volumetric flow. From the \(\lambda=0\) separation-of-variables solution of the Laplace equation.

438. specific : in a fluids context, usually means normalized by mass, by volume, or by some standard.

439. specific diameter: a normalized diameter indicative of what diameter would be required to pump a standardized \(\Delta p_0\) for a specific \(Q\) (pump specific diameter); or that diameter required to generate a standardized power \(P\) using a standardized \(\Delta p_0\) (turbine specific diameter).

440. specific enthalpy: sum of internal energy and work of compression, per unit mass denoted \(h=e+p/\rho\).

441. specific gravity : denoted SG. The ratio of the density of a fluid to the density of a reference fluid, typically water at 4C or air at STP.

442. specific heat: a measure of the energy involved in raising a fluid a specific amount. Can imply \(c_p\), the specific heat at fixed pressure, or \(c_v\), the specific heat at fixed volume.

443. specific-heat ratio: denoted \(\gamma\) and defined as \(\gamma=c_p/c_v\). A measure of how energy in the fluid links back to the equation of state.

444. specific speed: a normalized speed indicative of what speed would be required to pump a standardized \(\Delta p_0\) for a specific \(Q\) (pump specific speed); or that speed required to generate a standardized power \(P\) using a standardized \(\Delta p_0\) (turbine specific speed).

445. specific total enthalpy: sum of internal energy, work of compression, gravitational potential energy, and kinetic energy, reported per unit mass and denoted \(h_0=e+p/\rho+\tfrac12\rho U^2+gz\).

446. specific volume: denoted \(v\). volume per unit mass.

447. specific weight: denoted \(\gamma\). The weight per unit volume of a fluid. Given by \(\gamma=\rho g\).

448. speed: when describing fluid, a scalar description of fluid motion equal to the magnitude of the velocity. When describing a turbomachine, the angular frequency of its rotation.

449. speed of sound: the speed with which infinitesimal (isentropic) disturbances propagate in a fluid. Denoted \(a\) by those studying compressible flow, and usually by \(c\) by those studying acoustics. We will use \(a\). Given by \(a^2=\left.\partial p/\partial\rho\right|_s\) or, for ideal gases, as \(a^2=\gamma RT\).

450. spillway: at a dam, a path for fluid to flow from the impoundment to the tailwater. Usually meant as an emergency path for water flow to prevent overtopping.

451. stage : a combination of a rotor and a stator used in a turbomachine to increase pressure without building up swirl.

Transcription note: The specific-enthalpy formula and specific-heat-ratio symbols are mostly erased; they are restored from the definitions and clear earlier occurrences. The source’s twice-used \(\gamma\) denotes different quantities in entries443 and447.

Editorial corrections: The kinetic term in specific total enthalpy must be \(U^2/2\), not \(\rho U^2/2\), to have energy-per-mass units. Entry435’s second “speed of sound” should be fluid speed. Specific heat is energy per unit mass per unit temperature increase; entry442 omits the temperature and mass qualifications.


PDF page 577 — source_issue

452. stagnation : the property of being motionless or the process of decelerating fluid to motionlessness.

453. stagnation head: the height \(H_{\mathrm{stagnation}}=p_{\mathrm{stagnation}}/(\rho g)\) corresponding to a gravitational potential energy per unit mass equal to the stagnation pressure.

454. stagnation point : a point in a flow where the velocity is zero.

455. stagnation pressure: the pressure \(p_0\) a fluid would have if isentropically slowed to stagnation along a streamline. For a calorically perfect gas, \(p_0=p\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}2M^2\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}\). For an incompressible fluid, \(p_0=p+\tfrac12\rho U^2\).

456. stagnation temperature: the temperature \(T_0\) a fluid would have if isentropically slowed to stagnation along a streamline. For a calorically perfect gas, \(T_0=T\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}2M^2\right)\).

457. stall : the aerodynamic phenomenon in which the lifting surfaces (e.g., wings) exceed a critical angle of attack and the lift is drastically reduced. Stall is defined as high angle of attack, but is associated with low aircraft speed because aircraft often use high angle of attack when at low speed.

458. standard atmosphere : a mathematical model of the thermodynamic properties of an atmosphere, typically used to enable altimetry through pressure measurement.

459. standing wave : a wave (sound wave or shock wave) that is not moving, usually because of the superposition of waves moving in two directions. Cf. traveling wave.

460. startup : the process by which a flow changes from quiescence to steady-state motion following the application of pressure or the startup of boundary motion. Cf. decay.

461. state property : a holistic property of a system, specifically one that does not vary within the system.

462. static head: the height \(H=p/(\rho g)\) whose gravitational potential energy per unit mass is equivalent to the static pressure.

463. static pressure : equivalent to the thermodynamic definition of pressure. A parameter that describes the force per unit area that the fluid imparts on a control surface in the flow. If positive, describes compressive forces. If negative, describes tensile force.

464. stationary : means statistically unchanging with time. This term is used to describe a turbulent flow that is unsteady but whose time-averaged velocity is not changing with time. Not used to mean motionless.

465. stator : a stationary airfoil component of a motor or pump. Cf. rotor.

466. steady : unchanging with time. Compare to unsteady, meaning changing with time, and stationary, meaning statistically unchanging in time.

467. steady-state : a state at which all properties are steady.

468. steam turbine : a turbine that extracts energy from vapor. If the turbine were driven by a collocated combustion chamber, it would instead be a gas turbine. If by naturally occuring gas motion, it would be a wind turbine. If driven by liquid it would be a hydrodynamic turbine.

469. stoichiometric : with respect to a chemical equation, meaning that the reactants are in balance and can react completely to form products.

470. Stokes flow: flow in which \(Re\to0\). Synonymous with creeping flow.

471. Stokes equations: the Navier–Stokes equations with the unsteady and convective terms eliminated: \(0=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\vec u+\rho\vec g\). Used when \(Re\to0\) or when the flow is steady, unidirectional, and infinite.

472. Stokes’ theorem: Stokes theorem applied to a fluid velocity field (\(\int_{\mathcal A}\nabla\times\vec u\,dA=\int_{\mathcal C}\vec u\cdot ds\)) indicates that the net circulation around a closed contour is equal to the integral of the vorticity over the area enclosed by the contour.

473. STP: standard temperature and pressure. \(T=273.15\ \mathrm K\) and \(p=1\ \mathrm{atm}\).

Transcription note: The equality signs in the stagnation/static-head definitions and the stagnation-pressure formula are partly erased and restored from their named definitions.

Editorial corrections: Entries453/462 should say gravitational potential energy per unit volume (\(\rho gH\)), not per unit mass (\(gH\)), when equating it to pressure. Entry472 omits the surface-normal projection and the vector line element. The scalar Stokes relation is \(\int_{\mathcal A}(\nabla\times\vec u)\cdot\hat n\,dA=\oint_{\mathcal C}\vec u\cdot d\vec s\), with consistent right-hand orientation. Low Reynolds number removes convective inertia but does not alone guarantee negligible unsteady inertia; steady Stokes flow requires that additional assumption.


PDF page 578 — source_issue

474. strain rate : a dyadic tensor that describes the manner in which a fluid deforms.

475. strain-rate tensor: a dyadic tensor that describes the manner in which a fluid deforms. Given by \(\tfrac12(\nabla\vec u+\nabla\vec u^T)\).

476. streakline : a line that traces the Eulerian time history of the velocity of a location in a fluid flow as time elapses. Can be imagined as the line that would be traced out if a small trace of dye were released slowly into a fluid flow.

477. streamfunction: denoted \(\psi\). Scalar function defined for 2D flows equivalently as (a) \(\psi(A)=\int_O^A u\,dy-v\,dx\) or (b) \(u=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\) and \(v=-\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\), or (c) \(\vec u=\nabla\times\psi\hat z\). Incompressible 2D flows can be defined by \(\psi(x,y)\) because the existence of \(\psi(x,y)\) is mathematically equivalent to satisfying conservation of mass.

478. streamline : a line that is everywhere tangent to the instantaneous fluid velocity vector.

479. streamlined : in describing the shape of an object, implies that the shape of the object is roughly similar to the shape of naturally occurring streamlines—smooth, with gentle curvature.

480. streamline coordinates: the coordinates \(s,n,\) and \(\ell\), indicating streamwise, normal, and binormal directions. These directions refer respectively to \(s\): the direction in which the fluid is moving; \(n\): the direction in which the fluid is turning; \(\ell\): the direction \(\hat s\times\hat n\) indicating the axis around which the fluid path turns.

481. streamwise : in the direction of the flow i.e., along the streamlines.

482. stress : in Newtonian fluid mechanics, the word stress is used to denote either (a) a scalar force per unit area on a plane, (b) a vector force per unit area on a plane, and (c) a dyadic tensor that fully describes all forces per unit area that would be applied on any plane. Fluid mechanicians are cavalier about this because so many fluids are effectively incompressible and isotropic. Solid and continuum mechanicians call (a) a stress component (b) a traction and (c) the stress tensor. So beware of this in MAE3270 and MAE3280 and MAE4230.

483. stress tensor: denoted \(\vec{\vec\tau}\). A dyadic tensor that describes the magnitude and direction of the force per unit area that a fluid would put on any surface at that point. \(\vec{\vec\tau}\cdot\vec n\) is a vector that describes the magnitude and direction of the force per unit area that the fluid would put on a surface drawn normal to the unit outward normal vector \(\vec n\).

484. sublinear : having a dependence that is weaker than linear.

485. subsonic : having a speed lower than the speed of sound i.e., a Mach number less than one.

486. supersonic : having a speed higher than the speed of sound i.e., a Mach number greater than one.

487. supralinear : having a dependence that is stronger than linear.

488. surface force : a force that acts on a control volume through its surface. Examples include viscous stresses and pressure. These forces, at the atomistic level, operate through close interactions when molecules collide with each other. Compare to body force.

489. surface tension : equivalently, either the excess energy per unit area associated with an interface between two fluids, or the apparent “tension” of the interface that comes from the inherent minimization of surface area that comes from minimization of energy at equilibrium.

490. swash plate : an angled disk attached to a shaft, which transduces rotating motion into oscillatory motion. In a helicopter, causes rotor blade pitch angle to vary sinusoidally with rotor rotation.

491. swirl : the azimuthal motion added to a fluid moving through a turbomachine by the rotary element...

492. symmetric: for a tensor or matrix, invariant upon permutation of indices. For a dyadic tensor element, means that if the unit dyads are switched (i.e., \(xz\) for \(zx\)), that the value does not change. For a 2D matrix, means symmetric upon flipping over the diagonal.

Transcription note: The faded left side of the streamfunction integral is restored as \(\psi(A)=\); its lower endpoint is the reference point \(O\), consistent with the definition in chapter8. In475 the transpose applies to the whole gradient tensor, \((\nabla\vec u)^T\).

Editorial clarification: A streakline is the present set of fluid particles that previously passed through a specified point, rather than merely the velocity time history at that point. Continuous dye injection is the example intended here.


PDF page 579 — source_issue

493. system: an element of mass under study, which moves in space, expands, and/or contracts based on where the mass goes, but which does not exchange mass. Compare to control volume, which is a volume element that may move in space, expand, and/or contract as specified by our analysis, but which is not correlated to any particular element of mass.

494. tangential stress : in general, the force per unit area that a fluid applies tangent to a specified plane. Specifically, often used to describe the force per unit area that a fluid applies tangent to a solid surface. For Newtonian fluids at motionless surfaces, given by the viscosity multiplied by the partial derivative of the tangential velocity in the direction of the outward normal to the surface. Synonymous with shear stress.

495. tailwater : the water immediately downstream of a dam.

496. Taylor–Couette flow : the flow between two concentric cylinders moving with different angular velocities.

497. Taylor-series expansion: an infinite series that describes the value of a function \(f\) near a point \(\vec x\) in terms of the derivatives of \(f\) at \(\vec x\).

498. tensor: an order \(n\) tensor describes a property with a magnitude and \(n\) directional components. In introductory fluid mechanics, unless the order is specified, “tensor” typically means a dyadic or 2nd-order tensor e.g., the strain rate or stress.

499. throat : the narrowest section of a tube or nozzle.

500. throttle : as a verb, means to restrict. As a noun or as an adjective in throttle valve, refers to a valve that restricts airflow (and therefore fuel flow) into an engine. Open or full throttle means maximum air flow rate.

501. thrust : a motive force pointing in the direction of a vehicle or object’s desired motion.

502. toroidal : having the shape of a torus (donut). Or, with reference to a specific direction, meaning along the large circular ring of the torus. If a torus is a cylinder bent into a circle, the toroidal direction is the axial direction of the original cylinder.

503. torque converter : a turbomachine that transfers torque from an engine to a transmission by exchanging fluid with differing angular momentum back and forth between two sides of the device, one of which is connected to the engine and one to the input shaft of the transmission.

504. Torricelli’s relation: the observation that a free jet emanating from an orifice a distance \(h\) below the top of a reservoir exits with speed \(\sqrt{2gh}\).

505. total derivative : a derivative that indicates how a function changes as an argument changes, including indirect contributions from changes in other arguments.

506. total dynamic head: denoted TDH. The work per unit fluid volume (\(\Delta p_0\)) that a pump adds to its working fluid, described using the equivalent height (\(\mathrm{TDH}=\Delta p_0/(\rho g)\)). Equal to the difference in total head between inlet and outlet of the pump. Not equal to total head nor dynamic head, which are both properties of fluids at a location rather than a differential property describing the difference in fluid properties across a pump.

507. total head: a property \(H_{\mathrm{total}}=p_{\mathrm{total}}/(\rho g)\) which describes the equivalent height whose gravitational potential energy per unit volume is equal to the fluid’s total pressure.

508. total pressure: a property \(p_0=p+\tfrac12\rho u^2+\rho gz\), having units of pressure (or equivalently volumetric energy), which indicates storage of multiple forms of energy, including \(p\,dV\) work of compression (\(p\)), kinetic energy (\(\tfrac12\rho u^2\)), and gravitational potential energy \(\rho gz\).

509. trailing edge : the rearward-most part of an object in a fluid flow.

510. trajectory : for a vector field, a trajectory is a contour that is everywhere tangent to the vector field.

511. transpose: for a 2nd-order tensor or a matrix, means that the index order is switched e.g., \(\widehat{zx}\) is switched for \(\widehat{xz}\).

Editorial corrections: An order-\(n\) tensor in \(d\) dimensions has \(n\) indices and generally \(d^n\) components, rather than \(n\) components. A Taylor series equals its function where the function is analytic and the series converges. “Total pressure” in508 includes gravity and is the book’s Bernoulli-pressure convention; usual stagnation pressure excludes gravitational potential. Faded equalities in506–508 are restored from the definitions.


PDF page 580 — source_issue

512. transverse metacenter : the metacenter for rolling motion.

513. traveling wave : a wave (sound wave or shock wave) that is moving. Cf. standing wave.

514. tube : a hollow structure. Typically a tube is structural, not fluid-carrying, but the word tubing is sometimes used to describe copper and PVC pipe and hose. Usually rigid when discussed structurally, usually flexible when used to mean hose. Designated by nominal diameter and schedule, which describe approximate inner diameter and material thickness. Cf. pipe, hose.

515. turbine : a general term for any turbomachine that extracts energy from a fluid.

516. turbine specific diameter : often called power specific diameter. A speed-independent measure of how much power a turbine at max efficiency extracts given a pressure difference. For equivalent performance, a high-specific-diameter turbine will run faster and be smaller than a low-specific-speed turbine. Given by \(D_t=\frac{D\Delta p_0^{3/4}}{P^{1/2}\rho^{1/4}}\)..

517. turbine specific speed : often called power specific speed. A size-independent measure of how much power a turbine at max efficiency extracts given a pressure difference. For equivalent performance, a high-specific-speed turbine will be smaller and operate at higher speed than a low-specific-speed turbine. Given by \(\omega_t=\frac{\omega\rho^{3/4}P^{1/2}}{\Delta p_0^{5/4}}\)..

518. turbomachine : a machine that adds energy to or extracts energy from a fluid by use of a rotary element. Typically implies dynamic machines not positive-displacement machines.

519. turbulence model : a model that attempts to estimate a turbulent flow through something other than the Navier-Stokes equations. Usually, this involves using the Navier-Stokes equations to solve most of the physics, then adding the turbulence model to account for a specific spatial or temporal scale that we believe we can approximate well but is difficult to solve using the Navier-Stokes equations.

520. turbulence : the local instability and chaos of a fluid flow, leading to unsteadiness and fluctuations even if the flow is stationary.

521. turbulent : characterized by local instability and chaos.

522. turbulent flow : a fluid flow characterized by local instability and chaos, which exhibits unsteadiness even if the flow is stationary.

523. turbulent viscosity : also called eddy viscosity. A parameter that has the same units as viscosity and describes the effective diffusion of momentum in a time-averaged turbulent flow that is attributable to the unsteady component of the flow.

524. 2-D flow: A flow that is independent of one of the coordinates, for example a function of \(x\) and \(y\) but not \(z\) (plane-symmetric), or a function of \(r\) and \(\theta\) but not \(z\) (plane-symmetric), or a function of \(r\) and \(z\) but not \(\theta\) (axially symmetric).

525. underexpanded : referring to a nozzle or the jet that comes out of the nozzle: means that the pressure of the exhaust is higher than ambient, leading to expansion fans. A longer nozzle with larger exhaust area would lead to more thrust (but would cost and weigh more).

526. unidirectional : having only one direction component. Usually true only as an approximation.

527. uniform : unchanging in space. Compare to the adjective constant, which means unchanging with time.

528. unit normal : a vector of length one that points normal to a plane.

529. unit outward normal : a vector of length one that points normal to a control surface, and points outward, away from the control volume.

530. unsteady : changing with time, both in an immediate sense and in a time-averaged sense. Compare to stationary, which means having an unchanging time-averaged nature, and steady, which means unchanging with time.

Editorial corrections: At fixed output power, pressure rise, and density, the displayed specific diameter is proportional to actual diameter; “high-specific-diameter” does not imply smaller and faster as entry516 states. That description belongs to high specific speed (517). An unsteady flow can have a stationary time average, so “both” in530 is too restrictive. Independence of one coordinate does not necessarily eliminate a third velocity component (for example axisymmetric swirl).


PDF page 581 — source_issue

531. upstream : in the direction opposing fluid motion.

532. vacuum Venturi : a vacuum driven by a high-pressure source (rather than an electric fan or blower) which uses the high pressure to drive flow through a tube with a throat to generate a low-pressure region.

533. valve : a device that regulates, switches, or controls the flow of fluid.

534. vane :a surface that turns flow and causes pressure changes. Roughly synonymous with airfoil, hydrofoil, wing, and blade. Often chosen over the word blade when the vane is motionless.

535. vector : a property with magnitude and direction.

536. velocity : vector description of fluid motion.

537. velocity coefficient : ratio of the actual speed of fluid exiting an orifice to that predicted by the Bernoulli equation.

538. velocity-gradient tensor : the dyadic tensor obtained when one takes the gradient of the velocity vector. Describes deformation and rotation of fluid.

539. velocity head: given by \(H=\bar U^2/(2g)\). The height a fluid could be pumped to if the kinetic energy of its mean velocity were converted to gravitational potential energy. Synonymous with dynamic head.

540. velocity potential: denoted \(\phi\). Scalar function that specifies the velocity though \(\vec u=\nabla\phi\). irrotational flows can be defined by \(\phi(\vec r)\) because the existence of \(\phi(\vec r)\) is mathematically equivalent to specifying \(\nabla\times\vec u=0\).

541. Venturi : a tube with a constriction whose purpose is to generate a low-pressure region in the throat.

542. vertical rise : the height difference between a pump and the exhaust of a piping system.

543. vertical-speed indicator : a device that indicates vertical speed of an aircraft by measuring the time rate of change of the ambient static pressure, usually through use of a reservoir volume connected to ambient pressure through a calibrated leak.

544. viscosity: if denoted \(\mu\), the dynamic viscosity. A measure of fluid resistance to being deformed. For Newtonian fluids, proportional to the ratio of the fluid stress to fluid strain rate. If denoted \(\nu\), the kinematic viscosity \(\nu=\mu/\rho\). A measure of fluid’s ability to diffuse momentum.

545. viscous : related to the generation of local fluid stresses by local fluid shear strain rate.

546. viscous dissipation : in fluid mechanics, the irreversible process by which fluid kinetic energy is converted to heat by the action of viscosity.

547. viscous dissipation factor: a nondimensional coefficient used to characterize drop of the Bernoulli constant (and thus typically pressure) in a pipe. This is typically called the “friction” factor by other texts, but the word “friction” is physically incorrect and misleading so I don’t use that term. In this class we use the Darcy factor \(f_D=\frac{\Delta B}{\frac12\rho U^2}\frac dL\) but there are others e.g., Fanning factor with similar but slightly different definitions.

548. viscous flow : generally, means flow in which viscous effects are meaningful. Typically requires flow in domains with a no-slip boundary condition and at Re numbers that are not infinitely large.

549. viscous stress : in general, the force per unit area that a fluid applies at a point that is not explained by the thermodynamic pressure. For Newtonian incompressible fluids, this is synonymous with shear stress and is given by the viscosity multiplied by the strain rate..

550. volumetric : related to volume, or per unit volume.

551. volute : a casing i.e., housing of a centrifugal pump which has a spiral shape resembling a mollusc. Synonymous with scroll.

552. von Kármán vortex street : the alternating pattern of vortexes seen in the wake of bluff bodies in certain Reynolds number ranges.

Transcription note: The velocity-head equality and several symbols in the Darcy-factor formula are erased and restored from the corresponding clear definitions (entries171 and213).

Editorial correction: With the strain-rate tensor defined in475, viscous stress is \(2\mu\varepsilon\), not merely viscosity times that tensor; entry549 omits the factor2 and can also obscure viscous normal stress. A globally single-valued velocity potential requires appropriate topology in addition to zero curl.


PDF page 582 — source_issue

553. vortex: in irrotational flow: an idealized point or line doublet of vorticity. From the \(\lambda=0\) separation-of-variables solution of the Laplace equation. More generally: a region of vorticity.

554. vortex shedding : the process by which the vorticity created in a boundary layer of an objectleaves the surface, creating a region of rotating fluid in the wake of the object.

555. vorticity: A pseudovector denoted by \(\vec\omega\) and defined by \(\vec\omega=\nabla\times\vec u\), whose direction describes the axis around which the fluid is locally rotating and whose magnitude indicates exactly twice the angular rotation rate of the fluid around that axis.

556. wake : in single-phase fluid mechanics, the downstream region of a flow behind a object whose momentum flux has been decreased by the viscous interaction with the object. For boats, the pattern of disrupted surface following a moving boat.

557. water horsepower : Measure of useful power produced by a pump, or the useful power needed by a pump to drive flow through a given system. 1 hp = 746 W.

558. water wheel : an impulse turbine, technologically important in antiquity, consisting of a wheel with paddles that water flows over.

559. wavelength : the length \(\lambda\) of an acoustic wave i.e., the distance between peaks of pressure, density, or velocity variation. Important as it relates to the length of a resonator required to amplify a frequency.

560. wheel : in in impulse turbine, the rotating, bladed element. Equivalent to the runner of a reaction turbine or the impeller of a pump.

561. wind turbine : a turbine that extracts energy from naturally occurring gas motion. If the turbine were driven by a collocated combustion chamber, it would instead be a gas turbine. If by vapor, it would be a steam turbine. If driven by liquid it would be a hydrodynamic turbine.

562. wing : a control surface on a vehicle that turns flow and causes pressure changes, typically to generate lift. Used to describe a part of an airplane whereas blade and vane are more often parts of turbomachines and airfoil is more often used to describe the 2D geometry used to design the wing.

563. yaw : left-right rotation of an aircraft i.e., rotation around the vertical axis.

564. YEET : I do not know what this means, nor whether I am using it correctly, nor do I want to. I am not trying to be cool. I am making fun of you.

Editorial correction: An elementary point/line vortex has concentrated circulation; it is not a vortex doublet, which combines two opposite vortices in a limiting pair. The partly erased vorticity operators are restored from its definition; its magnitude is twice the local angular rotation rate as the source correctly states.

This text is designed to be used for introductory fluid mechanics for an engineering audience; it is used at Cornell for junior Mechanical Engineering students.

The text takes as its motivating framework the many machines that have fluid mechanics as its core: rocket nozzles, turbomachines, dams, boats, airplanes, quadcopters and helicopters, and machine components such as engines, transmissions, and bearings.

The fundamentals covered include the governing equations prescribing hydrostatics, irrotational flow, inviscid incompressible and compressible flow, viscous flow, and acoustics. A variety of analytical techniques are used, such as control-volume and control-mass formulations, solution of Laplace, Stokes, and Euler equations for velocity and pressure fields, and methods for determining net forces on objects. The mathematical presentation includes vector and dyadic tensor formulations of the governing equations with Gibbs notation.

Numerous haiku throughout are used to communicate key concepts or complain about pop culture trends that bemuse or annoy the author.

Brian J. Kirby is the Meinig Family Professor of Engineering in the Sibley School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering at Cornell University, where he directs the Cornell Micro/Nanofluidics Laboratory. He was educated at the University of Michigan and Stanford University.
